name: Absolute Negator Determinatives
pattern: NP[absolute negator determinative as fused head]

entry.name: Absolute Negator Determinatives
entry.pattern: NP[absolute negator determinative as fused head]

1.definition: Encodes clausal negation via an NP headed by an absolute negator determinative in fused determiner-head function
1.details: CGEL (Ch. 9, §3.2) treats no and none as dependent and independent forms of the determinative no, and nobody, no one, nothing, nowhere, no place as single-word compounds of no. These are determinatives, not pronouns; standing alone as NPs they occupy fused determiner-head function.

examples.note: Independent form of the determinative no

constraints.description: Negative property percolates from the negator NP to the clause.
Alternates with verbal negation plus any/either/ever (e.g., "didn't do anything").

relatedConstructions.notes: Same determinative no in dependent (determiner) function

grounds.note: no/none dependent and independent forms of the determinative no; compounds are single words

projection.target: Nobody and nothing can trigger a positive confirmation tag even when the finite VP has affirmative form. The same polarity cannot be inferred merely from the use of few or little in every context.
projection.evidence: CGEL discusses positive tags and the relation between absolute negative expressions and approximate negation.

curious.title: Negative words that stand in for a noun phrase
curious.summary: Words like nobody, nothing and none can make a whole sentence negative without a separate not.
curious.body: In Nobody knew where Kim was, the word nobody does two jobs. It fills the place of the person who knew, and it makes the whole sentence negative. The same goes for nothing in Kim had done nothing about it, and for none in We liked none of them. This dictionary treats nobody, nothing, nowhere, no one and no place as compounds of the word no, and none as another form of no. They aren't pronouns here. A sentence with one of them can be rephrased with a verb negated and a word like any, as in Kim didn't do anything about it.
curious.try: Take a sentence with nothing in it and say it again with didn't and anything. Do the two versions give the same message?

teacher.summary: Useful for showing that nobody, nothing and none carry the negation of the clause themselves.
teacher.explain: No and none are the dependent and independent forms of the determinative no. Nobody, no one, nothing, nowhere and no place are single-word compounds of no. All of these are determinatives. Standing alone as noun phrases, they are in fused determiner-head function: one word is both determiner and head. Their negative meaning is carried up to the whole clause, so the clause counts as negative without a separate not. The same message can be expressed with verbal negation plus any, either or ever, as in didn't do anything.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call nobody and nothing negative pronouns. This grammar treats them as determinatives, with none as a form of the determinative no and the others as compounds of no.

contrasts.text: Kim had done nothing about it.
contrasts.note: The negative word is the object.

contrasts.text: Kim hadn't done anything about it.
contrasts.note: Verbal negation plus any gives a parallel way to be negative.

watch_for: A learner might look for a separate not in Nobody knew where Kim was, when nobody itself makes the clause negative.
A learner might treat none as unrelated to no, when it is the independent form of the same determinative.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a set of sentences with nobody, nothing and none. Each pair rewrites each one with a negated verb and any, then says whether the message stays the same.

child.hook: How can a sentence say no without the word not?
child.explain: Words like nobody, nothing and none make a sentence mean no all by themselves. You don't need not. You can also say the idea another way, with didn't and anything.

examples.text: I didn't find anything under the bed.

child.play: Say a sentence with nobody or nothing. Then say it again with didn't and anybody or anything. Take turns.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher explanation and terms now say that no and none are the dependent and independent forms of the determinative no, while nobody, no one, nothing, nowhere and no place are single-word compounds of no (as the entry has it); terms no longer gives a rationale the entry lacks; curious 'try' question reworded to ask whether the two versions give the same message.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Absolute Negator Determinatives." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/absolute-negator-determinative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Absolute Supplement
pattern: supplement[Subject:NP + non-finite VP or verbless predicate]

entry.name: Absolute Supplement
entry.pattern: supplement[Subject:NP + non-finite VP or verbless predicate]

1.definition: Adds a circumstance with a subject of its own.
1.details: In Her hands shaking, Mia set the glass down, her hands is the subject of shaking. The supplement can instead be verbless, as in Her keys in her coat pocket, Mia left the house. The relation to the main situation can be simultaneous, explanatory, or sequential, as context permits.

examples.form: [Her hands shaking], Mia set the glass down.
examples.note: Constructed non-finite supplement with an overt subject.

examples.form: [Her keys in her coat pocket], Mia left the house.

relatedConstructions.notes: The supplement has its own subject and predicate.
The what with frame also licenses a separate subject and predicate.

grounds.note: Describes absolute forms and their discourse contributions.
Distinguishes absolute clauses from subjectless supplements and describes verbless counterparts.

projection.target: Removing the overt subject of the non-finite supplement changes who is understood to be shaking in the ordinary reading. The same frame can host a verbless predicate.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes absolute supplements from subjectless supplements. The FrameNet team gives non-finite, verbless, and related with-variants.

curious.title: A circumstance with its own subject
curious.summary: A phrase added to a sentence can have a subject of its own and describe the circumstances of the main action.
curious.body: In Her hands shaking, Mia set the glass down, the added phrase has its own subject, her hands, and its own predicate, shaking. It tells us the circumstances in which Mia set the glass down. The added phrase doesn't need a verb. Her keys in her coat pocket, Mia left the house works the same way. How the circumstance relates to the main action depends on context: it can happen at the same time, explain why, or be part of a sequence of events. On this dictionary's analysis, taking the subject away changes the ordinary reading: we would no longer understand it to be her hands that are shaking.

examples.text: [Her hands shaking], Mia set the glass down.
[Her keys in her coat pocket], Mia left the house.

curious.try: Add a short phrase of your own to the start of a sentence, giving it its own subject. Does it happen at the same time as the main action, explain it, or form a sequence with it?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, a supplement with its own subject, as in Her hands shaking, Mia set the glass down.
teacher.explain: An absolute supplement is added to a clause and has a subject of its own, followed by a non-finite VP or a verbless predicate. In Her hands shaking, her hands is the subject of shaking. In Her keys in her coat pocket the predicate is verbless. Context decides whether the circumstance is simultaneous, explanatory or sequential. Removing the overt subject changes who is understood to be shaking in the ordinary reading, so an absolute supplement should be kept apart from a supplement with no subject of its own. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: CGEL distinguishes absolute clauses from subjectless supplements, and describes verbless counterparts. This dictionary treats the pattern as a construction with a subject and a predicate of its own.

examples.text: [Her hands shaking], Mia set the glass down.
[Her keys in her coat pocket], Mia left the house.

contrasts.text: Her hands shaking, Mia set the glass down.
contrasts.note: The supplement has its own subject.

contrasts.text: Shaking, Mia set the glass down.
contrasts.note: No overt subject, so the understood subject of shaking changes.

watch_for: A learner might take her hands in Her hands shaking as a part of the main clause, when it is the subject of shaking.
A learner might assume the supplement has to name a reason, when context can also make it simultaneous or sequential.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as a main clause and a circumstance. They add an overt subject to the circumstance, put it first, and say whether it reads as simultaneous, explanatory or sequential.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body hedged the subject-removal claim as this dictionary's analysis (the entry's kind is provisional); curious.body 'come first' replaced by 'be part of a sequence of events' (the entry says only 'sequential'); curious.try dropped 'how' (manner is not among the entry's relations) and now names the entry's three relations. Also fixed (unflagged): teacher 'The entry'/'This entry' changed to 'This dictionary'. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Absolute Supplement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/absolute-supplement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: with Plus an Absolute Predication
pattern: PP[with + NP + participial or verbless predicate]

entry.name: with Plus an Absolute Predication
entry.pattern: PP[with + NP + participial or verbless predicate]

1.definition: Presents a background condition with its own subject and predicate.

examples.form: [With the shutters closed], the room stayed cool.

projection.target: The shutters are understood as closed. The relation to the main situation can be merely concomitant or explanatory, whereas what with conventionally gives a reason.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: With plus a thing and how it is
curious.summary: A phrase beginning with with can set a background condition by naming something and saying how it is.
curious.body: In With the shutters closed, the room stayed cool, the phrase tells us a condition that holds in the background: the shutters are closed. It has a subject of its own, the shutters, and a description of it, closed. The link to the main statement can be loose. The condition can simply go along with the main situation, or it can help explain it. The expression what with is different: it conventionally gives a reason.

examples.text: [With the shutters closed], the room stayed cool.
[With the lights off], we watched the film.

curious.try: Start a sentence with with, then a thing, then a word saying how it is. What does the phrase add?

teacher.summary: Shows a with phrase that contains its own subject and predicate, such as With the shutters closed.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a PP: with plus an NP plus a participial or verbless predicate. The NP and the predicate form a subject-predicate unit, so the shutters are understood as closed. The phrase presents a background condition for the main clause. Its relation to the main situation can be merely concomitant or explanatory. Compare what with, which conventionally gives a reason. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, and it treats the pattern as related to the absolute supplement.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call such a phrase an absolute construction. This dictionary treats it as a prepositional phrase headed by with.

examples.text: [With the shutters closed], the room stayed cool.
[With the lights off], we watched the film.

contrasts.text: With the shutters closed, the room stayed cool.
contrasts.note: A background condition that may simply accompany or explain.

watch_for: A learner might read the shutters closed as a noun phrase on its own, when the shutters is understood as the subject of closed.
A learner might treat with here and what with as the same, when what with conventionally gives a reason.
teacher.activity: Students match a with phrase to a main clause, then say whether the condition just accompanies the main situation or helps explain it.

child.hook: In "With the shutters closed", what is closed?
child.explain: Some sentences start with with, then a thing, then how that thing is. With the shutters closed tells us the shutters are shut. It sets the scene for the rest of the sentence.

examples.text: [With the shutters closed], the room stayed cool.
[With the lights off], we watched the film.

child.play: Start a sentence with with and a thing. Add how it is, like open or off. Then finish the sentence. Read it aloud to a partner.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "with Plus an Absolute Predication." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/absolute-with-predication-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Abstract Numeral Construction

dimensions.form: Cardinal noun as bare NP subject; no determiner or modifier
dimensions.meaning: Denotes abstract mathematical entity as subject of predication
dimensions.function: Names a number-as-object for mathematical or metalinguistic statements
dimensions.distribution: Subject position in clauses predicating properties of numbers

1.definition: Cardinal noun denotes an abstract mathematical object rather than a count or quantity

constraints.description: Cardinal noun heads a bare NP; resists determiners (*the seven is prime).
Resists attributive modifiers (*prime seven is odd).
Rigidly designates a particular abstract quantity via nominal number assignment.

projection.target: In Seven is prime, seven is an independent subject naming a number. In seven pages, seven supplies cardinal determination. Plural sevens can instead count instances of a written symbol or value.
projection.evidence: Reynolds distinguishes abstract-name, token, and quantificational uses by their distributions.

curious.title: Numbers as things we talk about
curious.summary: A bare number word can be the subject of a sentence about the number itself.
curious.body: In Seven is prime, seven isn't counting anything. It names a number, and the sentence says something about that number. The same goes for Twenty is even and Two plus two is four. Compare seven pages, where seven tells you how many pages there are. In the mathematical use, the number word stands alone, with no the or other describing word in front. It acts like a name for one particular number.
curious.try: Compare "Seven is prime" with "I read seven pages." In which sentence is seven counting something, and in which is it the thing being described?

teacher.summary: Shows number words used as names of numbers in mathematical statements, in contrast with number words that count.
teacher.explain: In Seven is prime, seven is a cardinal noun heading a bare NP in subject position. It denotes an abstract mathematical object, not a count or quantity, and rigidly designates a particular number. This dictionary notes that it resists determiners and attributive modifiers. Compare seven pages, where seven supplies cardinal determination. The plural sevens can instead count instances of a written symbol or value. This dictionary bases the distinction between abstract-name, token and quantificational uses on their distributions.
teacher.terms: Cardinal noun: a number word used as a noun.

contrasts.note: Seven names a number.
Seven counts pages.

watch_for: A learner might read Seven is prime as describing seven of something.
A learner might add the or an adjective in front of the number word, as in the seven is prime.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences into two piles, those where a number word names a number (Twenty is even) and those where it counts things (seven pages), then write one new sentence for each pile.

checked.note: Fixed: removed the cardinal determinative gloss from teacher.terms (the entry leaves the category of seven in seven pages unstated); replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Abstract Numeral Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/abstract-numeral-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Activity Weak Definite
pattern: Host expressing a conventional activity + NP[the + N]

entry.name: Activity Weak Definite
entry.pattern: Host expressing a conventional activity + NP[the + N]

1.definition: Invokes a conventional activity with a definite NP that need not identify a unique participant or object.
1.details: In take the bus, the transport activity can be understood without identifying which vehicle is involved. The same NP can identify a particular vehicle with a different predicate. The host and the noun both matter, and the activity frame may also allow an ordinary identifying reading in context.

examples.note: Conventional transport use. The NP sits inside the bracketed activity frame.
Constructed identifying control. The verb and activity are different, with the noun and article held fixed.

relatedConstructions.notes: The activity frame contains an NP with the definite article.
Definite form co-occurs with weaker semantic identification.

grounds.note: Tests which combinations of verb and noun license the weak reading.

projection.target: With a suitable host and noun, the hearer can recover the activity without identifying a unique participant of the kind denoted by the noun.
projection.evidence: CGEL's activity examples and Klein et al.'s Experiment 4, which combines and varies the verbs and nouns in licensing environments.

curious.title: The bus that isn't a particular bus
curious.summary: With some verbs and nouns, a phrase starting with the can name an everyday activity rather than one particular thing.
curious.body: When we say We took the bus, we're describing a way of travelling. The phrase the bus doesn't point to one particular vehicle that the listener must work out. Change the verb and the same words can pick out a particular bus: in Lee parked the bus, we're talking about a specific vehicle. Both the verb and the noun matter, and a sentence like We took the bus can also be read as naming one particular bus if the situation makes that clear.
curious.try: Say We took the bus and then Lee parked the bus. Which one needs you to know which bus is meant?

teacher.summary: Explains weak definites, where the plus a noun names a conventional activity without identifying a unique object.
teacher.explain: In We took the bus, the definite NP sits inside a conventional activity frame (transport use). The hearer can recover the activity without identifying which vehicle is involved. With a different predicate and the same noun and article, as in Lee parked the bus, the NP identifies a particular vehicle. So the host expression and the noun both matter, and the activity frame may still allow an ordinary identifying reading in context. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional; it relies on experimental work on which verb and noun combinations license the weak reading.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a weak definite. This dictionary calls the host plus NP an activity frame.

contrasts.note: Conventional transport use.
The same noun and article, a different verb, and a particular vehicle.

watch_for: A learner might assume the bus has to name a single vehicle both speaker and listener know, when the activity can be understood without that.
A learner might assume any verb with the bus gives the activity reading, when the verb matters.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a list of verb plus the bus phrases. They sort them into everyday activity readings and particular-vehicle readings, then compare sorting with another pair.

child.hook: When you say "We took the bus", do you mean one special bus?
child.explain: We took the bus can be about travelling, without one special bus in mind. Lee parked the bus is about one particular bus. The verb matters, and so does the noun.
child.play: Say each sentence and ask a partner, "Which bus?" Do you need to know which bus in each one? Try it with other sentences of your own.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain now says We took the bus can be about travelling (the entry allows an identifying reading in context); child.play no longer implies only one sentence invites 'Which bus?'. Also fixed (unflagged): curious summary typo; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; teacher terms hedged to 'sometimes called'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Activity Weak Definite." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/activity-weak-definite-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Adjectival Passive

1.definition: Predicates a state or property through an adjective with passive-like morphology.

relatedConstructions.notes: The door remained locked supports an adjective analysis. The door was locked by security at noon permits the verbal passive analysis with an event time and a by-phrase.

projection.target: Remain can select the stative predicate. A verbal passive with an agent and an explicitly dated event gives an event reading rather than the state interpretation illustrated here.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Describing a state with a word like locked
curious.summary: A word that looks like part of a passive verb can instead describe how something is.
curious.body: In The door remained locked, the word locked tells us the state of the door. Nobody is said to have done anything. This dictionary tentatively treats locked here as an adjective, because the verb remain can select a description of a state. Compare The door was locked by security at noon. There we can picture an event at a particular time, with someone doing the locking, so the verbal passive reading is possible. The two sentences share the same word shape, but the first describes a state and the second can describe an event.
curious.try: Say The door remained locked, then The door was locked by security at noon. Which one sounds like something happening at a particular time?

teacher.summary: Helps students tell a state described by an adjective (remained locked) from a verbal passive event (was locked by security).
teacher.explain: In the adjectival passive, a past-participle form heads an adjective phrase after be, seem or remain, and the clause ascribes a state or property to the subject. Remain supports the adjective analysis because it can select the stative predicate. A verbal passive with an agent and an explicitly dated event, such as The door was locked by security at noon, permits the verbal analysis and gives an event reading instead. This dictionary treats the adjectival passive as a specialization of the subject-ascriptive pattern and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Both patterns use a past-participial form. This dictionary calls the first an adjectival passive (adjective phrase) and the second a verbal be-passive.

contrasts.note: State of the door; adjective analysis supported.

contrasts.text: The door was locked by security at noon.
contrasts.note: Agent and dated event; verbal passive analysis permitted.

watch_for: A learner might read every past participle after be, seem or remain as an event with an agent, when remained locked describes a state.
A learner might assume seem or remain can't be followed by locked, when the pattern allows be, seem and remain.
teacher.activity: Students get sentence pairs built on the same participle, one with remain and one with a by-phrase and a time. They label each as state or event and say what clue decided it.

child.hook: Is "locked" something a person does, or how the door is?
child.explain: In The door remained locked, locked tells us how the door is. It doesn't say who locked it. In The door was locked by security at noon, we hear about something that happened.
child.play: Think of things that stay in a state, like closed or broken. Say a sentence with remained for each one, and tell a partner how the thing is.

checked.note: Fixed: child example The window remained open replaced by The window remained closed (the entry's pattern needs a past-participial base; open is not one); child.play dropped empty for the same reason; curious.body now says this dictionary tentatively treats locked as an adjective (the entry is provisional, confidence medium); teacher.terms 'look like be plus a past participle' changed to 'use a past-participial form' (the entry's example uses remain). Also fixed (unflagged): curious.examples dropped The door [was locked] by security at noon, which bolded a verbal passive as an instance of this pattern (the comparison stays in the body); watch_for item now says after be, seem or remain rather than be plus past participle; teacher 'The entry'/'This entry' changed to 'This dictionary'. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Adjectival Passive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/adjectival-passive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Raising with an Adjectival Predicative
pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + be + PredComp:AdjP[Adj + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]]

entry.name: Raising with an Adjectival Predicative
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + be + PredComp:AdjP[Adj + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]]

1.definition: Locates likelihood or a related assessment in the situation expressed by the infinitival.
1.details: Likely assesses the situation. It permits dummy there in the subject position because that position serves the infinitival predication. In determined to leave, the adjective ascribes determination to its subject and does not permit dummy there.

examples.form: [There is likely to be enough food left.]
examples.note: Dummy there is licensed within the existential situation assessed.
The situation remains the same in They were likely to be convinced by Liz.

relatedConstructions.notes: The matrix adjective takes an infinitival.
The tough construction instead links the matrix subject to a non-subject gap.

grounds.note: Records likely with an infinitival in the raising frame.

projection.target: Dummy subjects are compatible with the raising pattern. Substituting a passive description of the same situation need not shift the target of likely.
projection.evidence: CGEL tests matched raising and non-raising adjectives with dummy subjects, passive alternation and selection. CASA records the likely construction.

curious.title: Likely to, said of a whole situation
curious.summary: With a word like likely, the sentence judges a whole situation rather than describing the person it starts with.
curious.body: In Liz was likely to convince them, the word likely doesn't describe Liz. It assesses a situation: Liz convincing them. That's why They were likely to be convinced by Liz describes the same situation. It also explains There is likely to be enough food left, where the opening there isn't a person or thing that could be likely. Compare determined to leave, where the adjective says something about its subject: someone is determined. There the opening word can't be an empty there.

examples.text: [There is likely to be enough food left.]

curious.try: Say Liz was likely to convince them, and then They were likely to be convinced by Liz. Does the situation stay the same?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, shows how likely assesses a situation expressed by the infinitival, unlike determined.
teacher.explain: In the raising pattern, the subject belongs to the infinitival predication, and the adjective assesses the whole situation. Evidence in this dictionary: likely permits dummy there as subject (There is likely to be enough food left), and an active and a passive version describe the same situation (Liz was likely to convince them; They were likely to be convinced by Liz). In determined to leave, the adjective ascribes determination to its subject and does not permit dummy there. This dictionary sets raising apart from the tough construction, in which the matrix subject is linked to a non-subject gap.
teacher.terms: Raising adjective is the label used for likely in this pattern. Dummy there is the empty subject there.

examples.text: [There is likely to be enough food left.]

contrasts.text: Liz was likely to convince them.
contrasts.note: Likely assesses the situation of Liz convincing them.
Determined ascribes determination to Kim, so dummy there doesn't fit here.

watch_for: A learner might read Liz was likely to convince them as saying something about Liz herself, when likely assesses the situation.
A learner might treat likely and determined as the same pattern because both are followed by to, when this dictionary shows they differ.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of adjectives followed by to-infinitivals (likely and determined). They test each with an active and passive version of the same situation and decide which adjective stays about the same situation.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Raising with an Adjectival Predicative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/adjectival-raising-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Adjective

dimensions.form: Lexical stem; accepts degree morphology (-er/-est) or degree modifiers (very)
dimensions.meaning: Scalar, classificatory, state, evaluative, or referential feature bundles
dimensions.function: Modifier of nominal; predicative complement; rarely argument
dimensions.distribution: Attributive (prenominal), predicative, postpositive; some restricted to one position

1.definition: Denotes scalar feature bundle
1.details: Core semantic features that position entities on measurable dimensions

2.details: Semantic features that assign entities to categories or types

3.details: Semantic features describing temporary or permanent conditions

4.details: Semantic features expressing assessment or judgment

5.details: Semantic features establishing identity relations between entities

relatedConstructions.notes: Scalar adjectives share gradability semantics with degree constructions
Bidirectional; gradable adjectives license degree modification, degree modification cues scalar interpretation

stabilisers.evidence: early acquisition of adjective slots in NP and predicative complements
high-frequency descriptive adjectives anchor category use
need to encode properties for reference and predication

projection.target: A common central adjective can be both pre-head and predicative, as with an angry neighbour and the neighbour is angry. Former in former president lacks the corresponding reading after be. Neither semantic property description nor a single position suffices to identify every adjective.
projection.evidence: CGEL treats the central distribution as a cluster and describes restricted attributive and predicative members.

perturbations: reduced exposure to degree morphology weakens gradable diagnostics but leaves classificatory uses intact

known_boundary_items: fast
near
fun

curious.title: Words that describe things
curious.summary: Adjectives are words like tall, wooden or happy that say what something is like, and they don't all behave alike.
curious.body: Adjectives are words such as tall, fast, wooden, French, broken, happy, good and same. This dictionary groups what they tell us into five kinds: scale (tall), type (wooden), state (broken), evaluation (good) and reference (same). A common central adjective can come before a noun, as in an angry neighbour, and after be, as in the neighbour is angry. Not every adjective does both. The word former can come before a noun (a former president), but it doesn't have the matching use after be. So no single position or meaning picks out every adjective.
curious.try: Put a few describing words before a noun and after is. Do they all fit both places?

teacher.summary: Gives teachers a working description of adjectives as a cluster of properties, with attention to words that don't pattern alike.
teacher.explain: Adjective is a word category. Central members are modifiers of nouns (attributive, an angry neighbour) and predicative complements (the neighbour is angry), and gradable ones accept degree morphology (-er/-est) or degree modifiers like very. This dictionary lists five semantic groupings: scalar (tall, fast), classificatory (wooden, French), state (broken, happy), evaluative (good, correct) and reference (same, other). Classificatory adjectives resist degree modification. Some adjectives are restricted: former in former president lacks the corresponding reading after be. Fast, near and fun are listed as boundary items. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call adjectives describing words. In CGEL usage an adjective is a word category, and modifier and predicative complement are functions.

contrasts.note: Before the noun.
After be, a predicative use.

watch_for: A learner might assume every adjective can appear both before a noun and after be, when former in former president lacks the corresponding use after be.
A learner might sort words by meaning alone, when neither meaning nor a single position picks out every adjective.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of words (tall, wooden, happy, broken, same, former). They test each before a noun and after be, and record which fit where.

child.hook: Can you say "an angry neighbour" and also "the neighbour is angry"?
child.explain: Adjectives are words that tell us what something is like. Tall, wooden and happy are adjectives. They can go before a noun, and they can go after is.
child.play: Pick a describing word like tall, happy or wooden. Say it before a noun, then after is. Find three that work both ways.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Adjective." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/adjective-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Adjectival tough Construction
pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + be + PredComp:AdjP[Adj + to-infinitival Clause with non-subject gapᵢ]]

entry.name: Adjectival tough Construction
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + be + PredComp:AdjP[Adj + to-infinitival Clause with non-subject gapᵢ]]

1.definition: Characterizes the matrix subject by evaluating an action involving it.
1.details: In their argument was impossible to follow, the argument is understood as the object of follow. A preposition can supply the gap instead. The infinitival may have its own subject with for. Compare Kim was anxious to follow the argument, where Kim is the understood subject of follow. The construction makes an evaluation about the matrix subject, which excludes dummy there on this reading.

examples.note: The argument is the understood object of follow.

examples.form: [His performance was easy to find fault with.]
examples.note: The gap is the object of with.

examples.form: [The instructions were hard for us to follow.]
examples.note: Constructed with an overt subject in the infinitival.

relatedConstructions.notes: An adjectival predicative follows the matrix be.
The existing time-away entry uses the tough frame as an objecthood diagnostic.

grounds.note: Identifies the adjective and infinitival pattern with evaluation of an entity through an action.

projection.target: The matrix subject supplies a non-subject argument of the infinitival. The infinitival can separately identify who undertakes the action.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares hollow and ordinary infinitivals and contrasts their subject restrictions. CASA records the difficult-to-answer pattern.

curious.title: Easy to follow, hard to find fault with
curious.summary: In some sentences the adjective judges the opening noun by what we do to it, as in impossible to follow.
curious.body: In Their argument was impossible to follow, the argument is understood as the thing being followed, even though follow has no object after it. His performance was easy to find fault with works the same way: the performance is what we find fault with. The sentence evaluates the opening noun by an action involving it. The action can even have its own doer, as in The instructions were hard for us to follow. Compare Kim was anxious to follow the argument, where Kim is the one who follows.

examples.text: [His performance was easy to find fault with.]
[The instructions were hard for us to follow.]

curious.try: Say Their argument was impossible to follow. What is understood as the thing being followed?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, the tough construction, where the subject is understood as a non-subject of the infinitival.
teacher.explain: In the tough construction, the matrix subject is linked to a gap in the infinitival that is not a subject. In their argument was impossible to follow, the argument is the understood object of follow. A preposition can supply the gap instead (easy to find fault with). The infinitival may have its own subject introduced by for (hard for us to follow). The construction evaluates the matrix subject by an action involving it, and it excludes dummy there on this reading. Compare Kim was anxious to follow the argument, where Kim is the understood subject of follow.
teacher.terms: Tough construction is the usual name. This dictionary also uses hollow infinitival for the to-clause with a gap.

examples.text: [His performance was easy to find fault with.]
[The instructions were hard for us to follow.]

contrasts.text: Their argument was impossible to follow.
contrasts.note: The argument is the understood object of follow.

contrasts.text: Kim was anxious to follow the argument.
contrasts.note: Kim is the understood subject of follow.

watch_for: A learner might look for an object after follow in impossible to follow, when the subject is understood as the object.
A learner might read Kim was anxious to follow the argument like the tough pattern, when Kim is the one following.
teacher.activity: Give students tough-pattern sentences. They say what is understood as the object or prepositional object of the verb, then compare with anxious to follow.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Adjectival tough Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/adjective-hollow-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: have with a Past-Participial Predication

1.definition: Presents an outcome as arranged by or affecting the subject.

examples.form: We [had the roof replaced] in June.

projection.target: The subject can be an arranger, but had her bag stolen can describe an unwanted event she experienced. The post-have NP is understood as the affected participant of the participial.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Having something done
curious.summary: Have plus a noun phrase and a past-participle word presents an outcome as arranged by, or happening to, the subject.
curious.body: In We had the roof replaced in June, the roof is understood as the thing that got replaced, and we are the ones who arranged it. The same pattern can describe something unwanted that happened to the subject: Maya had her bag stolen on the train. So the subject can be an arranger, but it can also be the person affected. The noun phrase after have (the roof, her bag) is understood as the thing the action affected.

examples.text: We [had the roof replaced] in June.
Maya [had her bag stolen] on the train.

curious.try: Say We had the roof replaced. Then say Maya had her bag stolen. In which one did the subject arrange it?

teacher.summary: Shows have plus an NP plus a past participle, which can mean arranged or experienced.
teacher.explain: The pattern is have plus an NP plus a past-participial predicate (had the roof replaced). It presents an outcome as arranged by or affecting the subject. The subject can be an arranger, as in the roof example, but had her bag stolen can describe an unwanted event she experienced. The NP after have is understood as the affected participant of the participial. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the verb phrase and relates it to the be-passive. It is marked provisional.

examples.text: We [had the roof replaced] in June.
Maya [had her bag stolen] on the train.

contrasts.text: We had the roof replaced in June.
contrasts.note: The subject arranged the outcome.

contrasts.text: Maya had her bag stolen on the train.
contrasts.note: The subject experienced an unwanted event.

watch_for: A learner might read had her bag stolen as meaning she arranged the theft, when it can describe an unwanted event.
A learner might take the roof in had the roof replaced as the thing that does the replacing, when it is the affected participant.
teacher.activity: Give students short sentences with have plus an NP plus a participle. They mark each as arranged or experienced and underline the affected noun phrase.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "have with a Past-Participial Predication." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/affected-have-participial-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: all Modifier Restricting a Role
pattern: Nom[all + class-denoting nominal or adjective + N]

entry.name: all Modifier Restricting a Role
entry.pattern: Nom[all + class-denoting nominal or adjective + N]

1.definition: Restricts the occupants of a salient role associated with the head noun to one class.
1.details: With an all girls’ school the relevant role is eligibility to attend. The school can educate only some of the town’s girls and have men on staff. With an all-women team the team supplies the members. Genitive and plain-case nominal forms and adjectives support the interpretation. CGEL treats all girls’ as a genitive NP with peripheral all. The related patterns leave that token’s internal bracketing open.

examples.note: The restriction concerns who can attend the school.

grounds.locator: opening discussion, p. 1 of author manuscript

examples.note: Plain plural form. The same contingent is described by both published expressions.

grounds.locator: opening discussion, p. 1 of author manuscript

relatedConstructions.notes: The role-restricting expression combines with a nominal head.
CGEL analyzes the spelling girls’ in its example as genitive.

projection.target: The head helps select the set to which all applies. The restriction applies to students in the school case and members in the team case.
projection.evidence: CGEL's exclusivity gloss and the two expressions for the same Indian police contingent support the cross-form comparison.

curious.title: All as a restriction, as in an all girls' school
curious.summary: Putting all before a class word can say that only members of that class fill a role connected to the noun.
curious.body: In an all girls' school, the role at issue is who can attend. The school educates only girls, but it can serve only some of the town's girls and it can have men on staff. In an all-women team, the role is team membership, and the team supplies the members. The pattern works with several forms. There's a plural noun with an apostrophe (all girls'), a plain plural (all-women), and an adjective (all-female). The head noun helps decide which role all restricts.
curious.try: Think of a team, club or school described with all. Who does all say may be in it?

teacher.summary: Explains how all with a class word restricts a role, such as who attends or who belongs.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a nominal consisting of all plus a class-denoting nominal or adjective plus a noun. It restricts the occupants of a salient role associated with the head noun to one class. With an all girls' school the role is eligibility to attend, so the school can educate only some of the town's girls and have men on staff. With an all-women team, the team supplies the members. Genitive and plain-case nominal forms and adjectives all support the interpretation. CGEL treats all girls' as a genitive NP with peripheral all, while the internal bracketing of the other forms is left open. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: CGEL analyzes the apostrophe form girls' in its example as genitive.

contrasts.note: Adjectival class specification.
Plain plural form.

watch_for: A learner might read all girls' school as saying every girl in the town attends, when the restriction concerns who can attend.
A learner might assume all must restrict the same role in every phrase, when the head noun helps select the set.
teacher.activity: Students collect phrases with all and a class word (all-girls, all-female). For each, they say which role is restricted (attending, belonging) and who may fill it.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain no longer says the entry leaves the bracketing of the related patterns open; it now says the internal bracketing of the other forms is left open, as this dictionary does, and the provisional marking is attributed to this dictionary. Teacher terms now credits the genitive analysis of girls' to CGEL, as in this dictionary's example.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "all Modifier Restricting a Role." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/all-class-role-modifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: all of with a Stated Magnitude
pattern: all of + (approximator) + numeral expression, with no definite article after of

entry.name: all of with a Stated Magnitude
entry.pattern: all of + (approximator) + numeral expression, with no definite article after of

1.definition: Calls attention to a stated magnitude relative to an expectation.
1.details: The numeral gives the measured or counted magnitude. A distinct approximator can still make it inexact. All of the fifty volunteers instead quantifies over a separately identified group. The direction of the evaluation in the magnitude use remains open and can be tested by varying the expectation while holding the magnitude fixed.

examples.form: They had recruited [all of fifty] volunteers.
examples.note: The magnitude supplies a count of the recruits.
Overt approximation in an oral history.
Overt approximation in an oral history.

relatedConstructions.notes: The numeral supplies the magnitude independently of the all of expression.
All of fifty volunteers emphasizes a magnitude. All of the fifty volunteers ranges over the established group.

projection.target: The pattern can retain about and its approximation while inviting an assessment of whether the magnitude is noteworthy in context.
projection.evidence: CGEL's example and the two oral histories establish the form. The role of expectations is a proposal to test.

curious.title: All of before a number
curious.summary: Putting all of before a stated amount draws attention to that amount, as if it were noteworthy.
curious.body: In They had recruited all of fifty volunteers, the number is the point. The phrase asks us to notice the amount, compared with what we expected. The direction of that comparison is left open in this dictionary. A word like about can still make the number inexact, as in all of about five minutes. This isn't the same as all of the fifty volunteers, which talks about a group that has already been identified, and covers all of them.

examples.text: They had recruited [all of fifty] volunteers.

curious.try: Compare all of fifty volunteers with all of the fifty volunteers. Which one talks about a group we already know?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, all of before a numeral, which highlights a magnitude, versus all of the plus a known group.
teacher.explain: The pattern is all of plus an optional approximator plus a numeral expression, with no definite article after of. The numeral gives the measured or counted magnitude, and a distinct approximator such as about can still make it inexact. The effect is to call attention to the stated magnitude relative to an expectation. This dictionary says the direction of the evaluation remains open and could be tested by varying the expectation while holding the magnitude fixed. All of the fifty volunteers is different: it quantifies over a separately identified group. This dictionary rates its own confidence low.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats the numeral as supplying the magnitude independently of the all of expression.

examples.text: They had recruited [all of fifty] volunteers.

contrasts.text: They had recruited all of fifty volunteers.
contrasts.note: A magnitude, with no article after of.

contrasts.text: They had recruited all of the fifty volunteers.
contrasts.note: A separately identified group.

watch_for: A learner might read all of fifty volunteers as all of an already identified group, when the numeral gives the magnitude.
A learner might think about is incompatible with all of before a number, when all of about five minutes appears in this dictionary’s examples.
teacher.activity: Students write two sentences, one with all of plus a number and one with all of the plus a number and a group. They then say what each one is about, the amount or the group.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "all of with a Stated Magnitude." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/all-of-magnitude-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Concessive although Adjunct
pattern: PP[although + finite or licensed reduced predication]

entry.name: Concessive although Adjunct
entry.pattern: PP[although + finite or licensed reduced predication]

1.definition: Acknowledges a circumstance that might have counted against the main claim.

examples.form: [Although the steps were icy], we reached the door.
[Even if the steps are icy], we’ll reach the door.
examples.note: Constructed comparison. Conditional concession leaves the ice uncertain.

projection.target: Both the ice and the arrival are presented as actual. The contrast comes from an expectation about what the ice might impede.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Admitting a drawback with although
curious.summary: An although phrase acknowledges something that might have counted against the main claim.
curious.body: In Although the steps were icy, we reached the door, both things are presented as true. The steps were icy, and we reached the door. The contrast comes from an expectation about what the ice might have stopped. Even if works differently. In Even if the steps are icy, we'll reach the door, the ice is uncertain, so the sentence concedes a possibility rather than a fact.

examples.text: [Although the steps were icy], we reached the door.
[Even if the steps are icy], we’ll reach the door.

curious.try: Finish this sentence: Although it was late, ... Does your ending go against what late might lead us to expect?

teacher.summary: Shows although as a way to concede a circumstance that might have counted against the main claim.
teacher.explain: An although phrase is a PP with a finite clause or a licensed reduced predication. It acknowledges a circumstance that might have counted against the main claim. Both the ice and the arrival are presented as actual, and the contrast comes from an expectation about what the ice might impede. Compare even if, which gives a conditional concession and leaves the ice uncertain. This dictionary treats the although phrase as a specialization of PP and marks the analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: Textbooks may call although a subordinating conjunction. This dictionary treats although as the head of a PP.

examples.text: [Although the steps were icy], we reached the door.
[Even if the steps are icy], we’ll reach the door.

contrasts.text: Although the steps were icy, we reached the door.
contrasts.note: The ice is presented as actual.

contrasts.text: Even if the steps are icy, we'll reach the door.
contrasts.note: The ice is left uncertain.

watch_for: A learner might treat the although clause as uncertain, when both the ice and the arrival are presented as actual.
A learner might read the contrast as being between the two clauses alone, when it comes from an expectation about what the ice might impede.
teacher.activity: Students complete although sentences, then say what expectation each one goes against. They compare with the same ideas expressed with even if.

child.hook: What does "although" tell us might have stopped us?
child.explain: Although shows something that might have stopped us, but didn't. Although the steps were icy, we reached the door. The steps really were icy.

examples.text: [Although the steps were icy], we reached the door.
[Although it was raining], we played outside.

child.play: Start with although and a problem, like being tired or cold. Then say what happened anyway. Take turns with a partner.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Concessive although Adjunct." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/although-concessive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Singular Agreement with an Amount Expression
pattern: Clause[plural-shaped measure NP as subject + singular agreement]

entry.name: Singular Agreement with an Amount Expression
entry.pattern: Clause[plural-shaped measure NP as subject + singular agreement]

1.definition: Treats a multi-unit expression as a single amount for agreement.

relatedConstructions.notes: Three litres is enough treats a measurement as one amount. A collective NP such as the committee can allow plural agreement on a member-oriented reading.
A measure pseudopartitive can be the subject of singular amount agreement, as in Three litres of milk is enough.

projection.target: The singular is natural when the predicate evaluates a duration as a whole. An individually predicated series of hours can instead take plural agreement.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Three hours is enough
curious.summary: An amount that looks plural can take a singular verb when it's treated as one total.
curious.body: In Three hours is enough, the subject looks plural, but the verb is singular. The sentence treats three hours as a single amount of time. The same goes for Three litres is enough, where a measurement counts as one amount. On this dictionary's analysis, the singular fits when the sentence judges the duration as a whole. If the hours are being thought of one at a time, the plural can be used instead. A group word like the committee is a separate case: it can take a plural verb when we think of its members.
curious.try: Say Three hours is enough. Are you thinking of the hours as one total, or one by one?

teacher.summary: Explains why an amount expression such as three hours can take a singular verb.
teacher.explain: A plural-shaped measure NP can be the subject of a clause with singular agreement, as in Three hours is enough. The expression is treated as a single amount. On this dictionary's provisional analysis, the singular is natural when the predicate evaluates a duration as a whole. If a series of hours is predicated of individually, plural agreement can be used instead. A measure pseudopartitive can also be the subject of singular amount agreement (Three litres of milk is enough). This dictionary keeps this apart from collective agreement, where a collective NP such as the committee can take plural agreement on a member-oriented reading.
teacher.terms: Sometimes treated under notional concord (or notional agreement), a broader label for a verb agreeing with the meaning of its subject rather than its form, which also takes in collective nouns like the committee. This dictionary keeps the two apart and calls this pattern singular agreement with an amount expression.

contrasts.note: A measurement treated as one amount.

watch_for: A learner might expect the plural form of the verb because hours ends in a plural -s, when the whole duration is treated as one amount.
A learner might apply the same reasoning to the committee, when a collective NP can take a plural verb on a member-oriented reading.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with measure expressions (litres, hours, kilometres) as the subject and say whether each treats the amount as a whole total or one at a time.

child.hook: Three hours is more than one hour. So why can we say "three hours is enough"?
child.explain: Three hours is a plural-looking phrase, but we can treat it as one amount of time. Then we can say is. Three litres is enough works the same way.
child.play: Think of amounts like two hours, five kilometres or four litres. Say each one with is enough. Do they sound like one amount?

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms kept the textbook term but rephrased it as 'sometimes treated under notional concord (or notional agreement)', marked as a broader label that also covers collective nouns, which this dictionary keeps apart (Quirk et al. 1985, section 10.35 Note [a], puts singular agreement with plural measure phrases under notional concord; Leech's grammar glossary defines the term); curious.body and teacher.explain now hedge the whole-duration condition as this dictionary's (provisional) analysis (kind provisional, confidence medium). Also fixed (unflagged): child.hook said we say is 'and not are', and child.explain said 'So we say is', implying the plural is wrong, though the entry stars nothing and allows plural agreement for an individually predicated series; teacher 'The entry'/'This entry' changed to 'This dictionary'. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Singular Agreement with an Amount Expression." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/amount-singular-agreement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Anaphoric not with an Attitude Predicate

1.definition: Picks up the negative counterpart of a prior proposition.

projection.target: Not supplies the content that the screen is not broken. I don’t hope so can instead negate the hoping, and compatibility of the standalone not varies by predicate.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: I hope not
curious.summary: After a word like hope, not can stand in for a whole statement, the negative of something just raised in the conversation.
curious.body: Asked Is the screen broken?, someone can answer I hope not. The word not here stands in for the content the screen is not broken. So the answer means I hope the screen is not broken. This isn't the same as I don't hope so, which can instead deny that the speaker hopes. Not every attitude word allows the short answer, and which ones do depends on the word.
curious.try: Answer a yes-or-no question with I hope not. Then say what the full sentence would be.

teacher.summary: Shows how not can pick up a negative proposition after an attitude predicate, as in I hope not.
teacher.explain: In this pattern not follows a licensed predicate and picks up the negative counterpart of a proposition already in the discourse. In the exchange Is the screen broken? I hope not, not supplies the content that the screen is not broken. I don't hope so can instead negate the hoping. Whether the standalone not is compatible depends on the predicate, so each predicate has to be checked. This dictionary relates it to negative raising.
teacher.terms: Not here is anaphoric: it picks up the negative counterpart of an earlier proposition. This dictionary names the pattern anaphoric not with an attitude predicate.

contrasts.note: Not supplies the content that the screen is not broken.
Can instead negate the hoping.

watch_for: A learner might read I hope not as saying the speaker doesn't hope, when not supplies the negative content that is hoped for.
A learner might assume every attitude predicate can be followed by standalone not, when compatibility varies by predicate.
teacher.activity: Students ask each other yes-or-no questions and answer with I hope so and I hope not. They then write out the full sentence each short answer stands for.

child.hook: When someone says "I hope not", what do they hope?
child.explain: Someone asks, "Is the screen broken?" You answer, "I hope not." Not stands for the whole idea that the screen is not broken. It saves you from saying the whole sentence.
child.play: Ask a partner a yes-or-no question. They answer with I hope not. Then they say the whole sentence that those words stand for.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain cut the claim that the dictionary relates the pattern to anaphoric so (I hope so) as an alternate (the entry lists only negative-raising-001); teacher.terms now gives the entry's name, anaphoric not with an attitude predicate, and says not picks up the negative counterpart of an earlier proposition; curious.summary no longer says the negative statement was mentioned (the entry: not picks up the negative counterpart of a prior proposition). Also fixed (unflagged): child.explain 'saying it all again' changed to 'saying the whole sentence', since the negative was never said. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Anaphoric not with an Attitude Predicate." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/anaphoric-propositional-not-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Anaphoric so with an Attitude Predicate

1.definition: Picks up a prior proposition as the content of an attitude or utterance.

relatedConstructions.notes: I hope so and I hope not share an attitude predicate. So picks up the proposition in play. Not picks up its negative counterpart.

projection.target: So is interpreted as the proposition that the keys are inside. Substitution of do so gives an action anaphor and fails to express that content in this frame.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: I think so
curious.summary: After a word like think, so can stand in for a whole statement mentioned in the conversation.
curious.body: Asked Are the keys inside?, someone can answer I think so. Here so stands for the content the keys are inside. The full sentence would be I think the keys are inside. The same short form works with hope, as in I hope so. There the pair is I hope so and I hope not: so picks up the proposition in play, and not picks up its negative counterpart. It is different from do so, which stands in for an action rather than for something that is thought or said.
curious.try: Answer a yes-or-no question with I think so. Say the full sentence that so stands for.

teacher.summary: Shows how so can pick up a proposition after an attitude predicate, as in I think so.
teacher.explain: In this pattern so follows a licensed predicate and picks up a prior proposition as the content of an attitude or utterance. In the exchange Are the keys inside? I think so, so is interpreted as the proposition that the keys are inside. Do so gives an action anaphor, so it does not express that content in this frame. This dictionary places the pattern next to anaphoric not: I hope so and I hope not share an attitude predicate, with so picking up the proposition in play and not its negative counterpart.
teacher.terms: So is anaphoric here: it refers back to a proposition. This dictionary names the pattern anaphoric propositional so.

contrasts.note: So picks up the proposition in play.
Not picks up its negative counterpart.

watch_for: A learner might take so as meaning also or very, when it picks up a whole proposition as content.
A learner might swap in do so for so, when do so gives an action anaphor.
teacher.activity: Students ask each other yes-or-no questions and answer with I think so and I hope so. They then write out the whole sentence that so stands for.

child.hook: When someone says "I think so", what does "so" stand for?
child.explain: Someone asks, "Are the keys inside?" You answer, "I think so." The word so stands for the whole idea that the keys are inside. It saves you saying it all again.
child.play: Ask a partner a yes-or-no question. They answer with I think so. Then they say the whole sentence that those words stand for.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Anaphoric so with an Attitude Predicate." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/anaphoric-propositional-so-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Additive another before a Measure or Cardinal
pattern: NP[another + cardinal or measure expression + nominal]

entry.name: Additive another before a Measure or Cardinal
entry.pattern: NP[another + cardinal or measure expression + nominal]

1.definition: Adds another amount of the stated size to the relevant course or quantity.

projection.target: The added quantity can be plural, even though ordinary another with no intervening quantifier selects a singular count nominal. The example adds days rather than replacing the prior period.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Another three days
curious.summary: Another before a number or measure adds an amount of that size to what has gone before.
curious.body: In We stayed another three days, another adds three days to the stay. It doesn't replace the first period. It continues it. Ordinary another goes with a singular count noun, as in another day. Here, though, another comes before a plural, three days.
curious.try: Say We stayed another day, then We stayed another three days. What does another add each time?

teacher.summary: Shows how another before a cardinal or measure adds an amount of the stated size, even before a plural.
teacher.explain: In the pattern another plus a cardinal or measure expression plus a nominal, another adds another amount of the stated size to the relevant course or quantity. In We stayed another three days, the added quantity is plural, even though ordinary another with no intervening quantifier selects a singular count nominal. The example adds days to the earlier period and doesn't replace it. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the indefinite NP and relates it to the measure pseudopartitive. It is marked provisional.

contrasts.note: Another plus a cardinal and a plural noun, adding to the earlier period.
Ordinary another with a singular count noun.

watch_for: A learner might think another must be followed by a singular noun, when the cardinal allows a plural.
A learner might read another three days as a replacement for the earlier period, when the example adds days.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences such as We waited another ... with a number and a unit of time. They say what another added.

child.hook: We say "another day". Can we also say "another three days"?
child.explain: Another means one more. With a number it means that much more. We stayed another three days means three more days on top of the ones before.
child.play: Pick a number and a time, like two hours or five minutes. Say a sentence with another, like We waited another two hours. Then tell a partner how much more time another added.

checked.note: Fixed: child.play no longer asks for a total (the added time is the only amount given); teacher.activity now asks only what another added; cut the unsupported 'because' explanation in curious.body; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary' in teacher.explain.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Additive another before a Measure or Cardinal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/another-additive-measure-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Ordered Auxiliary Chain
pattern: VP[(modal) + (perfect have + past participle) + (progressive be + gerund-participle) + (passive be + past participle)]

entry.name: Ordered Auxiliary Chain
entry.pattern: VP[(modal) + (perfect have + past participle) + (progressive be + gerund-participle) + (passive be + past participle)]

1.definition: Composes several auxiliaries with locally selected verb forms and restricted relative order.

relatedConstructions.notes: In may have been waiting, perfect have follows the modal and selects the past-participial form been.
In has been waiting, progressive be follows perfect have and takes a gerund-participle.
In is being repaired, passive be follows progressive be and selects a past participle. The form being is selected by the progressive.

projection.target: Each auxiliary determines the immediately following form. The components normally retain the modal–perfect–progressive–passive order even when intermediate components are omitted.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Helper verbs in a fixed order
curious.summary: When several helper verbs come before a main verb, each shapes the next, and they keep a set order.
curious.body: In It might have been being repaired, four helper-style words come before the main verb: might, have, been and being. Each one decides the form of the word right after it. After have comes been, and after the progressive be comes being. The helpers keep a fixed order: first a modal like might, then perfect have, then progressive be, then passive be. Some can be left out, but the ones that remain keep that order.
curious.try: Build a sentence with just two helpers, such as may have waited. Then try adding a third helper in the same order.

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, the chain of auxiliaries and the verb form each one selects.
teacher.explain: The auxiliary chain is a VP in which up to four components appear in a fixed order: a modal, perfect have with a past participle, progressive be with a gerund-participle, and passive be with a past participle. Each auxiliary determines the form immediately following it. In may have been waiting, perfect have follows the modal and selects been. In has been waiting, progressive be follows perfect have and takes a gerund-participle. In is being repaired, passive be follows progressive be, and the progressive selects the form being. The order is kept when intermediate components are omitted.
teacher.terms: This dictionary’s four components are modal, perfect have, progressive be and passive be. Gerund-participle is the -ing form.
watch_for: A learner might expect each auxiliary to take the same verb form, when each selects the form that follows it.
A learner might think being and been are the same, when the perfect selects the past participle and the progressive selects the gerund-participle.
teacher.activity: Give students word cards (might, have, been, being, repaired). They arrange them into the longest acceptable chain, then drop one auxiliary and check that the order still holds.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Ordered Auxiliary Chain." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/auxiliary-chain-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Auxiliary-Stranding VP Ellipsis

1.definition: Recovers a predicate from the preceding discourse while pronouncing the auxiliary.

examples.form: Nora could repair it, and [Kai could too].

examples.note: Constructed comparison. The antecedent is positive and has a lexical preterite. The ellipsis host supplies negative do.

relatedConstructions.notes: Gapping leaves contrastive material on both sides of the omitted sequence.
In Jo has, too, an auxiliary remains before an unexpressed VP. In Jo tried to, the infinitival marker remains before an unexpressed predicate.
I don’t know who retains a wh-remnant and leaves the rest of the question unexpressed. Jo can retains the auxiliary before an unexpressed VP.

projection.target: The stranded auxiliary can differ in tense or polarity from the antecedent, as in Nora repaired it, but Kai didn't. A lexical verb does not freely strand in the same pattern.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Leaving out the rest after a helper verb
curious.summary: After a helper verb, the rest of the predicate can be left unsaid because we can recover it from earlier.
curious.body: In Nora could repair it, and Kai could too, the second part says only Kai could too. We understand it to mean Kai could repair it, because the earlier part tells us what the missing part is. The helper verb that remains doesn't have to match what came before. In Nora repaired it, but Kai didn't, the first part is positive and in the past, while the second supplies a negative did. A main verb doesn't freely get left alone like this.

examples.text: Nora could repair it, and [Kai could too].

curious.try: Say Nora could repair it. Then add and Kai could too. What is left unsaid after could in the second part?

teacher.summary: Teaches how a pronounced auxiliary can be followed by an unexpressed predicate recovered from the preceding discourse.
teacher.explain: In this pattern a clause has a subject and a finite auxiliary, with the complement left unexpressed and recovered from the preceding discourse. The auxiliary is pronounced. It can differ in tense or polarity from the antecedent: Nora repaired it, but Kai didn't has a positive antecedent with a lexical preterite, and the ellipsis host supplies negative do. A lexical verb does not freely strand in the same pattern. This dictionary relates it to gapping, to stranding of infinitival to (Jo tried to) and to sluicing.
teacher.terms: This pattern is called VP ellipsis. This dictionary names it auxiliary-stranding VP ellipsis.

examples.text: Nora could repair it, and [Kai could too].

contrasts.text: Nora could repair it, and Kai could too.
contrasts.note: The stranded auxiliary matches its antecedent.

contrasts.text: Nora repaired it, but Kai didn't.
contrasts.note: Positive antecedent with a lexical preterite; the host supplies negative do.

watch_for: A learner might expect the second clause to repeat the form of the verb in the first, when the stranded auxiliary can differ in tense or polarity.
A learner might try to leave a main verb stranded in the same way, when a lexical verb does not freely strand.
teacher.activity: Give pairs short sentences with a verb phrase. They write a second clause with a different subject and only the auxiliary, then say what has been left out.

child.hook: In "Kai could too", what is Kai able to do?
child.explain: You don't have to say the whole thing again. Nora could repair it, and Kai could too. We know Kai could repair it, because Nora's part told us.

examples.text: Nora could repair it, and [Kai could too].
Mia can swim, and [Ben can too].

child.play: Say something you can do, like skip. Your partner says and I can too. Then say what the second part left out.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the second part stops after could (the entry's example has too); try question and teacher summary now say the auxiliary is pronounced and the predicate after it is unexpressed and recovered, not 'stood for'; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Auxiliary-Stranding VP Ellipsis." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/auxiliary-vp-ellipsis-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Past Perfect Anteriority
pattern: Clause[preterite had + past-participial VP] with a past temporal anchor

entry.name: Past Perfect Anteriority
entry.pattern: Clause[preterite had + past-participial VP] with a past temporal anchor

1.definition: Places the event or state before a distinct past reference point.

examples.form: When I arrived, Jo [had already left].

projection.target: The departure precedes the arrival on the ordinary reading. The reference point can be supplied by the surrounding narrative without a separate time adjunct.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Had plus a verb for what came earlier
curious.summary: Had with a past-participle verb puts an event before another moment in the past.
curious.body: In When I arrived, Jo had already left, the leaving comes before the arrival on the ordinary reading. Had plus left puts the departure earlier than the past moment we're already talking about. The past moment we're looking back from doesn't have to be named by a phrase like when I arrived. The surrounding story can supply it, so no separate time phrase is needed.

examples.text: When I arrived, Jo [had already left].
By noon, she [had finished] her homework.

curious.try: Say When I arrived, Jo had already left. Which happened first, the arriving or the leaving?

teacher.summary: Shows how the past perfect places an event before a distinct past reference point.
teacher.explain: The past perfect is a clause with preterite had plus a past-participial VP and a past temporal anchor. It places the event or state before a distinct past reference point. In When I arrived, Jo had already left, the departure precedes the arrival on the ordinary reading. The reference point can be supplied by the surrounding narrative without a separate time adjunct. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of perfect have and relates it to the backshift of present forms. It is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the past perfect. This dictionary describes it as preterite had plus a past participle.

examples.text: When I arrived, Jo [had already left].

contrasts.text: When I arrived, Jo had already left.
contrasts.note: The departure comes before the arrival.

watch_for: A learner might read had left as simply past, when it places the leaving before another past point.
A learner might think a time phrase is required, when the narrative can supply the reference point.
teacher.activity: Students put two past events in a timeline, then write a sentence in which the earlier event uses had plus a participle and the later one uses the simple past.

child.hook: Which happened first, Jo leaving or the speaker arriving?
child.explain: When I arrived, Jo had already left. Here, Jo's leaving came first. Had plus a verb like left tells us that something happened earlier than another past moment.

examples.text: When I arrived, Jo [had already left].
By noon, she [had finished] her homework.

child.play: Draw a timeline with two past events. Say which came first, using had for the earlier one. Swap with a partner.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the earlier event is the one named by 'when I arrived' (that phrase names the later reference point); child hook now compares the leaving with the arriving; added 'on the ordinary reading' hedge; 'usual textbook name' changed to 'sometimes called'. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Past Perfect Anteriority." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/backshift-past-perfect-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Institutional Bare Singular
pattern: bare singular institutional noun in a licensed frame

entry.name: Institutional Bare Singular
entry.pattern: bare singular institutional noun in a licensed frame

1.definition: Refers to participation in an institutional activity or status.

relatedConstructions.notes: Went to school and took the bus both evoke an institutional activity. School is bare in the first frame, and bus keeps the in the second.

grounds.locator: Ch. 5 §8.5; Ch. 7, bare NPs after prepositions

projection.target: At school can describe the relevant institutional setting without selecting a particular building in the same way as at the school. Licensing depends on noun, context and variety.
