projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: At school, with no the
curious.summary: Some everyday nouns, such as school, can appear with no article when they refer to an activity or status.
curious.body: In The children are at school, the word school has no the or a before it. It can describe school as a setting for an activity, without picking out one particular building in the same way as at the school. At the school can instead point to a particular building. Not every noun works this way, and whether it does depends on the noun, the context and the variety of English. Went to school keeps school bare, while took the bus keeps the.
curious.try: Say The children are at school, then The children are at the school. Which one sounds like it's about a building?

teacher.summary: Explains institutional nouns like school that can be bare when they name an activity, not a particular place.
teacher.explain: A bare singular institutional noun can appear in a licensed frame and refer to participation in an institutional activity or status. At school can describe the relevant institutional setting without selecting a particular building in the same way as at the school. Licensing depends on the noun, the context and the variety. This dictionary relates it to the activity weak definite: went to school and took the bus both evoke an institutional activity, but school is bare in the first frame and bus keeps the in the second. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the bare NP and marks it provisional.
teacher.terms: Zero article is another way of describing the missing article. This dictionary calls this an institutional bare singular.

contrasts.note: The institutional setting.

contrasts.text: The children are at the school.
contrasts.note: Not selecting the setting in the same way; this can pick out a building.

watch_for: A learner might add the before school in at school, when the bare form names the institutional setting.
A learner might assume the same bare pattern works with every noun, when licensing depends on noun, context and variety.
teacher.activity: Give students nouns such as school, bus, church and hospital in frames with and without the. They discuss which frames express an activity and which a particular place, then compare with a dictionary or the teacher.

child.hook: What's the difference between "at school" and "at the school"?
child.explain: At school can be about taking part in school. At the school can point to the building. Some words let us leave out the, and some don't.
child.play: Say a sentence with at school, then one with at the school. Ask a partner which one talks about the building.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says at school means being a pupil (the dictionary speaks of institutional activity or status and a setting not tied to a particular building); softened the same gloss in curious.body; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary' in teacher text.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Institutional Bare Singular." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/bare-institutional-use-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Bare Singular Noun Coordination
pattern: Coordination[bare singular count form + and + bare singular count form]

entry.name: Bare Singular Noun Coordination
entry.pattern: Coordination[bare singular count form + and + bare singular count form]

1.definition: Presents two linked individuals or roles through one bare coordinate phrase.
1.details: The context may make the pair identifiable or introduce its members as new. In the invitation example, the preceding text introduces the bride and her dog, which lets the coordination refer to their depictions. The pairing can support an argument use whose individual bare nouns would require separate licensing.

examples.note: CGEL illustrates the pairing inside a PP.
Attested subject. The bride and dog are already salient from the description of the invitation.
Attested object introducing the two items.

relatedConstructions.notes: The pair has coordinate structure.
A separate construction licenses bare referential names, including some common-noun forms.

projection.target: Context can license the whole coordination as an argument, with a recoverable relationship between the individuals and either a familiar or a new pair.
projection.evidence: Le Bruyn and de Swart document both interpretations and the role of contextual links, extending the pattern beyond familiar collocations.

curious.title: Two bare nouns joined by and
curious.summary: Two singular nouns with no article can be joined by and to name a pair, as in husband and wife.
curious.body: In between husband and wife, neither noun has a the or a before it, yet together they name a pair. The same happens in He had pad and pencil, where the two items are introduced as new. Context can make the pair work as the subject or object of a sentence. In Bride and dog can be customized!, the bride and the dog were already described earlier, so the pair is easy to identify. The pair can be a familiar one or a new one, as long as the link between the two is recoverable.
curious.try: Think of a pair like pen and paper. Where can you use it with no article?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, bare singular count nouns coordinated into a pair that can serve as an argument.
teacher.explain: The pattern coordinates two bare singular count forms with and, presenting two linked individuals or roles through one phrase. Context may make the pair identifiable or introduce its members as new. In the invitation example, the preceding text introduces the bride and her dog, so the coordination can refer to their depictions. The pairing can support an argument use whose individual bare nouns would require separate licensing. This dictionary treats the pattern as a coordinate structure and marks it provisional. It relates it to a separate construction that licenses bare referential names.
teacher.terms: Bare here means without an article or other determiner. This dictionary calls the pattern bare singular noun coordination.

contrasts.note: Attested object introducing the two items.

contrasts.text: Bride and dog can be customized!
contrasts.note: Attested subject; the items are already salient.

watch_for: A learner might assume each noun in pad and pencil needs its own article, when the pair as a whole can work as an argument in context.
A learner might think the pair has to be already familiar, when this dictionary notes it can also introduce its members as new.
teacher.activity: Students collect attested pairs of bare nouns from texts. For each, they say whether the context made the pair familiar or introduced it as new.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Bare Singular Noun Coordination." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/bare-noun-coordination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Bare Role Construction
pattern: NP[Det:absent + Nom[Head:singular count role noun]], in a licensed role slot

entry.name: Bare Role Construction
entry.pattern: NP[Det:absent + Nom[Head:singular count role noun]], in a licensed role slot

dimensions.form: A singular count nominal, optionally modified, with no determiner
dimensions.meaning: Presents an office, assignment, or role that can be held or taken on
dimensions.function: Subject- or object-oriented predicative, complement of a preposition in a licensed frame, or ascriptive supplement
dimensions.distribution: Available in particular role-denoting senses and constructions. Ordinary referential subject and object positions generally require a determiner with the same singular count noun.

1.definition: Ascribes an office or institutional role, or gives the content of an office expression.
1.details: The same nominal can follow be, become, remain, appoint, or elect when the verb licenses a predicative complement. It can also occur with as and in role of or position of, in a matrix-licensed except phrase, or as an ascriptive supplement. In an appointment construction the direct object identifies the appointee and the bare NP gives the office.

examples.form: They appointed Lee [treasurer of the club].
examples.note: Constructed object-oriented predicative. In They questioned the treasurer of the club, the article-marked NP instead identifies the person questioned.
Constructed prepositional frame. Compare Lee applied for the position [of treasurer]. Both retain a bare role nominal.

examples.form: Faatulu was named [co-captain] along with fellow junior Jamie Peck.
examples.note: The sports report explicitly names two holders of the role.

grounds.locator: Paragraph beginning As one of the few upperclassmen

examples.note: Constructed after CGEL’s comparison. Lee is the secretary of the club can also specify the incumbent in answer to Who is the secretary?
The except phrase picks out a role from the alternatives made available by the matrix clause.

examples.form: Wilson, [Secretary to the Cabinet], had informed the Prime Minister immediately.
examples.note: Ascriptive supplement. The bare NP cannot replace Wilson as the referential subject.

2.definition: Ascribes a professional assignment construed as a post.
2.details: A workplace can make a particular assignment available for the construction. The availability of a bare form is sensitive to lexical choice and how a job title is used in the institution.

examples.form: They appointed Lee [lead counsel] for the appeal.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. In ordinary standard usage, became lawyer is degraded on the professional-class reading.

3.definition: Ascribes a relational or ceremonial role in a licensed frame.
3.details: A following relational dependent can specify whom the role is held in relation to. This use is limited to independently available role expressions. It is distinct from using a kin term as a form of address or as a standing name. Holding a kin role doesn't confer the kin term as a designation: Schneider and Homans report that when a child is reared from infancy by an aunt playing a maternal role, she “is still not called ‘mother’” (1955: 1203).

examples.form: They asked Lee to be [godfather to their son].
examples.note: Constructed relational example. The to-phrase supplies the other participant.

examples.form: There can likewise be only one person who is [father of the student I have in mind].
examples.note: CGEL’s own prose, discussing the identifiability of the father of the student; the sentence's opening In [2ii] is omitted. A kin noun heads the bare predicative, and of the student gives the relatum.

Constructed. A single kin noun, with the to-phrase giving the relatum. Kin nouns under this meaning are an adjudication (Brett, 2026-11-19): CGEL lists kin or similar relations separately from offices or roles (Ch. 4 §5.5.1(e)).

constraints.description: A bare role NP can describe the subject or object. It does not ordinarily occupy the subject or object position as a referential expression for the roleholder.
The choice of noun and context must support a role reading. Predicative function alone does not license removal of the article from become a miser or become a teacher.

The role can have multiple holders. A counterpart with an overt determiner can also ascribe a role, as in became a co-captain or remained our captain. With be, a counterpart with the can additionally identify the contextually relevant incumbent.

relatedConstructions.notes: This is one use of a determinerless NP headed by a nominal.
A bare role NP can ascribe a post to the subject.
In the appointment frame the predicand is realized as object.
A bare role NP can be the predicative complement of as or a complement of selected of or except.
Compare became co-captain and became a co-captain. Both can ascribe the same post.
Compare remained captain and remained our captain. The determiner adds a relation to the speaker’s group. With be, the captain can also give a specifying reading.
Compare Lee is secretary of the club and Lee is the secretary of the club. The latter can answer Who is the secretary?
Wilson, Secretary to the Cabinet shares the supplement packaging. Its bare supplement cannot replace Wilson as subject, which is CGEL’s diagnostic against apposition here.
Both license bare singular count NPs. Compare remained treasurer with went to school. The licensed slots and interpretations differ.
Role nouns can also occur bare as paired endpoints, as in from teacher to pupil. The pairing licenses a source–goal interpretation.
Compare Chair, may I respond? with Lee remained chair. The role noun serves as a form of address in the first example and a predicative in the second.

Both are determinerless singular NPs whose definite interpretation is relative to a domain, an organisation for treasurer and a household for Mom. Function distinguishes them: a bare role NP is predicative or in a licensed frame (Lee remained treasurer), while a strong proper name is a referential argument (Mom called; compare CGEL’s ∗I’m told treasurer strongly supports this proposal, p. 409). Inserting the keeps the ascription in Henry became the treasurer (p. 409) but loses the name in The mom called (constructed). A role form used as a standing name independently licenses referential argument uses.

grounds.locator: Ch. 4 §5.1 [5]; Ch. 5 §8.5 [19], p. 409; Ch. 7, pp. 637–638, predicative complements of as; Ch. 15 §5, [22ii]
grounds.note: Documents verbal, prepositional, and ascriptive supplementary uses and contrasts referential object uses.

grounds.locator: Ch. 4 §5.5.1(e), contrast with secretary of the bushwalking club; Ch. 5 §8.5 [19], p. 409
grounds.note: The role ascription and the identifying interpretation differ. Chapter 5 gives the stronger replacement claim.
Kin nouns in relational predicatives (father of the student) are instances of meaning 3; kin terms used as names (Dad called) are not, and belong to strong-proper-name-001.
An aunt who raises a child in a maternal role isn't thereby called mother: the role and the designation come apart.

known_boundary_items: Dad called, but Sam answered (constructed). Dad identifies a person as subject when the family uses it as a name: an instance of strong-proper-name-001, not of this construction.

Captain called, said of Lee, a former captain the team still calls Captain, while Sam holds the post (constructed). Captain identifies Lee, the captain identifies Sam, and Lee is captain is false: the designation outlasts the tenure, so the referential use belongs to strong-proper-name-001, not to this construction.

projection.target: In ordinary standard English, with a reading that ascribes an assignment or gives its content, a nominal such as treasurer can remain bare in She stayed treasurer, They appointed her treasurer, and As treasurer, she signed. Reuse as a stand-alone referential object, as in They questioned the treasurer, normally calls for a determiner. The same bare office ascription can apply to more than one holder.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares the same noun in predicative and object positions and documents the prepositional and supplementary uses. The Arizona State report documents shared tenure. Whether a counterpart with the preserves the bare reading depends on the frame and context.

curious.title: Jobs and roles without "the" or "a"
curious.summary: Words like treasurer or captain can describe the role someone holds without a word like the or a in front.
curious.body: Normally a word like treasurer needs company: we say the treasurer or a treasurer. But in some sentences it stands alone. They appointed Lee treasurer. Lee served as treasurer. Here the word doesn't point to a particular person. It says what role Lee has. Compare They questioned the treasurer. That sentence is about a person, so it normally needs the. The bare version works where a role is being given or described. The role can also have more than one holder, as when two people are named co-captain.

examples.text: They appointed Lee [treasurer of the club].
Faatulu was named [co-captain] along with fellow junior Jamie Peck.

curious.try: Say "They appointed her treasurer" and "They questioned the treasurer." In which sentence does treasurer name a role, and in which does it point at a person?

teacher.summary: Explains why role nouns such as secretary can lack a determiner in predicative and some prepositional frames.
teacher.explain: A singular count noun that names an office or post can appear with no determiner when the sentence ascribes the role to someone: after be, become, remain, appoint or elect, after as, after role of or position of, in an except phrase licensed by the main clause, or as an ascriptive supplement (Wilson, Secretary to the Cabinet, ...). The bare NP describes the subject or object. It doesn't normally stand as a referential subject or object for the role-holder, where a determiner is needed (They questioned the treasurer). The noun and context must support a role reading: the article stays in become a teacher. A version with the or a can also ascribe a role (became a co-captain), and with be, the secretary of the club can identify the current holder, answering Who is the secretary?
teacher.terms: Predicative complement: an NP such as treasurer in She stayed treasurer or They appointed her treasurer, which describes the subject or object. This dictionary treats this as a licensed use of a determinerless NP.

examples.text: They appointed Lee [treasurer of the club].
Wilson, [Secretary to the Cabinet], had informed the Prime Minister immediately.

contrasts.text: Lee is secretary of the club.
contrasts.note: Ascribes the role to Lee.

contrasts.text: Lee is the secretary of the club.
contrasts.note: Can also answer Who is the secretary?

contrasts.text: I'm told treasurer strongly supports this proposal.
contrasts.note: A bare role noun doesn't work as a referential subject here.

watch_for: A learner might assume any job noun can go without an article after become, when the choice depends on the noun and how the job title is used.
A learner might use a bare role noun as the subject for a particular person, as in I'm told treasurer strongly supports this proposal.
teacher.activity: Give students two columns of frames (appointed Lee ___, they questioned ___, served as ___, I spoke to ___). Students fill each with secretary or the secretary and explain which frames ascribe a role and which identify a person.

name: Verbal be-Passive
pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + Head:VP[be + VP[past participle, complementᵢ externalized, optional internalized by-PP]]]

entry.name: Verbal be-Passive
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:NPᵢ + Head:VP[be + VP[past participle, complementᵢ externalized, optional internalized by-PP]]]

1.definition: Realigns the verb’s arguments so an internal complement of the active can appear as subject.
1.details: In my surfboard was stolen by Pat, the active object becomes subject, and a by-phrase realizes the participant that would be active subject. The short form usually leaves that participant unexpressed. The by-phrase can supply an experiencer when the active subject is an experiencer. The externalized complement can also come from a preposition, as in the paper was referred to. The participial VP may have complements and verbal modifications. This entry covers the auxiliary be construction.

examples.note: Long passive with the active subject expressed as the complement of by.

examples.form: [Her paper is referred to by everyone.]
examples.note: The active would express the paper as object of to.

relatedConstructions.notes: The be-passive is a voice construction available in headed clauses.
Both use a past participle, with different auxiliary selection and argument syntax.

grounds.note: Documents long and short passives and the complement correspondence.
Records auxiliary be followed by a past-participial form.

projection.target: A verbal be-passive lacks a complement present in the corresponding active VP. The missing complement can correspond to the passive subject, and a by-phrase can realize the active subject independently of its semantic role.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s active/passive comparisons include direct objects, indirect objects, prepositional objects and non-agent subjects. CASA records the auxiliary and participle pairing.

curious.title: Putting the receiver first
curious.summary: In a passive sentence, the object of the matching active sentence becomes the subject, and the active sentence's subject can come later after by or be left out.
curious.body: In My surfboard was stolen by Pat, the surfboard comes first, though it's what Pat stole. The person who acted appears after by. In My surfboard was stolen, the doer is simply left out. The first thing can come from other places too. In Her paper is referred to by everyone, the paper is what everyone refers to, and the active version has it after the word to. This dictionary covers the passives made with the helper verb be, followed by a word like stolen.

examples.text: [Her paper is referred to by everyone.]

curious.try: Take an active sentence like Pat stole my surfboard and turn it around. What happens to Pat?

teacher.summary: Explains the be-passive as a way of realigning a verb's arguments so an active complement becomes the subject.
teacher.explain: In the verbal be-passive, an internal complement of the active verb appears as the subject, and the participial VP lacks that complement. A by-phrase can realize the participant that would be the active subject, and the short passive usually leaves that participant unexpressed. The externalized complement can be a direct object, an indirect object, or the object of a preposition, as in the paper was referred to. The by-phrase can supply an experiencer when the active subject is an experiencer. The participial VP may have complements and verbal modifications. Only the construction with auxiliary be is covered here.
teacher.terms: Long passive has a by-phrase, and short passive has none. Such clauses are sometimes said to be in the passive voice; this dictionary calls the version with be the verbal be-passive.

examples.text: [Her paper is referred to by everyone.]

contrasts.note: The active version.

contrasts.text: My surfboard was stolen by Pat.
contrasts.note: Long passive; the active subject is the complement of by.
Short passive.

watch_for: A learner might think the by-phrase is required, when a short passive can leave that participant out.
A learner might expect only a direct object to become the subject, when a prepositional object can too (Her paper is referred to).
teacher.activity: Students turn active sentences into long passives and then short passives. They say which participant becomes the subject and where the original subject went.

child.hook: In "My surfboard was stolen", who is missing from the sentence?
child.explain: You can start a sentence with the thing something happened to. My surfboard was stolen by Pat. If we don't need to say who did it, we can leave out by Pat.
child.play: Make up a sentence like Pat stole my surfboard. Turn it around so the thing comes first. Then try it without the doer.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms dropped the frequency claim 'the usual textbook term' and now says such clauses are sometimes said to be in the passive voice, with the be version being this dictionary's verbal be-passive (passive voice is a widely used term and CGEL's own heading for this topic, Ch. 16 section 10, the entry's cited source; it is broader than the be-passive, so it is not offered as a synonym). Also fixed (unflagged): teacher 'The entry covers' changed to 'Only the construction with auxiliary be is covered here'. Dismissed: none. After a Codex recheck: the curious summary now says the active object becomes the subject and the active subject can follow by (it had said the thing something happens to comes first, and called that participant the doer); teacher texts now hedge the short passive as the entry does.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Verbal be-Passive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/be-passive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Correlative both … and

1.definition: Explicitly presents the first two coordinates as jointly included.

examples.form: We need [both a permit and an inspection].

projection.target: Both signals the first coordinate and and marks the second. Both alone can be an NP quantifier, a use with a different structural relation to the following material.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Both a and b
curious.summary: Both before the first item and and before the second say outright that two things are included.
curious.body: In We need both a permit and an inspection, both comes before the first item and and comes before the second. Together they show clearly that we need the permit and the inspection. Both marks the first item, and and marks the second. Both can also appear alone before a noun phrase, but that's a different use, with a different relation to the words that follow.

examples.text: We need [both a permit and an inspection].

curious.try: Say We need a permit and an inspection. Then add both. What does both add?

teacher.summary: Shows both and and as paired markers on two coordinates.
teacher.explain: The pattern is coordination of two items with both before the first and and before the second. It explicitly presents the first two coordinates as jointly included. Both signals the first coordinate and and marks the second. Both on its own can be an NP quantifier, which has a different structural relation to the following material. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of coordination and relates it to either ... or. It is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Both and and form a correlative pair, as this dictionary’s name says.

examples.text: We need [both a permit and an inspection].

contrasts.text: We need both a permit and an inspection.
contrasts.note: Both marks the first coordinate and and marks the second.

contrasts.text: We need a permit and an inspection.
contrasts.note: Without both, the joint inclusion is not marked explicitly.

watch_for: A learner might read both as the same word in both of them and both a permit and an inspection, when the two uses have different structural relations.
A learner might leave out the second marker and, when both signals the first coordinate and and marks the second.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences starting We need both ... and ... with two items of their own. They then compare with the same sentence without both.

child.hook: What does "both" tell us in "both a permit and an inspection"?
child.explain: Both and and work together. Both comes first and and comes before the second thing. They tell us that we need the two things.

examples.text: We need [both a permit and an inspection].

child.play: Say what you like using both and and, like both apples and pears. Take turns with a partner and name two things each time.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Correlative both … and." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/both-and-coordination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Bare Deictic Calendar NP
pattern: NP[this/last/next + calendar noun or weekday] in temporal adjunct use

entry.name: Bare Deictic Calendar NP
entry.pattern: NP[this/last/next + calendar noun or weekday] in temporal adjunct use

1.definition: Uses the contextual present to select an adjacent or current calendar period.

projection.target: The NP can be a time adjunct without on. The relevant Tuesday is selected by the deictic expression, with some variation in how speakers resolve next.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Next Tuesday, with no on
curious.summary: Words like this, last and next before a day or calendar period say when something happens, measured from now.
curious.body: In I'll call next Tuesday, the phrase next Tuesday tells us when, and it needs no on in front. The word next picks out a Tuesday by counting from the present moment. This, last and next work this way. Which Tuesday counts as next can vary between speakers, since it depends on how next is resolved. The context of the present is what fixes the period.
curious.try: Say I'll call next Tuesday. Which Tuesday do you mean? Ask a friend which one they would pick.

teacher.summary: Shows how this, last and next with a weekday or calendar noun give a time adjunct without on.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an NP made of this, last or next and a calendar noun or weekday, used as a temporal adjunct. It uses the contextual present to select an adjacent or current calendar period. The NP can be a time adjunct without on. The relevant Tuesday is selected by the deictic expression, and this dictionary notes some variation in how speakers resolve next. This dictionary relates it to month-and-day dates and to year names, and treats the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls the pattern a bare deictic calendar NP, where the time is picked out by the context of the present.

contrasts.note: A deictic NP used as a time adjunct, without on.
A plain weekday with on.

watch_for: A learner might add on before next Tuesday, when the NP can be a time adjunct without on.
A learner might assume next Tuesday picks out the same day for every speaker, when speakers resolve next with some variation.
teacher.activity: Fix a date on the board. Students say which day they take next Friday and last Monday to be from that date, and compare their choices.

child.hook: Does "next Tuesday" mean the same day for everyone?
child.explain: Words like this, last and next can go right before a day. I'll call next Tuesday. We don't need on. Which Tuesday next means can change from person to person.
child.play: Look at a calendar and find today. Say which day you think next Friday is. Ask a partner if they agree.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher 'terms' no longer defines deixis as anchoring to the moment of speaking (the entry gives no such definition) and now restates the entry's wording; child game now says to look at a calendar and find today. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary' in teacher text.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Bare Deictic Calendar NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/calendar-deictic-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Cardinal Determinative

dimensions.form: Basic (0-99) or magnitude determinative; no number inflection
dimensions.meaning: Supplies a cardinal value. Interpretation as an exact total or as a lower boundary depends on context.
dimensions.function: Heads DPs functioning as determiners, factors, or fused heads
dimensions.distribution: Determiner in NP; factor in magnitude phrases; fused determiner-head

1.definition: Cardinal numerative that can determine a nominal by giving a numerical value

examples.form: The building has [one thousand twenty-four] rooms.

constraints.description: Functions as determiner in NP structure; can appear as fused head (e.g., "I bought three").

projection.target: A cardinal determiner in thirty copies can alternate with some copies. In two hundred, two is internal to the numerative and can coexist with an external determiner in a two hundred, on the token reading.
projection.evidence: Reynolds uses coexistence with an external determiner to distinguish determiner function from multiplicative modification.

curious.title: Number words before nouns
curious.summary: A number word such as three or twenty-six can come before a noun and say how many there are.
curious.body: In I saw three cats, the word three tells us how many cats. Longer numbers work the same way: twenty-six students, or one thousand twenty-four rooms. The number comes at the front of the noun phrase and supplies a value. A number word can also stand in for the whole noun phrase when the noun is understood, as in I bought three. And whether a number means exactly that many or at least that many depends on the context.

examples.text: The building has [one thousand twenty-four] rooms.

curious.try: Say I bought three and then I bought three cats. Is the number doing the same job in both?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining that a cardinal word can serve as a determiner in a noun phrase, and that the same word can also stand alone for the whole noun phrase.
teacher.explain: Cardinal words such as three, twenty-six and one thousand twenty-four are determinatives (a word category) that serve as determiners (a function) in a noun phrase. They supply a numerical value and have no number inflection. A cardinal can also be a fused determiner-head, standing for the whole noun phrase, as in I bought three. In two hundred, the first word is a factor in the magnitude phrase rather than a determiner of the noun. Whether a cardinal gives an exact total or a lower boundary depends on context.
teacher.terms: Cardinal number or numeral: the traditional names. This dictionary says cardinal determinative for the word and determiner for the function. Numerative is the dictionary's own word for number words and phrases.

examples.text: The building has [one thousand twenty-four] rooms.

contrasts.note: Three is a determiner in the noun phrase three cats.
Three stands alone as fused determiner-head.

watch_for: A learner might take three to mean exactly three cats in every context, when context decides between an exact total and a lower boundary.
A learner might treat three in I bought three as a different kind of word from three in three cats.
A learner might expect a number word that determines a noun to take a plural ending, though cardinal determinatives have no number inflection.
teacher.activity: Give students short texts with number words. They underline each number and mark whether a noun follows it (three cats) or whether it stands alone (I bought three).

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.summary no longer says a number word before a noun is always a determiner (the entry distinguishes factors such as two in two hundred).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Cardinal Determinative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/cardinal-determinative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Cardinal Noun

dimensions.form: Cardinal numerative in noun category; may be proper or common
dimensions.meaning: Denotes number entities, quantities, labels, or numerical tokens
dimensions.function: Heads NPs in various uses (naming, quantifying, labelling)
dimensions.distribution: Subject, object, complement; proper uses are bare, common uses take determiners

1.definition: Cardinal numerative used as a noun to denote a number entity or quantity concept

constraints.description: Denotes a number entity or quantity concept, not a determiner function.
Proper-noun uses head bare NPs; common-noun uses take determiners and plural.

relatedConstructions.notes: Cardinal determinatives vs cardinal nouns

projection.target: A quantifying or token use can take number inflection and another determiner, as in two tens. The naming use ten in Ten is even and the determinative use in ten cards lack that count-noun environment.
projection.evidence: Reynolds separates cardinal nouns used to name, count, or label from syntactic determiner function.

curious.title: Number words that act as nouns
curious.summary: A number word can name a number, label one thing or stand for a quantity, behaving like an ordinary noun.
curious.body: A number word can come before a noun, as in ten cards. But it can also be a noun in its own right. In Ten is even, ten names a number and doesn't count anything. In Room 101, the number labels one particular room. Other uses count or measure. You can say a ten, and in hundreds of people the number gives a large quantity. In these uses the number word can take a plural ending and another word before it, as in two tens. The naming use and the use before a noun, as in ten cards, don't work that way.
curious.try: Compare I have ten cards with I have two tens. In which one can you put a word like two in front of the number?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why a number word sometimes behaves like a noun, with its own plural and determiner, and sometimes doesn't.
teacher.explain: A cardinal noun is a number word used as a noun. Proper-noun uses head bare noun phrases: Ten is even (the number itself) and Room 101 (a numerical label). Common-noun uses take determiners and plural forms: a ten, two tens, hundreds of people. They denote number entities, quantities, labels or numerical tokens, and they are not determiners. Contrast ten cards, where ten is a determinative and the noun is cards.
teacher.terms: Cardinal number or numeral: the traditional names. This dictionary separates the cardinal determinative (ten cards) from the cardinal noun (Ten is even, two tens).

contrasts.note: Determinative use. Ten determines the noun cards.
Common-noun use. Tens is a plural noun with its own determiner.

watch_for: A learner might read Room 101 as one hundred and one rooms.
A learner might think ten in Ten is even is counting something, when it names the number.
A learner might expect ten cards to take a determiner before ten and a plural ending, as two tens does.
teacher.activity: Give students cards with ten cards, two tens, Ten is even and Room 101. They sort them into "number before a noun" and "number used as a noun", then say how they decided.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Cardinal Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/cardinal-noun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Causative have with a Bare Infinitival

1.definition: Presents an event as arranged, instructed or brought about by the subject.

relatedConstructions.notes: Had Kai replace the roof makes Kai the understood replacer. Had the roof replaced presents the roof as affected and can describe an arrangement. Had his phone stolen can describe an unwanted experience.

projection.target: Jo undertakes the checking. Have Jo check contrasts with perfect have checked and with affected have the figures checked.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Having someone do something
curious.summary: In a sentence like I'll have Jo check the figures, the speaker arranges for someone else to do the checking.
curious.body: In I'll have Jo check the figures, the subject arranges, instructs or brings about an event. Jo is the one who does the checking, and the verb after Jo is in its plain form, check, with no to. In Had Kai replace the roof, Kai is likewise the understood replacer. A nearby pattern looks similar but works differently. In Had the roof replaced, the roof is what is affected, and the sentence can describe an arrangement. Had his phone stolen can describe an unwanted experience instead.
curious.try: Say I'll have Jo check the figures. Who does the checking, you or Jo?

teacher.summary: Helps separate causative have from perfect have and from the affected-object pattern (had the roof replaced).
teacher.explain: In causative have, the subject presents an event as arranged, instructed or brought about, and the noun phrase after have (Jo) is the one who carries it out, followed by a bare infinitival (the infinitive without to). I'll have Jo check the figures: Jo undertakes the checking. Compare perfect have (Jo has checked the figures), where have is an auxiliary, and affected have (have the figures checked), where the object is what is affected and no one is named as the doer.
teacher.terms: Bare infinitival: an infinitival with no to; in this pattern it is check the figures. Perfect have is the auxiliary in has checked. Affected have is the pattern in had the roof replaced.

contrasts.text: I'll have Jo check the figures.
contrasts.note: Causative have. Jo is the one who checks.
Perfect have. Has is an auxiliary.
Affected have. The figures are what is affected.

watch_for: A learner might read have in have Jo check as perfect have.
A learner might take Jo to be the thing affected, when Jo is the understood checker.
A learner might expect to before check, though the pattern has a bare infinitival.
teacher.activity: Write sentences on strips using have Jo check, have the figures checked and has checked. Students sort them by whether someone is arranged to act, something is affected, or it is the perfect have in has checked.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms now gives the bare infinitival as check the figures, not the plain verb form alone; teacher.activity no longer defines perfect have as completion. Also fixed: teacher.explain tied to Jo as in the entry's example. Second round: fixed the perfect-have contrast note by cutting 'nothing is arranged' (this dictionary doesn't rule out an arrangement behind Jo has checked the figures); also fixed (unflagged) curious.body, which presented Had Kai replace the roof as a different pattern though this dictionary's note gives it as causative have with Kai as the understood replacer. Dismissed: the two flags on calling perfect have an auxiliary (CGEL's standard classification, which this dictionary presupposes in contrasting perfect have with causative have).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Causative have with a Bare Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/causative-have-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Causative and Inchoative Alternation
pattern: alternation[Subject + V + affected NP ↔ affected NP + V]

entry.name: Causative and Inchoative Alternation
entry.pattern: alternation[Subject + V + affected NP ↔ affected NP + V]

1.definition: Expresses a change either with an external causer as subject or with the changing participant as subject.

examples.form: The heat cracked the window, and [the window cracked].

relatedConstructions.notes: The causative member uses the changing participant as direct object.
The inchoative member uses it as subject.

projection.target: The affected participant has object function in the causative and subject function in the inchoative. The inchoative does not require a separate external causer argument.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A change with a cause, and without one
curious.summary: Some verbs can say who or what caused a change, or can simply say that the thing changed.
curious.body: The heat cracked the window, and the window cracked. In the first part, the heat is the cause and the window comes right after the verb as the thing that changed. In the second part, the window starts the sentence, and no cause is mentioned. The same thing, the window, turns up in a different place in each. The second version doesn't need a separate cause to be named.

examples.text: The heat cracked the window, and [the window cracked].

curious.try: Think of something that can melt or crack. Can you say who or what did it, and also say it with only the thing that changed?

teacher.summary: Useful for verbs that can be used with a causer, or with just the changing participant as subject.
teacher.explain: The alternation pairs a causative clause (subject + verb + affected noun phrase) with an inchoative clause (the affected noun phrase as subject). In The heat cracked the window, window is the direct object. In the window cracked, the same participant is subject, and the clause doesn't require a separate external causer. So the causative is monotransitive and the inchoative is simple intransitive.
teacher.terms: Causative: the member with a causer as subject and the changing participant as object. Inchoative: the member with the changing participant as subject.

examples.text: The heat cracked the window, and [the window cracked].

contrasts.note: Causer as subject; window is the direct object.
The changing participant is the subject.

watch_for: A learner might read the window in The heat cracked the window as the subject because it names what changed.
A learner might look for a hidden causer in the window cracked, when the clause doesn't require one.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of sentences about changes, one naming a cause and one naming only the thing that changed. They underline the subject and the direct object in each pair and say which participant is object in one and subject in the other.

child.hook: Can a window crack without anyone saying who cracked it?
child.explain: Sometimes a sentence tells who made a change. The heat cracked the window. Sometimes it just tells what changed. The window cracked.

examples.text: The heat cracked the window, and [the window cracked].
Mia melted the ice, and [the ice melted].

child.play: Think of a change, like melting or cracking. Say one sentence with a cause and one with only the thing that changed.

checked.note: Audit: fixed teacher.activity, which asked which noun phrase moved (the entry says the same participant is object in one clause and subject in the other, with no movement analysis).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Causative and Inchoative Alternation." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/causative-inchoative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Caused-Motion Construction

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb followed by an NP direct object and an object-oriented locative PP complement
dimensions.meaning: The subject referent causes the direct-object referent to move along a path, from a source, toward a direction, or to a goal
dimensions.function: Packages a causing event and the resulting change of location; the verb can supply manner or causal means
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal in active and passive clauses; productive with verbs that do not lexically license the object or locative complement

1.definition: The subject participant causes the direct-object theme to undergo the change of location described by the locative complement
1.details: The construction, not necessarily the verb's lexical valency, licenses the theme object and locative complement. In He sneezed his tooth right across town, sneeze supplies the causal event while the frame supplies the caused-motion relation. In CGEL terms, across town is an object-oriented locative complement with a path/goal construal, not an adjunct, a predicative complement, or a second object of the verb (CGEL pp. 257–59, 684–88; Goldberg 2006: 6, 33–35, 94, 98–100).

examples.note: Attested Munsch/Goldberg example with a path/goal construal; sneeze does not independently have a three-argument sense
The verb supplies the means; the frame supplies caused motion and goal

constraints.description: The NP after the verb is Od; the following PP is an object-oriented locative complement, not a second object and not a locative adjunct.
The external subject must be construable as the source of causal force; volition is not required, as sneeze and knock show.

The direct-object referent is construed as the moving theme, and the PP supplies source, path, goal, or direction. Static caused-location uses require a separate extension and are not included in this core pattern.
The verbal event must be construable as causally relevant means or manner; productivity is constrained by semantic similarity and statistical pre-emption.

projection.target: Recognizing the Head–Od–locative-complement frame predicts a causer subject, a moving-theme object, an object-oriented change-of-location PP, and a caused-motion reading even when the verb does not lexically license those dependents
projection.evidence: Novel sneeze examples isolate constructional licensing (Goldberg 2006: 6, 94, 98–100); child-directed-speech results support predictive association between the form and caused-motion meaning (pp. 106–10); CGEL p. 684 treats change-of-location dependents as complements in motion frames

grounds.note: Productive licensing with non-motion verbs and form-meaning association
Productivity and learning evidence support a stable form-meaning profile

core.property: NP direct object as moving theme

diagnostics: source, path, goal, or direction interpretation
verb contributes manner or means rather than all valency

known_boundary_items: Caused location, enabled motion, and prevented motion are established extensions, but they do not replace the core caused-motion meaning.
CGEL calls the PP a locative complement and keeps locatives distinct from predicative complements; causative path resultative is a construction-family label, not the CGEL function label.

relatedConstructions.notes: Caused motion is a VP-level argument-structure specialization
The moving-theme direct object is normally realized by an NP
The final dependent is a locative PP complement
Transitive sister of the intransitive motion/goal frame; caused motion adds an Od theme
The final locative complement can bear the source role

grounds.note: The post-object PP is an object-oriented locative complement bearing a change-of-location role
Constructional licensing and caused-motion semantics

curious.title: Making something move with a verb
curious.summary: A verb can be followed by a thing and a place phrase, showing that someone caused the thing to move.
curious.body: In She sneezed the foam off the cappuccino, the sneeze makes the foam move. Sneeze doesn't have a sense with a moving thing and a path of its own, but the pattern supplies both. Pat shoveled the hay into the wagon works the same way. The verb says how the causing happens, here shoveling, and the pattern adds the movement: someone makes something travel from a place, along a path, toward a direction or to a goal. The subject only has to be the source of the force. It doesn't have to act on purpose, as sneezing shows.
curious.try: Think of an action, like kicking or pushing. Can you say what it moved and where it went?

teacher.summary: Helps students see that some verbs get an object and a place phrase from the pattern itself, not from the verb alone.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb, a direct object noun phrase that is the moving theme, and a locative PP complement giving source, path, goal or direction. The subject causes the movement. The construction, not necessarily the verb, licenses the object and the PP: sneeze supplies the causing event, the frame supplies the caused motion. The PP is an object-oriented locative complement, not an adjunct, a predicative complement or a second object. The verb must be construable as the means or manner, and productivity is limited by semantic similarity.
teacher.terms: Caused-motion construction is the constructional name for the pattern. CGEL: the PP is an object-oriented locative complement. Od is the direct object.

contrasts.text: Pat shoveled the hay into the wagon.
contrasts.note: Direct object plus locative complement. The hay moves into the wagon.
Direct object only. There is no path phrase, so no caused-motion pattern.

watch_for: A learner might read into the wagon as a second object of the verb.
A learner might read the place phrase as a setting adjunct, when it describes where the object moves.
A learner might assume any verb can be used this way, when productivity depends on semantic similarity and on the verb's role as means or manner.
teacher.activity: Give students verbs such as kick, push and blow, plus a thing and a place. They build caused-motion sentences, then decide which show something moving from a source, along a path or to a goal.

child.hook: Can a sneeze send a tooth across town?
child.explain: Some sentences tell who made something move. Pat shoveled the hay into the wagon. Pat made the hay move, and the words into the wagon tell where the hay went.
child.play: Pick an action like kick, push or blow. Say what it moved and where it went. Can your friends guess the action?

checked.note: Fixed: child explain now names the hay and the words into the wagon instead of an unclear it. Also fixed (unflagged): child example bracketing now marks the object and the place phrase separately, as the entry's examples do. Frequency pass: teacher.activity verbs sneeze and shovel (about 7,600th and 8,000th in SUBTLEX-UK, counting their other forms) replaced by push and blow, as in the child play; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Caused-Motion Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/caused-motion-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Clause

dimensions.form: Phrase headed immediately by a VP, optionally with a Subject; the VP is ultimately headed by V
dimensions.meaning: Clause-level content organized around the situation profile of the VP and, when expressed, its Subject
dimensions.function: Main or subordinate predication; argument, complement, modifier, supplement, or complete utterance where licensed
dimensions.distribution: Occurs independently and in the dependent positions licensed for finite and non-finite Clauses

1.definition: A Phrase whose Head is a VP and whose Subject is optional
1.details: Clause is defined here without exception as a headed Phrase. Its immediate Head is VP and its ultimate Head is V. An overt Subject, when present, is a Clause-level dependent rather than part of the VP. Subjectless imperative and non-finite Clauses therefore satisfy the same pattern as subject-bearing Clauses. Markers, prenuclear elements, and other Clause-level dependents do not alter the Head relation. A constituent without a VP in Head function is not a Clause in this Constructionary; non-headed structures with clause-like interpretations are assigned to clause-analogue-001.

examples.note: Subjectless imperative Clause consisting overtly of its Head VP
The matrix Clause has Subject Clause leaving early and Head VP annoyed Pat

constraints.description: A Clause must have a VP in Head function; a constituent without a VP Head is not a Clause.
The Subject is optional in the general Clause pattern and, when present, is a dependent of Clause rather than VP.
Clause-level markers, prenuclear material, and supplements do not replace the VP as Head.
A coordination of Clauses is a non-headed coordination, not itself a Clause.

projection.target: Clause membership predicts availability of clause-level polarity, clause-type, subordination, and information-packaging contrasts, together with distribution as a main unit or as a clausal dependent; the VP Head predicts the Clause's internal complementation profile
projection.evidence: CGEL's canonical and non-canonical Clause systems preserve the VP-headed organization across polarity, clause type, voice, subordination, and information packaging, while non-finite data show that an overt Subject is not required

grounds.note: VP-headed membership projects Clause-level systems and distribution beyond the Head/Subject diagnostics
VP-headed structure persists across major Clause contrasts; non-finite Clauses establish the optionality of overt Subject

known_boundary_items: Constituents that CGEL calls verbless clauses have clause-like interpretations but no VP Head; they are excluded here
Attributive VPs are VPs but do not thereby instantiate a separate Clause node

relatedConstructions.notes: Clause specializes Phrase with VP as its immediate Head
The Clause's obligatory Head constituent is a VP
Both can convey clause-like content, but only Clause is formally headed by VP
Finite subject-bearing Clauses provide the Subject–verb configuration in which number agreement is realized
A coordination may contain Clauses as coordinates, but the coordination itself is non-headed and is not a Clause

grounds.note: Clause is a phrasal category whose Predicate/Head is VP, ultimately headed by V
Subjectless non-finites show that an overt Subject is not necessary for Clause status
Clause is strictly a Phrase headed by VP with an optional Subject; there is no verbless exception

curious.title: What counts as a clause
curious.summary: In this dictionary a clause is a group of words built around a verb and what goes with it, with or without a subject.
curious.body: A clause is built around a verb and whatever goes with it. Kim left early has someone doing something: Kim is who left, and left early is the verb part. Leave early! has only the verb part, and it's still a clause. Clauses can sit inside other clauses. In Leaving early annoyed Pat, the opening words Leaving early are a clause that acts as the subject of the whole sentence. Short phrases that carry a message but have no verb part aren't clauses here, though they can mean something clause-like.
curious.try: Find the verb in a sentence you wrote today. What are the words that go with it?

teacher.summary: Defines Clause strictly as a phrase headed by a VP, which separates it from verbless structures and from coordinations.
teacher.explain: A Clause is a phrase whose head is a VP, with an optional subject. In Kim left early, Kim is the subject and left early is the head VP. Leave early! is a subjectless imperative: the Clause is just its head VP. In Leaving early annoyed Pat, the matrix Clause has a subject that is itself a Clause. The subject is a dependent of the Clause, not part of the VP. Markers and other clause-level dependents don't replace the VP as head. A coordination of Clauses is non-headed and is not itself a Clause.
teacher.terms: CGEL also counts verbless clauses as clauses. This dictionary does not: a structure with a clause-like meaning but no VP head is not a Clause here; it is assigned to a separate category, the clause analogue.

contrasts.note: Subject plus head VP.
Head VP alone, with no subject.

watch_for: A learner might think a Clause must have a subject, when some Clauses, such as imperatives and non-finite Clauses, have none.
A learner might count a verbless phrase with clause-like meaning as a Clause, when it has no VP head.
A learner might treat Kim left early and Pat stayed as one Clause, when a coordination of Clauses is not itself a Clause.
teacher.activity: Give students a mix of sentences and verbless fragments. They circle the verb in each, mark the subject when there is one, and sort the items into clause and not a clause.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms now says structures with clause-like meanings but no VP head are assigned to clause analogues (not merely 'no VP head'); teacher.watch_for now says some Clauses, such as imperatives and non-finite Clauses, have no subject.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Clause-Analogue Construction

dimensions.form: A non-headed construction realized by one or more overt phrases, but with no VP and no constituent in Head function at the construction's own level
dimensions.meaning: A recoverable predication, situation, proposition, or speech-act update comparable to the interpretation of a Clause
dimensions.function: Construction-specific complement, adjunct, supplement, exclamation, echo, directive, or other stand-alone utterance
dimensions.distribution: Restricted to licensed non-verbal frames; it is not freely interchangeable with a Clause

1.definition: Conveys clause-like semantic or discourse content through a non-headed construction that is not a Clause
1.details: This node houses the constructions that CGEL calls verbless clauses while rejecting their assignment to the Clause category. Some have an overt subject-like expression plus a predicative expression (their hands above their heads; Dinner over); others consist overtly of a single NP, AdjP, PP, or predicative phrase whose subject or copular relation is recovered from the licensing construction or discourse (What a disaster!; No entry). The overt daughter phrases retain their own internal Heads, but none is Head of the higher clausal-semantics construction. Recovering an implicit predication or speech act in interpretation does not posit a silent VP in syntax.

examples.form: They stood with [their hands above their heads].
examples.note: Subject-like NP plus locative predicative, licensed as complement of with
Supplement with subject-like NP and predicative expression
Non-headed exclamative packaging with understood subject and copular relation
Non-verbal directive whose prohibition is supplied constructionally
Bare-predication polar echo with subject-like NP and predicative AdjP

constraints.description: No VP occurs in Head function; if the construction has a VP Head, it is a Clause instead.
Overt daughters may themselves be headed NPs, AdjPs, or PPs, but no daughter is Head of the higher clausal-semantics construction.
Clause-like content is recovered from the licensed construction and context; the analysis does not posit an unpronounced verbal Head.
Membership is construction-specific: an arbitrary non-verbal fragment does not automatically instantiate this construction.

projection.target: Recognizing the clause-analogue construction predicts recovery of an implicit predicational or speech-act relation and licensing in a delimited clause-like discourse or dependent function, while predicting the absence of verbal tense, auxiliary, and VP-complementation behavior
projection.evidence: CGEL documents recurrent, construction-specific correspondences between these non-verbal forms and finite or non-finite Clause interpretations across complements, supplements, exclamatives, echoes, and directives, even though this Constructionary draws the category boundary differently

grounds.note: The licensed non-verbal forms project recoverable predicational or speech-act content and restricted distributions
Documents recurrent form–interpretation pairings and their restricted complement, supplement, exclamative, and directive distributions

core.property: No Head at the construction's own level
diagnostics: no other daughter determines the construction's distribution
recognized supplement, echo, exclamative, or directive frame
NP/AdjP/PP utterance with conventional clause-like force

known_boundary_items: A Clause has a VP Head and is therefore formally disjoint from this construction
A headed NP or AdjP used merely as a referential fragment need not have clausal semantics
Coordination is also non-headed, but coordinate structure alone does not supply clausal semantics

relatedConstructions.notes: Shares clause-like semantic and discourse work but not the defining VP-headed form
Its daughters may be headed Phrases, but the higher clausal-semantics construction is not itself a Phrase
Both are non-headed constructions, but their internal organization and projections differ
Some non-headed exclamative realizations carry exclamation force, while many exclamations and many members of this construction fall outside that overlap

grounds.note: Detailed inventory and analysis of the structures CGEL calls verbless clauses
CGEL includes these non-VP-headed structures in Clause despite its general head-based Phrase architecture; the Constructionary does not
Anything without a VP Head is not a Clause; CGEL's verbless-clause residue belongs in this separate clause-analogue construction

curious.title: Sentence-like phrases with no verb
curious.summary: Some short phrases carry the meaning of a whole statement even though they contain no verb.
curious.body: A notice reading No entry means something like "you may not enter." What a disaster! means something like "that's a disaster." Neither has a verb, yet we understand a full message. Dinner over, they resumed their game works the same way: it tells us the dinner was over. This dictionary groups such phrases together. They get their clause-like meaning from the pattern they belong to and from the situation, not from a hidden verb. A clause here means a stretch of language built around a verb phrase, and these phrases aren't built that way. They also work only in particular frames, so an arbitrary scrap of words doesn't count.

examples.text: They stood with [their hands above their heads].

curious.try: Think of a sign or a short exclamation with no verb. What full sentence does it stand for?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, verbless but clause-like utterances such as No entry and Dinner over.
teacher.explain: This dictionary groups together non-headed constructions with a clause-like interpretation but no VP in head function. CGEL calls these verbless clauses; this dictionary rejects that label, reserving Clause for structures with a VP head. Some have a subject-like expression plus a predicative expression (their hands above their heads; Dinner over). Others are a single NP, AdjP or PP whose subject or copular relation is recovered from the frame or the discourse (What a disaster!; No entry). This dictionary doesn't posit a silent verb: the implicit predication or speech act is recovered in interpretation, not supplied by an unpronounced VP. Membership is construction-specific, so an arbitrary non-verbal fragment isn't automatically included.
teacher.terms: CGEL: verbless clause. This dictionary: clause-analogue, kept separate from Clause because it has no VP head.

examples.text: They stood with [their hands above their heads].

watch_for: A learner might assume No entry has a hidden verb in the sentence's structure, when this dictionary says the meaning is recovered without positing one.
A learner might think any short fragment, such as a bare noun phrase naming something, carries clause-like meaning.
teacher.activity: Collect short verbless signs and exclamations from around the school. Students write the full-sentence meaning of each and say whether it's a command, a statement, an exclamation or a question.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Clause-Analogue Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/clause-analogue-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Closed Interrogative Clause
pattern: Clause: (Subject:XP +) Head:VP[closed interrogative; main-clause subject–auxiliary inversion]

entry.name: Closed Interrogative Clause
entry.pattern: Clause: (Subject:XP +) Head:VP[closed interrogative; main-clause subject–auxiliary inversion]

dimensions.form: Clause headed by a VP; main clauses show clause-type-triggered subject–auxiliary inversion, while subordinate content clauses are normally marked by whether or if and retain basic Subject–Predicator order
dimensions.meaning: Characteristically presents a closed set of answers, prototypically the positive and negative values of a proposition
dimensions.function: Characteristically asks a closed question, but can perform directives, acknowledgements, statements, and other indirect speech acts
dimensions.distribution: Tensed main clauses and subordinate closed-interrogative content clauses

1.definition: A headed clause type characteristically used to present a closed question
1.details: Closed and open interrogatives are distinct primary clause types in CGEL, not syntactic subtypes defined by a shared interrogative form. In main closed interrogatives, clause type itself triggers subject–auxiliary inversion and do-support where no other auxiliary is available. Subordinate closed interrogatives normally use whether or if without inversion. Closed-question force is characteristic rather than necessary: Would you mind opening the door? is syntactically closed interrogative but conventionally functions as a directive (CGEL pp. 853–57, 865–72, 951–55).

examples.note: Main closed interrogative with subject–auxiliary inversion
Do-support supplies the auxiliary required by main-clause inversion

examples.form: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].
examples.note: Subordinate closed interrogative with whether and basic Subject–Predicator order
Closed interrogative conventionally used as an indirect directive

constraints.description: The construction remains a Clause headed by VP. In a main clause the finite auxiliary precedes the Subject through subject–auxiliary inversion; subordinate closed interrogatives normally have whether/if marking and no inversion.
The characteristic question defines a closed answer set; alternative questions are a use of coordination with closed-interrogative syntax, not a sixth clause type.
Inquiry force is not necessary: indirect directives and strongly biased or rhetorical uses retain closed-interrogative clause type.

projection.target: Clause-type-triggered inversion in a main clause, or subordinate whether/if marking, predicts a closed answer space and the corresponding main/subordinate distribution, while leaving room for indirect forces such as directives
projection.evidence: The inversion and subordinator diagnostics distinguish closed interrogatives from declaratives and open interrogatives independently of whether a particular utterance is used to inquire

grounds.note: Main inversion and subordinate whether/if marking project answer-space and distributional contrasts
The linked main/subordinate profile recurs independently of actual inquiry force

diagnostics: basic Subject–Predicator order in the standard variety

relatedConstructions.notes: Closed and open interrogatives are distinct primary clause types with different syntactic marking
A declarative question asks without subject–auxiliary inversion and carries a stronger same-polarity bias

grounds.note: Closed-interrogative syntax, closed questions, indirect-force uses, and main/subordinate contrast

curious.title: Questions with a fixed set of answers
curious.summary: Some clauses are built to ask a question with a closed set of answers, such as yes or no.
curious.body: Are you generous? and Did Kim finish the report? are built to ask a closed question, one with a fixed set of possible answers, such as yes or no. In these, the helping word (are, did) comes before the person. Inside a longer sentence the pattern changes. In I wonder whether Kim finished the report, the question is tucked into the sentence, introduced by whether, and the words keep their ordinary order. The form doesn't force the use. Would you mind opening the door? has the same build but works as a polite request.

examples.text: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].

curious.try: Take a statement, such as You are hungry. How do you turn it into a question with a yes or no answer?

teacher.summary: Covers yes/no questions in main and subordinate clauses, including do-support and indirect uses such as requests.
teacher.explain: A closed interrogative is a Clause that characteristically asks a closed question: the answers are a closed set, prototypically positive or negative. In a main clause the clause type triggers subject-auxiliary inversion, and do-support supplies an auxiliary when none is present (Did Kim finish the report?). A subordinate closed interrogative normally uses whether or if with ordinary subject-verb order. Closed-question force is characteristic, not necessary: Would you mind opening the door? is a closed interrogative that conventionally works as a directive.
teacher.terms: Yes/no question or polar question are sometimes-used labels for the positive-or-negative cases, and are narrower than closed interrogative, which also covers alternative questions. Open interrogatives (wh-questions) are a separate clause type.

examples.text: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].

contrasts.note: Declarative.
Closed interrogative. Do-support supplies the auxiliary that comes before the subject.

watch_for: A learner might read Would you mind opening the door? as only asking about willingness, when it is conventionally a request.
A learner might look for an auxiliary in Did Kim finish the report? and miss that do supplies one.
A learner might carry main-clause inversion into the subordinate clause after wonder.
teacher.activity: Students turn statements into closed questions (You are hungry, Kim finished the report) and then tuck each into I wonder whether. They say what changed in word order between the two versions.

child.hook: Which questions can you answer with yes or no?
child.explain: Some questions have a short set of answers, like yes or no. In Are you generous? the helping word are comes before the person. In Did Kim finish the report? the helping word did is added to make the question.
child.play: Turn You are hungry into a question. Which word moves in front of the person? Then turn Kim finished the report into a question. Which helping word gets added?

checked.note: Fixed: teacher terms now say yes/no and polar question are narrower labels than closed interrogative (which also covers alternative questions); child explanation and game now say did is added by do-support rather than moved.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Closed Interrogative Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/closed-interrogative-clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subordinate Closed Interrogative with if

1.definition: Introduces a closed question in licensed complement positions.

relatedConstructions.notes: Asked if Jo was ready embeds a question. If Jo was ready, we could leave makes readiness a condition on the main clause.

projection.target: The clause has embedded question interpretation and ordinary subject–verb order. In this use if cannot introduce a whether-to infinitival.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Questions inside sentences with if
curious.summary: After a verb like wonder or ask, if can introduce a question that the sentence reports.
curious.body: In I wondered if Lee had arrived, the question is whether Lee had arrived, but it's tucked inside the sentence. The sentence reports a question rather than asking one. The words inside keep an ordinary order, with the subject before the verb. This if is different from the if of a condition. Asked if Jo was ready reports a question. In If Jo was ready, we could leave, readiness is a condition on the main clause.
curious.try: Say I wondered if Lee had arrived. Now say If Lee had arrived, we could start. In which sentence does the if introduce a question?

teacher.summary: Useful for separating if that introduces an embedded question from conditional if, and for contrasting if with whether.
teacher.explain: Interrogative if introduces a finite subordinate closed interrogative clause in licensed complement positions. The embedded clause has embedded-question interpretation and ordinary subject-verb order. Conditional if is different: in If Jo was ready, we could leave, the if-clause makes readiness a condition on the main clause. Interrogative if cannot introduce a whether-to infinitival.
teacher.terms: Subordinate closed interrogative: an embedded yes/no question. Compare whether, which is related; see this dictionary's entry on whether.

contrasts.text: They asked if Jo was ready.
contrasts.note: Embedded question.

contrasts.text: If Jo was ready, we could leave.
contrasts.note: Condition on the main clause.

watch_for: A learner might read the if in asked if Jo was ready as a condition.
A learner might expect if to introduce a to-infinitival the way whether can.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with if. They sort them into embedded question (asked if Jo was ready) and condition (If Jo was ready, we could leave) and say how they decided.

checked.note: Fixed: removed 'only on that condition' (stronger than the entry's 'a condition on the main clause'); try question now says the if introduces a question; the whether-to infinitival restriction is stated of interrogative if explicitly. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subordinate Closed Interrogative with if." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/closed-interrogative-if-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subordinate Closed Interrogative with whether
pattern: whether + subordinate declarative-order nucleus, or whether + to-infinitival

entry.name: Subordinate Closed Interrogative with whether
entry.pattern: whether + subordinate declarative-order nucleus, or whether + to-infinitival

1.definition: Introduces an embedded closed question or choice between alternatives.

projection.target: Whether can introduce an infinitival, where interrogative if is unavailable. Certain finite prepositional and subject environments likewise favour or require whether.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Questions inside sentences with whether
curious.summary: Whether can introduce a question or a choice between alternatives inside a larger sentence.
curious.body: In Whether to reschedule still needs discussion, whether introduces a choice between alternatives, and the whole phrase acts as the subject of the sentence. Whether can be followed by a full clause or by to and a verb. It also works in places where the question word if isn't available, such as before to and a verb. Some other positions, including some where the phrase is the subject, favour whether or require it.

examples.text: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].

curious.try: Compare I wonder whether to go and I wonder whether we should go. Is the choice between alternatives the same in both?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining when whether, and not if, introduces an embedded closed question.
teacher.explain: Whether introduces an embedded closed question or choice between alternatives, followed either by a clause in declarative order or by a to-infinitival. It can introduce an infinitival where interrogative if is unavailable. Certain finite prepositional and subject environments likewise favour or require whether. When teaching embedded questions, show whether alongside if, so students see where whether is the form to use.
teacher.terms: Subordinate closed interrogative: an embedded closed question or choice between alternatives. Compare if, whose use is more restricted here; see the separate entry for if.

examples.text: I wonder [whether Kim finished the report].

watch_for: A learner might choose if where whether is favoured or required, as with whether to reschedule.
A learner might miss that a whether-phrase can itself be the subject of a sentence.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with a gap where whether or if could go. They decide where whether is needed or preferred, then say what each embedded clause asks.

checked.note: Audit: fixed teacher.terms, which glossed the pattern as an embedded yes/no question only (the entry also covers a choice between alternatives).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subordinate Closed Interrogative with whether." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/closed-interrogative-whether-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Cognate Event Object
pattern: VP[Head:V[event] + Od:NP[event nominal cognate with V]]

entry.name: Cognate Event Object
entry.pattern: VP[Head:V[event] + Od:NP[event nominal cognate with V]]

1.definition: Elaborates the event already described by the verb.
1.details: An otherwise intransitive verb such as die can occur with a cognate event noun and its modifiers. The object in died a long and agonising death adds duration and manner without introducing a second dying event. Modification is commonly needed to make the object informative. This entry targets the event-reading construction, including otherwise intransitive verbs.

examples.form: He [died a long and agonising death].
examples.note: The NP supplies information about how he died.
The event nominal elaborates the fight.
