relatedConstructions.notes: The cognate NP is internal to the verbal phrase.
The reaction NP identifies what is expressed rather than describing the verbal event.

grounds.note: Compares event-denoting cognates with reaction and superlative expressions.

projection.target: An intransitive verb can take an event NP when its head and the verb describe the same event type. The NP commonly adds information through modification.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the manner reading, and Bouso, Hundt and Van Driessche distinguish the event-denoting cognate from other object-like expressions.

curious.title: A verb and an object that name the same event
curious.summary: Some verbs can be followed by a noun naming the same event, which then lets you describe how it happened.
curious.body: In He died a long and agonising death, the verb already says what happened. The phrase after it doesn't add a second dying. It adds details about the one event: how long it lasted and what it was like. She fought a heroic fight works the same way. The noun fight repeats the idea in the verb, and the describing words give the extra information. Die is otherwise a verb with no object after it, yet it can take one here.

examples.text: He [died a long and agonising death].

curious.try: Take a verb like fought and a noun for the same event. What describing words could you add to say more about it?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining objects that repeat the verb's event noun and add manner or duration.
teacher.explain: In a cognate event object, an object noun phrase whose head is an event nominal related to the verb elaborates the event the verb already describes. It can occur with otherwise intransitive verbs such as die. In died a long and agonising death, the object adds duration and manner without introducing a second dying event, and in fought a heroic fight the nominal elaborates the fight. The object is internal to the verb phrase. A reaction object differs: it identifies what is expressed rather than describing the verbal event.
teacher.terms: Cognate object is the traditional name. Od is the direct object.

examples.text: He [died a long and agonising death].

contrasts.note: Verb alone.
The event noun adds a description of the same fighting.

watch_for: A learner might read died a long and agonising death as two events, dying and a death.
A learner might treat the object as a separate participant, when it describes the verb's own event.
teacher.activity: Give students bare verbs such as fought and died. They add an event noun related to the verb plus describing words, then say what the added words tell about the event.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Cognate Event Object." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/cognate-event-object-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Notional Agreement with a Collective NP
pattern: Clause[Subject headed by singular collective N + singular or plural finite agreement]

entry.name: Notional Agreement with a Collective NP
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject headed by singular collective N + singular or plural finite agreement]

1.definition: Allows agreement to track a collective unit or its members in appropriate varieties.

examples.form: The committee [have all signed] the report.

projection.target: Singular committee can control plural agreement where the members are foregrounded. Availability depends on variety and the particular predicate, and the noun itself stays singular.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Singular group nouns with plural verbs
curious.summary: A singular noun for a group, such as committee, can sometimes take a plural verb when the members are in mind.
curious.body: In The committee have all signed the report, committee is a singular noun, but the verb is plural. The plural verb follows the members of the committee, who each signed, rather than the group as one unit. The noun itself stays singular. Whether a plural verb is available depends on the variety of English and on the particular predicate. Agreement is the matching of the verb to the subject, and here it can follow the meaning.

examples.text: The committee [have all signed] the report.

curious.try: Compare The committee has signed the report with The committee have all signed the report. Which one has the members in mind?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining notional agreement with collective nouns, and why plural agreement isn't available in every case.
teacher.explain: With a subject headed by a singular collective noun, agreement can be singular or plural. Singular committee can control plural agreement where the members are foregrounded, as in The committee have all signed the report. The noun stays singular; the verb tracks the members. Whether plural agreement is available depends on the variety and on the particular predicate. This is notional agreement, with the verb following the meaning rather than only the form of the subject.
teacher.terms: Notional agreement: agreement that follows the meaning of the subject. Collective noun: a noun for a group, such as committee. See the separate entry on verb number agreement.

examples.text: The committee [have all signed] the report.

contrasts.text: The committee have all signed the report.
contrasts.note: Plural agreement. The members are foregrounded.

contrasts.text: The committee has signed the report.
contrasts.note: Singular agreement. The committee is treated as a unit.

watch_for: A learner might think committee becomes a plural noun when the verb is plural, when the noun stays singular.
A learner might expect plural agreement to be available with any predicate and in any variety, when availability depends on both.
teacher.activity: Students read The committee has signed the report and The committee have all signed the report aloud, say whether the unit or the members are in mind, and discuss which they would use in the varieties they know.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Notional Agreement with a Collective NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/collective-agreement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Collective Numeral Construction

dimensions.form: Plural cardinal noun in PP, often coordinated (twos and threes)
dimensions.meaning: Grouping or distribution by numerical size
dimensions.function: Specifies manner of grouping or arrangement
dimensions.distribution: Adverbial PP modifying manner of action

1.definition: Cardinal nouns denote group sizes for collective arrangement

examples.note: Magnitude reading, often large numbers rather than batches of exactly one hundred

constraints.description: Cardinal noun is a common noun; takes plural morphology.
Typically in PP with 'in' or 'by'.

projection.target: People entered in threes can describe an arbitrarily large crowd. Three counts the members in each group even though threes is itself grammatically plural. A phrase such as by the hundreds can instead indicate large numbers without fixed groups.
projection.evidence: Reynolds assigns the grouping use its own semantic role among cardinal nouns. The constructed contrast checks whether the number applies to the total or to the groups.

curious.title: Counting and arranging in groups
curious.summary: A plural number word after in or by can tell how people or things are grouped.
curious.body: In twos and threes describes people arriving or being arranged in small groups. The number tells the size of each group, not the total. People entered in threes could be an enormous crowd, since three counts the members of each group. Count by fives uses a number for grouping too. By the hundreds works a little differently. It suggests large numbers, not batches of exactly one hundred.
curious.try: Say People entered in threes. Does three tell you how many people there were in all, or how many in each group?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining plural number words that give group sizes after in or by.
teacher.explain: In this construction a plural cardinal noun in a PP with in or by gives the size of groups, and the PP is an adverbial modifying the manner of the action (arriving in twos and threes). The cardinal noun is a common noun and takes plural morphology. Three counts the members of each group even though threes is grammatically plural. By the hundreds works differently: it can indicate large numbers without fixed groups, rather than batches of exactly one hundred.
teacher.terms: Cardinal noun: a number word used as a noun. Compare a cardinal determinative, as in three people.

contrasts.note: Three counts the members of each group; the crowd can be of any size.
Three counts the total.

watch_for: A learner might read in threes as a total of three people.
A learner might read by the hundreds as batches of exactly one hundred.
teacher.activity: Students line up in twos, then in threes, and describe what happened using in twos and in threes. They then count aloud by fives and say what the number tells them.

child.hook: Can you count by fives?
child.explain: A number can tell how big each group is. In twos means two at a time. Count by fives means you jump five each time.
child.play: Line up your friends in twos, then in threes. Say what you did with in twos and in threes.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Collective Numeral Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/collective-numeral-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: come with a Motion or Sound Participial

entry.name: come with a Motion or Sound Participial

1.definition: Presents an approach with its manner or accompanying sound.
1.details: In came running, running supplies the manner. In came roaring past, roaring supplies sound during the movement and past supplies the path. The subject participates in the motion and the activity or sound. Compare came looking for us, where the participial can instead describe a purpose. This entry covers the manner and sound reading with come.

examples.form: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].
examples.note: Excerpt from the documented example. Running supplies manner.
Excerpt from a description of tanks. Roaring supplies the sound and past the path.

relatedConstructions.notes: Both the participial and any path expression are part of the motion description.
A goal expression can specify the destination of the movement.

grounds.note: Documents the motion frame and the distribution of manner and sound participles.

projection.target: A sound verb can describe how the movement unfolds, with a path expression that describes the movement rather than the direction of the sound.
projection.evidence: Patel’s Research Constructicon entry gives motion and sound examples. Fanego traces the corpus distribution of the broader movement-plus-participial pattern.

curious.title: Came running, came roaring
curious.summary: Come followed by an -ing word can show how someone approached or what sound came with the movement.
curious.body: In Sally came running excitedly into the room, running tells us how she arrived. In came roaring past, from a description of tanks, roaring is a sound heard during the movement, and past shows the path. The one who comes takes part in both the motion and the activity or sound. Compare came looking for us. There the -ing word can instead describe a purpose: they came in order to look for us.

examples.text: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].

curious.try: Say came running and then came looking for us. In which one does the -ing word tell how someone moved, and in which can it tell why they came?

teacher.summary: Helps students see come plus an -ing word as manner or sound of movement, and tell it apart from a purpose reading.
teacher.explain: In this pattern the head verb come is followed by a V-ing expression and optionally a path expression. In came running, running supplies the manner. In came roaring past, roaring supplies sound during the movement and past supplies the path; the path describes the movement, not the direction of the sound. The subject participates in the motion and in the activity or sound. A goal expression can also specify the destination. In came looking for us the participial can instead describe a purpose, a reading outside this pattern.
teacher.terms: V-ing form: the gerund-participial in CGEL, called the present participle in traditional grammar. Path and goal expressions are related to the goal complement entry.

examples.text: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].

contrasts.text: Sally came running into the room.
contrasts.note: Running is the manner of arrival.
The participial can describe a purpose instead.

watch_for: A learner might read came running as two separate events, coming and then running, when running describes how the coming happens.
A learner might read the -ing word as a purpose, as in came looking for us, when it supplies manner or sound.
A learner might take past in came roaring past as the direction of the sound, when it describes the movement.
teacher.activity: Students act out came running, came dancing and came looking for us. The class decides whether the -ing word tells how someone moved or why they came.

child.hook: What do you notice about the word after came in Sally came running into the room?
child.explain: You can add a word ending in -ing after came. It can tell how someone moved. Sally came running into the room.

examples.text: Sally [came running excitedly into the room].
The dog [came running into the kitchen].

child.play: Act out came running, came hopping and came skipping. Which word tells you how the person moved?

checked.note: Fixed: child.hook no longer asks for 'hurry' with only came (the entry says nothing of hurry) and now asks about the word after came; curious text now says the -ing word can describe a purpose in came looking for us, as the entry puts it; replaced 'this entry' in teacher text. Frequency pass: teacher.activity came skipping (skip about 3,300th in SUBTLEX-UK, counting its other forms) replaced by came dancing; child play unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "come with a Motion or Sound Participial." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/come-with-motion-participial-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Suppletive Adjectival Comparison

1.definition: Realizes grade in selected adjectives with different stems.

examples.form: This plan is [better] than the first.

grounds.locator: Ch. 6, grade inflection; Ch. 13 §6.3; Ch. 18, adjective inflection

projection.target: Better behaves like a comparative even though it has no transparently added -er ending. Better than and the best share a paradigm with plain good in the relevant readings.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Comparing with a different word
curious.summary: A few adjectives make their comparison forms from a different stem, such as good, better and best.
curious.body: Good has better and best as its comparison forms, and bad has worse and worst. These are built on different stems, not by adding something to the plain word. Better still works as a comparison form even though it has no added -er ending. This plan is better than the first compares two plans, just as a taller one would compare two heights. Better than and the best share a pattern with plain good.

examples.text: This plan is [better] than the first.

curious.try: Say the plain word, the comparison and the best for good and for bad. What do you notice about the endings?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining why good and bad compare with different words instead of added endings.
teacher.explain: Some adjectives realize grade through different stems: good has better and best, and bad has worse and worst. This is suppletion. Better behaves like a comparative even though it has no transparently added -er ending: it can introduce a than-phrase, as in better than the first. Better than and the best share a paradigm with plain good in the relevant readings.
teacher.terms: Suppletion: forming grade forms from a different stem. Comparative and superlative are the traditional names for the two grades; this dictionary says grade.

examples.text: This plan is [better] than the first.

contrasts.text: This plan is better than the first.
contrasts.note: Suppletive comparative of good.

contrasts.text: This plan is longer than the first.
contrasts.note: Regular comparative with the -er suffix.

watch_for: A learner might look for the -er ending in better and not see it as a comparison form.
A learner might treat better and good as unrelated words, when they belong to one paradigm.
teacher.activity: Students write the three forms (plain, comparison, best) for good and bad and for a regular adjective like long. They mark which forms are built by adding an ending and which come from a different stem.

child.hook: What comes after good, then better?
child.explain: Some words change into a different word when you compare. Good turns into better and best. Bad turns into worse and worst.

examples.text: This plan is [better] than the first.
This soup is [worse] than that one.

child.play: Finish the chain out loud. Good, better, and then what? Bad, worse, and then what? Make a sentence with each word.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Suppletive Adjectival Comparison." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/comparative-adjective-suppletion-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Comparative Correlative
pattern: the + fronted comparative in first unit, the + fronted comparative in second unit; also matrix comparative + final the-comparative unit

entry.name: Comparative Correlative
entry.pattern: the + fronted comparative in first unit, the + fronted comparative in second unit; also matrix comparative + final the-comparative unit

1.definition: Makes variation on one scale contingent on the value on another.
1.details: The more we pay them, the harder they work makes effort vary with pay. Reversing the order can make pay vary with effort, which licenses different inferences. The second comparative can stay in its ordinary position when the dependent unit comes last. Fronted pairs also allow reductions such as the sooner, the better. The comparative marker the also occurs before comparative AdjPs and AdvPs in this pattern.

examples.form: [The more we pay them, the harder they work.]
examples.note: Pay supplies the scale from which variation in effort is projected.

examples.form: [He becomes more cynical the older he gets.]

relatedConstructions.notes: An inflected comparative is one possible realization of each degree phrase.
Fully reduced pairs can express the relation with no overt VP.

grounds.note: Documents reduction in the comparative correlative.
Corpus study of the construction and its variants.

projection.target: Matched comparatives cue linked variation rather than two unconnected comparisons. The fronted pairing permits reduced units, and reversing which scale sets the condition can change truth conditions.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s order, dependency and reduction contrasts, CASA’s reduced pattern, and Hoffmann’s corpus study.

curious.title: Two comparisons that change together
curious.summary: Two matching the-parts show that one thing varies in step with another.
curious.body: In The more we pay them, the harder they work, both parts start with the and contain a comparison. Together they tell us that effort varies with pay. Order matters. Swapping the parts can make pay vary with effort instead, which supports different conclusions. The parts can be cut down, as in The sooner, the better. The dependent part can also come last, as in He becomes more cynical the older he gets.

examples.text: [The more we pay them, the harder they work.]
[He becomes more cynical the older he gets.]

curious.try: Say The more we pay them, the harder they work. Now swap the two parts. Does the meaning stay the same?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining the two the-comparatives pattern and why the two parts aren't two separate comparisons.
teacher.explain: The comparative correlative links variation on one scale to variation on another. In the fronted pairs, each unit has the followed by a fronted comparative: the more we pay them, the harder they work. The first unit sets the scale, and the second varies with it. Reversing the order can make pay vary with effort, which licenses different inferences. The second comparative can stay in its ordinary position when the dependent unit comes last (more cynical the older he gets), and fronted pairs can be reduced, as in the sooner, the better. The marker the also occurs before comparative AdjPs and AdvPs in this pattern.
teacher.terms: Comparative correlative: the name used here for the pattern. This dictionary calls the word the in this pattern a comparative marker.

examples.text: [The more we pay them, the harder they work.]
[He becomes more cynical the older he gets.]

contrasts.text: The more we pay them, the harder they work.
contrasts.note: Pay supplies the scale; effort varies with it.

contrasts.text: The harder they work, the more we pay them.
contrasts.note: Effort now supplies the scale, and pay varies with it.

watch_for: A learner might read the in the sooner, the better as the definite article.
A learner might read the two parts as unconnected comparisons, when they express linked variation.
A learner might assume that reversing the parts keeps the same meaning, when it can change which thing varies with which.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as the sooner, the better and the more we pay them, the harder they work. They decide which part sets the scale, then swap the parts and discuss what changes.

child.hook: How does The sooner, the better work?
child.explain: Sometimes two the-parts go together. What the second part says changes along with the first. The more you practise, the better you get.

examples.text: [The more you practise, the better you get.]

child.play: Here is one. The bigger the dog, the louder the bark. Now make your own by swapping in different things for the dog and the bark.

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer says the first thing 'grows' (the entry's examples include The sooner, the better) and now says the two parts change together; child game rewritten with a concrete instruction; curious body drops the causal 'change the pay' wording and keeps the entry's 'effort varies with pay'; teacher explanation limits the 'the + fronted comparative' description to the fronted pairs. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Comparative Correlative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/comparative-correlative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Comparative -er
pattern: XP[X + -er] where X < {tall, deep, soon, near, few, ...} >

entry.name: Comparative -er
entry.pattern: XP[X + -er] where X < {tall, deep, soon, near, few, ...} >

1.definition: Denotes scalar superiority
1.details: Semantic operation comparing two points on scale denoted by base

2.details: Semantic operation measuring interval between compared points

3.details: Semantic operation establishing reference point

projection.target: The same comparative relation can be expressed by a suffix with tall or by more with expensive. The suffix does not freely spread from one gradable adjective to another. Either realization can introduce a than-standard and accept a differential where the adjective allows it.
projection.evidence: CGEL treats comparative realization and the form of the standard as distinct choices and documents lexical variation in grade inflection.

relatedConstructions.notes: Longer than we expected pairs a comparative adjective with a than-clause whose missing degree is interpreted through the comparison.
Longer marks comparative grade with the regular suffix. Better expresses comparative grade with a suppletive form.

curious.title: Comparing with -er
curious.summary: Adding -er to a word like tall says that one thing ranks higher than another on a scale.
curious.body: Taller, deeper, sooner, nearer and fewer all compare two points on a scale. The -er form can also say by how much, as in much taller or two inches taller, and it can name what is being compared with, as in taller than Bill. Sometimes the comparison is left to context, as in the taller building. The same idea can come out as more with another adjective, as in more expensive. Which adjectives take -er varies from word to word.
curious.try: Compare two things near you with taller, deeper or nearer. Can you say by how much, and than what?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining -er comparatives, the than-phrase, and how a difference like two inches can be added.
teacher.explain: A comparative with -er compares two points on the scale named by its base: taller, deeper, sooner, nearer and fewer. It can also express a difference (much taller, two inches taller) and the basis of comparison, whether explicit (taller than Bill) or contextual (the taller building). The same comparative relation can be expressed by a suffix with tall or by more with expensive; the suffix does not freely spread from one gradable adjective to another. Either form can introduce a than-standard and accept a differential where the adjective allows it.
teacher.terms: Comparative: the traditional name. Standard of comparison: what follows than. Differential: the measured difference, as in two inches taller.

contrasts.note: Suffix comparative with an explicit standard.
The same relation expressed with more.

watch_for: A learner might expect -er wherever a comparison is wanted, though more expensive expresses the same relation with expensive.
A learner might read taller in the taller building as having no basis of comparison, when context supplies one.
teacher.activity: Students compare classroom objects. They use -er or more, add a measured difference (two inches taller), and add a than-phrase.

child.hook: Which is taller, you or your teacher?
child.explain: Add -er to words like tall and deep to compare two things. Tall becomes taller. Deep becomes deeper. Then say what you compare it with, like taller than Bill.

examples.text: The pool is [deeper] than the pond.

child.play: Compare two things in the room with an -er word. Add than and name the other thing.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain now limits -er to words like tall and deep, as the entry says the suffix does not freely spread (more expensive).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Comparative -er." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/comparative-er-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Multiplicative Measure Comparison

1.definition: Expresses a ratio between quantities on a scale.

examples.form: This cabinet is [twice as deep as that one].

projection.target: Twice measures the ratio of depths rather than repetition of the cabinet state. Twice as deep fixes a ratio in a way that two centimetres deeper does not.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how many times as much
curious.summary: A multiplier such as twice, followed by as and a measure word, compares two amounts as a ratio.
curious.body: This cabinet is twice as deep as that one says that one depth is two times the other. Twice here gives a ratio between two depths. It doesn't mean the cabinet is repeated. This is a different kind of comparison from two centimetres deeper. That version gives a difference between the depths, while twice as deep fixes how many times one is the other.

examples.text: This cabinet is [twice as deep as that one].

curious.try: Compare This cabinet is twice as deep as that one with This cabinet is two centimetres deeper than that one. Which one tells you a ratio?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining multiplier plus as...as comparisons and how they differ from comparisons that give a difference.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a multiplier + as + a gradable expression + an as-phrase, a specialization of the equative as...as. It expresses a ratio between quantities on a scale. In twice as deep as that one, twice measures the ratio of depths, not repetition of the cabinet state. That fixes the ratio in a way that a differential such as two centimetres deeper does not: the differential gives the size of the gap, not how many times one measure is the other.
teacher.terms: Equative: a comparison of equal degree, as in as deep as. Multiplier: a word like twice that scales the comparison. Differential: a measured difference, as in two centimetres deeper.

examples.text: This cabinet is [twice as deep as that one].

contrasts.text: This cabinet is twice as deep as that one.
contrasts.note: A ratio of depths.

contrasts.text: This cabinet is two centimetres deeper than that one.
contrasts.note: A difference between depths.

watch_for: A learner might read twice as saying the cabinet itself occurs twice, when it states a ratio of depths.
A learner might treat twice as deep as that one as a measured difference, when it states a ratio.
teacher.activity: Give students two objects and a ruler. They measure both and say a ratio sentence (one is twice as long as the other) and a difference sentence (one is two centimetres longer).

child.hook: If one rope is twice as long as another, how long is it?
child.explain: Twice as long as means two times the length. It compares two things and tells how many times as long one is.

examples.text: This cabinet is [twice as deep as that one].
This rope is [twice as long as that one].

child.play: Find two pencils or two strings. Can you find a pair where one is twice as long as the other? Say it as a sentence.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Multiplicative Measure Comparison." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/comparative-factor-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Object it with an Extraposed Content Clause
pattern: VP[V + it + predicative or other complement + content clause]

entry.name: Object it with an Extraposed Content Clause
entry.pattern: VP[V + it + predicative or other complement + content clause]

1.definition: Places propositional content after the other complements with it in an earlier object position.

examples.form: We [found it surprising that the lights were on].

projection.target: It fills the object slot and need not refer to a prior NP. The corresponding sequence found that the lights were on surprising is heavily degraded.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Putting it first and the clause last
curious.summary: A verb can take it right after the verb and put the real content in a clause at the end.
curious.body: In We found it surprising that the lights were on, the word it comes right after found, then comes surprising, and the clause that the lights were on comes last. The clause says what was surprising. Here it holds the place after the verb and doesn't point back to anything mentioned before. The content comes at the end instead. Putting the clause straight after found and moving the describing word to the end is heavily degraded.

examples.text: We [found it surprising that the lights were on].

curious.try: Say We found it surprising that the lights were on. What does it stand for in that sentence?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining object it with an extraposed that-clause after a predicative complement.
teacher.explain: In this verb phrase, a verb is followed by it in object position, then a predicative or other complement, and finally a content clause: found it surprising that the lights were on. It fills the object slot and need not refer to a previous noun phrase. The content clause, placed last, gives the propositional content. The corresponding order with the clause directly after the verb (found that the lights were on surprising) is heavily degraded.
teacher.terms: Extraposition: moving a content clause to the end, with it in its place. Content clause: a clause that gives propositional content, such as that the lights were on.

examples.text: We [found it surprising that the lights were on].

contrasts.text: We found it surprising that the lights were on.
contrasts.note: It is in object position, the content clause is last.
An ordinary noun phrase object with a predicative complement and no content clause.

watch_for: A learner might look for an earlier noun phrase that it refers to, when it need not refer to one.
A learner might put the content clause right after the verb, which is heavily degraded in this pattern.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences like We found it surprising that the lights were on. They underline it, the complement and the content clause, and say what the content clause tells you.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Object it with an Extraposed Content Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/complement-it-extraposition-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Complement Preposing

1.definition: Uses a fronted complement to link the clause to something evoked in the discourse.
1.details: In the muffin example the fronted NP occupies the position interpreted as the object of give. A contrast or a set of alternatives can make the link available without repeating the same words. A fronted adjunct can introduce a new setting with no prior link, and left dislocation instead leaves an overt expression in the nucleus.

examples.form: [A bran muffin I can give you.]
examples.note: The server has just said that the bagels are sold out. The muffins are an available alternative.

examples.form: About the forms, [two of them I have already signed].
examples.note: Constructed example with an explicit anchor for the preposed object.

relatedConstructions.notes: A complement occurs before the clause nucleus.
The detached-topic construction allows an overt resumptive expression.

grounds.note: Registers topicalization with a preposed complement.

projection.target: In its ordinary declarative use the preposed complement needs a discourse link even when the speaker has not mentioned the exact referent. An initial setting adjunct has no corresponding requirement.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts preposed complements and adjuncts, including links by repeated mention, subset, and contrasting alternative. CASA records topicalization.

curious.title: Moving a part to the front
curious.summary: Part of a sentence can be moved to the front to tie the sentence to something already in the conversation.
curious.body: Suppose a server has just said the bagels are sold out. A bran muffin I can give you moves the thing being given to the front, and the muffin is an available alternative to the bagels. In plain order it would come after the verb give. The moved part needs a link to the conversation. It might have been mentioned, belong to a set that was, or be a contrast with something else. A phrase that just sets the scene can open a sentence without such a link. And the moved part leaves no repeated copy behind.

examples.text: [A bran muffin I can give you.]
About the forms, [two of them I have already signed].

curious.try: Think of a conversation in which someone could say A bran muffin I can give you. What might they have just said?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining why a preposed object needs a discourse link, and how it differs from a fronted setting and from left dislocation.
teacher.explain: In complement preposing, a complement is fronted and the clause nucleus has a gap where it would normally appear: A bran muffin I can give you, where the fronted noun phrase is interpreted as the object of give. In its ordinary declarative use, the preposed complement needs a discourse link, even when the exact referent hasn't been mentioned. The link can be repeated mention, a subset, or a contrasting alternative. A fronted adjunct can introduce a new setting with no prior link. Left dislocation differs: it leaves an overt expression in the nucleus.
teacher.terms: Topicalization: another name for fronting a complement. Gap: the place in the clause where the fronted phrase is interpreted.

examples.text: [A bran muffin I can give you.]
About the forms, [two of them I have already signed].

contrasts.text: A bran muffin I can give you.
contrasts.note: Preposed complement. The muffin is the object of give; no copy remains in the clause.

contrasts.text: I can give you a bran muffin.
contrasts.note: The same content in ordinary order.

watch_for: A learner might front any object, when the fronted complement needs a discourse link.
A learner might confuse preposing with left dislocation, where an overt expression stays in the clause.
A learner might think a fronted setting needs a prior link, when an initial setting adjunct has no such requirement.
teacher.activity: Students role-play a cafe. One says what is sold out, and the other offers an alternative with a preposed complement (A cup of tea I can give you). They then say what linked the offer to the conversation.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.activity model line A bran muffin I can give you (bran about 24,700th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by A cup of tea I can give you; entry examples and the constructed contrast that pairs with them are unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Complement Preposing." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/complement-preposing-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Conative at

1.definition: Presents an action directed towards a target without committing to the usual result of the transitive use.
1.details: With kick, the direct object normally entails contact. The at-phrase identifies what the action was directed towards and permits either contact or a miss. With eat or nibble, related uses can instead involve small amounts or repetition. The entry concerns the directed-action reading with verbs that support the contrast, leaving ordinary uses such as look at to their own accounts.

examples.note: The action is directed at the speaker, who may have been missed.

examples.form: The striker [kicked at the ball] and caught it with the outside of her foot.
examples.note: Constructed. Success remains compatible with the at-form.

relatedConstructions.notes: The target is internal to the VP, as the object of at.
The target supplies a direction for the action, without an arrival or contact entailment.

grounds.note: Distinguishes attempted contact from repeated contact and partial ingestion.
Examines the contribution of the pattern by verb class.
Records the target-oriented action pattern.

projection.target: For contact verbs such as kick, at plus the target permits a continuation with a miss. A transitive object with the same verb normally rules that continuation out.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s alternation, Birmingham’s attempted-contact record and Perek’s evidence for different conative verb classes.

curious.title: Aiming an action at something
curious.summary: An at-phrase can show that an action was aimed at something, without saying it connected.
curious.body: The horse kicked at me and The horse kicked me differ in a useful way. The second says the kick landed. The first says the kick was aimed at me, and it may have connected or missed. The at-phrase names the target. It doesn't rule out success: The striker kicked at the ball and caught it with the outside of her foot. With a verb like kick, a direct object normally means contact happened, and at removes that commitment. Related uses with eat or nibble can involve small amounts or repetition.

examples.text: The striker [kicked at the ball] and caught it with the outside of her foot.

curious.try: Compare The horse kicked at me with The horse kicked me. In which one do you know for sure that the kick connected?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining at-phrases that present an action as directed at a target without the usual result of the transitive use.
teacher.explain: In the conative, a verb of action is followed by a PP headed by at, whose complement is the target. Kicked at me presents the action as directed towards the speaker without committing to the usual result. With kick, the direct object in The horse kicked me normally entails contact, while the at-phrase permits either contact or a miss. The target supplies a direction for the action, with no entailment of arrival or contact. Ordinary uses such as look at are left to their own accounts.
teacher.terms: Conative: the traditional name for this pattern. Comp is a complement; the target is the object of at.

examples.text: The striker [kicked at the ball] and caught it with the outside of her foot.

contrasts.note: Directed at the speaker. Contact or a miss.
Transitive control. Contact occurred.

watch_for: A learner might read kicked at as meaning the kick missed, when it permits either contact or a miss.
A learner might treat the at-phrase as a place adjunct, when it names what the action was directed towards.
teacher.activity: Students act out two versions of kicking a ball, once with contact and once with a miss. They describe each with kicked the ball and kicked at the ball, then discuss which description fits.

child.hook: Is kicking at a ball the same as kicking a ball?
child.explain: Kicked the ball means your foot hit it. Kicked at the ball means you aimed a kick at it. You might have missed.

examples.text: Mia [kicked at the ball] and missed.

child.play: Kick a soft ball or pretend to. Say what happened with kicked the ball or kicked at the ball.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Conative at." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/conative-at-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Concealed Passive in an -ing Complement
pattern: VP[need/want/require or other licensing V + gerund-participial]

entry.name: Concealed Passive in an -ing Complement
entry.pattern: VP[need/want/require or other licensing V + gerund-participial]

1.definition: Uses an active-shaped complement with a passive interpretation.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. The infinitival counterpart displays the passive overtly.

relatedConstructions.notes: The hinge needs oiling has a passive interpretation with an active gerund-participial. The hinge needs to be oiled expresses the passive overtly.

projection.target: The hinge is understood as what someone oils. A to-infinitival with analogous meaning normally requires passive morphology, as in needs to be oiled.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Active-looking words with a passive meaning
curious.summary: After verbs like need, an -ing word can have a passive meaning even though it looks active.
curious.body: The hinge needs oiling means the hinge should be oiled. The word oiling looks active, but the hinge isn't doing the oiling. The hinge is understood as what someone oils. The longer way to say it shows the passive on the surface: The hinge needs to be oiled. In the -ing version, nothing marks the passive. Verbs like need, want and require can take this kind of complement. The meaning of the passive is there, but its usual wording is hidden.
curious.try: Say The hinge needs oiling and The hinge needs to be oiled. Do they mean the same thing?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why needs washing means needs to be washed, with no passive marking.
teacher.explain: After a licensing verb such as need, want or require, a gerund-participial complement can have a passive interpretation while keeping active form: The hinge needs oiling. The hinge is understood as what someone oils. A to-infinitival with analogous meaning normally requires passive morphology, as in needs to be oiled, which displays the passive overtly. The gerund-participial version shows no passive marking.
teacher.terms: Gerund-participial: the -ing form of a verb. Concealed passive: this dictionary’s name for a passive meaning without passive form.

contrasts.note: Active form, passive meaning.

contrasts.text: The hinge needs to be oiled.
contrasts.note: The infinitival counterpart shows the passive overtly.

watch_for: A learner might think the hinge does the oiling, when it is understood as what someone oils.
A learner might look for be and a past participle in needs oiling and conclude there is no passive meaning.
teacher.activity: Students rewrite sentences like My bike needs washing as needs to be washed, then say who does the action in each and whether the sentence names them.

child.hook: Who does the oiling in The hinge needs oiling?
child.explain: Sometimes a word ending in -ing has a hidden meaning. The hinge needs oiling means someone should oil the hinge. The hinge doesn't oil itself.
child.play: Say each one the longer way. The hinge needs to be oiled. My bike needs to be washed. Make one for something in your room.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.summary and activity now use needs washing (as in the child edition) instead of needs oiling (oiling about 44,500th in SUBTLEX-UK); added the constructed teacher example My bike needs washing; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Concealed Passive in an -ing Complement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/concealed-passive-ing-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Constituent Negation with not

1.definition: Negates a non-verbal predicate or constituent within a clause

constraints.description: Occurs with predicative XP (AdjP/PP/NP) in a copular or similar frame.
Negates the property or relation expressed by the XP.

projection.target: In Lee came not on Tuesday but on Wednesday, the correction replaces a temporal expression while the coming remains asserted. The clause can take an ordinary negative tag expecting confirmation of that coming.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents local scope of not inside coordinates and distinguishes it from primary finite negation.

relatedConstructions.notes: Jo ordered tea, not coffee targets a constituent. Jo didn’t order coffee puts the negation with the finite auxiliary.

curious.title: Saying not about one part of a sentence
curious.summary: Not can deny one part of a sentence, such as a description or a time, instead of the whole action.
curious.body: In That is not a solution, not denies what is said about that: it isn't a solution. In She is not in the box, it denies a place. The description or relation is what gets negated. Not can also target one part while the rest stays asserted. In Lee came not on Tuesday but on Wednesday, the coming still happened. Only the time is corrected. Jo ordered tea, not coffee targets just the drink, unlike Jo didn't order coffee.

examples.text: Lee came [not on Tuesday] but on Wednesday.

curious.try: Say Jo ordered tea, not coffee. What does not apply to? Compare Jo didn't order coffee.

teacher.summary: Helps students see not as negating a particular part of a clause, and tell it apart from negation attached to the auxiliary.
teacher.explain: In constituent negation, not negates a non-verbal predicate or constituent within a clause. This dictionary’s examples have a predicative NP, AdjP or PP in a copular or similar frame (That is not a solution, She is not in the box), where not negates the property or relation the phrase expresses. Not can also have local scope inside coordinates: in Lee came not on Tuesday but on Wednesday, the correction replaces a time expression and the coming remains asserted. This differs from primary finite negation, as in Jo didn't order coffee, where the negation goes with the finite auxiliary.
teacher.terms: Constituent negation: negation of one part of a clause. Primary (finite) negation: negation attached to the finite auxiliary, as in didn't.

contrasts.note: Not targets one constituent.
Negation goes with the finite auxiliary.

watch_for: A learner might read Lee came not on Tuesday but on Wednesday as saying Lee didn't come, when the coming remains asserted.
A learner might treat not before a predicative phrase and not with the auxiliary as the same thing.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs like Jo ordered tea, not coffee and Jo didn't order coffee. They say what is denied in each and what is still asserted.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Constituent Negation with not." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/constituent-not-negation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Content-Level because Adjunct

1.definition: Presents a circumstance as the reason for the event or state asserted.

examples.form: Jo left [because the room was too cold].

projection.target: The cold explains the leaving on the content reading. In the reasoning use of because, its clause can instead supply evidence for making the assertion.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Because giving the reason for an event
curious.summary: A because-part can give the reason that something happened or was the case.
curious.body: In Jo left because the room was too cold, the because-part says why Jo left. The cold explains the leaving. This is the content reading: the circumstance is presented as the reason for the event or state asserted. Because has another use, in reasoning. There the because-part can give evidence for making the statement, not an explanation for an event.

examples.text: Jo left [because the room was too cold].
We stayed inside [because it was raining].

curious.try: Say Jo left because the room was too cold. What happened, and what is the reason it happened?

teacher.summary: Useful for separating because as a reason for an event from because as evidence for a claim.
teacher.explain: In the content use, a PP headed by because with a finite clause as its complement modifies the predication and presents a circumstance as the reason for the event or state asserted. In Jo left because the room was too cold, the cold explains the leaving. In the reasoning use, the because-clause can instead supply evidence for making the assertion. This dictionary covers the content reading; the evidential use has its own entry.
teacher.terms: Adverbial clause of reason: the traditional name. In this grammar because heads a PP whose complement is a finite clause.

examples.text: Jo left [because the room was too cold].

contrasts.text: Jo left because the room was too cold.
contrasts.note: The cold explains the leaving.

contrasts.text: We stayed inside because it was raining.
contrasts.note: The rain is the reason for staying inside.

watch_for: A learner might read every because-clause as explaining the event, when a reasoning use gives evidence for an assertion.
A learner might take the because-clause as a separate sentence, when it modifies the predication.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentence starters like Jo left because and We stayed inside because. They underline the reason and say which event or state it explains.

child.hook: Why did Jo leave?
child.explain: Because tells the reason something happened. Jo left because the room was too cold. The cold is why Jo left.

examples.text: Jo left [because the room was too cold].
We stayed inside [because it was raining].

child.play: Start a sentence with I wore a coat because. Ask a friend to finish it with a reason. Then swap.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Content-Level because Adjunct." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/content-because-adjunct-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Noun with a Declarative Content Complement

entry.name: Noun with a Declarative Content Complement

1.definition: Supplies the propositional content associated with a noun such as claim or fact.

examples.form: The [claim that Jo knew the code] surprised us.
The claim [that Jo rejected] surprised us.
examples.note: Constructed comparison. Integrated relative with a missing object corresponding to claim.

relatedConstructions.notes: The rumour that Jo had left gives the content of the rumour, with no noun-linked gap. The rumour that Jo spread has an object gap linked to rumour.

projection.target: The embedded knew the code has no gap linked to claim. In the claim that Jo rejected, the matching string that Jo rejected instead has an object gap.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Nouns that come with a that-clause
curious.summary: A noun such as claim or fact can be followed by a clause that spells out its content.
curious.body: In The claim that Jo knew the code surprised us, the that-clause says what the claim was: Jo knew the code. Nothing in that clause is missing or points back to claim. Compare The claim that Jo rejected surprised us. Here Jo rejected the claim, so the clause is missing something, the thing rejected, and that something is the claim. The rumour that Jo had left gives the content of the rumour. The rumour that Jo spread works like the second claim sentence: it has a missing object that is the rumour.

examples.text: The [claim that Jo knew the code] surprised us.
The claim [that Jo rejected] surprised us.

curious.try: Compare the rumour that Jo had left and the rumour that Jo spread. In which one is something missing from the clause?

teacher.summary: Helps students separate a noun's content clause from a relative clause that looks the same.
teacher.explain: A noun such as claim or fact can take a finite content clause that supplies the propositional content associated with it: the claim that Jo knew the code. The embedded clause (Jo knew the code) is complete and has no gap linked to claim. In the claim that Jo rejected, the string that Jo rejected, which opens like the content clause above, is an integrated relative clause with an object gap corresponding to claim. So a clause after a noun can be a content clause or a relative clause, and the difference is whether the clause has a gap linked to the noun.
teacher.terms: Content clause: a clause giving propositional content. Integrated relative: a relative clause closely tied to its noun.

examples.text: The [claim that Jo knew the code] surprised us.
The claim [that Jo rejected] surprised us.

contrasts.text: The rumour that Jo had left surprised us.
contrasts.note: Content clause. It gives the content of the rumour; nothing is missing.

contrasts.text: The rumour that Jo spread surprised us.
contrasts.note: Integrated relative. The clause has an object gap linked to rumour.

watch_for: A learner might treat the claim that Jo rejected as a content clause, when Jo rejected the claim and the clause has a gap.
A learner might assume that-clauses after a noun all work alike, when the gap test separates two types.
teacher.activity: Give students noun phrases like the rumour that Jo had left and the rumour that Jo spread. They test each by asking whether the clause has a gap linked to the noun (what was spread?), then label content clause or relative clause.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain no longer calls the two clauses the same string (that Jo knew the code vs that Jo rejected); teacher.activity uses the gap-linked-to-the-noun test the entry gives, not completeness on its own.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Noun with a Declarative Content Complement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/content-clause-in-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Content and Container Subject Alternation
pattern: Clause[content + V + in-location PP ↔ location + V + with-content PP]

entry.name: Content and Container Subject Alternation
entry.pattern: Clause[content + V + in-location PP ↔ location + V + with-content PP]

1.definition: Presents an activity either through its participants or as a state of the place they occupy.

projection.target: The courtyard is the subject and bees the with-complement, despite bees performing the activity. The location-subject form is restricted to suitable verbs and does not follow from general PP inversion.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Describing the place instead of the crowd
curious.summary: A busy scene can be described through the things doing the activity or through the place where it happens.
curious.body: You can report the same scene in two ways. One starts with what is doing the activity: Bees swarmed in the courtyard. The other starts with the place: The courtyard swarmed with bees. In the second, the courtyard is the subject of the sentence, and the bees come in a phrase beginning with. The second way presents the scene as a state of the place, rather than as something the bees are doing. This dictionary treats that analysis as provisional. It also notes that only suitable verbs allow the place-first form, so it can't be assumed to work wherever the other does.
curious.try: Take a sentence that says what something is doing in a place. Can you turn it round so the place comes first and the sentence says what the place is full of?

teacher.summary: Low priority for most classes: this dictionary's only example rests on swarm, which is relatively infrequent (about 16,500th among word forms in the SUBTLEX-UK subtitle counts, and swarmed about 47,600th), so treat it if it comes up rather than teaching it. Helps explain why a place can be the subject of a verb of activity, as in The courtyard swarmed with bees.
teacher.explain: The pattern pairs two ways of presenting one scene. In one, the content (the things performing the activity) is subject and the place is in a locative PP: Bees swarmed in the courtyard. In the other, the place is subject and the content is in a with-PP: The courtyard swarmed with bees. In the second, the courtyard is the subject and bees is the with-complement, even though the bees perform the activity. The place-subject form is restricted to suitable verbs and does not follow from general PP inversion. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary's name for the pattern is content and container subject alternation.

contrasts.note: Place as subject, content in a with-phrase.
Content as subject, place in an in-phrase.

watch_for: A learner might take bees to be the subject of The courtyard swarmed with bees because the bees do the swarming.
A learner might assume the place-subject form is available with any verb that allows the content-subject form.
teacher.activity: If the pattern comes up in a reading, write The courtyard swarmed with bees and Bees swarmed in the courtyard on the board. Students underline the subject of each sentence and say which phrase names the place and which names the bees.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.summary now opens by marking the entry low priority (swarm about 16,500th in SUBTLEX-UK); activity no longer has students produce place-subject sentences with verbs like swarm, and is now a recognition task on the two board sentences.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Content and Container Subject Alternation." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/content-container-alternation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Continuative away at

1.definition: Describes sustained or repeated activity directed at a target.
1.details: The activity can consist of many small effects on the target without presenting a finished result. The combination sometimes allows a verb that is markedly less acceptable with at alone. Away here has an aspectual contribution. A directional away from construction has a separate interpretation.

examples.form: Simmy was [carving away at the roast].
examples.note: Published comparison. The version without away was judged degraded.

examples.form: They [worked away at the problem] all afternoon.
examples.note: Constructed example. The duration concerns the work and does not imply a solution.

relatedConstructions.notes: The two patterns share a target at-phrase and differ in aspect and available verbs.
Both have nonlocative away, but the time-away pattern licenses a time object.

grounds.note: Distinguishes extended action and more specific readings.
Gives the carve contrast alongside other uses of aspectual away.

projection.target: Away favours an extended or repeated reading. In the published carve pair it also improves the target-at frame without adding a spatial direction.
projection.evidence: The Birmingham inventory separates duration, effort, bit-by-bit damage and ingestion. Jackendoff gives a comparison holding the verb and target fixed.

curious.title: Keeping at something with away
curious.summary: Adding away and at to a verb presents an activity as sustained or repeated, aimed at a target.
curious.body: In They worked away at the problem all afternoon, away doesn't mean that anyone went anywhere. It adds the idea that the work went on, without saying the problem was solved. The target of the effort comes after at. The same idea fits Simmy was carving away at the roast: the carving is presented as sustained, with no finished result announced. This dictionary also says that away can help a verb fit the at frame when it would be judged worse with at alone. A different pattern, with away from, is about direction and is a separate matter.

examples.text: Simmy was [carving away at the roast].
They [worked away at the problem] all afternoon.

curious.try: Compare They worked at the problem with They worked away at the problem. Which one sounds more like long, patient effort?

teacher.summary: Helps explain how away plus an at-phrase marks ongoing or repeated effort aimed at a target.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb followed by away and an at-phrase: V away at NP. Away contributes aspect, not direction. It presents the activity as sustained or repeated, possibly made of many small effects on the target, without a finished result. A published comparison (carve with and without away) suggests that away can also license a verb that is judged markedly less acceptable with at alone. The analysis is provisional. Don't confuse it with directional away from, which has a separate interpretation, or with the conative at pattern, which shares the target at-phrase but differs in aspect and available verbs.
teacher.terms: This dictionary describes away here as making an aspectual contribution, not a directional one.

examples.text: Simmy was [carving away at the roast].
They [worked away at the problem] all afternoon.

contrasts.text: They worked away at the problem all afternoon.
contrasts.note: Away marks sustained effort; the problem needn't be solved.

contrasts.text: They walked away from the problem.
contrasts.note: Away from is directional, a separate interpretation.

watch_for: A learner might read away in worked away at as movement away from something.
A learner might take worked away at the problem to mean the problem was solved.
teacher.activity: Students act out or describe tasks that take many small efforts (chipping ice, cleaning a pan, fixing a bike). They complete "She was ___ away at the ___" with working or chipping and say what the sentence leaves open about whether the job finished.

child.hook: What does away mean in "She worked away at her homework"?
child.explain: Sometimes away doesn't mean going anywhere. It means you keep doing something for a while. Working away at homework means working on it for a good while.

examples.text: They [worked away at the problem] all afternoon.
Dad was [chipping away at the ice].

child.play: Pick a job, like scrubbing or colouring. Say it with away at, then act it out for ten seconds. Does it feel like one quick action or like something that keeps going?

checked.note: Fixed: removed the claim that the work in the problem example consisted of many small efforts (the entry says only that it conveys duration and leaves the result open) and the matching many-small-cuts reading of the carving example; child explain and play now speak of keeping going rather than bit by bit. Frequency pass: teacher.activity tasks scrubbing and sanding (scrub about 8,900th in SUBTLEX-UK; sanding rarer) replaced by everyday tasks, and the frame is now filled with working or chipping; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Continuative away at." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/continuative-away-at-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Continuative Perfect
pattern: Clause[perfect have + past-participial VP + duration reaching the reference time]

entry.name: Continuative Perfect
entry.pattern: Clause[perfect have + past-participial VP + duration reaching the reference time]

1.definition: Presents a situation as holding through an interval ending at the relevant temporal anchor.

examples.form: Jo [had lived there since April] when we met.
examples.note: Constructed comparison. Past reference point supplied by the meeting.

relatedConstructions.notes: I’ve lived here since 2019 allows an ongoing-state reading. I’ve visited three times since 2019 counts completed episodes within the same interval.
Since 2019 supplies the start time in I’ve lived here since 2019. Since also combines with experiential uses, so it does not force continuity.

projection.target: With a suitable stative predicate and since-anchor, the ordinary reading extends residence to the present or other reference time. An experiential perfect need only locate an occurrence before that time.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Having done something up to now
curious.summary: Some have-sentences say that a situation has been going on through a stretch of time that ends at the moment being talked about.
curious.body: In Jo has lived here since April, Jo still lives here: the living-here stretches from April up to now. The sentence presents a situation as holding through an interval that ends at the relevant time. That time needn't be now. In Jo had lived there since April when we met, the stretch ends at the meeting. This reading goes with a suitable state, like living somewhere, and a phrase giving the starting point. A sentence like I've visited three times since 2019 is different: it counts separate occasions rather than describing something ongoing.

examples.text: Jo [had lived there since April] when we met.

curious.try: Say I've lived here since 2019, then I've visited three times since 2019. Which one describes something still going on?

teacher.summary: Helps explain the ongoing-state reading of the perfect, as in has lived here since April.
teacher.explain: The continuative perfect combines perfect have, a past-participial VP and a duration reaching the reference time. With a suitable stative predicate and a since-anchor, the ordinary reading extends the situation to the present, or to another reference time supplied by context (when we met). Contrast the experiential perfect, which only locates an occurrence before the reference time: I've visited three times since 2019 counts completed episodes within the same interval. Since does not force continuity, because it also combines with experiential uses. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Perfect have appears in what textbooks call the present perfect (has lived) and past perfect (had lived). Continuative and experiential name two readings of it.

examples.text: Jo [had lived there since April] when we met.

contrasts.note: Ongoing-state reading is available.
Counts completed episodes in the interval.

watch_for: A learner might read has lived here since April as a completed past event.
A learner might assume that since signals an ongoing state.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of since-sentences, some with states (live, know, work at) and some with countable events (visit, call). They sort them into "still going on" and "counted occasions" and discuss the cues.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Continuative Perfect." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/continuative-perfect-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Comparative Reduplication with and
pattern: AdjP/AdvP[comparative XP + and + identical comparative XP]

entry.name: Comparative Reduplication with and
entry.pattern: AdjP/AdvP[comparative XP + and + identical comparative XP]

1.definition: Presents degree as progressively increasing or decreasing over a relevant interval.

projection.target: Repeating the same comparative yields continued change rather than identifying two independent properties. The corresponding plain-grade repetition has other uses.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Fainter and fainter
curious.summary: Repeating a comparative word with and says that something keeps changing by degrees.
curious.body: In The sound grew fainter and fainter, the same word is said twice, joined by and. The sentence doesn't mention two different qualities. It says the faintness kept increasing. What's repeated has to be a comparative, the kind of form that compares degrees. Repeating the plain form has other uses, and this dictionary treats the pattern as a separate case. The analysis here is provisional.
curious.try: Finish the sentence "The music got ___ and ___" with one comparative word twice. What changes over time?

teacher.summary: Helps explain warmer and warmer and similar repetitions that mean progressive increase or decrease.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a coordination of two identical comparatives (AdjP or AdvP): fainter and fainter. Repeating the same comparative yields continued change over a relevant interval, not two independent properties, as separate adjectives would (cold and wet). This dictionary treats it as a specialization of coordination. The corresponding plain-grade repetition has other uses, so this reading belongs to the comparative form. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call the -er or more form the comparative degree. Here comparative is a grade of the adjective or adverb.

contrasts.text: The sound grew fainter and fainter.
contrasts.note: One property, increasing over the interval.

contrasts.text: The room was cold and wet.
contrasts.note: Two different properties, ordinary coordination.

watch_for: A learner might read fainter and fainter as two separate qualities rather than one that keeps increasing.
teacher.activity: Students describe a changing situation (a balloon inflating, a storm approaching, a sunset) using the pattern, then replace it with a sentence about two different properties and say how the meaning shifts.

child.hook: How would you say a sound is getting quieter and quieter?
child.explain: When we say a word like fainter or warmer twice with and, it can mean something keeps changing. The sound grew fainter and fainter. It means it kept getting fainter.
child.play: Pick a changing thing, like a balloon or the sun. Describe it with one word twice, like bigger and bigger. Can a friend guess what is happening?

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain now limits the pattern to a repeated comparative word like fainter or warmer, as the entry does; curious.body no longer ties the comparative to an ending; 'steady' changed to 'progressive' (teacher.summary); 'as time went on' and 'over time' changed to match the entry's 'relevant interval'. Second round: fixed curious.body, which said the repeated unit had to be a single comparative word (the entry repeats a comparative adjective or adverb phrase). Frequency pass: teacher.summary now names warmer and warmer (already a constructed example) instead of fainter and fainter (fainter about 42,600th in SUBTLEX-UK); the entry example is unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Comparative Reduplication with and." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/coordinate-degree-reduplication-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Coordination

dimensions.form: Two or more coordinates, optionally linked by coordinators (and, or, but, nor); no head
dimensions.meaning: Joint contribution of the coordinates (conjunction, disjunction, contrast, addition)
dimensions.function: Whatever function the coordinates jointly serve
dimensions.distribution: Distributes as its coordinates allow; category difference between coordinates is tolerated where there is likeness of function

1.definition: A non-headed constituent made up of coordinates; not a phrase
1.details: Coordinations contrast with phrases, which are headed (see phrase-001). No coordinate is the head; the coordination's distribution follows from the coordinates jointly, and a difference of category is generally tolerated where there is likeness of function (e.g., the DP + NP numerative coordinations in two thousand and twenty-seven).

examples.note: Numerative coordination; coordinates of different categories under likeness of function

constraints.description: No head; each coordinate could typically stand in the coordination's position alone.

projection.target: Identifying a constituent as a coordination predicts headlessness (no single element determines distribution), coordinate-wise distribution, and tolerance of category mixture under likeness of function
projection.evidence: Coordinate-category mixture under functional likeness is attested across the numerative coordinations and ordinary NP/AdjP coordination

grounds.note: Non-headed coordinate structure projects coordinate-wise distribution and functional likeness
The same non-headed profile recurs across coordination categories

relatedConstructions.notes: The headed constituent type; the contrast is definitional
Both are non-headed constituent types, but coordination is organized into coordinates rather than licensed by clausal semantics

curious.title: Joining things with and, or and but
curious.summary: Words like and, or and but can link two or more equal parts, and none of the parts is in charge.
curious.body: In bread and butter, two nouns sit side by side, linked by and. In slowly but surely, two adverbs are linked by but. Neither part is the boss of the other. A group like this is called a coordination, and it adds up the contributions of its parts: joining, choosing, contrasting or adding. A coordination can do whatever its parts do together in the sentence. Its parts needn't be exactly the same kind of word, as long as they do a similar job. Two thousand and twenty-seven joins two number expressions of different kinds this way. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Take a sentence with bread and butter in it. Can you take away and butter and still have a sentence?

teacher.summary: Helps explain coordinations as headless groups of equal parts joined by and, or, but or nor.
teacher.explain: A coordination is a non-headed constituent made up of two or more coordinates, optionally linked by a coordinator (and, or, but, nor). It isn't a phrase, because phrases are headed. No coordinate is the head, so the group's distribution follows from the coordinates jointly. Each coordinate could typically stand alone in the coordination's position. Coordinates can differ in category where their functions are alike, as in two thousand and twenty-seven. The meaning is the joint contribution of the coordinates: conjunction, disjunction, contrast or addition.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars call the linking words coordinating conjunctions. This grammar calls them coordinators and treats the group as a coordination rather than a phrase.

contrasts.note: Coordination of two nouns; no head.
A phrase, with a head noun and a dependent.

watch_for: A learner might look for a head word in bread and butter, as in a noun phrase, when neither noun is the head.
A learner might think the coordinates must be the same category, when a similar function is enough.
teacher.activity: Students write short coordinations with and, or and but (nouns, adjectives, adverbs). For each, they test whether either part could stand alone in the same sentence, and note the meaning the coordinator adds.

child.hook: What do the words and, or and but do when they join two things?
child.explain: Small words like and, or and but can join two things. In bread and butter, both words matter equally. Neither one is the boss.
child.play: Pick a food. Join it to another with and, then with or. Say each one in a sentence. How does the meaning change?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Coordination." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/coordination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Gapping in Coordination
pattern: coordination[Clause₁ + (Coordinator) + Clause₂ with a medial gap between remnants]

entry.name: Gapping in Coordination
entry.pattern: coordination[Clause₁ + (Coordinator) + Clause₂ with a medial gap between remnants]

1.definition: Contrasts corresponding elements of linked predications while leaving repeated medial material unspoken.
1.details: In Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne, the second clause is understood with lives. Both Pat and in Melbourne contrast with material in the first clause. The gap can contain more than the verb. The ordinary construction depends on a coordinate or closely parallel discourse relation.

examples.form: [Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne.]
examples.note: The second pair of contrasting expressions flanks the gap for lives.
Constructed example with two contrasting remnants in the second clause.

relatedConstructions.notes: The pattern can link coordinated clauses.
Jo ordered tea and Kai coffee allows recovery of ordered in the second clause. Jo gave Kim tea and Kai coffee can instead coordinate two argument clusters under one subject and verb.
Gapping leaves repeated predicative material unexpressed in a later coordinate. Right-edge sharing expresses a constituent once at the far right, with an interpretation in more than one coordinate.

grounds.note: Describes contrasting material around a shared medial sequence.
Documents gaps of different lengths and the relation to coordination.

projection.target: The repeated verb or overt medial sequence can be absent between two contrastive remnants. This distinguishes gapping from final VP ellipsis after a stranded auxiliary.
projection.evidence: FrameNet specifies the positions around the gap. CGEL documents multiword gaps and the relative restrictions on coordination.

curious.title: Leaving out the repeated middle
curious.summary: When two linked sentences share a verb, the second can leave it out and keep only the parts that differ.
curious.body: In Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne, the second part has no verb. We understand it with lives anyway: Pat lives in Melbourne. What's left is the contrast, Pat against Kim and Melbourne against Perth. The gap can hold more than just the verb. The shortcut works when the two parts are linked and parallel, as in Sam ordered tea and Lee coffee. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne.]

curious.try: Make up a sentence about two people who each do the same thing to different objects. Can you leave the second verb out?

teacher.summary: Helps explain how the second of two parallel clauses can omit a repeated verb, as in Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne.
teacher.explain: In gapping, a coordinated clause leaves repeated medial material unspoken between two contrasting remnants.
