In Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne, the second clause is understood with lives; Pat and in Melbourne each contrast with material in the first clause. The gap can contain more than the verb. The ordinary construction depends on a coordinate or closely parallel discourse relation. It differs from final VP ellipsis after a stranded auxiliary. Compare right argument cluster coordination, where two argument clusters share one subject and verb: Jo gave Kim tea and Kai coffee can be read that way instead.
teacher.terms: Gapping is the usual textbook name. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of coordination.

examples.text: [Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne.]

contrasts.text: Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne.
contrasts.note: Second clause understood with lives; remnants contrast with the first.

contrasts.text: Jo gave Kim tea and Kai coffee.
contrasts.note: Can instead coordinate two argument clusters under one subject and verb.

watch_for: A learner might read Pat in Melbourne as an incomplete sentence rather than one understood with lives.
A learner might think only the verb can be left out, when the gap can contain more.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of full parallel clauses (Sam ordered tea. Lee ordered coffee.). They join each pair into one sentence, leaving out the repeated verb, and say which words must stay to keep the contrast clear.

child.hook: Can you say two things in one sentence without saying the verb twice?
child.explain: Sometimes the second half of a sentence leaves out a word we already heard. Sam ordered tea and Lee coffee. We still know Lee ordered coffee.

examples.text: Kim lives in Perth, Pat in Melbourne.

child.play: Pick two friends and two foods they like. Say a sentence about the first. Then add the second friend and their food, but don't say the verb again.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Gapping in Coordination." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/coordination-gapping-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Corrective not X but Y

1.definition: Rejects one description and substitutes another as the intended one.

projection.target: Not applies to the rejected candidate, and but introduces the correction. This differs from concessive but, where both coordinated propositions can be asserted.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Not this but that
curious.summary: The not-but pattern turns down one description and puts another in its place.
curious.body: In I ordered not tea but coffee, not marks tea as the wrong candidate, and but brings in the correction. The speaker is saying what was ordered by ruling out one choice and naming the right one. This differs from the but in a sentence like It was cheap but good. There, both parts can be asserted. In the not-but pattern the first part is rejected and the second is offered in its place. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: She wanted [not a quick answer but a good one].

curious.try: Think of a time you corrected someone's guess. How would you say it with not and but?

teacher.summary: Helps explain not X but Y as a correction that rejects one description and substitutes another.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a coordination of the form not XP + but XP. Not applies to the rejected candidate, and but introduces the correction: I ordered not tea but coffee. This differs from concessive but, where both coordinated propositions can be asserted (It was cheap but good). This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of coordination and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls the pattern corrective not X but Y and sets it apart from concessive but.

examples.text: She wanted [not a quick answer but a good one].

contrasts.text: I ordered not tea but coffee.
contrasts.note: Corrective; tea is rejected, coffee substituted.
Concessive but; both parts are asserted.

watch_for: A learner might read not tea but coffee as concessive but, as if both were ordered.
A learner might attach not only to the verb rather than to the rejected candidate.
teacher.activity: Give students mistaken statements ("You ordered tea."). They correct each one aloud with a not X but Y sentence, then rewrite one as a concessive but sentence and compare the meanings.

child.hook: How do you tell someone they guessed wrong and give the right answer?
child.explain: You can say what something isn't and then what it is. I ordered not tea but coffee. The first thing is turned down. The second is the right one.

examples.text: We went to [not the park but the beach].

child.play: Make up two guesses about what's in a box. Correct each with not and but. Who can come up with the silliest right answer?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Corrective not X but Y." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/corrective-but-coordination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deadjectival Noun in -ity
pattern: N[adjectival base + -ity], sometimes with a stem alternation

entry.name: Deadjectival Noun in -ity
entry.pattern: N[adjectival base + -ity], sometimes with a stem alternation

1.definition: Names a quality or state associated with the adjective.
1.details: -ity typically stresses the syllable immediately before the ending. It may also alter the end of the base, as in curious and curiosity. Formations cluster with particular adjective types. The corresponding -ness formation typically preserves the base’s shape and stress.

examples.note: Existing derivative illustrating stress shift from eccentric and a change in the final consonant.
Existing derivative illustrating shift of stress and the form of the base.

relatedConstructions.notes: The output is a common noun.

grounds.note: Distinguishes the -ity nominal from -ness.
Documents stress, vowel changes, velar softening and stem alternation.

projection.target: Recognizable -ity derivatives generally have stress just before the suffix. The pattern allows changes to the base that the productive -ness pattern does not.
projection.evidence: CGEL gives matched stress and stem contrasts. CASA records -ity separately from -ness.

curious.title: Nouns ending in -ity
curious.summary: Adding -ity to an adjective can name the quality it describes, sometimes changing how the word sounds.
curious.body: Curious is an adjective, and curiosity names the quality of being curious. Eccentric becomes eccentricity in the same way. The ending -ity typically puts the stress on the syllable just before it. The base word can change too, as in curious and curiosity, where the end of the word is altered. The -ness ending does something similar, but it typically leaves the base word's shape and stress as they were. Which adjectives take -ity depends on the adjective type.
curious.try: Say eccentric and then eccentricity out loud. Where does the strongest beat fall in each?

teacher.summary: Helps explain -ity nouns such as ability and curiosity, including stress shift and changes to the base.
teacher.explain: The pattern forms a common noun from an adjective plus -ity, sometimes with a stem alternation. The noun names a quality or state associated with the adjective. -ity typically stresses the syllable immediately before the ending. It may also alter the end of the base, as in curious and curiosity, and as in eccentric and eccentricity, where the final consonant changes. Formations cluster with particular adjective types. The corresponding -ness formation typically preserves the base's shape and stress, so the two suffixes behave differently. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars call these abstract nouns formed by suffixation. This dictionary treats the output as a common noun.

contrasts.note: Stress shifts and the final consonant changes.
-ness keeps the base's shape.

watch_for: A learner might expect curiosity to keep the exact shape and stress of curious.
A learner might assume -ity and -ness are interchangeable on any adjective.
teacher.activity: Give students adjective and noun pairs (able, ability; kind, kindness). They mark the stressed syllable in each word and compare what -ity and -ness do to the base.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.summary now names ability and curiosity instead of curiosity and eccentricity (eccentricity about 32,700th in SUBTLEX-UK); added the constructed teacher example ability; activity pair curious, curiosity replaced by able, ability; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deadjectival Noun in -ity." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deadjectival-ity-noun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Change Verb in -ize

1.definition: Forms a verb for causing or undergoing a change connected to the adjectival base.

projection.target: In the transparent causative use stable specifies a result. The -ize family also has noun bases and lexicalized meanings beyond this construction.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Verbs ending in -ize
curious.summary: Adding -ize to an adjective can make a verb meaning to cause or undergo a change tied to that adjective.
curious.body: Stable is an adjective, and stabilize is a verb. In The update should stabilize the connection, the verb means to make the connection stable. The adjective names the result of the change. The -ize ending is also added to nouns, and some -ize verbs have meanings of their own that go beyond this pattern. This dictionary's pattern is the one built on an adjective, where the verb means causing or undergoing a change connected to that adjective. The analysis is provisional. The pattern is also written with the spelling -ise.
curious.try: Think of an adjective, such as stable, and add -ize. What would the new verb mean?

teacher.summary: Helps explain verbs like stabilize formed from an adjective with -ize or -ise. Stabilize itself is relatively infrequent (its British spelling stabilise is about 12,300th among word forms in the SUBTLEX-UK subtitle counts).
teacher.explain: The pattern forms a verb from an adjective base plus -ize (or -ise), meaning to cause or undergo a change connected to the adjective. In the transparent causative use, the adjective stable specifies the result of stabilize. The -ize family also has noun bases and lexicalized meanings beyond this construction, so the adjective's contribution may not be transparent. This dictionary links this pattern to the causative-inchoative entry and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call -ize a verb-forming suffix. This dictionary treats the pattern as a morphological construction from an adjective.

contrasts.note: The adjective names the result.

contrasts.text: The update should stabilize the connection.
contrasts.note: The verb causes the connection to become stable.

watch_for: A learner might assume every -ize verb comes from an adjective, when some have noun bases.
A learner might assume the meaning of every -ize verb follows from its base.
teacher.activity: Give students adjectives (stable, final, legal). They form verbs with -ize if the verb exists, write a sentence for each, and check each in a dictionary to see whether the result matches the adjective's meaning.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says this dictionary covers only the transparent-result case (the entry defines the pattern as a change connected to the adjective; transparent result is the causative use); 'causative-inchoative alternation' changed to 'entry'; 'derivational' changed to 'morphological' as in the entry. Frequency pass: teacher.summary now opens by marking the pattern as mainly useful for academic reading and writing (the British spelling stabilise alone is about 12,300th in SUBTLEX-UK; stabilize is rarer there), not low priority; activity unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Change Verb in -ize." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deadjectival-ize-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deadjectival Noun in -ness

1.definition: Names a property or state characterized by the base adjective.
1.details: The regular formation preserves the stress of the base. Novel formations are generally interpretable given a recognizable adjective. Some derivatives lexicalize specialized readings. Competing -ity may shift stress or alter the base.

examples.note: Constructed example with the stress of awkward preserved.

relatedConstructions.notes: The output is a common noun.
The core pattern selects an adjective as its base.
Both suffixes can create property nouns, as in kindness and opacity. The adjective base constrains the choice of suffix and can have a different stem form before -ity.

grounds.note: Distinguishes the two derivational patterns.
Documents stress, stem alternations and productivity in the two patterns.

projection.target: The regular -ness output retains base stress, and the pattern supports novel property nouns. A competing -ity formation can change the stress or shape of the base.
projection.evidence: CASA gives separate -ness and -ity records. CGEL documents their formal and productivity contrast.

curious.title: Nouns ending in -ness
curious.summary: Adding -ness to an adjective makes a noun naming the property or state the adjective describes.
curious.body: Clear is an adjective, and clearness names the property of being clear. In the clearness of the recording, the noun phrase talks about how clear the recording is. The same works with awkward and awkwardness. A regular -ness noun keeps the stress of the base word. New formations can generally be understood if the adjective is familiar, though some -ness words have specialized meanings of their own. The -ity ending competes with it: both can make property nouns, as in kindness and opacity, and -ity can change the base.
curious.try: Choose an adjective for how you feel today and add -ness. Does the new word make sense?

teacher.summary: Helps explain -ness nouns such as kindness, and how they differ from -ity nouns.
teacher.explain: The pattern forms a common noun from an adjective plus -ness, naming a property or state characterized by the adjective. The regular formation preserves the stress of the base. Novel formations are generally interpretable given a recognizable adjective, although some derivatives lexicalize specialized readings. Competing -ity may shift stress or alter the base: both suffixes can create property nouns, as in kindness and opacity, and the adjective base constrains the choice of suffix.
teacher.terms: These are sometimes treated under abstract nouns, a broader label. This dictionary treats the output as a common noun.

contrasts.note: -ness noun, built on kind.
-ity forms a property noun and can alter the base.

watch_for: A learner might think -ness and -ity can be swapped on any adjective.
A learner might assume every -ness noun means only the adjective's quality, when some have specialized readings.
teacher.activity: Students list familiar adjectives and add -ness to each, using the new nouns in sentences such as "The ___ of the ___ surprised us." They mark which words, if any, also have an -ity partner.

child.hook: What do you call being kind? What about being clear?
child.explain: You can add -ness to a describing word to name the quality. Kind becomes kindness. Kind is still right there inside kindness.

examples.text: I liked [the clearness of the recording].

child.play: Pick five describing words, like soft, bright and sad. Add -ness to each and use it in a sentence. Which new word is your favourite?

checked.note: Fixed: kindness (-ness) and opacity (-ity) no longer presented as examples of what -ity does; stress preservation stated of regular -ness formations; child line no longer claims the whole pronunciation is kept; child example with added words relabelled constructed; 'abstract nouns' flagged as a broader label. Dismissed: none. Frequency pass: teacher.summary now names kindness instead of clearness and awkwardness (about 91,500th and 37,200th in SUBTLEX-UK); constructed -ity contrast opacity (about 97,100th) replaced by ability; teacher.explain still quotes the entry's kindness and opacity; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deadjectival Noun in -ness." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deadjectival-ness-noun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Declarative Clause

dimensions.form: Clause headed by a VP, with an optional Subject and no interrogative, exclamative, or imperative clause-type marking
dimensions.meaning: Presents propositional content without encoding an open or closed question, remarkable degree, or imperative marking as clause type
dimensions.function: Characteristically makes a statement, but also supports directives, promises, questions, and other forces
dimensions.distribution: The default clause type; occurs as a main clause and as a subordinate content clause

1.definition: The default headed clause type, characteristically used to make a statement
1.details: Declarative is a category of syntactic form, not a statement-force category. Basic declaratives normally have Subject–Predicator order, but their actual force depends on construction and context: Passengers are requested to remain seated is a directive, and a declarative question adds question intonation to declarative syntax. Declaratives occur both as main clauses and as subordinate content clauses (CGEL pp. 853–55, 951–55).

examples.note: Main declarative in its characteristic statement use
Declarative clause used as a directive; force does not determine clause type

examples.form: She says [that Kim finished the report].

constraints.description: The construction is a Clause headed by VP, with an optional Subject; declarative is the default type and lacks the specialized type-marking properties of closed interrogatives, open interrogatives, exclamatives, and imperatives.
Statement is the characteristic use, not a necessary condition: declarative syntax is compatible with indirect questions and directives and with performative forces such as promising.

projection.target: Basic declarative clause structure predicts broad main- and subordinate-clause distribution and leaves illocutionary force comparatively open, while making statement force the unmarked interpretation in an independent assertion context
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts the declarative's default Subject–Predicator organization and broad content-clause distribution with the specialized marking and distribution of the other four major clause types

grounds.note: Default declarative form projects broad main/subordinate distribution without fixing illocutionary force
The form/distribution profile recurs independently of characteristic statement use

diagnostics: absence of interrogative, exclamative, or imperative type marking

grounds.note: Declarative as the default major clause type, distinct from statement force, in main and subordinate clauses

curious.title: The plain statement-shaped sentence
curious.summary: A declarative sentence is the default sentence shape, and it is built for making statements but can do other jobs too.
curious.body: Kim finished the report is the plainest kind of sentence. It has no question word, no exclamation form and no command form. This dictionary calls that shape declarative. It is the default type, and it turns up both as a sentence on its own and inside another sentence, as in She says that Kim finished the report. Making a statement is the characteristic use of this shape, but the shape doesn't fix the job. Passengers are requested to remain seated has the same shape and works as a directive. Declarative names a form, not a purpose. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: She says [that Kim finished the report].

curious.try: Look at a sign or announcement that sounds like a statement. Is it telling you something, or asking you to do something?

teacher.summary: Helps separate declarative as a clause form from statement as a use, since declarative clauses can also direct, promise and ask.
teacher.explain: A declarative clause is the default headed clause type: a Clause headed by a VP, with an optional Subject, and no interrogative, exclamative or imperative marking. Basic declaratives normally have Subject-Predicator order. Declarative is a category of syntactic form, not statement force. Statement is the characteristic use, but force depends on construction and context: Passengers are requested to remain seated is a directive, and a declarative question adds question intonation to declarative syntax. Declaratives occur as main clauses and as subordinate content clauses. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars call this the declarative sentence and tie it to making statements. This dictionary separates clause type (declarative) from force (statement, directive and so on).

examples.text: She says [that Kim finished the report].

contrasts.note: Declarative form, used to make a statement.

contrasts.text: Passengers are requested to remain seated.
contrasts.note: Same form, used as a directive.

watch_for: A learner might assume that a declarative clause must make a statement, when its force depends on construction and context.
A learner might treat a clause inside another sentence, as in She says that Kim finished the report, as not declarative, when declaratives also occur as subordinate content clauses.
teacher.activity: Students collect short declarative sentences from notices and announcements around the school. They sort each by what it does (states, directs, promises, asks) and discuss how they can tell.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Declarative Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/declarative-clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Declarative Content Clause

1.definition: Presents propositional content as part of a larger construction.
1.details: That can be optional after a verb such as say or in subject extraposition. It is required in ordinary fully expressed initial clausal subjects. Whether the proposition is reported, presupposed, or questioned depends on the matrix construction.

examples.form: [That they were lying] is now quite obvious.
examples.note: Initial clausal subject requires that in this example.
Constructed post-verbal complement. The bracketed that itself can be omitted.

relatedConstructions.notes: The subordinate pattern preserves declarative order in the nucleus.
Extraposition creates one position in which that is often optional.
That can mark either construction. In Jo said that Kai read it the content clause has its own object. In the book that Kai read the relative links an object gap to book.

grounds.note: Documents context-sensitive marking and functions of declarative content clauses.

projection.target: The same declarative content requires that in a canonical initial subject and can omit it in the corresponding extraposed subject.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares the same proposition and matrix predicate with the content clause in those two positions. CASA’s it-that record is one context for the broader pattern.

curious.title: When that can be left out
curious.summary: The part of a sentence that gives what someone believes or says can be introduced by that, which is sometimes optional and sometimes required.
curious.body: In I believe they were lying, the part they were lying gives the content of the belief, inside a larger sentence. The word that can introduce it: I believe that they were lying. After a verb like believe, that can be left out. It isn't always optional. When that part comes first as the subject of an ordinary, fully expressed sentence, as in That they were lying is now quite obvious, the sentence requires that. Whether the content is reported, taken for granted or questioned depends on the larger sentence around it. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [That they were lying] is now quite obvious.

curious.try: Take a sentence like I believe they were lying. Add that after believe. Does it still work? Now compare That they were lying is now quite obvious, where that is required.

teacher.summary: Helps explain when that is optional or required before a declarative content clause.
teacher.explain: A declarative content clause is a subordinate clause, optionally introduced by that, that presents propositional content as part of a larger construction. That can be optional after a verb such as say or believe, and in subject extraposition. It is required in ordinary fully expressed initial clausal subjects: That they were lying is now quite obvious. Whether the proposition is reported, presupposed or questioned depends on the matrix construction. The subordinate clause preserves declarative order. Don't confuse it with a relative clause: in Jo said that Kai read it the content clause has its own object, while in the book that Kai read the relative links an object gap to book.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call these that-clauses or noun clauses. This dictionary calls them declarative content clauses.

examples.text: [That they were lying] is now quite obvious.

contrasts.text: I believe that they were lying.
contrasts.note: That introduces the content clause after a verb.

contrasts.text: Jo said that Kai read it.
contrasts.note: Content clause with its own object.
Relative clause linked to book through an object gap.

watch_for: A learner might assume that can be dropped in every position, when it is required in an ordinary initial clausal subject.
A learner might treat that as the same in Jo said that Kai read it and the book that Kai read, when one introduces a content clause and the other a relative.
teacher.activity: Give students matrix verbs (say, believe, know) and a short statement. They build sentences with and without that, then try the statement as the subject at the start, noting where that must stay.

checked.note: Fixed: curious text no longer calls the embedded part a statement in its own right (in I believe they were lying it supplies the content of the belief; what is done with it depends on the larger construction); the requirement for that is now stated for ordinary, fully expressed initial clausal subjects, as in the entry.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Declarative Content Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/declarative-content-clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Declarative Question
pattern: Question[closed, same-polarity bias] applied to Declarative Clause + question intonation

entry.name: Declarative Question
entry.pattern: Question[closed, same-polarity bias] applied to Declarative Clause + question intonation

dimensions.form: Declarative Clause syntax, without subject–auxiliary inversion, combined with question intonation or corresponding question punctuation
dimensions.meaning: A polar question strongly biased toward the answer with the same propositional content and polarity as the declarative base
dimensions.function: Typically seeks confirmation of a proposition the speaker is already inclined to accept
dimensions.distribution: Independent declarative Clauses in confirmation-seeking and other strongly biased question contexts

1.definition: A declarative Clause used as a strongly same-polarity-biased question through question prosody
1.details: Positive declarative questions are biased toward a positive answer and negative declarative questions toward a negative answer. The expected answer therefore has the same propositional content as the question, and confirmatory responses such as That's right, Exactly, and Quite so are especially natural. Question is the semantic category applied to a syntactically declarative Clause, with question intonation marking the combination; the host does not change clause type. It is not an echo question, since it need not repeat or query the wording of a prior stimulus (CGEL pp. 879–83).

examples.note: Positive declarative question biased toward confirmation that they have finished
Negative declarative question biased toward confirmation that they have not finished

examples.form: [And the manager has been informed, of course?]
examples.note: Confidence marker reinforces the positive bias while remaining outside question scope

examples.form: [There isn't any chance of her changing her mind, I take it?]
examples.note: Natural confirmation-seeking declarative question with negative polarity

constraints.description: The Clause retains declarative syntax and is headed by VP; there is no clause-type-triggered subject–auxiliary inversion.
Question intonation in speech, or corresponding question punctuation in writing, supplies the question interpretation without changing declarative clause type.
Question is a semantic classification of the whole form–interpretation pairing, while declarative remains the syntactic type of the headed host Clause.
The construction is strongly epistemically biased toward the same-polarity answer and is infelicitous as a neutral request between equally open positive and negative alternatives.
No prior utterance is required. If the form instead queries whether particular wording was said or heard, the independent echo-question construction is involved.

projection.target: Declarative order plus question prosody predicts strong same-polarity bias, confirmation-seeking function, and compatibility with responses such as That's right or Exactly, in contrast to a neutral closed interrogative
projection.evidence: Positive and negative declarative questions consistently reverse neither polarity nor expected answer; their response profile and confidence-marker compatibility diagnose bias independently of declarative word order

grounds.note: Question interpretation applied to declarative form projects polarity bias and response profile
The same-polarity bias recurs across positive and negative declarative questions

known_boundary_items: She is a genius?: ordinary declarative question if it asks whether she is a genius; echo question if it asks whether the speaker said that she is

relatedConstructions.notes: Declarative Question is the same-polarity-biased subtype realized on a declarative Clause
The syntactic host retains declarative Clause type while receiving question semantics
Closed interrogatives use interrogative syntax and can be neutral; declarative questions retain declarative syntax and are strongly biased
Echo questions depend on a stimulus and question some aspect of that prior wording; ordinary declarative questions need not

grounds.note: Declarative questions as strongly biased indirect questions with same-polarity expectations and distinctive response patterns

curious.title: Asking by tone of voice
curious.summary: A statement-shaped sentence said with a questioning tone can ask for confirmation of something the speaker already expects.
curious.body: They've finished? has the word order of a statement. In speech, the questioning tone turns it into a question. The speaker expects the answer yes, and a reply like That's right fits naturally. The expectation matches the sentence. A positive one, They've finished?, expects a positive answer, and a negative one, They haven't finished?, expects a negative answer. This isn't the neutral question of Have they finished?, which leaves the answer more open. In writing, the question mark does the work of the tone.

examples.text: [And the manager has been informed, of course?]
[There isn't any chance of her changing her mind, I take it?]

curious.try: Say You're coming tonight? as a question. What answer do you expect? Now say Are you coming tonight? Does the expectation change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain statement-order questions that expect confirmation, as in They've finished?
teacher.explain: A declarative question keeps declarative syntax, with no subject-auxiliary inversion, and gets its question interpretation from question intonation, or question punctuation in writing. It's a closed question strongly biased toward the answer with the same propositional content and polarity as the declarative: positive toward positive, negative toward negative. Confirmatory responses such as That's right, Exactly and Quite so are especially natural. The host clause stays declarative, and question is a semantic category applied to the whole form. It is not an echo question, since it needn't repeat or query the wording of a prior utterance. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call these statement questions or rising-intonation questions. Closed interrogative is the inverted form (Have they finished?), which can be neutral.

examples.text: [And the manager has been informed, of course?]
[There isn't any chance of her changing her mind, I take it?]

contrasts.note: Declarative syntax; biased toward a positive answer.
Closed interrogative with inversion; can be neutral.

watch_for: A learner might treat They've finished? as a neutral question, when it is biased toward a positive answer.
A learner might take They haven't finished? to expect yes, when it expects the negative answer, that they haven't.
A learner might think a declarative question must echo something just said, when no prior utterance is required.
teacher.activity: Students role-play checking a fact they half-know (a friend's plans, a test date). They ask once with an inverted question and once with a declarative question, then say how much each one assumes the answer.

child.hook: How can you ask a question without changing any words?
child.explain: You can say a sentence in a questioning voice. They've finished? You think they have, and you want to check. The other person can answer, "That's right."
child.play: Say "You're hungry" two ways, as a plain statement and then as a question. Ask a friend to listen. Can they hear which one you want an answer to?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Declarative Question." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/declarative-question-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Definite Construction
pattern: Typical hosts include a determined NP, a name used referentially, or a referential pronoun

entry.name: Definite Construction
entry.pattern: Typical hosts include a determined NP, a name used referentially, or a referential pronoun

1.definition: Identifiable referent
1.details: Entity uniquely identifiable in context through shared knowledge or previous mention

examples.note: Standing designation in a community that can identify the intended bearer

2.details: Entity or set exhausting relevant context

examples.note: Contextually maximal group on the ordinary referential reading

3.details: Category-level reference

grounds.locator: Separation of structural and semantic profiles

projection.target: The plumber can identify an unmentioned person via an appointment already known to the hearer. On the usual weak reading of take the bus, the same article need not identify a particular vehicle. Familiarity and uniqueness are therefore subject to independent checks.
projection.evidence: CGEL describes recognitional and restricted activity readings. Reynolds treats deital syntax and definite interpretation as distinguishable.

curious.title: Pointing out which one you mean
curious.summary: A definite expression picks out something the listener can identify, such as one particular dog or the whole relevant group.
curious.body: When someone says the dog, the listener is expected to know which dog is meant, because it was mentioned before or because it is the obvious one in the situation. A name like John works similarly, as a standing label that a community can use to identify the person. This dictionary describes several ways this can work. The tallest student picks out the one thing that fits the description. The books can mean the whole relevant group. The lion and The dodo is extinct talk about a kind, and the Pope is familiar from shared culture. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Say the dog, then a dog. In which case do you expect your listener to already know which dog you mean?

teacher.summary: Helps explain definiteness as a matter of meaning (identifiable, unique, kind, familiar), separate from the form of the, this and similar words.
teacher.explain: This dictionary describes definiteness as a semantic profile with four strands. Identifiable referent: the dog, or a name such as John, picks out something the hearer can identify through shared knowledge or previous mention. Unique or maximal entity: the tallest student, the books. Kind or type: the lion, The dodo is extinct. Familiar entity: the Pope, that same dog. It keeps the semantic profile apart from the structural profile (deitality). The strands are subject to independent checks: the plumber can identify an unmentioned person via a known appointment, and on the usual weak reading of take the bus the same article need not identify a particular vehicle. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: The and a are determinatives (often called articles). Definite is a meaning label; the syntactic side is treated in deitality.

contrasts.note: Can identify an unmentioned person via an appointment the hearer knows about.
On the usual weak reading the same article need not identify a particular vehicle.

watch_for: A learner might assume every use of the identifies one particular thing, when kind uses and weak uses like take the bus don't.
A learner might assume that definiteness requires previous mention, when shared knowledge can supply the identification.
teacher.activity: Give students short passages with several the-phrases. They label each as previously mentioned, uniquely described, kind-level or culturally familiar, and note any that fit more than one label.

child.hook: When do we say the dog instead of a dog?
child.explain: We say the dog when our listener knows which dog we mean. Maybe we talked about it before. Maybe it's the only dog around.

examples.text: [The dog] barked at the mail carrier.

child.play: Look around a room and describe one thing with the, like the red book. Can a friend find it? What helped them know which one you meant?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Definite Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/definite-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: the two of us

1.definition: Identifies a group while explicitly giving its size.
1.details: The four of us can describe the group of four that includes the speaker. If a larger group is salient, the phrase needs a recoverable set of four. Without the, four of us can simply pick an unspecified subset of a larger us-group. The scope of the definite is the group picked out by the whole NP.

examples.form: There were six of us, and [four of us] had bikes.
examples.note: Constructed subset with the article absent.

examples.form: I was there with Jo, Lee and Pat. [The four of us] shared a tent.
examples.note: Constructed definite whose numeral matches the contextually salient group.

relatedConstructions.notes: The article determines the whole NP.
Cardinals with of-phrases can occur in ordinary partitive syntax.

grounds.note: Lists several cardinals and personal pronouns with the group-size function.
Notes the standard cardinal and the less widely accepted both variant.

projection.target: A cardinal with the can count members of an already identified group. Without the, the same numeral and pronoun also admit an unspecified subset of a larger salient group.
projection.evidence: CASA records the cardinal and pronoun slots and the group-size reading. CGEL explicitly contrasts the two of us with both of us and dialectal the both of us.

curious.title: The two of us, the four of us
curious.summary: The, a number and of plus a pronoun together name a group and say how many are in it.
curious.body: I was there with Jo, Lee and Pat. The four of us shared a tent. The phrase the four of us can point to a group of four that includes the speaker, and it gives the group's size at the same time. When a larger group is also in the picture, the phrase needs a set of four the listener can pick out. Without the, it works differently. In There were six of us, and four of us had bikes, four of us picks out some of a larger group rather than naming the whole group. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: I was there with Jo, Lee and Pat. [The four of us] shared a tent.
There were six of us, and [four of us] had bikes.

curious.try: Think of a group you were part of. How would you name it with the, a number and of us? What if only some of the group did something?

teacher.summary: Helps explain the four of us (a recoverable group of four) versus four of us (an unspecified subset of a larger group).
teacher.explain: The pattern is NP[the + cardinal + of + personal pronoun], as in the four of us. It identifies a group while explicitly giving its size, and the article determines the whole NP. The numeral must match a contextually recoverable group, so the four of us can describe the group of four that includes the speaker. Without the, four of us can simply pick an unspecified subset of a larger us-group. Cardinals with of-phrases can also occur in ordinary partitive syntax. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: The is a determinative (often called the definite article).

examples.text: I was there with Jo, Lee and Pat. [The four of us] shared a tent.
There were six of us, and [four of us] had bikes.

contrasts.text: The four of us shared a tent.
contrasts.note: Definite; the numeral matches the contextually salient group.
No the; can pick an unspecified subset of a larger group.

watch_for: A learner might read four of us, without the, as naming a whole group of four, when it can pick an unspecified subset of a larger group.
A learner might use the two of us for a pair that isn't the contextually identified group.
teacher.activity: Describe a picture of a group of six, with three friends sitting together. Students write sentences about the whole group and about parts of it, with and without the, and say which group each sentence names.

child.hook: What can you call a group of friends and say how many without naming each one?
child.explain: You can name a group by saying the, a number and of us. The four of us shared a tent. It points to a group of four that you can pick out from the situation.

examples.text: [The four of us] shared a tent.

child.play: Pick a group you were in, like a team or a table at lunch. Say how many were in it using the number and of us. Then say what some of the group did.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher summary and watch_for no longer say the four of us names the whole group (the entry allows it to pick a recoverable set of four within a larger salient group, and says four of us without the can pick an unspecified subset); contrast note reworded; 'can describe' replaces 'describes'; child explanation now says the group can be picked out from the situation. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "the two of us." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/definite-cardinal-of-pronoun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Degree
pattern: XP[{more|less} + X] | XP[X + -er] | XP[{most|least} + X] | XP[X + -est] | XP[as + X + as]

entry.name: Degree
entry.pattern: XP[{more|less} + X] | XP[X + -er] | XP[{most|least} + X] | XP[X + -est] | XP[as + X + as]

1.definition: Denotes relative scale position
1.details: Semantic features encoding comparative, superlative and equative scale relations

2.details: Semantic features encoding degree of difference between scale points

3.details: Semantic features encoding reference sets for comparison

examples.form: taller than average/most expensive of all
as tall as expected/least expensive option

stabilisers.evidence: early acquisition of comparative frames
high-frequency degree templates reinforce usage
need to encode relative scale positions
short comparative morphology favored in production

projection.target: The same dimension can have an explicit differential in two centimetres wider and a simple comparative in wider. An equality comparison can instead supply a standard with as wide as. The constructions test comparison structure separately from the particular scale chosen.
projection.evidence: CGEL discusses equality and inequality and separates differential modification from the standard phrase.

perturbations: loss of degree morphology shifts toward periphrastic comparatives

activation_states.effect: degree frames degraded with absolute adjectives

variation.speaker_variation: analytic vs synthetic comparative preference by register

known_boundary_items: unique
dead

coupling.mechanism: bidirectional inference between scale construal and degree morphology

curious.title: Comparing things on a scale
curious.summary: English has a few ways to say where something sits on a scale, such as taller than, the tallest and as tall as.
curious.body: Words like tall, expensive or short describe a scale, and English has patterns for placing things on it. Taller than and more expensive than compare two things. The tallest and the most expensive pick out the end of the scale. As tall as says two things are level. The patterns can also say how big the difference is: much taller, two feet taller. And they can compare against a group or a standard, as in taller than average or most expensive of all. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Pick two objects in the room and compare them with taller than, then with as tall as. Now try the least expensive thing you can see.

teacher.summary: Helps explain comparatives, superlatives and equatives as ways of placing something on a scale.
teacher.explain: Degree constructions denote relative scale position. The comparative (-er or more/less: taller, more expensive), the superlative (-est or most/least: tallest, most expensive) and the equative (as tall as) encode scale relations. Measure and differential phrases denote intervals (much taller, two feet taller), and comparison classes supply a reference set or standard (taller than average, most expensive of all). The patterns apply to gradable adjectives and adverbs. This dictionary notes that degree frames are degraded with absolute adjectives and lists unique and dead as boundary items. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary's term for the broader scale meaning is degree.

contrasts.note: A simple comparative.
The same scale with an explicit differential.
An equality comparison that supplies a standard.

watch_for: A learner might expect degree frames to work with any adjective, when absolute adjectives such as unique and dead are boundary items.
A learner might treat much taller and two feet taller as the same kind of difference, when this dictionary treats much taller as a relative interval and two feet taller as a measured interval.
teacher.activity: Students measure or rank classroom objects, then write sentences with a comparative, a superlative, an equative and a measure phrase. They swap and check that each sentence matches the facts.

child.hook: How do you say one thing is more than another?
child.explain: We compare things with words like taller, tallest and as tall as. Taller than compares two things. The tallest in the class means no one in the class is taller. As tall as says they match.

examples.text: Sam is [the tallest] in the class.

child.play: Compare three objects, like pencils or shoes. Make a sentence with taller, one with the tallest and one with as tall as. Can a friend tell which object you mean?

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.watch_for[1] now states the entry's distinction (much taller as a relative interval, two feet taller as a measured interval). Also relabelled examples that the entry quotes from constructed to entry. Second round: fixed teacher.terms by cutting the claim about what traditional grammars call these patterns (this dictionary makes no such claim); fixed child.explain, whose 'picks out one at the end' introduced no scale, by saying what the tallest in the class means.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Degree." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/degree-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Degree-Adjective-Indefinite (Big Mess Construction)

1.definition: Degree word and adjective precede the indefinite article, expressing degree or extent of the adjectival property
1.details: A degree-marked adjective phrase, including certain comparatives, precedes the indefinite article, inverting the normal order (cf. "a big mess" → "how big a mess"). Only compatible with indefinite "a(n)", not definite "the" (*"how big the mess"). The "how" variant can function as an interrogative phrase, fronting to clause-initial position. Variants differ in register. An intervening of is especially familiar in North American varieties and is more available with some degree phrases than others.

examples.form: It was [too big a problem] to ignore.
She's [so good a student] that she skipped a year.
It's not [as big a deal] as you think.
I've never seen [so big a crowd].
examples.note: "So" variant; more literary than other degree words

examples.form: It's not [that big of a deal].
examples.note: Of-insertion variant; common in North American English

examples.form: [more interesting a job] than I thought
examples.note: Published comparison. The fronted adjective phrase is comparative.

constraints.description: Eligible phrases include those with how, so, too, that and as and certain comparatives. Ordinary very uses a different word order.
Article must be indefinite a(n); definite the is ungrammatical
"How" variant can be interrogative, fronting to clause-initial position
Acceptability and register depend on the degree phrase and the availability of the intervening of variant.

dimensions.form: Degree word + adjective + indefinite article + noun
dimensions.meaning: Expresses degree/extent of adjectival property; scalar semantics
dimensions.function: Degree modification with displaced adjective
dimensions.distribution: Common in speech and writing; competes with such a big N and a N that big

relatedConstructions.notes: Requires indefinite article; incompatible with definite
Specialized degree construction with unusual word order

projection.target: An eligible degree phrase can precede a in too serious a problem. Ordinary very yields a very serious problem. Comparatives are also documented, and acceptability of of varies with the particular degree expression and variety.
projection.evidence: The FrameNet chapter gives the comparatives alongside so, as, how, that and too. It explicitly leaves the distribution of intervening of open.

curious.title: How big a mess, too big a problem
curious.summary: With words like how, too, so, that and as, the adjective can move in front of a or an.
curious.body: In a big mess, the adjective sits between a and the noun. But after words such as how, so, too, that and as, the adjective moves forward and a follows it. So we say how big a mess, too big a problem, so good a student, not that good a teacher. The word a or an has to stay: this pattern doesn't work with the. In some varieties you can also add of, as in that big of a deal, though whether of is acceptable depends on the degree word and the variety. The ordinary word very doesn't do this, and takes the usual order: a very serious problem.

examples.text: It was [too big a problem] to ignore.
She's [so good a student] that she skipped a year.
It's not [as big a deal] as you think.

curious.try: Start from a big mess and ask how big a mess. Then try the same with the, and see whether it still works.

teacher.summary: Explains inverted order after degree words (how big a mess) and the a(n)-only restriction.
teacher.explain: A degree word plus an adjective can precede the indefinite article, reversing the usual order: a big mess becomes how big a mess. Eligible phrases include those with how, so, too, that and as, and certain comparatives (more interesting a job). The article must be indefinite a(n); the doesn't fit, as in how big the mess. The how version can be an interrogative phrase, fronted to the start of the clause. Ordinary very uses a different word order (a very serious problem). An intervening of (that big of a deal) is especially familiar in North American varieties and is more available with some degree words than others. Register differs among the variants.
teacher.terms: Degree word: a word such as how, so, too or as that modifies the adjective. Indefinite article: a or an, the words CGEL classes as determinatives.

examples.text: It was [too big a problem] to ignore.
It's not [that big of a deal].
[more interesting a job] than I thought

contrasts.note: Ordinary order, with the adjective after a.
This dictionary stars this version with the.
Very keeps the usual order.

watch_for: A learner might put the definite article into the pattern, as in how big the mess.
A learner might expect very to behave like how and so, and move the adjective in front of a.
A learner might assume that of is available with every degree word, though this dictionary notes this varies with the degree word and variety.
teacher.activity: Give students a big mess, a good teacher and a serious problem. They build how, too, so and as versions, then check each with a different noun and say which degree words they can use.

checked.note: Dismissed: teacher.terms a/an as determinatives (GLM: unsupported) is CGEL's standard classification and consistent with the entry; reworded to say CGEL classes them so rather than that this grammar does. Also fixed (unflagged): removed 'Usually' (a frequency word) from curious.body; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'. Second round: dismissed teacher.terms a/an as determinatives, flagged again (CGEL's standard classification, consistent with the entry's indefinite article).

name: Deictic here or there with Inversion
pattern: Clause[stressed locative here/there + V + full NP], or here/there + pronoun + V

entry.name: Deictic here or there with Inversion
entry.pattern: Clause[stressed locative here/there + V + full NP], or here/there + pronoun + V

1.definition: Draws attention to an arrival, presence or departure in the relevant perceptual setting.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. Ordinary order when the subject is a personal pronoun.

projection.target: A full NP typically follows come. A personal pronoun occurs before it in Here it comes. The locative can receive pointing stress, unlike the dummy subject of an existential.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Here comes the bus
curious.summary: Starting a sentence with a stressed here or there, then the verb, points out something arriving, present or leaving.
curious.body: In Here comes the bus, here points to the place you are, the verb comes next, and the thing arriving comes last. The sentence draws attention to an arrival, a presence or a departure in what you can see or hear around you. The word here can get pointing stress, as if the speaker were pointing. When the arriving thing is a pronoun, the order is the ordinary one: Here it comes. A full noun phrase, like the bus, follows the verb. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Say Here comes the bus, then Here it comes. Where does the thing arriving go in each?

teacher.summary: Helps explain Here comes the bus and Here it comes, where here or there with inversion draws attention to what is in view.
teacher.explain: The pattern has a stressed locative here or there, a verb and a full NP: Here comes the bus. It draws attention to an arrival, presence or departure in the perceptual setting. When the subject is a personal pronoun, the order is ordinary, with the pronoun before the verb: Here it comes. A full NP typically follows come. The locative can receive pointing stress, unlike the dummy subject of an existential. Compare presentational there, where there is a dummy subject. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may describe here or there at the start as adverbs. This dictionary describes the locative as a deictic, pointing to the setting.

contrasts.note: Full NP follows the verb.
Pronoun subject in ordinary order.

watch_for: A learner might treat here in Here comes the bus as a dummy subject like existential there, when it can take pointing stress.
A learner might think a pronoun should follow the verb in the same way a full noun phrase does.
teacher.activity: Students look out a window or at a picture and describe what is arriving or leaving with Here comes or There goes, using both a full noun phrase and a pronoun. They note where the stress falls.

child.hook: What do you say when you spot the bus coming?
child.explain: You can point at something with the word here at the start. Here comes the bus. When you use a word like it, it goes before the verb. Here it comes.
child.play: Stand at a window and watch. When something arrives, point and describe it with Here comes and the thing. Then say it again with just it.

name: Deitality
pattern: Structural profile over determination: there-resistance + partitive domain establishment + identificational hosting

entry.name: Deitality
entry.pattern: Structural profile over determination: there-resistance + partitive domain establishment + identificational hosting

dimensions.form: Prototype: the demonstratives (this, that, these, those); core members include the, personal genitives, genitive NPs in determiner function; graded membership beyond the core
dimensions.meaning: Strongly but imperfectly correlated with semantic definiteness; the correlation is leaky in principled ways
dimensions.function: Domain establishment for reference; anchors partitive and identificational structure
dimensions.distribution: Resists neutral existential there pivots; supplies the domain-establishing complement in true partitives; hosts identificational material

1.definition: A structural (morphosyntactic) profile of English determination, distinct from semantic definiteness, for which English grammar previously had no agreed name
1.details: Reynolds, Definiteness and Deitality in English (LingBuzz 009369). Prototype: the demonstratives (deictic, and the historical source of the). Core diagnostics, ranked: resistance to neutral existential there pivots; domain establishment in true partitives; ready hosting of identificational material. A narrow bare-one substitution pattern supplies corroborating residue, not a core diagnostic. Definiteness and deitality usually coincide, which is why they get run together; weak definites, generic definites, narrative this, and proper names each mark a point where they separate. See data/indices/deitality-status.yaml for the provisional membership inventory.

examples.form: two of [the] dogs / *two of [some] dogs (true partitive)
examples.note: Domain-establishing complement in a true partitive

constraints.description: Membership is graded; status labels are deital, non-deital, mixed, and provisional (see the inventory index).

grounds.locator: SS4 diagnostics; SS5 sources and stabilizers

projection.target: Locating a form or construction in the deital profile predicts which diagnostic residues survive semantic mismatch, which diagnostics split under prosodic and specificity manipulation, and where dialectal and acquisitional variation appears
projection.evidence: Convergence of the ranked diagnostics across the core inventory; decoupling cases (weak definites, generic definites, narrative this, proper names) behave as the profile predicts

core.property: Resistance to neutral existential there pivots

stabilisers.evidence: Demonstrative > article grammaticalization; demonstratives are the profile's prototype and the historical source of the
Learners acquire deital distribution before full definiteness semantics

perturbations: Weak and generic definites weaken semantic definiteness while deital marking survives
Narrative this recruits deital form for non-identifiable referents

known_boundary_items: weak definites
generic definites
narrative this
proper names

coupling.mechanism: Correlated kinds: strong, bidirectional, but imperfect alignment; the paper argues sources and stabilizers across timescales, so the maintained tier is plausible pending rung review

relatedConstructions.notes: The correlated semantic kind; deital form cues definite interpretation, definite intention licenses deital form, with principled leaks
Deitality is the structural profile that ranks and organizes the determination system's diagnostics

curious.title: Words that behave like this and that
curious.summary: This dictionary uses deitality for a pattern of grammatical behaviour shared by the, this, that and similar words, separate from what they mean.
curious.body: Words like this, that, these, those and the behave alike in ways that have nothing to do with pointing. They resist the neutral there was pattern: There was the dog in the yard doesn't work in the ordinary, neutral way. They can name the group a partitive is drawn from, as in two of the dogs. And they readily host extra identifying material, as in that idiot Larry. This dictionary calls that bundle of behaviour deitality. It is related to definiteness, which is about meaning, but the two don't line up perfectly. Membership in the pattern is a matter of degree, and the analysis is provisional.
curious.try: Compare two of the dogs with two of some dogs. Which one works? What does that tell you about the?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: a grammatical profile (there-resistance, partitive domain, identificational hosting) that goes with, but isn't the same as, definiteness.
teacher.explain: Deitality is a structural (morphosyntactic) profile of English determination, distinct from semantic definiteness. The prototype is the demonstratives (this, that, these, those). Core members include the, personal genitives and genitive NPs in determiner function. Three diagnostics are ranked: resistance to neutral existential there pivots; domain establishment in true partitives; ready hosting of identificational material. Definiteness and deitality usually coincide, which is why they get run together; weak definites, generic definites, narrative this and proper names each mark a point where they separate. Membership is graded, with status labels deital, non-deital, mixed and provisional. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: The, this, that, these and those are determinatives; Determiner is their function. The there-resistance is labelled the definiteness effect in this dictionary. Here it counts as one diagnostic of a structural profile, not as definiteness itself.

contrasts.text: There was [the] dog in the yard.
contrasts.note: There-resistance under neutral prosody.
Domain-establishing complement in a true partitive.
Not acceptable as a true partitive.

watch_for: A learner might treat deitality and definiteness as the same thing, when weak definites, generic definites, narrative this and proper names show where they separate.
A learner might expect a form to be either deital or not, when membership is graded.
teacher.activity: Students test the, this, that, a and some in the frames there was ___ dog in the yard, two of ___ dogs and ___ idiot Larry, tallying which words fit each frame and discussing why the results line up with, but don't exactly match, meaning.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deitality." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deitality-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

pattern: coordination[XP₁ ... gap + Coordinator + XP₂ ...] + shared right-edge constituent

entry.name: Delayed Right Constituent in Coordination
entry.pattern: coordination[XP₁ ... gap + Coordinator + XP₂ ...] + shared right-edge constituent

1.definition: Expresses shared right-edge material once while contrasting what precedes it.
1.details: In She knew of but never mentioned the proposal, the proposal completes both knew of and mentioned. Its functions differ across the two coordinates. Delay can foreground the contrast between the predicates.

examples.form: She [knew of but never mentioned the proposal].
examples.note: Constructed after the CGEL model with a PP complement in one coordinate and a direct object in the other.

examples.form: I am [interested in but worried about the new plan].
examples.note: Constructed example where different prepositions precede the delayed NP.

relatedConstructions.notes: The first parts occur in a coordinate structure.

grounds.note: Lists Shared_completion, also known as right-node raising.
Shows different syntactic functions for the delayed element.

projection.target: The single pronounced NP can satisfy two distinct local frames. The preposition inside the first coordinate can select that NP even though the second frame takes a direct object.
projection.evidence: The CGEL examples control which constituent is delayed and show different complement selections. FrameNet names the Shared_completion construction.

curious.title: One ending shared by two halves
curious.summary: In a linked pair of phrases, the shared last part can be said once, at the very end.
curious.body: In She knew of but never mentioned the proposal, the phrase the proposal finishes both parts of the sentence. She knew of the proposal, and she never mentioned the proposal. Saying it only once, at the end, lets the speaker set the two verbs against each other. The shared ending does a different job in each half. After knew of it is the object of a preposition, and after mentioned it is a direct object. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: She [knew of but never mentioned the proposal].
I am [interested in but worried about the new plan].

curious.try: Combine two short sentences about the same thing, such as I like it and I fear it, into one with a single it at the end. Which parts come before it?

teacher.summary: Helps explain right-edge sharing, where a final phrase completes two coordinated parts, as in knew of but never mentioned the proposal.
teacher.explain: In this construction, the first parts occur in a coordinate structure and a single constituent at the right edge is expressed once. In She knew of but never mentioned the proposal, the proposal completes both knew of and mentioned, though its functions differ across the two coordinates: it is the complement of a preposition in one and a direct object in the other. In I am interested in but worried about the new plan, different prepositions precede the delayed NP. Delay can foreground the contrast between the predicates. The pronounced NP satisfies two distinct local frames. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Right-edge sharing is sometimes called right-node raising.

examples.text: She [knew of but never mentioned the proposal].
I am [interested in but worried about the new plan].

contrasts.text: She knew of but never mentioned the proposal.
contrasts.note: The shared NP is a prepositional complement in one coordinate and a direct object in the other.

contrasts.text: I am [interested in but worried about the new plan].
contrasts.note: Different prepositions precede the delayed noun phrase.

watch_for: A learner might think the proposal is the direct object of both verbs, when it follows the preposition of in the first part.
A learner might expect each half to have its own ending, when the shared ending is said once.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of sentences about one object (I like it. I fear it.) and prepositional pairs (interested in, worried about). They combine each pair into one sentence with one shared ending and mark what comes before it in each part.

checked.note: Fixed: removed all statements about gapping (the entry does not discuss it), including the constructed gapping contrast, replaced with the entry's second example, and a watch_for item on shared endings. Right-node raising is now given as a name sometimes used, per this dictionary's sources.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Delayed Right Constituent in Coordination." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/delayed-right-constituent-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Demonstrative Determinative in Fused Determiner-Head Function

entry.name: Demonstrative Determinative in Fused Determiner-Head Function

1.definition: A demonstrative determinative realizes fused determiner-head function in an NP and refers deictically to a salient entity or situation
1.details: CGEL treats this, that, these, and those as determinatives; independent NP use does not reclassify them as pronouns.

examples.note: That is a demonstrative determinative in fused determiner-head function, referring to the current situation.

constraints.description: The fused determiner-head must be realized by this, that, these, or those.

relatedConstructions.notes: The demonstratives are the prototype of the deital profile

projection.target: That can be an entire NP subject in That is strange. In That plan is strange, it instead determines a nominal. A prior proposition can supply the deictic target even with no physical object indicated.
projection.evidence: CGEL treats the two syntactic realizations separately and documents discourse-deictic demonstratives.

curious.title: This and that standing on their own
curious.summary: Words like this and that can stand alone as a whole phrase, pointing to something in the situation.
curious.body: In That is incredible!, that isn't attached to a noun. It stands on its own and points to something in the situation, such as what has just happened or been said. A prior statement can supply the target even when no physical object is pointed at. This dictionary counts this, that, these and those as a kind of word called determinatives, and it keeps them in that category even when they stand on their own. In That plan is strange, by contrast, that goes with a noun. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Hear someone say That is incredible! What could that be pointing to? Now say That plan is incredible. What changes?

teacher.summary: Helps explain this, that, these and those used alone, and why this grammar keeps them as determinatives.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an NP where a demonstrative determinative realizes fused determiner-head function: one word does the jobs of determiner and head. In That is incredible!, that is an entire NP referring to the current situation. In That plan is strange, it instead determines a nominal. The fused head must be this, that, these or those. A prior proposition can supply the deictic target even with no physical object indicated. This grammar treats these words as determinatives, and independent NP use doesn't reclassify them as pronouns. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars call this use a demonstrative pronoun. This grammar keeps this, that, these and those as determinatives (a word category) in fused determiner-head function.

contrasts.note: That alone is the whole NP, referring to the situation.
That determines a nominal, plan.

watch_for: A learner might reclassify that as a pronoun when it stands alone, when this grammar keeps it a determinative.
A learner might look for a physical object that that points to, when a prior proposition can supply the target.
teacher.activity: Students collect sentences with this, that, these and those, sort them into stand-alone and followed-by-a-noun, and say what each one points to in the situation or in the previous sentence.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Demonstrative Determinative in Fused Determiner-Head Function." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/demonstrative-determinative-fused-head-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deictic Demonstrative Determination

1.definition: Directs attention to a referent and presents it as proximal or distal in a relevant deictic dimension.

examples.form: Could you pass me [that blue folder] over there?

projection.target: This and that can select different candidates without a prior noun-phrase antecedent. Spatial distance is one dimension and is not obligatory in discourse-deictic uses.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: This one or that one
curious.summary: This, that, these and those direct attention to something and can present it as near or far.
curious.body: In Could you pass me that blue folder over there?, that points to one folder among others, and over there adds where it is. The demonstrative words are this and that, with these and those for more than one. They present the thing as near or far in some relevant dimension. Distance in space is one such dimension, but it isn't required. This and that can also pick out different candidates without any earlier noun phrase to point back to, and they can refer to things said earlier. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: Could you pass me [that blue folder] over there?

curious.try: Point at two similar objects, one near and one farther away. Which would you call this one and which that one?

teacher.summary: Helps explain this, that, these and those as words that direct attention and mark proximal or distal position.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an NP with a demonstrative determiner: this or that with a singular, these or those with a plural. It directs attention to a referent and presents it as proximal or distal in a relevant deictic dimension. This and that can select different candidates without a prior noun-phrase antecedent. Spatial distance is one dimension and isn't obligatory in discourse-deictic uses. The determiner function is realized by determinatives: this, that, these and those. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars call this, that, these and those demonstrative adjectives or demonstrative pronouns. In this grammar they are determinatives, and Determiner is their function.

examples.text: Could you pass me [that blue folder] over there?

contrasts.text: Could you pass me that blue folder over there?
contrasts.note: Distal demonstrative, with spatial distance.

contrasts.text: Could you pass me this blue folder?
contrasts.note: Proximal demonstrative.

watch_for: A learner might think this and that must mark physical distance, when the dimension can be something else in discourse.
A learner might use a singular this or that where the noun is plural, instead of these or those.
teacher.activity: Place several similar objects around the room, some near and some farther away. Students ask a partner to pass or point to particular ones using this, that, these and those, and discuss what each choice picks out.

child.hook: When do you say this one and when do you say that one?
child.explain: Words like this and that help you point out one thing. You might use this for something close and that for something farther away. For more than one, say these or those.

examples.text: Could you pass me [that blue folder] over there?

child.play: Put two toys on a table, one close and one far. Ask a friend to pass one using this or that. Then add more toys and use these and those.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deictic Demonstrative Determination." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/demonstrative-distance-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Demonstrative with an Oblique Genitive

1.definition: Picks out a referent through a demonstrative and a genitive relation, including a uniquely possessed referent.
1.details: Barker analyzes a demonstrative construction in which that nose of his is usable for an ordinary person with one nose, though the nose of his is degraded. He links the use to focus on the head and speaker affect. The extent to which affect is required across CGEL’s examples remains open.

examples.note: The phrase can be tested in a setting with a single husband.
Plural demonstrative in CGEL's oblique-genitive series.
Published judgment in comparison with the nose of his.

relatedConstructions.notes: The demonstrative marks the NP as definite.
The of-phrase takes an independent genitive NP.

grounds.note: Distinguishes the demonstrative pattern from oblique genitives subject to anti-uniqueness.

projection.target: The demonstrative form can license an oblique genitive even when the relation supplies only one relevant referent.
projection.evidence: Barker's controlled contrast and the range of relations in CGEL's demonstrative series.

curious.title: That husband of Mary's
curious.summary: A demonstrative plus a phrase like of Mary's can pick out a person or thing through a relation, even when only one fits.
curious.body: In that husband of Mary's, the word that points to the husband, and the phrase of Mary's says whose husband he is. The same pattern appears in those green eyes of Mary's and that nose of his. The pattern works even when there is only one husband, or one nose, in the picture. This dictionary links this use to focus on the head noun and to speaker feeling, but how far feeling is needed across all the examples remains open. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Compare that nose of his with his nose. Does the first one feel different?

teacher.summary: Helps explain that husband of Mary's and similar phrases with a demonstrative and an of-phrase containing a genitive.
teacher.explain: The pattern is NP[demonstrative determiner + nominal with an of-phrase containing a genitive NP]. The demonstrative marks the NP as definite, and the genitive relation picks out a referent, including a uniquely possessed one: that husband of Mary's can be tested in a setting with a single husband. A published analysis (Barker, 1998) distinguishes this demonstrative pattern from oblique genitives subject to anti-uniqueness, and links the use to focus on the head and speaker affect. How far affect is required across CGEL's examples remains open. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: The of-phrase contains an independent genitive (Mary's, his), This grammar says genitive rather than possessive.

contrasts.note: Demonstrative with an oblique genitive; usable where Mary has one husband.
Plain genitive in determiner function; no demonstrative.

watch_for: A learner might think that husband of Mary's must mean Mary has several husbands, when the pattern can be used with a single one.
A learner might treat the demonstrative as only a pointing word, when the use is linked to focus and speaker affect.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as that husband of Mary's and Mary's husband. They say in which setting each would be natural and discuss whether the demonstrative version carries extra feeling.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Demonstrative with an Oblique Genitive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/demonstrative-oblique-genitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Denominator Numeral Construction

dimensions.form: Cardinal noun with determiner; may take plural morphology
dimensions.meaning: Denotes a token of a numerical type (score, label, symbol)
