dimensions.function: Refers to instances of numerals as objects
dimensions.distribution: Object position; count noun syntax

1.definition: Cardinal noun denotes a token numeral (score, written symbol, etc.)

examples.note: Plural cardinal noun for multiple tokens

constraints.description: Behaves as count noun; takes determiners and plural morphology.
Denotes a token or instance of a numeral, not an abstract number.

projection.target: I rolled three tens describes three tokens of the value ten, rather than a count of ten objects. The lexical noun takes its own plural marking and appears under a separate cardinal determiner.
projection.evidence: The numeral paper distinguishes the count noun for a token or score from arithmetic name and quantificational uses.

curious.title: A ten, three tens
curious.summary: A number word can work like an ordinary noun, naming an instance of a number such as a score.
curious.body: In I rolled a ten, the word ten isn't counting anything. It names a score of ten. It behaves like an ordinary noun: it has a determiner, a, and it can be plural, as in She drew three tens. Three tens means three instances of the value ten, not ten objects. The same works for ratings, as in That's a perfect ten. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of a game or contest with scores. How would you name a score of seven as an item, with a before it?

teacher.summary: Helps explain number words used as count nouns, such as a ten and three tens.
teacher.explain: In this use, a cardinal functions as a noun denoting a token or instance of a numeral (a score, a label, a written symbol), not an abstract number. It behaves as a count noun: it takes determiners and plural morphology. I rolled three tens describes three tokens of the value ten, not a count of ten objects. The noun takes its own plural marking and appears under a separate cardinal determinative, as in three tens. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Cardinal here is a noun, not the determinative use of a number as in three dogs.

contrasts.note: Three tokens of the value ten.
Ten is a determinative counting objects.

watch_for: A learner might read three tens as ten objects counted three times, when it means three tokens of the value ten.
A learner might think a cardinal cannot take a plural ending when it is used as a noun.
teacher.activity: Students play a dice or card game and describe their results with a number noun (I rolled a six, I drew two fives). They then say whether the number counts objects or names a score.

child.hook: Can a number word have a plural, like tens?
child.explain: A number can name a score or a card. I rolled a ten. You can even add an s, as in three tens. That means three of them, each one a ten.
child.play: Roll two dice or draw cards a few times. Describe each result with a number word, like a six. If you get the same number twice, give it an s.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says the three tens are rolls (the entry's example is a card draw); curious.body now says 'a score of ten'; cut the unsupported traditional-names sentence in teacher.terms.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Denominator Numeral Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/denominator-numeral-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Depictive Secondary Predication
pattern: Clause[primary VP + secondary AdjP/NP predicated of a participant]

entry.name: Depictive Secondary Predication
entry.pattern: Clause[primary VP + secondary AdjP/NP predicated of a participant]

1.definition: Ascribes a condition to a participant during the primary event.

relatedConstructions.notes: Ate the fish raw gives the state of the fish at the time of eating. Cooked the fish dry presents dryness as a result.

projection.target: The patient can already have been unconscious before being carried. That temporal compatibility distinguishes the depictive reading from a caused-result reading.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how someone or something was at the time
curious.summary: A word added after the verb phrase can tell you what state someone or something was in during the action.
curious.body: In They carried the patient unconscious, the word unconscious describes the patient while the carrying happens. The patient could already have been unconscious before anyone picked them up. The extra word describes a condition, not an outcome of the action. That is the difference from a sentence where the action causes the state. Ate the fish raw gives the state of the fish at the time of eating. Cooked the fish dry presents dryness as a result of the cooking. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Compare She ate the fish raw with She cooked the fish dry. In which one was the fish already in that state?

teacher.summary: Helps explain depictives such as unconscious in carried the patient unconscious, and how they differ from resultatives.
teacher.explain: A depictive is a secondary predicate (an AdjP or NP) added to a primary VP and predicated of a participant, ascribing a condition to that participant during the primary event: They carried the patient unconscious. The patient can already have been unconscious before being carried, and that temporal compatibility distinguishes the depictive reading from a caused-result reading. Compare Ate the fish raw, which gives the state of the fish at the time of eating, with Cooked the fish dry, which presents dryness as a result. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Secondary predicate is a textbook name for the added predicate. Resultative is the name for the caused-result pattern.

contrasts.note: Depictive; the fish was raw when eaten.
Resultative; dryness results from the cooking.

watch_for: A learner might read unconscious in carried the patient unconscious as the result of the carrying.
A learner might think the added word describes the verb's subject, when here it describes the patient.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as ate the fish raw and cooked the fish dry. For each, they ask whether the added word describes the participant during the action or presents a result of it, and sort the pairs into depictive and resultative.

child.hook: Was the fish raw before you ate it, or did eating make it raw?
child.explain: Sometimes a word after the verb tells what something was like while it happened. She ate the fish raw. The fish was already raw when she ate it.
child.play: Say what a person or thing was like while something happened, such as ate the apple whole. Ask a friend what the apple was like while it was eaten.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher activity sorts by whether the word describes the participant during the action or presents a result (not by whether the state held beforehand); child game asks what the thing was like while it happened; cut the term 'depictive predicative'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Depictive Secondary Predication." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/depictive-predication-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Descriptor + Identifier Label
pattern: NP[descriptor + identifier: number, letter name, or alphanumeric code]

entry.name: Descriptor + Identifier Label
entry.pattern: NP[descriptor + identifier: number, letter name, or alphanumeric code]

1.definition: Identifies a bearer by an assigned label within a naming system.
1.details: The descriptor gives the kind of bearer. The following identifier picks out a bearer within the relevant naming system. Gen in Gen Z supplies the kind in the same way as Ward in CGEL’s Ward 17. Descriptor describes a contribution within the naming construction. In CGEL an embellishment is a semantically nonrestrictive dependent accompanying a proper name. The shared pattern leaves the syntactic head and the identifier’s word category open.

examples.note: Cornell gives these two designations for the same space in Appel Commons.

grounds.locator: Info Session Locations, Appel Commons Community Center

examples.note: Gen identifies the referent as a generation and Z supplies its conventional label. Cohort boundaries can vary across sources.

relatedConstructions.notes: Room 302A realizes naming through a type-denoting descriptor and an assigned code. The identification depends on the code assignment at the relevant site.
Room 101 and Kim both occur as bare argument NPs. In Room 101 the noun supplies the type of bearer and the assigned code supplies its identity.

Dr Patel also places a nominal before an identifying form. Dr is an appellation giving the bearer’s status in a personal name. Room in Room 101 gives the type of entity and the following code is interpreted within the site.

Compare Room 101 with the river Wye. Both pair a type expression with an identifier. The latter has an overt determiner and is analyzed as an integrated appositive. The comparison leaves the headedness of Room 101 open.

grounds.note: Lists Ward 17 among names with a descriptor that indicates the kind of entity named.

Calls Room an embellishment rather than an attributive modifier (n. 9). The wider construction uses CGEL’s descriptor for the type-denoting element, and CGEL’s embellishments include nominal attributive modifiers (p. 520).

projection.target: A descriptor can be followed by a number, a letter or a mixed code in the same naming role. Changing a label may change the bearer, or leave it fixed if the two labels are aliases. Any quantity or rank associated with the code depends on the local allocation convention.
projection.evidence: Cornell uses Room 101 and Room 302A, and gives Multipurpose Room A for the same space as Room 302A. CGEL gives Ward 17. Pew uses Gen Z as a cohort label.

known_boundary_items: In 101 rooms, 101 determines how many rooms. In Room 101, it identifies a room.
In a type specification such as a type A personality, the designation supplies a class inside an ordinary count NP. Compare bare Gen Z for an identified cohort.

curious.title: A kind of thing plus its label
curious.summary: A word naming a kind of thing, followed by a number or letter code, can pick out one particular thing.
curious.body: Many names are built from two parts: a word that says what kind of thing it is, and a label that says which one. In Room 302A, Room gives the kind and 302A is the label. In Gen Z, Gen tells you it's a generation and Z is its label. The label can be a number, a letter or a mix of both. What the label means depends on the system it belongs to. A university, for instance, can give the same space two designations, Room 302A and Multipurpose Room A. Changing the label might change which thing you mean, unless the two labels are just different names for the same thing.
curious.try: Think of a place you know that has a kind word plus a code, like a room, a gate or a ward. Does the code tell you anything beyond "this one"?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why Room 302A and Gen Z are naming patterns, not descriptions with a number or letter attached.
teacher.explain: These names pair a descriptor (the word giving the kind of bearer, such as Room or Gen) with an identifier (a number, letter name or mixed code) that picks out a bearer within a naming system. The same pattern covers Ward 17, Room 302A and Gen Z. In CGEL, an embellishment is a semantically nonrestrictive dependent accompanying a proper name. This dictionary leaves open which element is the syntactic head and what word category the identifier has. Any quantity or rank the code suggests depends on how the codes were allocated locally. Contrast 101 rooms, where 101 counts rooms, with Room 101, where it identifies one.
teacher.terms: Descriptor: CGEL's term for the element that indicates the kind of entity named, as in Ward 17. Embellishment: CGEL's term for a nonrestrictive dependent accompanying a proper name.

contrasts.note: The number identifies one room.
The number says how many rooms.

watch_for: A learner might read Room 302A as a count or ranking of rooms rather than a label for one room.
A learner might treat Gen Z as a description of a person's character rather than as the label for a generation.
teacher.activity: Students collect descriptor-plus-code names from their school or neighbourhood (rooms, buses, forms, teams), then sort the codes into numbers, letters and mixed codes and say what kind each code names.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Descriptor + Identifier Label." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/descriptor-identifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Determination

1.definition: Licenses a nominal as an NP and marks it for definiteness or indefiniteness
1.details: Realized by basic determiners (determinatives), subject-determiners (genitive NPs), and a limited set of minor determiners (plain-case NPs or PPs).

examples.note: PP determiner in a measure NP

constraints.description: Determiner is a dependent within NP structure.

Singular count nominals generally require determination; bare plural and non-count nominals can be determinerless, and a small set of bare singular count frames are licensed (institutional/time/iteration).

peripheral.property: Tendency to align with semantic definiteness

stabilisers.evidence: Demonstrative > article grammaticalization stabilizes determiner distribution across generations.
Learners acquire determiner distribution before full definiteness semantics.
Interactive alignment reinforces determiner placement in NP.
Prestige selection shapes which determiner variants persist in a community.

projection.target: The slot can be filled by the DP this or by a genitive NP such as Jo’s. The relation holds in this book and Jo’s book though the dependent belongs to a different category.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates determiner function from determinative category and documents multiple realizations.

perturbations: Weak definites (go to the hospital) weaken semantic definiteness while preserving deital marking.
Generic definites (The tiger is endangered) shift to kind reference.
Proper names are semantically definite without deital marking.

variation.speaker_variation: Dialectal bare-noun patterns (in hospital, at university) shift deitality distribution.

known_boundary_items: weak definites
generic definites
proper names

curious.title: Words that open a noun phrase
curious.summary: A noun phrase can start with a small word or phrase that marks it as a complete phrase and signals whether we mean a particular thing or not.
curious.body: In the new car and one new car, the first word does a job: it marks the phrase as a full noun phrase and tells us whether the car is a definite one or an indefinite one. That job is called determiner. Several kinds of expression can do it. There are small words like the and one, a name with 's added, as in Ally's new car, and in a few frames a whole phrase, as in what size hat or over 20 times. The job is the same each time even though the expression filling it differs. Plural and non-count nouns can go without one, but a singular count noun generally needs one.
curious.try: Look at a noun phrase in a sentence near you and see whether you can find a word or phrase that does this job, like the or Ally's. If you do, is it a small word, a name with 's, or something longer?

teacher.summary: Helps explain that determiner is a function in the noun phrase, filled by several kinds of expression, not only by the and a.
teacher.explain: In this grammar determiner is a function, a function in the NP that licenses a nominal as an NP and marks it for definiteness or indefiniteness. Determinative is the word category. The slot is filled by determinatives (the, one), by genitive NPs (Ally's), and, in a limited set of cases, by plain-case NPs or PPs (what size, over 20). This dictionary says singular count nominals generally need determination, while bare plural and non-count nominals can be determinerless, and a small set of bare singular count frames is licensed. The analysis is marked provisional, and this dictionary notes that weak definites (go to the hospital) and proper names complicate the link between determiner marking and semantic definiteness.
teacher.terms: Traditionally, the and a are called articles; here they are determinatives in determiner function.
watch_for: A learner might take determiner to mean only the words the and a, when Ally's and what size fill the same slot.
A learner might treat determiner and determinative as one term, though one names a function and the other a word category.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a set of noun phrases (the new car, one new car, Ally's new car, what size hat, over 20 times). They underline the determiner in each, then sort the phrases by what kind of expression fills the slot.

checked.note: Fixed: determiner no longer defined as the slot at the front of an NP (function within the NP); try prompt allows for noun phrases without a determiner; removed 'possessives' term (CGEL says genitive). Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Determination." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/determination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deverbal Adjective in -able
pattern: Adj[verb base + -able], with related forms in -ible

entry.name: Deverbal Adjective in -able
entry.pattern: Adj[verb base + -able], with related forms in -ible

1.definition: Characterizes a potential participant of an action by the possibility or suitability of that action.
1.details: Readable normally describes what people can read. The productive transitive pattern is therefore oriented to the base verb’s object. A prepositional verb can supply an oblique participant, as in dependable. Intransitive-base and lexicalized readings, such as perishable, extend beyond the central pattern.

examples.note: Constructed example. The document is what one can search.

examples.form: A [dependable] source is hard to find.
examples.note: Constructed example with depend on as the relevant verb and preposition.

relatedConstructions.notes: The derived form is adjectival.
The central reading is typically paraphrasable with a modal passive.
Washable and This fabric washes well can describe suitability for washing. One derives an adjective and the other forms a clause with an active verb.

grounds.note: Registers the -able and -ible adjective family.
Documents base types, modal interpretation and participant contrasts.

projection.target: For a new transparent formation with a transitive base, the default referent is what can undergo the action. Prepositional verbs can supply a different participant.
projection.evidence: CASA registers the -able and -ible family. CGEL describes the productive modal use and records prefixed, oblique and other departures from it.

curious.title: Adjectives ending in -able
curious.summary: In its central pattern, adding -able to a verb gives an adjective that says something can have that action done to it.
curious.body: Searchable describes a document that someone can search. Readable normally describes what people can read. So a new -able adjective built on a verb that takes an object normally describes the thing the action would be done to, not the person doing it. There are related forms in -ible. Some verbs bring a small word along. Dependable is built on depend on, and it describes what you can depend on. Not every case fits. Perishable doesn't simply mean that something can be perished, so some -able words go beyond this central meaning.

examples.text: A [dependable] source is hard to find.

curious.try: Take a verb you use and add -able. Does the new word describe the thing the action would happen to?

teacher.summary: Helps explain that an -able adjective built on a transitive verb is oriented to the verb's object, and that its central reading can be paraphrased as can be Xed.
teacher.explain: A deverbal adjective in -able (or -ible) characterizes a potential participant of an action by the possibility or suitability of that action. With a transitive base the adjective is oriented to the base verb's object: readable describes what people can read. The central reading can typically be paraphrased with a modal passive (can be searched). A prepositional verb can supply an oblique participant, as in dependable (depend on). Intransitive-base and lexicalized readings, such as perishable, extend beyond this central pattern.
teacher.terms: The paraphrase can be called a modal passive.

examples.text: A [dependable] source is hard to find.

contrasts.note: A related idea in a clause with an active verb; washable is the adjective counterpart.

watch_for: A learner might read dependable as describing the person who depends, when it describes what can be depended on.
A learner might assume every -able word means can be Xed, though perishable and other lexicalized forms extend beyond that pattern.
teacher.activity: Students list verbs from a class text, add -able where it makes a word they know, and paraphrase each as can be Xed. They flag any word that doesn't paraphrase that way.

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary and body and teacher summary now confine object orientation to the central (transitive-base) pattern, as the entry does, and mention readings that go beyond it; dropped the claim that some -able words 'drifted' from the central meaning; dropped the unsupported 'verbal adjectives' traditional-term mapping.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deverbal Adjective in -able." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deverbal-able-adjective-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deverbal Noun in -er

1.definition: Forms a noun for a participant characteristically associated with the action of the base verb.
1.details: The central reading identifies a person who undertakes the activity, as in singer. Instrument readings occur with forms such as mixer. A verbal object can have a corresponding of-phrase with many agent nouns. The same ending in islander supports a separate noun-base pattern.

examples.note: Constructed example of a reviewer’s complement corresponding to the object of review.
Constructed instrument reading with a verbal base.

relatedConstructions.notes: The derivation forms an ordinary common noun.
The base verb’s object can supply the argument of an of-phrase.

grounds.note: Separates verbal and nominal bases and related -or nouns.
Documents meanings and the argument correspondence.

projection.target: A transparently agentive -er noun can license an of-phrase corresponding to the base verb’s object. The -er pattern also admits conventional instruments.
projection.evidence: CASA separately records verbal and nominal bases. CGEL documents agent, instrument and other readings and traces complements back to verbal argument structure.

curious.title: Nouns made by adding -er to a verb
curious.summary: Adding -er to a verb gives a noun for someone or something tied to that action.
curious.body: A singer is a person who sings. The central reading names the person who does the activity. Some -er words name a tool instead, as in mixer. Agent nouns like these can carry a complement that matches the object of the verb. In the reviewer of the manuscript, the manuscript is what gets reviewed. The same ending also shows up in islander, but that follows a different pattern, because it starts from a noun rather than a verb.
curious.try: Think of a verb for a job. Add -er. Is the new word a person or a tool?

teacher.summary: Helps explain agent and instrument nouns in -er and the of-phrase that matches the verb's object.
teacher.explain: A deverbal noun in -er names a participant characteristically associated with the action of the base verb. The central reading identifies the person who does the activity (singer). Instrument readings occur with forms such as mixer. With many agent nouns, the verb's object has a corresponding of-phrase, as in the reviewer of the manuscript. The same ending in islander supports a separate noun-base pattern, so not every -er word comes from a verb.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars call the person-naming ones (singer) agent nouns; instrument readings such as mixer are a further reading of the same pattern. This dictionary treats the result as an ordinary common noun.
watch_for: A learner might assume every -er noun names a person, when mixer names an instrument.
A learner might read islander as built on a verb, when its base is a noun.
teacher.activity: Students match verbs (sing, teach, mix) to -er nouns, then say whether each names a person or a tool, and add an of-phrase to the people words where it fits.

child.hook: What do you call a person who sings?
child.explain: Add -er to a word for an action and you can get a word for who does it, like singer. Sometimes the -er word is a tool instead, like mixer.

examples.text: Dad used a [mixer] for the cake.

child.play: Take sing, paint and teach. Add -er to each one. Say who does each job. Then find a word ending in -er that is a tool.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher terms no longer applies 'agent nouns' to the whole class; it now limits it to the person-naming reading and notes that instrument readings such as mixer belong to the same pattern. Frequency pass: teacher.activity verb review (reviewer about 30,300th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by teach; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deverbal Noun in -er." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deverbal-er-noun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deverbal Noun in -ing
pattern: N[verb base + derivational -ing] with nominal dependents

entry.name: Deverbal Noun in -ing
entry.pattern: N[verb base + derivational -ing] with nominal dependents

1.definition: Names an activity, result, or product using nominal syntax.

examples.form: [The careful sorting of the files] took hours.

projection.target: Careful modifies the noun and of introduces the former object argument. A gerund-participial can instead have carefully and take the files as a direct object.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Activity nouns ending in -ing
curious.summary: Some words in -ing name an activity or its result and behave like nouns, taking words like careful and of.
curious.body: In The careful sorting of the files took hours, sorting names an activity, but it acts like a noun. It takes the adjective careful in front of it, and the files comes after of. The same idea can be said another way. Carefully sorting the files uses the adverb carefully, and the files follows the verb directly. Here the -ing word acts like a verb. This dictionary treats the two patterns as different, and the first as a noun pattern.

examples.text: [The careful sorting of the files] took hours.

curious.try: Compare careful sorting of the files with carefully sorting the files. Which one has of? Which one has an adverb?

teacher.summary: Helps contrast an -ing noun with its nominal dependents against the verb-like -ing form.
teacher.explain: A deverbal noun in -ing names an activity, result or product using nominal syntax. In The careful sorting of the files took hours, careful modifies the noun and of introduces what was formerly the object. A gerund-participial can say the same thing with carefully and take the files as a direct object. This dictionary’s confidence in this analysis is marked medium.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call the noun a verbal noun and the verb-like form a gerund.

examples.text: [The careful sorting of the files] took hours.

contrasts.text: Carefully sorting the files took hours.
contrasts.note: The verb-like version, with an adverb and a direct object.

watch_for: A learner might use careful with the verb-like form, or carefully with the noun-like form, when each pattern takes its own kind of modifier.
teacher.activity: Students rewrite each noun-pattern sentence in the verb-like pattern and back, marking where of appears and where the adverb appears.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deverbal Noun in -ing." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deverbal-ing-nominal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deverbal Noun of-Argument
pattern: NP[(Det) + deverbal Nom + PP[of + argument NP]]

entry.name: Deverbal Noun of-Argument
entry.pattern: NP[(Det) + deverbal Nom + PP[of + argument NP]]

1.definition: An of-phrase expresses an argument of a deverbal noun
1.details: The of-PP expresses a participant in the event denoted by the deverbal noun. Its role is selected by the noun and construction. With a transitive source, a preceding genitive can express the agent while of expresses the affected participant. The of-complement can help identify an event, and an indefinite determiner remains possible.

examples.note: Argument is the entity that failed; the argument helps identify which failure is meant
Argument is the entity that arrived
Argument is the entity that died
The genitive supplies the destroyer and the of-phrase the affected entity
Constructed comparison with an indefinite determiner and an of-argument

constraints.description: Head noun is deverbal (nominalized verb)
Of-PP is complement to the deverbal noun
Of-NP expresses a semantic argument of the underlying verb, typically non-agentive
The of-complement can help identify the nominal referent. It also occurs with indefinite determination.

dimensions.form: NP with deverbal head and of-PP complement
dimensions.meaning: Deverbal expression with a participant specified by an of-phrase
dimensions.function: Refers to events while maintaining argument structure of underlying verb
dimensions.distribution: Common in formal and narrative registers; alternates with genitive construction

relatedConstructions.notes: "The failure of WM" ~ "WM's failure"; genitive preferred for agents, of-PP for non-agentive arguments
An of-argument can contribute to identification. The determiner alternation tests the two properties separately.

projection.target: In the repainting of the hall, of the hall can supply the participant repainted. A repainting of the hall also occurs under an indefinite determiner. Argument realization does not by itself select the definite article.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents complements with nominalized heads, and the constructed determiner alternation holds the head and of-dependent constant.

curious.title: Event nouns followed by of
curious.summary: A noun made from a verb can be followed by of and a phrase naming someone or something involved in the event.
curious.body: In the arrival of the guests, arrival names an event, and of the guests says who arrived. In the destruction of the city, the city is the thing destroyed. The of-phrase names a participant in the event, and the noun decides which role that participant has. When the event has someone who does it, that person can come first with 's, as in the enemy's destruction of the city: the enemy did the destroying, and the city was destroyed. The of-phrase can also help pin down which event is meant, as in the failure of Washington Mutual.
curious.try: Turn a verb you know into a noun (arrive, fail, destroy). Which words can follow it with of?

teacher.summary: Helps explain how an of-phrase after a deverbal noun carries a participant of the underlying verb.
teacher.explain: In an NP with a deverbal noun head, the of-PP is a complement that expresses a semantic argument of the underlying verb, such as the entity that arrived or the entity destroyed. The noun and the construction select the role. With a transitive source, a genitive can express the agent and the of-phrase the affected participant (the enemy's destruction of the city). The of-complement can help identify the event, and an indefinite determiner remains possible (a repainting of the hall). This dictionary notes that the genitive form alternates with the of-form (the failure of WM and WM's failure), with the genitive preferred for agents and the of-PP for non-agentive arguments.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call such nouns nominalizations or verbal nouns.

contrasts.note: The of-phrase names the entity that failed.
The genitive alternative for the same participant.

watch_for: A learner might read the of-phrase in the destruction of the city as the one doing the destroying, when it is the thing destroyed.
A learner might think a noun with an of-argument must be definite, though a repainting of the hall has an indefinite determiner.
teacher.activity: Give students event nouns (arrival, destruction, death, failure). They add an of-phrase to each and say who or what it names and what role that participant has in the event.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deverbal Noun of-Argument." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/deverbal-noun-of-argument-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Difference Complement after different

1.definition: Specifies the referent or situation from which something differs.

examples.form: The result was [different from what we expected].

projection.target: The choice of marker depends on variety and complement form. Than can introduce a finite comparison in uses where from requires a nominal or other licensed complement.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: What something is different from
curious.summary: The word different can be followed by a phrase that names what something differs from.
curious.body: In The result was different from what we expected, the phrase after different says what the result is compared with. This dictionary's pattern lists three small words that can introduce that phrase: from, to and than. The phrase can name a thing or a whole situation. Here it is what we expected, a situation the result is measured against.

examples.text: The result was [different from what we expected].
This road is [different from the old one].

curious.try: Finish the sentence My day today was different from ... in your own words. What did you compare it with?

teacher.summary: Gives the pattern for the standard of comparison after different.
teacher.explain: Different heads an AdjP whose complement specifies the referent or situation from which something differs. The pattern in this dictionary lists from, to and than as introducers of that standard. The standard can be a plain NP or a clause-like expression, as in different from what we expected. This dictionary gives only one illustration and relates the pattern to same-as comparison and to than-reduced clauses.

examples.text: The result was [different from what we expected].
This road is [different from the old one].

watch_for: A learner might not realize that the standard of comparison is what the phrase after different supplies.
teacher.activity: Show two pictures. Students write one sentence about each difference using different from, naming the picture the first thing is compared with.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Difference Complement after different." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/difference-than-from-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Measure Differential in a Comparative

1.definition: Gives the numerical difference between a degree and its standard.

examples.form: The replacement is [two centimetres wider] than the old bracket.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. In the plain-grade measurement frame the measure gives the total width.

projection.target: Two centimetres measures the difference, not the total width. Explicitly naming the comparison standard can therefore fix the implied total independently.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how much bigger, in numbers
curious.summary: A measurement placed before a comparison word, such as wider, says by how much the two things differ.
curious.body: In The replacement is two centimetres wider than the old bracket, two centimetres is the gap between the two brackets. The two centimetres measures that difference, not the total width of the new bracket. Compare It was two centimetres wide. Here there's no comparison word, and the measure gives the total width. The same measurement phrase does two different jobs, depending on whether the adjective is in its comparative form.

examples.text: The replacement is [two centimetres wider] than the old bracket.

curious.try: Say how much taller you are than a friend or a chair, using a number and taller.

teacher.summary: Helps contrast a measure phrase giving a difference (two centimetres wider) with one giving a total (two centimetres wide).
teacher.explain: A measure NP before a comparative AdjP or AdvP gives the numerical difference between a degree and its standard. In two centimetres wider than the old bracket, the measure is the difference between the two widths. In the plain-grade frame, as in two centimetres wide, the same kind of measure gives the total width. The contrast helps learners see that the comparative form changes what the measure means.

examples.text: The replacement is [two centimetres wider] than the old bracket.

contrasts.text: The replacement is [two centimetres wider] than the old bracket.
contrasts.note: The measure is the difference.
The measure is the total width.

watch_for: A learner might read two centimetres wider as the total width of the new bracket.
teacher.activity: Students measure two objects in the room and write two sentences about them, one with a measure plus a comparative (three centimetres longer than ...) and one with a measure plus the plain adjective (twenty centimetres long).

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body no longer says the new bracket isn't two centimetres wide in total; it says only that the measure is the difference, not the total width, as the entry does.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Measure Differential in a Comparative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/differential-measure-comparative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Direct Quotation with Reporting Predicate
pattern: quotation + reporting predicate or reporting predicate + quotation

entry.name: Direct Quotation with Reporting Predicate
entry.pattern: quotation + reporting predicate or reporting predicate + quotation

1.definition: Presents words as directly voiced or displayed against a reporting frame.

relatedConstructions.notes: Jo said, “I’m ready” presents a quotation in the original speaker’s terms. Jo said that she was ready reports content from the reporting context.

projection.target: I and tomorrow are anchored to the quoted speech. A verbal question can retain root inversion inside the quote, unlike the ordinary indirect question complement.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Quoting someone's exact words
curious.summary: A direct quotation presents words as the speaker voiced them, set against a frame saying who spoke.
curious.body: In "I'll call tomorrow," Jo said, the quoted words come first and the frame Jo said follows. The frame can also come first. Either way, the quotation presents the words in the original speaker's terms. Reporting the same message differently changes the wording. Jo said, "I'm ready" quotes her words, and Jo said that she was ready reports what she meant from the point of view of the person doing the reporting.

examples.text: Jo said that she was ready.

curious.try: Tell a friend what you said earlier in the day, first in your exact words and then in a report that starts with that.

teacher.summary: Helps contrast a direct quotation with an indirect report of the same message.
teacher.explain: A direct quotation presents words as directly voiced or displayed against a reporting frame, either quotation plus reporting predicate or the reverse. The quotation keeps the original speaker's terms. An indirect report, by contrast, reports content from the reporting context, which is why the pronoun and verb form in Jo said that she was ready differ from those in Jo said, "I'm ready". This dictionary relates direct quotation to indirect reports and to closed interrogative clauses.
teacher.terms: Traditionally, direct speech versus indirect (reported) speech.

contrasts.note: Direct quotation, in the original speaker's terms.

contrasts.text: Jo said that she was ready.
contrasts.note: Indirect report, with content from the reporting context.

watch_for: A learner might treat Jo said, "I'm ready" and Jo said that she was ready as identical in how they present the words.
teacher.activity: Students write down a short remark from a partner as a direct quotation, then rewrite it as an indirect report, and mark which words changed.

child.hook: How do you tell someone exactly what a friend said?
child.explain: You can say a person's exact words and then say who spoke. Or you can say who spoke first. Jo said, "I'm ready" repeats her words. Jo said that she was ready tells what she meant.
child.play: Ask a friend to say one sentence. Write it down in quotation marks and add who said it. Then tell it again without the exact words.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Direct Quotation with Reporting Predicate." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/direct-quotation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Directive had better

1.definition: Recommends a course of action, often implying an adverse consequence otherwise.

projection.target: Had can contract to ’d but ordinarily cannot be replaced by present have. The directive refers to prospective rather than past action.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Advice with had better
curious.summary: Had better recommends a course of action and often hints at a bad result if it isn't followed.
curious.body: In You had better bring the receipt, the speaker recommends bringing it. The words had better work together as a fixed unit, and the verb after them, bring, is in its plain form. The recommendation often carries a hint of what could go wrong otherwise, so it can feel stronger than a simple suggestion.
curious.try: Think of a time you gave someone strong advice. Could you have said it with had better?

teacher.summary: Helps explain had better as a fixed unit recommending an action, followed by the plain form of a verb.
teacher.explain: The directive had better is a VP with fixed had and better followed by a plain infinitival, as in You had better bring the receipt. It recommends a course of action, often implying an adverse consequence otherwise. This dictionary relates it to modal verbs with plain complements, because the verb after it is the plain form, as it is after a modal.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats it as a fixed VP pattern related to modal verbs.
watch_for: A learner might add to before the verb, though the pattern takes the plain form (bring).
A learner might hear had as signalling past time, when the pattern recommends an action.
teacher.activity: Give students short scenarios (a rainy day, a test, a train leaving). They write one had better sentence advising a character, then add what might go wrong otherwise.

child.hook: What do you say when you really need a friend to hurry?
child.explain: Had better is how you tell someone what is a good idea to do. It can hint that something bad might happen if they don't.
child.play: Make a had better sentence for each picture in a story. Then say what might go wrong.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Directive had better." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/directive-had-better-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Directive-Ostensive Construction

1.definition: Alerts addressee to attend to referent in shared environment
1.details: Directs addressee's attention to something present or imminent. Ostensive in the Sperber & Wilson sense - showing rather than describing. Typically exclamatory intonation with fall or rise-fall. Not syntactically integrated as a clause argument. Normal NP determination applies.

constraints.description: Normal NP determination (singular count nouns require a determiner; non-count and plural can be bare)
Referent must be present or imminent in shared environment
Exclamatory intonation, typically fall or rise-fall
Referent is NOT the addressee (distinguishes from vocative)

1.notes: Both are non-argumental NPs with directive function; vocative addresses hearer, directive-ostensive alerts hearer to something else

relatedConstructions.notes: Environment-directed packaging of the ostensive NP
Both direct attention but differ in target (addressee vs. environment)
Prototypically exclamatory, but murmured reminders show the profiles can come apart

projection.target: Membership predicts full NP-internal determination despite extra-clausal status (contrast block language: A snake! vs headline Snake found in library), introduction of a discourse referent available to anaphora (contrast interjections: A snake! It's moving vs Ouch! *It...), orientation-type rather than verbal response (contrast interrogatives), and immediacy construal (referent present or imminent)
projection.evidence: The determination and anaphora contrasts separate the construction from its nearest neighbours (block language, interjections); acquisitional continuity with joint-attention pointing is a testable CHILDES prediction

diagnostics: non-count and plural can be bare

stabilisers.evidence: Need to rapidly alert others to threats or opportunities
High-frequency alerting expressions (Fire!, Watch out!)

curious.title: Shouting a noun phrase to point something out
curious.summary: A speaker can call attention to something present or about to happen by saying just a noun phrase, such as The bus!
curious.body: Sometimes one noun phrase is the whole message. Someone shouts A snake! or The bus!, and the listener looks, because the thing is right there or about to happen. The speaker is showing something rather than describing it. It is typically spoken as an exclamation, with a falling or rising-then-falling tune, though a murmured reminder can lack that tone. The thing named isn't the listener, which separates this from calling someone's name. The noun phrase follows the ordinary rules: a singular count noun like snake comes with a word such as a, while a plural (Robbers!) or a non-count noun (Fire!) can stand bare.
curious.try: Imagine something about to happen that you want a friend to notice. What would you say in just a few words, and is the thing you name the friend?

teacher.summary: Helps explain single noun phrases used as attention-getting exclamations, and how they differ from vocatives.
teacher.explain: The directive-ostensive is a non-argumental NP that alerts the addressee to a referent in the shared environment. The referent must be present or imminent, and it is not the addressee, which separates the pattern from a vocative. It is typically exclamatory, with a fall or rise-fall, though murmured reminders show that the exclamatory profile can come apart from the function. The NP follows ordinary determination: singular count nouns require a determiner (A snake!), while plural and non-count nouns can be bare (Robbers!, Fire!). It isn't an argument of any clause.
teacher.terms: This dictionary relates the pattern to exclamations and contrasts it with the vocative.

contrasts.note: Alerts the addressee to something imminent; the bus is not the person addressed.
A vocative, which names the person addressed.

watch_for: A learner might take The bus! to address a listener called the bus, when it points the listener at the bus.
A learner might assume a determiner is required, though plural Robbers! and non-count Fire! are bare.
teacher.activity: Students act out scenes (a bus leaving, a snake, lost keys). A partner says one noun phrase to alert another, who says what the speaker pointed out. Then they change one to a vocative, such as a name.

child.hook: What do you shout when you see the bus leaving?
child.explain: Sometimes a few words are all you need to make someone look. You say the name of the thing that is there or about to happen. You aren't talking about the person you shout to.
child.play: Pick a scene, such as a bus, a snake or lost keys. Say just a few words to make a friend look. Can they guess what you mean?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body now says the exclamatory delivery is typical rather than invariant, as the entry does (it notes murmured reminders can lack it).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Directive-Ostensive Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/directive-ostensive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Dispositional Middle
pattern: Clause[Theme Subject + active transitive-capable V + optional ease/manner modifier]

entry.name: Dispositional Middle
entry.pattern: Clause[Theme Subject + active transitive-capable V + optional ease/manner modifier]

1.definition: Presents a referent as having a disposition affecting how an action can be carried out on it.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. An eventive passive with a specific occasion, in contrast to the dispositional middle.

relatedConstructions.notes: This fabric washes well attributes a disposition with active verb forms. This fabric was washed at noon reports a particular event in the passive.
This fabric washes well invites an interpretation involving a washer. The door opened can simply report a change of state without invoking an implicit opener.

projection.target: The subject corresponds to the ordinary object, yet the verb is active. The default generic assessment contrasts with an event report such as This fabric was washed at noon.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Things that wash well
curious.summary: A sentence with an ordinary verb can describe how an action can be carried out on something.
curious.body: This fabric washes well describes the fabric, and the verb washes looks like any active verb. But the sentence is about a quality of the fabric: how an action can be carried out on it. The sentence suggests someone doing the washing. Compare The fabric was washed at noon. That reports a particular event on a particular occasion, so it isn't a statement about the fabric's qualities.
curious.try: Think of an object around you and a verb for something done to it. Can you say how well it does under that action, as in This fabric washes well?

teacher.summary: Helps explain active-form clauses that describe a property of the subject, not an event, and contrast them with passives.
teacher.explain: The dispositional middle is a clause whose subject is the theme, with an active transitive-capable verb and an optional ease or manner modifier. It presents a referent as having a disposition affecting how an action can be carried out on it. This fabric washes well attributes a disposition with active verb forms; This fabric was washed at noon reports a particular event in the passive. This dictionary notes that This fabric washes well invites an interpretation involving a washer, unlike The door opened, which can simply report a change of state without an implicit opener.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the middle construction, or simply the middle.

contrasts.note: An eventive passive with a specific occasion.
Can simply report a change of state without an implicit opener.

watch_for: A learner might read This fabric washes well as describing something the fabric does by itself.
A learner might treat This fabric washes well and This fabric was washed at noon as the same, though the first attributes a disposition and the second reports a particular event.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences about objects (the bread cuts easily, the tickets were sold yesterday) and ask them to sort them into disposition statements and event reports.

checked.note: Fixed: removed the comparison with the adjective washable (this dictionary makes no such comparison). Also fixed (unflagged): replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'. Second round: fixed teacher.terms by dropping 'traditionally' and 'middle voice' (a broader label this dictionary doesn't use); fixed teacher.watch_for[1] to contrast this dictionary's two example sentences rather than middles and passives in general; curious.summary no longer singles out ease (this dictionary includes manner); the door contrast now says it can simply report a change of state. Also fixed (unflagged): teacher.explain ties the implied washer to This fabric washes well, as this dictionary does, not to middles in general.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Dispositional Middle." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/dispositional-middle-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Distributive Rate with each or apiece
pattern: measure or counted NP + each/apiece, with a group supplied by context

entry.name: Distributive Rate with each or apiece
entry.pattern: measure or counted NP + each/apiece, with a group supplied by context

1.definition: Assigns the stated amount to each unit or participant.

projection.target: The six dollars is the price of an individual ticket. With six dollars altogether, the same amount instead applies to the whole set.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Prices and amounts per item
curious.summary: Words like apiece and each after an amount say the amount applies to every item or person in a group.
curious.body: In The tickets cost six dollars apiece, six dollars is the price of one ticket, not the price of all of them together. Apiece gives the amount to each ticket in the group. The group isn't named in the amount phrase itself. The context supplies it, here the tickets. Each can do the same job.
curious.try: Say the price of three things you know, using each or apiece after the amount.

teacher.summary: Worth teaching with each (two dollars each); apiece is relatively infrequent (about 9,000th among word forms in the SUBTLEX-UK subtitle counts), so treat it if it comes up rather than teaching it. Helps explain each and apiece after an amount as a rate assigned to each member of a group.
teacher.explain: A measure or counted NP followed by each or apiece assigns the stated amount to each unit or participant, with the group supplied by context. In The tickets cost six dollars apiece, six dollars is the rate per ticket. The pattern is related to indefinite rates and to floating distributives.
teacher.terms: This dictionary labels the pattern a distributive rate.

contrasts.note: The amount applies to each ticket.

contrasts.text: The tickets cost six dollars altogether.
contrasts.note: A total for the group, for contrast.

watch_for: A learner might read six dollars apiece as the total for all the tickets.
A learner might look for the group in the amount phrase, when context supplies it.
teacher.activity: Students write price tags for a class shop using each, then a partner states the total for three items.

child.hook: If pens are two dollars each, how much is one pen?
child.explain: Each and apiece tell the price of one thing. The tickets cost six dollars apiece means one ticket costs six dollars. The talk around it tells you which things.
child.play: Set up a pretend shop. Give each thing a price using each or apiece. Then tell a friend what three of them would cost.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer implies the group comes from an earlier sentence (the group can be named in the same sentence); cut the description of floating distributives, which the entry does not give. Frequency pass: teacher.summary now says to teach the pattern with each and treat apiece (about 9,000th in SUBTLEX-UK) if it comes up; teacher.activity price tags now use each only.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Distributive Rate with each or apiece." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/distributive-rate-apiece-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Ditransitive VP (Double-object Construction)

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb with two internal core complements: indirect object followed by direct object
dimensions.meaning: Role alignment is centred on recipient and theme, but extends to goods-beneficiary, prevention, source, loss, and other affected-participant interpretations
dimensions.function: Packages two participants as indirect and direct object
dimensions.distribution: Licensed by particular verb senses; many, but not all, have a related monotransitive VP with a to- or for-PP

1.definition: The indirect object denotes a recipient of the entity, information, or experience denoted by the direct object
1.details: CGEL defines ditransitive complementation syntactically for clauses and verb uses by Oi + Od; both objects are internal to the VP and licensed by its head verb. This entry records that complementation pattern at VP level, not a necessary caused-possession meaning. Goldberg instead organizes the double-object pattern around a caused-receipt or giving prototype with related extensions (CGEL Ch. 4 §§1–1.1, 4.3, 8.2, pp. 215–17, 248–51, 308–13; Goldberg 2006: 20–28).

2.definition: The indirect object denotes the intended beneficiary or recipient of goods created or obtained
2.details: CGEL restricts the central beneficiary alternation mainly to beneficiaries of goods rather than services; the interpretation normally includes intended transfer of the direct-object referent (CGEL pp. 310–11).

examples.note: Goods-beneficiary use; contrast service-beneficiary *I'll do you the washing-up

3.definition: The indirect object denotes a prevented recipient, source, loser, or other affected participant rather than an actual recipient
3.details: These participants are still indirect objects on syntactic evidence. CGEL includes Oi-only permission and refusal verbs and source-role uses of charge, cost, and fine (pp. 309, 311–13); Goldberg analyzes prevented receipt and loss as extensions of the giving prototype.

examples.note: Ed is source rather than recipient

constraints.description: Licensing is lexeme- and sense-specific: give allows Oi or to, explain is to-only, buy allows Oi or for, borrow is for-only, and spare has Oi-only senses.
In the canonical VP, Oi precedes Od. Some chiefly BrE varieties allow Od–Oi when both are personal pronouns, as in He gave it her.
A to- or for-PP is not an indirect object. In sent a copy to Sue, the VP is monotransitive: a copy is Od, the to-PP is a complement, and Sue is oblique within that PP.
With only one object in a canonical active VP, that object is Od even when its semantic role corresponds to the Oi of a ditransitive alternant.
Recipient, animacy, and caused receipt are central tendencies, not necessary conditions for membership in the CGEL syntactic class.

projection.target: A verb sense attested in the canonical Head–NP–NP frame predicts reduced frontability and postposability of the first NP relative to the second, preference for first-object passivization, and an animate, given, and topical bias in the first-object slot
projection.evidence: CGEL documents fixed order and extraction asymmetries on pp. 248–50, passive asymmetries on pp. 249–50, information-packaging preferences on pp. 309–10, and role and alternant classes on pp. 308–13

grounds.note: Order, extraction, passive, information-packaging, and alternant diagnostics
The Oi/Od asymmetries recur across independently defined verb-sense classes

core.property: Two internal core-complement objects, Oi and Od
diagnostics: contrast with Od plus PP and Od plus predicative complement
Oi-or-to, to-only, Oi-or-for, for-only, and Oi-only lexical classes

peripheral.property: Recipient or goods-beneficiary bias for Oi

diagnostics: Od plus to-PP or for-PP for many, but not all, verb senses
Oi-corresponding passive subject generally preferred over Od-corresponding passive subject

activation_states.context: Both objects are personal pronouns in some BrE varieties

activation_states.effect: Passive acceptability is generally lower and more speaker-variable

variation.speaker_variation: Judgements vary for second passives, for-beneficiary passives, and some service-beneficiary double-object VPs.

known_boundary_items: sent a copy to Sue: Od plus PP, hence monotransitive, not ditransitive
considered Ed a fool: Od plus NP predicative complement, not two objects
sent Kim to the back: Od plus locative-goal PP, hence monotransitive and not ditransitive
teaches the students: its sole object is Od despite matching the semantic role of a ditransitive Oi

relatedConstructions.notes: Ditransitive complementation is a specialization of VP structure
The two object slots are normally realized by NPs
Caused motion has one Od plus a locative PP complement and is therefore monotransitive, not ditransitive

grounds.note: Ditransitive complementation is the syntactic Head-Oi-Od pattern, not a semantic transfer class
Caused-receipt prototype and extensions in the double-object semantic network

curious.title: Verbs that take two objects
curious.summary: Some verbs can be followed by two noun phrases in a row, such as someone who receives and the thing received.
curious.body: In I sent Sue a copy, the verb sent is followed by two things: Sue, who gets the copy, and a copy, what is sent. The first is called the indirect object and the second the direct object. Each is a full noun phrase, and the verb allows both. The pattern isn't only about handing things over. It also fits She baked Kim a cake, where the cake is meant for Kim, and It cost Mel his job, where Mel loses something. Which verbs allow it depends on the verb: some also allow a version with to or for, as in I sent a copy to Sue, and some don't.
curious.try: Say I sent Sue a copy, then say I sent a copy to Sue. Does the meaning change? Now try the same with other verbs, such as baked or told.

teacher.summary: Helps explain double-object verbs, what counts as an indirect object, and how they differ from verbs with a to- or for-phrase.
teacher.explain: A ditransitive VP has a verb followed by two internal objects, the indirect object (Oi) and then the direct object (Od), as in sent Sue a copy. This dictionary treats this as a syntactic pattern, not a meaning class: the Oi tends to be a recipient or beneficiary of goods, but can also be a prevented recipient, a source or a loser (refused Kim permission, charged Ed ten dollars, cost Mel his job). Which verb senses allow it is lexically specific: give allows Oi or a to-phrase, explain takes only to, buy allows Oi or for, and borrow takes only for. A to- or for-phrase is not an indirect object: in sent a copy to Sue, a copy is the direct object and the verb is monotransitive.
teacher.terms: Indirect object and direct object are the usual terms. Double-object construction is another name for the same pattern.

contrasts.note: Two objects, indirect then direct.

contrasts.text: I sent a copy to Sue.
contrasts.note: One object plus a to-phrase; monotransitive.
One object plus a predicative NP, not two objects.

watch_for: A learner might treat the to-phrase in sent a copy to Sue as an indirect object.
A learner might assume any verb that can take a to-phrase can also take two objects, though licensing depends on the verb sense.
A learner might read the two NPs in considered Ed a fool as two objects, when a fool describes Ed.
teacher.activity: Give students verb cards (give, send, bake, explain, buy). They try each in a double-object sentence and in a to- or for-phrase sentence, sort the results, and compare with a dictionary or the teacher.

child.hook: Can you give a friend a pencil without saying "to"?
child.explain: Some verbs can be followed by who something is for and then the thing itself. Dad baked Kim a cake. The cake is meant for Kim. The words come in that order.
child.play: Make up sentences with who gets something, then what they get. Try sent, told and baked. Then say each one again with to or for and a name at the end.

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer says Kim gets the cake (the entry says the cake is intended for Kim); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; 'often' replaced by 'tends to be' (the entry calls recipient a central tendency). Cut the unsupported term 'dative alternation' (narrower to-phrase label, not in the entry).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Ditransitive VP (Double-object Construction)." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/ditransitive-vp-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Domain Adjunct with -wise

1.definition: Restricts the dimension within which the following claim is assessed.

projection.target: The same van can be worse in comfort without contradiction. The adjunct sets the assessment domain rather than describing how better is realized.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Narrowing a claim with -wise
curious.summary: A word ending in -wise at the start of a sentence says which aspect the rest of the sentence is about.
curious.body: In Cost-wise, the smaller van is better, the opening word cost-wise limits the claim. The smaller van is better as far as cost goes, and the sentence doesn't say it is better in every way. The opening expression sets the dimension within which the following claim is judged. It stands at the front of the sentence, apart from the main statement.
curious.try: Take a choice you've made recently. Can you say which aspect it was better in, starting with a word in -wise?

teacher.summary: Helps explain a front-placed -wise word that restricts the dimension of a claim.
teacher.explain: A domain adjunct in -wise is an initial expression in -wise followed by a clause. It restricts the dimension within which the following claim is assessed. In Cost-wise, the smaller van is better, the claim holds for cost. This dictionary relates the pattern to gradation and cites CGEL's treatment of adverbial word formation.
watch_for: A learner might read the -wise word as describing the van, when it names the dimension of the comparison.
A learner might read the claim as holding in every respect, when the -wise word limits it.
teacher.activity: Students compare two options (two phones, two routes) and write two -wise sentences, each naming a different dimension where a different option wins.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Domain Adjunct with -wise." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/domain-wise-adjunct-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Postverbal Durational long
pattern: VP[... + long in a non-affirmative duration frame]

entry.name: Postverbal Durational long
entry.pattern: VP[... + long in a non-affirmative duration frame]

1.definition: Describes a potentially long duration, typically under negation, a question, or a conditional.
1.details: Plain long in the postverbal position is natural in They didn’t stay long and Will they stay long? The ordinary affirmative They stayed long is markedly less natural for many speakers. Modified forms can behave differently, as in They stayed too long. The category analysis varies across sources. A separate use before the main verb is possible in affirmative They have long known.

examples.note: Negated example used in CGEL's temporal duration discussion.

relatedConstructions.notes: A polar question can license durational long.
A conditional antecedent can also license it.

grounds.note: Documents environments and proposes an NP analysis for the postverbal use.
Gives reasons for an adverb analysis and records the duration and polarity contrast.

projection.target: Changing polarity or clause type while holding the duration predicate fixed can make plain postverbal long natural. Degree modification can change the distribution.
projection.evidence: FrameNet supplies documented questions, negation, conditional clauses and a separate preverbal use. CGEL independently marks the usual affirmative restriction for plain long.

curious.title: Asking or denying "long" after a verb
curious.summary: Plain long after a verb works in a question, a negative or an if-clause to describe a potentially long time.
curious.body: They didn't stay long and Did you wait long? both use long to talk about how much time passed. The word fits in a question such as Will they stay long?, and in a negative. This dictionary says a conditional can license it too. This dictionary says the plain affirmative They stayed long is markedly less natural for many speakers. Adding a modifier changes things, as in They stayed too long. Linguists analyse the word differently, so this dictionary leaves its category open.
curious.try: Say a sentence with long after a verb in a question and one in a negative. Then try an if-clause.

teacher.summary: Helps explain how postverbal durational long fits question, negative and conditional frames.
teacher.explain: Postverbal long describes a potentially long duration, typically in a non-affirmative frame: a negative (They didn't stay long), a polar question (Did you wait long?) or a conditional antecedent. This dictionary says the ordinary affirmative They stayed long is markedly less natural for many speakers. Modified forms can behave differently, as in They stayed too long. A separate use before the main verb is possible in affirmative They have long known. The category analysis varies across sources: CGEL gives reasons for an adverb, and the Constructicon draft proposes an NP analysis for the postverbal use.
teacher.terms: Duration adverbial; non-affirmative (or polarity-sensitive) contexts.

contrasts.note: A modified form, which can behave differently from plain long.
A separate use before the main verb.

watch_for: A learner might assume that the question and negative frames carry over to every affirmative sentence with long, though this dictionary describes the plain affirmative as markedly less natural.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences with long into question, negative, conditional and affirmative frames, and discuss which affirmative versions are natural.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Postverbal Durational long." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/durational-long-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: each in a Partitive NP

1.definition: Distributes a predication over every member of an established group.

examples.form: [Each of the six drawers] has a lock.

relatedConstructions.notes: Each of the six drawers uses a partitive domain and distributes the predication over every drawer in it.

projection.target: The of-phrase has a plural complement, while each favours singular verbal agreement. Every without a following one does not normally form the same construction.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Each of the group
curious.summary: Each followed by of and a known group says something about every member of that group.
curious.body: In Each of the six drawers has a lock, the six drawers are a group already in view. The sentence says that every one of them has a lock, one by one. The word each singles out the members, and the phrase after of names the group they belong to. The group is expressed with a plural and a definite word such as the.

examples.text: [Each of the six drawers] has a lock.
[Each of the boys] has a bike.

curious.try: Pick a group you both know, such as the books on a table. Say something true of each one, starting with each of.

teacher.summary: Helps explain each of plus a plural definite NP as a way to apply a statement to every member of a known group.
teacher.explain: In each + PP[of + plural definite NP], each distributes the predication over every member of an established group, as in Each of the six drawers has a lock. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the true partitive: the of-phrase gives a partitive domain, and the predication is distributed over every drawer in it. This dictionary also relates the pattern to grammatical number, since the group is plural and the distribution works member by member.

examples.text: [Each of the six drawers] has a lock.
[Each of the boys] has a bike.

watch_for: A learner might use each of with a group that hasn't been established, though the pattern distributes over a known group.
A learner might treat each of the six drawers as describing the drawers together, when it describes them one by one.
teacher.activity: Students look at a picture of a group (six drawers, a team) and write a sentence saying something true of each member, beginning each of the.

child.hook: Can one word talk about every drawer in turn?
child.explain: Each of the six drawers has a lock means every drawer has one. You count them one at a time. The group is one you already know about.

examples.text: [Each of the six drawers] has a lock.
[Each of the girls] has a bike.

child.play: Look at a group of things in the room. Say one true thing about each one, starting with each of the.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "each in a Partitive NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/each-of-partitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Echo Question
pattern: Question[echo] applied to Host:Clause[clause type preserved] / Non-headed clausal-semantics construction + echo prosody (+ variable phrase in situ)

entry.name: Echo Question
entry.pattern: Question[echo] applied to Host:Clause[clause type preserved] / Non-headed clausal-semantics construction + echo prosody (+ variable phrase in situ)

dimensions.form: An independently typed Clause or licensed clause-analogue construction echoes a prior utterance, often with rising or rise-fall prosody; a questioned constituent may be replaced by an in-situ variable phrase
dimensions.meaning: Questions what the previous speaker said or meant, rather than directly questioning the echoed proposition
dimensions.function: Requests repetition or clarification of a prior utterance, often also conveying surprise or incredulity
dimensions.distribution: Response to a linguistic stimulus; overlays declarative, closed-interrogative, imperative, and other Clause types without replacing them, and also licenses non-headed echo hosts

1.definition: Repeats all or part of a prior utterance to ask whether that is what the previous speaker said
1.details: The echo question is not a sixth clause type. Question is a semantic category applied as a stimulus-dependent layer while a clausal host preserves its grammatical type and a non-headed host remains non-headed. Its implicit propositional content concerns the prior speech act: an echo of Is he resigning? asks approximately whether the previous speaker asked that question, not whether he is resigning (CGEL pp. 853–54, 886–90).

examples.form: A: She is leaving on Saturday. B: [She is leaving on Saturday]?
examples.note: Repetition echo with declarative clause type preserved

examples.form: A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
examples.note: The echo remains a closed interrogative Clause

examples.form: A: Ed is quite competent. B: [Ed quite competent]?
examples.note: Bare-predication echo with a non-headed host; question semantics does not make it a Clause

2.definition: Replaces a poorly heard or understood part of the stimulus with an in-situ variable phrase to request clarification
2.details: Variable echoes normally retain the word order and clause type of the stimulus rather than acquiring ordinary open-interrogative syntax. Reduction and deictic adjustment are common because the stimulus came from another speaker.

examples.form: A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
examples.note: Variable echo superimposed on an imperative Clause

examples.form: A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?
examples.note: Variable echo superimposed on a closed interrogative Clause, with deictic shift

constraints.description: Requires a recoverable linguistic stimulus whose wording or interpretation is being repeated or clarified.

The echo overlay does not determine syntactic category: an underlying declarative, closed-interrogative, imperative, or other headed Clause retains its defining syntax, and a licensed non-headed host does not become a Clause.
Variable echoes may leave the questioned phrase in the position corresponding to the stimulus and may reduce other recoverable material.

projection.target: Recognizing an echo question predicts preservation of the host's syntactic classification, stimulus-bound deictic adjustment, possible in-situ variable replacement, and answers directed to what was said or meant rather than directly to the echoed proposition
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts echo with ordinary questions through clause-type preservation, stimulus dependence, deictic shift, variable placement, and response interpretation on pp. 853–54 and 886–90

grounds.note: Clause-type preservation, stimulus dependence, and variable placement recur across echo subtypes

diagnostics: response targets what was said or meant

known_boundary_items: Declarative questions such as They've finished? seek confirmation of a proposition using declarative syntax but need not echo a linguistic stimulus.
Ordinary open interrogatives are typed by an interrogative phrase and normally front a non-subject phrase; variable echoes preserve stimulus order.

relatedConstructions.notes: Echo Question specializes Question by making the questioned content a prior linguistic stimulus
Many echoes overlay an independently typed headed Clause without becoming a clause type
A licensed non-headed expression can host echo-question semantics without becoming a Clause
Declarative questions have declarative syntax and confirmation bias but do not require a linguistic stimulus
Variable echoes may contain similar forms but preserve stimulus order rather than instantiating ordinary open-interrogative syntax

grounds.note: Echo questions overlay independently determined clause types and seek repetition or clarification

curious.title: Repeating what someone said as a question
curious.summary: A speaker can repeat all or part of what was just said, in the form of a question, to check it or to ask for clarification.
curious.body: If someone says She is leaving on Saturday, you can reply She is leaving on Saturday? with a questioning tune. You're asking whether that is what they said. You aren't asking whether she is leaving. You can also swap a part you didn't hear or understand for a question word. After Give it to Angela, the reply Give it to who? keeps the original order and asks about the missing piece. The echo depends on what the other person just said.

examples.text: A: She is leaving on Saturday. B: [She is leaving on Saturday]?
A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?

curious.try: Next time you didn't catch a word, say back what you heard and swap the missing part for who or what.

teacher.summary: Helps explain echo questions as a layer over a prior utterance that keeps the clause type of what is echoed.
teacher.explain: An echo question repeats all or part of a prior utterance to ask whether that is what the previous speaker said.
