This dictionary says it isn't a sixth clause type: it's a semantic layer on a stimulus, and the clausal host keeps its grammatical type (declarative, closed interrogative, imperative). A non-headed host stays non-headed, as in Ed quite competent? Echoing Is he resigning? asks approximately whether the previous speaker asked that, not whether he's resigning. A variable echo replaces a poorly heard or understood part with an in-situ variable phrase and keeps the stimulus's word order and clause type, sometimes with reduction and deictic shift (Did I use a what?).
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats the echo question as a stimulus-dependent layer over a host, not as a clause type.

examples.text: A: She is leaving on Saturday. B: [She is leaving on Saturday]?
A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
A: Ed is quite competent. B: [Ed quite competent]?
A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?

contrasts.text: A: Is he going to resign? B: [Is he going to resign]?
contrasts.note: The echo stays a closed interrogative.

contrasts.text: A: Did you use a macro? B: [Did I use a what]?
contrasts.note: Variable echo with deictic shift (you becomes I).

watch_for: A learner might read the reply Is he going to resign? as asking about his resigning, when it checks what the previous speaker asked.
A learner might expect a variable echo to take ordinary question-word order, though it keeps the stimulus's order.
teacher.activity: Pairs take turns saying a sentence with one word hard to hear. The listener echoes it back, swapping the missed word for who or what, and the speaker repeats the word.

child.hook: What do you say when you didn't hear a word?
child.explain: You can say back what you heard as a question. You can swap the missing word for who or what. Someone says Give it to Angela. You say Give it to who?

examples.text: A: Give it to Angela. B: [Give it to who]?
A: I found a snake. B: [You found a what]?

child.play: Whisper a sentence to a friend and mumble one word. They say it back and swap the mumbled word for who or what.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Echo Question." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/echo-question-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Correlative either … or

1.definition: Introduces alternatives with an overt marker at the left edge.

examples.form: Pick [either the blue folder or the red one].

projection.target: Either signals a forthcoming alternative. Exclusion of both can be imposed by context without being a universal truth-condition of or.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Offering two choices with either and or
curious.summary: Either at the start and or between marks a pair of alternatives.
curious.body: In Pick either the blue folder or the red one, the word either warns at the left edge that two alternatives are coming, and or introduces the second. The two options are the blue folder and the red one. The pattern puts the overt marker at the left edge. This dictionary relates it to a neighbouring pattern with neither and nor.

examples.text: Pick [either the blue folder or the red one].
You can have [either tea or juice].

curious.try: Offer a friend two choices for lunch, using either and or.

teacher.summary: Helps explain correlative coordination with either and or, where either marks the alternatives at the left edge.
teacher.explain: Either ... or is a correlative coordination: either, an overt marker at the left edge, introduces the alternatives, and or links them. The pattern is either + XP + or + XP, so the choices are two phrases, here two NPs. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of coordination and relates it to neither ... nor.
teacher.terms: Traditionally, either and or are correlative conjunctions.

examples.text: Pick [either the blue folder or the red one].
You can have [either tea or juice].

watch_for: A learner might place either before the second option instead of at the left edge.
A learner might confuse either ... or with neither ... nor, which is a related but separate pattern.
teacher.activity: Students write choices for a menu using either ... or, then swap papers and mark the two alternatives in each.

child.hook: How do you offer someone two choices at once?
child.explain: Either goes before the first choice. Or goes before the second. You can say Pick either the blue folder or the red one.

examples.text: Pick [either the blue folder or the red one].
You can have [either tea or juice].

child.play: Offer a friend two snacks using either and or. They pick one and say which they chose.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Correlative either … or." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/either-or-coordination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Emphatic Polarity Response Family
pattern: hell + yeah | shit + no | fuck + {yeah, yes, no} | fucking + {yes, no} | hell fucking no

entry.name: Emphatic Polarity Response Family
entry.pattern: hell + yeah | shit + no | fuck + {yeah, yes, no} | fucking + {yes, no} | hell fucking no

dimensions.form: Documented linear combinations of an emphatic expression with a polarity response; the expanded hell fucking no is included without a commitment about its internal bracketing
dimensions.meaning: Emotional emphasis on the response expressed through yeah, yes or no
dimensions.function: An emphatic response, sometimes followed by a longer turn; the conversational action depends on context
dimensions.distribution: Independent response uses and documented turn-preface uses; excludes nominal answer expressions and questions presenting answer alternatives

1.definition: Adds emotional emphasis to an affirmative or negative response while preserving the response orientation of yeah, yes or no
1.details: This is a family of related local patterns, not a claim that every emphatic form combines freely with every response word. Norrick (2009: 880) analyzes hell in hell yeah and shit in shit no as intensifiers; the whole hell yeah or fuck yeah expression can function as a pragmatic marker before a longer turn. Intensifier describes an internal contribution, while pragmatic marker describes a use of the whole. Neither label settles lexical category. Following CGEL (2002: 848), response polarity must be distinguished from agreement, refusal and other conversational actions. Emotional emphasis need not raise epistemic certainty or express approval of the event.

examples.note: Published response token: Norrick (2009: 880), SCoSE Football; response to did you burn anything?

examples.form: [fuck yeah] it placed third in the derby in his year.
examples.note: Published turn preface: Norrick (2009: 880), WSC DPC032; the excerpt ends before a further continuation
Published author example, not a corpus attestation: Mackenzie (2019: 69), example (43a)

examples.form: [Fuck no], you don’t care about the money.
examples.note: Published scripted-dialogue example: Moreau (2024: 8), Table 3, Orange Is the New Black; preceding turn not supplied
COCA supplied concordance, Green Street Hooligans, year label 2005, MOV: response to a football-draw announcement; source/date metadata not independently checked

grounds.locator: Green Street Hooligans; COCA year 2005, MOV; supplied 2026-11-14

examples.note: COCA supplied concordance, V/H/S Viral, year label 2014, MOV: response to Was he bleeding?; source/date metadata not independently checked

grounds.locator: V/H/S Viral; COCA year 2014, MOV; supplied 2026-11-14

examples.note: COCA supplied concordance, The Bronze, year label 2015, MOV: negative response; source/date metadata not independently checked

grounds.locator: The Bronze; COCA year 2015, MOV; supplied 2026-11-14

constraints.description: This is a provisional descriptive family. Its predictive advantage over listing the documented local patterns has not been established; no independent projection target or securing tier is claimed.
The reversed sequence no shit has a different idiomatic interpretation (Norrick 2009: 881) and is outside this family.

The pattern enumerates documented combinations, not a Cartesian product or an unrestricted slot-filling rule. The labels emphatic expression and polarity response specify contributions, not lexical categories.

Use is form-, context- and potentially variety-sensitive. Mackenzie (2019: 69, example 43) stars fucking yes/no; supplied COCA contexts attest both bare forms. Retain this source contrast without extending one judgment to all English speakers or claiming to know its cause.

Norrick explicitly reports one intonation unit and primary stress on hell for the SCoSE hell yeah example. This does not establish a uniform stress rule for the other combinations. Commas do not determine intonation, Discourse Act boundaries or internal bracketing.

Nominal answer expressions such as a big fucking yes/no are a separate environment. Their nominal packaging does not establish that bare response yes/no is nominal. Alternative questions such as yes or fucking no, no idea, no before a noun, and verbal fucking are also outside this entry.
The internal analysis of hell fucking no remains open: the string alone does not decide nested modification, multiple emphatic dependents or a stored larger formula.

relatedConstructions.notes: Some emphatic responses have exclamatory force; response use alone does not establish the exclamation entry's prosodic and force profile

grounds.note: Distinguishes intensification inside the combination from pragmatic-marker use of the whole and from independent turn-initial markers
Expressive attributives, adjective/adverb pairs and context-dependent response actions; these comparisons do not classify the components of the present patterns
Permits fuck yes/no and stars fucking yes/no; the latter restriction does not cover the full supplied COCA range
Supplies fuck no with a following clause; the interjection label is the source's analysis, not an adopted lexical classification here

curious.title: Adding force to yes and no
curious.summary: Informal speakers put an emphatic word in front of yeah, yes or no to give the answer extra feeling.
curious.body: You can answer a question with a plain yeah or no. You can also put an emphatic word in front, as in hell yeah, to show you feel strongly about the answer. The word added doesn't change the answer: hell yeah still means yes, and hell fucking no still means no. It adds emotion. Some of these combinations use profane words. They're also a small, specific set, not a rule that lets any emphatic word go with any answer. Some are also used to start a longer reply, with the rest of the turn following.
curious.try: Notice a time someone answered a question with extra force. Was the answer itself different from a plain yes or no, or only the feeling?

teacher.summary: Likely relevant only for advanced or register-focused classes; this dictionary covers informal, profane emphatic responses.
teacher.explain: This is a family of related local patterns where an emphatic expression precedes a polarity response (yeah, yes, no), adding emotional emphasis while keeping the response's orientation. It is not a free combination: this dictionary documents particular forms, such as hell yeah, shit no, fuck yes and hell fucking no. Norrick (2009: 880) treats hell in hell yeah and shit in shit no as intensifiers, and the whole expression can work as a pragmatic marker before a longer turn. The reverse order no shit has a different idiomatic meaning and falls outside the family. Emotional emphasis doesn't necessarily raise certainty or express approval of the event.
teacher.terms: Intensifier describes the internal contribution of the emphatic word; pragmatic marker describes a use of the whole expression. This dictionary says neither label settles the word's lexical category.

examples.text: [fuck yeah] it placed third in the derby in his year.
[Fuck no], you don't care about the money.

contrasts.note: One published source gives fuck yes and fuck no but excludes fucking yes and fucking no.
A corpus concordance line supplied for this dictionary attests the bare fucking yes.

watch_for: A learner might treat an emphatic response as a free pattern in which any emphatic word can precede any answer word.
A learner might take emphatic hell yeah to express approval of the event, when this dictionary says emphasis need not mean approval.
A learner might read no shit as the same pattern reversed, although it has a different idiomatic meaning.
teacher.activity: Students discuss, in pairs, when a plain yes or no would be heard as flat and when an emphatic response would be out of place in a class, workplace or home setting, then rewrite two emphatic replies into neutral ones.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Emphatic Polarity Response Family." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/emphatic-polarity-response-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Adjective in -ful

1.definition: Characterizes something as having or displaying the substance or property associated with the base.

projection.target: The output is adjectival and can modify reply. Noun formations like cupful have a separate measure interpretation and can take plural morphology.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Adjectives ending in -ful
curious.summary: Adding -ful to a noun gives an adjective saying something has or displays what the noun names.
curious.body: A thoughtful reply is one that shows thought. The -ful adjective describes something as having or displaying the substance or property associated with the base word. The base is typically a noun. Colour gives colourful, a word for something that has colour or displays it. A related ending, -less, works in the opposite direction.
curious.try: Add -ful to a noun such as joy or help. What does the new word say about something?

teacher.summary: Helps explain -ful adjectives as formed from a base meaning having or displaying that property.
teacher.explain: An adjective in -ful characterizes something as having or displaying the substance or property associated with the base, typically a noun. In The chair gave a thoughtful reply, thoughtful describes a reply that displays thought. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the adjective construction and relates it to the privative -less pattern, which marks lack.
watch_for: A learner might read thoughtful as describing the chair, when it describes the reply.
A learner might confuse -ful with its related privative pattern -less, which marks the opposite idea.
teacher.activity: Students list nouns (care, help, use), add -ful, and write a sentence with each new adjective. A partner restates it as has or shows the noun.

child.hook: What word describes a reply that shows thought?
child.explain: Add -ful to a word like thought and you get a word saying someone has it or shows it. A thoughtful reply shows thought. A colourful kite has colour.
child.play: Try adding -ful to joy, help and care. Use each new word in a short sentence.

checked.note: Frequency pass: constructed teacher example The colourful kite flew high (colourful about 4,600th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by She is a careful driver; teacher.activity noun joy (joyful is rare) replaced by use; child block unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Adjective in -ful." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/endowed-ful-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Sufficient Degree enough with an Infinitival

1.definition: Presents a degree as meeting the threshold for the specified outcome.

examples.form: The wall is [high enough to hide the bins].

relatedConstructions.notes: Ripe enough to eat places the degree at or above a lower threshold. Too ripe to eat places it above an upper threshold.

projection.target: Meeting the threshold does not assert that the bins are currently behind the wall. In the ordinary adjectival pattern enough follows the gradable adjective.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Enough to do something
curious.summary: Enough after a describing word says that a quality reaches the level needed for a stated result.
curious.body: In The wall is high enough to hide the bins, high enough says the wall's height meets the threshold, and to hide the bins names the outcome that the height is measured against. The pattern presents a degree as meeting the threshold for the specified outcome. Ripe enough to eat works the same way, with ripeness at or above a lower threshold. A neighbouring pattern, too ripe to eat, puts the degree above an upper threshold instead.

examples.text: The wall is [high enough to hide the bins].
The fruit is [ripe enough to eat].

curious.try: Finish this with your own words: The box is big enough to ...

teacher.summary: Helps explain enough plus a to-infinitival as marking a degree sufficient for an outcome, in contrast with too.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a gradable adjective or adverb followed by enough and a to-infinitival. It presents a degree as meeting the threshold for the specified outcome: high enough to hide the bins. Ripe enough to eat places the degree at or above a lower threshold, whereas too ripe to eat places it above an upper threshold. This dictionary relates the pattern to gradation and to the too-degree infinitival.
teacher.terms: Compare the too pattern.

examples.text: The wall is [high enough to hide the bins].
The fruit is [ripe enough to eat].

contrasts.text: The fruit is [ripe enough to eat].
contrasts.note: The degree meets a lower threshold.

contrasts.text: The fruit is too ripe to eat.
contrasts.note: The degree exceeds an upper threshold.

watch_for: A learner might think enough and too express the same meaning, when one marks a lower threshold and the other an upper one.
A learner might read the to-infinitival as a separate sentence, when it names the outcome the degree allows.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentence frames (The bag is big enough to ..., This soup is hot enough to ...) and then write a matching too sentence for the same adjective.

child.hook: How tall must a wall be to hide the bins?
child.explain: Enough after a describing word means there is as much of it as you need. Then to and a verb say what it lets you do. The wall is high enough to hide the bins.

examples.text: The wall is [high enough to hide the bins].
The box is [big enough to hold the toys].

child.play: Look around the room. Make sentences like The table is big enough to ... Then say what is not big enough.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the height achieves the outcome (the entry says only that the degree meets the threshold, and does not assert the bins are hidden); removed the traditional-term mapping that classed enough as a degree adverb and the infinitival as a result construction, which the entry does not state. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Sufficient Degree enough with an Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/enough-degree-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Epistemic Modal over Perfect

1.definition: Assesses an earlier situation from a later point of view.

relatedConstructions.notes: Perfect have locates the assessed event before the reference time.

projection.target: On the inferential reading, must expresses the current conclusion and have places the rain earlier. A past requirement ordinarily calls for had to rather than this construction.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Judging the past with must have
curious.summary: A modal verb of judging, followed by have and a past participle, assesses an earlier situation from a later point of view.
curious.body: In It must have rained last night, the speaker is judging what happened earlier. The modal must brings the speaker's assessment, and have followed by the past participle (rained) places the event before the point of view the speaker is judging from. The pattern assesses an earlier situation from a later point of view. It is built from a modal verb followed by perfect have.
curious.try: Look at a clue in the room, such as wet shoes. What could you say about what happened earlier, starting with must have?

teacher.summary: Helps explain an epistemic modal followed by perfect have as an assessment of an earlier situation.
teacher.explain: The pattern is VP[epistemic modal + have + past participle]. It assesses an earlier situation from a later point of view: in It must have rained last night, the modal supplies the assessment and perfect have locates the assessed event before the reference time. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the modal-plus-plain-complement pattern and as containing perfect have.
teacher.terms: Epistemic modal; perfect (have + past participle).
watch_for: A learner might read have in must have rained as showing possession.
A learner might read must as an obligation, when here it belongs to an assessment of an earlier situation.
teacher.activity: Present clues (wet pavement, an empty plate). Students write a sentence for each, assessing what happened earlier with must have or may have.

child.hook: You see wet grass. What can you say about the night?
child.explain: You can use must have to say what you work out from a clue about something earlier. It must have rained last night.
child.play: Look at a picture clue, like muddy boots. Say what must have happened. Can a friend think of another idea?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary now says the modal is a judging (epistemic) one and that the assessed situation is earlier than a later point of view, as the entry defines it, without tying it to the speaker's present; child.explain rewritten in simpler words that connect must have to working something out from a clue; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Epistemic Modal over Perfect." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/epistemic-perfect-modal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Scalar Equative as … as

1.definition: Compares a degree with a standard without asserting a greater degree in the positive form.

examples.form: The new shelf is [as wide as the old one].

projection.target: The first as sets up a degree standard and the second introduces it. At least as wide explicitly allows a greater width and not as wide ordinarily implies a lower degree.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Comparing with as ... as
curious.summary: As ... as sets one thing's degree against another's without saying the first has more.
curious.body: In The new shelf is as wide as the old one, the pattern compares the new shelf's width with the old one's. The positive form doesn't say that the new shelf is wider. The first as comes before the describing word, and the second as introduces what you're measuring against, here the old one.

examples.text: The new shelf is [as wide as the old one].
Max is [as tall as his sister].

curious.try: Compare two things in the room with as ... as, such as two bags or two books.

teacher.summary: Helps explain the as ... as equative that compares a degree with a standard without asserting a greater one.
teacher.explain: The scalar equative has the form as + gradable expression + as-phrase or clause. In its positive form it compares a degree with a standard without asserting a greater degree. In The new shelf is as wide as the old one, the old shelf supplies the standard. This dictionary relates the pattern to gradation and to than-reduced clauses.
teacher.terms: Traditionally called a comparison of equality; compare the comparative with than.

examples.text: The new shelf is [as wide as the old one].
Max is [as tall as his sister].

watch_for: A learner might think as wide as asserts that the new shelf is wider.
A learner might leave out the first as, though the pattern has two.
teacher.activity: Students pick pairs of objects and write sentences with as ... as, naming the standard each time.

child.hook: How do you say two things match in size?
child.explain: Put as before a describing word and as before the thing you're comparing with. The new shelf is as wide as the old one. It doesn't say the new shelf is wider.

examples.text: The new shelf is [as wide as the old one].
Max is [as tall as his sister].

child.play: Pick two things you can see. Say how they compare using as ... as, such as as long as or as tall as.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Scalar Equative as … as." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/equative-as-as-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Evaluative Adjective with of and an Infinitival
pattern: Clause[dummy it + be + Adj + PP[of + NPᵢ] + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

entry.name: Evaluative Adjective with of and an Infinitival
entry.pattern: Clause[dummy it + be + Adj + PP[of + NPᵢ] + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

1.definition: Evaluates a person’s conduct in doing or contemplating the action named by the infinitival.
1.details: In It was kind of you to call, of you supplies the participant whose action is evaluated. Compare It was difficult for you to call, where the assessment concerns the difficulty of your calling. With the relevant evaluative adjectives a context can supply the action instead, as in That was kind of you.

examples.form: [It is good of you to help.]
examples.note: You is the understood helper as well as the person being evaluated.

examples.form: [It was careless of Pat to leave the gate open].
examples.note: Constructed example with an unfavourable evaluation.

relatedConstructions.notes: Both occur with it and a following infinitival.
How kind of you to call uses the evaluative frame with exclamative packaging.

grounds.note: Separates kind-of-you and difficult-for-you patterns.

projection.target: The of-phrase can remain with a referential that when the action is supplied by the context. In the corresponding difficult for pattern, who undertakes the difficult act is part of the clause with for.
projection.evidence: CASA lists this adjective-of frame separately from the it-for-event frame. The contrast can be tested using the same action and participant.

curious.title: Judging a person's action with "kind of you"
curious.summary: A sentence like It was kind of you to call judges a person by what they did or considered doing.
curious.body: In It is good of you to help, the speaker judges you for helping. You are both the person being judged and the one who helps. The sentence evaluates a person's conduct in doing the action named after to. Compare It was difficult for you to call. There, the assessment is about how hard the call was, not about you as a person. When the context makes the action clear, the shorter That was kind of you also works.

examples.text: [It is good of you to help.]
[It was careless of Pat to leave the gate open].
It was kind of you to call.

curious.try: Think of something kind a friend did. Say it to them starting with It was kind of you to ...

teacher.summary: Helps contrast evaluating a person (kind of you) with assessing difficulty (difficult for you).
teacher.explain: The pattern is dummy it + be + adjective + of + NP + to-infinitival, where the NP after of is also the understood subject of the infinitival. It evaluates a person's conduct in doing or contemplating the action: in It was kind of you to call, you is the person whose action is evaluated. Compare It was difficult for you to call, where the assessment concerns the difficulty of the calling. With relevant evaluative adjectives a context can supply the action, as in That was kind of you. This dictionary relates the pattern to subject extraposition and to exclamative packaging (How kind of you to call).
teacher.terms: This dictionary separates the kind-of-you pattern from the difficult-for-you pattern.

examples.text: [It is good of you to help.]
[It was careless of Pat to leave the gate open].

contrasts.text: It was kind of you to call.
contrasts.note: Evaluates the person who called.

contrasts.text: It was difficult for you to call.
contrasts.note: Assesses how hard calling was.

watch_for: A learner might treat of you and for you as interchangeable, though the assessments differ.
A learner might read It was careless of Pat to leave the gate open as a comment on the gate, when it evaluates Pat's conduct.
teacher.activity: Students sort adjectives (kind, difficult, silly, easy) by whether they judge the person or the task, then write one sentence of each kind.

child.hook: How do you thank a friend for something kind?
child.explain: Some sentences tell what you think of a person for something they did. It was kind of you to share. The words after of tell who did it. The words after to tell what they did.

examples.text: It was [kind of you to share].
[It is good of you to help.]

child.play: Think of something kind or careless someone did. Say what you think of them with of you or of and a name.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.activity adjective careless (about 10,400th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by silly; the entry example with careless and the child block are unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Evaluative Adjective with of and an Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/evaluation-of-person-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Evaluative Binominal
pattern: NP[... Nom₁ of NP₂], with Nom₁ predicated of the referent of NP₂

entry.name: Evaluative Binominal
entry.pattern: NP[... Nom₁ of NP₂], with Nom₁ predicated of the referent of NP₂

1.definition: Evaluates the person or thing introduced by the second nominal.
1.details: A nitwit of a husband evaluates the husband as a nitwit. Material and measure expressions such as a statue of bronze and a cup of water supply different relations. The usual singular oblique takes a(n). Kim and Sells document bare plural obliques. The evaluation can apply to a complex first nominal, as when destroyer of education is predicated of the minister. That semantic grouping leaves the attachment of the outer PP open.

examples.note: The husband is the target of the evaluation.
BNC example with a bare plural oblique.

examples.form: [that destroyer of education of a minister]
examples.note: Published judgment. Education is what the minister destroys.

relatedConstructions.notes: The whole expression can serve as an NP.

grounds.note: Reports bare plural obliques and argues for a constructional analysis.

projection.target: The first nominal supplies a description of the referent contributed by the second. A bare plural second nominal can support that relation.
projection.evidence: CGEL's clausal paraphrase and the published singular and plural cases investigated by Kim and Sells.

curious.title: A noun of a noun, used to judge
curious.summary: In a phrase like a nitwit of a husband, the first noun is a judgment about the person or thing named by the second.
curious.body: In her stupid nitwit of a husband, the husband is the target of the evaluation. The first noun, nitwit, is said of the husband. This is different from a statue of bronze or a cup of water, where of expresses a material or a measure. The first part can be bigger than one word. In that destroyer of education of a minister, the education is what the minister destroys, and destroyer of education is the judgment passed on the minister.

examples.text: [that destroyer of education of a minister]

curious.try: Think of a judgment you could pass on a person with a noun, then fit it into a phrase of that shape.

teacher.summary: Helps explain evaluative noun of noun phrases, and how they differ from material and measure of-phrases.
teacher.explain: In an evaluative binominal, the first nominal is predicated of the referent of the second: a nitwit of a husband evaluates the husband as a nitwit. Material and measure expressions such as a statue of bronze and a cup of water supply different relations. This dictionary notes that the usual singular oblique takes a(n) and that Kim and Sells document bare plural obliques (wobbly jellies of men). The evaluation can apply to a complex first nominal, as in destroyer of education of a minister, where education is what the minister destroys; that grouping leaves the attachment of the outer PP open.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls the judging use an evaluative binominal.

examples.text: [that destroyer of education of a minister]

contrasts.note: The first noun evaluates the man.
Of expresses the material.
Of expresses a measure.

watch_for: A learner might read a nitwit of a husband as two people, a nitwit and a husband.
A learner might read of in a statue of bronze as evaluating, when it gives a material.
teacher.activity: Students sort phrases with of (a giant of a man, a cup of water, a statue of bronze) by whether of expresses a judgment, a material or a measure.

checked.note: Frequency pass: constructed contrast and activity phrase a nitwit of a husband (nitwit about 68,600th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by a giant of a man; explain and watch_for still quote the entry's nitwit of a husband; the material and measure contrasts are unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Evaluative Binominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/evaluative-binominal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Clause-Orientated Evaluative Adjunct
pattern: evaluative AdvP + clause, often separated prosodically

entry.name: Clause-Orientated Evaluative Adjunct
entry.pattern: evaluative AdvP + clause, often separated prosodically

1.definition: Expresses the speaker’s evaluation of the reported situation.

projection.target: Fortunately evaluates the situation as a whole. It does not describe a fortunate manner in which the backup operated.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Showing how you feel about what happened
curious.summary: An adverb such as fortunately can open a sentence and express the speaker's evaluation of what is reported.
curious.body: In Fortunately, the backup worked, the word fortunately doesn't describe how the backup worked. It shows how the speaker feels about the fact that it worked. The evaluation is attached to the whole reported situation. These adverbs are often separated from the rest of the sentence by a pause in speech.
curious.try: Start a sentence about something that happened today with a word that shows how you feel about it.

teacher.summary: Helps explain a clause-initial adverb that gives the speaker's evaluation of the situation.
teacher.explain: An evaluative adverb phrase before a clause expresses the speaker's evaluation of the reported situation. In Fortunately, the backup worked, the adverb is the speaker's assessment of the whole situation. This dictionary says it is often separated prosodically from the clause, and relates the pattern to evidential because.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls it a clause-orientated evaluative adjunct.
watch_for: A learner might read fortunately as describing how the backup worked, when it gives the speaker's view of the situation.
teacher.activity: Give students short events (the bus came, the test was cancelled). They add an evaluative adverb at the start and say what the speaker thinks.

child.hook: What word shows how you feel about something that happened?
child.explain: A word like fortunately can start a sentence. It shows how the speaker feels about what happened. Fortunately, the backup worked.
child.play: Say something that happened today. Start it with a word that shows how you feel about it.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Clause-Orientated Evaluative Adjunct." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/evaluative-sentence-adverb-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Concessive Conditional even if

1.definition: Holds a consequence fixed under a condition presented as unfavourable or extreme.

projection.target: The sentence can be uttered while rain is uncertain. The plan is presented as holding even in that case, unlike the ordinary expectation suggested by a bare conditional.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Plans that survive bad news
curious.summary: Even if names a condition that might seem to threaten a plan and says the plan holds anyway.
curious.body: In Even if it rains, we'll go, the speaker says the plan stays fixed under a condition that looks unfavourable. Rain is the awkward case, and the plan is presented as holding even then. The speaker can say this while not knowing whether it will rain. The sentence doesn't settle the weather. It settles what happens either way. This differs from the ordinary expectation a plain if sentence suggests, and the even is what changes it.

examples.text: [Even if you're late], we'll wait for you.
[Even if the road is closed], they'll find a way.

curious.try: Say Even if it rains, we'll go. Does the speaker need to know whether it will rain?

teacher.summary: Helps explain how even if differs from a plain if in conditional sentences.
teacher.explain: An even-if adjunct (even if plus a finite clause) holds the main clause's consequence fixed under a condition presented as unfavourable or extreme. It is a specialization of the if-conditional. The sentence can be used while the condition is still uncertain: Even if it rains, we'll go doesn't need the rain to be settled. The plan is presented as holding in that case, unlike the ordinary expectation a bare conditional suggests. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence, and rests on CGEL's discussion of concessive conditionals.
teacher.terms: Concessive conditional is the name used here for even if clauses.

examples.text: [Even if you're late], we'll wait for you.

contrasts.text: Even if it rains, we'll go.
contrasts.note: The plan holds even in the unfavourable case.
A bare conditional, with the ordinary expectation this dictionary mentions.

watch_for: A learner might read even if as a plain if with extra emphasis, and miss that the consequence is presented as holding regardless.
A learner might think the speaker of Even if it rains, we'll go knows that it will rain.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a plan ("We'll start at noon") and a possible obstacle (heavy traffic, a late guest). Each pair writes one sentence with even if and one with a plain if, then explains aloud what changes.

child.hook: What does the speaker mean by Even if it rains, we'll go?
child.explain: Even if tells you the plan won't change. Rain might come, and that's the bad news. The people will go anyway.

examples.text: [Even if you're late], we'll wait for you.

child.play: Make a plan, like going to the park. Then think of something that could get in the way. Say your plan with Even if at the start.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Concessive Conditional even if." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/even-if-concessive-conditional-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: every inch with a Nominal Predicative

1.definition: Emphasizes that someone exemplifies a role or type in the relevant respects.
1.details: Every inch marks completeness in the characterization. CGEL identifies this use as idiomatic and contrasts the predicative with an unacceptable use as a by-agent. The relation to every bit as good remains open.

examples.note: The relevant respects come from the description philosopher.

relatedConstructions.notes: Every inch strengthens the characterization.
Both concern nominal predication. The every inch pattern shown here contains an article.

grounds.note: Identifies idiomatic every inch and compares its predicative and nonpredicative distribution.

projection.target: The idiomatic frame favours predicative use and an interpretation over respects in which the description applies.
projection.evidence: CGEL's predicative versus by-agent comparison and its note on idiomatic every inch. A constructed test replaces inch with centimetre.

curious.title: Being a philosopher in every way
curious.summary: Every inch a philosopher says that someone fully fits a role or type, in the respects that matter for it.
curious.body: In She is every inch a philosopher, the words every inch add emphasis. They suggest nothing is missing from the description: she is a philosopher completely. The respects that count come from the description itself. Here the word philosopher tells us what to look at, so the phrase is about her qualities as a philosopher, not about her height. The phrase is an idiom, and in this example it describes the person after a form of be.
curious.try: Swap philosopher for another role, such as leader. Which qualities does every inch now cover?

teacher.summary: Low priority for most classes: inch is relatively infrequent (about 4,200th among word forms in the SUBTLEX-UK subtitle counts), so treat this idiom if it comes up rather than teaching it. Helps with the idiom every inch a ..., which emphasizes that someone fully fits a role or type.
teacher.explain: Every inch plus a or an plus a nominal works as a predicative complement and marks completeness in the characterization: the subject exemplifies the role or type in the relevant respects. The respects come from the noun (philosopher), not from any measurement. CGEL identifies this use as idiomatic and contrasts the predicative use with an unacceptable use as a by-agent. This dictionary’s relation to every bit as good remains open, and this dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Predicative complement is this grammar's term. Textbooks sometimes call it a subject complement or predicate nominative.

contrasts.text: She is every inch a philosopher.
contrasts.note: Adds completeness to the characterization.
Same description without the emphasis on completeness.

watch_for: A learner might read inch literally, as a measure of height or size.
A learner might not see that the noun after a decides which respects every inch covers.
teacher.activity: If the idiom comes up in a reading, write She is every inch a philosopher and She is a philosopher on the board. Students say what the first sentence adds and which qualities of a philosopher it covers.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.summary now opens by marking the idiom low priority (inch about 4,200th in SUBTLEX-UK); activity no longer has students write every inch a sentences and is now a recognition task on the entry example and its constructed contrast.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "every inch with a Nominal Predicative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/every-inch-predicative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Speech-Act or Evidential because

1.definition: Gives grounds for making the preceding claim or directive.

examples.form: Jo must be home, [because her keys are on the table].

projection.target: The keys motivate the speaker’s conclusion. Their being on the table need not be what caused Jo to be home.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Giving your reason for saying something
curious.summary: A because phrase can explain why the speaker says something, not why the thing happened.
curious.body: In Jo must be home, because her keys are on the table, the keys are the speaker's reason for concluding that Jo is home. They motivate the conclusion. Their being on the table need not be what caused Jo to be home. So the because part is added after the main clause to give grounds for making the claim. It can do the same for a directive, an instruction or request. A because phrase can also give a cause in the world, and this dictionary keeps that use apart from the reason-for-speaking use.

examples.text: Jo must be home, [because her keys are on the table].
He must be asleep, [because the lights are off].
Take an umbrella, [because the sky looks dark].

curious.try: Finish this sentence two ways. She must be tired, because ... (a clue that makes you think so), then because ... (what made her tired).

teacher.summary: Helps students tell a because that explains an event from a because that explains why the speaker says something.
teacher.explain: A supplementary because-PP follows a clause and gives grounds for making the preceding claim or directive. In Jo must be home, because her keys are on the table, the keys motivate the speaker's conclusion, and their being on the table need not be what caused Jo to be home. CGEL distinguishes act-related from content-related cause, and this construction is discussed in that connection. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional (medium confidence) and lists a related construction, epistemic modals with perfect have.
teacher.terms: Evidential or speech-act because are the labels used here. CGEL's contrast is act-related versus content-related cause.

examples.text: Jo must be home, [because her keys are on the table].
Close the window, [because it's cold in here].

contrasts.text: Jo must be home, because her keys are on the table.
contrasts.note: The keys are the speaker's grounds for the conclusion.

contrasts.text: Jo is late because the bus broke down.
contrasts.note: The because phrase gives a cause of the event itself.

watch_for: A learner might read the because part as the cause of Jo's being home, when it gives the speaker's reason for saying so.
A learner might think because can follow only a statement, when this dictionary says it can also give grounds for a directive.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as "The grass is wet, because it rained" and "It must have rained, because the grass is wet". They say, for each, whether because explains the event or the speaker's conclusion.

child.hook: Why does the speaker think Jo is home?
child.explain: Sometimes because tells why something happened. Sometimes it tells why you think something. The keys are a clue that Jo is home. They help the speaker guess it.

examples.text: Jo must be home, [because her keys are on the table].
She must be asleep, [because the lights are off].

child.play: Be a detective. Spot a clue, like wet boots by the door. Say what it makes you think, then add because and the clue.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher explanation now says the keys need not be the cause (as the entry does) instead of ruling the causal link out; the related-construction link is stated as epistemic modals with perfect have rather than epistemic must; child explanation no longer says what did or didn't make Jo go home. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; the claim that the entry places this use with the act-related kind was cut as unsupported. Second round: fixed the teacher contrast note, because clause changed to because phrase (the entry's pattern is a because-PP).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Speech-Act or Evidential because." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/evidential-because-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Exclamation
pattern: Utterance with exclamatory prosody and heightened-stance force

entry.name: Exclamation
entry.pattern: Utterance with exclamatory prosody and heightened-stance force

dimensions.form: Realized by interjections, exclamative clauses, extra-clausal NPs, or prosodically marked declaratives
dimensions.meaning: Heightened speaker stance toward a referent, situation, or degree
dimensions.function: Expressive force; stands alone as a complete utterance
dimensions.distribution: Utterance-level; resists syntactic integration and at-issue challenge

1.definition: An utterance-level force category, expressing heightened speaker stance with exclamatory prosody
1.details: Terminology: exclamative is the clause type (syntactic), exclamatory the property of uses, exclamation the utterance-level force category (pragmatic). This entry is a Constructionary pragmatic profile, not a claim that CGEL recognizes a unified grammatical class: CGEL p. 923 treats exclamation as structurally nebulous and samples several formally distinct realizations. Membership here is graded: interjections are the prototype; exclamative clauses are core; directive-ostensive NPs are prototypically members; vocatives enter only via the summons/call use; declaratives join by prosody alone (That's amazing!). The category cross-cuts ostensive-np-001 rather than containing it: tag vocatives are structural-yes/force-no, while exclamatory declaratives are force-yes/structural-no.

examples.note: Interjection; the prototype (pure force, no discourse referent)
Non-headed construction with exclamative clausal semantics; cf. the headed Clause What a lovely day it is!

constraints.description: Not at-issue; the force resists direct denial (That's false cannot target the exclamatory stance).
Exclamatory prosody is non-reducible; deaccenting removes membership.

projection.target: Locating an utterance in the exclamation profile predicts stand-alone viability, non-reducible exclamatory prosody, heightened-stance interpretation, and resistance to at-issue denial, across formally unrelated realizations
projection.evidence: The projections hold from interjections through exclamative clauses to recruited declaratives; the profile is realizationally promiscuous but functionally uniform

stabilisers.evidence: High-frequency expressive routines (interjections, formulaic exclamatives)
Need to express heightened stance rapidly, without clausal assembly

known_boundary_items: CGEL does not posit a well-defined grammatical class of non-exclamative exclamations; this entry proposes a cross-form pragmatic profile
tag and address vocatives (structural profile without exclamatory force)
exclamatory declaratives (force without the extra-clausal structure)
murmured reminders (Your keys, said flatly)

relatedConstructions.notes: Cross-cutting, not containment; the leak cases are the boundary items
The exclamative packaging of the indeterminates feeds core members (what/how exclamatives)
Only via the summons/call use
A headed exclamative Clause is a core realization of exclamation force
A declarative Clause can be recruited as an exclamation by prosody
Phrase-only exclamative forms realize the force without instantiating Clause

grounds.note: CGEL treats exclamation as structurally nebulous; this entry proposes a cross-form pragmatic profile

curious.title: Short bursts of strong feeling
curious.summary: An exclamation is an utterance that expresses strong feeling, and the way it's said is part of what makes it one.
curious.body: Ouch! is the clearest exclamation. It's a complete utterance on its own and it just expresses feeling. But the category is wider than that. What a lovely day! and A snake! can be exclamations too, and so can an ordinary-looking statement like That's amazing! What these share is an exclamatory tone of voice and a heightened feeling. With Ouch! that is pure feeling; with the others it is directed at something. Take away the tone and the exclamation goes with it. The feeling also can't be argued with in the usual way: replying That's false doesn't target the feeling expressed. This dictionary treats exclamation as a pattern of use, and notes that the grammar book it draws on doesn't recognize it as one tidy class.
curious.try: Say That's amazing in a flat voice, then say it as if you've just seen something astonishing. Which one is an exclamation?

teacher.summary: Helps separate exclamation (a use of language with a heightened-stance tone) from exclamative (a clause type).
teacher.explain: This dictionary offers a pragmatic profile, not a claim that CGEL recognizes a unified grammatical class; CGEL treats exclamation as structurally nebulous. Exclamation is an utterance-level force: heightened speaker stance with exclamatory prosody, complete on its own. Realizations vary. Interjections are the prototype, exclamative clauses are core, directive-ostensive NPs are prototypical members, vocatives qualify only as summons or calls, and a declarative joins through prosody alone (That's amazing!). Keep three terms apart: exclamative is a clause type, exclamatory describes uses, exclamation is the force category. The stance isn't at-issue, so it resists direct denial.
teacher.terms: Interjection is the traditional name for words like Ouch. Exclamative clause is the clause type.
watch_for: A learner might treat the exclamation mark as the whole test, when the core properties in this dictionary include exclamatory prosody.
A learner might use exclamation and exclamative as one word, though exclamative names a clause type and exclamation a use.
A learner might expect That's false to answer the stance in That's amazing!, though the force resists direct denial.
teacher.activity: Students say That's amazing three ways (flat, bored, astonished) and vote on which are exclamations. Then they look at Ouch, What a lovely day and A snake, note that each is a complete utterance said with feeling, and note how differently they're built.

child.hook: How do you say That's amazing when you are really amazed?
child.explain: An exclamation shows a big feeling. How you say it matters. Ouch! and A snake! are exclamations. So is That's amazing! if you say it with feeling.
child.play: Say That's amazing like a sleepy robot. Now say it like you just saw a rocket. Only one is an exclamation. Which?

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.activity no longer sorts What a lovely day as a clause (the entry calls it a non-headed construction); curious.body says Ouch! is pure feeling and the others are directed at something; removed the 'exclamatory sentences' gloss in teacher.terms; child.hook no longer implies Hello is not an exclamation; replaced 'the entry'/'This entry' with this dictionary. Second round: fixed curious.summary by cutting 'about something' (this dictionary's prototype, Ouch!, is pure force with no discourse referent); teacher.watch_for[0] now names exclamatory prosody as one of the core properties rather than the only test.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Exclamation." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/exclamation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Exclamative Clause

dimensions.form: Tensed Clause headed by a VP and marked by an exclamative phrase based on what or how; normally the exclamative phrase is initial and Subject precedes the Predicator
dimensions.meaning: Presents a proposition as holding to a remarkable degree or in a remarkable way relative to a contextual norm
dimensions.function: Characteristically makes an exclamatory statement, without being identical to the broader pragmatic category of exclamation
dimensions.distribution: Main clauses and subordinate exclamative content clauses

1.definition: A headed clause type marked by an exclamative what/how phrase and characteristically used for an exclamatory statement
1.details: Exclamative what and how mark clause type while also performing a core role inside the exclamative phrase. Headed exclamatives are normally tensed and usually have Subject–Predicator order, although subject postposing and subject–auxiliary inversion are possible. Clause type must be kept distinct from force: exclamative is one syntactic source of exclamatory statements, while the wider exclamation profile also includes interjections, NPs, and recruited declaratives. Phrase-only What a disaster! is not a headed Clause in this project and belongs with clause-analogue semantics (CGEL pp. 853–57, 918–23).

examples.form: I realised [what a bargain it was].
[How happy would he be if he could see her once more!]
examples.note: Marked but licensed subject–auxiliary inversion in a headed exclamative

constraints.description: The construction is a Clause headed by VP and contains an exclamative phrase based on what or how; Subject–Predicator order is usual but not invariant.
A phrase-only expression such as What a disaster! is not an instance of this headed construction; its clausal interpretation belongs under clause-analogue-001.
Exclamatory statement is the characteristic use, but exclamative clause type is not coextensive with exclamation or with exclamatory prosody.

projection.target: An exclamative what/how phrase inside a headed Clause predicts remarkable-degree interpretation, a strong preference for Subject–Predicator order, and availability in both main and subordinate exclamative environments
projection.evidence: What/how marking covaries with evaluative degree semantics across main and subordinate headed clauses, while the order possibilities distinguish this construction from open interrogatives without defining it by punctuation or force

grounds.note: Exclamative marking projects remarkable-degree interpretation and main/subordinate distribution
The form-meaning-order profile recurs across headed exclamatives

relatedConstructions.notes: Exclamative what/how supplies both a core phrasal role and the feature marking the Clause as exclamative
Exclamative clauses characteristically realize exclamatory force, but the pragmatic exclamation profile is broader than this clause type
What and how can mark either type, but role, order, meaning, and context distinguish them
Phrase-only exclamatory expressions receive clausal interpretations without being headed Clauses

grounds.note: Exclamative clause marking, syntax, characteristic meaning, and distinction from the wider class of exclamations

curious.title: What and how sentences of surprise
curious.summary: Some sentences start with what or how to present something as remarkable.
curious.body: What a fine player she is! and How generous you are! both present something as remarkable, as measured against what we'd expect. Each starts with a what or how phrase, then normally the person or thing, then the verb. These are clauses, meaning groups of words built around a verb. They can stand alone, as above, or sit inside a bigger sentence: I realised what a bargain it was. The usual order can change, as in How happy would he be if he could see her once more!, which is a marked but allowed pattern. A phrase with no verb, such as What a disaster!, isn't counted here.

examples.text: I realised [what a bargain it was].
[How happy would he be if he could see her once more!]

curious.try: Make your own sentence that starts with What a or How. Where does the verb come, before or after the person or thing?

teacher.summary: Helps students recognize what and how exclamatives as verb-headed clauses, and tell them from questions and from phrase-only exclamations.
teacher.explain: An exclamative clause is a clause headed by a VP (normally tensed) and marked by an exclamative phrase based on what or how. It presents a proposition as holding to a remarkable degree or in a remarkable way, and characteristically makes an exclamatory statement. The exclamative phrase is normally initial and the Subject precedes the Predicator, though subject postposing and subject-auxiliary inversion are possible. It occurs in main clauses and as a subordinate content clause. Clause type isn't the same as force: exclamation is a wider pattern of use. Phrase-only What a disaster! isn't a headed clause in this dictionary; see the clause-analogue entry. What and how can also mark open interrogatives, and role, order, meaning and context separate the two.
teacher.terms: Exclamative clause is CGEL's term. Sentences like these are sometimes called exclamatory sentences.

examples.text: I realised [what a bargain it was].
[How happy would he be if he could see her once more!]

watch_for: A learner might treat any sentence beginning with what or how as an exclamative, when the same words can start an open interrogative.
A learner might take Subject-Predicator order as required, though the how-happy example shows a licensed inversion.
A learner might count What a disaster! as a verb-headed clause, when this dictionary treats it as phrase-only.
teacher.activity: Students get strips with what/how sentences, some exclamatives and some questions (What did she play? alongside What a fine player she is!). They sort them and mark where the verb and subject fall.

child.hook: Which sentence shows surprise, What a fine player she is or What did she play?
child.explain: Some sentences start with What a or How to show something is remarkable. What a fine player she is!
child.play: Look at a picture. Say something amazing about it that starts with What a or How.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body and teacher.explain no longer make tense part of what a clause is or require it (the entry says headed exclamatives are normally tensed); child.explain no longer states subject-before-verb order as a rule (the entry allows subject postposing and inversion); curious.body says normally for the order.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Exclamative Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/exclamative-clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Exclamative Use of Indeterminates

dimensions.form: Only what and how from the indeterminate series; exclamative what is an adjective, while exclamative how is adverbial
dimensions.meaning: The open variable is packaged as evaluation against a contextual norm
dimensions.function: Marks exclamative clause type and, in its core role, remarkable degree or quality
dimensions.distribution: Exclamative clauses (What children they are!, How fast she ran!) and exclamative NPs

1.definition: Expresses evaluation of the variable's value against a contextual standard or expectation
1.details: Membership is the tightest of the three packagings: what and how only. Exclamative how is adverbial, modifying an adjective, degree determinative, adverb, or verb. Exclamative what is an adjective functioning as external or internal modifier in NP structure; this contrasts with interrogative what, which is a determinative in determiner use but a pronoun when it heads an NP (CGEL pp. 397–98, 918–20). Exclamative uses pattern non-deitally on the deitality inventory; such (a) and so many/much pattern with them in exclamatory NPs without being indeterminates.

examples.note: Adjective in modifier function; notable children evaluated against a norm
Adverb modifying an adjective; remarkable speed
Exclamative NP with singular count noun

relatedConstructions.notes: Exclamative uses pattern non-deitally (Reynolds, deitality inventory)
Exclamative what/how marks headed exclamative Clauses
Exclamative what/how also occurs in non-headed constructions with exclamative clausal semantics

grounds.note: Exclamative what is an adjective; interrogative what a determinative

projection.target: An independent What a mess! uses a in the singular count case, while What awful weather! does not. How odd! can supply its own exclamatory force without an overt subject. An ordinary open interrogative uses related forms in a different clause construction.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares exclamatives with open interrogatives and gives the phrasal uses and internal NP restrictions.

curious.title: What and how as words of amazement
curious.summary: Of the question words, only what and how are used in exclamations to present something as remarkable.
curious.body: In What a day it's been! and How fast she ran!, the words what and how aren't asking anything. They present the day or the speed as standing out against what we'd expect. Only these two words from the family of question words are used this way. How goes with a describing word or an action, as in how fast. What comes before a noun, as in what children or what a day. In a question, the same words do a different job in a different kind of sentence.
curious.try: Compare How fast she ran! with How fast did she run? What is the speaker doing in each?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: exclamative what and how, and how exclamative what differs in word class from question what.
teacher.explain: Exclamative use is the tightest packaging of the indeterminate series: only what and how, and the open variable is evaluated against a contextual norm. Exclamative what is an adjective functioning as an external or internal modifier in NP structure (what children, what a day). Exclamative how is adverbial and modifies an adjective, degree determinative, adverb or verb. Interrogative what is different: a determinative in determiner use and a pronoun when it heads an NP. In a singular count case, an independent What a mess! uses a, while What awful weather! does not. Such (a) and so many/much pattern with exclamative what in exclamatory NPs without belonging to the series.
teacher.terms: Indeterminate series is this grammar's name for the what/who/how family, sometimes called wh-words.

contrasts.text: What a lovely day it is!
contrasts.note: Exclamative what, an adjective in modifier function within the noun phrase.
Interrogative what, here a pronoun heading an NP.

watch_for: A learner might give what the same word class in What a day it's been! and What do you want?
A learner might treat how in How fast she ran! as a question word asking for a speed.
teacher.activity: Students list five things that surprise them and write each as a what or how exclamation. They then underline what or how and say what it modifies.

checked.note: Fixed: summary now limits the what/how restriction to the question-word (indeterminate) series, as this dictionary does; the what a lovely day contrast note no longer says what modifies day and instead says exclamative what is an adjective in modifier function within the NP. Terms: wh-words now 'sometimes called'. Second round: fixed teacher.explain, which now gives exclamative what as an external or internal modifier in NP structure, as the entry does; teacher.activity no longer limits what is modified to a noun or a describing word (the entry lets how modify a degree determinative or a verb as well). Dismissed the low flag on the contrast note (within the noun phrase covers both external and internal modifiers).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Exclamative Use of Indeterminates." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/exclamative-word-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Alternative Exhaustive Conditional

1.definition: States that the outcome holds whichever of the presented alternatives obtains.

examples.form: [Whether Lee comes or not], the meeting goes ahead.

relatedConstructions.notes: I asked whether Jo stayed or left seeks the answer. Whether Jo stayed or left, the lights stayed on puts both alternatives in the adjunct and asserts the same consequence across them.

projection.target: The adjunct does not ask or report an unresolved question. It asserts that the consequence holds on both alternatives.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: The same result whichever way it goes
curious.summary: A whether phrase with two alternatives says the result holds on either one.
curious.body: In Whether Lee comes or not, the meeting goes ahead, both possibilities are named: Lee comes, or Lee doesn't. The sentence says the meeting goes ahead on either one. The speaker isn't asking a question. Compare I asked whether Jo stayed or left, where whether introduces a question the speaker wants answered. In Whether Jo stayed or left, the lights stayed on, both alternatives sit in the opening phrase, and the same result is asserted across them.

examples.text: [Whether Lee comes or not], the meeting goes ahead.
[Whether Jo stayed or left], the lights stayed on.
[Whether it snows or rains], the match will be played.

curious.try: Finish this: Whether you win or lose, ... Does your ending depend on which one happens?

teacher.summary: Helps explain whether...or adjuncts that assert one result across two alternatives, and how they differ from embedded questions.
teacher.explain: An alternative exhaustive conditional is an adjunct built from whether plus alternatives linked by or. It states that the outcome holds whichever of the presented alternatives obtains. The adjunct neither asks nor reports an unresolved question; it asserts that the consequence holds on both alternatives. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional, with medium confidence, and relates it both to the if-conditional and to the closed interrogative whether. The contrast with the interrogative use is the main point to teach.

examples.text: [Whether Lee comes or not], the meeting goes ahead.
[Whether Jo stayed or left], the lights stayed on.

contrasts.text: Whether Jo stayed or left, the lights stayed on.
contrasts.note: Both alternatives in the adjunct, one consequence across them.

contrasts.text: I asked whether Jo stayed or left.
contrasts.note: Whether introduces a question that seeks the answer.

watch_for: A learner might read the whether clause as a question the speaker is asking.
A learner might read the construction as an if sentence that holds for only one alternative, when both alternatives lead to the same result.
teacher.activity: Give students a result ("the party starts at eight") and a pair of alternatives (rain or shine, guests early or late). They write whether...or sentences, then rewrite one as an embedded question with ask and compare.

child.hook: What does Whether Lee comes or not tell you about the meeting?
child.explain: Whether Lee comes or not names two things that could happen. The meeting goes ahead either way. The sentence isn't asking a question.

examples.text: [Whether Lee comes or not], the meeting goes ahead.
[Whether it snows or rains], the match will be played.

child.play: Name two things that could happen, like sun or rain. Join them with whether and or. Then say what happens either way.

checked.note: Fixed: removed 'isn't leaving anything unresolved' from curious.body (the sentence can leave open which alternative obtains); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; reworded one watch_for item.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Alternative Exhaustive Conditional." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/exhaustive-alternative-conditional-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Existential no with a Gerund-Participial

1.definition: Presents an action as unavailable in the circumstances.
1.details: There was no moving it normally suggests that moving it was impossible or impracticable. In a constructed context where moving the crate was easy and nobody chose to do it, nobody moved it fits directly and there was no moving it calls for further explanation. A rule can also be the obstacle, as in a prohibitive use. The availability and source of this modal force are open.

examples.note: Chapter 5 mentions the pattern in its survey of what can head an NP.

examples.form: [There was no telling what he might do next.]
examples.note: The action at issue is telling what he might do.
A future action is presented as unavailable.
Constructed test. Compare a crate bolted to the floor with one that people simply chose to leave.

relatedConstructions.notes: The fixed form no is shared with ordinary negative NPs.

grounds.note: Treats no plus a gerund-participial as hybrid and observes a strong restriction to existential there.

projection.target: On the impossibility reading, the form invites an explanation of what blocks the action even when its nonoccurrence is already given.
projection.evidence: CGEL's contrast between existential and nonexistential hosts supports the distribution. The feasibility comparison is a proposed test of the interpretation.

curious.title: There was no stopping her
curious.summary: There plus be plus no plus an -ing verb presents an action as unavailable in the circumstances.
curious.body: There was no stopping her says that stopping her couldn't be done. The pattern is there, a form of be, the word no, and a verb ending in -ing. It presents an action as unavailable in the circumstances. There was no moving it normally suggests that moving it was impossible or impracticable. If someone could easily have moved a crate and just chose not to, Nobody moved it fits directly, and There was no moving it would call for more explanation. A rule can be the obstacle too. Where this sense of "can't" comes from is left open in this dictionary.

examples.text: [There was no telling what he might do next.]

curious.try: Picture two crates, one bolted to the floor and one that people simply left where it was. For which does There was no moving it fit better?

teacher.summary: Helps explain the idiomatic There was no -ing pattern, which presents an action as unavailable.
teacher.explain: The pattern is existential there, BE, no, and a gerund-participial VP. It presents an action as unavailable in the circumstances: There was no moving it normally suggests that moving it was impossible or impracticable, and a rule can also be the obstacle (a prohibitive use). A test: where a crate was easy to move and nobody did, Nobody moved it fits directly and There was no moving it calls for further explanation. CGEL treats no plus a gerund-participial as hybrid and observes a strong restriction to existential there. The source of the modal force is open, and this dictionary’s confidence is low.
teacher.terms: Gerund-participial is CGEL's name for the -ing form, covering what traditional grammars split into gerund and present participle.

examples.text: [There was no telling what he might do next.]

contrasts.note: Fits a crate bolted to the floor.
Fits a crate that was easy to move and was simply left.

watch_for: A learner might read There was no moving it as a plain report that nobody moved it.
A learner might try the no plus -ing pattern with other kinds of subject, though this dictionary notes a strong restriction to existential there.
teacher.activity: Give students two scenarios for a stuck door, one where it's jammed and one where people just didn't bother. They decide which fits There was no opening it and which fits Nobody opened it, and explain why.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Existential no with a Gerund-Participial." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/existential-no-gerund-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Existential there with be
pattern: Clause[dummy there + finite be + pivot NP]

entry.name: Existential there with be
entry.pattern: Clause[dummy there + finite be + pivot NP]

1.definition: Introduces a candidate referent or asserts its presence, availability, or occurrence.

projection.target: There inverts in Is there a seat? and can occur in a tag. In the central presentational use the pivot favours new information, even though some definites are licensed in appropriate contexts.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Sentences that start with there
curious.summary: There plus be can introduce something, or say that it's present, available or going on.
curious.body: In There are two spare seats, the word there doesn't point to a place. It opens the sentence so that the thing being introduced, two spare seats, comes after the verb. Sentences like this introduce something new into the conversation, or assert that it's present, available or happening. The word there moves around like a subject. It switches places with the verb in a question (Is there a seat?) and can turn up in a tag at the end. The thing introduced favours information that's new to the listener, though some definite things are allowed in the right context.

examples.text: [There is a cat] on the roof.

curious.try: Say There are two spare seats, then turn it into a question. What happens to the word there?

teacher.summary: Helps explain existential there, the there that doesn't mean a place, and what comes after be.
teacher.explain: In an existential clause, dummy there is followed by finite be and a pivot NP: There are two spare seats. The clause introduces a candidate referent or asserts its presence, availability or occurrence. There inverts in Is there a seat? and can occur in a tag. In the central presentational use the pivot favours new information, even though some definites are licensed in appropriate contexts. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Dummy there is also called expletive there. The pivot is the NP after be.

contrasts.note: Dummy there, no place meaning.

contrasts.text: There are two spare seats, aren't there?
contrasts.note: There can occur in a tag.

watch_for: A learner might read there in There are two spare seats as the adverb of place.
A learner might expect a definite pivot to be ruled out, though some definites are licensed in appropriate contexts.
teacher.activity: Students write three sentences about their classroom starting with There is or There are. They turn each into a question, then swap with a partner and underline the pivot.

child.hook: Does the word there in There are two spare seats point to a place?
child.explain: Some sentences start with there just to introduce something. There are two spare seats. The seats are the news. You can ask about them too: Is there a seat?

examples.text: [There is a cat] on the roof.

child.play: Look around the room. Say what you can find with There is or There are. Then turn each one into a question starting with Is there or Are there.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Existential there with be." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/existential-there-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Experiential Perfect
pattern: Clause[perfect have + past-participial VP], with experiential time span

entry.name: Experiential Perfect
entry.pattern: Clause[perfect have + past-participial VP], with experiential time span

1.definition: Places one or more previous occurrences within a time span understood as relevant now.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. The simple preterite is natural for the specifically dated occurrence.

projection.target: Ever can ask about any occurrence before the reference time. A finished, explicitly dated occasion normally favours the simple preterite over the present perfect in the standard contrast.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Asking whether something has ever happened
curious.summary: A have plus past-participle sentence can place earlier happenings within a stretch of time that matters now.
curious.body: Have you ever driven a bus? asks whether at least one earlier occasion fits. The speaker isn't asking about a particular day. The word ever can ask about any occurrence before the time of speaking. Compare Did you drive the bus yesterday? Once the occasion is finished and has a definite date, the simple past is the natural choice. So have plus a verb like driven fits the experience question, and did drive fits the dated one.
curious.try: Ask a friend Have you ever ... about something they might have done. Then ask about one particular day. Which verb form fits each question?

teacher.summary: Helps explain when the present perfect asks about experience and when the simple past is used for a dated occasion.
