teacher.explain: The experiential perfect (perfect have plus a past-participial VP) places one or more previous occurrences within a time span understood as relevant now. Ever can ask about any occurrence before the reference time. A finished, explicitly dated occasion normally favours the simple preterite over the present perfect in the standard contrast. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence, and cites CGEL on the perfect.
teacher.terms: Present perfect of experience is a common textbook label. The simple preterite is the simple past.

contrasts.text: Have you ever driven a bus?
contrasts.note: Any earlier occasion counts.

contrasts.text: Did you drive the bus yesterday?
contrasts.note: A specific dated occasion; the simple preterite is natural.

watch_for: A learner might combine the present perfect with an explicit past date like yesterday, when the simple preterite is the natural choice.
A learner might read Have you ever driven a bus? as asking about right now rather than any earlier time.
teacher.activity: Students interview each other with Have you ever ...? questions. When a partner says yes, they ask a follow-up about one particular occasion, and note which verb form each question needs.

child.hook: How do you ask if someone has done something at least once?
child.explain: Have you ever driven a bus? asks if you did it at some time before now. It doesn't ask when. If you ask about yesterday, you say Did you drive the bus yesterday?
child.play: Ask three friends Have you ever ... about animals, places or foods. Then ask one of them about a single day with Did you ... yesterday?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Experiential Perfect." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/experiential-perfect-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Extended Existential with a Predicate
pattern: Clause[dummy there + be + pivot NP + integrated location or secondary predication]

entry.name: Extended Existential with a Predicate
entry.pattern: Clause[dummy there + be + pivot NP + integrated location or secondary predication]

1.definition: Introduces a referent and characterizes its position or current situation.

projection.target: Ringing predicates an activity of the alarms. A free event adjunct can instead modify the whole existential assertion without predicating a property of the pivot.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: There were two alarms ringing
curious.summary: A there sentence can introduce something and then say where it is or what it's doing.
curious.body: In There were two alarms ringing, the sentence introduces two alarms and then says what they were doing: ringing. The word ringing tells us about the alarms themselves. A different kind of added phrase works another way. It can comment on the whole situation without describing the thing introduced. So the same sentence shape can hold either a description of the alarms or a comment on the whole event, and this dictionary keeps the two apart.

examples.text: [There was a light shining] in the window.

curious.try: In There were two alarms ringing, who or what is doing the ringing?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: there sentences that add a location or a predicate about the introduced NP.
teacher.explain: An extended existential has dummy there, be, a pivot NP, and an integrated location or secondary predication: There were two alarms ringing. It introduces a referent and characterizes its position or current situation. Ringing predicates an activity of the alarms. A free event adjunct can instead modify the whole existential assertion without predicating a property of the pivot. This dictionary is a specialization of existential there, marked provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Pivot NP is the NP after be. Secondary predication is a predicate that describes the pivot.

examples.text: [There was a light shining] in the window.

watch_for: A learner might treat every phrase after the pivot as describing the pivot, when a free event adjunct can modify the whole assertion.
A learner might take ringing as a separate clause, when it predicates an activity of the alarms.
teacher.activity: Students write There was/were sentences about a picture, adding what each thing is doing. Pairs then check that each added phrase describes the thing just introduced.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Extended Existential with a Predicate." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/extended-existential-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Spatial Extent with a Measure NP

entry.name: Spatial Extent with a Measure NP

1.definition: Measures traversed distance or the spatial extent of a configuration.

relatedConstructions.notes: Walked three kilometres measures distance. Walked for an hour measures the duration and uses a for-PP.

projection.target: The NP answers how far and usually lacks an ordinary active-object/passive-subject alternation. A goal phrase can independently say where the walking led.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how far
curious.summary: After a verb of movement, a measured distance can answer the question "how far".
curious.body: In We walked three kilometres before lunch, the phrase three kilometres says how far the walking went. It measures the distance covered, or the spatial extent of something. That differs from a measure of time. Walked three kilometres measures distance, while walked for an hour measures how long the walking lasted and uses a for phrase. A separate phrase can also say where the walking led.

examples.text: They ran [two kilometres] along the river.

curious.try: Say how far you walk to school, or to a shop. Which words in your sentence give the distance?

teacher.summary: Helps explain measure phrases like three kilometres after a motion verb, and how they differ from objects and duration phrases.
teacher.explain: A measure NP after a motion or spatial verb measures traversed distance or the spatial extent of a configuration: We walked three kilometres before lunch. The NP answers how far and usually lacks an ordinary active-object/passive-subject alternation, so it doesn't behave like a typical object. A goal phrase can independently say where the walking led. Distance (three kilometres) is kept apart from duration (for an hour, a for-PP). This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Measure phrase is the usual name. Traditional grammar sometimes treats such phrases as adverbials of distance.

contrasts.note: Measures distance, answering how far.
Measures duration with a for phrase.

watch_for: A learner might treat three kilometres as an ordinary object that could become the subject of a passive.
A learner might mix up a distance phrase (three kilometres) with a duration phrase (for an hour).
teacher.activity: Students write how far they went on a recent trip, then rewrite it to say how long it took. They label each phrase as distance or duration.

child.hook: How could you answer How far did we walk?
child.explain: You can say a distance right after the verb. We walked three kilometres. The words three kilometres tell how far.

examples.text: They ran [two kilometres] along the river.

child.play: Pick a way to move, like walking, running or swimming. Say a sentence that tells how far you went. Then say how long it took, using for.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Spatial Extent with a Measure NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/extent-measure-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Postposed Relative Modifier
pattern: Clause[NP with its relative realized later in the clause]

entry.name: Postposed Relative Modifier
entry.pattern: Clause[NP with its relative realized later in the clause]

1.definition: Separates a relative from its antecedent when packaging allows the nominal to be short and the relative later.

relatedConstructions.notes: In A problem arose that we hadn’t anticipated, only the relative is postposed. Heavy NP shift places the whole object NP after another dependent.

grounds.locator: Ch. 16 §4, postposed dependents in NP structure; Ch. 12 §3

projection.target: Who is linked to visitors despite intervening arrived. A matching relative can occur adjacent to the antecedent without changing that dependency.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Describing a noun from a distance
curious.summary: The words that describe a noun can sit later in the sentence instead of right beside it.
curious.body: In Several visitors arrived who hadn't registered, the words who hadn't registered describe the visitors, even though arrived sits between them. The speaker keeps the noun phrase short and puts the describing part later. A describing part like this is called a relative clause. In A problem arose that we hadn't anticipated, only that part moves away. The same description could sit right next to its noun without changing who or what it's about.

examples.text: A problem arose [that we hadn't anticipated].
A package came [that I wasn't expecting].

curious.try: Take Several visitors arrived who hadn't registered and put who hadn't registered right after visitors. Who is it still about?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: relatives separated from their noun, as in Several visitors arrived who hadn't registered.
teacher.explain: A postposed relative is a relative modifier separated from its antecedent: the NP stays short and the relative comes later in the clause. In Several visitors arrived who hadn't registered, who is still linked to visitors despite the intervening arrived. A matching relative can occur adjacent to the antecedent without changing that dependency. Only the relative is postposed; in heavy NP shift the whole object NP is placed after another dependent. This dictionary cites CGEL on postposed dependents in NP structure, and is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Extraposition from NP is sometimes used as a textbook name for this pattern. Relative modifier is used here for what traditional grammar calls a relative clause.

examples.text: A problem arose [that we hadn't anticipated].

contrasts.text: Several visitors arrived who hadn't registered.
contrasts.note: The relative is postposed.

contrasts.text: Several visitors who hadn't registered arrived.
contrasts.note: The relative sits next to its antecedent; the dependency is the same.

watch_for: A learner might attach who hadn't registered to the nearest word, arrived, instead of visitors.
A learner might confuse this with heavy NP shift, where the whole NP moves rather than only the relative.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with a postposed relative. They draw an arrow from the relative to the noun it describes, then rewrite each with the relative next to the noun.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer defines a relative clause as one starting with who or that (the entry states no such requirement); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; 'common textbook name' hedged to 'sometimes used'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Postposed Relative Modifier." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/extraposed-relative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Factive Predication with a Content Clause
pattern: matrix factive predicate + subordinate declarative content

entry.name: Factive Predication with a Content Clause
entry.pattern: matrix factive predicate + subordinate declarative content

1.definition: Treats the content as already true or taken for granted in ordinary uses.

examples.form: Jo didn’t [regret that the shop closed].

projection.target: The closure normally remains taken for granted under matrix negation. Context and predicate choice can alter projection, so factivity must be checked per use.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Taking something as already true
curious.summary: Some verbs treat what follows them as a fact, and the sentence keeps treating it that way even when it's negative.
curious.body: In Jo didn't regret that the shop closed, the shop closing is taken for granted. The speaker doesn't say Jo failed to regret something that didn't happen. The closure stands as a fact, and the negative is only about Jo's feelings. That is the normal behaviour for this pattern, but context and the choice of word can change it. So whether a particular sentence treats its content as already true has to be checked each time.

examples.text: Jo didn't [regret that the shop closed].

curious.try: Say Jo didn't regret that the shop closed. Did the shop close?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: predicates that take a that-clause as already true, even under negation.
teacher.explain: A factive predication pairs a matrix factive predicate with a subordinate declarative content clause, and in ordinary uses treats the content as already true or taken for granted. In Jo didn't regret that the shop closed, the closure normally remains taken for granted under matrix negation. Context and predicate choice can alter this projection, so factivity must be checked per use. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence, and relates the pattern to the declarative content clause.
teacher.terms: Factive predicate is the usual name. The taken-for-granted content is also described as presupposed.

examples.text: Jo didn't [regret that the shop closed].

watch_for: A learner might think negating the main verb cancels the content clause, so that Jo didn't regret that the shop closed leaves open whether it closed.
A learner might assume any verb followed by a that-clause treats its content as true, when factivity must be checked for each use.
teacher.activity: Give students the example sentence and ask three questions about it (Did Jo regret something? Did the shop close? Who thinks the shop closed?). Discuss which answers survive the negation.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Factive Predication with a Content Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/factive-content-complement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Finite do Support
pattern: Clause[finite do + plain-form VP] in inversion or clause negation

entry.name: Finite do Support
entry.pattern: Clause[finite do + plain-form VP] in inversion or clause negation

1.definition: Supplies a finite auxiliary when the construction requires one and the ordinary positive clause has a lexical verb.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. An available finite modal supplies the operator.

relatedConstructions.notes: Imperative do also occurs before be.
Did Jo leave? inserts finite do when the clause needs inversion and has no other auxiliary. Has Jo left? inverts the auxiliary already present.
Jo didn’t leave uses do to host negation. Jo hasn’t left uses the existing auxiliary.

projection.target: The tense feature is expressed on do, and check is plain. An available modal in Can you check? occupies the finite auxiliary position directly.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: The helper word do
curious.summary: When a sentence needs a helper verb and has none, English supplies did, does or do.
curious.body: In Did you check the hinge?, the question starts with did, and check stays in its plain form. The did is the helper, and it carries the past tense. English supplies it when a question or a negative needs a helper and the sentence has only an ordinary verb. If a helper such as can is already there, no do is needed: Can you check the hinge? The same goes for Has Jo left?, where the helper has is already present. For a negative, Jo didn't leave uses do to carry the not, while Jo hasn't left uses the helper that's already there.
curious.try: Turn Jo left into a question. Which little word do you add, and what happens to left?

teacher.summary: Helps explain when English adds finite do, in questions and negatives, and when an existing auxiliary does the job.
teacher.explain: Finite do support supplies a finite auxiliary when the construction (inversion or clause negation) requires one and the positive clause has a lexical verb. The tense is expressed on do and the verb is plain: Did you check the hinge? If a finite modal is available, it occupies the auxiliary position directly: Can you check the hinge? Likewise Has Jo left? inverts the auxiliary already present, and Jo hasn't left uses the existing auxiliary, whereas Did Jo leave? and Jo didn't leave insert do. Imperative do also occurs before be. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Also called do-support. The finite auxiliary that inverts or hosts negation is sometimes called the operator.

contrasts.note: No other auxiliary, so do is supplied and check is plain.
The modal already occupies the finite auxiliary position.
The existing auxiliary inverts, so no do.

watch_for: A learner might put the tense on both did and check.
A learner might add did when a modal or another auxiliary is already present.
teacher.activity: Students get statements with plain verbs (Jo left, You checked) and with auxiliaries (Jo has left, You can check). They turn each into a question and a negative, and sort the results by whether do was added.

child.hook: Which little word helps you ask Did you check the hinge?
child.explain: In Did you check the hinge?, the question begins with did, and check stays plain. English adds did when the question needs a helper word and there isn't one. With can, you don't need did.
child.play: Take a statement like Jo left and ask it as a question starting with did. What happens to left? Then ask Jo can swim as a question. Do you need did?

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer says do-support applies to every question about an ordinary verb, no longer says did shows 'it happened before' (the entry puts the tense on do, in constructions that require an auxiliary), and the play task now states the plain-form change (Did Jo leave?). Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Finite do Support." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/finite-do-support-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Floating each
pattern: Clause[plural participant NP + separately positioned each]

entry.name: Floating each
entry.pattern: Clause[plural participant NP + separately positioned each]

1.definition: Distributes the predication over individual members associated with a nearby argument.

examples.form: The three hikers [each carried a radio].

projection.target: Each can follow the subject across a finite auxiliary in The hikers had each carried a radio. The linked NP can have its own determiner and is not contained in each.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Each, placed away from its group
curious.summary: The word each can sit after a group of people or things and say the action applies to every member separately.
curious.body: In The three hikers each carried a radio, each isn't stuck to a noun. It sits later and says the carrying applies to the hikers one by one: every hiker carried a radio. The word can follow the subject even across a helper verb, as in The hikers had each carried a radio. The group it's linked to can have its own the, and the group isn't contained inside each.

examples.text: The three hikers [each carried a radio].
The hikers had [each carried a radio].
The two sisters [each wrote a letter].

curious.try: Say The three hikers each carried a radio. Then say Each of the hikers carried a radio. Is the meaning the same?

teacher.summary: Helps explain floating each, which distributes an action over the members of a nearby plural noun phrase.
teacher.explain: Floating each is separately positioned from the plural participant NP it is associated with, and it distributes the predication over the individual members: The three hikers each carried a radio. Each can follow the subject across a finite auxiliary, as in The hikers had each carried a radio. The linked NP can have its own determiner and isn't contained in each. This dictionary relates the pattern to the each-of partitive and to each in subject determiner function, and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Each in this position is sometimes called a floating quantifier. Distributive each is used for its meaning.

examples.text: The three hikers [each carried a radio].
The hikers had [each carried a radio].

contrasts.text: The three hikers each carried a radio.
contrasts.note: Each sits away from the group it distributes over.

contrasts.text: Each of the hikers carried a radio.
contrasts.note: Each heads a partitive and is next to the group.

watch_for: A learner might read each as modifying radio rather than distributing over the hikers.
A learner might think each has to sit right next to its subject.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences about a group (the three hikers, two sisters) and place each in different spots, before and after a helper verb. They check that it still distributes over the group.

checked.note: Audit: fixed teacher.summary, plural subject changed to nearby plural noun phrase (the entry says a plural participant NP, a nearby argument); also The entry changed to This dictionary in teacher.explain.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Floating each." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/floating-distributive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Duration with for
pattern: clause with adjunct PP[for + measure NP of time]

entry.name: Duration with for
entry.pattern: clause with adjunct PP[for + measure NP of time]

1.definition: Measures how long a state, process or maintained result holds.

relatedConstructions.notes: Wrote for an hour measures time spent writing. Wrote the letter in an hour measures elapsed time to completion.

projection.target: The adjunct measures holding time. With a normally punctual predicate it can favour a repeated-event or resulting-state construal where supported by context.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how long with for
curious.summary: A for phrase with a length of time says how long something lasted.
curious.body: In Jo stayed outside for fifteen minutes, for fifteen minutes measures how long Jo's staying outside lasted. It can measure how long a state or an activity held, or a result was maintained. Compare time measured by in. Wrote for an hour measures the time spent writing, while wrote the letter in an hour measures the time it took to finish. With a very quick action, the for phrase can suggest repetition or a result that lasts, where the context supports that.

examples.text: Jo wrote the letter [in an hour].

curious.try: Say how long you spent on something today, using for. Then say how long a finished job took, using in.

teacher.summary: Helps explain for-phrases that measure how long, and how they differ from in-phrases that measure time to completion.
teacher.explain: A for-PP with a measure NP of time is an adjunct that measures how long a state, process or maintained result holds: Jo stayed outside for fifteen minutes. Wrote for an hour measures time spent writing, while wrote the letter in an hour measures elapsed time to completion. With a normally punctual predicate, the adjunct can favour a repeated-event or resulting-state construal where context supports it. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the PP and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: For-phrases like this are sometimes called duration adverbials.

contrasts.note: Measures time spent writing.

contrasts.text: Jo wrote the letter in an hour.
contrasts.note: Measures time elapsed to completion.

watch_for: A learner might mix up for an hour (time spent) and in an hour (time to finish).
A learner might read for fifteen minutes with a quick action as one long event, when context can favour a repeated-event reading.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of activities, some open-ended (reading, waiting) and some with an endpoint (writing a letter, cleaning a room). They add for or in plus a time and explain what each phrase measures.

child.hook: How do you say how long Jo stayed outside?
child.explain: For and a length of time tell how long something lasted. Jo stayed outside for fifteen minutes. The time is how long she stayed.
child.play: Tell a partner something you did today. Say how long it lasted using for. Your partner guesses what you did.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Duration with for." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/for-duration-adjunct-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: for-Infinitival with an Overt Subject
pattern: for + Subject:NP[accusative if personal pronoun] + to-infinitival VP

entry.name: for-Infinitival with an Overt Subject
entry.pattern: for + Subject:NP[accusative if personal pronoun] + to-infinitival VP

1.definition: Introduces an infinitival with a syntactically expressed subject.

examples.form: [For them to leave now] would be awkward.

projection.target: Them is the subject of leave, not the object of a purpose preposition in this use. In subject position this infinitival normally requires for before its overt subject.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: For, then who, then to
curious.summary: A phrase made of for, a person or thing, and to plus a verb can say who would do the action.
curious.body: In For them to leave now would be awkward, the words for them to leave now say what would be awkward, and them is the one who would leave. Here for isn't linking them to something as a preposition would. The person doing the leaving is them. When the whole phrase is the subject of a sentence, it normally needs for before the person or thing. A pronoun for a person takes its them-type form here.

examples.text: [For them to leave now] would be awkward.
[For Ana to win] would be wonderful.

curious.try: In For them to leave now would be awkward, who is leaving?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: the for NP to-VP pattern, where the NP is the subject of the infinitive.
teacher.explain: The for-infinitival introduces an infinitival with a syntactically expressed subject: for, Subject NP, then a to-infinitival VP. A personal pronoun takes accusative form (for them to leave). In For them to leave now would be awkward, them is the subject of leave, not the object of a purpose preposition in this use. In subject position this infinitival normally requires for before its overt subject. This dictionary cites CGEL on infinitival clauses and is marked provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Accusative is also called objective case. This pattern is sometimes called a for-to infinitive.

examples.text: [For them to leave now] would be awkward.
[For Ana to win] would be wonderful.

watch_for: A learner might analyze for them as a prepositional phrase with them as its object.
A learner might expect for to be optional in subject position, where it normally isn't.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences beginning For ___ to ___ with different people and verbs. They underline the subject of the infinitive and say who does the action.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "for-Infinitival with an Overt Subject." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/for-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Anaphoric Adjective in a Fused-Head NP
pattern: NP[Det + AdjP with a contextually supplied nominal description]

entry.name: Anaphoric Adjective in a Fused-Head NP
entry.pattern: NP[Det + AdjP with a contextually supplied nominal description]

1.definition: Uses a modifier to distinguish a referent while leaving the descriptive noun recoverable.

examples.form: I took the dry cloth and left [the damp].

projection.target: The inferred kind comes from cloth, and agreement follows the recovered nominal. The human-class reading of the wealthy instead needs no such antecedent.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Leaving out the noun when it's obvious
curious.summary: A describing word with the can stand for a noun mentioned earlier, as in the damp for the damp cloth.
curious.body: In I took the dry cloth and left the damp, the damp means the damp cloth. The noun isn't repeated because the earlier word cloth makes it clear, and the describing word damp takes over the job of naming. The kind of thing comes from cloth, and any agreement follows the recovered noun. This is different from the wealthy, which refers to a group of people without needing an earlier noun to fill in.

examples.text: I took the dry cloth and left [the damp].
She chose the red scarf and I chose [the blue].

curious.try: Say I took the dry cloth and left the damp. What exactly was left?

teacher.summary: Helps explain an adjective standing in for a noun recovered from context, and how it differs from the wealthy.
teacher.explain: In an anaphoric fused-head NP, a determiner plus an adjective phrase distinguishes a referent while the descriptive noun is recoverable from context: I took the dry cloth and left the damp. The inferred kind comes from cloth, and agreement follows the recovered nominal. The human-class reading of the wealthy instead needs no such antecedent. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the fused-head construction, related to the adjective NP and to pro-nominal one, and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: This is sometimes described as an adjective used as a noun. Fused head is this grammar's term for an NP whose head function is carried by another constituent, here the adjective.

examples.text: I took the dry cloth and left [the damp].
She chose the red scarf and I chose [the blue].

contrasts.text: I took the dry cloth and left the damp.
contrasts.note: The noun is recovered from cloth.

contrasts.text: I took the dry cloth and left the damp one.
contrasts.note: Here one overtly stands in for cloth.

watch_for: A learner might treat the damp as a noun with no link to the earlier cloth.
A learner might expect the wealthy to need an earlier noun, when its human-class reading doesn't.
teacher.activity: Students get sentences with two contrasting things (the red car and the blue car). They rewrite them without repeating the noun and underline what supplies the missing noun.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.activity model pair the dry cloth and the damp cloth (damp about 3,200th, cloth about 5,500th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by the red car and the blue car, matching the colour pattern of the constructed example the blue; entry example unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Anaphoric Adjective in a Fused-Head NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/fused-adjective-anaphoric-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Fused Determiner-Head Construction

dimensions.form: DP with no following nominal head
dimensions.meaning: Quantity, identity, or person reference with the head interpretation recovered anaphorically, from a partitive complement, or from the determinative's own content
dimensions.function: Determiner and head functions fused in one constituent
dimensions.distribution: Any NP position; may license a partitive of-complement

1.definition: A DP functions simultaneously as determiner and head of the NP, with no separate nominal head
1.details: CGEL Ch. 5 §9. Covers anaphoric uses, partitives, the compound determinatives in -body/-one/-thing/-where (traditional 'indefinite pronouns'), and demonstratives standing alone. These are not pronouns; the category stays determinative while the head function is fused. This entry is a determiner-head subtype of the broader fused-head construction. Contested: Reynolds, Determinatives as nouns in English (LingBuzz 009939), analyzes determinatives as a fourth noun subclass, with simple independent uses (Some left) as ordinary Head rather than fused Det-Head, narrowing fusion to a residue. If adopted, this entry shrinks accordingly.

examples.form: She bought twenty books, but I bought [twenty-two].

examples.note: Partitive; independent form of the determinative no
Compound determinative, not an indefinite pronoun
Demonstrative determinative standing alone, not a demonstrative pronoun

constraints.description: The fused element is a DP; NPs headed by pronouns are a different construction (np-pron-001).

relatedConstructions.notes: Determinative-head subtype of the broader fused-head family
Absolute negators standing alone as NPs instantiate this construction

projection.target: Several of these can serve as an argument without an overt nominal following several. Some of the fruit admits a non-count partitive domain. Several of the fruit does not admit that same reading. A determiner-like expression as an entire NP need not uniformly be anaphoric.
projection.evidence: CGEL tests partitive complements and non-anaphoric special readings. The head analysis is the one adopted in this record and alternatives are separately noted.

curious.title: Words like twenty-two or everybody standing alone
curious.summary: Some words that normally come before a noun can fill a whole noun phrase by themselves.
curious.body: In She bought twenty books, but I bought twenty-two, the word twenty-two stands alone: no noun follows it. Words like none, everybody and those do the same in We liked none of them, Everybody left early and Those are mine. What each one stands for comes from earlier in the sentence, from an of phrase after it, or from the word's own meaning. These words belong to the class this dictionary calls determinatives, the class that includes the, some and those. They aren't treated as pronouns here. One competing analysis, noted in this dictionary, would treat some of these uses as ordinary nouns; if that were adopted, this pattern would shrink.

examples.text: She bought twenty books, but I bought [twenty-two].

curious.try: In She bought twenty books, but I bought twenty-two, what are the twenty-two? Where in the sentence does that come from?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: determinatives like twenty-two, none, everybody and those standing alone as a whole NP.
teacher.explain: In a fused determiner-head NP, a determinative phrase serves as determiner and head at once, with no separate nominal head: bought twenty-two, liked none of them, Everybody left early, Those are mine. The head interpretation is recovered anaphorically, from a partitive complement, or from the determinative's own content. The word stays a determinative; these are not pronouns, and NPs headed by pronouns are a different construction. This dictionary covers anaphoric uses, partitives, the compound determinatives in -body/-one/-thing/-where and standalone demonstratives. It's contested: another analysis treats simple independent uses (Some left) as ordinary Head, which would narrow fusion to a residue.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar calls everybody an indefinite pronoun and those a demonstrative pronoun. This grammar calls both determinatives. Fused head is the CGEL analysis.

examples.text: She bought twenty books, but I bought [twenty-two].

watch_for: A learner might label everybody or those a pronoun, when this dictionary keeps them as determinatives.
A learner might look for a missing noun after Everybody, though the meaning comes from the word itself.
A learner might assume a determinative standing alone must recover its meaning from earlier text, when this dictionary says it need not be uniformly anaphoric.
teacher.activity: Students collect standalone determinatives from a short text (some, none, everybody, those, twenty-two). For each, they say where its meaning comes from: earlier text, an of phrase, or the word itself.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Fused Determiner-Head Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/fused-determiner-head-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Fused-Head Construction

dimensions.form: A non-nominal constituent realizes the NP without an overt nominal head
dimensions.meaning: Head interpretation is recovered from the constituent itself, context, or a licensed complement structure
dimensions.function: Head-like realization of an NP slot by a determiner, modifier, or related constituent
dimensions.distribution: NP positions where a nominal head is omitted, absent, or constructionally unrecovered

1.definition: A non-nominal constituent functions as the head of an NP without an overt nominal head
1.details: This family covers fused determiner-head uses and fused modifier-head uses. The overt constituent may be a DP, an adjective phrase, a participial phrase, or a related non-nominal expression, depending on the subtype. The point of the construction is that the NP's head interpretation is supplied without an overt noun.

constraints.description: The construction lacks an overt nominal head and is realized by a non-nominal constituent whose head interpretation is recoverable.
Fused determiner-head and fused modifier-head uses are subtypes of this broader family.

relatedConstructions.notes: The fused constituent realizes a complete NP without a separate nominal head.

grounds.note: CGEL's fused-head analysis covers determiner-head and modifier-head uses

projection.target: The contrast between some left and the poor left is not merely the same omitted noun. The rich can denote humans without a recoverable nominal, while an anaphoric adjective NP can take its interpretation and number from the previously named nominal.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes fusion of determiner and modifier with head and separates simple, partitive, and special interpretations.

curious.title: Noun phrases with no noun
curious.summary: Some phrases work as a full noun phrase even though the main word isn't a noun.
curious.body: A noun phrase is a phrase that can name people or things. In Everybody left early and The rich were taxed more heavily, the phrases work that way, yet neither has a noun in it. Rich is a describing word, and the phrase has no separate noun after it. In each phrase, the job of the noun is done by another word. We still know what is meant, because the meaning is supplied by the word itself, by the context, or by what follows. This dictionary calls the pattern a fused head.
curious.try: In The rich were taxed more heavily, what noun could you add after rich? Does the sentence need it?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: NPs whose head is a determinative or modifier with no overt noun.
teacher.explain: In a fused-head NP, a non-nominal constituent functions as the head without an overt nominal head, and the head interpretation is supplied without a noun. The family covers fused determiner-head uses (Everybody left early) and fused modifier-head uses (The rich were taxed more heavily). The overt constituent may be a determinative phrase (DP), an adjective phrase, a participial phrase or a related expression, depending on the subtype. The difference between some left and the poor left isn't just the same omitted noun: the rich can denote humans without a recoverable nominal, while an anaphoric adjective NP can take its interpretation and number from the nominal named earlier.
teacher.terms: Fused head is CGEL's analysis. Everybody is traditionally an indefinite pronoun, and the rich is sometimes described as an adjective used as a noun.

examples.text: She chose the red scarf and I chose [the blue].

contrasts.text: The rich were taxed more heavily.
contrasts.note: Human-class reading with no recoverable noun.

contrasts.text: She chose the red scarf and I chose the blue.
contrasts.note: The noun is recovered from the earlier scarf.

watch_for: A learner might think every fused head is just a noun that was deleted, when the rich needs no recoverable noun.
A learner might treat a determinative and an adjective as the same kind of fused head, when this dictionary separates fused determiner-head and fused modifier-head subtypes.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences with no overt noun (Everybody left; the rich; I chose the blue) by where the meaning comes from: the word itself, context, or an earlier noun.

checked.note: Fixed: removed the claim that Everybody belongs with words like every and some (the entry only gives Everybody as a fused determiner-head example); in teacher text, the list of possible overt constituents now gives DP as determinative phrase, as in the entry.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Fused-Head Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/fused-head-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Free-Choice Fused Relative in -ever

1.definition: Picks out an eligible participant without requiring the speaker to identify which one.

examples.form: [Whoever is on duty] can sign it.

projection.target: In a generic or future context the identity can be left open. The whole phrase occupies an NP position and can also have a specific unknown referent in a suitable episodic context.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Whoever and whatever as noun phrases
curious.summary: A word like whoever starts a phrase that picks out someone eligible, without saying who.
curious.body: In Whoever is on duty can sign it, the speaker picks out a person by a condition rather than by name. The speaker doesn't need to know who that is. The whole phrase, whoever is on duty, fills a noun's place in the sentence. In a general or future situation the identity can stay open. In a suitable one-off situation it can also point to one specific person the speaker doesn't know.

examples.text: [Whoever is on duty] can sign it.

curious.try: Say Whoever is on duty can sign it. Does the speaker need to know who is on duty?

teacher.summary: Helps explain -ever phrases like whoever is on duty, which pick out an unspecified eligible person or thing.
teacher.explain: A free-choice fused relative is an NP made of a relative wh-ever word plus a dependent clause. It picks out an eligible participant without requiring the speaker to identify which one. In a generic or future context the identity can be left open, and the whole phrase occupies an NP position. In a suitable episodic context it can also have a specific unknown referent. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the fused relative NP, distinct from the unconditional wh-adjunct, and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Fused relative is CGEL's term. Free relative is a common textbook name.

examples.text: [Whoever is on duty] can sign it.

watch_for: A learner might think the speaker must know who is on duty.
A learner might look for a separate noun that whoever modifies, when the whole phrase fills an NP position.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences beginning Whoever, Whatever or Whichever, giving each a role in the sentence (subject or object). They then say whether the speaker needs to know who or what is meant.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Free-Choice Fused Relative in -ever." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/fused-relative-no-matter-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Fused Relative NP

1.definition: Identifies a person, thing, or quantity through the relation expressed inside the NP.
1.details: In what she wrote, the initial expression supplies both the nominal reference and a dependent of wrote. The resulting NP can denote written material. The same word sequence can form an embedded interrogative about the identity of that material. In subject position a plural fused relative licenses plural agreement, whereas a clausal subject takes default singular agreement.

examples.note: Fused relative contrasted with the interrogative after wonder.

examples.form: [What books she has] are in the attic.
examples.note: The NP has plural agreement despite containing a finite clause.

relatedConstructions.notes: The whole expression distributes as an NP.
A relative expression helps identify the nominal referent.
The same string can express an embedded question in another construction.
The variable expression of a pseudo-cleft is a fused relative.

projection.target: Identical-looking subordinate strings can differ in agreement and complement distribution. A plural fused relative can control plural agreement where an open interrogative cannot.
projection.evidence: CGEL uses agreement, extraposition and selection as diagnostics independent of the referential contrast. The NP is also the variable expression in the CASA wh-cleft.

curious.title: A what phrase that acts as a noun phrase
curious.summary: A phrase like what she wrote names the thing that was written, much as a noun phrase would.
curious.body: In I really liked what she wrote, the phrase what she wrote names the thing that was written. The word what does two jobs: it supplies the thing referred to, and it fills the place after wrote where that thing would go. The same words can instead be a question about identity, as after wonder. One clue to the difference is the verb. In What books she has are in the attic, the phrase takes the plural are, where a clause on its own as subject would take a singular verb.

examples.text: [What books she has] are in the attic.

curious.try: Compare I really liked what she wrote with I wonder what she wrote. In which one is what she wrote a thing you could point at?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: what she wrote as a noun phrase, and how it differs from an embedded question.
teacher.explain: A fused relative NP identifies a person, thing or quantity through the relation expressed inside the NP. In what she wrote, the initial expression supplies both the nominal reference and a dependent of wrote, so the NP can denote written material. The same string can form an embedded interrogative about the identity of the material. Diagnostics independent of the referential contrast include agreement, extraposition and selection: a plural fused relative as subject licenses plural agreement (What books she has are in the attic), whereas a clausal subject takes default singular agreement. The variable expression of a pseudo-cleft is a fused relative. Confidence in this dictionary is high.
teacher.terms: Fused relative is CGEL's term. Free relative and nominal relative are sometimes used for the same thing.

examples.text: [What books she has] are in the attic.

contrasts.text: I really liked what she wrote.
contrasts.note: Fused relative; the NP denotes written material.
The same words as an embedded question about identity.

watch_for: A learner might read what she wrote in I really liked what she wrote as a question.
A learner might choose a singular verb after What books she has, because the phrase contains a finite clause.
teacher.activity: Students get pairs like I liked what she wrote and I wonder what she wrote. They decide which is a noun phrase naming something and which is a question. They can check by the verb: What books she has are in the attic.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Fused Relative NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/fused-relative-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Genitive with every

1.definition: Quantifies over instances delimited by their relation to the genitive.
1.details: Her every move ranges over her movements. CGEL contrasts each in the same position. Postma and Rooryck discuss body-part nouns alongside actions and contrast the form with every move of John’s. To test how the genitive sets the domain, keep bone fixed and compare bones of a person’s skeleton with bones that person owns as specimens.

examples.note: The genitive delimits the movements under consideration.

relatedConstructions.notes: A genitive appears in determiner function before every.

grounds.note: Argues for a relational restriction and compares the oblique genitive.

projection.target: The kind of relation to the genitive can affect whether the pattern is available, even when the head noun is held fixed.
projection.evidence: CGEL's every versus each contrast and the published discussion of actions and body parts. The owned-specimen comparison is a proposed test.

curious.title: Her every move
curious.summary: A genitive before every picks out all the instances tied to a person or thing, as in her every move.
curious.body: In They scrutinised her every move, her sets the territory and every counts the instances inside it. Her every move means every one of her movements. The same words with each in that spot work differently, and this dictionary notes the contrast. The kind of relation between the person and the noun can affect whether the pattern is available, even when the noun stays the same. Think of bone: do the bones of a person's skeleton and the bones a person owns as specimens feel the same here?
curious.try: Say her every move, then her every word. Which things can belong to her in that way?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: the genitive-plus-every pattern, as in her every move.
teacher.explain: In genitive every, a genitive NP in determiner function precedes every plus a singular nominal. It quantifies over instances delimited by their relation to the genitive: her every move ranges over her movements. CGEL contrasts each in the same position. A published discussion treats actions and body-part nouns together and contrasts the form with every move of John's. To test how the genitive sets the domain, keep bone fixed and compare bones of a person's skeleton with bones that person owns as specimens. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Genitive is this grammar's term for the 's form and for her, his, their in determiner function; traditional teaching calls these possessives.
watch_for: A learner might assume the genitive plus every can be swapped freely with the of-genitive form (every move of John's), though the published discussion contrasts the two.
A learner might expect the pattern to work with any noun after a genitive, though the kind of relation can affect availability.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with a genitive before every, using nouns such as move, word and step. They say what the genitive restricts the instances to, then compare with each in the same position.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Genitive with every." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/genitive-every-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Genitive Subject in a Gerund-Participial

1.definition: Expresses an overt subject in the genitive inside a gerund-participial.

relatedConstructions.notes: Compare We objected to their blocking the exit and We objected to them blocking the exit. The case varies in this frame. Availability depends on the higher construction and variety.
Their carefully sorting the files has a verbal predicate with an adverb and direct object. Their careful sorting of the files has adjective and of-complement in a nominal.

projection.target: The verb can retain adverbial modification and take a direct object. The genitive marks its subject rather than turning the following verb into a noun.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Their arriving so late
curious.summary: A word like their can sit in front of a verb ending in -ing to say who is doing the action.
curious.body: In I disliked their arriving so late, the word their says who arrived. What follows is still verb-like: arriving keeps its own add-on, so late. The word their marks the one who does the action, rather than turning arriving into an ordinary noun. The same job can be done by a different form. We objected to their blocking the exit and We objected to them blocking the exit both fit. This dictionary notes that which form is available depends on the larger pattern and on the variety of English.

examples.text: We objected to [their blocking the exit].
We objected to [them blocking the exit].

curious.try: Say We objected to their blocking the exit, then We objected to them blocking the exit. Which one would you say, and does the other sound natural to you?

teacher.summary: Useful when students ask why a genitive appears before a verb in -ing, or how it differs from a noun with of.
teacher.explain: This is a gerund-participial clause whose subject is an overt genitive NP: their arriving so late, with their as subject and arriving so late as the verb phrase. This dictionary’s key point is that the verb stays verbal. It can keep adverbial modification and take a direct object, so the genitive marks the subject and does not turn the -ing word into a noun. An oblique subject is an alternative in some frames (them blocking the exit); this dictionary says the case varies and that availability depends on the higher construction and variety. This analysis is marked provisional in this dictionary.
teacher.terms: Gerund-participial is the CGEL-style label for the clause. Traditional grammars may call the -ing word a gerund.

examples.text: We objected to [their blocking the exit].
We objected to [them blocking the exit].

contrasts.note: Verbal: adverb and direct object.

contrasts.text: Their careful sorting of the files
contrasts.note: Nominal: adjective and of-complement.

watch_for: A learner might treat their arriving as a noun phrase with an ordinary noun, when the -ing word keeps verb features such as adverbs and a direct object.
A learner might treat their blocking the exit and their blocking of the exit as the same structure.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a short list of -ing phrases with a genitive in front. Students add an adverb or a direct object to each (their arriving ...), then try a version with careful and of, and say which one keeps the verb's own add-ons.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Genitive Subject in a Gerund-Participial." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/genitive-ing-subject-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Genitive 's

1.definition: Indicates possession/ownership
1.details: Marks the NP as possessor or controller

2.details: Indicates inherent connection rather than ownership

3.details: Marks the creator or source

6.details: Indicates the doer/experiencer of an action/state

projection.target: With the person next door’s bicycle, the genitive marker is adjacent to door but the possessor is the whole person next door. The semantic relation also varies across uses such as Monday’s meeting and our uncle’s bicycle.
projection.evidence: CGEL uses phrasal placement to separate the marker’s host from the genitive’s semantic argument.

curious.title: The 's ending
curious.summary: Adding 's to a noun phrase marks it as a genitive, and the relation it expresses can be of several different kinds.
curious.body: The 's ending marks a word or phrase as a genitive. In Mary's book, it means the book is Mary's. In the tree's branches, the branches are part of the tree. In Shakespeare's plays, Shakespeare wrote them. And in tomorrow's meeting, it ties the meeting to a time. The 's form can also stand alone, as in That car is John's. The ending doesn't have to sit right next to the person it describes. In the person next door's bicycle, the 's is attached to door, but the owner is the whole phrase, the person next door.
curious.try: Pick a noun phrase of several words, such as the person next door, and add 's. Where does your 's land, and who does the phrase point to?

teacher.summary: Covers the 's genitive, its range of meanings, and where the marker goes on a longer phrase.
teacher.explain: The genitive 's attaches to a noun phrase and marks it as a genitive. This dictionary lists a range of relations: ownership (Mary's book), part-whole (the tree's branches), creation or authorship (Shakespeare's plays), time (a day's work, tomorrow's meeting), property (the metal's strength), a doer (the sun's rise) and social or institutional role (Mary's brother). The relation varies across these uses. Position matters: in the person next door's bicycle, 's is adjacent to door but the possessor is the whole person next door. The 's form can also stand alone, as in That car is John's (an independent genitive). This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars sometimes call this the possessive, but the relation can be something other than ownership. Independent genitive is the name this dictionary uses for That car is John's.

contrasts.note: The 's is attached to door, but the possessor is the whole phrase.

watch_for: A learner might read every 's phrase as ownership, when this dictionary lists part-whole, authorship, time and role uses as well.
A learner might expect 's on the head noun of a longer phrase, though in the person next door's bicycle it is attached to door.
teacher.activity: Give students a set of 's phrases from this dictionary on slips. They sort them by relation (owner, part, author, time, role) and then compose one of each type with their own nouns.

child.hook: What does the little 's tell you in Mary's book?
child.explain: The 's ending can show who something belongs to. It can also show where something comes from or what it is part of. Mary's book is the book that is Mary's. The tree's branches are the branches on the tree.
child.play: Look around the room and name five things with 's, like Mia's pencil or the door's handle. Then find one that is about a time, like tomorrow's lesson.

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary and body no longer say 's links a noun phrase to a following noun (the entry includes the independent genitive That car is John's, now mentioned in the body); teacher explanation no longer says the meaning comes from context rather than from 's and now says only that the relation varies across uses. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary' in teacher text. Second round: fixed teacher.explain, which called the person next door the genitive NP; it now says the possessor is the whole person next door, as this dictionary does. Also fixed (unflagged): teacher.watch_for[1] no longer implies a judgment on placing 's after the head noun (nothing is starred); it now describes where the marker sits in this dictionary's example.

name: get Passive
pattern: Clause[affected Subject + get + verbal past participle]

entry.name: get Passive
entry.pattern: Clause[affected Subject + get + verbal past participle]

1.definition: Presents the subject as undergoing a passive event, often with subject relevance or affectedness.

relatedConstructions.notes: Jo got promoted and Jo was promoted can describe the same event. Get foregrounds the change or its relevance to Jo. Be is also available in stative uses such as is widely believed.

grounds.locator: Ch. 16 §10.1.3, verbal get-passive versus adjectival get

projection.target: An apparent positive outcome can occur, so adverse consequence is unnecessary. The construction can admit an agent by-phrase and contrasts with get plus an ordinary adjective.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Got promoted
curious.summary: Using got with a past-participle word, as in Jo got promoted, presents someone as undergoing something that happened to them.
curious.body: In Jo got promoted last week, something happened to Jo: someone promoted her. The sentence puts the spotlight on the change and on what it means for Jo. The plain version, Jo was promoted, can describe the same event. This dictionary says that got foregrounds the change or its relevance to Jo, while was also covers cases that describe a state, such as is widely believed. A good outcome is possible too, so the pattern doesn't need to be about something bad.
curious.try: Take a sentence like The window was broken and try it with got. Does the focus shift?

teacher.summary: Useful for showing learners the get-passive as an alternative to the be-passive, with a different focus.
teacher.explain: The get-passive has an affected subject, get, and a verbal past participle: Jo got promoted. It alternates with the be-passive (Jo was promoted), and both can describe the same event. This dictionary says get foregrounds the change or its relevance to Jo, while be is also available in stative uses such as is widely believed. A get-passive can have a positive outcome, so adverse consequence is not required, and it can admit a by-phrase naming the agent. It contrasts with get plus an ordinary adjective. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Get-passive is the usual name. This dictionary treats it as a passive with the verb get in place of be.

contrasts.note: Get foregrounds the change or its relevance to Jo.
Can describe the same event.

watch_for: A learner might assume a get-passive must describe something bad for the subject, when this dictionary says a positive outcome is possible.
A learner might treat get plus a participle as get plus an ordinary adjective, when this dictionary distinguishes the two.
teacher.activity: Give students short event sentences with be-passives. They rewrite each with get, then discuss whether the focus on the change or on the person affected shifts.

child.hook: What is the difference between Jo was picked and Jo got picked?
child.explain: Got can show that something happened to someone. Jo got promoted means somebody promoted Jo. The sentence is about Jo and what happened to her.
child.play: Tell a partner something that happened to you using got, like I got invited. Then say the same thing with was and see whether it sounds different.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "get Passive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/get-event-passive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Goal Locative-Complement Construction

dimensions.form: Verb head with a goal-denoting PP in locative-complement function; the PP may be transitive or complementless
dimensions.meaning: Directed motion toward a final location; the frame can impose the motion reading
dimensions.function: Locative complement of the verb, bearing the semantic role goal
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal with motion verbs and constructionally coerced manner or emission verbs

1.definition: A VP contains a locative complement bearing the goal role, yielding directed motion toward a final location
1.details: Goal is a semantic role, while locative complement is the CGEL syntactic function. Realizations include to-PPs (go to the shop), compound goal PPs headed by into or onto (run into the garden), and unmarked goal PPs headed by complementless locative prepositions (go home, head abroad). Direction PPs headed by towards or compass terms form a distinct category. *Go to home is excluded by to's NP-object complementation, not by the goal construction (CGEL pp. 257–59, 686–88).

examples.note: Goal-role locative complement headed by transitive to
To-PP with a bare institutional NP object
Goal-role locative complement realized by a one-word PP
Complementless-P realization of the goal slot

2.definition: The frame coerces a directed-motion reading onto a verb without lexical direction or goal semantics
2.details: This is the constructional residue: the verb contributes manner or emission while the frame supplies motion and the goal (Goldberg 1995, intransitive-motion construction).

examples.note: The frame supplies directed motion toward the goal

constraints.description: The PP is integrated as a locative complement in the directed-motion VP, not added as a locative adjunct.
When the verb does not lexically encode direction or a goal, the frame supplies the directed-motion relation while the verb contributes manner or emission.

projection.target: A manner or emission verb followed by an integrated locative PP predicts a coerced directed-motion reading even when the verb lacks lexical direction or goal semantics; established goal instances range across to-PPs, compound into/onto PPs, and unmarked locative PPs
projection.evidence: Manner and emission verbs acquire directed-motion readings in this frame (Goldberg 1995), while CGEL distinguishes goal realizations from direction on pp. 686–88

grounds.note: Manner and emission verbs acquire constructionally licensed directed-motion readings
Productive coercion supports a recurrent form-meaning profile

diagnostics: manner or emission verbs acquire directed-motion readings

known_boundary_items: off, back, or down followed by a to-PP: the sequence may contain two separate PP complements because each first P also has a complementless use
from under the bed proves only that from can take a PP complement; it does not establish PP-internal goal complementation
the way construction: related but distinct frame
caused motion: transitive sister frame with an Od theme

relatedConstructions.notes: The goal-role locative complement is licensed within VP structure
The goal-role locative complement is a PP
Sister semantic roles within the locative-complement family

grounds.note: Goal is a semantic role borne by a PP in locative-complement function
Intransitive motion construction; coercion of manner verbs

curious.title: Phrases that say where the movement ends
curious.summary: With a verb of movement, a short phrase can say where the movement ends, as in go to the shop.
curious.body: In go to the shop, to the shop says where the going ends up. The same job is done by go home, where one word names the place, and by run into the garden. The frame can also bring the movement itself. In The bottle floated into the cave, floated says how the bottle moved, and into the cave gives the direction and the end point. The same happens with The fly buzzed into the room and She danced into the hall, even though buzzed and danced don't themselves carry a direction or a goal.
curious.try: Compare The fly buzzed with The fly buzzed into the room. What does the second one add?

teacher.summary: Helps explain how a place phrase after a verb marks the end point of movement, including with manner verbs like float.
teacher.explain: The goal role is a semantic role; the syntactic function is locative complement. This dictionary lists three realizations: to-PPs (go to the shop), compound goal PPs headed by into or onto (run into the garden), and one-word PPs headed by a complementless preposition (go home, head abroad). Direction PPs headed by towards or compass terms are a distinct category. With manner or emission verbs the frame itself supplies the directed motion: floated into the cave. The PP is a complement integrated into the motion VP, not an adjunct.
teacher.terms: Goal is the semantic role. Locative complement is the CGEL function. This dictionary cites Goldberg for the intransitive-motion construction that supplies the motion reading with manner verbs.
watch_for: A learner might put to before home, when this dictionary treats go home as a goal PP of one word, with to-PPs a separate realization.
A learner might read danced into the hall as two actions, dancing and entering, when the frame supplies the movement.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of verbs (float, buzz, dance, go, run). They pair each with a goal phrase (into the room, home, to the shop) and say which verbs already carry a direction or goal and which get it from the frame.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body now says buzzed and danced lack lexical direction or a goal (not that they can't describe movement); title and teacher.activity now speak of where movement ends and of direction or goal rather than movement itself; replaced the try prompt with a pair the entry exemplifies; replaced 'the entry' with this dictionary. Frequency pass: teacher.activity goal phrases ashore and into the cave (ashore about 10,900th, cave about 4,100th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by to the shop and into the room, both from the entry; the verb list is unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Goal Locative-Complement Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/goal-complement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: God knows with an Indeterminate Expression
pattern: fixed authority expression + knows + indeterminate XP, including inside an argument or modifier

entry.name: God knows with an Indeterminate Expression
entry.pattern: fixed authority expression + knows + indeterminate XP, including inside an argument or modifier

1.definition: Marks a value as unknown or left unspecified, often with an emphatic stance.
1.details: In He filed God knows how many pages, the expression supplies an indefinite quantity inside the object NP. In She put God knows what in the soup, it supplies the unknown item. The source lists variants with Heaven, the Lord and goodness. An independent sentence such as God knows how many pages he filed can also make a literal claim about knowledge.

examples.form: They packed [God knows what] in these boxes.
examples.note: Constructed NP object use with an unknown item.

examples.form: He filed [goodness knows how many pages].
examples.note: Constructed example where the unknown value is the number inside the object NP.

relatedConstructions.notes: An indeterminate identifies the open value.
An independent verb of knowing can instead take an ordinary embedded question.

grounds.note: Records the stance formula and attested slot types.

projection.target: An expression with the shape of a finite clause can occur within the matrix object NP and mark an unknown content or quantity. A fully literal knowledge clause does not generally have that distribution.
projection.evidence: CASA lists the formula and the range of indeterminates. The constructed insertion contrasts test the embedded use. Its internal constituency is open.

curious.title: God knows what
curious.summary: A phrase like God knows what, placed inside a larger phrase, marks something as unknown or left unspecified, often with feeling.
curious.body: In They packed God knows what in these boxes, the speaker doesn't say what the items were. In He filed goodness knows how many pages, the number of pages is the unknown value. Both put the phrase right inside the object and mark an open value with emphasis. This dictionary lists variants with Heaven, the Lord and goodness in place of God. A separate sentence such as God knows how many pages he filed can also make a literal claim about who knows, so what the phrase does depends on where it sits.

examples.text: They packed [God knows what] in these boxes.
He filed [goodness knows how many pages].
She put [God knows what] in the soup.

curious.try: Finish this sentence with your own version: She bought heaven knows ... Does the phrase stand in for a missing item or amount?

teacher.summary: Mostly for advanced classes, an idiomatic stance formula that fills a slot for an unknown item or amount.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a fixed authority expression plus knows plus an indeterminate expression such as what or how many, placed inside an argument or modifier: God knows what in They packed God knows what in these boxes. It marks a value as unknown or left unspecified, often with an emphatic stance. Variants use Heaven, the Lord and goodness. In an independent sentence such as God knows how many pages he filed, it can also be a literal claim about knowledge. This dictionary says that a literal knowledge clause does not generally have the embedded distribution, and that the internal constituency of the formula is open.
teacher.terms: Indeterminate is this dictionary’s term for words like what and how many that identify an open value.

examples.text: They packed [God knows what] in these boxes.
He filed [goodness knows how many pages].
She put [God knows what] in the soup.

contrasts.text: God knows how many pages he filed.
contrasts.note: As an independent sentence, can make a literal claim about knowledge.

watch_for: A learner might read God knows what in an object slot as a literal claim about divine knowledge.
A learner might expect the variant with goodness or Heaven to work only as an independent sentence.
teacher.activity: Give students three sentences with a blank in the object slot (He filed ..., She cooked ..., They bought ...). Students fill them with an authority word plus knows and an indeterminate, then say what is left unspecified.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "God knows with an Indeterminate Expression." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/god-knows-indeterminate-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Prospective be going to

1.definition: Presents an event as prospective in light of an intention or present indications.

relatedConstructions.notes: Compare I’m going to leave and I’m going to the station. The prospective construction takes an infinitival and allows subjects with no motion interpretation.

projection.target: The weather subject requires no mover and no physical destination. The prospective use can therefore be distinguished from motion in going to the station.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Going to as a way of looking ahead
curious.summary: Be going to followed by a verb can present something as coming up, because of a plan or because of what is happening now.
curious.body: In It's going to freeze tonight, nothing is travelling anywhere. The words going to simply look ahead, presenting the freeze as coming because of present signs. In I'm going to leave, the same words present an event as coming in light of an intention. Compare I'm going to the station, where going is a real journey and to the station is the place. In I'm going to leave, a verb follows to.
curious.try: Say It's going to rain, then think of a sentence where going is a real journey. How do you tell the two apart?

teacher.summary: Helps separate prospective be going to from the motion verb go in sentences like I'm going to the station.
teacher.explain: Prospective be going to presents an event as upcoming in light of an intention or present indications: It's going to freeze tonight. The form is be, going and a to-infinitival. It takes an infinitival, and it allows subjects with no motion interpretation, such as the weather subject in the example, which has no mover and no physical destination. In I'm going to the station, by contrast, going is a motion verb and to is a preposition. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the going-to future. This dictionary calls it the prospective construction.

contrasts.note: Prospective, takes an infinitival.
Motion verb with a destination.

watch_for: A learner might read going to in It's going to freeze as movement toward a place.
A learner might treat going to leave and going to the station as the same structure.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of sentences with going to. They sort each one as a journey or a look ahead and discuss what in the sentence helped them decide.

child.hook: Is It's going to rain about a trip?
child.explain: Going to can talk about what is coming next. It's going to freeze tonight tells us what to expect. Nobody is travelling. I'm going to the station is different, because there you go to a place.
child.play: Sort sentences with going to into two piles, trips and what's coming next. Talk about how you decided.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.activity and child.play no longer give 'a place or a verb after to' as a sorting test (a journey can also take a purpose infinitive); removed the teacher.explain sentence turning the weather example into a general no-destination test; curious.body no longer says nobody has to be moving. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; 'Often taught' changed to 'Sometimes called'. Second round: dismissed teacher.explain to as a preposition in going to the station (CGEL's standard classification of to before a noun phrase, consistent with the entry's contrast with motion to a destination).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Prospective be going to." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/going-to-future-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Gradation

1.definition: Denotes scalar property
1.details: Core semantic features encoding measurable dimensions

2.details: Semantic features encoding scale topology

3.details: Semantic features encoding comparison class

projection.target: Positive tall relies on a contextually set standard. Six feet tall can place someone on the scale without settling whether they count as tall for a basketball player.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes scalar comparison and standards from positive-grade property ascription.

curious.title: Words for things that come in degrees
curious.summary: Words like tall, deep and quick describe something you can measure on a scale, and what counts as tall depends on what you compare it with.
curious.body: Tall is about height, and quick is about speed. Each picks out a scale, and a person or thing sits somewhere along it. Scales come in different shapes. Full and empty have a closed scale, while long and short have an open one. The standard matters too: tall for a child is judged against children, and perfectly clean sets an absolute standard. Six feet tall places someone on the height scale without deciding whether that person counts as tall for a basketball player. That is a separate question, set by the context.
curious.try: Think of someone you'd call tall. Would you still call them tall if they stood on a basketball team?

teacher.summary: Gives a vocabulary for talking about scales and standards when teaching gradable adjectives.
teacher.explain: Gradation is the semantic side of gradable properties. This dictionary separates three things: the scalar property itself (tall on a height scale, quick on a speed scale), the shape of the scale (full and empty, closed; long and short, open), and the standard of comparison (tall for a child, which is class-relative, and perfectly clean, which is absolute). Positive tall relies on a contextually set standard. Six feet tall places someone on the scale without settling whether they count as tall for a basketball player. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Gradable is the usual word for adjectives that can be placed on a scale. This dictionary uses the CGEL-style distinction between scalar comparison and positive-grade property ascription.
watch_for: A learner might think tall names a fixed height, when the standard is set by context.
A learner might take six feet tall as settling whether someone counts as tall for any group.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as tall and short, full and empty, long and short. They place each on a scale, say what standard is in play, and try adding for a child or perfectly.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Gradation." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/gradation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Grammatical Definiteness
