pattern: Semantic feature implemented through nominal determination

entry.name: Grammatical Definiteness
entry.pattern: Semantic feature implemented through nominal determination

dimensions.form: Typically realized by deital determiners (the, this, that, dependent genitive pronouns, genitive NPs) or bare proper nouns
dimensions.meaning: Identifiability, uniqueness, discourse familiarity
dimensions.function: Establishes referent accessibility; anchors information structure
dimensions.distribution: NPs in argument and predicative positions

1.definition: Identifiability status
1.details: Whether entity can be uniquely identified in context

2.details: Whether reference exhausts contextual set

examples.note: An established group versus a subset, on the ordinary referential readings

3.details: Whether entity is established in discourse

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional interface; definite interpretation cues deital form in production, deital form cues definite interpretation in comprehension
Grammatical definiteness is realized through definite construction
Paradigmatic contrast in the definiteness system

grounds.locator: Ranked formal diagnostics and interpretation mismatches

projection.target: Shared knowledge can make the only exit identifiable at first mention. Conversely, the in take the train can mark the lexicalized activity without distinguishing a specific train. Familiarity, unique reference, and structural diagnostics need separate predictions.
projection.evidence: CGEL and Reynolds document structural and interpretive departures from the simple definite/familiar mapping.

curious.title: Pointing out which one you mean
curious.summary: Words like the, this and that, or a name such as John, can show that the listener is able to work out which one is meant, in contrast with a or some.
curious.body: Saying the cat signals that the listener can work out which cat. A cat or some person does not. The same pairs show other contrasts: the students against some students is an established group against a subset, and the winner against a winner is unique against arbitrary. These contrasts aren't a simple switch tied to one word. Shared knowledge can make the only exit identifiable the first time it's mentioned. And in take the train, the word the can mark the activity itself without pointing to a specific train.
curious.try: Compare the book and a book in your own talk. When do you say each?

teacher.summary: Frames definiteness as identifiability, reference scope and discourse status, with known mismatches.
teacher.explain: Grammatical definiteness is a semantic feature implemented through nominal determination. This dictionary distinguishes identifiability (the cat against a cat), reference scope (the students against some students; the winner against a winner) and discourse status (given against new). Form is typically realized by the, this, that, dependent genitive pronouns, genitive NPs or bare proper nouns. Familiarity, unique reference and structural diagnostics need separate predictions: shared knowledge can make the only exit identifiable at first mention, and the in take the train can mark a lexicalized activity without distinguishing a specific train. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary describes the forms as typically deital determiners (a function, filled by the, this, that, dependent genitive pronouns or genitive noun phrases) or bare proper nouns. The and a are determinatives (often called articles), and their function in the NP is determiner.

contrasts.note: Given versus new.
A name is inherently identifiable; some person is not.

watch_for: A learner might think the requires that the listener has seen the thing before, when shared knowledge or a lexicalized activity can also license it.
A learner might take the train in take the train as pointing to one specific train.
teacher.activity: Give students short texts with the and a. They underline each, say whether the referent is new, given or identifiable from shared knowledge, and discuss any that don't fit.

checked.note: Fixed: summary no longer says definiteness shows the speaker has a particular thing in mind (this dictionary allows the in take the train without a specific train) and now speaks of identifiability; the train example no longer calls the activity familiar; teacher terms no longer says the forms form a word class called deital determinatives and instead gives this dictionary's wording (deital determiners, genitive NPs, bare proper nouns). Second round: fixed curious.summary to say these words can show identifiability (this dictionary allows the in take the train without an identifiable train) and curious.body to say the can mark the activity; fixed teacher.terms to list genitive noun phrases among the realizations of deital determiners, as this dictionary does, not as a separate alternative. Dismissed: the flag on 'The and a are determinatives' (CGEL's standard classification, presupposed by this dictionary's account of the determiner function).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Grammatical Definiteness." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/grammatical-definiteness-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Grammatical Number
pattern: Applies to nouns and agreement targets

entry.name: Grammatical Number
entry.pattern: Applies to nouns and agreement targets

dimensions.form: Singular/plural morphology on nouns; agreement on demonstrative determinatives, verbs, pronouns
dimensions.meaning: Cardinality, individuation, countability status
dimensions.function: Enables reference tracking; supports quantification
dimensions.distribution: Nouns, determinatives, verbs, pronouns; agreement domain extends across clause

1.definition: Specifies cardinality features
1.details: Core semantic features relating to quantity/cardinality of referents

2.details: Indicates whether referents are construed as countable units

3.definition: Encodes the tight/loose hierarchy of count diagnostics
3.details: Tight diagnostics (a/an, low cardinals, distributives) require higher individuation precision than loose diagnostics (many, high round numerals, plural agreement).

stabilisers.evidence: early acquisition of singular/plural contrasts
high-frequency noun paradigms anchor agreement
community convergence on agreement targets
consistent marking across generations
need to track individuation and plurality in discourse

projection.target: The standard count singular three-hour span contrasts with three hours is enough, where a morphologically plural measure can take singular agreement. This rules out deriving all agreement directly from the number of units in the situation.
projection.evidence: CGEL treats amount agreement as an override alongside the ordinary singular and plural agreement construction.

perturbations: reduced transmission or contact leads to erosion of number marking

variation.speaker_variation: register and dialect differences in agreement

known_boundary_items: cattle
police
furniture

coupling.mechanism: bidirectional inference between construal and morphosyntax

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional; singular form cues singular construal, singular construal licenses singular form
Bidirectional; plural form cues non-singular construal, non-singular construal licenses plural form
Boundary items showing ordered dissociation of count diagnostics

curious.title: One or more than one
curious.summary: Nouns like cat change form to show one thing or more than one, and words nearby change to match.
curious.body: Cat and cats show one against more than one, and this and these do the same for the word pointing at it. The verb can follow along too. The pattern is about more than counting. Rice and rices show that a word can be treated as something you can count or as an amount you can't, and the choice shows up in the grammar. Some words sit in between: many cattle is fine, while three cattle isn't. In three hours is enough, a plural measure takes a singular verb, so the grammar doesn't just tally the units.
curious.try: Say There's a cat in the garden and then change cat to cats. What else in the sentence has to change?

teacher.summary: Covers singular and plural marking, agreement, and the count/non-count boundary, including odd cases like three hours is enough.
teacher.explain: Grammatical number covers singular and plural morphology on nouns and agreement on demonstrative determinatives, verbs and pronouns. It also reflects whether a referent is construed as countable: rice against rices shows non-count against count construal. This dictionary ranks count diagnostics: the tight ones (a/an, low cardinals, distributives) need more individuation precision than the loose ones (many, high round numerals, plural agreement). Quasi-count nouns show the ranking, as in many cattle against three cattle. Amount agreement is a further override: three hours is enough has a plural measure with singular agreement, so agreement doesn't follow directly from the number of units. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Demonstrative determinatives are this/these and that/those. Non-count is the CGEL term (traditionally mass). Cattle, police and furniture are listed as boundary items.

contrasts.note: Quasi-count pattern; compare many cattle.

watch_for: A learner might take plural form to guarantee plural agreement, as in three hours is enough.
A learner might assume a noun that works with the loose diagnostics also works with low cardinals, as with cattle.
teacher.activity: Give students cards with nouns (cat, rice, furniture, hours). They test each with a/an, three, many and a verb, record what works, and sort the nouns into groups.

child.hook: How can you tell one cat from more than one cat?
child.explain: Nouns like cat change when there's more than one. One cat becomes two cats. Words nearby can change too, like this cat and these cats.
child.play: Pick five things in the room and say each as one and as more than one. Then say this or these in front of each.

checked.note: Frequency pass: cattle (about 3,700th in SUBTLEX-UK; the quasi-count entry is now marked low priority) dropped from teacher.summary and from the activity's noun cards; the starred entry contrast three cattle and the explain, terms and watch_for mentions are unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Grammatical Number." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/grammatical-number-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Phrasal Genitive at the NP Edge
pattern: NP[Determiner:genitive extended NP whose rightmost host is not its nominal head + Nom]

entry.name: Phrasal Genitive at the NP Edge
entry.pattern: NP[Determiner:genitive extended NP whose rightmost host is not its nominal head + Nom]

1.definition: Places genitive marking at the right edge of a possessor expression.

examples.form: It was [the person next door’s ladder].

projection.target: Door is the rightmost host of the marker, though the ladder is associated with the person. The possessor reading is determined by the whole genitive NP.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: The 's at the end of a longer phrase
curious.summary: When the owner is described by a long phrase, the 's goes at the very end of that phrase, not on the main word.
curious.body: In It was the person next door's ladder, the owner is the person next door. The 's doesn't go on person, the main word, but at the end of the whole phrase, on door. So the word right next to the 's isn't the one the ladder belongs to. The ladder belongs to the person, and the reading comes from the whole phrase the 's closes off.

examples.text: It was [the person next door's ladder].

curious.try: Describe a friend with a phrase of three or four words, such as the girl at the bus stop. Say whose bag it is, and notice where the 's goes.

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, where the genitive 's goes when the possessor is a long phrase.
teacher.explain: The genitive marker attaches at the right edge of an extended possessor: the person next door's ladder. Door is the rightmost host of the 's, though the ladder is associated with the person. The possessor reading is determined by the whole genitive NP, not by the word that hosts the marker. This dictionary treats this as a specialization of the genitive 's pattern, with a genitive NP in determiner function, and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Phrasal genitive is this dictionary’s name. It is sometimes called a group genitive.

examples.text: It was [the person next door's ladder].

watch_for: A learner might put the 's on person, the head noun, instead of at the end of the whole phrase.
A learner might take door as the owner because it hosts the 's.
teacher.activity: Give students noun phrases with a modifier after the head (the woman at the desk, the boy next door). They add 's and a noun and then say who owns the object.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Phrasal Genitive at the NP Edge." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/group-genitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Habitual used to

1.definition: Presents a habitual situation or state as characteristic of a past period.

examples.form: The shop [used to close] at noon.

projection.target: Used to can describe a past state, as in Jo used to own it. The present counterpart use to does not express a parallel current habit in ordinary affirmative clauses.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Used to
curious.summary: Used to followed by a plain verb describes a habit or a state that belonged to a past period.
curious.body: The shop used to close at noon tells us that closing at noon was the regular pattern at some earlier time. Used to can also describe a past state, as in Jo used to own it. The present-tense counterpart, use to, doesn't parallel this by describing a current habit in an ordinary affirmative sentence.

examples.text: The shop [used to close] at noon.

curious.try: Say something about a place near you that has changed, starting with It used to ...

teacher.summary: Helps students use used to for past habits and states and see how it differs from the present.
teacher.explain: The pattern is used to plus a plain-form verb: The shop used to close at noon. It presents a habitual situation or state as characteristic of a past period, so it covers habits and states: Jo used to own it. This dictionary says the present counterpart use to does not express a parallel current habit in ordinary affirmative clauses. It treats it as a specialization of VP structure, related to the past tense, and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Often taught as the past habitual or used to + infinitive.

examples.text: The shop [used to close] at noon.

watch_for: A learner might use use to for a present habit in an affirmative sentence, when it doesn't parallel used to.
A learner might think used to covers only repeated actions, when it also covers states like owning.
teacher.activity: Students write two sentences with used to about how their town has changed, one a habit and one a state, then swap and decide which is which.

child.hook: How do you talk about how things were?
child.explain: Used to talks about how things were in the past. The shop used to close at noon.

examples.text: The shop [used to close] at noon.

child.play: Tell a partner two things that used to be true for you. Start each with I used to.

checked.note: Fixed: cut the unsupported 'the form for talking about how things were' (curious.body); child.explain no longer introduces 'state' undefined; child.play no longer asks children to sort habits from states; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Habitual used to." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/habitual-used-to-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: have had it up to here (with X)
pattern: Clause[experiencer + perfect have had it up to here + (with + stimulus NP)]

entry.name: have had it up to here (with X)
entry.pattern: Clause[experiencer + perfect have had it up to here + (with + stimulus NP)]

1.definition: Presents the speaker or reported experiencer as having reached a limit of tolerance.
1.details: Here locates a figurative threshold. A gesture can give it a physical locus, and the idiom is also available in writing. The with-phrase can identify what has become intolerable. A literal liquid-level description lacks the experiencer and tolerance interpretation.

examples.form: We have [had it up to here with typical politicians].
examples.note: Excerpt from the annotated FAU example with an explicit stimulus.
Constructed example where the stimulus is clear in context.

relatedConstructions.notes: The core verbal expression has a largely fixed lexical form.
The canonical form of this idiom has perfect have.

grounds.locator: verbal pattern and inherited gesture variants
grounds.note: Records the negative-stimulus role and the threshold reading.

projection.target: The with-phrase identifies the source of frustration. An optional height gesture can highlight the threshold, while a distance phrase does not freely substitute for here with the same idiomatic reading.
projection.evidence: The FAU records distinguish the verbal idiom from two established gesture combinations and give an example with an explicit with-phrase.

curious.title: I've had it up to here
curious.summary: Have had it up to here says someone has reached the limit of what they can put up with, and with names the cause.
curious.body: I've had it up to here doesn't describe a liquid level. It says the speaker has reached a limit of tolerance, with here marking a figurative line. A gesture can show where that line is. A with-phrase can say what has become too much: We have had it up to here with typical politicians. The expression is also available in writing, and a literal description of liquid height lacks the tolerance meaning.

examples.text: We have [had it up to here with typical politicians].

curious.try: Say I've had it up to here with ... and hold a hand at a height. Does the gesture change how strong it sounds?

teacher.summary: An idiom for reaching the limit of tolerance, with an optional with-phrase naming the cause.
teacher.explain: The idiom is perfect have plus had it up to here, optionally followed by a with-phrase: We have had it up to here with typical politicians. It presents the speaker or a reported experiencer as having reached a limit of tolerance. Here locates a figurative threshold, which a gesture can give a physical locus. The with-phrase identifies the source of frustration. A distance phrase does not freely substitute for here with the same idiomatic reading, and a literal liquid-level description lacks the experiencer and tolerance interpretation. This dictionary says the core expression has a largely fixed lexical form.
teacher.terms: Idiom is the usual word. This dictionary calls the with-phrase's referent the stimulus.

examples.text: We have [had it up to here with typical politicians].

watch_for: A learner might read it as a literal measurement of where something reaches.
A learner might replace here with a distance phrase and expect the same idiomatic reading.
A learner might leave out the perfect have, though this dictionary gives that as the canonical form.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of annoyances (a noisy neighbour, a late bus). They write I've had it up to here with ... for each, then compare a literal sentence about water height to the idiom.

child.hook: What does it mean to have had it up to here?
child.explain: This means you can't put up with something any more. A hand held up high can show where your limit is. I've had it up to here with the noise.

examples.text: [I've had it up to here with the noise].

child.play: Hold your hand up high and say you've had it up to here with something silly, like broken pencils.

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation now says a raised hand shows where your limit is, not how full you are (which could suggest food); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "have had it up to here (with X)." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/had-it-up-to-here-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Heavy Complement Postposing
pattern: VP[V + short dependent + relatively heavy NP complement]

entry.name: Heavy Complement Postposing
entry.pattern: VP[V + short dependent + relatively heavy NP complement]

1.definition: Places a bulky complement after a lighter dependent of the same verb.

examples.form: She [handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits].

projection.target: Substituting a short pronoun produces strongly degraded handed to the chair it. Relative length and information status affect the postposed order.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saving the long part for last
curious.summary: When one part of a sentence is long, it can be placed after a shorter part of the same verb.
curious.body: In She handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits, the long phrase a folder containing all the amended exhibits comes last. The short phrase to the chair comes before it, even though both belong to the same verb. This dictionary says the order depends on how long the phrase is and on how much is already known about it. A short word in that spot gives a strongly degraded result: handed to the chair it doesn't work well. So the pattern suits a bulky phrase.

examples.text: She [handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits].

curious.try: Think of a sentence where you have to describe something long, such as a folder containing all the amended exhibits. Where do you put it?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, a word-order pattern where a long complement follows a short dependent of the same verb.
teacher.explain: In heavy complement postposing, a verb has a short dependent (to the chair) followed by a relatively heavy NP complement (a folder containing all the amended exhibits). The heavy NP is placed after the lighter dependent. Substituting a short pronoun gives strongly degraded handed to the chair it. Relative length and information status affect the postposed order. This dictionary relates the pattern to transitive verbs with a recipient to-phrase and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Heavy NP shift is the textbook name. This dictionary calls the pattern heavy complement postposing.

examples.text: She [handed to the chair a folder containing all the amended exhibits].

watch_for: A learner might treat the postposed order as free for any complement, when this dictionary says relative length and information status affect it.
A learner might place a short pronoun last, as in handed to the chair it, which this dictionary calls strongly degraded.
teacher.activity: Give students a sentence with a short object and a long object after a verb. They try both orders aloud, then replace the long phrase with a pronoun and notice which order resists.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Heavy Complement Postposing." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/heavy-np-shift-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Proposal with how about
pattern: how about + NP, gerund-participial or licensed clause

entry.name: Proposal with how about
entry.pattern: how about + NP, gerund-participial or licensed clause

1.definition: Offers an item or course of action for consideration.

relatedConstructions.notes: How about a short break? and What about a short break? can both propose a break. What about the budget? can also take up an outstanding topic.
How about taking a break? proposes an option with a gerund-participial. Why not take a break? puts forward a proposal using a plain verbal predicate.

projection.target: The response can accept or reject the proposal. The phrase need not ask how a break would be carried out.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: How about a short break?
curious.summary: How about followed by a thing or an activity puts it forward as an option for the listener to consider.
curious.body: How about a short break? doesn't have to be a question about how a break would happen. It's a proposal: here's an option, what do you think? The listener can accept or reject it. How about can be followed by a noun phrase, or by an activity ending in -ing, as in How about taking a break? What about a short break? can propose the same thing, though What about the budget? can also bring up a topic that's still outstanding. Why not take a break? also proposes a break, using a plain verb.
curious.try: Next time you want to suggest an activity, try How about ... and notice how people answer.

teacher.summary: Gives learners a way to make a suggestion, with variants using a noun phrase or an -ing form.
teacher.explain: How about plus an NP, a gerund-participial or a licensed clause offers an item or course of action for consideration: How about a short break? The response can accept or reject the proposal. The phrase need not ask how a break would be carried out, so the phrase works as a proposal. What about a short break? can propose the same thing, but What about the budget? can also take up an outstanding topic. Why not take a break? proposes with a plain verbal predicate, while How about taking a break? uses a gerund-participial. This dictionary marks this analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Gerund-participial is the CGEL-style label for the -ing clause after how about.

contrasts.note: Can take up an outstanding topic.

watch_for: A learner might read How about a short break? as asking in what way a break would be carried out.
A learner might treat How about taking a break? and Why not take a break? as the same form, when one uses -ing and the other a plain verb.
teacher.activity: Give pairs planning scenarios (a weekend, a lunch). One proposes with How about, and the partner accepts or rejects. They swap to Why not and notice the change in wording.

child.hook: How do you suggest something to a friend?
child.explain: How about can offer an idea. How about a short break? means maybe we could take one. Your friend can say yes or no.
child.play: Take turns suggesting things with How about. Your partner says yes or no. Try one with a thing and one with an -ing word.

checked.note: Fixed: contrast note for What about the budget? now says only what the entry says (can take up an outstanding topic; the proposal reading is shown with What about a short break?); dropped the broader 'pragmatic use, not a how-question' distinction; hedged curious body as 'doesn't have to be'. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Proposal with how about." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/how-about-proposal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Phrasal Exclamation with how

1.definition: Expresses an affective reaction to a degree judged remarkable.

projection.target: The phrase already supports an exclamation without an overt subject or predicate. The corresponding full exclamative can supply the evaluated situation explicitly.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: How odd!
curious.summary: How followed by an adjective can stand alone as an exclamation, showing a strong reaction to how far something goes.
curious.body: How odd! has no subject and no verb, yet it's a complete exclamation. It expresses a reaction to a degree the speaker finds remarkable. A longer version can spell out the situation being judged, such as How odd it is. The short form works by itself, without a subject or predicate.
curious.try: Think of something that surprised you. Say it with How and one adjective.

teacher.summary: Covers the short exclamation How plus an adjective, and how it relates to the full exclamative.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an independent AdjP made of exclamative how plus a gradable adjective: How odd! It expresses an affective reaction to a degree judged remarkable. The phrase already supports an exclamation without an overt subject or predicate. The corresponding full exclamative can supply the evaluated situation explicitly. This dictionary relates the pattern to other verbless clause-like utterances and marks its analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Exclamative how is this dictionary’s term for how in this use. Gradable adjectives are those that can be placed on a scale.
watch_for: A learner might treat How odd as a question about manner, when the pattern expresses a reaction.
A learner might add a subject and verb to the short exclamation, when this dictionary says the phrase already supports an exclamation without them.
teacher.activity: Show students surprising pictures. Each writes a short exclamation with How and an adjective, then expands it into a full sentence naming the situation.

child.hook: What can you say when something surprises you?
child.explain: How and a describing word can show a big feeling. How odd! is a whole exclamation. You don't need any more words.
child.play: Find something surprising in a picture and say how it is, with How and one word.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Phrasal Exclamation with how." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/how-adjective-exclamative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Explanatory how come

1.definition: Asks for an explanation of an actual or apparently actual state of affairs.

projection.target: Ordinary why questions allow Why is the gate open? How come normally retains subject-before-auxiliary order in the corresponding main-clause question.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: How come
curious.summary: How come asks for an explanation of something that seems to be the case.
curious.body: How come the gate is open? asks why the gate is open. It treats the open gate as a fact that needs explaining. The pattern differs from an ordinary why question. Why is the gate open? puts the verb before the subject. How come keeps the subject first: how come the gate is open.
curious.try: Ask the same question with Why and with How come. Which word order does each one use?

teacher.summary: Shows learners how come as a way to ask for an explanation, with different word order from why.
teacher.explain: How come plus a subject and finite predicate asks for an explanation of an actual or apparently actual state of affairs: How come the gate is open? An ordinary why question allows Why is the gate open?, with the verb before the subject. How come normally keeps subject-before-auxiliary order in the corresponding main-clause question. This dictionary relates it to open interrogative clauses and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Open interrogative is this dictionary’s term for questions with a question word, traditionally wh-questions.

contrasts.note: Verb before subject.

contrasts.text: How come the gate is open?
contrasts.note: Subject first.

watch_for: A learner might read How come as asking in what way something happened.
A learner might put the verb first after how come, as after why.
teacher.activity: Give students a set of observed situations (a light on, a late bus). They ask each with Why and with How come, and mark where the subject sits.

child.hook: What is another way to ask why?
child.explain: How come can ask why. How come the gate is open? means the same as asking why it is open. How come starts the question, then the gate comes next.
child.play: Ask a friend about something odd you see with How come. Then ask with Why and notice which words move.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Explanatory how come." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/how-come-explanation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Open and Remote if-Conditionals
pattern: Clause with an adjunct PP[if + finite declarative clause]

entry.name: Open and Remote if-Conditionals
entry.pattern: Clause with an adjunct PP[if + finite declarative clause]

1.definition: Sets out a condition and presents a consequence in relation to it.
1.details: The open variant treats the condition as an open possibility. The remote variant characteristically combines a preterite or irrealis form in the condition with a remote modal in the consequence. That preterite can be compatible with an explicitly future time. Present or past remotes often suggest that the condition fails, while a future remote can describe an unsettled possibility.

examples.form: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won’t have to rush.]
examples.note: Open variant with a future time.

examples.form: [If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn’t have to rush.]
examples.note: Remote counterpart. Tonight keeps the condition in the future.

relatedConstructions.notes: The consequent and conditional adjunct are packaged in one construction.
A regular preterite can mark remoteness as well as past time.
A separate use of if introduces an embedded yes/no question.

grounds.note: Catalogues open and more remote condition frames.
Analyzes the open and remote forms and their interpretations.

projection.target: A preterite form in a remote if-clause can describe the same future time as the corresponding present in an open conditional. Remoteness can be marked without asserting that the condition is false.
projection.evidence: CGEL provides matched forms and separates the interpretation from context-dependent implicatures. CASA groups the open and remote variants in three records.

curious.title: If this, then that
curious.summary: An if-phrase sets out a condition, and the rest of the sentence says what follows from it.
curious.body: In If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush, the if-part sets a condition and the rest says what follows. The condition is treated as an open possibility. A second version changes the wording: If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush. Both are about tonight, so the changed wording doesn't point to the past. The second marks the possibility as more remote, but that doesn't mean the condition is false.

examples.text: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.]
[If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.]

curious.try: Say a sentence about tomorrow with If and takes. Now say it with took and would. What changes in the feel of it?

teacher.summary: Helps students tell open from remote conditionals, and see that a past form in an if-clause can refer to future time.
teacher.explain: The if-part is an adjunct PP containing a finite declarative clause, and the sentence presents a consequence in relation to it. The open variant treats the condition as an open possibility. The remote variant characteristically combines a preterite or irrealis form in the condition with a remote modal in the consequence. The preterite can be compatible with explicitly future time, as with tonight. Present or past remotes often suggest that the condition fails, while a future remote can describe an unsettled possibility. Remoteness can be marked without asserting that the condition is false. A separate use of if introduces an embedded yes/no question.
teacher.terms: Preterite is the CGEL term for the past tense form. Open and remote are this dictionary's two variants.

examples.text: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.]
[If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.]

contrasts.text: If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.
contrasts.note: Open variant with a future time.

contrasts.text: If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.
contrasts.note: Remote counterpart. Tonight keeps the condition in the future.

watch_for: A learner might read took in the if-clause as past time, when with tonight it is future.
A learner might assume a remote if-clause says the condition is false.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of open and remote conditionals about plans. They mark the time of each, say what the verb form signals, and rewrite from open to remote.

child.hook: What does if add to a sentence?
child.explain: An if-part names a possibility. The rest says what follows from it. If he takes the later plane tonight, he won't have to rush.

examples.text: [If he takes the later plane tonight he won't have to rush.]
[If he took the later plane tonight he wouldn't have to rush.]

child.play: Say the two example sentences aloud. Which words change? Then make up your own if sentence about tonight, saying the possibility first and then what follows.

checked.note: Fixed: child.play now points at the two example sentences instead of an open-ended task followed by a single verb change; teacher.explain no longer calls the whole adjunct both a clause and a PP (the PP contains the finite clause); replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Open and Remote if-Conditionals." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/if-conditional-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Optative if only
pattern: standalone if only + finite clause, often modally remote

entry.name: Optative if only
entry.pattern: standalone if only + finite clause, often modally remote

1.definition: Expresses a wish concerning a possibility or unrealized state.

examples.form: [If only we had brought a torch!]

relatedConstructions.notes: Only if imposes a condition, while if only can express a wish.

projection.target: A consequence can remain unexpressed, and the utterance conveys a wish. In We can enter only if we bring a torch, only if instead sets a necessary condition.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: If only
curious.summary: If only, standing alone, expresses a wish about something that isn't the case or might not be.
curious.body: If only we had brought a torch! is a wish. A result can be left unsaid, and the sentence still conveys the wish. If only is different from only if. We can enter only if we bring a torch sets a necessary condition. If only expresses a wish, and the clause that follows is often remote in its wording.

examples.text: [If only we had brought a torch!]
We can enter only if we bring a torch.

curious.try: Think of something you wish had gone differently. Start the sentence with If only.

teacher.summary: Teaches learners to express a wish with if only, and to tell it from only if.
teacher.explain: Optative if only stands alone with a finite clause, often modally remote: If only we had brought a torch! It expresses a wish concerning a possibility or unrealized state. A consequence can remain unexpressed, and the utterance conveys a wish. Only if instead sets a necessary condition, as in We can enter only if we bring a torch. This dictionary relates the pattern to ordinary if-conditionals and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Optative is this dictionary’s term for the wish use.

examples.text: [If only we had brought a torch!]
We can enter only if we bring a torch.

contrasts.text: If only we had brought a torch!
contrasts.note: A wish.

contrasts.text: We can enter only if we bring a torch.
contrasts.note: A necessary condition.

watch_for: A learner might treat if only as the same as only if, when if only expresses a wish and only if imposes a condition.
A learner might look for a main clause after if only, when the consequence can remain unexpressed.
teacher.activity: Give students situations where something went wrong. They write a wish with If only and a related condition with only if, and say how the two differ.

child.hook: How do you say what you wish had happened?
child.explain: If only can show a wish. If only we had brought a torch! means we wish we had one. It's a wish, so no other part is needed.

examples.text: [If only we had brought a torch!]

child.play: Think of a wish about something that didn't happen. Begin with If only and say it with feeling.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Optative if only." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/if-only-wish-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: no sooner X than Y
pattern: No sooner + inverted primary clause + than + second clause

entry.name: no sooner X than Y
entry.pattern: No sooner + inverted primary clause + than + second clause

1.definition: Presents one event as occurring almost immediately after another.

examples.form: [No sooner had we parked than the rain started].

grounds.locator: Ch. 8 §§6, 10; Ch. 9, inversion after initial negation

projection.target: The comparative-shaped than-clause supplies the subsequent event. Fronted no sooner licenses inversion in the initial clause.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: No sooner ... than
curious.summary: No sooner ... than presents one event as following almost at once after another.
curious.body: In No sooner had we parked than the rain started, the rain starts almost as soon as the parking is done. The sentence starts with no sooner, and the helper word had comes before we. The second part begins with than, which brings in the later event. Placing no sooner first is what brings in the changed word order in the first part.

examples.text: [No sooner had we parked than the rain started].

curious.try: Say something that happened right after something else, beginning with No sooner had ...

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, a fronted negative expression with inverted order, and a than-clause for the later event.
teacher.explain: The pattern is No sooner plus an inverted primary clause, then than plus a second clause: No sooner had we parked than the rain started. It presents one event as occurring almost immediately after another. The comparative-shaped than-clause supplies the subsequent event. Fronted no sooner licenses inversion in the initial clause. This dictionary relates the pattern to negative-initial inversion and marks it as provisional.
teacher.terms: Subject-auxiliary inversion is the usual textbook name for the word order in the first part.

examples.text: [No sooner had we parked than the rain started].

watch_for: A learner might leave the first clause in ordinary order after no sooner, instead of inverting it as had we parked.
A learner might replace than with another word in the second part.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of events in time order. They combine each with No sooner ... than, then say aloud which event came first.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "no sooner X than Y." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/immediate-following-no-sooner-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Imperative Plus and with Conditional Force

1.definition: Interprets an imperative-shaped first coordinate as a sufficient condition in context.

examples.form: [Touch that wire and the alarm will ring].

projection.target: The first coordinate can warn against touching, with no instruction to do it. The consequent interpretation depends on performing the mentioned act.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A command that works like an if
curious.summary: A command followed by and can work like an if-sentence, saying what will happen if you do the thing.
curious.body: Touch that wire and the alarm will ring has the shape of a command, but it isn't telling anyone to touch the wire. It can warn against touching. The second part says what will happen if you do. The result depends on the act in the first part being performed. So the sentence reads much like If you touch that wire, the alarm will ring.

examples.text: [Touch that wire and the alarm will ring].

curious.try: Say a sentence that starts like a command but warns of a result, such as Open that door and ...

teacher.summary: Helps learners read an imperative joined by and to a consequence as an if-condition.
teacher.explain: An imperative-shaped first coordinate is interpreted as a sufficient condition in context, followed by and and a declarative consequence: Touch that wire and the alarm will ring. The first coordinate can warn against touching, with no instruction to do it. The consequent interpretation depends on performing the mentioned act. This dictionary relates the pattern to imperative clauses and to if-conditionals, and marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [Touch that wire and the alarm will ring].

watch_for: A learner might read the first part as an order to touch the wire.
A learner might expect the alarm to ring whether or not the wire is touched.
teacher.activity: Give students warning signs written as imperative plus and. They paraphrase each as an if-sentence and say whether the writer wants the act performed.

child.hook: Does Touch that wire and the alarm will ring tell you to touch it?
child.explain: It sounds like a command, but it works as a warning. It tells you what will happen if you touch the wire.

examples.text: [Touch that wire and the alarm will ring].

child.play: Make up warnings that start with a command and say what will happen next. Then say each one again with if.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the result 'only' follows if the act is performed (the entry treats the first part as a sufficient condition and says the consequent interpretation depends on performing the act); 'can warn' as in the entry. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary' in teacher text.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Imperative Plus and with Conditional Force." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/imperative-and-conditional-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Imperative Clause

dimensions.form: Clause headed by a plain-form VP; a second-person Subject is normally optional, and imperative do-support has properties distinct from declarative negation
dimensions.meaning: Presents a potential situation for addressee-oriented realization, while also permitting wishes, conditionals, and other non-directive interpretations
dimensions.function: Characteristically issues a directive
dimensions.distribution: Normally a main clause; English lacks a general subordinate imperative construction

1.definition: A headed clause type with plain-form VP and optional second-person Subject, characteristically used as a directive
1.details: Imperative is defined by its grammatical profile, not by directive force. The Subject is often absent and normally understood as second person, but overt you and third-person-like quantified Subjects are licensed. The verb is plain-form; supportive do is required for verbal negation, emphatic polarity, and code even with be. Sleep well illustrates a wish use rather than a directive. Non-finite and non-headed directives do not thereby become imperative clauses (CGEL pp. 853–57, 924–43).

examples.note: Imperative with quantified overt Subject and plain-form verb
Imperative clause used to express a wish rather than a directive

constraints.description: The construction is a Clause headed by a plain-form VP. A second-person Subject is omissible; an overt Subject precedes the positive VP but normally follows don't in a negative imperative.
Supportive do is required in verbal negation and emphatic polarity even with be; imperative clauses are normally restricted to main-clause distribution.

Directive force is characteristic, not necessary: wishes and conditional interpretations retain imperative clause type, while interrogative, declarative, non-finite, and non-headed expressions can convey directives without becoming imperatives.

projection.target: Plain-form imperative VP syntax predicts optional second-person Subject, special do-support with be, and main-clause distribution; directive force is the default pragmatic inference but can be overridden by wish or conditional uses
projection.evidence: The linked cluster of plain-form inflection, Subject optionality, imperative negation, and main-clause restriction holds independently of whether a token is actually used to direct the addressee

grounds.note: Plain-form imperative syntax projects Subject optionality, special do-support, and main-clause distribution
The linked grammatical profile recurs across directive and non-directive uses

relatedConstructions.notes: Non-finite and non-headed directives can convey directive meaning without being imperative Clauses

grounds.note: Imperative syntax, Subject optionality, do-support, characteristic directive use, and absence of a general subordinate imperative

curious.title: Commands, requests and wishes
curious.summary: An imperative is a sentence built around a plain-form verb, like Be generous, and it can express more than an order.
curious.body: Be generous, Everybody stand up and Don't be late all use the plain form of a verb (be, stand). When the subject is left out, as in Be generous, the person being spoken to is normally understood as the one who acts. You be careful shows that an overt you is possible too, and Everybody stand up has a different overt subject. Giving an order is the characteristic use, but not the only one. Sleep well is a wish, not an order. This dictionary defines the pattern by how the sentence is built, not by what it's used for.
curious.try: Think of a sentence that begins with a plain verb but isn't an order, like Sleep well. What is it doing instead?

teacher.summary: Defines the imperative by its grammar, with optional subject and special do-support, and separates it from directive force.
teacher.explain: An imperative clause has a plain-form VP head and an optional second-person subject; the subject is normally understood as second person, but overt you and quantified subjects are licensed (You be careful; Everybody stand up). Supportive do is required for verbal negation and emphatic polarity, even with be (Don't be late). An overt subject precedes a positive VP but normally follows don't in a negative imperative. Imperatives are normally main clauses, and English lacks a general subordinate imperative construction. Directive force is characteristic, not necessary: Sleep well is a wish, while interrogative, declarative, non-finite and non-headed expressions can convey directives without becoming imperatives. This dictionary marks its analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Imperative is the clause type; directive is the use. Plain form is the CGEL name for what traditional grammars call the base form.

contrasts.note: Subjectless; the subject is understood as second person.
Overt second-person subject.
An imperative clause used as a wish.

watch_for: A learner might think every imperative gives an order, when Sleep well is a wish.
A learner might use isn't or aren't to negate be in an imperative, when this dictionary requires do-support in Don't be late.
A learner might treat any directive as an imperative clause, though other forms can convey directives.
teacher.activity: Give students a mixed set of directives, wishes and requests. They mark which are imperatives, using this page's examples as models, and which are other forms that convey a directive.

child.hook: Does every sentence like Be generous give an order?
child.explain: Be generous tells someone what to do. The word you can be left out. Sleep well is a wish, not a command.
child.play: Say five sentences like Be generous or Sleep well. Which ones are orders and which are wishes?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary and body define the imperative by its plain-form verb rather than by a sentence-initial plain verb; Everybody stand up is described as having an overt subject; subject omission is stated as normal, as in the entry; teacher.activity now includes imperatives with an overt subject; replaced 'the entry' with this dictionary. Second round: fixed child.hook and child.play, which relied on the unexplained term plain verb; both now point to the examples Be generous and Sleep well.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Imperative Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/imperative-clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Imperative Negation with do-support

1.definition: Issues a negative directive (prohibitive imperative)
1.details: Uses do-support for negation in imperatives, even when an auxiliary could negate in declaratives.

constraints.description: Imperative clause with base-form VP.
Negation is expressed with do-support (do not/don't) in imperatives.

relatedConstructions.notes: Negative imperative retains imperative clause type and its special do-support requirement

projection.target: A prohibitive imperative can use don’t with be, as in Don’t be late, while an ordinary finite declarative uses She isn’t late. The negative inclusive Let’s not leave instantiates a different imperative subtype.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the distinctive imperative do distribution and the order alternatives in negatives with let’s.

curious.title: Telling someone not to
curious.summary: To tell someone not to do something, English uses don't or do not, even with be.
curious.body: Don't look at me and Don't be afraid are negative commands. Don't comes first, and the rest follows. The pattern uses don't even where a plain statement wouldn't. A statement uses She isn't late, but a negative command uses Don't be late. A speaker can add you for emphasis, as in Don't you look at me!, or use a word like everyone, as in Don't everyone shout it out.
curious.try: Tell a friend not to be late, then not to be noisy. Do you say don't each time?

teacher.summary: Teaches negative commands with don't, including the contrast with be in declaratives.
teacher.explain: A prohibitive imperative uses do-support for negation: Don't look at me. This dictionary notes this holds even with be, where an auxiliary could negate in a declarative: Don't be afraid, against She isn't late. An overt subject can follow don't, as in the emphatic Don't you look at me! and in a quantified subject such as Don't everyone shout it out. The negative inclusive Let's not leave is a different imperative subtype. This dictionary marks its analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Do-support is the usual name. Prohibitive imperative is this dictionary’s term for a negative command.

contrasts.note: Imperative with do-support despite be.
Declarative negation without do.

watch_for: A learner might negate be in an imperative as in a declarative, when this dictionary requires do-support.
A learner might treat Let's not leave as the same subtype as Don't be late.
A learner might place an overt subject before don't instead of after it.
teacher.activity: Give students positive commands including some with be. They turn each into a negative command, then contrast with a statement such as She isn't late.

child.hook: How do you tell someone not to do something?
child.explain: You can start with Don't. Don't look at me is a negative command. Don't be afraid uses Don't too, even with be.
child.play: Tell your partner five things not to do, starting with Don't. Include one with be, like Don't be late.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Imperative Negation with do-support." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/imperative-negation-do-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Imperative Plus or with a Warning

1.definition: Presents the second state of affairs as what may happen if the directive is ignored.

projection.target: The fall is associated with failure to hold still, rather than offered as an equally intended alternative action.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A command followed by a warning
curious.summary: A command joined by or to a result tells you what may happen if you ignore it.
curious.body: In Hold still or you'll fall, the second part says what may happen if the command is ignored. The fall goes with failing to hold still. The sentence doesn't offer two equal choices, to hold still or to fall. The fall is a warning, and the speaker doesn't intend it as something the listener might do instead.
curious.try: Say a warning that starts with a command and has or after it, such as Wait here or ...

teacher.summary: Helps learners read a command plus or plus a result as a warning, not a choice.
teacher.explain: An imperative is followed by or and a declarative consequence: Hold still or you'll fall. The second state of affairs is presented as what may happen if the directive is ignored. The fall is associated with failure to hold still, rather than offered as an equally intended alternative action. This dictionary relates the pattern to imperative-plus-and and to either-or coordination, and marks the analysis as provisional.
watch_for: A learner might read the two parts as equal options, to hold still or to fall.
A learner might treat the second part as an instruction to follow.
teacher.activity: Give students warning signs with or. They paraphrase each as If you don't ... and say what the writer wants the reader to do.

child.hook: Does Hold still or you'll fall give you two choices?
child.explain: No. The first part tells you what to do. The second part tells you what may happen if you don't.
child.play: Take turns giving a command and then a warning with or. Say what the speaker really wants.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Imperative Plus or with a Warning." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/imperative-or-warning-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Indefinite Object Omission
pattern: VP[transitive-capable V used without an overt object]

entry.name: Indefinite Object Omission
entry.pattern: VP[transitive-capable V used without an overt object]

1.definition: Leaves a usual participant nonspecific while asserting the activity or event.

relatedConstructions.notes: Compare Jo ate lunch with Jo ate. The second leaves the food unspecified. Availability depends on the verb and its use.

projection.target: The implied food need not have been mentioned. Leaving the relevant object unexpressed is natural for eat, even when plausible near-synonyms such as consume strongly favour a stated object.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Leaving out what was eaten
curious.summary: Some verbs that can take an object can also be used without one, with the object left unspecified.
curious.body: Have you eaten yet? doesn't say what was eaten. The food is left open. Compare Jo ate lunch with Jo ate, where the second leaves the food unspecified. The food need not have been mentioned earlier. Leaving out the object is natural for eat, though a near-synonym such as consume strongly favours a stated object. Whether it works depends on the verb and how it's used.
curious.try: Try the same with other verbs, like read or write. Which ones sound complete without an object?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why some verbs are fine without an object, while a near-synonym may need one.
teacher.explain: A verb that can take an object is used without one, leaving a usual participant nonspecific while presenting the activity or event itself: in Have you eaten yet? the food is left open. The implied food need not have been mentioned. This dictionary says leaving the relevant object unexpressed is natural for eat, even when plausible near-synonyms such as consume strongly favour a stated object. Availability depends on the verb and its use. This dictionary relates the pattern to simple intransitive and monotransitive VPs and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called object omission or the intransitive use of a transitive verb.

contrasts.note: Object stated.
Object left unspecified.

watch_for: A learner might assume any near-synonym of eat can drop its object, when consume strongly favours a stated one.
A learner might look for a specific food in Have you eaten yet?, when the food is left unspecified.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of verbs with similar meanings (eat and consume). They test each with and without an object, record which works, and discuss what is left unspecified.

child.hook: Can you say Have you eaten yet? without saying what?
child.explain: Some verbs can leave out what the action was done to. Have you eaten yet? doesn't say what. It only asks whether you ate.
child.play: Say Jo ate lunch. Then say it again without the word lunch, like Jo ate. What did the second one leave out? Try it with your own sentences about eating.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body and teacher.explain no longer say the activity is asserted in Have you eaten yet? (that example is a question); child.play no longer asks children to spot an object in several verbs and instead shows what to drop (lunch). Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Indefinite Object Omission." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/implicit-object-use-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Precautionary in case

1.definition: Supplies the possibility against which the main action is a precaution.

examples.form: Take a key [in case the door locks].

projection.target: The taking is appropriate before it is known whether the door will lock. An if-adjunct can instead make taking conditional on the door locking.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Doing something just in case
curious.summary: A phrase beginning with in case names a possibility that you're guarding against, so the main action is a precaution.
curious.body: In Take a key in case the door locks, the part after in case names a possibility. The taking happens as a precaution against it. You don't need to know yet whether the door will lock. That makes it different from a version with if. Take a key if the door locks makes the taking depend on the door locking. With in case, the taking is appropriate before anyone knows how things will turn out.

examples.text: Take a key [in case the door locks].
Pack a coat [in case it rains].

curious.try: Compare Take a key in case the door locks with Take a key if the door locks. When would you pick up the key in each one?

teacher.summary: Useful for learners who treat in case as interchangeable with if.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a prepositional phrase made of in case plus a finite clause. It supplies the possibility against which the main action is a precaution. The main action is appropriate before it is known whether the possibility will come about. An if-adjunct can instead make the main action conditional on that possibility. So the two forms invite different readings of the same main clause, as in Take a key in case the door locks versus Take a key if the door locks. The dictionary marks this dictionary as provisional and relates it to the general prepositional phrase and to if-conditionals.
teacher.terms: Sometimes described as a precautionary or contingency use of in case. The if version is a conditional adjunct.

examples.text: Take a key [in case the door locks].
Bring an umbrella [in case it rains].

contrasts.text: Take a key in case the door locks.
contrasts.note: Precaution; taken before it's known whether the door will lock.

contrasts.text: Take a key if the door locks.
contrasts.note: Taking depends on the door locking.

watch_for: A learner might treat in case and if as having the same meaning in Take a key in case the door locks.
A learner might think the in case clause describes something that has already happened.
teacher.activity: Give pairs of sentences that differ only in in case and if. Students say what you would do, and when, in each version, then write their own pair.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Precautionary in case." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/in-case-contingency-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Completion in a Time Span
pattern: clause with adjunct PP[in + measure NP of time]

entry.name: Completion in a Time Span
entry.pattern: clause with adjunct PP[in + measure NP of time]

1.definition: Measures the time to a bounded occurrence or endpoint.

examples.form: Jo sealed the cartons [in fifteen minutes].

examples.note: Constructed comparison. Temporal location reading of the same form.

projection.target: With a completed-event preterite the interval normally measures time to completion. With a prospective reading in fifteen minutes can instead locate an event fifteen minutes from now.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Finishing in a stretch of time
curious.summary: A phrase like in fifteen minutes can say how long something took, but the same words can also say when something will start.
curious.body: In Jo sealed the cartons in fifteen minutes, the phrase in fifteen minutes measures the time up to the point where the job was done. It tells you how long the sealing took. The same words can do something different. In Lee will start in fifteen minutes, they say when the starting will happen, fifteen minutes from now. So one form carries two readings, and the rest of the sentence helps you tell which one you've got.

examples.text: Jo sealed the cartons [in fifteen minutes].

curious.try: Say Jo sealed the cartons in fifteen minutes, then Lee will start in fifteen minutes. Which one tells you how long the job took, and which tells you when something begins?

teacher.summary: Helps with in plus a time measure, which can mean time taken or time until a future event.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause with an adjunct of the form in plus a noun phrase measuring time. With a completed event in the preterite, the interval normally measures the time to completion, as in Jo sealed the cartons in fifteen minutes. With a prospective reading, the same form can instead locate an event fifteen minutes from now, as in Lee will start in fifteen minutes. The first measures the time to a bounded occurrence or endpoint. The second gives a temporal location. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a duration adjunct or a time-frame adverbial. This dictionary treats it as a prepositional phrase adjunct.

examples.text: Jo sealed the cartons [in fifteen minutes].

contrasts.text: Jo sealed the cartons in fifteen minutes.
contrasts.note: Time taken to reach completion.

contrasts.text: Lee will start in fifteen minutes.
contrasts.note: Locates the start fifteen minutes from now.

watch_for: A learner might read Lee will start in fifteen minutes as saying that the starting takes fifteen minutes.
A learner might think in fifteen minutes has one fixed meaning whatever the verb and tense are.
teacher.activity: Write sentences with in and a time measure on strips, some past and some future. Students sort them into "how long it took" and "how long until it happens", then explain which clue in the sentence decided it.

checked.note: Fixed: the curious try question used an invented sentence pair that presupposed the future sentence locates the start; it now uses this dictionary's two examples, which are the readings the dictionary assigns. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' wording in teacher explain.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Completion in a Time Span." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/in-duration-completion-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Incongruity what is X doing Y?
pattern: interrogative[what + be + Subject + doing + location or V-ing expression]

entry.name: Incongruity what is X doing Y?
entry.pattern: interrogative[what + be + Subject + doing + location or V-ing expression]

1.definition: Asks for an explanation of a state, presence or action presented as anomalous.

examples.form: [What’s that ladder doing in the hall?]

projection.target: A ladder in a hall need not be performing an action. The same string shape with a human subject and an activity can also support an ordinary literal what-question.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: What is that ladder doing in the hall?
curious.summary: A question shaped like What is X doing there? can ask for an explanation of something that seems out of place.
curious.body: Take What's that ladder doing in the hall? A ladder needn't be performing any action. The question asks why the ladder is there, and it presents its being there as strange. The same shape of words can also be an ordinary question. With a person and an activity, such as asking what someone is doing in the hall, it can simply ask what that person is up to. The shape of the words alone doesn't settle which reading is meant.

examples.text: [What’s that ladder doing in the hall?]
What's that muddy boot doing on the table?

curious.try: Think of something you found in an odd spot. How would you ask why it was there, using this pattern?

teacher.summary: Covers the idiomatic What is X doing Y? question that asks for an explanation of something presented as odd.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an interrogative built from what, a form of be, a subject, doing and then a location or an -ing expression. Its meaning is to ask for an explanation of a state, presence or action presented as anomalous. A ladder in a hall need not be performing an action, so the doing isn't literal. The same string shape with a human subject and an activity can also support an ordinary literal what-question, so the shape alone doesn't settle which reading is meant. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the open interrogative clause and marks it provisional. It cites discussion in CGEL, in Kay and Fillmore, and in Goldberg.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the What's X doing Y? construction.

examples.text: [What’s that ladder doing in the hall?]
What's your bike doing on the lawn?

contrasts.text: What's that ladder doing in the hall?
contrasts.note: Asks why it's there, presented as odd.

contrasts.text: What's Dad doing in the hall?
contrasts.note: Can be an ordinary question about an activity.

watch_for: A learner might answer What's that ladder doing in the hall? by describing an action the ladder performs.
A learner might not realize the speaker is presenting the situation as strange.
teacher.activity: Place a few out-of-place objects around the room. Students ask What's the X doing Y? about each, and a partner supplies an explanation.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary now says the pattern can ask for an explanation (the same shape can be an ordinary literal question); cut the claim that a subject's ability to act tells the readings apart; cut the unsupported origin of the name in teacher.terms.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Incongruity what is X doing Y?." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/incongruity-whats-doing-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Indefinite Construction
pattern: Indefinite determination or contextually indefinite bare plural/non-count NP

entry.name: Indefinite Construction
entry.pattern: Indefinite determination or contextually indefinite bare plural/non-count NP

1.definition: Refers without presenting the referent as already uniquely identifiable
1.details: The speaker may know the identity. The construction does not require the hearer to resolve it from prior information.

2.details: Entity being introduced to discourse

3.details: Under certain directives or permissions an indefinite can leave the choice of individual open. Choice and permitted quantity are separate.

grounds.locator: Deital form and interpretation, including non-deital residual cases

projection.target: A student phoned can refer to a particular student known to the speaker. A student can enter allows a general reading. The article alone does not rule out specific reference or supply an any-member permission.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes referential from non-referential uses and documents both specific and nonspecific interpretations. A determinerless role predication does not itself introduce a novel reference.

curious.title: Noun phrases that don't present a thing as already identifiable
curious.summary: Phrases such as a dog or some students refer without treating the thing as one the listener can already pick out.
curious.body: When you say a dog, you refer to something without presenting it as already uniquely identifiable to the listener. You may know exactly which dog you mean. The phrase just doesn't ask the listener to work that out. This kind of phrase can introduce something new, as in there is a solution. It can leave the choice open, as in take a card, where any card will do. And it can say what kind of thing someone is, as in is a teacher. The word a alone doesn't settle which of these you've got, and A student phoned can even be about one particular student the speaker knows.
curious.try: Say A student phoned and A student can enter. In which one might the speaker have one particular student in mind?

teacher.summary: Explains that indefinite noun phrases don't mark the referent as identifiable, and that the same form covers several uses.
teacher.explain: This dictionary describes indefinite reference as referring without presenting the referent as already uniquely identifiable. The speaker may know the identity, and the construction doesn't require the hearer to resolve it from prior information. It lists four uses: reference without presenting the referent as already identifiable (a dog, some students), a new discourse entity (there is a solution, first mention), an arbitrary instance where the choice is left open (take a card), and type membership (is a teacher, is some kind of expert). Choice and permitted quantity are separate. The article alone doesn't rule out specific reference or supply an any-member permission. A student phoned can refer to a particular student known to the speaker, while A student can enter allows a general reading. This analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditionally, a and an are called indefinite articles. In CGEL terms they're determinatives, and the noun phrase can include bare plural or non-count forms. The specific and non-specific readings are the textbook names for the contrast between a particular referent and a general one.

contrasts.note: Can refer to a particular student known to the speaker.
Allows a general reading.

watch_for: A learner might assume that a means the speaker doesn't know which one is meant.
A learner might read take a card as allowing any number of cards.
A learner might read is a teacher as introducing a new person rather than naming a category the person belongs to.
teacher.activity: Give students short sentences with a, some and bare plurals. They label each as introducing something new, leaving a choice open, or naming a category, and note any sentence that could fit more than one.

checked.note: Fixed: curious title no longer implies the thing is unknown (the entry allows a particular individual known to the speaker); teacher explanation no longer turns the first meaning into a novelty requirement, and says 'this dictionary' for 'the entry'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Indefinite Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/indefinite-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Indefinite NP with a Modified Personal Name
pattern: NP[a/an + attributive AdjP + personal name form]

entry.name: Indefinite NP with a Modified Personal Name
entry.pattern: NP[a/an + attributive AdjP + personal name form]

1.definition: Presents a named person in a condition associated with a particular occasion.
1.details: In a visibly shaken Giuliani, the name identifies a person already introduced in the report. The adjective supplies his state within the NP, and the clause predicates what he did. One analysis takes the modifier to characterize the bearer directly. Another takes the NP to pick out a manifestation, understood as the bearer in one of several possible states.

examples.form: [A visibly shaken Giuliani] noted the tragic circumstances during a hospital press conference.
examples.note: The report has already named Rudolph Giuliani and described his emotional state.

grounds.locator: Paragraph before the quotation about Father’s Day

examples.note: The modified name is a preposition’s complement within the description of a photograph.
An evidential adverb can qualify the attribution made by the adjective.

grounds.locator: §7 [62], from the GB section of NOW, 23 February 2017

relatedConstructions.notes: The overt article takes determiner function in an NP with an adjective and a personal name form.
Poor Henry and a visibly shaken Giuliani both characterize an identifiable bearer. The former illustrates the restricted class of adjectives in bare embellishments.

The analyses overlap if a visibly shaken Giuliani selects one manifestation. In the Paris of my youth, a contextually delimited period is explicitly identified, whereas the CBS token provides an occasion-specific description in a report about a single event.

Both patterns can characterize a participant during an event. Compare They carried an unconscious Kim with They carried Kim unconscious. In the former, the adjective is internal to the object NP. In the latter, it is a secondary predicative outside that NP.

grounds.note: The selected COCA comparisons favour a/an with short-lived conditions. Berezowski analyses the contrast in terms of name-bearer manifestations and ordinary indefinite reference.
The authors discuss an angry Blair as nonrestrictive with respect to the person and contrastive with respect to that person’s possible states.
CGEL describes bare and the-marked adjectival embellishments and treats the selection of a manifestation separately.

projection.target: A temporary-state adjective can make a/an available with an already identified name bearer, in subject position and within a PP. The determiner choice varies with the adjective and the construal of its contribution.
projection.evidence: CBS supplies the previously identified bearer. Berezowski’s selected COCA comparisons give more a/an tokens than the or bare tokens for angry, smiling, beaming, relaxed and tired. His young and old comparisons are predominantly bare.

known_boundary_items: Poor Henry supplies an attribution in a bare NP. CGEL also gives the distraught Empress Alexandra with the and a temporary state.
Another Roosevelt describes a person by resemblance. A visibly shaken Giuliani keeps Giuliani as the bearer whose state is described.

curious.title: A shaken Giuliani, a smiling Johnson
curious.summary: Putting a or an and a describing word in front of a person's name can present that person in a particular state on a particular occasion.
curious.body: In A visibly shaken Giuliani noted the tragic circumstances, the name belongs to someone the report has already introduced.
