The describing word tells us his state at the time, and the rest of the sentence says what he did. Why a rather than the or nothing? One analysis says the description is directly about the person. Another says the phrase picks out one version of the person, as he was in one of several possible states. This dictionary treats the question as open. The pattern also turns up after prepositions, as in next to a smiling Hootie Johnson.

examples.text: [A visibly shaken Giuliani] noted the tragic circumstances during a hospital press conference.

curious.try: Think of a news photo caption. Could you write a smiling and a name there, such as a smiling Maria? What does adding the describing word tell you about that moment?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, a or an with an adjective and a personal name, as in a visibly shaken Giuliani.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a noun phrase made of a or an, an attributive adjective phrase and a personal name form. The article is in determiner function. In the Giuliani example the name identifies a person already introduced in the report, and the adjective supplies his state on an occasion. This dictionary reports two analyses: the modifier characterizes the bearer directly, or the phrase picks out a manifestation, understood as the bearer in one of several possible states. It cites a corpus comparison in which a/an used with angry, smiling, beaming, relaxed and tired gives more tokens than the or bare forms, while young and old comparisons are predominantly bare. The analysis is provisional, so present the analysis as open.
teacher.terms: Sometimes discussed under the heading of proper names used with an indefinite article. This dictionary treats the whole phrase as a noun phrase in which a or an is the determiner.

examples.text: [A visibly shaken Giuliani] noted the tragic circumstances during a hospital press conference.

contrasts.note: The adjective is inside the object noun phrase.
The adjective is outside it, as a secondary predicative.

watch_for: A learner might read a smiling Hootie Johnson as introducing a second person with the same name.
A learner might treat unconscious in They carried Kim unconscious as part of the object noun phrase.
teacher.activity: Give students short news-style captions with a name and a temporary state. They rewrite each with the adjective after the name, as in the second contrast sentence, and say whether the adjective is inside or outside the noun phrase.

checked.note: Fixed: prior introduction of the bearer now stated of the Giuliani example, not of the whole pattern; removed the claim that the personal name form is head (the entry says only that the article takes determiner function). Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Indefinite NP with a Modified Personal Name." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/indefinite-modified-name-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Rate with an Indefinite Denominator
pattern: quantity or frequency expression + NP[a(n) + singular unit nominal]

entry.name: Rate with an Indefinite Denominator
entry.pattern: quantity or frequency expression + NP[a(n) + singular unit nominal]

1.definition: Expresses a ratio by pairing a numerator with a unit denominator.
1.details: Fifty miles an hour supplies a speed, even if the measured motion lasts only a minute. Fifty miles every hour can instead assert successive hourly totals. The same form supports price, salary, and frequency. A per-phrase can often express the same ratio and is more flexible with stacked or complex denominators.

examples.form: He was going at [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].
examples.note: Constructed frequency example; the numerator can be multiplicative.

relatedConstructions.notes: The denominator is an indefinite singular NP.
Both combine with a stated magnitude, with different interpretations.

grounds.note: Compares the indefinite denominator with an every-time adjunct and a per-phrase.

projection.target: The second NP is interpreted as a unit denominator. The construction can describe a rate without asserting one complete occurrence of that unit.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes the a- and per-forms. The FrameNet account controls the duration of motion in the comparison with every hour.

curious.title: Fifty miles an hour
curious.summary: Putting a or an before a unit, as in $20 a yard, turns an amount into a rate.
curious.body: In He was going at 50 miles an hour, the words an hour don't mean one particular hour. They say what the 50 miles is measured against, so the whole phrase gives a speed. The same pattern gives a price, as in $20 a yard, and a frequency, as in twice a day. The speed holds even if the trip lasts only a minute. Fifty miles every hour is different: it can claim fifty miles in each successive hour. A phrase with per can often say the same thing, and it copes better with longer or stacked units.

examples.text: He was going at [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].

curious.try: How would you say what a bicycle costs for each hour you rent it, using a and an hour or a day?

teacher.summary: Covers rates like fifty miles an hour, where a or an plus a unit expresses a ratio.
teacher.explain: The pattern pairs a quantity or frequency expression with a noun phrase made of a or an and a singular unit noun. It expresses a ratio: a numerator over a unit denominator. Fifty miles an hour gives a speed even if the motion lasts only a minute, whereas fifty miles every hour can assert successive hourly totals. The same form supports price, salary and frequency. The second noun phrase is interpreted as a unit denominator, and the construction describes a rate without asserting one complete occurrence of that unit. A per-phrase can often express the same ratio and is more flexible with stacked or complex denominators.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a distributive use of a/an. The a/an here is the indefinite article in traditional terms, a determinative in CGEL terms.

examples.text: He was going at [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].

contrasts.text: He was going at 50 miles an hour.
contrasts.note: A rate, whatever the length of the trip.
Can assert successive hourly totals.

watch_for: A learner might read an hour in fifty miles an hour as one particular hour.
A learner might assume the trip must last a whole hour for fifty miles an hour to be true.
teacher.activity: Students collect rates from signs, menus and timetables (price a kilo, trains an hour). They say each aloud with a or an, then restate it with per.

child.hook: How fast does a car go in "fifty miles an hour"?
child.explain: Sometimes a means "for each." Fifty miles an hour means fifty miles for each hour. A yard of ribbon at $20 a yard costs $20 for each yard.

examples.text: The car went [50 miles an hour].
The nurse checked it [twice a day].

child.play: Find prices and speeds on signs or packages. Say each one with a or an, such as three dollars a bag. Then say what it means with for each.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Rate with an Indefinite Denominator." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/indefinite-rate-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Independent Genitive Pronoun

1.definition: Indicates possession/ownership
1.details: Marks the pronoun as possessor or controller

2.details: Indicates inherent connection rather than ownership

3.details: Marks the creator or source

examples.note: Property of it (independent its is rare but attested)

6.details: Indicates the doer/experiencer of an action/state

projection.target: Mine contrasts with my in This is mine versus my copy. With whose and his, identical surface forms can appear in independent or dependent slots. Independent its is rare rather than ruled out.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates dependent and independent genitive realizations. Its warning about the exceptional distribution of its limits any paradigm-wide prediction.

curious.title: Mine, yours and theirs
curious.summary: Words like mine, yours, hers and theirs can stand on their own as a whole phrase, where my, your, her and their need a noun after them.
curious.body: My copy needs a noun to lean on. Mine doesn't. In This is mine, the word stands alone. Words in this group include mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs and whose, as in Whose is this? Some of these look the same whether or not they stand alone. His and whose are examples. Its is a special case: standing alone it is rare, but it isn't ruled out. The dictionary notes that the relationship between the person and the thing can be ownership, but can also be something broader.
curious.try: Say This is my copy and then This is mine. What did you drop, and what did mine do for you?

teacher.summary: Helps explain the stand-alone forms mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs against the forms that precede a noun.
teacher.explain: The independent genitive pronouns are mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs and whose. They contrast with dependent forms: This is mine versus my copy. CGEL separates dependent and independent genitive realizations. Some forms, such as his and whose, can look identical in both slots. This dictionary treats independent its as rare rather than ruled out, and CGEL's warning about the exceptional distribution of its limits any paradigm-wide prediction. The relationship expressed can be ownership or control, as in That car is mine and These policies are theirs. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Mine, yours, theirs and the like are sometimes called possessive pronouns. In this dictionary's terms they're independent genitive pronouns, and the forms before a noun are dependent genitives.

contrasts.note: Independent form, no noun follows.
Dependent form, a noun follows.

watch_for: A learner might add a noun after mine, yours or theirs, as one would after my, your or their.
A learner might assume the independent form of every genitive differs from the dependent form, though his and whose can look the same in both slots.
teacher.activity: Students take pairs of sentences with my/your/their and a noun and rewrite them with mine/yours/theirs and no noun. They then find two forms that stay the same.

child.hook: What is the difference between "my book" and "the book is mine"?
child.explain: My needs a word after it, like my book. Mine can stand alone. You can say the book is mine.
child.play: Point to things in the room and say whose they are. Try it two ways, such as "my pencil" and "this pencil is mine."

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms kept possessive pronouns, rephrased as 'sometimes called' (CGEL Ch. 5 section 16.4, the entry's cited source, says traditional grammar analyses the independent genitives as possessive pronouns), and cut absolute possessives (not verified as widely used). Also fixed (unflagged): curious.body cut the gloss that mine means something like 'my one' (not in the entry); teacher 'The entry' changed to 'This dictionary'. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Independent Genitive Pronoun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/independent-genitive-pronoun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Indeterminate Word

dimensions.form: Closed series sharing historical wh- orthography (how included); internal paradigm structure (whose, whom as case forms of who); productive -ever derivation
dimensions.meaning: Contributes an open variable restricted to a sort (person, thing, selection, possessor, place, time, reason, manner/degree)
dimensions.function: Feeds interrogative, relative, and exclamative packagings; the marked property percolates upward, with non-subject fronting where the packaging requires it
dimensions.distribution: Availability and lexical category vary by member and packaging; non-subject phrases are fronted in the relevant constructions

1.definition: Contributes an open variable restricted to a sort, available to different clause-type packagings
1.details: Term: indeterminate (cf. Kuroda 1965 for the Japanese analogue). Not a CGEL lexical category: the set cross-cuts lexical categories, and category may differ by packaging and function—interrogative what is a determinative in determiner use (what size) but a pronoun when it heads an NP (What did you see?), whereas exclamative what is an adjective; how is adverbial. Three projections support the overarching set: (i) sortal-variable semantics across packagings; (ii) upward percolation of the interrogative, relative, or exclamative property, plus non-subject fronting where required; (iii) the -ever series (whoever, whatever, whichever, wherever, whenever, however) derives from this base set. Packaging-specific category facts live in the specialization entries and lexicon layer.

examples.note: Open variable over things (fused relative packaging)

2.definition: Marks scalar degree, a point or extent on an implicit or explicit scale
2.details: Degree is one of the sorts the series ranges over

relatedConstructions.notes: Deitality status varies by packaging: ignorance-reading fused relatives pattern deitally; free-choice readings are mixed; exclamative uses are non-deital (Reynolds, deitality inventory)

grounds.note: Indeterminate as the term for the analogous Japanese series

projection.target: The same sortal form can occur in what Jo wrote after admire or wonder. With admire, the expression can denote an entity or text. With wonder, it presents an open question. The lexical shape does not determine the packaging.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares matching clause-like strings across fused relatives and embedded interrogatives and gives independent agreement and distributional tests.

curious.title: The who, what, where family of words
curious.summary: Words like who, what, where, when, why and how share one job, which is to stand for something left open, and different sentence types put them to different uses.
curious.body: Who, what, which, where, when, why and how all leave something open. Who leaves open a person, where a place, when a time. This dictionary calls them indeterminates, and the same word can serve a question, a relative phrase or an exclamation. Compare what she saw with who came. In what she saw, the word stands for a thing. In who came, it stands for a person, and the sentence asks which one. Words ending in ever, such as whoever and whenever, come from the same set. Degree belongs here too: how tall asks about a point on a scale.
curious.try: Take who, where and when. What kind of thing does each one leave open?

teacher.summary: Gives the overarching idea behind wh-words across questions, relatives and exclamatives, and warns they don't form one word category.
teacher.explain: This dictionary treats who, whom, whose, what, which, where, when, why and how, plus the -ever series, as one set whose members contribute an open variable restricted to a sort: person, thing, selection, possessor, place, time, reason, manner or degree. The set isn't a CGEL lexical category, because it cross-cuts categories. Interrogative what is a determinative in what size but a pronoun when it heads an NP, as in What did you see?; exclamative what is an adjective; how is adverbial. The same form can occur in what Jo wrote after admire or wonder: after admire it can denote an entity or text, and after wonder it presents an open question. The lexical shape doesn't determine the clause type. This analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call the interrogative uses wh-words or question words. This dictionary's term for the wider set, which also covers relative and exclamative uses and the -ever series, is indeterminate.

contrasts.note: Can denote an entity or text; compare the next line.
Presents an open question.

watch_for: A learner might assume that who, what and how all belong to one word class in CGEL, though this dictionary says the set cross-cuts classes.
A learner might assume a form such as what has one category in every use, though interrogative what is a determinative in what size and a pronoun in What did you see?
teacher.activity: Give sentences with what, who, where and how in questions, relatives and exclamations. Students sort the uses by clause type and name the kind of thing each word leaves open.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.watch_for no longer presents what size and What did you see? as a change of clause type (both are interrogative; they illustrate category differing by function); teacher.terms now limits wh-word and question word to the interrogative uses and says the dictionary's set is wider; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Indeterminate Word." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/indeterminate-word-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Indirect Speech Report

1.definition: Reports propositional or interrogative content from the reporter’s perspective.

examples.form: Jo said [that she would call the next day].

relatedConstructions.notes: The that-clause in Jo said that she was ready supplies the content of the speech report.

projection.target: Person, tense and calendar anchoring can adapt to the reporting context. The reported clause need not reproduce the words used in the prior utterance.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Reporting what someone said
curious.summary: An indirect report gives the content of what someone said from the reporter's point of view, without repeating their exact words.
curious.body: In Jo said that she would call the next day, the reporter tells us what Jo said. The reporter doesn't quote Jo. The person, the tense and the way the day is named can be adjusted to fit the reporter's situation. So the reported part need not repeat the words Jo used. It reports the content, and it can report a statement or a question.

examples.text: Jo said [that she would call the next day].

curious.try: Think of something a friend said to you. Can you report it to someone else without using the friend's exact words?

teacher.summary: Introduces reported speech as a reporting predicate plus a content clause.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a reporting predicate followed by a content clause. It reports propositional or interrogative content from the reporter's perspective, as in Jo said that she would call the next day. Person, tense and calendar anchoring can adapt to the reporting context, and the reported clause need not reproduce the words of the earlier utterance. The that-clause supplies the content of the report. This dictionary relates this pattern to the declarative content clause and to present backshift, and marks it provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditionally called indirect speech or reported speech. The matching quotation of the speaker's exact words is traditionally called direct speech; this dictionary doesn't cover it.

examples.text: Jo said [that she would call the next day].
Sam told us [that he was ready].

watch_for: A learner might assume the reported clause must repeat the speaker's exact words.
A learner might keep the speaker's original person and calendar words, such as tomorrow, when the reporting context calls for adjusting them.
teacher.activity: Students write down one short statement each. Partners report it to the class without repeating the exact words, then check which parts changed.

child.hook: Can you tell someone what a friend said without copying the exact words?
child.explain: You can tell what someone said without using their exact words. Jo said that she would call the next day. The words can change to fit who is telling it.

examples.text: Jo said [that she would call the next day].

child.play: Say one sentence to a partner. They tell the class what you said, starting with "said that." Did the words change?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Indirect Speech Report." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/indirect-report-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Infinitival Open Interrogative
pattern: interrogative XP + to-infinitival with a linked gap

entry.name: Infinitival Open Interrogative
entry.pattern: interrogative XP + to-infinitival with a linked gap

1.definition: Presents an unresolved choice about an envisaged action.

projection.target: Which route supplies the missing object and the action is prospective or modal. The corresponding finite question can ask instead what was actually done.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Which route to take
curious.summary: A question word followed by to and a verb, as in which route to take, presents an open choice about something that could be done.
curious.body: In They discussed which route to take, the part after discussed is a question with to and a verb instead of a full clause. Which route fills in what's missing after take. The question is about an action that's being considered, not one that has been carried out. A full finite question can ask instead what was actually done, so the two forms can ask different things.
curious.try: Finish the sentence We can't decide... with a question word and to plus a verb.

teacher.summary: Covers embedded questions such as which route to take, which have a question phrase and a to-infinitival.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an interrogative phrase followed by a to-infinitival with a linked gap. It presents an unresolved choice about an envisaged action. In They discussed which route to take, which route supplies the missing object of take, and the action is prospective or modal. The corresponding finite question can ask instead what was actually done. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the open interrogative clause and relates it to for-infinitivals. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an infinitival wh-question or an embedded infinitival interrogative.

contrasts.text: They discussed which route to take.
contrasts.note: An envisaged action, still undecided.

contrasts.text: They discussed which route they took.
contrasts.note: A finite question can ask what was actually done.

watch_for: A learner might read which route to take as asking about a past action.
A learner might treat which route as separate from the verb take, when it supplies the missing object of take.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences that start with I don't know, using a question word plus to and a verb. They then rewrite each with a finite clause and compare the meanings.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Infinitival Open Interrogative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/infinitival-open-interrogative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Infinitival Purpose Adjunct

1.definition: Presents a desired outcome as the purpose of the main situation.

examples.form: Jo borrowed the van [to move the chairs].
Jo borrowed the van [to move the chairs], but the plan fell through.
examples.note: Constructed comparison. The purpose can remain unrealized.

projection.target: The chair-moving need never occur. The clause can be expanded with in order, unlike many result infinitivals that report a realized later event.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Doing something to reach a goal
curious.summary: A to plus a verb after a clause can say what the action was for, as in borrowing a van to move the chairs.
curious.body: In Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs, the part with to says why Jo borrowed the van. It presents a wanted outcome as the purpose of what happened. A purpose doesn't have to come true. Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs, but the plan fell through is fine: the chairs may never have moved. You can also spell the purpose out with in order, as in in order to move the chairs.

examples.text: Jo borrowed the van [to move the chairs].
Jo borrowed the van [to move the chairs], but the plan fell through.

curious.try: Say Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs. Does it tell you the chairs got moved?

teacher.summary: Explains to plus a verb as a purpose adjunct, and why the purpose need not be realized.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause followed by a to-infinitival adjunct. It presents a desired outcome as the purpose of the main situation. The purpose can remain unrealized: in Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs, but the plan fell through, the chair-moving need never occur. The clause can be expanded with in order, which is a useful test. This dictionary contrasts this with a result infinitival, which reports a realized later event. It relates the pattern to for-infinitivals. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditionally called an infinitive of purpose or purposive infinitive. The related result use is covered under infinitival of subsequent outcome.

examples.text: Jo borrowed the van [to move the chairs].
Jo borrowed the van [to move the chairs], but the plan fell through.

contrasts.text: Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs.
contrasts.note: Purpose; can be expanded with in order.

contrasts.text: Jo borrowed the van in order to move the chairs.
contrasts.note: The same purpose, spelled out.

watch_for: A learner might assume the purpose clause describes something that did happen.
A learner might read the to-phrase as describing the van rather than the purpose of borrowing it.
teacher.activity: Students write why-questions and answer with to plus a verb. They add but the plan fell through to some answers and discuss whether the purpose was achieved.

child.hook: Why did Jo borrow the van?
child.explain: To plus a verb can tell why someone did something. Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs. That was the plan. It doesn't say the chairs got moved.

examples.text: Jo borrowed the van [to move the chairs].
I grabbed a pencil [to draw a map].

child.play: Ask a partner why they did something today. Answer with "to" and a verb. Add "but it didn't work" to one answer.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Infinitival Purpose Adjunct." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/infinitival-purpose-adjunct-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Infinitival Relative Modifier
pattern: Nom + to-infinitival with an antecedent-linked gap

entry.name: Infinitival Relative Modifier
entry.pattern: Nom + to-infinitival with an antecedent-linked gap

1.definition: Characterizes a referent by a possible or appropriate action involving it.

examples.form: We need a bench [to sit on].

projection.target: The bench supplies the complement of on. The relative often has a modal reading and can differ from a purpose adjunct describing why a matrix action occurred.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A bench to sit on
curious.summary: A to plus a verb after a noun can describe the thing by what could be done with it, as in a bench to sit on.
curious.body: In We need a bench to sit on, the part to sit on describes the bench. It says what the bench is for or could be used for. The bench is the thing you'd sit on, so it fills the gap after on. The to part can have a sense of possibility or fitness. It differs from a purpose phrase, which tells why someone did something. We need a bench to sit on is about the bench, not about the reason for an action.

examples.text: We need a bench [to sit on].
She wants a book [to read on the train].

curious.try: Finish this sentence: I need something to ... What does the thing do for you?

teacher.summary: Covers noun phrases like a bench to sit on, where a to-infinitival modifies the noun.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a nominal followed by a to-infinitival with a gap linked to the antecedent. It characterizes a referent by a possible or appropriate action involving it. In We need a bench to sit on, the bench supplies the complement of on. The relative can have a modal reading, and it can differ from a purpose adjunct describing why a main-clause action occurred. This dictionary relates it to the integrated relative modifier and to the infinitival purpose adjunct, and marks it provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an infinitival relative clause or a to-infinitive modifying a noun.

examples.text: We need a bench [to sit on].
She wants a book [to read on the train].

contrasts.text: We need a bench to sit on.
contrasts.note: Describes the bench; the bench is what you sit on.

contrasts.text: Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs.
contrasts.note: A purpose phrase telling why the action happened.

watch_for: A learner might not notice that the bench is what fills the gap after on.
A learner might read to sit on as the reason for the needing rather than as a description of the bench.
teacher.activity: Students complete noun phrases such as a pen to ... and a box to ... and mark the gap where the noun would go in the verb phrase. They compare with a purpose sentence.

child.hook: What's a bench to sit on?
child.explain: To plus a verb can describe a thing by what you could do with it. A bench to sit on is a bench you could sit on. You sit on the bench.

examples.text: We need a bench [to sit on].
I found a rope [to climb on].

child.play: Pick something in the room. Describe it with to plus a verb, such as a chair to sit on. Can a partner guess it?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Infinitival Relative Modifier." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/infinitival-relative-modifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Infinitival of Subsequent Outcome

1.definition: Presents a later situation as an outcome or unexpected sequel.

examples.form: Jo opened the parcel [only to find it empty].

projection.target: The finding is presented as having occurred in the narrative. Expanding to in order to changes the reading to purpose.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Opening the parcel only to find it empty
curious.summary: A to plus a verb added after a clause can report what happened next, as an outcome or an unexpected sequel.
curious.body: In Jo opened the parcel only to find it empty, the part with to doesn't say why Jo opened the parcel. It reports a later event, the finding, as an outcome or an unexpected sequel. The finding is presented as having happened in the story. That separates it from a purpose phrase. If you expand it with in order to, the sentence is read as a purpose instead.

examples.text: Jo opened the parcel [only to find it empty].

curious.try: Say Jo opened the parcel only to find it empty. Then replace only to with in order to. Does the sentence now say why Jo opened it?

teacher.summary: Distinguishes a to-infinitival that reports a later outcome from one that gives a purpose.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause plus a supplementary to-infinitival. It presents a later situation as an outcome or unexpected sequel. In Jo opened the parcel only to find it empty, the finding is presented as having occurred in the narrative. Expanding to in order to changes the reading to purpose, so the expansion test separates the two uses. This construction sits beside the infinitival purpose adjunct, which presents a desired outcome whose realization isn't required. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an infinitive of result.

examples.text: Jo opened the parcel [only to find it empty].

contrasts.text: Jo opened the parcel only to find it empty.
contrasts.note: A later event reported as an outcome.

contrasts.text: Jo borrowed the van to move the chairs.
contrasts.note: A purpose; the moving need not happen.

watch_for: A learner might read only to find it empty as the reason Jo opened the parcel.
A learner might think the finding is a plan that may not have come true.
teacher.activity: Students write two-part stories with only to and a verb, then swap with a partner who says what happened next and whether it was expected.

checked.note: Audit: fixed curious.try, which compared the sentence with and without only (the entry's test is expansion to in order to). Also replaced This entry and The entry in teacher.explain, and cut resultative to-infinitive from teacher.terms (it could be confused with the resultative construction).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Infinitival of Subsequent Outcome." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/infinitival-result-adjunct-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Infinitival to Stranding

1.definition: Realizes an infinitival complement with overt to and a contextually recoverable predicate.

examples.form: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].

projection.target: To can remain in the position where the full infinitival would occur. The same speaker can recover go without substituting lexical do so.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Ending a sentence with to
curious.summary: After words like wanted, the word to can stand without a verb after it when the listener can work out what verb is meant.
curious.body: In I didn't go, but I wanted to, the sentence stops at to. You know the missing verb is go, because it was just mentioned. The to stays where a full phrase such as to go would have been. This lets a speaker avoid repeating a verb. It's a different way of recovering the meaning from using do so in its place.

examples.text: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].
She asked me to help, and I'm happy [to].

curious.try: Say I wanted to go, then say it again, dropping go. What does the listener supply?

teacher.summary: Explains to with an unexpressed verb phrase, as in I wanted to.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an infinitival complement realized with overt to and a contextually recoverable predicate. In I didn't go, but I wanted to, to stays in the position where the full infinitival would occur, and the listener recovers go from context. The same speaker can recover go without substituting lexical do so. This dictionary relates the pattern to the do so anaphor and marks it provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called VP ellipsis after to or a stranded to. This dictionary describes it as a to-infinitival with an unexpressed verb phrase.

examples.text: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].
She asked me to help, and I'm happy [to].

contrasts.text: I didn't go, but I wanted to.
contrasts.note: To stranded; go recovered from context.

contrasts.text: I didn't go, but I wanted to go.
contrasts.note: The full infinitival, verb expressed.

watch_for: A learner might think a sentence ending in to is unfinished.
A learner might look for a verb after to in the same clause rather than recovering it from context.
teacher.activity: Students read short exchanges with a stranded to and write what verb the listener recovers. They then repeat the exchange with the full infinitival.

child.hook: Can a sentence end with the word "to"?
child.explain: Sometimes a sentence ends with to, and you still know the verb. I didn't go, but I wanted to. You know the missing word is go.

examples.text: I didn’t go, but I [wanted to].
Mia asked me to play, and I [wanted to].

child.play: Tell a partner something you didn't do but wanted to, like I didn't swim, but I wanted to. Stop after to. Can your partner say the missing verb?

checked.note: Fixed: child game rewritten as one concrete step (say something you didn't do but wanted to, stopping at to, with an example that gives the partner the verb). Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary' in teacher text.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Infinitival to Stranding." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/infinitival-to-stranding-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Instrumental with-PP
pattern: PP[with + instrument NP] as an adjunct

entry.name: Instrumental with-PP
entry.pattern: PP[with + instrument NP] as an adjunct

1.definition: Identifies an object that mediates or enables an action.

examples.form: Lee opened the case [with a small screwdriver].

projection.target: A screwdriver has a means role here. With the watchman can instead identify an accompanying participant under a distinct interpretation.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Doing something with a tool
curious.summary: A phrase with with and a thing can name what was used to do something.
curious.body: In Lee opened the case with a small screwdriver, the phrase with a small screwdriver names what Lee used. The screwdriver helped the action happen. The same words with can introduce someone who came along, as in with the watchman. That's a different meaning, so the sentence around it matters.

examples.text: Lee opened the case [with a small screwdriver].
She stirred the soup [with a wooden spoon].

curious.try: Say Lee opened the case with a screwdriver, then Lee opened the case with the watchman. How does the meaning of with change?

teacher.summary: Covers with plus a noun phrase naming the instrument used in an action.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a prepositional phrase of with plus an instrument noun phrase, used as an adjunct. It identifies an object that mediates or enables an action: in Lee opened the case with a small screwdriver, the screwdriver has a means role. With the watchman can instead identify an accompanying participant, which is a distinct interpretation. This dictionary treats the phrase as a specialization of the prepositional phrase and relates it to by plus gerund means phrases. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditionally called an adverbial of instrument. This dictionary treats it as an adjunct prepositional phrase.

examples.text: Lee opened the case [with a small screwdriver].
She stirred the soup [with a wooden spoon].

contrasts.text: Lee opened the case with a small screwdriver.
contrasts.note: The with-phrase names the means.

contrasts.text: Lee opened the case with the watchman.
contrasts.note: Can identify an accompanying participant.

watch_for: A learner might read with the watchman as naming a tool.
A learner might think every with-phrase names an accompanying person.
teacher.activity: Students ask How did you do it? about classroom actions and answer with with plus a tool. They then replace the tool with a person and discuss how the meaning shifts.

child.hook: What do you use to do things, and how do you say it?
child.explain: With can name a tool you used. Lee opened the case with a small screwdriver. The screwdriver is what helped him do it.

examples.text: Lee opened the case [with a small screwdriver].
I drew the picture [with a blue pen].

child.play: Act out a job without saying the tool. A partner says what you did, ending with the tool, such as "with a spoon."

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Instrumental with-PP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/instrumental-with-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Integrated Relative Modifier
pattern: Nominal[... antecedent ... + relative clause containing a linked gap]

entry.name: Integrated Relative Modifier
entry.pattern: Nominal[... antecedent ... + relative clause containing a linked gap]

1.definition: Adds a clause to the nominal description of a referent or set of referents.
1.details: A nominal containing a relative can describe a subset, as with the books Kim bought. It can also add a property of a referent already uniquely identified. Wh-marking, that, and bare forms can package the link. Bare finite relatives generally permit an object gap but exclude a gap in the subject position of the relative clause itself.

examples.form: The books [that Kim bought] are on the desk.
examples.note: Constructed object relative. The books Kim bought has a bare variant.

examples.form: The books [that arrived today] are on the desk.
examples.note: Constructed subject relative. Omitting that here does not give the same integrated NP.

relatedConstructions.notes: The relative is a dependent within a nominal.
One form registers the relative link with a relative word.
A fused relative can form an NP without a separately expressed antecedent.

In the books that arrived, the integrated clause helps identify the books. In The books, which arrived yesterday, are upstairs, the supplementary clause adds a separate comment on a referent already supplied.

grounds.note: Records relative postmodification.
Distinguishes the types and documents the conditions on bare relatives.

projection.target: An integrated relative can be bare with a close object gap but normally needs a marker with a gap as its immediate subject. Restriction of reference is a frequent interpretation.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes integration from semantic restriction and limits the omission generalization to the relevant gap configuration. CASA supplies the relative-postmodifier frame.

curious.title: The books that Kim bought
curious.summary: A clause can be attached to a noun to help say which things you mean, as in the books that Kim bought.
curious.body: In The books that Kim bought are on the desk, the part that Kim bought is joined directly to books. It helps pick out which books: the ones Kim bought. The word that can be left out here, giving the books Kim bought. Other cases need the marker. In The books that arrived today are on the desk, the books themselves are what arrived, and omitting that doesn't give the same kind of phrase. A relative clause can also add a fact about something already identified, so it needn't narrow things down.

examples.text: The books [that Kim bought] are on the desk.
The books [that arrived today] are on the desk.

curious.try: Say The books Kim bought are on the desk. Now try leaving that out of The books that arrived today. What changes?

teacher.summary: Explains relative clauses that are part of a noun phrase and help identify its referent.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a nominal containing an antecedent plus a relative clause with a linked gap. It can describe a subset, as in the books Kim bought, or add a property of a referent already uniquely identified. Wh-marking, that and bare forms can package the link. Bare finite relatives generally permit an object gap but exclude a gap in the subject position of the relative clause itself. So an integrated relative can be bare with a close object gap but normally needs a marker when the gap is its immediate subject. Restriction of reference is a frequent interpretation. This contrasts with the supplementary relative, as in The books, which arrived yesterday, are upstairs. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditionally called a restrictive relative clause. This dictionary says integrated, since integration is distinct from semantic restriction, and calls the other kind supplementary (traditionally non-restrictive).

examples.text: The books [that Kim bought] are on the desk.
The books [that arrived today] are on the desk.

contrasts.text: The books that arrived today are on the desk.
contrasts.note: Integrated, the relative helps identify the books.

contrasts.text: The books, which arrived yesterday, are upstairs.
contrasts.note: Supplementary, a separate comment on books already supplied.

watch_for: A learner might think that must appear in every relative clause, though the books Kim bought is given as a variant.
A learner might think every relative clause narrows down the referent, though this dictionary says one can also add a property of a referent already uniquely identified.
teacher.activity: Students rewrite pairs of sentences into one noun phrase with a relative clause, and test which can drop that. They then compare with a comma version using which.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Integrated Relative Modifier." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/integrated-relative-modifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Intensifying to death

1.definition: Intensifies an action or the experience it causes.
1.details: In the dog scared me to death, to death conventionally expresses extreme fright. With a killing verb or an appropriate context, the same phrase instead identifies a literal result. A literal outcome and an intensified experience can thus differ without a change in surface order.

examples.form: The alarm [scared me to death], but everyone was fine.
examples.note: Constructed context selects the degree interpretation.

examples.form: The fox [bit the hare to death].
examples.note: Constructed comparison with a fatal outcome.

relatedConstructions.notes: The literal construction presents death as an achieved result.
The figurative use locates the experience high on an intensity scale.

grounds.note: Distinguishes intensity, stimulating emotion and a literal killing outcome.

projection.target: A later report of survival is compatible with the emotional intensity reading. The same continuation contradicts the literal outcome reading.
projection.evidence: Birmingham distinguishes a general intensifier entry, its emotional subtype and a literal killing construction. The continuation tests make the difference assessable.

curious.title: Scared to death, but fine
curious.summary: The words to death after a verb can mean extreme feeling, as in scared me to death, or a literal fatal outcome, depending on the verb and the context.
curious.body: In The alarm scared me to death, but everyone was fine, to death expresses extreme fright. Nobody died. The continuation about everyone being fine fits that reading. With a killing verb, the same words identify a literal result, as in The fox bit the hare to death. The word order is the same in both. A later report of survival fits the extreme-feeling reading and contradicts the literal one.

examples.text: The alarm [scared me to death], but everyone was fine.
The fox [bit the hare to death].

curious.try: Add but I'm fine to the end of The dog scared me to death. Does it still make sense? Now compare The fox bit the hare to death. What does that sentence say happened to the hare?

teacher.summary: Distinguishes figurative to death as an intensifier from literal to death as a fatal result.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb, optionally an object, and to death. It intensifies an action or the experience it causes. In The dog scared me to death, to death conventionally expresses extreme fright. With a killing verb or an appropriate context, the same phrase identifies a literal result, as in The fox bit the hare to death. The two readings can differ without any change in surface order. A later report of survival is compatible with the emotional intensity reading and contradicts the literal outcome reading, which makes a useful classroom test. This dictionary relates the literal use to object resultatives and the figurative use to degree, and marks itself provisional.
teacher.terms: The figurative use is sometimes described as an intensifier. The literal use is related to the object resultative construction, which presents death as an achieved result.

examples.text: The alarm [scared me to death], but everyone was fine.
The fox [bit the hare to death].

contrasts.text: The alarm scared me to death, but everyone was fine.
contrasts.note: Extreme fright; survival is compatible.

contrasts.text: The fox bit the hare to death.
contrasts.note: A literal fatal outcome.

watch_for: A learner might read scared me to death as reporting that someone died.
A learner might assume the figurative and literal uses differ in word order.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences ending in to death into extreme feeling and literal outcome. They test each by adding a later report that the one said to have died was fine, and checking whether it fits.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.try and teacher.activity now test survival of the one said to have died (the hare), not the narrator or everyone; removed the 'hyperbolic phrase' gloss and tied the literal use to the object resultative, as the entry relates them; replaced 'the entry' with this dictionary.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Intensifying to death." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/intensifying-to-death-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Interrogative Sluicing
pattern: interrogative XP with the remaining clause unexpressed

entry.name: Interrogative Sluicing
entry.pattern: interrogative XP with the remaining clause unexpressed

1.definition: Recovers a question with only the questioned part overt.

examples.form: Someone moved the keys, but I don’t know [who].

grounds.locator: discussion of clause-level ellipsis in Construction Grammar

projection.target: The mover role can be recovered from the preceding clause. A more explicit interrogative XP such as which person can likewise remain overt.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: I don't know who
curious.summary: A question can be reduced to its question word when the rest can be recovered from what came before.
curious.body: In Someone moved the keys, but I don't know who, the word who stands for the whole question who moved the keys. The first part of the sentence supplies what's missing. A longer question phrase can stay too, as in which person. Only the part being asked about is spoken, and the listener fills in the rest.

examples.text: Someone moved the keys, but I don’t know [who].
Mia left early, but I don't know [why].

curious.try: Complete this: Someone called me, but I don't know... What does the listener understand you left out?

teacher.summary: Explains reduced questions that keep only the question phrase, as in I don't know who.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an interrogative phrase with the rest of the clause unexpressed. It recovers a question with only the questioned part overt. In Someone moved the keys, but I don't know who, the mover role is recovered from the preceding clause. A more explicit interrogative phrase such as which person can likewise remain overt. This dictionary relates the pattern to open interrogative clauses and cites CGEL and Goldberg and Perek (2019). It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Sluicing is the standard name in the linguistics literature. Some textbooks call this a reduced or elliptical wh-question.

examples.text: Someone moved the keys, but I don’t know [who].
Mia left early, but I don't know [why].

contrasts.text: Someone moved the keys, but I don't know who.
contrasts.note: Only the question word is overt.

contrasts.text: Someone moved the keys, but I don't know who moved the keys.
contrasts.note: The full question, spelled out.

watch_for: A learner might think I don't know who is incomplete.
A learner might not see that the earlier clause supplies the missing part of the question.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences that begin with someone or something, then add but I don't know followed by a question word. They write out the full question each one stands for.

child.hook: What does "I don't know who" leave out?
child.explain: Sometimes you say only the question word. Someone moved the keys, but I don't know who. You and your listener both know the rest: who moved the keys.

examples.text: Someone moved the keys, but I don’t know [who].
Mia left early, but I don't know [why].

child.play: Say "Someone took my pencil, but I don't know" and stop at the question word. Can a partner say the whole question?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Interrogative Sluicing." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/interrogative-sluicing-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Interrogative Use of Indeterminates

dimensions.form: Full indeterminate series; non-subject interrogative phrases are normally fronted, while interrogative subjects remain in basic position and echoes may remain in situ
dimensions.meaning: The open variable is packaged as a request for its value
dimensions.function: Marks the focus of the question; question-answer congruence
dimensions.distribution: Main and subordinate open interrogatives; main-clause inversion follows a fronted non-subject, while subordinate interrogatives and interrogative subjects normally retain subject–verb order

1.definition: Asks for the value of the indeterminate's open variable, constraining its sort
1.details: All members of the indeterminate series participate in this packaging

examples.note: Interrogative subject in basic subject position; no subject–auxiliary inversion

constraints.description: The interrogative property percolates from the indeterminate to its phrase and clause. Non-subject phrases are normally fronted and trigger subject–auxiliary inversion in main clauses; subjects are not fronted, subordinate clauses normally do not invert, and echoes may leave the phrase in situ.

relatedConstructions.notes: Variable echoes may use similar forms in situ but preserve the stimulus's independently determined clause type
Interrogative words mark headed open-interrogative Clauses through upward percolation
Interrogative words contribute variables to open-question semantics
An interrogative phrase can form a non-headed question construction without instantiating Clause
Deitality diagnostics are largely undefined for fronted interrogatives (clause-type dependent)

projection.target: In Whose coat did Jo borrow?, the whole phrase whose coat fronts while whose supplies the open variable for the possessor. With an interrogative subject, Who left? has no corresponding auxiliary inversion.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates the interrogative feature of a word from that of its containing phrase and tests subject versus non-subject distributions.

curious.title: Question words
curious.summary: Who, what, where, when, why, how and their relatives mark a question by asking for the missing piece of information.
curious.body: A question word asks for the value of something left open. Whose book asks about the owner, and Who came asks about a person. Each word limits what kind of answer fits: a person, a place, a time. Question words normally come first in the question, as in Whose coat did Jo borrow? When the question word is the subject, as in Who left?, it stays in its usual place and the verb needn't move. A question inside a longer sentence, such as I wonder where she went, keeps ordinary word order.
curious.try: Turn Jo borrowed the red coat into a question about the colour, then into a question about whose coat it was. Where did your question word end up?

teacher.summary: Covers wh-words used to ask questions, including where they go and whether the verb moves.
teacher.explain: In this packaging, a member of the indeterminate series asks for the value of its open variable, constraining its sort. The interrogative property passes from the word to its phrase and clause. Non-subject phrases are normally fronted and trigger subject-auxiliary inversion in main clauses. Subjects are not fronted, so Who left? has no inversion, and subordinate interrogatives normally keep subject-verb order, as in I wonder where she went. In Whose coat did Jo borrow?, the whole phrase whose coat fronts while whose supplies the open variable for the possessor. Echo questions may leave the phrase in its original position. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditionally called wh-words or interrogative pronouns, adverbs and determiners. This dictionary groups them as interrogative uses of the indeterminate series.

contrasts.note: A fronted non-subject phrase; subject and auxiliary swap places.
Interrogative subject; no inversion.

watch_for: A learner might invert the subject and verb in Who left?
A learner might invert in the subordinate question I wonder where she went.
teacher.activity: Students turn statements into questions about each part, then sort them by whether the question word is the subject, and note when the verb order changes.

child.hook: What do question words ask for?
child.explain: Question words ask for the missing piece. Who asks about a person. Where asks about a place. The question word normally comes first.
child.play: Pick a sentence like "Jo borrowed a coat." Ask a question about each part of it, using who, what or whose. What would each answer be?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Interrogative Use of Indeterminates." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/interrogative-word-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: into-Causative
pattern: VP[Head:V + Od:NPᵢ + Comp:PP[into + gerund-participial Clause with understood subjectᵢ]]

entry.name: into-Causative
entry.pattern: VP[Head:V + Od:NPᵢ + Comp:PP[into + gerund-participial Clause with understood subjectᵢ]]

1.definition: Presents the object’s action or change of mental state as a result of what the matrix verb describes.
1.details: In talk someone into leaving, talk supplies a means and the object supplies the understood subject of leaving. The pattern can give an otherwise intransitive use of a verb an object. The result inference concerns an affirmative, completed instance. A conditional, an attempt or negation can suspend it. Into followed by a locative NP can have the distinct caused-motion interpretation.

examples.note: BNC example. He is both the affected participant and the understood subject of going.

grounds.locator: V n into -ing, example with talk

examples.note: Constructed extension. The laughter can be understood as the means by which he was induced to join.

relatedConstructions.notes: Causation is expressed through the object and into-phrase inside the VP.
Both pair an object with an endpoint. Here the endpoint is a situation expressed by a gerund-participial clause.
Both can license an object to which the result applies.

grounds.note: Describes the object and into-phrase in one pattern.
Investigates verb choice, innovative uses and the relation to caused-motion and resultative constructions.

projection.target: The postverbal NP supplies the participant who carries out or experiences the result expressed after into, even with verbs that do not ordinarily take that object.
projection.evidence: The CASA and Hunston inventories document diverse verbs. Kim and Davies use corpus evidence to distinguish this form from literal caused motion and related frames.

curious.title: Talking someone into going
curious.summary: A verb, a person and into plus an -ing verb can say how someone was brought to do something.
curious.body: In talked him into going to London, talking is the means, and him is the person who ends up going. He's both the one affected and the one doing the going. The same pattern works with other verbs. In They laughed him into joining in, the laughter is understood as the means by which he was induced to join. The result is claimed only for an actual completed case. A conditional, an attempt or a negation can suspend it. Into followed by a place, by contrast, describes movement.
curious.try: Say She talked him into going. Who goes? Now say She tried to talk him into going. Did he go?

teacher.summary: Covers verb plus object plus into plus a gerund-participial clause, as in talked him into going.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb, an object, and a prepositional phrase with into plus a gerund-participial clause whose understood subject is the object. It presents the object's action or change of mental state as a result of what the matrix verb describes. In talked him into going to London, talk supplies a means and him supplies the understood subject of going. The pattern can give an otherwise intransitive use of a verb an object. The result inference concerns an affirmative, completed instance; a conditional, an attempt or negation can suspend it. Into followed by a locative noun phrase can have the distinct caused-motion interpretation. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: No widely used traditional name is given in this dictionary. It is related to caused-motion and object resultative constructions.

contrasts.text: talked him into going to London
contrasts.note: Into plus a gerund-participial clause; him is the understood subject of going.

contrasts.text: They pushed the cart into the barn.
contrasts.note: Into plus a place; caused motion.

watch_for: A learner might read talked him into going as saying that he talked.
A learner might take She tried to talk him into going to mean that he went.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with a verb, a person and into plus -ing. They then add a conditional, an attempt or a negative and discuss whether the result still follows.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "into-Causative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/into-causative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Intransitive Preposition Use

dimensions.form: Preposition heading a PP without an NP object; it may be complementless or take a PP, clause, or predicative complement
dimensions.meaning: Varies with the head and complement: location, direction, time, reason, comparison, and other relations
dimensions.function: Heads an intransitive PP in complement, modifier, adjunct, or predicative function
dimensions.distribution: The full CGEL objectless class; complementless locative members occupy the same PP positions as full locative PPs

1.definition: A preposition used without an NP object, whether or not it has another kind of complement
1.details: Intransitive means no object, not no complement. A complementless member such as outside heads a one-word PP, but an intransitive preposition may instead take a PP complement (owing to the rain), a predicative complement (as satisfactory), or a clause complement (because it rained). Ago is intransitive-only and occurs with an obligatory pre-head measure modifier (ten years ago; cf. ten years before Christ). The category remains preposition throughout (CGEL p. 272); the analysis of ago deliberately rejects CGEL p. 632.

examples.note: Complementless intransitive use; the same lexeme also has transitive outside the door
Intransitive preposition with a PP complement
Intransitive preposition with a predicative complement
Intransitive preposition with a clause complement
Intransitive-only, with an obligatory pre-head measure modifier (*I went ago); the measure phrase is a modifier, not a complement (cf. ten years before Christ)
Complementless intransitive preposition heading a one-word PP in particle use

constraints.description: The head has no NP object in this use; the presence of a non-object complement does not make the PP transitive.
Within the complementless locative subset, right/straight modification and from-embedding help distinguish PPs from AdvPs (right outside, straight home, from abroad).

projection.target: Outside can occur alone in We waited outside or with a complement in We waited outside the gate. The ability to say from outside supplies a test beyond merely counting overt NP complements.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes intransitive uses and documents PP embedding by from and other prepositions.

curious.title: Prepositions with no object
curious.summary: Some prepositions can do their job without a noun phrase after them, as outside does in She waited outside.
curious.body: Take in the garden: the preposition in has an object, the garden. But in She waited outside, outside stands alone. It has no object, yet it's still the same kind of word, a preposition. No object doesn't mean nothing follows. A preposition can take a phrase, as in owing to the rain, a description, as in as satisfactory, or a whole clause, as in because it rained. What it lacks is a noun phrase object.
curious.try: Say We waited outside and We waited outside the gate. What does the gate add?

teacher.summary: Explains that prepositions can be intransitive, lacking an object, without lacking a complement.
teacher.explain: Intransitive here means no object, not no complement. A preposition without an NP object can be complementless, as in outside, or can take a PP complement (owing to the rain), a predicative complement (as satisfactory), or a clause complement (because it rained). The category remains preposition throughout. The PP can function as complement, modifier, adjunct or predicative. For complementless locative members such as outside, right or straight modification and from-embedding help distinguish PPs from adverb phrases: right outside, straight home, from abroad. This dictionary gives ago as intransitive-only, with an obligatory pre-head measure modifier, as in ten years ago. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: A word like outside in this use is sometimes called an adverb. CGEL, and this dictionary, treat them as prepositions heading PPs without an object.

contrasts.note: No object.
The same word with a noun phrase object.

watch_for: A learner might think a preposition must be followed by a noun phrase.
A learner might read no object as meaning no complement, when to the rain (after owing) and it rained (after because) are complements.
teacher.activity: Students list prepositions from a text and sort each use by whether a noun phrase object follows. They then find uses with a PP, predicative or clause complement.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body now separates the preposition in from the phrase in the garden; teacher.watch_for names the complements as to the rain and it rained, not the strings with the prepositions. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Intransitive Preposition Use." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/intransitive-preposition-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Inverted Conditional
pattern: conditional Clause[had, were, or should + Subject + residual predicate]

entry.name: Inverted Conditional
entry.pattern: conditional Clause[had, were, or should + Subject + residual predicate]

1.definition: Introduces a condition through auxiliary–subject order without if.
1.details: Had you known corresponds to If you had known. Were and should license the same order in their own conditional uses. Other auxiliaries do not freely enter this frame. In the central standard pattern the negative is separate, as in Had you not called.

examples.form: [Had you called], we could have picked you up.
[Should you need help], call this number.
[Were I in charge], I would change it.

relatedConstructions.notes: An if-clause can supply an equivalent condition in ordinary order.
The same auxiliary–subject order can express a question, with a wider range of auxiliaries.
Had Jo known introduces a condition without if. Never had Jo seen it uses the same auxiliary–subject order in a clause with a preposed negative expression.

grounds.note: Distinguishes conditional from other auxiliary-initial clauses.
Compares interrogative and inverted conditional uses and records marginal historical or literary forms.

projection.target: The inverted conditional is restricted to a small set of auxiliaries. Substituting an ordinary modal such as would fails to preserve the construction.
projection.evidence: FrameNet identifies the auxiliary restriction and compares conditional inversion with interrogative uses of the same order. CGEL records the core restriction and rare literary extensions.

curious.title: Conditions without if
curious.summary: Putting had, were or should before the subject can set up a condition without using if.
curious.body: Had you called, we could have picked you up corresponds to If you had called, we could have picked you up. The auxiliary comes before the subject, and if drops out. Were and should work the same way, as in Were I in charge, I would change it and Should you need help, call this number. Other auxiliaries don't freely enter this frame. In the central standard pattern the negative comes after the subject, as in Had you not called.

examples.text: [Had you called], we could have picked you up.
[Should you need help], call this number.
[Were I in charge], I would change it.

curious.try: Rewrite If you had known, I'd have told you without if. Which word moves, and where does it go?

teacher.summary: Covers had/were/should plus subject conditionals such as Had you called, an alternative to if.
teacher.explain: The pattern introduces a condition through auxiliary-subject order without if. Had you known corresponds to If you had known, and were and should license the same order in their own conditional uses. Other auxiliaries don't freely enter this frame, and substituting an ordinary modal such as would fails to preserve the construction. In the central standard pattern the negative is separate, as in Had you not called. The same order can express a question, with a wider range of auxiliaries. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called conditional inversion. This dictionary treats the order as the same auxiliary-subject order seen in closed interrogatives.

examples.text: [Had you called], we could have picked you up.
[Should you need help], call this number.
[Were I in charge], I would change it.

contrasts.text: If you had called, we could have picked you up.
contrasts.note: Ordinary order with if.

contrasts.text: Had you called, we could have picked you up.
contrasts.note: Auxiliary before subject, no if.

watch_for: A learner might think any auxiliary or modal can start such a clause.
A learner might confuse Had you called with a question, since the word order is the same.
teacher.activity: Students rewrite if-conditionals with had, were and should, then try rewriting one with another auxiliary and discuss what the dictionary says about that.

checked.note: Fixed: removed 'formal' from the teacher summary (this dictionary assigns no register to the pattern). Also fixed (unflagged): cut the term 'if-less conditional', which this dictionary does not use; 'the entry' wording; curious body now says the sentence corresponds to the if-version, as this dictionary does.

name: Irrealis were
pattern: Clause[1sg/3sg Subject + were] in selected remote environments

entry.name: Irrealis were
entry.pattern: Clause[1sg/3sg Subject + were] in selected remote environments

1.definition: Realizes a distinct irrealis form of be in the first or third person singular.

projection.target: Remote if may also have was for many speakers. The matrix-like were in Were I taller is licensed under inversion, where replacing it by was fails in standard usage.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: I wish I were taller
curious.summary: In some wishing and imagining sentences, a form of be, were, appears with I or with he, she or it.
curious.body: In I wish I were taller, were is the form of be used with I. The sentence is about something that isn't the case. This distinct form is called irrealis, and it shows up in the first and third person singular. With remote if, was may also be used by many speakers. But in Were I taller, where were comes before the subject, was fails in standard usage.

examples.text: [Were I taller], I'd reach the shelf.

curious.try: Say I wish I were taller. Then think of another wish beginning I wish she... Which form of be fits?

teacher.summary: Explains the irrealis were that remains in first and third person singular clauses.
teacher.explain: This dictionary treats were as a distinct irrealis form of be, realized in the first or third person singular in selected remote environments, as in I wish I were taller. Remote if may also have was, for many speakers. The matrix-like were in Were I taller is licensed under inversion, where replacing it by was fails in standard usage. It relates this to if-conditionals and to the inverted conditional, and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the subjunctive were. This dictionary calls it a distinct irrealis form of be.

examples.text: [Were I taller], I'd reach the shelf.

contrasts.note: Irrealis were with I.

contrasts.text: If I were taller, I'd reach the shelf.
contrasts.note: Remote if; was may also occur.

watch_for: A learner might think were is plural-only and cannot be used with I.
A learner might be unsure which of were and was to use after remote if.
teacher.activity: Students complete I wish... and If I... sentences about things that aren't so. They underline the form of be and compare it with the plain past in real past-time sentences.

child.hook: How could you finish the wish "I wish I were ..."?
child.explain: Sometimes we say were with I. I wish I were taller. It's a wish about something that isn't true right now.
child.play: Make wishes that start with I wish I were. Then say what you'd do if the wish came true.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms no longer claims a dictionary-wide naming policy about mood; child.hook no longer implies was after I wish is avoided (the entry's only negative judgment about was concerns inversion); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Irrealis were." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/irrealis-were-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Vowel Alternation in Irregular Verb Inflection
pattern: selected verb stems with present, preterite and participial vowel alternants

entry.name: Vowel Alternation in Irregular Verb Inflection
entry.pattern: selected verb stems with present, preterite and participial vowel alternants

1.definition: Distinguishes verbal inflectional forms through lexicalized changes in the stem vowel.

examples.form: Jo [sang] yesterday and has [sung] twice today.

relatedConstructions.notes: The perfect selects the past participle, here sung.

projection.target: Sang and sung correspond to different slots for this verb. Other verbs can share one form across those slots, so the exact mapping is lexical.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Sing, sang, sung
curious.summary: Some verbs show different forms by changing the vowel inside the word, and the changes belong to each verb.
curious.body: In Jo sang yesterday and has sung twice today, the vowel in the middle of the word changes: sing, sang, sung. Each form fills a different slot. Sang is the past form, and sung is the form that goes after has. Other verbs can use one form for more than one slot, so the exact pattern belongs to each verb individually.

examples.text: Jo [sang] yesterday and has [sung] twice today.

curious.try: Say Jo sings today, Jo sang yesterday, Jo has sung. Which vowel changes at each step?

teacher.summary: Covers verbs whose past and participle forms are marked by a stem vowel change, as in sing, sang, sung.
teacher.explain: This dictionary describes selected verb stems with present, preterite and participial vowel alternants. The changes are lexicalized and distinguish verbal inflectional forms. For sing, sang and sung correspond to different slots. The perfect selects the past participle, here sung. Other verbs can share one form across those slots, so the exact mapping is lexical, and each verb has to be learned. This dictionary relates the pattern to regular -ed past tense and to the perfect with have. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars sometimes call these strong verbs, a label that may be broader than this pattern, and ablaut is a textbook word for stem-vowel change of this kind. This dictionary calls the pattern vowel alternation in irregular verb inflection.

examples.text: Jo [sang] yesterday and has [sung] twice today.

contrasts.note: The preterite form.
The past participle after has.

watch_for: A learner might mix up which of sang and sung fills which slot.
A learner might expect every verb to add -ed for its past.
teacher.activity: Students list verbs with a vowel change and write each in a pair of sentences, one with the past form and one with has and the participle. They note any verb that uses one form for both.

child.hook: What changes in the word sing when you say yesterday?
child.explain: Some words change their middle sound. Today I sing. Yesterday I sang. Today I have sung. Each word has its own pattern.

examples.text: Jo [sang] yesterday and has [sung] twice today.

child.play: Say sing, sang and sung with a partner. Find other words whose middle sound changes, and test each one.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher terms no longer claim the dictionary's title contains 'ablaut' (the title is 'Vowel Alternation in Irregular Verb Inflection'); strong verbs hedged as possibly broader; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; curious summary no longer says the vowel shows 'tense' alone (the entry says inflectional forms). Second round: fixed curious.body by cutting 'you can't predict the pattern from a rule' (this dictionary says only that the exact mapping is lexical).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Vowel Alternation in Irregular Verb Inflection." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/irregular-ablaut-verb-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Stem-Vowel Alternation in Noun Plurals
pattern: selected noun stem alternation, e.g. tooth ↔ teeth

entry.name: Stem-Vowel Alternation in Noun Plurals
entry.pattern: selected noun stem alternation, e.g. tooth ↔ teeth

1.definition: Realizes a lexical noun plural by internal vowel change.

examples.form: One tooth had broken and [two teeth] were loose.

projection.target: Plural agreement is expressed without ordinary -s. The pattern is confined to established pairs and does not productively pluralize arbitrarily similar nouns.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Plurals made by changing a vowel
curious.summary: A few English nouns make their plural by changing a vowel inside the word instead of adding an ending.
curious.body: The plural of tooth is teeth. Nothing is added at the end; the vowel inside the word changes. That's different from the ordinary plural, which adds an -s. The pattern is tied to particular words. It belongs to established pairs, such as tooth and teeth, and it doesn't turn just any similar-looking noun into a plural. To use it, you have to know the pair. This dictionary lists two related entries, one for the ordinary -s plural and one for nouns whose plural looks the same as the singular.

examples.text: One tooth had broken and [two teeth] were loose.

curious.try: Say the plural of tooth out loud. What changed inside the word, and what stayed the same?

teacher.summary: Useful when learners meet plurals that don't take -s, and need to see that these come as fixed pairs.
teacher.explain: Some nouns realize the plural by changing the stem vowel (tooth, teeth), not by adding the ordinary -s. This dictionary treats this as a pattern confined to selected, established pairs. It doesn't productively pluralize arbitrary nouns that resemble them. So the practical message is that each pair is learned as a pair. It helps to teach the vowel-change plural beside the ordinary -s plural and the zero plural (where singular and plural look alike), since this dictionary treats all three as related.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an irregular plural. In this dictionary the pattern is a stem-vowel alternation in a noun plural, related to the ordinary -s plural and to the zero plural.

examples.text: One tooth had broken and [two teeth] were loose.
