contrasts.text: One tooth had broken and two teeth were loose.
contrasts.note: Singular and plural differ by the vowel inside the word, with no -s.

watch_for: A learner might add the ordinary -s ending to a noun that already forms its plural by vowel change.
A learner might apply the vowel change to other nouns that look similar, when the pattern is confined to established pairs.
teacher.activity: Put singular-plural pairs on cards, some with -s, some with a vowel change and some where the two forms look the same. Students sort the cards into three piles and say each pair aloud in a sentence.

child.hook: How do you say more than one tooth?
child.explain: One tooth, two teeth. The word doesn't get an s at the end. The middle of the word changes instead. Only some words do this.

examples.text: One tooth was loose and [two teeth] were sore.

child.play: Say one tooth, then two teeth. Listen for the part that changes. Then think of other words that change in the middle when there's more than one. Ask a grown-up whether you found any.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Stem-Vowel Alternation in Noun Plurals." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/irregular-vowel-plural-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Clitic it’s in Auxiliary Uses

1.definition: Realizes a reduced auxiliary on the pronoun it.

relatedConstructions.notes: The following participial form helps determine the contracted auxiliary.

projection.target: The host and following participial environment distinguish has in It’s been repaired from is in It’s being repaired. Genitive its instead combines with a nominal in its ordinary dependent use.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: The 's in it's can stand for is or has
curious.summary: The short form it's can mean it is or it has, and a participle after it, such as been or being, can show which.
curious.body: The 's in It's been repaired stands for has, so it means It has been repaired. The 's in It's being repaired stands for is, so it means It is being repaired. The participle after the 's, been or being, helps you work out which one it is. Don't confuse either of these with its, the word that goes before a noun to show belonging. It has no apostrophe and doesn't stand for is or has.
curious.try: Say It's been repaired and It's being repaired, then say each one in full. Which short word did you put back in each?

teacher.summary: Helps learners decide whether 's after it is is or has, and keep it's apart from its.
teacher.explain: After the pronoun it, 's can be a reduced auxiliary, either is or has. The host (it) and the participial form that follows together distinguish them. A following participle such as been signals has (It’s been repaired), while being signals is (It’s being repaired). The genitive its is different: it combines with a nominal in its ordinary dependent use and isn't a reduced auxiliary. The analysis is marked provisional and rests on two cited CGEL sections and a constructed illustration, so keep the explanation to these two contrasts.
teacher.terms: Contraction of is or has. In this dictionary, a clitic: a reduced auxiliary attached to it. The genitive its is a separate word.

contrasts.note: The 's is has, because been follows.
The 's is is, because being follows.

watch_for: A learner might read the 's in It's been repaired as is, when the following participle signals has.
A learner might write it's where the genitive its belongs, though only its combines with a following noun as a dependent.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with it's followed by different forms. They expand each 's to is or has, circle the participle (been or being) that told them where there is one, and then add one sentence using the genitive its.

child.hook: What two words can hide inside it's?
child.explain: It's can be short for it is or for it has. Words like been and being can show which. It's been repaired means it has been repaired. It's being repaired means it is being repaired.
child.play: Say each example, then say it again with the short word spelled out in full. Look at been or being after it's. Does it help you choose between is and has?

checked.note: Fixed: removed the claim that the following word always settles is versus has (the entry gives the been/being contrast only); activity and child text limited to participles such as been and being; 'short discussion in CGEL' replaced by what the entry cites. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Clitic it’s in Auxiliary Uses." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/it-auxiliary-clitic-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: it-Cleft
pattern: Clause[Subject:it + be + PredComp:XP + cleft relative Clause]

entry.name: it-Cleft
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:it + be + PredComp:XP + cleft relative Clause]

1.definition: Specifies the value of a variable whose descriptive content is supplied by the cleft relative.
1.details: In it was Kim who was sacked, Kim supplies the value and the relative sets out the background proposition that somebody was sacked. This packaging can present new information as background. The position after be marks grammatical foregrounding. Main stress can fall inside the relative instead. CGEL distinguishes this structure from a referential it with an integrated relative inside an NP, using contexts where the surface wording is the same.

examples.form: [It was peace and quiet that he wanted most.]
[It was to Boston that I flew.]
examples.note: A PP can occupy the foregrounded slot.

examples.form: [It wasn’t Kim who took the keys.]
examples.note: Constructed. The denial normally targets Kim’s identification, with somebody’s taking the keys treated as background.

relatedConstructions.notes: The construction is headed by a VP in a matrix clause.
The cleft relative can be marked by a relative word; that and zero relatives also occur.
It was Jo who opened the window identifies the focused value. It was surprising that Jo opened the window places the content of the evaluation after the predicate.

grounds.note: Distinguishes foregrounded syntax, discourse availability of the presupposition, and accent.
Documents the cleft frame across foregrounded phrase types.

projection.target: The relative supplies a background proposition and the post-be phrase provides a value. In an ordinary identifying context, negating the identification can leave that background proposition in place.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s integrated-relative contrast and two kinds of presupposition. CASA documents different foregrounded phrase types.

curious.title: Putting one phrase in the spotlight with it was
curious.summary: A sentence can start with it was and a phrase, then a clause that sets out the background.
curious.body: In It was Kim who was sacked, the sentence picks out Kim as the person who was sacked. The part after Kim, who was sacked, sets out the background: somebody was sacked. This way of packaging a sentence can present new information as if it were background. The phrase in the spotlight comes right after was. It isn't limited to a person. It can be a noun phrase like peace and quiet, or a phrase such as to Boston. If you deny the sentence, as in It wasn't Kim who took the keys, you normally reject only the claim about Kim. In a context like this, the background, that somebody took the keys, can stay in place.

examples.text: [It was peace and quiet that he wanted most.]
[It was to Boston that I flew.]
[It wasn’t Kim who took the keys.]

curious.try: Take a plain sentence such as Kim was sacked. Which word would you spotlight to start a sentence with it was?

teacher.summary: Useful for advanced learners who need to see how it was lets a speaker foreground one phrase and treat the rest as background.
teacher.explain: An it-cleft has it as subject, a form of be, a foregrounded phrase, and a cleft relative. The foregrounded phrase supplies a value; the relative supplies the descriptive content of a variable, so in It was Kim who was sacked, Kim is the value and somebody was sacked is the background. The phrase after be can be an NP or a PP, and the relative may be marked by who or another relative word, or by that or nothing. Negating the identification (It wasn’t Kim who took the keys) normally leaves the background in place. Compare subject extraposition, which doesn't foreground a value.
teacher.terms: Sometimes taught as a cleft sentence. In this dictionary: the it-cleft, with the phrase after be as the foregrounded element and the following clause as the cleft relative.

examples.text: [It was peace and quiet that he wanted most.]
[It was to Boston that I flew.]
[It wasn’t Kim who took the keys.]

contrasts.text: It was Jo who opened the window.
contrasts.note: Identifies the value, Jo, and treats the opening of the window as background.

contrasts.text: It was surprising that Jo opened the window.
contrasts.note: Subject extraposition, not a cleft. The content of the evaluation comes after the predicate.

watch_for: A learner might read the clause after the foregrounded phrase as a separate sentence, when it is the background part of the same sentence.
A learner might take a negated cleft to deny the whole event, when the denial normally targets the identification, as in It wasn't Kim who took the keys.
A learner might think only noun phrases can follow was, though a prepositional phrase such as to Boston can too.
teacher.activity: Give students a plain sentence such as Jo opened the window. They write two it-clefts, spotlighting a different phrase each time, then say which phrase each one picks out.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary no longer says the clause sets out what everyone already takes as background (the dictionary says the packaging can present new information as background); softened the negation sentence to say the background can stay in place in an ordinary identifying context; reworded 'answer to a question' / 'what question each one answers' as picking out the value. Second round: fixed teacher.activity, three it-clefts changed to two (Jo opened the window offers two phrases to foreground, Jo and the window). Dismissed the low flag on the curious spotlight sentence (the entry places the foregrounded phrase after be).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "it-Cleft." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/it-cleft-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Kin Title with a Personal Name
pattern: NP[Nom[pre-head kin term + personal name]], with no determiner

entry.name: Kin Title with a Personal Name
entry.pattern: NP[Nom[pre-head kin term + personal name]], with no determiner

dimensions.form: A kin term such as aunt, uncle, grandma, grandpa or nana before a given name or surname, with no determiner. The NP's head is the proper noun, and the kin term is a pre-head modifier.
dimensions.meaning: Designates one relative: the kin term gives a kin class and the personal name picks out a member of it.
dimensions.function: Referential argument, subject-determiner in a genitive, or vocative.
dimensions.distribution: In the caregiver lines cited, grandparental titles occur with given names (Grandma Sharon) and with a surname (Grandma Baum). Schneider and Homans's American informants most often designated aunts and uncles this way.

1.definition: Designates a relative by combining a kin title with that person's name.
1.details: Schneider and Homans report that an uncle may be addressed or referred to by uncle plus first name, by first name alone or by uncle alone, and similarly an aunt (1955: 1195). Among their informants the combination was the most frequently employed term for aunts and uncles (p. 1199), and they write that the American system “classes all uncles together and then subdivides members of the class” (p. 1201). CGEL calls pre-head modifiers of personal names such as Queen, Sister, Captain and Dr appellations, expressing the status of the individual, and notes that it is arguable whether they form part of the name (pp. 518–519). Its list of appellations doesn't include kin terms. Treating the kin term here as a modifier of the same kind extends that analysis and isn't itself grounded in CGEL.

examples.form: Well, we are actually leaving for [Grandma Sharon] and [Grandpa Dale] in three days.
examples.note: Attested, mother to child. Coordinated NPs as object in a PP; the transcript's pause mark is omitted.

examples.form: I like the ones that [Grandmama Linda] made though.
examples.note: Attested, mother. Subject of a relative clause.
Attested. The speaker is herself a grandmother (participant Kate); a surname follows the kin title.

examples.form: That reminds me of [grampa Charlie]'s story, Julia.
examples.note: Attested, mother to child. The NP is subject-determiner in a genitive.

constraints.description: The kin term takes no determiner of its own. With a genitive determiner the structure differs: in it's your brother Ben's birthday (CHILDES Peters, 010621a.cha, line 20), brother is head, your is its determiner and Ben is an integrated appositive. CGEL draws the same contrast between architect Norman Foster, where architect is an omissible embellishment, and the architect Norman Foster, where architect is head and the name an appositive dependent (p. 520).
The kin term assigns the bearer to a kin class, and the personal name selects one member of it (Schneider and Homans 1955: 1201).

The same relative can be designated in other ways. Schneider and Homans's informants used first name alone as the principal term for an uncle or aunt where there was strong positive or negative affect (1955: 1200). One informant called his father's brother Uncle Bill when speaking with his father, Bill when speaking with the uncle directly and my uncle when telling a friend about him (p. 1196).

relatedConstructions.notes: In referential argument use the NP is a strong proper name (leaving for Grandma Sharon); in address it isn't (Thanks, Aunt Sarah). Test: hold the referent fixed and drop the personal name. Bare Grandpa has a simple head and is itself the name, while in Grandpa Dale the kin term modifies a proper noun.

Both place a title before a personal name with no determiner, the pattern CGEL calls appellation plus name (pp. 518–519). That entry's titles identify an office, qualification or style (Sir James, Dr Patel); a kin title identifies a kin class. Test: drop the personal name. A kin title can remain as a name for the same person: Schneider and Homans's informants addressed or referred to an uncle by uncle plus first name or by uncle alone (1955: 1195), and bare Aunty occurs as an argument (Do the duck for Aunty?, CHILDES Peters, 010410c.cha, line 605). Sir can't: dropping the name from Sir James opened the ceremony leaves ∗Sir opened the ceremony (constructed). Some occupational appellations pass the test, as in CGEL's Have you seen Nurse? (p. 518), so it separates kin titles from Sir, not from every office title.
The NP is used as a relative's name; proper name stays the semantic classification.
Compare it's your brother Ben's birthday, where brother is head and Ben an integrated appositive, with grampa Charlie's story, where the kin term modifies the name and no determiner occurs.
The same NP serves in address (Thanks, Aunt Sarah, constructed).
The NP can be subject-determiner in a genitive (grampa Charlie's story).

grounds.locator: Ch. 5 §20.2.2, [4ii] and Appellations, pp. 518–519; nominal modifiers and appositives, p. 520
grounds.note: Appellations as pre-head modifiers of personal names, with royal, clerical, military, political, judicial and academic kinds; kin terms aren't among them. Contrasts architect Norman Foster with the architect Norman Foster.
Aunt- or uncle-plus-first-name as the most frequent designation among the informants, its alternation with first name alone, uncle alone and my uncle, and the classing and subdividing of uncles.

grounds.locator: Weist, Matt/040610.cha line 899; Brent, j1/010001.cha line 392; Snow, 030019b.cha line 3596; Hall, WhitePro/jub.cha line 15237; Peters, 010621a.cha line 20 and 010410c.cha line 605; Brown, Sarah/040118.cha line 296
grounds.note: Title-plus-name arguments and genitives in caregiver speech, a determined kin noun with an appositive name, a bare kin title used alone, and a clerical appellation.

projection.target: Knowing that a kin title plus a personal name is a family's designation for a relative predicts that it occurs with no determiner in argument functions, as a genitive subject-determiner and in address, and that the same person can also be designated by the first name alone, the kin term alone or a relational NP such as my uncle, depending on audience and relationship.
projection.evidence: Schneider and Homans (1955: 1195–1201) document the combination and its alternatives for aunts and uncles among their American informants. The CHILDES lines attest argument and genitive uses in caregiver speech. The analysis of the kin term as a pre-head modifier extends CGEL's account of appellations, which doesn't list kin terms.

known_boundary_items: Sister Margareta, said of a school principal (CHILDES Brown, Sarah/040118.cha, line 296). Sister here is a clerical appellation in CGEL's list (p. 519), not a kin title.
my Aunt Sarah or my aunt Sarah (constructed). With a genitive determiner the kin noun can be head and the name an appositive, as in the architect Norman Foster; the spelling varies.
Courtesy aunts and uncles (Schneider and Homans 1955: 1203). The kin term is applied to someone who isn't a relative, though there is “never any doubt about their status as courtesy kin”.

curious.title: Family titles before a name
curious.summary: A family word such as Grandma or Aunt placed before a name works as the name of one relative.
curious.body: A relative can be called by a family word plus a name: Grandma Sharon, Aunt Sarah, Grandpa Dale. The two parts do different jobs. The family word says what kind of relative it is, and the name picks out which one. There's no the or my in front. You can say we're leaving for Grandma Sharon, or call out Thanks, Aunt Sarah. The same person can be named in other ways too, depending on who is listening: one study found a man calling his father's brother Uncle Bill, Bill or my uncle, depending on whom he was speaking to.

examples.text: Well, we are actually leaving for [Grandma Sharon] and [Grandpa Dale] in three days.
That reminds me of [grampa Charlie]'s story, Julia.

curious.try: What do you call your relatives when you talk to them, and what do you call them when you talk about them to a friend? Is it always the same?

teacher.summary: Explains kin titles used as part of a name (Grandma Sharon) and how they differ from titles like Dr or Sir.
teacher.explain: In Grandma Sharon, the head of the NP is the proper noun Sharon, and the kin term is a pre-head modifier with no determiner of its own. The kin term gives a kin class, and the personal name picks out one member of it. The NP can be a referential argument, the subject-determiner in a genitive (grampa Charlie's story), or a vocative (Thanks, Aunt Sarah). This dictionary treats the kin term as a modifier of the same kind as CGEL's appellations (Queen, Sister, Captain, Dr), but notes that CGEL's list doesn't include kin terms, so this extends CGEL's analysis. With a genitive determiner the structure differs: in your brother Ben's birthday, brother is head and Ben an appositive.
teacher.terms: Appellation: CGEL's term for a pre-head modifier of a personal name that expresses the status of the individual, such as Dr or Queen. Kin title: a family word such as Aunt, Uncle or Grandma used before a name.

examples.text: Well, we are actually leaving for [Grandma Sharon] and [Grandpa Dale] in three days.
I like the ones that [Grandmama Linda] made though.
That reminds me of [grampa Charlie]'s story, Julia.

contrasts.note: The kin term modifies the name, and there's no determiner.
With the determiner your, brother is the head and Ben is an appositive.

watch_for: A learner might add a determiner and treat Aunt Sarah as if it had the same structure as my aunt Sarah.
A learner might take a courtesy aunt or uncle (a kin term used for someone who isn't a relative) to be a blood relation.
teacher.activity: Students list the ways they or their characters name one relative (Uncle plus name, name alone, my uncle) and decide which would suit speaking to the person, speaking about the person to a friend, and writing a card.

child.hook: Do you say "Grandma" and then a name for one of your relatives?
child.explain: People can call a relative by a family word plus a name, like Aunt Sarah. The family word tells who she is to you. The name tells which aunt you mean.
child.play: List your relatives. For each one, write the family word and the name together. Then try calling the same person by the name alone, or by "my" plus the family word.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Kin Title with a Personal Name." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/kin-title-name-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Left Dislocation with a Pronoun

1.definition: Presents a referent before making a predication about it within the clause.
1.details: A pronoun in the clause takes the referent of the initial NP. The pronoun may be a subject, an object, or a genitive determiner. In complement preposing the relevant position has a gap. The left-dislocated NP can introduce a new referent.

examples.form: [Her parents, I don’t like them at all.]
[Some guys, they just show up without even calling first.]
examples.note: The initial NP can introduce a class of people to the discourse.

relatedConstructions.notes: The clause nucleus supplies Head:VP.
The linked NP can also follow the nucleus, with different discourse conditions.
Preposing uses a gap instead of an overt pronoun.

grounds.note: Records the detached initial NP and the following clause with a linked pronoun.

projection.target: An overt pronoun can appear inside an NP as a genitive determiner while the initial referent is outside the clause nucleus. The referent can be new to the discourse.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares preposing with matched left dislocation and documents genitive and discourse-new cases. CASA records the linked pronoun.

curious.title: Naming something first, then using a pronoun for it
curious.summary: A speaker names a person or thing at the start, then makes a statement about it using a pronoun.
curious.body: In Her parents, I don't like them at all, the speaker first puts Her parents out there and then says something about them with the pronoun them. The opening phrase and the pronoun point to the same people. The pronoun can be the subject or the object of what follows, or a word like her or their that goes before a noun. The opening phrase can also bring someone new into the conversation: in Some guys, they just show up without even calling first, the speaker introduces a group of people, then talks about them.

examples.text: [Her parents, I don’t like them at all.]
[Some guys, they just show up without even calling first.]

curious.try: Pick someone you know and start with their name, then say something about them using a pronoun. What did the opening name do for the listener?

teacher.summary: Helps explain a sentence where a noun phrase comes first and a pronoun repeats it inside the clause.
teacher.explain: In left dislocation, an NP comes before a clause, and an overt personal pronoun inside the clause takes the referent of that NP. The pronoun can be a subject, an object, or a genitive determiner. The initial NP can introduce a new referent into the discourse. Compare complement preposing, where the position inside the clause has a gap and no pronoun is present. This dictionary also records a right-dislocation counterpart, where the linked NP follows the clause instead.
teacher.terms: Left dislocation is the name this dictionary uses. The related pattern where a gap replaces the pronoun is complement preposing in this dictionary.

examples.text: [Her parents, I don’t like them at all.]
[Some guys, they just show up without even calling first.]

contrasts.text: Her parents, I don't like them at all.
contrasts.note: The pronoun them is overt.
Complement preposing: a gap, no pronoun.

watch_for: A learner might treat the pronoun as an error because it repeats the opening phrase, when the pattern requires an overt pronoun.
A learner might assume the initial phrase must already be known to the listener, when it can introduce a new referent.
teacher.activity: Give students plain sentences such as I don't like her parents. They rewrite each with the noun phrase first and a pronoun in its old place, then rewrite it again with a gap and compare the two.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher summary no longer calls the pattern spoken-style (the entry assigns it no register); teacher terms no longer claims 'the usual name'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Left Dislocation with a Pronoun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/left-dislocation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: X, let alone Y
pattern: utterance with contrasting focus A + let alone + corresponding focus B; shared material can follow both foci

entry.name: X, let alone Y
entry.pattern: utterance with contrasting focus A + let alone + corresponding focus B; shared material can follow both foci

1.definition: Uses a contrast on a contextually supplied scale to justify dismissing a further alternative.
1.details: On the usual negative pattern, the first alternative is easier, smaller, or otherwise more attainable. If even it fails, the harder one can be dismissed. The material after let alone can consist of a phrase whose interpretation uses the shared material of the first part. Negation and other downward-oriented environments are favoured. The original study also discusses positive uses and speaker variation.

examples.form: [Few people have seen the document, let alone know what’s in it.]
examples.note: The scale links seeing the document and knowing its contents.

examples.form: [We couldn’t fit a bicycle, let alone a whole sofa, through that doorway.]
examples.note: Constructed NP contrast. Through that doorway applies to both alternatives.

relatedConstructions.notes: CGEL treats the connective as a candidate marginal coordinator.

grounds.note: Analyzes paired foci, licensing contexts and scalar inference.
Reports let alone among well-studied constructions omitted from the chapter’s worked survey.

projection.target: A short paired focus after let alone receives a fuller interpretation from the shared material, with the ordering of the alternatives constrained by the discourse scale and polarity context.
projection.evidence: Fillmore, Kay and O’Connor give paired-focus, shared-material, polarity and scale diagnostics. CGEL records the link between finite VPs.

curious.title: Setting aside a bigger claim with let alone
curious.summary: Let alone pairs a smaller claim with a bigger one on a scale. On the usual negative pattern, if even the smaller one fails, the bigger one can be set aside.
curious.body: In Few people have seen the document, let alone know what's in it, the speaker names something easier first (seeing the document) and then something harder (knowing what's in it). If even the easier thing is rare, the harder one can be set aside. The two parts line up on a scale, such as how hard something is. On the usual negative pattern, the first is the easier, smaller or otherwise more attainable one, and the second is the harder one. Sentences with a negative, as in We couldn't fit a bicycle, let alone a whole sofa, through that doorway, are the favoured setting. What comes after the sofa, through that doorway, belongs to both parts.

examples.text: [Few people have seen the document, let alone know what’s in it.]
[We couldn’t fit a bicycle, let alone a whole sofa, through that doorway.]

curious.try: Think of something hard you haven't done, and something even harder. Can you join them with let alone?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: how let alone joins an easier and a harder alternative and, on the usual negative pattern, dismisses the harder one.
teacher.explain: Let alone pairs two contrasting foci, A and B, with shared material that can follow both. On the usual negative pattern, B is dismissed because A, which is easier, smaller or otherwise more attainable on a contextual scale, already fails. Negation and other downward-oriented environments favour the pattern. The material after let alone can be a short phrase whose interpretation draws on the shared material, so a whole sofa is read together with through that doorway. CGEL treats let alone as a candidate marginal coordinator. The original study also discusses positive uses and speaker variation, so don't present the negative pattern as the only one.
teacher.terms: CGEL treats let alone as a candidate marginal coordinator, so it is related to coordination in this dictionary.

examples.text: [Few people have seen the document, let alone know what’s in it.]
[We couldn’t fit a bicycle, let alone a whole sofa, through that doorway.]

contrasts.text: We couldn't fit a bicycle, let alone a whole sofa, through that doorway.
contrasts.note: A and B are both NPs; through that doorway applies to both.

watch_for: A learner might put the harder alternative before let alone, when on the negative pattern the first alternative is the easier one.
A learner might use let alone to join two alternatives with no contextual scale ordering them, when the two are ordered on a contextual scale.
teacher.activity: Give students a scale such as walking a block, a kilometre, a marathon. They write sentences with a negative and let alone, choosing the easier alternative first, and swap to check whether each pair is ordered correctly.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary, curious.body, teacher.summary, teacher.explain and teacher.watch_for now tie the failure-of-the-easier-alternative account to the usual negative pattern and allow other contextual scales, as the entry does.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "X, let alone Y." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/let-alone-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: let Permissive with a Bare Infinitival

1.definition: Presents an action as permitted or allowed to proceed.

projection.target: Let licenses a plain form after Jo. An ordinary verbal passive with let and to is unavailable in this use, unlike Jo was allowed to use the key.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Letting someone do something
curious.summary: Let can be followed by a person and then a plain verb to say that an action is allowed to go ahead.
curious.body: In They let Jo use the key, the speakers allow Jo to do something. The pattern is let, then the person, then the verb in its plain form, as in use. The meaning is permission. The action is presented as allowed to proceed. Some other ways of giving permission work a little differently. For example, you can say Jo was allowed to use the key, but the ordinary passive with let and to isn't available in this use.

examples.text: Jo was allowed to use the key.

curious.try: Say They let Jo use the key. Who is giving permission, and who gets to act?

teacher.summary: Helps explain let plus a person plus a plain verb as permission, and why it lacks the passive that allow has.
teacher.explain: In this use, let takes an NP and a bare infinitival: let Jo use the key. The sentence presents an action as permitted or allowed to proceed. The verb after the NP is in the plain form, and let licenses it directly. The passive behaves differently from other permission verbs. An ordinary verbal passive with let and to is unavailable in this use, unlike Jo was allowed to use the key. Teaching let beside allow makes the difference easy to see.
teacher.terms: The bare infinitival is sometimes called a bare infinitive. This dictionary also calls the form after Jo the plain form of the verb.

contrasts.text: They let Jo use the key.
contrasts.note: Let with a plain form after Jo.

contrasts.text: Jo was allowed to use the key.
contrasts.note: Allow has an ordinary passive with to.

watch_for: A learner might put to before the verb after Jo because allow takes to in Jo was allowed to use the key.
A learner might try to form the passive of let in this use the way the passive of allow is formed.
teacher.activity: Students write four sentences about permission at school with let followed by a person and a plain verb. A partner rewrites each one with allow and compares the two verbs.

child.hook: What do you call it when a grown-up says you can do something?
child.explain: When someone lets you do something, they allow it. Say let, then who gets to do it, then the action. Dad lets Mia use his bike. The action word stays plain.
child.play: Finish this sentence three ways, with a different person and a different action each time. My teacher lets ... Then read your three sentences aloud to a friend.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "let Permissive with a Bare Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/let-permissive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Inclusive let’s Imperative

1.definition: Proposes a course of action involving speaker and addressee or the relevant joint group.

projection.target: The preferred negative counterpart can be Let’s not take a break. The ’s form identifies the inclusive pattern and is unavailable in a literal command to release someone.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Suggesting something to do together
curious.summary: Let's followed by a plain verb proposes that the speaker and the listener, or a group, do something together.
curious.body: Let's take a break proposes an action for the speaker and the listener to do together. The group involved can also be a wider one that includes them. The 's after let identifies this joint pattern. The preferred negative counterpart can be Let's not take a break. The 's form also can't be used for a literal command to release someone, which is a different use of let.
curious.try: Think of something you'd like to do with a friend. Start with let's and suggest it. Who is included?

teacher.summary: Helps explain let's as a joint proposal, and keeps it apart from let meaning allow.
teacher.explain: Let's plus a plain-form VP proposes a course of action involving the speaker and addressee, or the relevant joint group. Teach it as a special kind of imperative: the proposal includes the speaker, so it isn't an order aimed only at the listener. The negative counterpart can be Let's not take a break. The 's form identifies the inclusive pattern and isn't available in a literal command to release someone. For the permission sense, see the related permissive let entry.
teacher.terms: An imperative in this dictionary, with the inclusive 's marking joint action. Related to let permissive, which means allow.

contrasts.note: Joint proposal: speaker and addressee.

contrasts.text: They let Jo use the key.
contrasts.note: Permission: let allows someone else to act.
A negative counterpart of the joint proposal.

watch_for: A learner might read Let's take a break as a command aimed only at the listener, when the speaker is included.
A learner might confuse the 's in let's with the 's of a genitive or of is.
teacher.activity: Students suggest group activities with let's, then each suggestion is answered with Let's not and another idea. Discuss who is included in each proposal.

child.hook: When you say let's, who is going to do it?
child.explain: Let's means you and others, together. You suggest something to do as a group. Let's take a break means we rest together.
child.play: Think of three things to suggest to a friend, each starting with let's. Then say one more with let's not. Does it still include you both?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body no longer says the release sense is covered in a separate entry, and no longer calls the negative 'the negative version' built with not (it now says only that the preferred negative counterpart can be Let's not take a break); teacher.explain points to the related permissive let entry that the entry links. Second round: fixed child.explain, which required everyone being addressed to take part (this dictionary allows the speaker and addressee or the relevant joint group); curious.body now says the 's identifies the inclusive pattern, as this dictionary does, rather than that it makes the proposal.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Inclusive let’s Imperative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/lets-inclusive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Letter-Case Modifier Construction

dimensions.form: Premodifying adjective phrase (often hyphenated) naming letter case.
dimensions.meaning: Signals lowercase vs uppercase interpretation of the modified label.
dimensions.function: Marks ordinary vs institutional/proper readings within NP structure.
dimensions.distribution: Premodifier of category labels and role nouns.

1.specialization: Encodes letter-case as a premodifier (small-c, big-D), specifying the intended interpretive status.

examples.note: Ordinary descriptive sense; not the institution.

relatedConstructions.notes: Realized as an adjectival pre-head modifier in nominals.

grounds.locator: Literal case contrast, as the comparison for the constructed modifier

projection.target: The compact modifier big-D in a big-D Democrat can disambiguate the label before its head. The full PP with a capital D can follow the label and express an equivalent literal contrast.
projection.evidence: The lexical meanings of capital and small supply the comparison. The position and interpretation contrast uses constructed forms rather than claims about regional frequencies.

curious.title: Small-c and big-D labels
curious.summary: A word like small-c or big-D placed before a label tells the reader which kind of meaning the label has.
curious.body: Putting small-c before a word tells you to read it in its ordinary, descriptive sense, not as the name of an institution. Putting big-D before a word does the opposite. In She is a big-D Democrat, the label points to the party, while small-c catholic in He's a small-c catholic points to the ordinary sense. The little modifier names a letter and whether it's capital or small. It works as a quick instruction about how to read the word that follows. The longer version puts a phrase with a capital D after the label.
curious.try: Pick a word you could write with a capital or a small first letter. How could you tell a reader which meaning you intend?

teacher.summary: Explains compact modifiers like small-c and big-D that tell a reader how to interpret a label.
teacher.explain: This is the compact form of letter-case specification. A premodifying adjective phrase, often hyphenated, names a letter and its case (small, big, little) and signals how to read the label that follows: ordinary or descriptive, versus institutional or party-affiliated. It sits before the head in the nominal, like other pre-head adjectival modifiers. The same contrast can be expressed with a full PP after the label, such as with a capital D. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional; it rests on dictionary definitions of capital and small, so treat these as constructed illustrations.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats it as a metalinguistic modifier: a modifier about how a word is written, used to guide how it is read.

contrasts.text: She is a Democrat with a capital D.
contrasts.note: The full PP after the label expresses an equivalent contrast.
The compact modifier before the label.

watch_for: A learner might read small-c as describing size, when it names the case of the letter.
A learner might expect the modifier to come after the label, when the compact form sits before it.
teacher.activity: Write pairs of sentences that need a capital letter to show an institutional meaning and a small letter to show an ordinary one. Partners explain each sentence in their own words and then add the compact modifier before the label.

checked.note: Fixed: removed the claim about textbook categories from teacher terms (this dictionary says nothing about it). Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' wording; the longer-version sentence in the curious body now matches this dictionary's projection note.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Letter-Case Modifier Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/letter-case-modifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Letter-Case Specification Construction
pattern: Case-specifying phrase or modifier attached to a label (e.g., with a small X, with a lowercase X, small-X)

entry.name: Letter-Case Specification Construction
entry.pattern: Case-specifying phrase or modifier attached to a label (e.g., with a small X, with a lowercase X, small-X)

dimensions.form: PP or adjectival modifier naming a letter and its case (small/big/capital/uppercase/lowercase).
dimensions.meaning: Specifies orthographic case to disambiguate the sense or status of a label.
dimensions.function: Metalinguistic instruction about how a label should be written and interpreted.
dimensions.distribution: Adjunct to category labels; often parenthetical after the label.

1.definition: Specifies the capitalization of a letter in a label.
1.details: Capitalization can distinguish institutional and descriptive uses. Name conventions and ordinary spelling supply other uses. The capital-letter format can also emphatically present an example as fully deserving its label.

relatedConstructions.notes: Lowercase specifications align with common-noun readings.
Case specification often disambiguates proper-name readings.
Letter-case cues interact with proper-noun orthography.

grounds.locator: Entries for capital letter and its contrast with small letter
Idiom entry, attributing a strong degree

projection.target: With a capital R can distinguish the Romantic movement from a descriptive adjective. A quality with a capital letter can also express emphatic exemplarity. Neither the letter case nor the verbal specification determines noun subclass independently.
projection.evidence: The dictionary contrasts labels by written case and lists the emphatic idiom separately.

curious.title: Saying which letter case you mean
curious.summary: A phrase like with a small c tells the reader how a label is spelled and, with it, what it means.
curious.body: Sometimes the letter at the start of a word changes what the word means. Catholic with a small c points to a non-institutional, descriptive sense. A big-D Democrat points to the party. The phrase naming the letter is a quick instruction about how to read the label. Another use presents something as fully deserving a label. Saying a person is generous with a capital G suggests that the person fully deserves the label. The case of the letter doesn't decide by itself what kind of word the label is.
curious.try: Say the same label twice, once with a small first letter and once with a capital. Does the meaning change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain phrases like with a small c that tell the reader which sense of a label is meant.
teacher.explain: A PP or adjectival modifier names a letter and its case and attaches to a label. This dictionary treats it as a metalinguistic instruction: it tells the reader how to write or interpret the label, such as institutional versus descriptive. Name conventions and ordinary spelling supply other uses. The capital-letter format can also present an example as fully deserving its label, so a quality with a capital letter is emphatic. Neither letter case nor the specification fixes noun subclass by itself. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on dictionary entries.
teacher.terms: Related entries in this dictionary: common noun, proper name, proper noun.

contrasts.note: Non-institutional, descriptive sense.

contrasts.text: She's generous with a capital G.
contrasts.note: Emphatic, presenting her as fully deserving the label generous.

watch_for: A learner might take with a capital G as an instruction about spelling only, when it can also mean that the quality fully applies.
A learner might assume the capital letter by itself shows whether a word is a proper noun, when neither case nor the specification settles the noun subclass.
teacher.activity: Give students labels that have both an institutional and a descriptive sense. They write two sentences for each, using a phrase naming the letter case to show which sense they mean.

checked.note: Fixed: cut 'Not a standard textbook category' (teacher.terms, unsupported); 'perfect example' changed to 'fully deserving the label' (curious.body, teacher.contrasts); cut 'not a corpus'; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Letter-Case Specification Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/letter-case-specification-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Anaphoric do so

1.definition: Uses an anaphoric expression as a VP in its own right.

examples.form: Kai tied the bundle, and [did so] again the next day.

grounds.locator: Ch. 17 §§7.5–7.6, do so versus do it/that; Ch. 3 §2.1.4

projection.target: Do so can be infinitival in promised to do so, and in its ordinary use favours an action antecedent. Stranded auxiliary do has a wider range of antecedents.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Do so standing in for an action
curious.summary: Do so can replace a phrase that has already named an action, so the speaker doesn't have to repeat it.
curious.body: In Kai tied the bundle, and did so again the next day, did so stands in for tied the bundle. Instead of repeating the action, the speaker points back to it. This works as a phrase in its own right, so it can appear in different forms. In She promised to do so, it follows to. In its ordinary use, do so looks back to an action that was named earlier. This dictionary has a separate entry on a related pattern, where the helper word do is left standing with the rest unsaid, as in Jo did too, and that one allows a wider range of earlier phrases.

examples.text: Kai tied the bundle, and [did so] again the next day.

curious.try: Say a sentence about something you did, then add and did so again. What does did so replace?

teacher.summary: Helps explain do so as a stand-in for an earlier action phrase, and how it differs from stranded auxiliary do.
teacher.explain: Do so is an anaphoric expression that functions as a VP in its own right. It refers back to an earlier action, so in Kai tied the bundle, and did so again the next day, did so picks up tied the bundle. Because it's a VP, it can be infinitival, as in promised to do so. Its ordinary use favours an action antecedent. Stranded auxiliary do, the pattern in Jo did too, has a wider range of antecedents. This analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Do so can be described as a pro-form for a verb phrase. In this dictionary: anaphoric do so, with stranded auxiliary do as a separate, related entry.

examples.text: Kai tied the bundle, and [did so] again the next day.

contrasts.text: Kai tied the bundle, and did so again the next day.
contrasts.note: Do so is a VP in its own right and looks back to an action.

contrasts.text: Kai tied the bundle, and Jo did too.
contrasts.note: Stranded auxiliary do, a related pattern with a wider range of antecedents.

watch_for: A learner might think do so is only a finite form, when this dictionary shows it can be infinitival, as in promised to do so.
A learner might use do so to refer back to something that isn't an action, when its ordinary use favours an action antecedent.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences naming an action and then rewrite the second mention with do so. They then compare with a version that uses did too and say what each form refers back to.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer describes stranded do as following another helper word (do is itself the auxiliary there); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary' and the provisional status stated.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Anaphoric do so." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/lexical-do-so-anaphor-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Light Verb with an Event Nominal

entry.name: Light Verb with an Event Nominal

1.definition: Packages an event in a nominal while the verbal head carries tense and complementation.

examples.form: We [took a quick look] at the charts.

projection.target: The nominal can take attributive modification or be counted, as in two quick looks. Its lexical collocation with the light verb constrains substitution.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Taking a look instead of looking
curious.summary: A plain verb such as took can carry the tense while a noun, such as look, names the event.
curious.body: In We took a quick look at the charts, the event is the look. The verb took does little more than carry the tense and the rest of the sentence's structure. The noun look names what happened. Because look is a noun here, it can be treated like other nouns. It can have a describing word before it, as in quick look, and it can be counted, as in two quick looks. The pairing of verb and noun depends on the particular words involved, so you can't freely swap in a different verb.

examples.text: We [took a quick look] at the charts.
We took [two quick looks] at the charts.

curious.try: Think of an action you could describe with a verb and a noun, like took a look. Can you count it, or describe it with an adjective?

teacher.summary: Helps explain verb plus event noun patterns like took a look, and why the verb can't be swapped freely.
teacher.explain: A light verb with an event nominal packages the event in an NP while the verb carries tense and complementation. In We took a quick look at the charts, the event is expressed by the noun look, and the direct object is the noun phrase a quick look. The nominal can take attributive modification (quick) and can be counted (two quick looks). Which light verb goes with which noun is a matter of lexical collocation, which constrains substitution. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional, so teach it through a few set collocations.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a light verb construction, a delexical verb or a support verb construction. In this dictionary, the verb is a light verb and the object is an event nominal.

examples.text: We [took a quick look] at the charts.
We took [two quick looks] at the charts.

contrasts.text: We took a quick look at the charts.
contrasts.note: The event is in the noun, which is modified by quick.

contrasts.text: We took two quick looks at the charts.
contrasts.note: The nominal is counted.

watch_for: A learner might choose a different light verb than the one that fits the noun, when the collocation constrains substitution.
A learner might look for the main meaning in the verb took, when the event is carried by the noun look.
teacher.activity: Give students event nouns such as look, walk or swim, each on a card. They find which light verb pairs with each one, then add an adjective and a number to each noun phrase.

child.hook: Do you take a look or just look?
child.explain: You can say we took a quick look. Here the word look names what happened, and took just goes with it. Because look is a noun here, you can count it: two quick looks.

examples.text: We [took a quick look] at the charts.
We took [two quick looks] at the charts.

child.play: Say we took a look. Now put a describing word in front of look, and then try two looks. What do the changes tell you about the word look?

checked.note: Fixed: direct-object function assigned to the noun phrase a quick look rather than to the noun look; child line says look can be counted because it is a noun here, not 'a thing'; 'fixed' pairing softened to 'depends on the particular words'. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Light Verb with an Event Nominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/light-verb-event-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Locative Location-Object Frame

1.definition: Presents a location as the principal affected object and the material as a with-dependent.

relatedConstructions.notes: In sprayed the panel with paint, the with-phrase gives the material applied. In painted the panel with a brush, it gives the instrument.

projection.target: The location can be the passive subject. The location-object variant favours an affected-region reading, which need not literally cover every part of the site.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Putting the surface right after the verb
curious.summary: With some verbs, the place that gets treated comes right after the verb and the material comes after with.
curious.body: They sprayed the panel with paint puts the panel, the place that gets sprayed, straight after the verb. The paint, the material, follows with. The sentence presents the panel as the main thing affected. This way of saying it favours reading the panel as the affected area, though not every part needs to be covered. In a with-phrase like this, with gives the material. In painted the panel with a brush, it gives the tool instead.

examples.text: They [painted the panel with a brush].

curious.try: Say They sprayed the panel with paint and then They painted the panel with a brush. What does with give in each one?

teacher.summary: Helps explain the frame in which the location is the direct object and the material comes in a with-phrase, as in sprayed the panel with paint.
teacher.explain: In this frame the location is the direct object and the material is a with-dependent: sprayed the panel with paint. The location can also be the passive subject (The panel was sprayed with paint). The frame favours an affected-region reading, which need not literally cover every part of the site. Don't confuse the material with-phrase with the instrument with-phrase in painted the panel with a brush.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls this the location-object frame.

contrasts.text: They sprayed the panel with paint.
contrasts.note: The location is the object; with gives the material.

contrasts.text: They painted the panel with a brush.
contrasts.note: The with-phrase gives the instrument, not the material.

watch_for: A learner might think the panel must be covered completely, when the frame favours an affected-region reading that need not cover every part.
A learner might read the with-phrase in painted the panel with a brush as a material, when it is an instrument.
teacher.activity: Give students verb cards such as spray and paint. They build sentences with the place right after the verb, swap them with a partner, and mark whether the with-phrase names a material or an instrument.

checked.note: Fixed: removed every claim about an alternate frame in which the material is the object (onto-phrases, 'theme-object frame', the locative alternation, which verbs take both), since this dictionary does not describe it; the second curious example is now painted the panel with a brush, which this dictionary contrasts with the material with-phrase; try and activity reworded to match. Second round: fixed curious.body, affected as a whole changed to the affected area (the entry says an affected-region reading that need not cover every part).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Locative Location-Object Frame." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/locative-location-variant-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Locative Theme-Object Frame

1.definition: Presents a material or moved entity as direct object and a location as goal.

relatedConstructions.notes: In sprayed paint onto the panel the material is the object. In sprayed the panel with paint the location is the object. The alternation depends on the verb and sense.

projection.target: What was sprayed? can ask about the material. The goal need not be understood as comprehensively affected, unlike the customary implication of the corresponding location-object variant.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Putting the material right after the verb
curious.summary: With some verbs, the material or moved thing comes right after the verb and the place comes later.
curious.body: In They sprayed paint onto the panel, the paint comes straight after the verb and the panel follows. The paint is the thing that was moved, and the panel is where it ended up. You can ask about the paint with What was sprayed? There's a second way of saying it, in which the panel comes first: They sprayed the panel with paint. Which verbs allow both depends on the verb and its sense. When the panel is placed later, it needn't be understood as affected throughout, whereas the panel-first version customarily suggests more of the surface was affected.

examples.text: They sprayed the panel with paint.

curious.try: Ask a question about the thing that was sprayed. Which word in the sentence answers it?

teacher.summary: Helps explain the frame where the material is the object and the location is a goal PP.
teacher.explain: In this frame the material or moved entity is the direct object and the location is a goal PP: sprayed paint onto the panel. A question can target the material (What was sprayed?). The goal needn't be understood as comprehensively affected, unlike the customary implication of the corresponding location-object variant. It alternates with sprayed the panel with paint, but whether a verb takes both depends on the verb and sense. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of caused motion.
teacher.terms: Part of what is sometimes called the locative alternation. In this dictionary it is the theme-object frame, paired with the location-object frame.

contrasts.text: They sprayed paint onto the panel.
contrasts.note: The material is the object; the panel is a goal.

contrasts.text: They sprayed the panel with paint.
contrasts.note: The location is the object; with gives the material.

watch_for: A learner might think the panel in sprayed paint onto the panel must be covered completely, when the goal needn't be understood that way.
A learner might assume every verb allows both frames, when the alternation depends on the verb and sense.
teacher.activity: Students ask What was sprayed? of a sentence in this frame and then rewrite it with the location as object, discussing whether the second version suggests more of the surface was affected.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Locative Theme-Object Frame." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/locative-theme-variant-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Long-Distance Open Interrogative
pattern: fronted interrogative XPᵢ + clause containing a subordinate clause with gapᵢ

entry.name: Long-Distance Open Interrogative
entry.pattern: fronted interrogative XPᵢ + clause containing a subordinate clause with gapᵢ

1.definition: Questions a dependent associated with a predicate inside an embedded clause.

examples.form: [Which tool did Lee say Jo had borrowed?]

examples.note: Constructed comparison. Local counterpart. The same interrogative is associated directly with the main verb.

projection.target: The tool is interpreted as the object of borrowed. Licensing varies with the intervening construction, and experiments find gradient effects associated with how strongly the embedded content is backgrounded.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A question word reaching into a later clause
curious.summary: A question word at the front of a sentence can ask about something that belongs to a verb in a later clause.
curious.body: In Which tool did Lee say Jo had borrowed? the question word phrase sits at the front, but the tool is what Jo borrowed, not what Lee said. The question reaches into the clause that follows say. Compare the shorter Which tool did Jo borrow? Here the question phrase is tied directly to the main verb. In the longer version, the same link is stretched across another clause. Not every sentence of this kind sounds equally natural. How well it works depends on the construction in between, and experiments find gradient effects, linked to how strongly the embedded content is backgrounded.

examples.text: [Which tool did Lee say Jo had borrowed?]

curious.try: Say Which tool did Lee say Jo had borrowed? Which verb does Which tool belong to?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: how a question phrase at the front is understood as belonging to a verb in a lower clause.
teacher.explain: A long-distance open interrogative fronts an interrogative phrase and associates it with a gap inside an embedded clause. In Which tool did Lee say Jo had borrowed?, the tool is interpreted as the object of borrowed. The local counterpart, Which tool did Jo borrow?, ties the phrase directly to the main verb. Licensing varies with the intervening construction, and experiments report gradient effects associated with how strongly the embedded content is backgrounded. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, so don't present a simple rule for which embeddings allow it.
teacher.terms: Open interrogative is the term here; a wh-question is another name for the same kind of question. The link across clauses is a long-distance dependency.

examples.text: [Which tool did Lee say Jo had borrowed?]

contrasts.text: Which tool did Lee say Jo had borrowed?
contrasts.note: Long-distance. The tool is the object of borrowed.
Local counterpart. The phrase is tied to the main verb.

watch_for: A learner might link the question phrase to say, when the tool is the object of borrowed.
A learner might expect every embedding to allow the pattern equally, when licensing varies with the intervening construction.
teacher.activity: Give students a statement like Lee said Jo had borrowed a tool. They turn it into a question about the tool, then check each question by identifying which verb the question phrase belongs to.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Long-Distance Open Interrogative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/long-distance-open-interrogative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Long-Distance Dependency in an Integrated Relative
pattern: antecedent nominal + relative with an antecedent-linked gap inside an embedded clause

entry.name: Long-Distance Dependency in an Integrated Relative
entry.pattern: antecedent nominal + relative with an antecedent-linked gap inside an embedded clause

1.definition: Identifies a referent by a dependency that crosses into an embedded predication.

examples.form: We need the tool [which Lee said Jo had borrowed].
We need the tool [which Jo borrowed].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. Local counterpart with no intervening clause.

grounds.locator: experiments comparing questions and relatives in the same base constructions

projection.target: The tool fills the object role of borrowed. The relative and a corresponding question differ in their discourse functions, and the acceptability of both depends on the intervening construction.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A relative clause that reaches into a later clause
curious.summary: A phrase that describes a noun can link back to the noun from inside a later clause.
curious.body: In We need the tool which Lee said Jo had borrowed, the part starting with which tells us which tool is wanted. The tool is what Jo borrowed, not what Lee said, so the link reaches past say into the clause that follows. Compare the shorter We need the tool which Jo borrowed. The same link is there, with no extra clause in between. A related question pattern and this relative pattern differ in their discourse functions, and how well each works depends on the construction in between.

examples.text: We need the tool [which Lee said Jo had borrowed].
We need the tool [which Jo borrowed].

curious.try: Say We need the tool which Lee said Jo had borrowed. Which verb does the tool belong to?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes: how a relative clause links a noun to a position inside a lower clause.
teacher.explain: In a long-distance integrated relative, the relative contains an antecedent-linked gap inside an embedded clause. In We need the tool which Lee said Jo had borrowed, the tool fills the object role of borrowed. The local counterpart, We need the tool which Jo borrowed, has no intervening clause. The relative and a corresponding question differ in their discourse functions, and acceptability of both depends on the intervening construction. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, so avoid stating a simple rule for which embeddings are allowed. See also the related entry on long-distance open interrogatives.
teacher.terms: Integrated relative is CGEL's term. A restrictive relative clause is another name for it. The link across clauses is a long-distance dependency.

examples.text: We need the tool [which Lee said Jo had borrowed].

contrasts.text: We need the tool which Lee said Jo had borrowed.
contrasts.note: Long-distance. The tool is the object of borrowed.

contrasts.text: We need the tool which Jo borrowed.
contrasts.note: Local counterpart with no intervening clause.

watch_for: A learner might link which to said, when the tool is the object of borrowed.
A learner might expect every embedding to allow the pattern, when acceptability depends on the intervening construction.
teacher.activity: Students combine pairs such as We need a tool and Jo borrowed it, first locally, then with Lee said inserted. They name which verb the tool belongs to each time.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Long-Distance Dependency in an Integrated Relative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/long-distance-relative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Magnitude Quantifier Construction

dimensions.form: Plural magnitude noun (hundreds, thousands) with of-PP complement
dimensions.meaning: Approximate large quantity; vague quantification
dimensions.function: Quantifies without precise count; emphasizes scale
dimensions.distribution: Heads quantificational NPs in subject, object, and other NP positions

1.definition: Plural magnitude noun quantifies an approximate large number

constraints.description: The core pattern uses plural magnitude nouns such as hundreds and thousands. Non-magnitude quantity nouns such as dozens have a related quantified use.
Distinct from partitive (two of the cats) where numerative is DP in fused-head function.
The of-complement NP may be indefinite (unlike true partitives).

projection.target: Hundreds of enquiries permits a bare plural complement. Exact two of the enquiries instead selects a subset from an established group. Plural hundreds of can give an approximate scale without fixing how many groups of a hundred there were.
projection.evidence: Reynolds distinguishes the plural magnitudes’ quantifier use from exact cardinal expressions and identifies dozen as outside the paper’s technical magnitude class.

curious.title: Hundreds of, thousands of, millions of
curious.summary: A plural word for a large size, followed by of, gives a rough, large amount without saying exactly how many.
curious.body: In hundreds of people, the word hundreds doesn't give an exact count. It gives a rough, large amount, and the speaker is emphasizing scale. The same pattern appears in millions of stars, and it can be stacked, as in tens of thousands of dollars. These are plural words followed by of and a noun phrase. Hundreds of people doesn't say how many groups of a hundred there were. That makes it different from an exact phrase such as two of the cats, which picks a smaller group out of a group already known. A related use with dozens is treated separately in this dictionary.
curious.try: Say hundreds of people and then two of the people. Which one tells you how many, and which picks some out of a known group?

teacher.summary: Helps explain hundreds of, thousands of and millions of as rough quantifiers, and why they differ from exact numbers.
teacher.explain: A plural magnitude noun (hundreds, thousands, millions) plus of and an NP quantifies an approximate large number. In hundreds of people, hundreds isn't a count of hundreds. It gives a rough scale without fixing how many groups of a hundred there were, and it can be nested (tens of thousands of dollars). The of-complement can be indefinite, unlike a true partitive such as two of the cats, which selects a subset from an established group. A word like dozens has a related quantified use but sits outside the core magnitude class. Mention that exact two of the enquiries is a different pattern.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an indefinite numeral, or a large-number noun. In this dictionary, a magnitude noun heads a quantifier construction, and a partitive is a separate pattern.

contrasts.note: Approximate scale; the complement can be a bare plural.
Exact, and selects a subset from an established group.

watch_for: A learner might read hundreds of people as exactly one hundred people, when it gives only an approximate scale.
A learner might treat hundreds of as a true partitive like two of the cats, when the of-complement can be indefinite.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of quantity phrases, some with hundreds, thousands or millions of and some with exact numbers. They sort them into rough and exact, then explain what each tells the reader.

child.hook: How do you say a really big number when you don't know the exact one?
child.explain: Words like hundreds, thousands and millions can tell you roughly how many. We say hundreds of people when we mean a big crowd. It doesn't tell us the exact number.

examples.text: We saw [hundreds of people] at the fair.

child.play: Look at the night sky or a big crowd. Make up sentences that start with hundreds of, thousands of or millions of, and add a noun. Which one would you pick for a huge number?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Magnitude Quantifier Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/magnitude-quantifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Mandative should
pattern: content clause[(that) + Subject + should + plain-form VP]

entry.name: Mandative should
entry.pattern: content clause[(that) + Subject + should + plain-form VP]

1.definition: Realizes a requirement or recommendation with a specialized modal.

examples.form: It is essential [that the gate should remain closed].

projection.target: Should is possible with strongly requiring predicates such as essential. This modal need not weaken the strength of the matrix requirement.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Should after a strong requirement
curious.summary: After a word that states a strong requirement, a that-clause can use should to say what is required.
curious.body: In It is essential that the gate should remain closed, the should is part of the requirement. The clause after that tells us what has to happen to the gate. A word like essential strongly requires something, and should can follow it in this way. The should doesn't weaken the requirement. It doesn't turn the sentence into a mild piece of advice. This dictionary also has a related entry for a version without should, which can replace it in the same kind of sentence.

examples.text: It is essential [that the gate should remain closed].

curious.try: Say It is essential that the gate should remain closed. Is the requirement strong or weak?

teacher.summary: Helps explain should in that-clauses after strongly requiring words like essential, and why it doesn't soften the requirement.
teacher.explain: In a mandative content clause, should can follow the subject and take a plain-form VP: that the gate should remain closed. The pattern realizes a requirement or recommendation. Should is possible with strongly requiring predicates such as essential, and the modal need not weaken the strength of the matrix requirement. This dictionary has a separate entry for the alternating form without should. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and short.
teacher.terms: Mandative construction is the usual name. The related form without should is called the subjunctive mandative in this dictionary.

examples.text: It is essential [that the gate should remain closed].

contrasts.text: It is essential that the gate should remain closed.
contrasts.note: Strongly requiring predicate with should; the requirement isn't weakened.

watch_for: A learner might hear should as mild advice, when here it need not weaken the strength of the requirement.
A learner might read should as a prediction about the gate, when it states what is required.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences beginning It is essential that ... with a subject and should plus a plain verb, then discuss how strong each requirement feels.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Mandative should." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/mandative-should-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Matched Bare Endpoints

1.definition: Uses two bare nouns to set the endpoints of a path, transfer, or transition.
1.details: The predicate and context determine what traverses the path and what the bare nouns describe. With from student to teacher, an object can pass from one person to another, or a person can move between two roles. A context can supply particular endpoints. The availability of either form alone is an independent test.

examples.note: A pair of related roles in the Chapter 5 list.
Source and goal in a transfer.
The conference abstract uses the phrase of the handing down of techniques.
Constructed change-of-role use. Compare The manuscript went from student to teacher.

relatedConstructions.notes: A different configuration makes two bare nouns available as a pair.
A source use can participate in the paired frame.
A goal use can participate in the paired frame.

grounds.note: Proposes a pair-level construction for the meanings of these bare-noun sequences.

projection.target: The same bare-noun pair can specify transfer between people, a role transition, or another route, depending on the host.
projection.evidence: Zwarts analyzes the construction over a pair. CGEL and the UNESCO abstract give distinct role pairings, and the audit records matched transfer and change-of-role contexts.

curious.title: From one role to another, with no the or a
curious.summary: Two nouns with no the or a, joined by from and to, mark the two ends of a path, a handing-over or a change.
curious.body: In from father to son and from teacher to pupil, each noun stands alone, with no the or a. The pair marks the two ends: where something starts and where it ends up. What moves between the ends depends on the rest of the sentence. With from student to teacher, an object can pass from one person to another. It can also be a person who moves between two roles. Compare The manuscript went from student to teacher with Lee went from student to teacher. A context can also supply particular people to fill the two ends.
curious.try: Think of two roles, such as teacher and pupil. What kinds of things could pass from one to the other?

teacher.summary: Helps explain from N to N phrases that mark the two ends of a transfer or change of role, with no articles.
teacher.explain: In from NP to NP with bare nouns, the two nouns set the endpoints of a path, a transfer or a transition. The same pair can specify transfer between people (from teacher to pupil), a role transition (Lee went from student to teacher) or another route, depending on the host. The predicate and context decide what traverses the path and what the bare nouns describe. This dictionary follows an analysis that treats the pair as a construction in its own right, and lists the source and goal uses as related entries.
teacher.terms: A bare noun is one with no determiner. This dictionary treats the whole from N to N pair as one pattern, related to separate source and goal complements.

contrasts.text: Lee went from student to teacher.
contrasts.note: Change of role.

contrasts.text: The manuscript went from student to teacher.
contrasts.note: Transfer between people.

watch_for: A learner might add the or a before each noun, when the pattern sets the endpoints with bare nouns.
A learner might read from student to teacher as a transfer of something, when with a person it can be a change of role.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of roles such as parent and child, coach and player. They write one sentence about something passing between the two and one about a person changing from one role to the other, then compare.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Matched Bare Endpoints." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/matched-bare-endpoints-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Means by with a Gerund-Participial

1.definition: Presents an activity as the means by which another outcome is obtained.

examples.form: Jo reopened the file [by restoring a backup].
Jo reopened the file [after restoring a backup].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. After supplies temporal order and leaves the means relation to context.

projection.target: The restoring is interpreted as part of the method, not merely as a coincidental event in the same time period.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how with by and an action word
curious.summary: By followed by an action that ends in ing says how something was done.
curious.body: In Jo reopened the file by restoring a backup, the restoring is the method. It's how Jo got the file back. The sentence presents the activity as the means by which the outcome was reached. Compare Jo reopened the file after restoring a backup. After gives the order of events but leaves the connection to context. By says more: the restoring is part of the method, not merely something that happened around the same time.

examples.text: Jo reopened the file [by restoring a backup].
Jo reopened the file after restoring a backup.

curious.try: Say how you got to school today, starting with by and an ing word. What would change if you used after instead?

teacher.summary: Helps explain by plus an ing phrase as the means by which something was done, and how it differs from after.
teacher.explain: A PP with by and a gerund-participial clause presents an activity as the means of obtaining another outcome: Jo reopened the file by restoring a backup. The restoring is interpreted as part of the method, not merely a coincidental event in the same time period. Compare after restoring a backup, which supplies temporal order and leaves the means relation to context.
