This dictionary treats the by-phrase as a specialization of the prepositional phrase and relates it to infinitival purpose adjuncts.
teacher.terms: The ing form after a preposition is traditionally called a gerund. In this dictionary it is a gerund-participial clause inside a PP.

examples.text: Jo reopened the file [by restoring a backup].

contrasts.text: Jo reopened the file by restoring a backup.
contrasts.note: The restoring is the means.

contrasts.text: Jo reopened the file after restoring a backup.
contrasts.note: After gives temporal order; the means relation is left to context.

watch_for: A learner might read by restoring a backup as showing only when something happened, when it gives the method.
A learner might treat after restoring a backup as saying the restoring was the method, when it supplies temporal order and leaves the means to context.
teacher.activity: Students write what they did and how, using by and an ing phrase, then change by to after. Partners say whether the meaning changed and how.

child.hook: How did you get your shoes on this morning?
child.explain: You can say how you did something with by and an ing word. I opened the box by cutting the tape. The cutting is how the box got opened.

examples.text: I opened the box [by cutting the tape].
Jo reopened the file [by restoring a backup].

child.play: Say how you do something with by. I got warm by ... I made a friend by ... Finish each one with an ing word, then try after instead of by with a partner.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Means by with a Gerund-Participial." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/means-by-gerund-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Measurement with a Scale Adjective
pattern: measure NP + scale Adj, or [number-unit.SG-scale Adj] before a noun

entry.name: Measurement with a Scale Adjective
entry.pattern: measure NP + scale Adj, or [number-unit.SG-scale Adj] before a noun

1.definition: Gives the position of a referent on a scale such as height, length, or age.
1.details: The same length is expressed by six feet long in a predicate and six-foot-long before a noun. The unit usually has ordinary number inflection in the predicative form and remains singular in the pre-head modifier. Corpus examples show variation in both directions. Only selected scale adjectives take the frame. Fifteen-pound turkey works without an adjective, while fifteen-pound-heavy turkey is excluded in the ordinary pattern.

examples.note: Constructed counterpart with the singular unit and conventional written hyphens.

relatedConstructions.notes: The adjective supplies the dimension measured.
The pre-head variant modifies a following noun.

grounds.note: Documents both forms, selection among scale adjectives and exceptions to the ordinary unit number.

projection.target: The placement of the expression predicts a difference in default unit inflection. The frame is selective even among adjectives that denote measurable properties.
projection.evidence: The FrameNet team compares predicative and attributive subtypes and gives BNC exceptions to the default number pattern.

curious.title: Six feet long and six-foot-long
curious.summary: A measurement followed by an adjective like long tells where something falls on a scale such as length.
curious.body: The board is six feet long uses a measurement (six feet) and an adjective (long) to say where the board falls on a scale. Before a noun, the same length is written six-foot-long, as in a six-foot-long board. Notice the unit. In The board is six feet long, it has its ordinary plural, feet. Before the noun it stays singular, foot, and the written form has hyphens. Examples collected from real writing show variation in both directions, so this is a description, not a rigid rule. Only certain adjectives fit the frame. A phrase like fifteen-pound turkey works without any adjective at all.
curious.try: Describe something near you with a number, a unit and an adjective, like six feet long. Now put the same measure before a noun. Does the unit change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain six feet long versus six-foot-long, and why the unit is singular before the noun.
teacher.explain: A measure NP plus a scale adjective gives the position of a referent on a scale such as height, length or age. In a predicate the unit usually has its ordinary number inflection (six feet long). In a pre-head modifier it remains singular and is hyphenated in writing (a six-foot-long board). Corpus examples show variation in both directions, so present this as the default pattern. Only selected scale adjectives take the frame, even among adjectives that denote measurable properties. A modifier like fifteen-pound turkey works without an adjective. This dictionary relates the pre-head variant to modification of a following noun.
teacher.terms: The pre-head form is sometimes taught as a compound adjective or compound modifier. In this dictionary the predicative and attributive forms are two placements of one pattern.

contrasts.text: The board is six feet long.
contrasts.note: Predicative placement, plural unit.
Pre-head placement, singular unit, written with hyphens.
Works without an adjective after the unit.

watch_for: A learner might expect the unit to take the same form in both positions, when this dictionary describes the pre-head form as singular by default (six-foot-long).
A learner might think any adjective can follow a measure, when only selected scale adjectives take the frame.
teacher.activity: Give students measure cards (six feet, two years, ten metres) and scale adjectives. They write one sentence after the verb and one before a noun for each, then check the unit and the hyphens.

child.hook: How long is the board?
child.explain: You can say the board is six feet long. Before a noun, you can say a six-foot-long board. There, feet has changed to foot.
child.play: Pick something in your room and measure it. Say how long it is in feet. Then put the measure before the thing, like a six-foot-long board.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher watch_for no longer presents a plural unit before the noun as a learner error (the entry reports variation in both directions and calls the singular the default); child explanation no longer states an exceptionless rule; teacher explanation says 'usually' as the entry does. Second round: fixed child.explain, whose 'with just one foot' could be read as a measurement of one foot; it now says only that feet has changed to foot. Also fixed (unflagged): curious.body said the plural unit comes 'after the noun' (it now names The board is six feet long); teacher.terms now applies the compound-adjective label to the pre-head form only; child.play no longer asks for a hyphen in speech.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Measurement with a Scale Adjective." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/measure-adjective-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Measure Genitive Premodifier

1.definition: Specifies a duration or monetary measure within a nominal.

projection.target: Two hours’ gives the duration of the wait and can be embedded within the scope of a preceding determiner. A personal genitive has an independently referential or participant interpretation.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Time measured with an apostrophe
curious.summary: A measure of time or money with an 's ending can come before a noun to say how long or how much.
curious.body: In We had another two hours' wait, the phrase two hours' says how long the wait was. It sits inside the noun phrase, before the noun wait, and the word another before it applies to the whole thing. The apostrophe here isn't about who owns something. Compare Jo's wait, where Jo is a person involved in the wait. The measure form gives a duration, or a money amount, not a participant.
curious.try: Say how long you waited for something, using a time measure with an apostrophe before the noun. Does the phrase say who waited?

teacher.summary: Helps explain two hours' wait, where an apostrophe measure gives a duration rather than a person.
teacher.explain: A measure genitive is a genitive NP naming a duration or monetary measure inside a nominal: two hours’ wait. It gives the duration of the wait and can be embedded within the scope of a preceding determiner (another two hours’ wait). A personal genitive such as Jo’s wait has an independently referential or participant interpretation. The measure genitive isn't a possessor. Some textbooks call the 's form possessive; this dictionary says genitive. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and short.
teacher.terms: Some textbooks call the 's form possessive; this dictionary says genitive. A measure genitive is a specialization of the genitive 's pattern.

contrasts.text: We had another two hours’ wait.
contrasts.note: The genitive gives the duration of the wait.
A personal genitive, with a participant interpretation.

watch_for: A learner might read two hours' as naming someone who owns or has the wait, when it gives the duration.
A learner might leave out the apostrophe in the measure, when the genitive marks the measure phrase.
teacher.activity: Students write measure phrases before nouns, such as a time before wait or holiday. Partners say whether each genitive gives a duration or names a person.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Measure Genitive Premodifier." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/measure-genitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Measure Pseudopartitive with of
pattern: NP[quantified measure expression + of + substance or plural nominal expression]

entry.name: Measure Pseudopartitive with of
entry.pattern: NP[quantified measure expression + of + substance or plural nominal expression]

1.definition: Uses a unit or container expression to specify quantity.

examples.form: They bought [three litres of the milk from yesterday].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. The construction can instead pick a quantity out of an established stock.

projection.target: Milk supplies the substance measured without referring to a definite stock of which the purchase was a subset. Compare three litres of the milk, which can select from such a stock.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Amounts and containers followed by of
curious.summary: A unit or container word followed by of says how much of a substance or how many things were involved.
curious.body: In They bought three litres of milk, three litres says how much milk. The milk isn't a particular stock of milk the shopper chose from. It's just the substance being measured. Compare They bought three litres of the milk from yesterday. Here the speaker picks a quantity out of an established stock: the milk from yesterday. Adding the changes the meaning from measuring a substance to selecting from one already known.

examples.text: They bought [three litres of the milk from yesterday].

curious.try: Say three litres of milk, then three litres of the milk. Which one points to milk you've already been talking about?

teacher.summary: Helps explain three litres of milk, where a unit or container word measures a substance, and how it differs from picking out part of a known stock.
teacher.explain: A measure pseudopartitive uses a unit or container expression plus of to specify quantity: three litres of milk. The milk supplies the substance measured and doesn't refer to a definite stock of which the purchase was a subset. Compare three litres of the milk from yesterday, which can select from such a stock. The pattern takes a substance or a plural nominal after of. This dictionary treats it as a kind of noun phrase and relates it to the measurement adjective pattern (six feet long).
teacher.terms: Pseudopartitive is the textbook name. A true partitive, as in two of the cats, selects from an established stock, and the measure pseudopartitive does not.

contrasts.text: They bought three litres of milk.
contrasts.note: Milk is the substance measured.

contrasts.text: They bought three litres of the milk from yesterday.
contrasts.note: Can instead pick a quantity out of an established stock.

watch_for: A learner might read three litres of milk as a portion of milk already mentioned, when it measures the substance.
A learner might think adding the changes only the wording, when it can shift the sense from measuring to selecting.
teacher.activity: Give students unit and container words, such as litres, bags and cups, with substances and plural nouns. They build sentences with of, then add the plus a definite phrase to one of them and explain what changed.

child.hook: How do you say how much milk you want?
child.explain: You can name an amount or a container, then say of, then say what it holds. Three litres of milk. The word of links the amount to the stuff.
child.play: Look in the kitchen. Name a container or a measure, then say of and what is inside. Make three sentences, like a bag of apples or a cup of tea.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Measure Pseudopartitive with of." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/measure-pseudopartitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Metalinguistic more … than
pattern: more XP than YP with competing descriptions of one item

entry.name: Metalinguistic more … than
entry.pattern: more XP than YP with competing descriptions of one item

1.definition: Ranks alternative descriptions by their appropriateness.

examples.form: The proposal was [more optimistic than realistic].

projection.target: The same referent is evaluated under alternative labels. Even expressions lacking a common numerical scale can be compared for adequacy of description.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Choosing the better description with more than
curious.summary: More ... than can compare two descriptions of the same thing and say which one fits better.
curious.body: In The proposal was more optimistic than realistic, the speaker is weighing two labels for the same proposal and saying that optimistic fits better than realistic. Here there is one thing, the proposal, and two competing descriptions of it. The descriptions don't have to share a numerical scale, yet they can still be compared for how well each one describes the thing.

examples.text: The proposal was [more optimistic than realistic].
The meal was [more filling than tasty].

curious.try: Think of something you've seen or eaten. Can you say which of two descriptions fits it better, using more ... than?

teacher.summary: Helps explain more ... than used to rank two descriptions of one item.
teacher.explain: In this metalinguistic use, more XP than YP ranks alternative descriptions by their appropriateness: The proposal was more optimistic than realistic. The same referent is evaluated under two labels, and expressions lacking a common numerical scale can still be compared for adequacy of description. This dictionary relates the pattern to than-reduced clauses and to gradation.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a metalinguistic comparative. In this dictionary: metalinguistic more ... than.

examples.text: The proposal was [more optimistic than realistic].
The meal was [more filling than tasty].

contrasts.text: The proposal was more optimistic than realistic.
contrasts.note: One referent, two competing descriptions.

contrasts.text: The new proposal was more optimistic than the old one.
contrasts.note: A comparison between two proposals.

watch_for: A learner might read more optimistic than realistic as comparing two different things, when it weighs two descriptions of the same thing.
A learner might try to find a second item to compare, when the comparison is between two labels for one referent.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with more X than Y about a film, a meal or a plan, choosing two adjectives that could both describe it. They explain why one fits better.

checked.note: Fixed: removed the claim that an ordinary comparison sets two things side by side or compares on one scale, which the entry does not state; the texts now say only that the pattern weighs two descriptions of one item.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Metalinguistic more … than." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/metalinguistic-more-than-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Metalinguistic Negation and Correction
pattern: negated expression followed or contextualized by correction of wording or scale

entry.name: Metalinguistic Negation and Correction
entry.pattern: negated expression followed or contextualized by correction of wording or scale

1.definition: Rejects the wording, implication, or strength of a description as inadequate.

projection.target: An ordinary scalar reading of scorching would imply warmth. The emphatic correction licenses negation of the weaker label while preserving the stronger characterization.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying not that word, but a stronger one
curious.summary: A speaker rejects a description as too weak, then corrects it with a stronger one.
curious.body: In It isn't warm. It's scorching, the speaker doesn't mean that the weather is cold. They mean that warm is too weak a word. The correction, scorching, is the stronger description. This works because scorching on its own would imply warmth. The correction rejects the weaker label while keeping the stronger characterization. So the negation targets the wording, its implication or its strength, not the plain facts about the temperature.
curious.try: Think of two words for the same thing, one weaker and one stronger. Can you say it isn't the weaker, then give the stronger?

teacher.summary: Helps explain a negation that rejects the strength or wording of a description and corrects it.
teacher.explain: In metalinguistic negation, a negated expression is followed or contextualized by a correction of wording or scale. It rejects the wording, implication or strength of a description as inadequate: It isn't warm. It's scorching. An ordinary scalar reading of scorching would imply warmth. The emphatic correction licenses negation of the weaker label while preserving the stronger characterization. This dictionary relates it to constituent negation with not and to metalinguistic more ... than.
teacher.terms: Metalinguistic negation is the standard name. In this dictionary it is related to constituent-not negation.

contrasts.note: Rejects the weaker label and gives a stronger one.

watch_for: A learner might read It isn't warm as saying the weather is cool, when the speaker is rejecting the label as too weak.
A learner might drop the correction, when the stronger description is what makes the negation clear.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of words on a scale, such as warm and scorching. They write a pair of sentences that reject the weaker word and give the stronger, and say what the speaker is correcting.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Metalinguistic Negation and Correction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/metalinguistic-negation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Minimizer under Non-Affirmative Polarity
pattern: minimal quantity expression in a negative or otherwise licensed context

entry.name: Minimizer under Non-Affirmative Polarity
entry.pattern: minimal quantity expression in a negative or otherwise licensed context

1.definition: Uses a minimal unit to emphasize absence of any relevant amount.

projection.target: Under negation even the minimal unit is denied. An inch can otherwise denote a literal distance without that emphatic interpretation.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Naming the smallest amount to deny everything
curious.summary: In a negative sentence, naming a tiny unit such as an inch can stress that there was none of the thing at all.
curious.body: When someone says They didn't budge an inch, the tiny unit isn't there to measure anything. Under negation, naming even the smallest amount denies every amount, so the sentence stresses that there was no movement at all. An inch can also mean a real distance, as in a window that opened an inch. The emphatic, nothing-at-all reading comes from the setting: a negative sentence, or another setting that allows it. This dictionary treats that analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Say They didn't budge an inch. Does it sound as if they moved a little, or not at all?

teacher.summary: Low priority for most classes: this dictionary's only example rests on budge, which is relatively infrequent (about 11,900th among word forms in the SUBTLEX-UK subtitle counts), so treat it if it comes up rather than teaching it. Explains why a minimal unit under negation reads as "not even a little".
teacher.explain: A minimizer is a minimal quantity expression that, in a negative or otherwise licensed context, emphasizes the absence of any relevant amount. In They didn't budge an inch, the negation denies even the smallest unit, so the whole sentence is emphatic. Outside such a context, an inch can simply denote a literal distance. Teach it as a pattern tied to a context, not as a property of the noun alone. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and the evidence as medium confidence; its one example is a constructed illustration.
teacher.terms: Minimizer is the term used here. Negative polarity item is a textbook name for expressions that need a licensing context; this dictionary links the pattern to polarity-sensitive ever.

contrasts.note: Emphatic denial of any movement.
A literal distance, with no emphatic reading.

watch_for: A learner might read budge an inch as a measurement of how far something moved.
A learner might expect the emphatic reading of an inch in a plain positive sentence, when this dictionary ties it to negative or otherwise licensed contexts.
teacher.activity: If the expression comes up in a reading, write They didn't budge an inch on the board. Ask what the speaker is claiming about movement. Then show The window opened an inch and have students explain how the same words mean something different in each sentence.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.summary now opens by marking the entry low priority (budge about 11,900th in SUBTLEX-UK); activity reframed as a recognition task for when the expression comes up in reading.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Minimizer under Non-Affirmative Polarity." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/minimizer-negative-polarity-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Minor Determiner (Plain NP/PP)

1.definition: Non-determinative phrase realizes determiner function in a restricted set of NP types

constraints.description: Restricted to specific NP types (interrogatives, measure/quantity frames).

grounds.locator: Ch. 5 §4.1, p. 357, property-value NPs and PP determiners

projection.target: What size hat asks for the hat’s size, whereas over thirty hats sets a lower boundary on their number. Those slots license different phrases even though neither is an ordinary bare determinative lexeme.
projection.evidence: CGEL gives restricted phrase realizations of determiner function, including paired word orders for property-value NPs.

curious.title: Whole phrases that sit before a noun
curious.summary: In a few frames, a phrase such as what size or over thirty can come before a noun the way a small word like the or some does.
curious.body: In what size hat, the words what size ask about the hat. In this size shoes, this size tells us which size of shoes. In over thirty ties, over thirty sets a lower limit on how many ties. Each of these opening groups is a whole phrase, not a single small word, yet it works in the slot before the noun where words like the and some work. This dictionary treats the pattern as restricted. It shows up in questions about size and in frames that measure or count, so it doesn't turn any phrase at all into an opener for a noun.
curious.try: Ask a shop assistant's question about size, beginning with what size. Which noun follows it?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, phrases rather than single words that fill the determiner slot in a few frames such as what size hat.
teacher.explain: Determiner is a function; determinatives like the and some are the words that fill it elsewhere. Here the function is filled by a phrase instead: a plain noun phrase (what size, this size) or a prepositional phrase (over thirty) before the noun. This dictionary's pattern is a noun phrase or prepositional phrase plus a noun, and it is restricted to certain noun-phrase types: interrogatives and measure or quantity frames. What size hat asks for the hat's size. Over thirty ties sets a lower boundary on the number of ties. Present it as a limited set of frames, not as a general rule.
teacher.terms: Minor determiner is this dictionary's label for a phrase, not a determinative word, in determiner function. Property-value noun phrase is the CGEL term for the what size hat type.

contrasts.note: The prepositional phrase over thirty sets a lower boundary on the number of hats.
The noun phrase what size asks for the size of the hat.

watch_for: A learner might take what size or over thirty to be a single determinative word like the.
A learner might assume any phrase can fill the determiner slot, when this dictionary restricts it to interrogative and measure or quantity frames.
teacher.activity: Give students shop-sign prompts (a hat shop, a shoe shop, a tie sale). They write one question with what size and one statement with over thirty, then circle the phrase that comes before each noun.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Minor Determiner (Plain NP/PP)." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/minor-determiner-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Modal Interrogative Request
pattern: polar interrogative with can/could/will/would and second-person subject

entry.name: Modal Interrogative Request
entry.pattern: polar interrogative with can/could/will/would and second-person subject

1.definition: Uses interrogative form to request the addressee’s action.

projection.target: Lowering the shade can satisfy the utterance. In a capacity-testing context the same form can instead invite an answer about ability.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Questions that are really requests
curious.summary: A yes-or-no question with can, could, will or would and you can be a way to ask someone to do something.
curious.body: Could you lower the shade? has the form of a question, but the speaker wants the shade lowered. The listener can satisfy it by doing that, rather than by answering yes or no. The pattern is a yes-or-no question with can, could, will or would and you as the subject. The same words can also be a real question. If the setting is a test of what someone is able to do, Could you lower the shade? can invite an answer about ability instead.
curious.try: Next time you ask someone for help with Can you ... or Could you ..., notice whether they answer in words or just do it.

teacher.summary: Useful for teaching requests: the interrogative form with a modal and you asks for action.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a polar interrogative with can, could, will or would and a second-person subject, used to request the addressee's action. The same form can also be a literal question; the use differs. Could you lower the shade? can be satisfied by lowering the shade. In a capacity-testing context the same form can invite an answer about ability. Teachers can contrast it with the imperative, which this dictionary lists as a related construction. This dictionary classes the pattern as pragmatic: it concerns how the form is used.
teacher.terms: Indirect speech act or indirect request are textbook names for this kind of use.

contrasts.note: A request; lowering the shade satisfies it.
The related imperative.

watch_for: A learner might answer Could you lower the shade? with only yes, taking it as a question about ability.
teacher.activity: Students write three requests with can, could or would and you for a classroom situation (a closed window, a lost pen). In pairs, one reads the request and the other responds with an action, not words. Discuss when a spoken answer would be expected instead.

child.hook: When someone asks "Can you pass the salt?", do they want just a yes?
child.explain: Some questions are really ways of asking for something. Could you lower the shade? asks you to lower it. You can answer by doing it.
child.play: Ask a friend to do something with Could you or Will you. They answer by doing it, not by speaking. Then swap.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain no longer mentions willingness questions (the entry supports only the capacity-testing ability reading). Also fixed (unflagged): removed 'polite' from curious.summary and teacher.summary and cut the watch_for about a future reading, since the entry supports neither.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Modal Interrogative Request." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/modal-interrogative-request-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Central Modal with a Plain-Form Complement

entry.name: Central Modal with a Plain-Form Complement

1.definition: Combines central modal marking with a plain-form verbal complement.

projection.target: Might selects plain have, and the modal itself has no third-person singular suffix. Ordinary central modals cannot occupy the complement slot of perfect have.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Little helper verbs and the plain verb after them
curious.summary: Words like might come before a verb in its basic form, and they have no -s ending of their own.
curious.body: In Jo might have missed the train, the word might comes first and the plain form have follows it. Might doesn't change for different subjects: there's no third-person -s on the modal itself. The verb after it stays in its basic form. This dictionary calls words like might central modals. This dictionary also notes that an ordinary central modal can't fill the slot after perfect have. The modal comes first and have comes after it.
curious.try: Put might, must or will in front of a verb, then change the subject from I to she. Does the modal change at all?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why verbs after modals stay in the plain form and why modals have no -s form.
teacher.explain: A central modal combines with a plain-form verb phrase. Might selects plain have in Jo might have missed the train, and the modal has no third-person singular suffix. This dictionary adds that ordinary central modals cannot occupy the complement slot of perfect have: the modal comes first, and have follows it. The pattern is a specialization of the general verb phrase. Teachers may want to pair it with the perfect, which this dictionary lists as related.
teacher.terms: Plain form is sometimes called the base form or bare infinitive. Central modal is the CGEL name; modal auxiliary is sometimes used in textbooks.

contrasts.text: Jo might have missed the train.
contrasts.note: Modal first, then plain have.
Perfect have with a third-person singular form, and no modal.

watch_for: A learner might add -s to a modal after he or she, since other verbs take it.
A learner might use have or has before the modal rather than after it.
A learner might use a verb form with -ing or -ed after might instead of the plain form.
teacher.activity: Give students subjects (I, she, they) and modals (might, must, will). They build sentences with a plain verb, then with have and a past participle, and compare the endings on each verb.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Central Modal with a Plain-Form Complement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/modal-plain-complement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Adjectivally Modified Personal Pronoun NP

1.definition: Picks out a stage or aspect of the person or group identified by a pronoun.
1.details: In the five-year-old you, the pronoun anchors the reference to the addressee and the adjective specifies an age. In subject position the whole NP can take third-person verbal agreement. A coreferential reflexive can still carry the person of the pronoun. Some age-modified uses are bare. The category of the head and the explanation for the agreement split remain open.

examples.form: Questions [A Younger Me] Would Ask Myself
examples.note: In the reported title, the object reflexive retains first person.

2.definition: Characterizes the person identified by the pronoun as being in a particular state.
2.details: In an exhausted me, the speaker is still identified by me. The adjective adds the state in which the speaker experienced the situation. Halm compares this use with a visibly irritated Mr Andrews and distinguishes it from a reading that explicitly selects a stage or aspect.

examples.note: Excerpt from Halm’s example of the state-characterizing interpretation.

relatedConstructions.notes: The whole expression can occupy a subject or object slot. An attributive adjective combines with a form otherwise used as a personal pronoun.
The younger me has overt determination. Halm also reports bare age-modified forms, including 12 year old me as the subject of a relative clause.
An exhausted me and a visibly shaken Giuliani combine a/an with an adjective that characterizes a participant identified independently by the pronoun or name.
The young Isaac Newton and the five-year-old you can each pick out a life stage, anchored by a name in the first case and by the addressee pronoun in the second.
In we linguists, we occupies the determiner slot and precedes a lexical head. In the younger us, the article occupies that slot and us follows the modifier.

grounds.note: Reports adjectivally modified forms across person and number, split agreement and third-person anaphora when stages are juxtaposed.
The general personal-pronoun examples in CGEL restrict pre-head dependents and give ordinary subject–reflexive person agreement.

projection.target: The modified NP can take a singular verb form unavailable to ordinary you, while an antecedent containing me can support myself. A stage contrast can also support third-person anaphora.
projection.evidence: Halm’s contrasts separate finite agreement from the selection of coreferential forms. The article alone leaves the head’s lexical category open.

known_boundary_items: Poor old me is CGEL’s bare evaluative pattern. The younger me can pick out a life stage and occurs in a pattern that also permits a younger me.
A he or a she can denote a person of a category and lacks the ordinary speaker or addressee anchoring tested here.

curious.title: Adjectives in front of me, you and us
curious.summary: A pronoun such as you or me can take an adjective in front of it to pick out a stage of a person's life or the state they were in.
curious.body: In The five-year-old you was so cute!, the word you still means the person being addressed. The adjective adds an age, so the phrase picks out one stage of that person. In An exhausted me has felt, the word me still means the speaker, and exhausted adds the state the speaker was in. These phrases show a split. The verb in the first example is was, not the were that ordinary you goes with, yet a phrase containing me can still go with myself, as in Questions A Younger Me Would Ask Myself. This dictionary says that what kind of word the head is, and why the split happens, remain open.

examples.text: Questions [A Younger Me] Would Ask Myself

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, personal pronouns modified by an adjective, as in the five-year-old you or an exhausted me.
teacher.explain: An attributive adjective can combine with a form otherwise used as a personal pronoun. The pronoun anchors the reference (the addressee, the speaker); the adjective picks out a stage or aspect of that person (the five-year-old you), or characterizes the person's state (an exhausted me). In subject position the whole phrase can take third-person verb agreement, as in the five-year-old you was. A coreferential reflexive can keep the pronoun's person (A Younger Me ... Myself). This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional: the category of the head and the explanation for the split agreement remain open.

examples.text: Questions [A Younger Me] Would Ask Myself

contrasts.text: The five-year-old you was so cute!
contrasts.note: The verb is was, which contrasts with ordinary second-person you were.

contrasts.text: Questions A Younger Me Would Ask Myself
contrasts.note: The reflexive keeps first person.

watch_for: A learner might assume the verb must agree with you as an ordinary second-person pronoun, as in you were.
A learner might take Poor old me, which this dictionary lists as a separate bare evaluative pattern, to be the same construction as the younger me.
A learner might read an exhausted me as picking out a different person, when me still identifies the speaker.
teacher.activity: Students write a sentence about themselves at an earlier age, starting with The ... me or The ... you, and one about a state (tired, nervous). Compare how the verb and any reflexive look in each, without deciding which analysis is right.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Adjectivally Modified Personal Pronoun NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/modified-personal-pronoun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Monotransitive VP

1.definition: Realizes one participant as a direct object of the verb.

projection.target: The object can bear accusative pronoun case and, with a suitable verb, correspond to the subject of a passive. A PP complement has different internal syntax.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Verbs with one object
curious.summary: Some verbs are followed by a single phrase naming the thing the action is done to.
curious.body: In The carpenter replaced the hinge, the verb replaced is followed by one phrase, the hinge. That phrase is the direct object. It names the thing that was replaced, and the verb has no other object after it. Two tests help you spot a direct object. A pronoun in that position takes its object form, as in She thanked him. And with a suitable verb, it can become the subject of a passive sentence: The hinge was replaced. A phrase that begins with a preposition, as in waited for the hinge, has different internal structure.

examples.text: The hinge was [replaced] by the carpenter.

curious.try: Take a sentence with a verb and one object, such as She thanked him. Can you turn it round so the object becomes the subject, as in He was thanked?

teacher.summary: Basic transitive verbs with a single direct object, and how to tell an object from a prepositional phrase.
teacher.explain: A monotransitive verb phrase has a head verb and one direct object (Od) realized by a noun phrase, as in replaced the hinge. Two tests support object status: an object can bear accusative pronoun case (thanked him), and with a suitable verb it corresponds to the subject of a passive (The hinge was replaced). A prepositional phrase complement, as in waited for the hinge, has different internal syntax and isn't a direct object. The pattern specializes the general verb phrase, and this dictionary lists the passive as related. The analysis is marked provisional with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Transitive verb is the traditional term; monotransitive is used here to contrast with ditransitive, which takes two objects.

contrasts.note: A noun phrase direct object.

contrasts.text: The carpenter waited for the hinge.
contrasts.note: A prepositional phrase complement, with different internal syntax.

watch_for: A learner might treat the preposition phrase in waited for the hinge as a direct object.
A learner might assume every verb with a noun phrase after it allows a passive, though this dictionary says only a suitable verb does.
teacher.activity: Give students verb cards (replace, thank, wait). They write a sentence with each, mark the direct object where there is one, and try the passive for each.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Monotransitive VP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/monotransitive-vp-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Month-First Calendar Date

1.definition: Identifies a day by its ordinal position within the named month.
1.details: In June fourteenth, the final numeral identifies the day of the month. The same convention can be written June 14. The month name and day number can do this without an article or a preposition inside the date. A separately formed expression such as the fourteenth of June identifies the same date by a different order and marking.

examples.note: Published example with month followed by an ordinal.
Constructed example in the articleless written format.

relatedConstructions.notes: The two patterns conventionally pick out different calendrical units by number.
The day numeral identifies a position in a conventional system.

grounds.note: Gives Month-plus-Date as a worked example of constructional annotation.

projection.target: A day numeral after a month name is interpreted as an index within that month, with the same interpretation available to ordinal forms and written digits.
projection.evidence: The FrameNet chapter identifies the two slots and their contributions. The restricted month-first pattern leaves other date formats to separate accounts.

curious.title: Dates written month first
curious.summary: A month name followed by a number picks out a day, as in June 14 or November 18.
curious.body: In June 14th, the number after the month tells you which day of that month is meant. It can be written as a digit, June 14, or as an ordinal, June fourteenth. The date needs no the or of inside it. The same date can also be said in another order, with extra words: the fourteenth of June. That pattern uses different order and marking. This dictionary describes only the month-first pattern here and leaves other date formats to separate accounts.
curious.try: Write today's date in the month-first way. Then say it again the other way, starting with the number.

teacher.summary: Helps with month-first dates and how the day number relates to the month name.
teacher.explain: A month name followed by a day number identifies a day by its ordinal position within that month. The number can be written as a digit or an ordinal (June 14, June 14th, June fourteenth). No article or preposition appears inside the date. The fourteenth of June identifies the same date with a different order and marking, so teach it as a separate pattern. This dictionary's high-confidence account covers the month-first pattern only. The number works as an index in a conventional system, like the numeral in a numerical label.
teacher.terms: Ordinal number is the traditional term for fourteenth. Month-first is this dictionary's label for the order.

contrasts.note: Month first, with no article or preposition.
The same date with a different order and marking.

watch_for: A learner might read the 14 in June 14 as counting something rather than naming a day.
A learner might add the or of inside a month-first date.
A learner might think June 14 and the fourteenth of June name different days.
teacher.activity: Students write their birthdays in the month-first way, then say them aloud with ordinal numbers. Next they say each birthday in the other order and compare what words changed.

child.hook: Can you say your birthday starting with the month?
child.explain: A month name followed by a number can name a day. June 14th is the fourteenth day of June. You can also say the fourteenth of June.
child.play: Write your birthday starting with the month. Then say it out loud using the number word, like fourteenth. Try a friend's birthday too.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Month-First Calendar Date." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/month-day-date-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Common Noun

dimensions.form: Noun stem; typically uncapitalized; takes number and case inflection
dimensions.meaning: Denotes class or category of entities; supports count/non-count distinction
dimensions.function: Head of Nom; provides descriptive content for reference
dimensions.distribution: Heads Nom in common NPs; modifier position in N-N compounds

1.definition: Provides a nominal description usable with ordinary NP determination when the count and number profile permits it

relatedConstructions.notes: Parallel noun category

projection.target: A use like the tallest building can identify a unique referent while keeping a common lexical head. Identification alone therefore does not predict the distribution of a proper noun.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates proper-noun specialization from syntactic determination and reference.

curious.title: Words for kinds of things
curious.summary: Common nouns like dog and city name a kind or category, not one particular individual.
curious.body: Dog and city are common nouns. Each names a class or category of things. Common nouns take endings for number (dog, dogs) and are typically written without a capital letter. A common noun can still lead to one particular thing. In the tallest building, the phrase can pick out a single building, yet building is still a common noun. Picking out one thing doesn't, by itself, make a word a name.
curious.try: Pick a word for a kind of thing in the room. Does it also name one particular thing, or the whole kind?

teacher.summary: Teaches the basic noun category, and how it differs from the proper noun.
teacher.explain: A common noun denotes a class or category of entities. It is the head of a nominal, supplies descriptive content for reference, takes number and case inflection, and supports the count and non-count distinction. Dog and city are this dictionary's examples. The pattern provides a nominal description usable with ordinary determination when the count and number profile permits it. Identification alone doesn't make a noun proper: the tallest building can identify a unique referent while keeping a common noun as its head. Compare with the proper noun, a parallel noun category.
teacher.terms: Common noun is the traditional term and the one used here. Countable and uncountable nouns are sometimes called count and non-count nouns; this dictionary prefers non-count.

contrasts.note: Identifies one building, but the head word building is still a common noun.

watch_for: A learner might treat a noun as proper whenever a phrase points to one individual, such as the tallest building.
A learner might assume every common noun can follow a cardinal number, though this dictionary says the count and number profile has to permit it.
teacher.activity: Students list five common nouns from the classroom. For each, they say whether it can follow a, much or a cardinal number, then compare lists with a partner.

child.hook: Which words name a kind of thing, like dog?
child.explain: Words like dog and city name a kind of thing. They don't name just one special one. Even in the tallest building, the main word is still building.
child.play: Look around. Say five words for kinds of things, like chair or tree. Then say one special name for each, like a friend's name for their pet.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Common Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/n-common-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Plural Common Noun

1.definition: Plural-marked common noun; plural agreement and determinative selection. Typically denotes more than one instance, though lexicalized and non-canonical plurals diverge

projection.target: Cats licenses plural verbal agreement and cardinals greater than one. A plural-only form such as scissors also takes plural agreement, while counting individual instruments ordinarily uses pairs of scissors.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts ordinary plurals and plural-only nouns, including restrictions on count determination.

curious.title: Plural words for kinds of things
curious.summary: A plural common noun such as dogs or cities typically names more than one of something and goes with plural verbs.
curious.body: Dogs and cities are plural common nouns. They go with plural verbs, and with numbers greater than one: Two cats are asleep. They typically stand for more than one of something. Some plural words work differently. Scissors takes a plural verb too, but it names a single tool made of two blades. To count the tools one by one, people ordinarily say pairs of scissors. This dictionary notes that special and irregular plurals can depart from the typical meaning.
curious.try: Think of something you own more than one of. Say a short sentence about them. Does the verb change from the one-thing version?

teacher.summary: Covers plural common nouns, the verb and number words they go with, and plural-only nouns such as scissors.
teacher.explain: A plural common noun is plural-marked, selects plural agreement and plural-selecting determinatives, and typically denotes more than one instance. Cats licenses plural verbal agreement and cardinals greater than one. Lexicalized and non-canonical plurals diverge from that typical meaning. A plural-only form such as scissors also takes plural agreement, but counting individual instruments ordinarily uses pairs of scissors. The pattern interfaces with verb-number agreement, and this dictionary lists the quasi-count noun as a related construction.
teacher.terms: Plural-only nouns are sometimes called pluralia tantum.

contrasts.note: Cardinal above one with a plural verb.

contrasts.text: She bought two pairs of scissors.
contrasts.note: Individual tools are counted with pairs of.

watch_for: A learner might think every plural form names more than one thing, when scissors names one tool.
A learner might use a singular verb after a plural noun.
teacher.activity: Students sort a list of plural nouns (dogs, cities, scissors) into those that name more than one thing and those that don't, then write one sentence for each with the right verb form.

child.hook: How do you count scissors?
child.explain: Plural nouns tell us about more than one thing, like dogs or cities. But scissors is a plural word for one tool. To count them, we say pairs of scissors.
child.play: Find a plural word for things you use. Say a sentence about two of them. Try scissors with pairs of.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Plural Common Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/n-common-pl-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Non-count Noun

1.definition: Non-count morphosyntax with a default substance/aggregate construal

stabilisers.evidence: early mapping of substance terms to non-count frames
high-frequency non-count nouns anchor quantifier patterns
stable non-count marking conventions across generations
need to distinguish substance from individuated reference

projection.target: In much coffee, coffee has non-count distribution. Two coffees permits a count reading because the context supplies portions or varieties. The individual lexical form alone does not decide the syntactic use.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares count and non-count uses of the same substance nouns, including drink names.

perturbations: portioning practices or registers promote count conversion

known_boundary_items: beer
chicken
paper
furniture
cattle
police

curious.title: Words for stuff you don't count
curious.summary: Non-count nouns such as water and rice name something thought of as stuff, not as separate items.
curious.body: Water and rice are non-count nouns. They name something thought of as undifferentiated stuff. They reject cardinal numbers, they take much and less, and they default to singular agreement: much coffee. The same word can sometimes shift. Two coffees works because the context supplies portions or varieties, such as cups or kinds. So the word alone doesn't decide how it's used, and this dictionary lists beer, chicken, paper, furniture, cattle and police as words near the boundary. The analysis is provisional.
curious.try: Think of something you pour or scoop. Does it go with much? Can you shift it to mean cups or kinds?

teacher.summary: Teaches the count and non-count distinction, with flexible cases such as two coffees as context-dependent shifts.
teacher.explain: A non-count noun has non-count morphosyntax and, by default, a substance or aggregate construal. Diagnostics: it rejects cardinals, takes much and less, and defaults to singular agreement. In much coffee, coffee has non-count distribution; Two coffees permits a count reading because the context supplies portions or varieties. The individual lexical form alone doesn't decide the syntactic use, and speakers vary on how flexible particular words are. Near the boundary are beer, chicken, paper, furniture, cattle and police. This dictionary treats the category as a provisional profile.
teacher.terms: Mass noun and uncountable noun are traditional names for non-count nouns. This dictionary uses non-count.

contrasts.note: Non-count distribution with much.
A count reading; context supplies cups or kinds.

watch_for: A learner might assume a noun that names a substance can't ever appear with a number, though context can supply portions or varieties.
A learner might take chicken, paper or beer to belong to one category only, when this dictionary lists them near the boundary.
teacher.activity: Students sort a list of food and drink words (water, rice, coffee, beer, paper). They test each with much, then with a number. Discuss which words shift when the context supplies cups, portions or kinds.

child.hook: Why do we say much rice but count apples?
child.explain: Some words name stuff, like water and rice. We don't count the stuff itself. We say much water. But two coffees can mean two cups of coffee.
child.play: Find words for stuff in the kitchen. Try each one with much. Then think of a cup or a bowl that lets you count it.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Non-count Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/n-non-count-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Plural Noun

1.definition: Plural number form; selects plural agreement and combines with cardinals above one. Typically construes referents as more than one unit, but the category is morphosyntactic, not semantic (cf. pluralia tantum)

projection.target: Plural noun form does not require the spelling -s or direct counting. Sheep can show plural agreement with no suffix, and scissors typically needs a unit expression to count individual instruments.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s irregular and plural-only forms supply independent contrasts for number marking and countability.

curious.title: Plural nouns without -s
curious.summary: A plural noun is defined by how it behaves in a sentence, not by an -s ending or by meaning more than one.
curious.body: Cats and books are plural nouns. They go with plural verbs and with numbers above one. But a plural noun doesn't need to end in -s. Sheep can go with a plural verb with no ending at all. Plural doesn't have to mean more than one thing. Scissors is plural, yet counting individual tools needs a phrase such as pairs of scissors. This dictionary calls plural a form category, not a meaning category: it typically suggests more than one unit, but that isn't what defines it.
curious.try: Find a plural word that doesn't end in -s. Put it in a sentence and see which verb fits.

teacher.summary: Explains that plural is a grammatical form, with irregular and plural-only nouns as test cases.
teacher.explain: A plural noun has the plural number form: it selects plural agreement and combines with cardinals above one. It typically construes the referents as more than one unit, but the category is morphosyntactic, not semantic (cf. plural-only nouns). A plural doesn't require the spelling -s or direct counting: sheep can show plural agreement with no suffix, and scissors typically needs a unit expression to count individual instruments. This dictionary's irregular and plural-only forms offer independent contrasts for number marking and countability. Zero plurals and plural common nouns are related patterns.
teacher.terms: Plural-only nouns are sometimes called pluralia tantum, the term this dictionary uses.

contrasts.text: The sheep are in the field.
contrasts.note: Plural agreement with no -s on the noun.

contrasts.text: She bought two pairs of scissors.
contrasts.note: Counting tools needs a unit expression.

watch_for: A learner might assume every plural noun ends in -s.
A learner might assume that plural has to mean more than one thing, though this dictionary says the category is a form category, not a semantic one.
teacher.activity: Students sort nouns into those with -s plurals, those with other plurals, and those that behave as plural only. They write each in a sentence with a plural verb.

child.hook: Is it one sheep or two sheep? Does the word change?
child.explain: Plural nouns tell us about more than one thing. Some end in -s, like cats and books. But sheep can be plural without changing. We say the sheep are in the field.
child.play: Say a sentence about two cats. Then say one about two sheep. Notice which word changes and which does not.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Plural Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/n-pl-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Proper Noun

dimensions.form: Noun specialized to head proper names; morphologically simple or compound. Normally written with an initial capital, subject to lexical and stylistic exceptions.
dimensions.meaning: Individual-specific, archetypal, institutional, or geographical features
dimensions.function: Head of proper NP; licenses bare NP without determiner
dimensions.distribution: Heads Nom in proper NPs; modifier position in N-N compounds

1.definition: Denotes individual-specific feature bundle
1.details: Core semantic features characterizing a particular individual

2.details: Characteristic semantic features that can ground metaphorical extension

3.details: Semantic features associated with institutional entities

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional syntax-semantics interface; proper nouns cue proper-name interpretation, proper-name intention licenses proper noun choice
Proper noun formally heads proper NP (via Nom)

projection.target: Proper noun and proper name need not have the same extent. New Zealand is a multiword name, and a noun normally used as a name can appear in an explicitly descriptive NP such as another Einstein.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates the word category from the whole designation and documents secondary uses.

curious.title: Names and the words that make them
curious.summary: A proper noun is a word specialized to serve as the main word of a name, such as Einstein, Waterloo, Harvard or Everest.
curious.body: Einstein, Waterloo, Harvard, Pacific and Everest are all proper nouns. Each is the main word of a name, and each carries associations. Einstein brings to mind a particular person. Waterloo brings to mind defeat, Harvard a university and Everest a mountain. A name can be longer than the word that heads it: New Zealand is a name of more than one word. A word normally used as a name can also appear in a descriptive phrase, as in another Einstein. Proper nouns are normally written with a capital letter, with some exceptions.
curious.try: Think of a name for a person, a place and a group. Which of them could have a descriptive phrase around it, such as another one?

teacher.summary: Separates the proper noun as a word category from the proper name, with secondary uses such as another Einstein.
teacher.explain: A proper noun is a noun specialized to head proper names. It is morphologically simple or compound and normally written with an initial capital, subject to lexical and stylistic exceptions. A proper noun heads a proper noun phrase and can appear without a determiner. In this dictionary, proper noun is a syntactic category and proper name a semantic one, and they need not have the same extent: New Zealand is a multiword name, and a noun normally used as a name can occur in a descriptive phrase such as another Einstein. This dictionary groups features as individual (Einstein), archetypal (Waterloo), institutional (Harvard) and geographical (Pacific, Everest).
teacher.terms: Proper noun is the traditional term and the one used here. This dictionary separates it from proper name, which it treats as a semantic category.

contrasts.note: A multiword name; the proper noun and the name differ in extent.
A name-type noun in a descriptive phrase.

watch_for: A learner might think the capital letter alone makes a word a proper noun.
A learner might treat New Zealand as one word because it is one name.
A learner might think proper noun and proper name are the same category.
teacher.activity: Students list names of people, places and institutions. For each name, they say whether it is a single word or several, and they write one descriptive phrase using a name, such as another one.

child.hook: Why does Kim get a capital letter but dog doesn't?
child.explain: A proper noun is a word used as a name, like Einstein or Everest. New Zealand is one name made of two words. A name normally starts with a capital letter.
child.play: Write names of a person, a pet, a town and a mountain. Circle the capital letters. Which names have more than one word?

checked.note: Fixed: child explain no longer uses the unexplained technical sense of 'heads a name'; it now says a proper noun is a word used as a name, with Einstein and Everest as examples and New Zealand as a two-word name. Also fixed (unflagged): curious summary and body replaced 'heads a name' with 'the main word of a name' for the same reason.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Proper Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/n-proper-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Singular Noun

1.definition: Singular number form; selects singular agreement and singular-selecting determinatives. Typically construes the referent as a single unit, but the category is morphosyntactic, not semantic

projection.target: Cat combines with a and singular agreement, while rice can take singular agreement without permitting a in its substance use. Singular agreement by itself does not identify singular count syntax.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates morphological number, countability, and formal agreement.

curious.title: Singular nouns
curious.summary: Singular is a form of a noun that selects singular agreement, and it's a matter of form, not of counting one.
curious.body: Cat and book are singular nouns. They go with a, as in a cat, and with singular verbs, as in The cat sleeps. They typically stand for a single unit. Singular is a matter of form, not of meaning. Rice, in its substance sense, can go with a singular verb but doesn't take a. So a singular verb on its own doesn't show that a noun is a singular count noun. This dictionary treats morphological number, countability and verb agreement as separate things.
curious.try: Pick a word for a thing and a word for stuff. Which one goes with a?

teacher.summary: Explains singular as a form category, with rice as a case where singular agreement does not mean singular count syntax.
teacher.explain: A singular noun has the singular number form: it selects singular agreement and singular-selecting determinatives, and typically construes its referent as a single unit. The category is morphosyntactic, not semantic. Cat combines with a and singular agreement, while rice can take singular agreement without permitting a in its substance use. Singular agreement by itself therefore doesn't identify singular count syntax. This dictionary separates morphological number, countability and formal agreement, and lists the non-count noun and verb-number agreement as related patterns.
teacher.terms: Singular is the traditional term. Singular count noun names the pattern with a.

contrasts.note: A singular count noun with a.
Singular agreement, but this is a non-count use that doesn't take a.

watch_for: A learner might assume that a singular verb shows that a noun is a singular count noun.
A learner might assume singular nouns have to name exactly one unit, when the category is a form category.
teacher.activity: Students list singular count nouns (cat, book) and write a sentence with each, using a and a singular verb. They then try rice in its substance use and compare.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.activity no longer lists rice as a singular noun alongside cat and book (the entry gives rice as singular agreement without a); curious.summary no longer reads as a general test for singular form.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Singular Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/n-sg-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Negative Concord
pattern: clause with verbal negation and/or multiple negative expressions interpreted together

entry.name: Negative Concord
entry.pattern: clause with verbal negation and/or multiple negative expressions interpreted together

1.definition: Expresses a single negation through more than one negative-marked item in the relevant variety.

projection.target: In concord varieties this can mean nobody was told. A two-negation interpretation is also possible in other systems or with a specially contrastive context.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Two negative words, one negation
curious.summary: In some varieties of English, more than one negative word in a clause can express a single negation.
curious.body: In I didn't tell nobody about it, both didn't and nobody are negative words. In varieties with negative concord, the sentence expresses one negation and can mean that nobody was told. Other systems can read two negative words differently, as two negations. A specially contrastive context can also bring out that two-negation reading. The reading depends on the variety, not on the words alone.
curious.try: Listen for a sentence with two negative words, such as didn't and nobody. Does the speaker seem to mean one negation or two?

teacher.summary: Explains how multiple negative expressions can express a single negation, with the reading depending on the variety.
teacher.explain: Negative concord is a pattern in which a clause with verbal negation and/or multiple negative expressions is interpreted as expressing a single negation. In I didn't tell nobody about it, the interpretation in a concord variety is that nobody was told. A two-negation interpretation is also possible in other systems or with a specially contrastive context. Related patterns include primary-auxiliary negation and the determinative no.
teacher.terms: Negative concord is the term this dictionary uses for the single-negation interpretation.

contrasts.text: I didn't tell nobody about it.
contrasts.note: In a concord variety, one negation, meaning nobody was told.

watch_for: A learner might read two negative words as cancelling each other to give a positive meaning, when in a concord variety they express one negation.
A learner might assume that every variety interprets two negative words the same way.
teacher.activity: Discuss with students how the sentence I didn't tell nobody about it would be understood in a variety with negative concord and in a system with two negations. Ask them to explain the difference in meaning each reading gives.

checked.note: Fixed: cut the 'double negative / double negation' term from teacher terms (the entry does not support it as a label for the form); curious body trimmed a sentence claiming the dictionary describes each reading, which the entry does not do.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Negative Concord." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/negative-concord-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Inversion after Preposed Negative or Restrictive Expression
pattern: Clause[preposed negative/restrictive dependent + finite Aux + Subject + VP]

entry.name: Inversion after Preposed Negative or Restrictive Expression
entry.pattern: Clause[preposed negative/restrictive dependent + finite Aux + Subject + VP]

1.definition: Uses auxiliary-first order within the nucleus after certain negative or restrictive expressions.

examples.form: [Only after the meeting did I find out].

examples.note: Constructed comparison. The non-restrictive fronted adjunct does not trigger inversion.

projection.target: Only after the meeting triggers inversion in this use. After the meeting I found out differs in auxiliary placement, and only modifying the subject does not trigger it.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Flipping the helper verb after a restricting opening
curious.summary: After an opening phrase such as only after the meeting, the helper verb comes before the subject.
curious.body: In Only after the meeting did I find out, the helper verb did comes before the subject I. The opening phrase narrows the claim, and that is what triggers the flip. Compare After the meeting I found out. Here the opening phrase doesn't narrow the claim, the subject stays first, and no helper verb is needed. This dictionary describes the flip as tied to certain negative or restrictive opening phrases, not to opening phrases in general.

examples.text: [Only after the meeting did I find out].

curious.try: Start a sentence with only after and finish it. Where does the helper verb go?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, auxiliary-first order after a preposed negative or restrictive expression.
teacher.explain: After certain preposed negative or restrictive expressions, a clause uses auxiliary-first order: finite auxiliary, then subject, then verb phrase. Only after the meeting did I find out shows it. In After the meeting I found out, the non-restrictive fronted adjunct doesn't trigger inversion. Only modifying the subject doesn't trigger it either. In the example the finite auxiliary is did. This dictionary lists finite do-support and complement preposing as related patterns, and marks the analysis provisional with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called subject-auxiliary inversion, a broader label than this dictionary's pattern, which covers inversion after preposed negative or restrictive expressions.

examples.text: [Only after the meeting did I find out].

contrasts.text: Only after the meeting did I find out.
contrasts.note: A restrictive fronted phrase triggers auxiliary-first order.

contrasts.text: After the meeting I found out.
contrasts.note: A non-restrictive fronted adjunct leaves the subject first.

watch_for: A learner might invert the subject and auxiliary after any fronted phrase.
A learner might expect the subject to come right after the opening phrase, as it does in After the meeting I found out.
teacher.activity: Students front only after the meeting, only then or similar phrases and rewrite each sentence with auxiliary-first order. Then they front a non-restrictive phrase and compare the word order.

checked.note: Fixed: removed the general rule about supplying do (the entry only illustrates did and lists finite do-support as related); replaced the matching watch_for item; qualified the subject-auxiliary inversion term as broader. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Inversion after Preposed Negative or Restrictive Expression." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/negative-initial-inversion-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Polarity-Sensitive Temporal ever
pattern: temporal ever in a licensing environment

entry.name: Polarity-Sensitive Temporal ever
entry.pattern: temporal ever in a licensing environment

1.definition: Ranges over occasions or times, especially under negation or questioning.

relatedConstructions.notes: Have you ever seen it? licenses ever in a question and supplies no negative assertion. Jo never saw it has negation within the temporal adverb.

projection.target: The affirmative counterpart Lee has ever sailed solo is marked without a special licensor. Superlatives and other suitable environments also permit ever.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: The word ever in questions and negatives
curious.summary: Ever meaning at any time fits in questions, negatives and some other settings, but is marked in a plain positive statement.
curious.body: In Has Lee ever sailed solo?, the word ever asks about any occasion at all. It fits in questions and under negation. It also fits in other suitable settings, such as superlatives. A plain positive statement is different: the affirmative counterpart of the question is marked, because it has no special licensor. This dictionary links the use to the setting it appears in, not to the word on its own. Have you ever seen it? asks a question and doesn't state anything negative.
curious.try: Ask a question with ever, then change the question into a plain statement. What changes?

teacher.summary: Explains temporal ever as a polarity-sensitive adverb that needs a licensing context.
teacher.explain: Temporal ever ranges over occasions or times, especially under negation or questioning. The affirmative counterpart, Lee has ever sailed solo, is marked without a special licensor, while superlatives and other suitable environments also permit ever. Have you ever seen it? licenses ever in a question and supplies no negative assertion, whereas Jo never saw it has negation within the temporal adverb. This dictionary links the pattern to the experiential perfect and notes the analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Negative polarity item is the textbook name for an expression like ever that needs a licensing context.

contrasts.note: Ever in a question; no negative assertion.
Negation is inside never.

watch_for: A learner might think ever is negative itself, when a question can license it without any negative assertion.
A learner might use ever in a plain positive statement without a licensing context.
teacher.activity: Students write three questions with ever and three statements with never, then say which setting each one uses. Discuss that a question with ever makes no negative assertion.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Polarity-Sensitive Temporal ever." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/negative-polarity-ever-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Inferred Embedded Negation under a Matrix Negative
pattern: matrix negation + opinion/expectation predicate + content clause

entry.name: Inferred Embedded Negation under a Matrix Negative
entry.pattern: matrix negation + opinion/expectation predicate + content clause

1.definition: Often invites a negative interpretation in the subordinate content while expressing negation in the matrix.

examples.form: I [don’t think the shop is open].
I [don’t believe the gate is open], but I have no view on whether it is closed.
examples.note: Constructed comparison. The continuation can cancel the ordinary interpretation that the speaker believes it closed.

projection.target: The natural interpretation often approximates I think the shop isn’t open. The two differ if the speaker lacks an opinion either way. The availability depends on the matrix predicate and context.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Negatives that apply to the clause after them
curious.summary: With verbs like think, a negative in the main clause can invite a negative meaning in the clause after it.
curious.body: I don't think the shop is open often invites a negative meaning in the clause after think: roughly, I think the shop isn't open. The negation sits in the first clause, but the meaning is about the second. The two sentences can differ if the speaker has no opinion either way. I don't believe the gate is open, but I have no view on whether it is closed cancels the reading that the speaker believes it closed. This dictionary adds that how available the reading is depends on the main verb and the context.

examples.text: I [don't think the shop is open].
I [don't believe the gate is open], but I have no view on whether it is closed.

curious.try: Say I don't think it will rain. Does it sound like I think it won't rain, or like I'm not sure?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, a main-clause negative that is interpreted as negating the content clause.
teacher.explain: With a matrix negation, an opinion or expectation predicate and a content clause, the interpretation often shifts to a negative in the subordinate content. I don't think the shop is open is naturally read as approximating I think the shop isn't open. The two differ if the speaker lacks an opinion either way, as the comparison with I don't believe the gate is open shows. The availability of the reading depends on the matrix predicate and context. This dictionary treats the effect as an interpretive inference, not a change in the grammar of the clause.
teacher.terms: Negative raising or neg-raising is the traditional name for this effect.

examples.text: I [don't think the shop is open].
I [don't believe the gate is open], but I have no view on whether it is closed.

contrasts.text: I don't think the shop is open.
contrasts.note: Naturally read as I think the shop isn't open.

contrasts.text: I don't believe the gate is open, but I have no view on whether it is closed.
contrasts.note: The continuation cancels the ordinary interpretation.

watch_for: A learner might read I don't think as meaning I think not, though this dictionary notes the two differ when the speaker has no opinion.
A learner might assume any verb allows the negative reading, when this dictionary says it depends on the predicate and context.
teacher.activity: Students read pairs such as I don't think ... and I think ... isn't ... aloud and judge whether the meanings are the same. Then they add a continuation that says the speaker has no view, and discuss the difference.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Inferred Embedded Negation under a Matrix Negative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/negative-raising-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Correlative Coordination with neither … nor

1.definition: Negates both conjuncts in a coordination

examples.form: He [neither] knew [nor] cared where his children were.

constraints.description: Correlative markers neither and nor introduce paired coordinates.
Both coordinated alternatives fall under negation.

projection.target: The coordinator can link two phrases as in neither Jo nor Kai or two verb phrases as in neither called nor wrote. The construction differs from additive neither did Jo, which depends on a preceding negative assertion.
