projection.evidence: CGEL describes the correlative frame and the wider use of nor and neither following negative clauses.

curious.title: Neither this nor that
curious.summary: Neither ... nor links two things and says that neither of them applies.
curious.body: In Neither Kim nor Pat replied, the pair neither ... nor joins Kim and Pat, and the sentence denies the reply for both. It also joins actions: He neither knew nor cared where his children were says that he did not know and did not care. Both items fall under the negation. The pair can link two phrases, as in neither Jo nor Kai, or two verb phrases, as in neither called nor wrote. It is different from the neither in neither did Jo, which depends on a negative statement that came before it.

examples.text: He [neither] knew [nor] cared where his children were.

curious.try: Pick two friends. Say a sentence with neither and nor that denies something for both.

teacher.summary: Helps teach correlative neither ... nor, which negates both of two coordinated items.
teacher.explain: Neither ... nor is a correlative coordination: the markers neither and nor introduce paired coordinates, and both coordinated alternatives fall under negation. It can coordinate noun phrases (Neither Kim nor Pat replied) or verb phrases (He neither knew nor cared where his children were). It differs from additive neither, as in neither did Jo, which depends on a preceding negative assertion. This dictionary treats neither ... nor as a specialization of coordination and lists absolute negator determinatives and so-neither inversion as related.
teacher.terms: Correlative conjunction is a traditional name; this dictionary prefers correlative coordination, with nor as the coordinator.

examples.text: He [neither] knew [nor] cared where his children were.

contrasts.note: Neither and nor pair two noun phrases.

contrasts.text: Kim didn't call, and neither did Jo.
contrasts.note: Additive neither, which follows a negative statement.

watch_for: A learner might read Neither Kim nor Pat replied as saying only one of them did not reply.
A learner might treat the neither in neither did Jo as the paired neither ... nor.
teacher.activity: Students write pairs of true statements about two classmates (Kim doesn't sing, Pat doesn't sing). They combine each pair into a neither ... nor sentence, once with noun phrases and once with verb phrases.

child.hook: How can you say that two people both didn't do something?
child.explain: Neither and nor go together. Neither Kim nor Pat replied means Kim didn't reply and Pat didn't either.
child.play: Say something two friends both didn't do. Then say it again starting with neither and putting nor between their names.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Correlative Coordination with neither … nor." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/neither-nor-coordination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Adverbial Negation with never

1.definition: Negates occurrence over time (no instances at any time)

constraints.description: Adverbial negator modifying VP.
Negates the occurrence across the relevant time span.

projection.target: They never replied can take the positive tag did they? No auxiliary do is needed to host never in the declarative. Its temporal quantification and clausal polarity are independently testable.
projection.evidence: CGEL supplies the confirmation tag and compares never with negation plus ever.

curious.title: A word that means at no time
curious.summary: The adverb never says that something did not happen at any time.
curious.body: In She never called, the word never denies calling across the whole relevant stretch of time. It means that no calling events occurred. In I have never been there, it means that there are no prior occasions in the speaker's experience. Never doesn't need a helper verb: She never called has no did before it. It also changes the sentence's polarity. After They never replied, a confirmation tag such as did they? fits. This dictionary treats the time meaning and the negative sentence as two things that can be tested separately.
curious.try: Say something you've never done. Does the sentence need a helper such as did?

teacher.summary: Covers never as an adverb of negation, with a confirmation tag as a polarity test.
teacher.explain: Never is an adverbial negator modifying the verb phrase. It negates occurrence across the relevant time span, meaning no instances at any time. No auxiliary do is needed to host it in the declarative. A clause such as They never replied can take the positive confirmation tag did they?, which shows the clause is negative. Its temporal quantification and its clausal polarity are independently testable. This dictionary compares never with negation plus ever.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls it an adverbial negator, a negative adverb that modifies the verb phrase.

contrasts.note: The positive tag confirms that the clause is negative.
Negation plus ever, which this dictionary compares with the adverb.

watch_for: A learner might assume a helper do is needed to carry the adverb, though this dictionary says no auxiliary do is needed in the declarative.
A learner might think a negative adverb means the clause is not negative.
teacher.activity: Students write three sentences with the adverb, one in the simple past and two in the perfect. They add a positive confirmation tag to each and say whether it fits.

child.hook: What does never tell you about when something happens?
child.explain: Never means at no time. She never called means she didn't call even once. I have never been there means I have not been there before.
child.play: Say three things you have never done. Start each one with I have never.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Adverbial Negation with never." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/never-adv-negation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Negative determinative no in determiner function

1.definition: Negatively quantifies a nominal by asserting zero instances

constraints.description: A DP headed by the determinative no functions as determiner within the NP.
Construes the NP as having zero members or instances.

projection.target: No can determine a singular count, plural count, or non-count nominal. A clause with We saw no damage normally licenses a positive confirmation tag, linking the local determiner to wider clausal polarity.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the distributions of no and the distinct polarity diagnostics. Those are separable from the claim that a contextually relevant quantity is zero.

curious.title: No before a noun
curious.summary: Put before a noun, no says that there were zero instances of whatever the noun names.
curious.body: In no books and no evidence, the word no tells you that there were zero instances. No books means no books at all, and no evidence means an absence of evidence. No can go before a singular count noun, a plural count noun or a non-count noun. A clause with We saw no damage also normally takes a positive confirmation tag, such as did we? That ties the word before the noun to the sentence as a whole: it makes the whole sentence negative.
curious.try: Say We saw no damage, then add did we? Does the sentence still feel negative?

teacher.summary: Teaches no as a determinative that quantifies a noun phrase down to zero, with clause polarity as a test.
teacher.explain: No is a determinative in determiner function: a determinative phrase headed by no is the determiner in the noun phrase. It construes the noun phrase as having zero members or instances. It can determine a singular count, plural count or non-count nominal. We saw no damage normally licenses a positive confirmation tag, which links the local determiner to wider clausal polarity. This dictionary separates those polarity diagnostics from the claim that the relevant quantity is zero. This dictionary treats no as interfacing with primary-auxiliary negation.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls no a determinative (the word category) and uses determiner for the function it has in the noun phrase.

contrasts.text: We saw no damage, did we?
contrasts.note: The positive tag shows the clause is negative.
No before a singular count noun.

watch_for: A learner might think no needs a plural noun after it.
A learner might expect no to need a negative verb as well, when We saw no damage already makes the clause negative.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with no before a plural noun, a singular noun and a non-count noun. They add a confirmation tag to one and compare it with the plain clause.

child.hook: What does no mean in no books?
child.explain: When no comes before a word for a thing, it means zero, none at all. No books means there are no books. No evidence means there isn't any evidence.
child.play: Look around your room. Make a sentence that starts with There is no or There are no, naming something that is missing.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says no means zero before any word; it now ties the zero meaning to no before a noun, as in no books (the dictionary assigns it to no as a determiner in a noun phrase).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Negative determinative no in determiner function." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/no-determiner-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Nominal Construction
pattern: Optional modifiers + Required head (n-common-001 + {singular-001 | plural-001}) + Optional post modifiers/complements

entry.name: Nominal Construction
entry.pattern: Optional modifiers + Required head (n-common-001 + {singular-001 | plural-001}) + Optional post modifiers/complements

dimensions.form: Head noun with optional pre- and post-modifiers; number marking
dimensions.meaning: Descriptive content that restricts or elaborates the head's denotation
dimensions.function: Provides the core descriptive content of NP; hosts modification
dimensions.distribution: Immediately dominated by NP; can be bare in certain contexts

1.definition: Specifies/restricts feature bundles
1.details: Modifies/narrows the feature bundle denoted by the head

2.details: Extends relational aspects of feature bundle through complements

relatedConstructions.notes: Nom formally contains N as head
Nominal structure supplies the complement of the determiner function.

projection.target: An expansion of chair to old chair can fit inside the frame the __ without adding another determiner. The resulting old chair still normally requires a determiner as an independent singular count argument.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes the noun-headed phrase that determination combines with from the resulting NP.

curious.title: A noun with its describing words
curious.summary: The part of a noun phrase made of a noun and its modifiers, not counting the word like the in front.
curious.body: In wooden chair, the noun chair is described by wooden. In mother of three, of three adds more about the relation. In knowledge that it is true, the clause after knowledge tells you what the knowledge is about. This dictionary calls such a unit a nominal: a head noun with optional modifiers before it and optional modifiers or complements after it. It supplies the core description in a noun phrase. A nominal such as old chair fits in a frame like the ___ without adding another determiner.
curious.try: Start with a plain noun, such as chair. How many describing words can you add before and after it?

teacher.summary: Explains the nominal as the head noun plus its modifiers and complements, apart from the determiner.
teacher.explain: A nominal has a required head noun, optional pre-head modifiers and optional post-head modifiers or complements. Its descriptive content restricts or elaborates the head's denotation: wooden chair restricts material features and mother of three elaborates a relation. It is immediately dominated by the noun phrase and can be bare in certain contexts. An expansion of chair to old chair can fit inside the frame the ___ without adding another determiner, but the resulting old chair normally still requires a determiner as an independent singular count argument.
teacher.terms: Nom is the CGEL label used here. Some generative textbooks call a comparable unit N-bar.

contrasts.note: The determiner the plus the nominal old chair.
A nominal with a pre-head modifier.

watch_for: A learner might treat the determiner as part of the nominal.
A learner might assume the nominal can stand on its own as a full noun phrase, when old chair normally still needs a determiner as a singular count argument.
teacher.activity: Students take a plain noun, add a modifier before and a complement after (chair, old chair, mother of three), and say where a determiner would go.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Nominal Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/nom-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Adjectival Pre-head Modifier in Nominal

1.definition: Property attribution to nominal head

examples.note: Direct property attribution; Attribution of age property to men
Special case where property is relative to context; Complement set relation

constraints.description: Mod must be AdjP with head Adj
AdjP occurs in pre-head position in Nom

relatedConstructions.notes: Specific type of pre-head modification

grounds.locator: Ch. 5 §14.2; Ch. 6, attributive versus predicative functions

projection.target: In a former president, former modifies the relation expressed by president. The president is former does not give the same reading. A pre-head adjective need not have a matching predicative use.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes attributive uses and discusses adjectives restricted to particular functions.

curious.title: Describing words in front of a noun
curious.summary: An adjective phrase placed before a noun says something about it, as in old men.
curious.body: In old men, the word old says something about the men: they are old. The describing word comes before the noun it describes. Not every case is that direct. In other men, the property depends on the context. And in a former president, former doesn't describe the person in the way old describes men. It modifies the relation that president expresses. This dictionary notes that an adjective placed before a noun doesn't have to work in the same way after the verb be.
curious.try: Say an adjective before a noun, such as old men. Then try the adjective after is or are. Does it still say the same thing?

teacher.summary: Teaches pre-head adjective phrases in the nominal, and why attributive adjectives need not have predicative uses.
teacher.explain: A pre-head adjective phrase attributes a property to the head noun: in old men, old attributes age to the men. Other men is a special case where the property is relative to context, with a complement-set relation. The modifier must be an adjective phrase headed by an adjective, in pre-head position in the nominal. A pre-head adjective needn't have a matching predicative use: in a former president, former modifies the relation expressed by president, and the president is former doesn't give the same reading. This dictionary treats this as a specific type of pre-head modification.
teacher.terms: Attributive adjective is the traditional term for an adjective before the noun; predicative adjective is the traditional term for one after a verb such as be.

contrasts.note: Direct property attribution.
Property relative to context; complement-set relation.

watch_for: A learner might think every adjective before a noun can also follow be with the same meaning.
A learner might read other in other men as describing a property of the men themselves, as old does.
teacher.activity: Students write short noun phrases with an adjective before the noun. For each, they decide whether the adjective states a plain property or depends on context, and compare answers.

child.hook: Which word tells you more about the men in old men?
child.explain: A describing word can come before a noun. In old men, the word old tells us about the men. The describing word comes first.
child.play: Pick a noun, like dog or house. Add a describing word before it. Then try a different one, and see how the picture changes.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Adjectival Pre-head Modifier in Nominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/nom-adjp-mod-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Nominal Pre-head Modifier in Nominal

1.definition: The first nominal specifies the type or category of the second nominal.
1.details: Constraints: semantic: The first nominal denotes a type or category that the second nominal belongs to. Related constructions: n-common-001 (can-fill-left); n-common-001 (can-fill-right)

examples.note: Specifies the type of breeder: one who breeds dogs.
Specifies the type of factory: one that makes toys.

2.definition: The first nominal indicates the purpose or function of the second nominal.
2.details: Constraints: semantic: The first nominal denotes a purpose or function associated with the second nominal. Related constructions: n-common-001 (can-fill-left); n-common-001 (can-fill-right)

examples.note: A cup intended for holding coffee.

3.definition: The first nominal specifies the origin or location of the second nominal.
3.details: Constraints: semantic: The first nominal denotes a location or origin associated with the second nominal. Related constructions: n-common-001 (can-fill-left); n-common-001 (can-fill-right)

examples.note: Indicates the council is associated with a particular city.
Music originating from or associated with a particular country.

4.definition: The first nominal describes a defining characteristic of the second nominal
4.details: Constraints: semantic: The first nominal denotes a defining characteristic of the second nominal Related constructions: np-commonized-pron-001 (can-fill); n-common-001 (can-fill-left); n-common-001 (can-fill-right)

examples.note: The first nominal describes a defining characteristic of the second nominal
The first nominal describes a defining characteristic of the second nominal

5.definition: The first nominal has a relationship with the second nominal that is similar to that expressed by a genitive construction, indicating a relationship such as possession, association, or inalienable part.
5.details: Constraints: semantic: The relationship between the two nominals can often be paraphrased using a genitive construction (e.g., using 'of' or ''s'). Related constructions: np-gen-dep-001 (semantically-related-to); np-gen-indep-001 (semantically-related-to); n-common-001 (can-fill-left); n-common-001 (can-fill-right)

examples.note: Could be paraphrased as 'the government's land'.

constraints.description: A nominal functions as a pre-head modifier within a larger noun phrase.
The first nominal modifies the second nominal (which is the head of the larger NP). The head of the modifying nominal is a Noun.
The modifying nominal typically restricts or specifies the meaning of the head nominal.

relatedConstructions.notes: Original relationship: can-fill.
Original relationship: can-be-part-of.

projection.target: Dog breeders normally pluralizes the head breeders. In book review the first nominal can supply the topic or object of a reviewing event. In coffee cup it supplies a conventional purpose. The word order alone does not select the semantic relation.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes noun-headed phrases and compounds and analyzes dependents independently of the inferred relation.

curious.title: A noun in front of another noun
curious.summary: A noun can come before another noun to say what kind, what for or where from.
curious.body: In dog breeder, the first noun tells you what kind of breeder: one who breeds dogs. In coffee cup, it gives a purpose: a cup for holding coffee. In city council, it points to where the council belongs, and in baby food, it means food for babies. Word order alone doesn't say which relation is meant. In dog breeders, the plural normally goes on the second noun. In book review, the first noun can supply the topic or object of a reviewing event.
curious.try: Choose a noun, such as school. What different nouns can you put after it, and what relation does each one show?

teacher.summary: Covers noun-noun modification in the nominal, with several relations that word order alone doesn't signal.
teacher.explain: A nominal can modify the head noun of a larger nominal. The relation between the two isn't signalled by word order, and this dictionary lists several: type (dog breeder), purpose (coffee cup), origin or location (city council, country music), a defining characteristic, and a relation like a genitive (student representative, government land, baby food). Plural normally goes on the head noun: dog breeders. In book review the first nominal can supply the topic or object of a reviewing event. This dictionary distinguishes this pre-head modifier from the noun-noun compound, which it lists as a related construction.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats the first nominal as a pre-head modifier and lists the noun-noun compound as a separate, related construction.

contrasts.note: The first noun gives the type.
The first noun gives the purpose.
The first noun gives a location or origin.

watch_for: A learner might expect one fixed relation for every noun-noun pair, when word order alone doesn't select it.
A learner might put the plural on the first noun in dog breeders, when the head noun normally takes it.
teacher.activity: Students make cards with nouns (dog, coffee, city, baby) and heads (owner, cup, council, food). They combine each pair and explain the relation, and then compare with a partner who chose a different relation.

child.hook: What is a coffee cup? What is a dog breeder?
child.explain: A noun can come before another noun. A coffee cup is a cup for coffee. A dog breeder is someone who breeds dogs. The first word tells us more about the second.
child.play: Pick the word cup and put a different noun before it. Then do the same with food. What does each new pair mean?

checked.note: Fixed: teacher terms no longer equates the construction with noun-noun compound or noun adjunct (the entry distinguishes noun-headed phrases from compounds and lists the compound as related); plural-on-the-head statements now say 'normally' and the book review reading 'can' supply the topic or object, as in the entry. Frequency pass: teacher.activity head noun breeder (about 13,800th in SUBTLEX-UK, counting breeders) replaced by owner; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Nominal Pre-head Modifier in Nominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/nom-n-mod-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Pre-head Modifier in Nominal

1.definition: Modification of nominal head through pre-head constituent

curious.title: Words that come before the noun
curious.summary: A modifier can come before the head noun, as in old book or dog breeder.
curious.body: In old book, the word old comes before the noun book and modifies it. In dog breeder, the noun dog comes before breeder and modifies it. Both are examples of a pre-head modifier: something placed before the head noun in the nominal. This dictionary describes two kinds in these examples. In old book the modifier is an adjective. In dog breeder it is a noun. Each modifier is part of a nominal whose head is the noun after it.
curious.try: Choose a noun, such as book, and add a word before it. Is the word you added an adjective or a noun?

teacher.summary: The general pattern behind adjective-before-noun and noun-before-noun combinations.
teacher.explain: A nominal can contain a pre-head modifier: a constituent placed before the head noun. This dictionary's two examples show two types: an adjectival modifier (old book) and a nominal modifier (dog breeder). This dictionary treats this as the general pattern, and the adjective and nominal versions as more specific types. This dictionary gives only a definition and two examples for this pattern, so teach it as an umbrella over the two specific patterns.
teacher.terms: This dictionary's term is pre-head modifier; attributive adjective is a textbook term for the adjective case.

contrasts.note: Adjectival pre-head modifier.
Nominal pre-head modifier.

watch_for: A learner might think the modifier is the head of the whole phrase, when book and breeder are the heads.
A learner might treat the two examples as the same kind of modifier, when one is an adjective and the other a noun.
teacher.activity: Students write five short phrases with a word before a noun. They underline the head noun and mark each modifier as an adjective or a noun.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Pre-head Modifier in Nominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/nom-premod-000/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Nominal Pre-head Modifier

1.definition: A nominal that includes a pre-head modifier

projection.target: The head remains the source of the nominal’s ordinary number possibilities. Compare dog breeders, where breeders pluralizes, with old books, where books pluralizes. Premodifier category can be tested independently.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s account of nominal heads and internal modifiers separates the function from how an adjunct realizes it.

curious.title: Words placed before a noun to describe it
curious.summary: A noun can have a describing word in front of it, and that word can be an adjective or another noun.
curious.body: In old book, the word old sits in front of book and says what kind of book it is. In dog breeder, the word dog sits in front of breeder, and it's a noun doing a describing job. So the word in front can be a different kind of word each time. The word at the end keeps its ordinary number possibilities. It's the one that is made plural in dog breeders and old books.
curious.try: Put a describing word in front of a noun, then make the phrase plural. Which word changes?

teacher.summary: Useful for showing that a word before a noun can be an adjective or a noun, while the final noun keeps its own plural.
teacher.explain: This dictionary treats a nominal with a pre-head modifier as a pattern defined by the modifier's position, not its category. In old book the modifier is an adjectival one; in dog breeder it's a nominal one. The head noun keeps its ordinary number possibilities: dog breeders and old books both pluralize at the head. The category of the premodifier can therefore be tested separately from the function. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Premodifier is another name for a pre-head modifier. Attributive adjective is sometimes used for old in old book, and noun modifier for dog in dog breeder.
watch_for: A learner might look to the first word to mark the plural, when dog breeders and old books pluralize the head noun.
A learner might think the word before a noun must be an adjective.
teacher.activity: Give pairs of students a list of head nouns (owner, book, car). They add one adjective and one noun in front, then write the plural of each phrase and underline the word that changed.

child.hook: In dog breeder, which word tells you about the other one?
child.explain: A word can go in front of a noun to say more about it. In old book, old is describing the book. In dog breeder, dog is a noun, but it describes the breeder.
child.play: Pick a noun like book. Add three different words in front of it. Then make it plural. Which word changes?

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.watch_for no longer presents dogs breeder as a learner error (the entry does not assess it) and now says the head noun pluralizes in dog breeders and old books; curious.body limited to the head noun's ordinary number possibilities. Frequency pass: teacher.activity head nouns breeder and lamp (about 13,800th and 4,000th in SUBTLEX-UK, counting plurals) replaced by owner and car; entry examples unchanged.

name: Non-count NP for Material from Countable Things
pattern: NP[(Det compatible with non-count syntax) + noun ordinarily used in count syntax]

entry.name: Non-count NP for Material from Countable Things
entry.pattern: NP[(Det compatible with non-count syntax) + noun ordinarily used in count syntax]

1.definition: Describes material from identifiable objects or organisms without counting the original individuals.
1.details: Apple in there’s apple all over the floor can denote apple matter rather than whole apples. In the culinary reading the material is specifically meat, as with some rabbit. A determiner like the can leave count and non-count readings open. Which material a noun makes accessible depends on lexical convention and context.

examples.form: The toddler got [apple] all over the high chair.
examples.note: Constructed example with material distributed over a surface.
Constructed example with a culinary interpretation.

relatedConstructions.notes: The resulting use has non-count grammar.
Some chicken can use a count-associated noun for material. Two coffees gives a non-count-associated noun a portion reading and allows numeral and plural marking.

grounds.note: Distinguishes material, meat and renewed count interpretations.

projection.target: The non-count use permits amount expressions and suspends counting the source individuals. A shared surface form such as the rabbit can still be ambiguous between an animal and its meat.
projection.evidence: FrameNet contrasts general material construal with the culinary interpretation and shows that a culinary construal can in turn feed a portion reading.

curious.title: Treating a countable thing as stuff
curious.summary: A word for a single thing, like apple or rabbit, can be used for the material it's made of instead of for individual things.
curious.body: We think of apples as things we can count. But in The toddler got apple all over the high chair, apple means apple matter, the mushy stuff, not whole apples. Nobody is counting anything. The same shift happens in The stew contains some rabbit. Here rabbit means the meat, not an animal. The sentence is about how much, not how many. Which material a word brings to mind depends on the word and on the situation.

examples.text: The toddler got [apple] all over the high chair.

curious.try: Think of a word for a single thing, such as an animal or a fruit. Can you use it to mean the stuff it's made of?

teacher.summary: Helps explain how a count noun can be used with non-count grammar to mean material, including meat.
teacher.explain: A noun ordinarily used in count syntax can appear in an NP with non-count syntax, and then it describes material from identifiable objects or organisms without counting the individuals. Apple in there's apple all over the floor means apple matter. In the culinary reading the material is specifically meat, as in some rabbit. The resulting use has non-count grammar, and amount expressions are permitted. A determiner like the can leave both readings open, so the rabbit can be an animal or its meat. Which material a noun makes available depends on lexical convention and context. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the grinding use of a count noun. Non-count is the term used here in place of mass.

examples.text: The toddler got [apple] all over the high chair.

contrasts.text: The rabbit is in the garden.
contrasts.note: A count reading, an animal.
A non-count reading, meat.

watch_for: A learner might read apple in apple all over the floor as one whole apple.
A learner might take the rabbit to mean only the animal, when the same form can be ambiguous between an animal and its meat.
teacher.activity: Show pairs of pictures (a whole fruit; a smear of the same fruit). Students write one sentence for each, using a non-count phrase for the second, then share and compare.

child.hook: Does "apple" have to mean one whole apple?
child.explain: Sometimes a word for a thing can mean the stuff it's made of. If a toddler gets apple all over the chair, it's a mess, not a whole apple.

examples.text: The toddler got [apple] all over the high chair.

child.play: Pick a fruit and make two sentences. In one, use a whole fruit. In the other, use the fruit as stuff on a table or a floor.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Non-count NP for Material from Countable Things." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/non-count-material-construal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Additive not only … but also

1.definition: Asserts both contributions with the second presented as additional or noteworthy.

examples.form: She [not only signed it but also delivered it].

projection.target: The first contribution is included despite the overt not. Preposing not only plus a constituent can trigger inversion when the first coordinate is a clause.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Not only this, but that too
curious.summary: A pair of words, not only and but also, joins two things and presents the second as an extra.
curious.body: In She not only signed it but also delivered it, both things happened. The words not only might make you expect a denial, but the first part is still included: she did sign it. The second part is presented as something added, or something worth noticing. When the first part is a whole clause and not only comes first, the sentence can change its word order.

examples.text: She [not only signed it but also delivered it].

curious.try: Take two things someone did and join them with not only and but also. Do both things still count as true?

teacher.summary: Explains not only ... but also as a way of joining two items that both hold, with the second as an addition.
teacher.explain: Not only X but (also) Y is a coordination construction that asserts both contributions, with the second presented as additional or noteworthy. Despite the overt not, the first contribution is included. The dictionary treats it as a specialization of ordinary coordination. When not only plus a constituent is preposed and the first coordinate is a clause, inversion can follow. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a correlative conjunction, or a correlative pair. Here it's treated as a kind of coordination.

examples.text: She [not only signed it but also delivered it].

watch_for: A learner might read not only as negating the first part, when the first contribution is still included.
A learner might drop but when building the second part.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of simple facts about one person. They join each pair with not only and but also, then say whether both facts are true.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.watch_for no longer treats leaving out also as an error (the entry writes also in parentheses, so it is optional); it now mentions only but.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Additive not only … but also." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/not-only-but-also-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Noun Phrase
pattern: (Det:licensed XP +) Head:Nom, with independently licensed fused-head and pronominal realizations

entry.name: Noun Phrase
entry.pattern: (Det:licensed XP +) Head:Nom, with independently licensed fused-head and pronominal realizations

dimensions.form: Headed by N or pronoun; optional determiner, modifiers
dimensions.meaning: Referential or predicative; can denote entities, concepts, or properties
dimensions.function: Argument, topic, focus; anchors discourse referents
dimensions.distribution: Subject, object, complement of preposition, predicative complement

1.definition: Can refer to entities, concepts, or be purely grammatical
1.details: This is the most general NP construction, serving as a parent for all other NP types.

constraints.description: Must be a valid NP constituent

relatedConstructions.notes: NP formally contains Nom as immediate constituent
Fusion supplies a complete NP without an ordinary overt noun head.

projection.target: A complete nominal expression such as the small box can appear as subject and object. In those positions replacing it with the small alone ordinarily requires a recoverable noun or another independently licensed fused-head use.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares the distribution of NPs and nominals in larger constructions and describes the fused-head exceptions separately.

curious.title: Phrases that name things
curious.summary: A noun phrase is a word or group of words built around a head, which is ordinarily a noun or pronoun. It can point to a person, thing or idea.
curious.body: John, the book and he can all do the same job in a sentence: each one names or points to something. John is a name, the book is a noun with a small word in front, and he is a pronoun. Such a phrase can be the subject of a sentence or its object. It can also describe something, and it can point to things, ideas or qualities. This is the most general kind of noun phrase, and the dictionary uses it as a parent for more specific kinds.
curious.try: Pick a sentence and swap its subject for another phrase that names something. Does the sentence still work?

teacher.summary: Gives the general picture of a noun phrase and its realizations before more specific types are taught.
teacher.explain: The NP construction is headed by a noun or pronoun, with an optional determiner and modifiers. It can refer to entities and concepts, or be used predicatively. It occurs as subject, object, complement of a preposition and predicative complement. This is the most general NP construction and the parent of the more specific ones. A fused head supplies a complete NP without an ordinary overt noun. A complete nominal expression such as the small box can be subject or object, and replacing it with the small alone ordinarily needs a recoverable noun or another licensed fused-head use. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Noun phrase is the traditional name. Determiner is a function; the and a are determinatives (often called articles).
watch_for: A learner might think a noun phrase must contain a determiner, when a name such as John is a full noun phrase.
A learner might expect the small to stand in for the small box anywhere, when that ordinarily needs a recoverable noun or another licensed fused-head use.
teacher.activity: Write a short sentence on the board. Students underline each noun phrase, then say whether its head is a noun, a pronoun or something else (as in the small, said of cups).

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary now allows a single word as a noun phrase (this dictionary's examples John and he); teacher explain now uses this dictionary's wording 'complete nominal expression' and 'ordinarily'; watch_for on the small restated with 'ordinarily' and the licensed fused-head alternative. Dismissed in part: the, a as determinatives kept (standard CGEL classification, consistent with the determiner function this dictionary assumes); this and the demonstratives gloss cut. Second round: fixed curious.summary, which now says a noun phrase can point to a person, thing or idea rather than defining it by that use (the entry also allows predicative and purely grammatical uses). Dismissed the and a as determinatives again (CGEL's standard classification), and the flags on taking the head to be a noun or pronoun in curious.summary and teacher.activity (the entry's form is headed by N or pronoun, with fused heads licensed separately).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Noun Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Bare NP Construction

1.definition: Refers to/predicates non-count substance
1.details: Refers to or predicates non-count substance/material

2.definition: Uses a bare plural for kind reference, classification, or an indefinite set
2.details: Bare plurals can receive a kind, generic, predicative, or episodic interpretation from the construction around them.

examples.note: Episodic use with a contextually supplied set of dogs

3.definition: Ascribes a role with a bare singular count NP
3.details: A licensed role NP can be bare as a predicative, in certain prepositional frames, or as an ascriptive supplement. The same role noun generally needs a determiner when used as an ordinary argument referring to the incumbent.

4.details: Refers to uniquely identifiable individual through proper name

5.details: Refers to or predicates generic activity type

examples.note: Activity reference (the adjectival modifier supports the noun analysis; bare "playing piano" is a gerund-participial clause, not an NP)

6.details: Refers to or predicates temporal point/period

examples.note: Articleless place name with a nominal head
Specifies a place by its name

8.details: Refers to or predicates abstract notion/quality

projection.target: A bare NP can be singular count in a restricted role or naming use, while bare plurals and non-count nouns can normally be arguments. Compare Lee became chair, Chair called on the name reading, and We bought chairs.
projection.evidence: CGEL provides independent distributional grounds for these kinds of bare uses. Absence of a determiner alone does not fix their interpretation.

relatedConstructions.notes: The NP consists of its nominal and has no overt determiner.
Dogs barked and Those dogs barked share the same nominal. The overt demonstrative in the second selects a contextually identifiable set.

curious.title: Noun phrases with no small word in front
curious.summary: Some noun phrases stand alone with no the, a or similar word, and still work as subjects, objects and names.
curious.body: Water is essential. Dogs are loyal. Monday works. Toronto was the next stop. None of these phrases has a small word like the or a in front of its noun, yet each is a complete phrase. Which meaning you get depends on the sentence around the phrase. Dogs are loyal talks about dogs as a kind, while Dogs barked all night is about a set of dogs the context supplies. Role words can go bare too: Lee stayed president. A word like chair needs something in front of it in other sentences, but in Jo became chair it can stand alone.
curious.try: Say Dogs are loyal and Those dogs barked. What does the extra word those change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain when a noun phrase can appear without a determiner and why the reading depends on the construction.
teacher.explain: A bare NP consists of a nominal with no overt determiner. The dictionary lists uses for non-count substances (Water is essential), bare plurals (Dogs are loyal; Those are bears; Dogs barked all night), proper names, activities, times, places and abstract concepts. A singular count noun can be bare only in restricted roles or naming uses (Lee stayed president, Jo became chair), whereas bare plurals and non-count nouns can normally be arguments. Not having a determiner doesn't fix the interpretation: kind, classification, or an episodic set all depend on the surrounding construction. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a determinerless NP or a bare noun phrase. Bare plural is the usual name for dogs with no determiner.

contrasts.note: Bare plural, with a set of dogs supplied by context.
Same nominal with an overt demonstrative, selecting a contextually identifiable set.

watch_for: A learner might think a missing determiner means the sentence is incomplete.
A learner might use the same bare noun for the incumbent of a role as an ordinary argument, though the dictionary notes that such a noun needs a determiner there.
A learner might read Dogs are loyal and Dogs barked all night as having the same kind of meaning.
teacher.activity: Give students a set of sentences with bare noun phrases (water, dogs, Monday, president). They sort them into kind, set, time, role and substance, and discuss how they decided.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Bare NP Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-bare-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Common Noun Phrase

1.definition: NP whose nominal head is a common noun; compatible with definite or indefinite, and unique or non-unique, reference

examples.note: Specific reference to a set of books

constraints.description: The nominal head must be a common noun

relatedConstructions.notes: Dogs can be both bare and headed by a common noun. The dogs has the same head category with an overt determiner.
The dogs is both determined and headed by a common noun. Dogs has the same head category without an overt determiner.

projection.target: A common noun such as river heads either the river or a river. A particular identifiable referent need not therefore be named through a proper noun.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts the lexical noun classes and distinguishes referential status from noun class.

curious.title: Phrases built on everyday nouns
curious.summary: A common noun phrase is built around an ordinary noun like river or book, not a name.
curious.body: Ordinary nouns such as dog, river and book head phrases like the books or a river. A phrase like this can point to something definite or something indefinite, and to one particular thing or to something less specific. So a particular, identifiable thing doesn't have to be named with a name. The river can point to one particular river, and the books to a set of books.
curious.try: Think of something you can point to in the room. Can you refer to it without using a name?

teacher.summary: Separates the kind of noun heading a phrase from whether the phrase is definite or identifies one referent.
teacher.explain: A common noun phrase has a common noun as its nominal head. It's compatible with definite or indefinite reference and with unique or non-unique reference. The noun class and the referential status are different matters: a noun such as river heads either the river or a river, so a particular identifiable referent need not be named with a proper noun. Dogs and the dogs share the same head category; the first has no overt determiner and the second has one.

contrasts.note: No overt determiner.
Overt determiner, same head.

watch_for: A learner might think a definite NP has to contain a proper noun.
A learner might think a common noun phrase must contain a determiner.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Common Noun Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-common-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Definite NP Construction
pattern: Definite determiner + Nominal | referential personal pronoun | NP used as a proper name

entry.name: Definite NP Construction
entry.pattern: Definite determiner + Nominal | referential personal pronoun | NP used as a proper name

dimensions.form: Deital determiner (the, this, that, dependent genitive pronoun, or genitive NP) + Nom, or personal pronoun, or bare proper-noun NP
dimensions.meaning: Identifiable, unique, or familiar referent; anchors discourse-established entity
dimensions.function: Topic-worthy argument; hosts identificational predication
dimensions.distribution: Argument positions; existential there-resistance; partitive licensing

1.definition: Refers to/predicates identifiable instance
1.details: Refers to or predicates property of instance of nominal's type as uniquely identifiable in context

2.details: Refers to or predicates property of all contextually relevant instances of nominal's type

examples.note: The group is delimited by the context

3.details: Refers to or predicates property of unique occupant/instance of role described by nominal

4.details: Refers to or predicates property of entire species/type

examples.form: The wolf has returned to the region
examples.note: Kind-level statement in a context about species distribution

5.details: Refers to or predicates property taken as generally characteristic

2.notes: Original type: elaborates. Related to meaning 1.

relatedConstructions.notes: The structural and interpretive profiles often co-occur. Weak definites and context-dependent identifications qualify the association.
Paradigmatic contrast in the definiteness system

grounds.locator: Diagnostics and the weak-definite boundary cases

projection.target: The keys normally identifies an accessible set and can supply a domain in two of the keys. The radio in Jo listened to the radio can still have a conventional activity reading without identifying one physical radio.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents both ordinary definites and restricted non-referential readings. Reynolds uses partitive domain establishment as a structural test rather than relying on identifiability alone.

curious.title: Phrases that point to a particular thing
curious.summary: Phrases like the dog, she or London can pick out something particular that the listener can work out.
curious.body: In The dog barked, the phrase the dog points to one particular dog that the listener can identify from the situation. The same kind of phrase can stand for a whole group the context makes clear, as in The students passed, or for the one person holding a role, as in The CEO resigned. It can also talk about a whole kind, as in The dodo is extinct. Not every use points to a single physical thing: in Jo listened to the radio, the phrase can have a conventional activity reading without picking out one particular radio.
curious.try: Say The dog barked to someone who doesn't know about any dog. What do they ask you?

teacher.summary: Lays out the meanings of definite NPs, from an identifiable referent to a role or a kind, and shows where they can be weaker.
teacher.explain: A definite NP consists of a definite determiner (the, this, that, a dependent genitive pronoun, or a genitive NP) with a nominal, or a referential personal pronoun, or a bare proper-name NP. The dictionary lists readings: an identifiable instance (The dog barked), a maximal set delimited by context (The students passed), a unique role (The CEO resigned), a kind (The dodo is extinct) and a generally characteristic property (The lion is dangerous). The keys normally identifies an accessible set and can supply a domain in two of the keys, but in Jo listened to the radio a conventional activity reading doesn't identify one radio. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: The is a determinative, often called the definite article. Weak definite is a name used for cases like the radio in Jo listened to the radio, which can have a conventional activity reading without identifying one physical radio.

contrasts.note: The indefinite alternative; the dog's identity is left unstated.

watch_for: A learner might think the has to point to one specific physical thing.
A learner might treat the dodo and the lion as naming one animal when they name a kind.
teacher.activity: Give students short story openings. They underline each definite NP and say what the listener is expected to identify (a thing, a group, a role or a kind).

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body no longer says the listening is a habit (the entry gives a conventional activity reading); teacher.terms now ties 'weak definite' to the entry's radio example instead of every case where the does not identify one thing.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Definite NP Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-def-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Determined Noun Phrase

1.definition: Nominal with a determiner function, forming an NP marked as definite or indefinite

constraints.description: Determiner function is a dependent in NP structure.
Singular count nominals generally require determination; bare plural and non-count nominals can be determinerless in some contexts.

relatedConstructions.notes: The overt determiner in the new car, a new car, and Jo’s new car realizes the determiner function.
An overt determiner combines with the nominal.
The book satisfies both patterns. A book has a determiner and is indefinite. A referential bare name such as London can be definite.
A book satisfies both patterns. The book has a determiner and is definite. The bare NP dogs in We saw dogs can be indefinite.

grounds.locator: Ch. 5 §4, determiner function and non-DP realizations

projection.target: Holding the target size fixed, that size shoes and shoes that size can share a property specification. Only the first puts the property NP before the head in determiner function in CGEL’s analysis.
projection.evidence: CGEL provides the matching property-value forms and treats non-determinative realizations as restricted.

curious.title: Noun phrases that start with a pointing or counting word
curious.summary: Some noun phrases begin with a small word or phrase that tells us which one or how much.
curious.body: In the new car, the word the points to a car we can pick out. In one new car, the word one counts it. In Ally's new car, Ally's does the same job, and in what size hat, the words what size ask about the hat. The words that do this are all in the same slot in front of the rest of the phrase. Singular nouns like car generally need something there. Plural nouns and non-count nouns can sometimes go without it.
curious.try: Take the phrase new car and add different words at the front. How does the meaning change?

teacher.summary: Shows that the determiner slot can be filled by different kinds of words and phrases, not only the and a.
teacher.explain: In a determined NP, a determiner function is filled in front of a nominal, and the NP is marked as definite or indefinite. The determiner can be realized by a determinative (the, one), by a genitive NP (Ally's), or by a plain NP in interrogatives (what size hat). Singular count nominals generally require determination; bare plural and non-count nominals can be determinerless in some contexts. Following CGEL, determinative is a word category and determiner is a function. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: The and a are determinatives, often called articles. Ally's is a genitive NP, sometimes called a possessive. Determiner function is sometimes called determination.
watch_for: A learner might think the only words that can fill this slot are the and a.
A learner might treat the position as a word class, when it's a function that different words and phrases can fill.
teacher.activity: Give students a nominal such as new car. They add as many different front-slot words as they can (the, one, Ally's, my), then sort them by kind.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Determined Noun Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-det-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Independent Genitive NP

1.definition: An NP in independent genitive form without an overt head noun

projection.target: Jo’s can occur without an overt following noun in Jo’s is blue when the relevant kind is established. In This one is Jo’s, the genitive can instead express a possessive relation predicatively.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes independent genitives with nominal recovery from a distinct predicative-genitive construction.

curious.title: Owner words that stand on their own
curious.summary: Words like mine and yours, and names with 's like Jo's, can stand in for a whole phrase about who owns something.
curious.body: Mine and yours stand on their own here, with no noun after them. In Jo's is blue, Jo's does the same job: the noun is left out, once it's clear what kind of thing we're talking about. A different use looks similar. In This one is Jo's, the 's form says who owns this one. It isn't standing in for a missing noun.
curious.try: Point at something of yours and say what colour it is without naming the thing, as in Mine is blue.

teacher.summary: Shows owner forms that function as a full noun phrase with no following noun, and separates them from a predicative use.
teacher.explain: An independent genitive NP is in independent genitive form with no overt head noun, as with mine and yours. Jo's can occur without an overt following noun in Jo's is blue when the relevant kind is established, so the missing nominal is recovered from context. In This one is Jo's, the genitive can instead express a possessive relation predicatively, which is a separate construction. This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Mine and yours are sometimes called possessive pronouns; this dictionary calls them independent genitive pronouns.

contrasts.note: Independent genitive; a noun such as the kind of thing is recovered from context.
A predicative genitive, a separate construction.

watch_for: A learner might look for a noun after mine or yours, though the independent genitive has no overt head noun.
A learner might treat the Jo's of This one is Jo's as standing in for a missing noun.
teacher.activity: Students put an object of theirs on the desk. In pairs they describe the objects without naming them, starting with mine, yours or a name with 's, as in Mine is blue or Jo's is red.

child.hook: How can you talk about your things without naming them?
child.explain: Words like mine and yours can stand on their own. Mine is blue doesn't name the thing, but we know what is meant. A name with 's can do it too, as in Jo's is blue.
child.play: Put two toys on a table. Point at your own and say Mine is, then its colour. Your friend points at a toy of theirs and does the same.

checked.note: Fixed: child examples were predicative (The red one is mine), which this dictionary separates from the independent genitive, so they now use Mine is blue and Yours is red, with explanation and game rewritten to match; curious body no longer glosses Jo's as 'Jo's one'; cut the term 'absolute possessive' (unsure it maps exactly). Second round: fixed child.explain, which said nothing comes after mine in Mine is blue; it now says Mine is blue doesn't name the thing. Curious.body no longer limits mine and yours to owners; teacher.terms now maps possessive pronouns to this dictionary's independent genitive pronouns instead of stating a general rule. Also fixed (unflagged): curious.try, teacher.activity and child.hook invited answers like It's Jo's, the predicative use this dictionary separates, and now model Mine is blue; teacher.watch_for[0] no longer presents a noun after mine as an error (nothing is starred).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Independent Genitive NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-gen-indep-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Indefinite NP Construction
pattern: Indefinite determiner + Nominal | Existential quantifier + Nominal | Bare plural/non-count Nominal

entry.name: Indefinite NP Construction
entry.pattern: Indefinite determiner + Nominal | Existential quantifier + Nominal | Bare plural/non-count Nominal

dimensions.meaning: Non-identifiable, novel, or arbitrary referent; introduces new discourse entity
dimensions.function: Introduces new referents; hosts existential predication
