1.definition: Refers to/predicates non-identifiable instance
1.details: The expression may introduce an individual or contribute the nominal as a predicate. The speaker can still have a specific individual in mind.

examples.note: Indefinite introduction, with the dog’s identity left unstated

2.details: Refers to or predicates property of some subset of nominal's type

3.definition: Describes a role instance or classifies someone as a roleholder
3.details: An article-marked NP can refer generically to a roleholder or ascribe occupational class membership. A bare role assignment has a different constructional license.

4.details: Refers to or predicates property of type subset

examples.form: That is a type of fish

5.details: Refers to or predicates property as typical possibility

6.details: Refers to or predicates existence of instance(s) of nominal's type

examples.form: There's a dog in the yard

examples.note: Bare non-count NP denoting the substance involved

7.details: Refers to or predicates membership in taxonomic category

examples.form: This is a new kind of problem

2.notes: Original type: elaborates. Related to meaning 1.

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional interface; indefinite form cues non-identifiable interpretation in comprehension, non-identifiable intention licenses indefinite form in production

grounds.locator: Identification, existential pivots, and the relation between deitality and interpretation

projection.target: In a neutral opening, There was a spare key in the box introduces a possible referent without assuming it is already identifiable. In She is a teacher, the same article can head a classification with no independent referent for the predicate.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes predicative and referential uses and documents definiteness effects in existentials. Those effects depend on information status as well as nominal marking.

curious.title: Phrases that bring in something new
curious.summary: Phrases like a dog or some students bring something into the conversation without assuming the listener already knows which one.
curious.body: In A dog barked, the phrase a dog brings in a dog without saying which one. The speaker may know exactly which dog it was, but the sentence leaves it unstated. Some students passed works the same way for a part of a group. The same small word can also sort things into a type instead of pointing to something. In She is a teacher, a teacher tells us what she is. And There was a spare key in the box introduces a key that nobody has mentioned yet.
curious.try: Say A dog barked and then The dog barked. When would you pick each one?

teacher.summary: Shows indefinite NPs introducing new referents, classifying, or describing a role, and how they contrast with definite NPs.
teacher.explain: An indefinite NP consists of an indefinite determiner (a, an, some) with a nominal, or an existential quantifier with a nominal, or a bare plural or non-count nominal. The dictionary lists readings: a non-identifiable instance (A dog barked), a partial set (Some students passed), a role instance or classification (She became a manager), a subkind (That is a type of fish), a characteristic property, existence (There's a dog in the yard) and a taxonomic type. Even in A dog barked the speaker can have a specific dog in mind. In She is a teacher, the same article heads a classification with no separate referent. Definiteness effects in existentials depend on information status as well as nominal marking. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: A and an are determinatives, often called the indefinite article. Existential there is the there in There's a dog in the yard.

contrasts.note: Non-identifiable; introduces a dog.
Definite; the dog is identifiable.

watch_for: A learner might think a means the speaker has no particular dog in mind.
A learner might read a teacher in She is a teacher as naming a separate person.
teacher.activity: Give students a short story opening. They underline each indefinite NP and mark whether it introduces something new or classifies someone.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Indefinite NP Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-indef-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Pronominal Noun Phrase

1.definition: Anaphoric reference - refers back to a previously mentioned entity (antecedent)
1.details: The interpretation can recover an earlier linguistic antecedent in the same sentence or the surrounding discourse.

2.definition: Cataphoric reference - refers forward to an entity mentioned later in the discourse
2.details: A following antecedent is possible in suitable structural and discourse settings.

examples.form: Before [he] entered the room, John switched off his phone.
examples.note: 'He' refers forward to 'John' in this reading.

3.definition: Exophoric reference - refers to an entity in the extralinguistic context (situation, shared knowledge)
3.details: Salience in the situation can identify the referent without any antecedent expression.

examples.note: Said about someone not present, referring to a shared understanding of who 'he' is.

4.definition: Bound variable reference - refers to an entity whose referent varies depending on a quantifier
4.details: The value can vary with the quantified antecedent.

examples.note: 'they' refers to each student, and its referent varies with each student.

5.definition: Dummy pronoun - has no referential meaning, serves a grammatical function
5.details: Dummy it and there occupy grammatical positions without identifying entities.

examples.note: 'It' does not refer to anything; it's a grammatical placeholder.
'There' does not refer to a place; it introduces the existence of something.

constraints.description: Must consist of a pronoun functioning as the head of the NP

relatedConstructions.notes: Traditional 'indefinite pronouns' (everybody, something, nobody) are compound determinatives in fused determiner-head function, not pronouns
Some interrogative forms are pronouns.
Some relative forms are pronouns.

projection.target: They and them can pick up a prior referent but change realization with subject versus object function. Dummy it can fill a subject slot with no antecedent, so antecedence is neither necessary for pronominal NP status nor sufficient to pick its case.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates pronominal form and syntax from anaphoric, deictic and dummy uses.

curious.title: Words that stand in for a noun phrase
curious.summary: A pronoun like he, they or it can take the place of a whole noun phrase and still work as the subject or object.
curious.body: In John arrived. He looked tired, the word he points back to John. In Before he entered the room, John switched off his phone, he can point forward to John. Said about someone who isn't there, He's late again points to a person the speakers both know about. Some uses point to a different person for each case: in Every student thinks they are smart, they follows each student. And in It is raining, the word it doesn't point to anything. It just fills the spot a subject normally fills.

examples.text: Before [he] entered the room, John switched off his phone.

curious.try: Find a sentence with it and ask whether the word it points to anything. What does it stand for in It is raining?

teacher.summary: Covers the different ways a pronoun NP finds its meaning, from earlier and later mentions to the situation and dummy uses.
teacher.explain: A pronominal NP consists of a pronoun as head. The dictionary distinguishes anaphoric uses (He looked tired, pointing back to John), cataphoric uses (Before he entered the room, John switched off his phone), exophoric uses (He's late again, with the referent supplied by the situation), bound variable uses (Every student thinks they are smart) and dummy uses (It is raining; There is a problem), where the pronoun doesn't identify an entity. Having an antecedent is neither necessary for pronominal NP status nor sufficient to pick its case: they and them can pick up a prior referent but change form with subject versus object function. In this grammar, everybody, something and nobody are compound determinatives, not pronouns. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Anaphora, cataphora and exophora are the usual names for pointing back, forward and out to the situation. Dummy it is sometimes called expletive it. Indefinite pronouns is the traditional name for everybody, something and nobody, which this grammar treats differently.

examples.text: Before [he] entered the room, John switched off his phone.

watch_for: A learner might assume every it points to a thing, including the it in It is raining.
A learner might think a pronoun has to follow the noun phrase it points to, when it can point forward.
teacher.activity: Give students short texts with highlighted pronouns. They draw an arrow to what each one points to, or write "nothing" for dummy uses.

child.hook: In "It is raining", what does "it" stand for?
child.explain: Words like he can take the place of a name. In John arrived. He looked tired, he means John. In It is raining, it doesn't mean anything. It just fills the spot.
child.play: Read a short story aloud. Every time you hear he or she, point to the person it means. Does every it point to something?

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer defines every pronoun as standing in for a name or noun phrase (dummy it does not); play task limited to he and she, since the entry gives they a bound-variable use. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Pronominal Noun Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-pron-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Independent Interrogative Genitive Pronoun NP

1.definition: Interrogative independent genitive pronoun functioning as an NP

projection.target: Whose can occur as a clause-level complement in Whose is this? and as an interrogative fused head in Whose did you borrow? The dependent use in Whose key is this? includes a separate nominal.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes three slots for whose and gives an independent NP use with nominal interpretation recovered from context.

curious.title: Asking whose it is
curious.summary: The word whose can stand alone as a question about the owner of something.
curious.body: In Whose is this?, the word whose asks who the owner is, and it stands alone with no noun after it. We can leave the noun out because the situation shows what we're talking about. Whose can also show up in other places. In Whose did you borrow?, it again stands for the thing and its owner together. In Whose key is this?, a noun follows it, so that's a different pattern.
curious.try: Hold up something that belongs to someone else and ask whose it is. Do you need to say what it is?

teacher.summary: Covers whose used as a freestanding NP in a question, and how it differs from whose before a noun.
teacher.explain: The independent interrogative genitive pronoun is a form of whose that functions as an NP with no following noun. It asks for the possessor, as in Whose is this? The dictionary distinguishes three slots for whose: a clause-level complement (Whose is this?), an interrogative fused head (Whose did you borrow?), and a dependent use with a separate nominal (Whose key is this?). In the independent use, the nominal interpretation is recovered from context. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Whose is sometimes called an interrogative possessive. This grammar says genitive instead of possessive.

contrasts.note: Independent; no noun follows.
Dependent; a separate nominal follows.

watch_for: A learner might think whose must be followed by a noun.
A learner might read the whose of Whose did you borrow? as asking about a person, when it asks about the owner of the thing borrowed.
teacher.activity: Collect a few items from the class. Students ask each other whose each one is, once with a noun and once without, and note where the noun can be left out.

child.hook: Which tiny word asks who owns something?
child.explain: The word whose asks who owns something. You can use it alone. You might hold up a jacket and ask, "Whose is this?"
child.play: Collect three things from around the room. Ask "Whose is this?" for each one, and see who can answer.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Independent Interrogative Genitive Pronoun NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-pron-interrog-gen-indep-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Independent Personal Genitive Pronoun NP

1.definition: Independent personal genitive pronoun functioning as an NP

projection.target: A form such as mine can occupy an NP slot without an overt noun, as in mine fell. The dependent counterpart my requires a nominal. His is formally shared across the two slots.
projection.evidence: CGEL lists independent and dependent forms and describes their different distributions.

curious.title: Mine, yours, hers and the rest
curious.summary: The words mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs can stand alone as a full phrase, with no noun after them.
curious.body: In The red one is mine, the word mine says whose the red one is, and nothing follows it. Those seats are theirs works the same way. Each of these words fills a whole phrase's spot on its own. Compare my. It goes before a noun, as in my book. The word his is the same in both uses: his book and The book is his.
curious.try: Say my book. Now say whose book it is using just one word and no noun.

teacher.summary: Teaches the stand-alone forms mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs and how they differ from my, your and their before a noun.
teacher.explain: An independent personal genitive pronoun is one of mine, yours, his, hers, ours or theirs, functioning as an NP. A form such as mine can occupy an NP slot without an overt noun, as in Mine fell. The dependent counterpart, such as my, requires a nominal. His is formally shared across the two slots. The dictionary lists independent and dependent forms and shows their different distributions. It marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called absolute possessive pronouns or possessive pronouns. This grammar uses genitive, not possessive, and calls my, your and the like dependent genitive pronouns.

contrasts.note: Dependent form, followed by a noun.
Independent form, no noun follows.

contrasts.text: That is [his] book. That book is [his].
contrasts.note: The same form fills both slots.

watch_for: A learner might add a noun after mine, yours or theirs.
A learner might expect his to change form between the two uses, when it stays the same.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of sentences with my, your, her and their before a noun. They rewrite each with the stand-alone form and no noun.

child.hook: Can one little word say who owns the whole thing?
child.explain: Words like mine, yours and theirs can stand alone. They say who owns something without naming it. The red one is mine.
child.play: Point to things in the room. Say who owns each one using only mine, yours, his, hers, ours or theirs.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Independent Personal Genitive Pronoun NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-pron-personal-gen-indep-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Reciprocal Anaphor
pattern: NP[each other or one another], optionally genitive

entry.name: Reciprocal Anaphor
entry.pattern: NP[each other or one another], optionally genitive

1.definition: Relates members of an antecedent group to other members of that group.
1.details: In Kim and Pat defended each other, Kim defended Pat and Pat defended Kim on the ordinary reading. A possessive counterpart occurs in each other’s clients. Larger groups can permit weaker readings, such as relations only between neighbours in a line. The genitive is available even though reflexives lack corresponding genitives.

examples.note: The reciprocal occurs in genitive determiner function.

relatedConstructions.notes: The core expression is a reciprocal pronoun.
The nearby antecedent links a reflexive to its own referent, while a reciprocal relates group members.
Reciprocity can instead be part of a nominal predicate with a with-phrase.

grounds.note: Records each other and one another.
Distinguishes reciprocity readings and tests the genitive contrast.

projection.target: Each other and one another can occur as genitive determiners. A reflexive form is excluded in the same genitive slot.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares the distribution of reciprocals and reflexives and gives examples where full pairwise reciprocity is too strong. CASA lists the two reciprocal forms.

curious.title: Each other and one another
curious.summary: Each other and one another say that the members of a group do the same thing to one another.
curious.body: In Kim and Pat defended each other, Kim defended Pat and Pat defended Kim. The phrase each other points back to the group, and it works as the object of the verb. It also has an owner form, each other's, as in They blamed each other's parents. For bigger groups the meaning can be looser: the relation might hold only between neighbours in a line. The other form is one another.
curious.try: Say Kim and Pat defended each other. Who defended whom? Does it change if you use one another?

teacher.summary: Explains each other and one another as reciprocal anaphors and contrasts them with reflexives.
teacher.explain: A reciprocal anaphor relates members of an antecedent group to other members of that group. In Kim and Pat defended each other, the ordinary reading is that Kim defended Pat and Pat defended Kim. Each other and one another can occur as genitive determiners, as in each other's parents, whereas reflexives lack corresponding genitives. For larger groups, weaker readings occur, such as relations only between neighbours in a line, so full pairwise reciprocity is too strong in some cases. A reflexive links a pronoun to its own referent, while a reciprocal relates group members. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Reciprocal pronoun is the usual name for each other and one another. This grammar groups them as a reciprocal anaphor.

contrasts.note: Reciprocal; each defends the other.
Reflexive; the object is the same person as the subject.

watch_for: A learner might use each other when the object is the same person as the subject.
A learner might think a reciprocal means every member relates to every other member, when larger groups can have weaker readings.
teacher.activity: Students stand in pairs and say what they did to each other (high-fived, thanked). Then groups of five say what happened and decide whether each person really did it to every other person.

child.hook: What do two friends do to each other?
child.explain: Each other says that two people do the same thing to one another. If Kim and Pat defended each other, Kim defended Pat and Pat defended Kim.
child.play: Pick two friends. Say what they did, using each other. Then say the same thing with one another.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Reciprocal Anaphor." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-pron-reciprocal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Direct-Object Reflexive Anaphor
pattern: NP[Pron.REFLᵢ] as direct object with local Subject:NPᵢ

entry.name: Direct-Object Reflexive Anaphor
entry.pattern: NP[Pron.REFLᵢ] as direct object with local Subject:NPᵢ

1.definition: Interprets a direct-object personal pronoun as having the same referent as the subject of the verb.
1.details: Sue defended herself has a local antecedent for herself. In the ordinary transitive reading, Sue defended her is about Sue defending someone else. This entry covers the simple direct-object pattern. A reflexive used for emphasis or in a picture NP can have different licensing.

examples.note: The reflexive is co-referential with the subject Sue.
Constructed plural example with a matching local antecedent.

relatedConstructions.notes: A personal pronoun appears in its reflexive form.
A reciprocal can occupy the same object position with a different relation among participants.

grounds.note: Lists reflexive forms as reference constructions.
Separates the simple object pattern from other reflexive uses.

projection.target: Changing a simple direct-object reflexive to the corresponding accusative usually removes the local co-reference reading. The reflexive form tracks the antecedent’s person and number.
projection.evidence: CGEL examines the basic verb-domain pattern and explicitly distinguishes override and emphatic reflexives. CASA lists corresponding members of the paradigm.

curious.title: Words like herself and themselves
curious.summary: A word like herself, as the object of a verb, points back to the person doing the action.
curious.body: In Sue defended herself, the word herself means Sue. The one doing the defending and the one being defended are the same person. Change it to Sue defended her, and the ordinary reading is that Sue defended someone else. The reflexive form matches the person it points back to in person and number, which is why we get The players congratulated themselves. This dictionary covers only the simple pattern with a verb and its object. Reflexives used for emphasis, or inside a phrase like a picture of herself, follow other rules.
curious.try: Say Sue defended herself and Sue defended her. Who is defended in each one?

teacher.summary: Explains the basic direct-object reflexive and its contrast with an ordinary object pronoun.
teacher.explain: In the simple pattern, a reflexive pronoun serves as direct object with a local subject antecedent: Sue defended herself. The personal pronoun in reflexive form has the same referent as the subject of the verb. In the ordinary transitive reading, Sue defended her is about Sue defending someone else. The reflexive form tracks the antecedent's person and number, so changing it to the plain accusative usually removes the local co-reference reading. The pattern here doesn't cover emphatic reflexives or those in picture noun phrases, which can have different licensing. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Reflexive pronoun is the traditional name. Her in Sue defended her is an ordinary personal pronoun in accusative form.

contrasts.note: The object is Sue, the subject.
The ordinary reading is about someone else.

watch_for: A learner might use her for the subject's own referent, as in Sue defended her, meaning Sue.
A learner might choose a reflexive that doesn't match its antecedent in person and number.
teacher.activity: Give students a set of sentences with a blank after a transitive verb. They fill in either a reflexive or a plain pronoun and say who each one refers to.

child.hook: When does "herself" mean the very same person?
child.explain: Words like herself and themselves point back to the person doing the action. When Sue defended herself, Sue was defended. When Sue defended her, it's someone else.
child.play: Think of two sentences with the same verb, one ending in herself or himself and one ending in her or him. Who is the object in each?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Direct-Object Reflexive Anaphor." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-pron-reflexive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Proper Noun Phrase

1.definition: NP whose nominal head is a proper noun; prototypically used as a proper name identifying a unique entity

relatedConstructions.notes: Realizes the proper name function

projection.target: London can occur without an article when it identifies the city. A construction such as two Kims uses a nomenclatural form with numeral determination and plural marking, so name form alone need not determine the NP’s referential status.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes proper nouns from whole names and documents secondary uses and complex names.

curious.title: Phrases built on names
curious.summary: A phrase built on a proper noun, such as London or the Thames, can identify one particular place, person or thing.
curious.body: London names a particular city, and it doesn't need a small word like the in front. The Thames is a name too, but it comes with the. Both kinds of phrase point to one particular thing. A name's form doesn't settle how the phrase works. In two Kims, the name Kim takes a number and a plural ending.
curious.try: Think of a name. Can you say two of them, like two Kims?

teacher.summary: Covers noun phrases headed by proper nouns, and shows that name form doesn't fix referential status.
teacher.explain: A proper noun phrase has a proper noun as its nominal head, and is prototypically used as a proper name identifying a unique entity. London can occur without an article when it identifies the city, while the Thames takes the. A construction such as two Kims uses a nomenclatural form with numeral determination and plural marking, so name form alone need not determine the NP's referential status. The dictionary also records secondary uses of proper names and complex names, and marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Proper noun is the traditional term for the word class, and proper name for the use of identifying a unique entity. The dictionary keeps the two apart.

contrasts.note: A name that identifies a city, with no article.
A name with a numeral and plural marking.

watch_for: A learner might think a proper noun can't take a determiner or a plural.
A learner might treat the Thames as a common noun phrase because it has the.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of names (London, the Thames, Kim). They sort them by whether the name has an article, then try adding a number to each name where it makes sense.

child.hook: Can a name be plural?
child.explain: A name points to one particular person, place or thing. London is a name, and so is the Thames. Sometimes you can count names too. If two people are called Kim, you know two Kims.
child.play: Think of a name that two people share. Say how many people have that name using a number and the name.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Proper Noun Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-proper-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Property-Value NP in a Nominal
pattern: NP[Det:NP[property value] + Nom] or Nom[N + Mod:NP[property value]]

entry.name: Property-Value NP in a Nominal
entry.pattern: NP[Det:NP[property value] + Nom] or Nom[N + Mod:NP[property value]]

1.definition: Uses an NP to supply or ask for the value of a property of the head noun’s referent.
1.details: The dependent NP supplies both a property and a value, as in shoes that size. In what size hat, the value is the requested information. CGEL analyzes the pre-head NP as determiner and the post-head NP as modifier. This entry records the shared interpretation. The lexical range of each position and the relation to predicative my age remain open.

examples.note: The interrogative NP asks for a value.
CGEL's preferred post-head variant for this example.

examples.form: [a house that size and that price]
examples.note: Coordinated post-head property specifications in a building-code hearing.

relatedConstructions.notes: The post-head variant modifies the nominal.
The pre-head variant has determiner function in CGEL.

projection.target: The dependent is interpreted as a property with a value to match or supply, in either of CGEL's two positions.
projection.evidence: CGEL gives paired examples with the same property. The hearing shows that two property values can be specified together.

curious.title: Asking for and giving a size
curious.summary: A noun phrase like that size can sit before or after another noun to say which value of some property we mean.
curious.body: In what size hat, the words what size ask for the size of the hat. In They don't stock shoes that size, the words that size say which size of shoes. Each one names a property (size) and, in the answer, a value for it. The phrase can go before the noun, as in that size shoes, or after it, as in shoes that size. The second is the preferred wording for this example. Two values can be given together: a house that size and that price.

examples.text: [a house that size and that price]

curious.try: Ask for something by size, like what size hat. How else could you say it?

teacher.summary: Shows a noun phrase supplying or asking for the value of a property of a head noun's referent, before or after the noun.
teacher.explain: A property-value NP supplies both a property and a value, as in shoes that size. In what size hat, the value is the requested information. CGEL analyzes the pre-head NP as determiner and the post-head NP as modifier, and this dictionary records the shared interpretation. Two values can be coordinated, as in a house that size and that price. The lexical range of each position, and the relation to predicative my age, remain open. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Pre-head NP in determiner function is a CGEL analysis; the post-head NP is a modifier.

examples.text: [a house that size and that price]

contrasts.note: Pre-head variant, with the property NP in determiner function.
Post-head variant, CGEL's preferred form for this example, with the property NP as a modifier.

watch_for: A learner might read that size as an ordinary determiner such as the.
A learner might think the pre-head and post-head versions mean different things.
teacher.activity: Give students a clothing-store role-play. They ask and answer using what size hat and shoes that size, and compare where the property phrase goes.

checked.note: Fixed: removed the claim about traditional names for the two positions; retitled so it no longer suggests age and other properties are established applications (the dictionary leaves the lexical range open); removed 'the dictionary prefers' since the preference for the post-head variant is CGEL's.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Property-Value NP in a Nominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-property-value-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Agreement through a Number-Transparent Nominal
pattern: Clause[Subject with number-transparent N + of-PP + finite agreement]

entry.name: Agreement through a Number-Transparent Nominal
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject with number-transparent N + of-PP + finite agreement]

1.definition: Allows the number of an embedded complement to determine agreement in a licensed nominal frame.

relatedConstructions.notes: The plural in A number of applicants were waiting follows the of-complement. Compare an amount reading with singular agreement in Three litres of milk was enough.

projection.target: The plural is licensed despite singular number. With the number of applicants, the nominal normally denotes the numerical quantity and takes singular agreement.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: When the verb follows the noun after of
curious.summary: In a number of applicants, the verb agrees with applicants, not with the singular word number.
curious.body: In A number of applicants were waiting, the word number is singular, yet the verb is plural. The verb follows the plural applicants after of. Compare The number of applicants. There, number normally names a quantity, and the verb goes with it: singular. Three litres of milk was enough works the same way, with a singular verb for an amount.

examples.text: The number of applicants was small.
Three litres of milk was enough.

curious.try: Say A number of applicants were waiting. Then say The number of applicants was small. Why does the verb change?

teacher.summary: Explains why a plural verb can follow a singular noun like number when an of-phrase supplies the plural.
teacher.explain: In a licensed frame, a number-transparent nominal lets the number of the embedded complement determine agreement. In A number of applicants were waiting, the plural is licensed despite the singular number, so the verb follows applicants. With the number of applicants, the nominal normally denotes a numerical quantity and takes singular agreement. Compare an amount reading with singular agreement, as in Three litres of milk was enough. This is a specialization of verb-number agreement. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

contrasts.note: Plural agreement follows the of-complement.
Number names a quantity, so agreement is singular.

watch_for: A learner might make the verb agree with the singular noun number in A number of applicants.
A learner might use a plural verb after the number of applicants.
teacher.activity: Give students sentence frames with a number of and the number of. They choose the verb form, then explain which word the verb agrees with.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Agreement through a Number-Transparent Nominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/number-transparent-agreement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Numerative Addition Coordination (without and)

dimensions.form: Asyndetic coordination; juxtaposition without 'and'
dimensions.meaning: Same additive semantics as syndetic variant
dimensions.function: Builds complex numeratives recursively
dimensions.distribution: Preferred in AmE; faster/less formal registers

1.definition: Additive numerative formed by juxtaposing magnitude and addition without and

constraints.description: Coordination targets numerative constituents; the coordinator and is omitted.
Recursive: the addition coordinate can itself be a basic numerative or a magnitude phrase; its category may be DP or NP (category difference is tolerated under likeness of function).
Strongly preferred in AmE and in faster or less formal registers.

projection.target: In two hundred five, five is added to a complete magnitude phrase. It contributes the same remainder as five in two hundred and five even though there is no spoken coordinator. This differs from a factor selecting a magnitude, as in five hundred.
projection.evidence: The paper compares asyndetic addition, marked addition, and multiplicative modification by word order and prosody.

curious.title: Big numbers said without and
curious.summary: Some numbers are built by putting a small number straight after a large one, with no and between them.
curious.body: In two hundred five, the five is added to two hundred, even though nothing joins them. It means the same as two hundred and five. Two thousand seven works the same way. This dictionary says the version without and is strongly preferred in American English and in faster or less formal speech. The five here is an addition to a complete amount. That differs from five hundred, where five says how many hundreds.
curious.try: Say two hundred five and two hundred and five. Do they mean the same number?

teacher.summary: Shows that two hundred five is addition with no spoken and, parallel to the version with and.
teacher.explain: This construction adds a smaller number to a complete magnitude phrase by juxtaposition, with the coordinator and omitted: two hundred five means 200 + 5. The dictionary analyzes it as coordination without a spoken coordinator. The addition coordinate can itself be a basic numerative or a magnitude phrase, so the pattern is recursive. In two hundred five, five contributes the same remainder as in two hundred and five. This differs from five hundred, where a factor selects a magnitude. The dictionary notes that this form is strongly preferred in American English and in faster or less formal registers. It marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Numerative is this grammar's term for number words, where a textbook may say numeral. Asyndetic means joined without a coordinator.

contrasts.note: Addition with no and (200 + 5).
Addition with and (200 + 5).
Multiplication, not addition (a factor selects a magnitude).

watch_for: A learner might think a number without and is missing something.
A learner might read two hundred five as two hundred multiplied by five.
teacher.activity: Dictate numbers such as 205, 2007 and 3006. Students write them in digits, then say each aloud in both styles, with and and without it.

name: Numerative Addition Coordination (with and)

dimensions.form: Coordination with overt 'and' marker; right-branching
dimensions.meaning: Additive composition of magnitude and addition
dimensions.function: Builds complex numeratives recursively
dimensions.distribution: Preferred in BrE; more formal registers

1.definition: Additive numerative formed by coordinating magnitude units and additions

constraints.description: Coordination targets numerative constituents; additions are coordinates (DP or NP).
Recursive: the addition coordinate can itself be a basic numerative or a magnitude phrase; its category may be DP or NP (category difference is tolerated under likeness of function).

projection.target: In three hundred and seven, each of three hundred and seven can denote a number independently. The whole normally denotes their sum and does not treat seven as another multiplier of hundred.
projection.evidence: Reynolds treats additions as coordinates and separates their distribution from that of factors.

curious.title: Big numbers said with and
curious.summary: Some numbers are built by joining a large amount and a small addition with the word and.
curious.body: In two hundred and five, the word and joins two hundred and five. Together they make the sum. Two thousand and seven is built the same way: 2000 plus 7. Each part can stand as a number on its own, and the whole means their sum. The seven in three hundred and seven isn't a second multiplier of hundred. This dictionary notes that this version is preferred in British English and in more formal speech.
curious.try: Say three hundred and seven aloud. Which parts could you say on their own as numbers?

teacher.summary: Shows that numbers like two hundred and five are additions, coordinating a magnitude and a smaller number.
teacher.explain: This construction forms an additive numerative by coordinating magnitude units and additions with and: two hundred and five means 200 + 5. The addition is a coordinate, and it can itself be a basic numerative or a magnitude phrase, so the pattern is recursive. In three hundred and seven, each of three hundred and seven can denote a number independently. The whole normally denotes their sum and doesn't treat seven as another multiplier of hundred. The dictionary notes that this form is preferred in British English and in more formal registers. It marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Numerative is this grammar's term for number words, where a textbook may say numeral. Syndetic means joined with a coordinator.

contrasts.note: Addition with and (200 + 5).
The same sum with no spoken and.

watch_for: A learner might read and in two hundred and five as joining two separate items rather than adding.
A learner might treat the seven in three hundred and seven as multiplying hundred.
teacher.activity: Students write number words for 105, 207 and 3004. They mark the large part and the addition, then compare with a partner.

name: Basic Numerative Lexeme (0–99)

dimensions.form: Lexical unit (simple, derived, or compound); no internal syntax
dimensions.meaning: Specifies cardinality from zero to ninety-nine
dimensions.function: Can serve as factor or addition in complex numeratives
dimensions.distribution: Determiner, factor, addition; resists internal modification/coordination

1.definition: Lexical numeratives from zero to ninety-nine

constraints.description: Behaves as a lexical unit for syntax (no internal coordination or modification).

projection.target: Twenty-four can supply the single lexical unit that ordinal morphology targets in twenty-fourth. A construction such as three hundred twenty-four has additional phrasal structure, which is recoverable in reduced alternatives in an appropriate context.
projection.evidence: Reynolds combines prosody, ordinal morphology and ellipsis evidence for the lexical versus syntactic analysis.

curious.title: Number words from zero to ninety-nine
curious.summary: The number words from zero to ninety-nine each work as a single unit, with no internal parts that can be joined or described.
curious.body: Five, ten, twelve, nineteen, forty and twenty-six all count as one word each. Even twenty-six is a single unit, not a phrase. The evidence points to the same thing. Twenty-four gives twenty-fourth, which changes the whole unit. A number like three hundred twenty-four is different: it has extra structure, and in the right context a shorter version can recover the missing parts.
curious.try: Make twenty-four into its ordinal form. Where does the change land?

teacher.summary: Explains why 0 to 99 are treated as lexical units, and where phrasal structure begins.
teacher.explain: The basic numerative lexemes are the number words from zero to ninety-nine. They include simple words (five, ten), irregular and regular teens (twelve, nineteen), decade words (forty) and compounds (twenty-six). They behave as lexical units for syntax, with no internal coordination or modification, and can serve as determiner, factor or addition in larger numbers. Twenty-four supplies the single lexical unit that ordinal morphology targets in twenty-fourth. Three hundred twenty-four has additional phrasal structure. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Numerative is this grammar's term for number words, where a textbook may say numeral. Cardinal numeral is the traditional name for these counting words.

contrasts.note: One lexical unit; ordinal twenty-fourth.
Phrasal, with internal structure.

watch_for: A learner might think twenty-six is a phrase with two separate words.
A learner might treat three hundred twenty-four as one word.
teacher.activity: Students list number words they can build ordinals from (five, twelve, twenty-four) and say each ordinal aloud. Then they try one for a larger number and see which part changes.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Basic Numerative Lexeme (0–99)." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-basic-lexeme-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Complex Numerative (Phrasal >99)

dimensions.form: Syntactic phrase or coordination; magnitude head with factor modifier
dimensions.meaning: Multiplicative and additive composition for values above 99
dimensions.function: Same functions as basic numeratives but with internal syntactic structure
dimensions.distribution: Prosodic breaks at magnitude boundaries; allows internal modification

1.definition: Phrasal numeratives above the lexical 0–99 range, built from magnitude phrases with optional additions

constraints.description: Requires a magnitude head with a factor; additions are coordinated constituents.
Applies above the basic numerative lexicon (0–99).

relatedConstructions.notes: Phrasal construction headed by cardinal determinatives; not a specialization of the lexical category (lexeme/phrase boundary at 99, Reynolds 2026 EL&L)

projection.target: Two hundred and four has an internal phrase two hundred which can also stand independently. Where the context supports the intended scale, the second coordinate of between two hundred and four and six can recover material and mean two hundred and six.
projection.evidence: Reynolds uses reduction and coordination to diagnose structure above the basic lexical inventory. A shorter coordinate can also get a literal small-number reading in other contexts.

curious.title: Number words above ninety-nine
curious.summary: Numbers above ninety-nine are built as phrases, from a multiplied amount like two hundred plus an optional addition.
curious.body: Two hundred and five and one thousand twenty-four are made of parts. In each, a multiplied amount (two hundred, one thousand) comes first, and a smaller number (five, twenty-four) is added after it. Two hundred, for instance, can also stand alone as a number. That's what separates these from smaller number words. Up to ninety-nine, this dictionary treats each number as a single word. Above that, the number has an inside, and context can sometimes fill in missing pieces. In between two hundred and four and six, the second number can be understood as two hundred and six.
curious.try: Say one thousand twenty-four aloud. Which part could you say on its own as a number?

teacher.summary: Explains numbers above 99 as phrases with internal structure, built from a factor, a magnitude and an optional addition.
teacher.explain: A complex numerative is a phrase above the lexical range of zero to ninety-nine. It requires a magnitude head with a factor, and additions are coordinated constituents, with or without and: one thousand twenty-four, two hundred and five. Two hundred and four has an internal phrase two hundred which can also stand independently. Where the context supports the intended scale, the second coordinate of between two hundred and four and six can recover material and mean two hundred and six. A shorter coordinate can also get a literal small-number reading in other contexts. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Numerative is this grammar's term for number words, where a textbook may say numeral.

contrasts.note: A single lexical unit.
A phrase, with factor, magnitude and addition.

watch_for: A learner might take the second coordinate in between two hundred and four and six as the small number six, when context can sometimes supply two hundred and give two hundred and six.
A learner might think a large number is one long word rather than a phrase.
teacher.activity: Students break written numbers such as one thousand twenty-four into parts and label the factor, the magnitude and the addition.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the addition goes onto 'it' (two hundred) for both examples; it now says a smaller number is added after the multiplied amount in each; teacher watch_for no longer suggests a reading of the first coordinate as 4 and states the entry's context-dependent reading of the second coordinate. Second round: fixed curious.body, which now attributes the single-word treatment of numbers up to ninety-nine to this dictionary (its lexical range) and puts the phrasal boundary above ninety-nine, as the entry does.

name: Compound Basic Numerative (Decade + Single-digit)

dimensions.form: Decade + single-digit compound; hyphenated; lexically atomic
dimensions.meaning: Specifies cardinality from twenty-one to ninety-nine
dimensions.function: Same distribution as simple basic numeratives
dimensions.distribution: Determiner, factor, addition; resists internal coordination (*twenty and one)

1.definition: Specifies a cardinality formed by additive composition of tens and ones

constraints.description: Requires a decade base with a single-digit addition; excludes *twenty-ten.

projection.target: Forty-three expresses one lexicalized sum and supplies a base for forty-third. A coordinator inside forty and three produces a separate structure and is not the ordinary lexical compound.
projection.evidence: Reynolds argues from word formation and prosody for lexical compounding below the magnitude boundary.

curious.title: Numbers like twenty-one and ninety-nine
curious.summary: Numbers such as twenty-one, forty-two and ninety-nine join a tens word and a ones word.
curious.body: Twenty-one is twenty plus one. Forty-two is forty plus two, and ninety-nine is ninety plus nine. Each is typically written with a hyphen and counts as one word. A number like forty-three also supplies the base for forty-third. A version with and inside, like forty and three, would be a different structure, not the ordinary word.
curious.try: Turn forty-three into forty-third. Which part of the word changes?

teacher.summary: Explains two-part numbers from 21 to 99 as single lexical units formed from a decade and a single digit.
teacher.explain: A compound basic numerative is a decade word followed by a single-digit word, typically hyphenated: twenty-one is 20 + 1. It's a lexical compound below the magnitude boundary, with the same distribution as simple basic numeratives (determiner, factor, addition). Forty-three expresses one lexicalized sum and supplies a base for forty-third. It requires a decade base with a single-digit addition. A coordinator inside, as in forty and three, produces a separate structure and isn't the ordinary lexical compound. This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Numerative is this dictionary's term for number words, where a textbook may say numeral.

contrasts.note: Internal coordination isn't part of the ordinary compound.
The pattern requires a single-digit addition to a decade.

watch_for: A learner might put and inside a number from 21 to 99, as in twenty and one.
A learner might try to build a number such as twenty-ten, when the pattern requires a single-digit addition to a decade.
teacher.activity: Give students decade cards and single-digit cards. They build every number they can from 21 to 99, hyphenate each one, and say its ordinal.

child.hook: How do we say numbers like twenty-one?
child.explain: Some numbers are made of two parts. Twenty-one is twenty and one put together. We typically write a hyphen between the parts.
child.play: Pick a tens word, like forty. Add each ones word to it, from one to nine. Say each number and write it with a hyphen.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary no longer claims every number from twenty-one to ninety-nine is tens plus ones (exact tens like thirty fall outside the pattern); hyphenation stated as typical, as in the entry; removed the 'common name' claim for compound numeral from teacher.terms; sharpened the twenty-ten watch_for to the entry's constraint. Second round: fixed curious.body, which said forty-three takes an ordinal ending because it is a single word; it now says, as this dictionary does, that forty-three supplies the base for forty-third. Also fixed (unflagged): the child example The page is ninety-nine used the number as a label, not a cardinality, and now counts years.

name: Decade Numerative

dimensions.form: Single-digit base + -ty suffix (twenty through ninety)
dimensions.meaning: Specifies cardinality in tens (20, 30, ..., 90)
dimensions.function: Base for compound formation; determiner, factor
dimensions.distribution: Combines with single-digits to form compounds (twenty-one)

1.definition: Specifies a cardinality in tens (20, 30, …, 90)

projection.target: Sixty can stand by itself and can supply the first component of sixty-four. The relation to six is transparent, but a new decade form cannot automatically be generated from any numerical expression by adding -ty.
projection.evidence: CGEL treats the decade endings as lexical word formation. Reynolds uses decade-based compounds as evidence for the basic lexicon.

curious.title: Number words for whole tens
curious.summary: The words twenty to ninety each name a number of tens.
curious.body: Twenty means 20, and seventy means 70. These words name whole tens, from twenty up to ninety, and each is built from a single-digit base with the ending -ty. Sixty stands by itself as a word, and it also supplies the first part of sixty-four. Its link to six is easy to see. But you can't make a new tens word by adding -ty to just any number expression.
curious.try: Say all the tens words from twenty to ninety. Which one reminds you of its single-digit number?

teacher.summary: Covers the tens words twenty to ninety, built with -ty, as the base for numbers like sixty-four.
teacher.explain: A decade numerative specifies a cardinality in tens (20, 30, ..., 90), formed from a single-digit base and the suffix -ty. It's a basic numerative, so it can serve as determiner or factor, and it combines with single digits to form compounds such as twenty-one. Sixty can stand alone and can supply the first component of sixty-four. The relation to six is transparent, but a new decade form can't automatically be generated from any numerical expression by adding -ty. The dictionary treats the decade endings as lexical word formation, and marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Numerative is this grammar's term for number words, where a textbook may say numeral. Decade numerals or tens words are common informal names.
watch_for: A learner might think any number word can take -ty to make a tens word.
A learner might miss that sixty relates to six, though the link is transparent.
teacher.activity: Students write the tens words from twenty to ninety, circle each ending, and match each with its single-digit base. Then they build three compound numbers from them.

child.hook: What do twenty, thirty and forty all end with?
child.explain: Words like twenty, seventy and ninety name whole tens. They end in -ty. Seventy means 70. You can count by tens with them.
child.play: Count by tens out loud, from twenty up to ninety. Stop at each -ty word, and clap on each one.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Decade Numerative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-decade-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Factor + Magnitude Numerative

dimensions.form: Basic numerative (0-99) + magnitude; factor is modifier, not determiner
dimensions.meaning: Multiplicative composition (factor × magnitude)
dimensions.function: Factor scales magnitude head; near-obligatory in most contexts
dimensions.distribution: Factor precedes magnitude head; prosodic break after magnitude

1.definition: Multiplicative numerative built by combining a factor with a magnitude head

constraints.description: Factor is a modifier of the magnitude head, not a determiner of the NP.
Factor is drawn from the basic numeratives (0–99).

grounds.locator: §4, obligatory factors and their grammatical function

projection.target: Two multiplies hundred in two hundred. It can be embedded under a separate determiner in a count noun use such as two two hundreds. A second determiner analysis would obscure why both numerals occur and contribute differently.
projection.evidence: Reynolds tests factor modification against the co-occurrence of actual external determiners and against argument-selection tests.

curious.title: Number words built by multiplying
curious.summary: In phrases like two hundred and forty-two million, a smaller number multiplies a big round one.
curious.body: In two hundred, the word two says how many hundreds there are: two times a hundred. In forty-two million, forty-two says how many millions. The smaller number is called the factor, and the big round word (hundred, thousand, million) is the one it multiplies. This dictionary takes the factor to be one of the basic number words, from zero to ninety-nine. It describes the factor as scaling the round word, not as a separate word that introduces the whole phrase, though that analysis is marked provisional.
curious.try: Pick a number like five hundred. Can you find the smaller number that multiplies the big round one?

teacher.summary: Explains why, in two hundred, the first number word is a multiplier of the second rather than a determiner of the noun phrase.
teacher.explain: A multiplicative numerative combines a factor with a magnitude head: two hundred is 2 × 100, and forty-two million is 42 × 1,000,000. The factor comes from the basic numeratives (0 to 99) and is a modifier of the magnitude head. It isn't a determiner of the NP. This dictionary's reasoning is that a separate determiner can still appear in a count-noun use (it cites two two hundreds), so treating the factor as the determiner would hide why both numerals are there and why each contributes differently. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Numeral is the traditional word for number words in general. This dictionary says numerative, and calls the multiplier a factor and the big round word a magnitude head.
watch_for: A learner might take two in two hundred as a determiner of the whole noun phrase, when this dictionary treats it as scaling hundred.
A learner might read forty-two million as forty-two plus a million, when it is forty-two times a million.
teacher.activity: Make cards with factors (two, seven, forty-two) and magnitude words (hundred, thousand, million). Pairs draw one of each, say the number aloud, and state the multiplication it stands for.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Factor + Magnitude Numerative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-factor-modifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Fractional Noun
pattern: Cardinal base → fractional noun (-th or suppletive)

entry.name: Fractional Noun
entry.pattern: Cardinal base → fractional noun (-th or suppletive)

dimensions.form: Cardinal base + -th or suppletive (half, quarter); count noun
dimensions.meaning: Denotes denominator in fraction; partitive semantics
dimensions.function: Heads nominal in fraction NPs; numerator is determiner
dimensions.distribution: Inflects for number (one fifth, two fifths); licenses factors

1.definition: Fractional noun denoting a denominator; used in fraction NPs with a numeral determiner

constraints.description: Fractional noun heads a nominal; numerator functions as determiner in fraction NPs (e.g., one fifth).
Fractional noun inflects for number (one third vs two thirds); half/quarter are suppletive.

projection.target: Fifths in three fifths accepts plural marking and a cardinal determiner. Fifth in fifth place is adjectival and does not take plural marking there. The two distributions persist where the forms are partly identical.
projection.evidence: CGEL and Reynolds distinguish fractional nouns from ordinal adjectives despite the shared morphological material.

curious.title: Fraction words as nouns
curious.summary: In a fraction like one fifth, the word fifth names the size of the pieces and behaves like a noun.
curious.body: In one fifth, the word fifth names the size of the pieces, and the number in front counts them. Because it's a noun, it takes a plural ending when there's more than one: one third, but two thirds. Some fraction words are made by adding -th to a number word, as in fifth. Others, such as half and quarter, are separate words that aren't built that way. This dictionary treats fifth in a fraction as different from fifth in fifth place, where it describes a position and takes no plural, even though the two look the same.
curious.try: Say one fifth, then two fifths. What happens to the end of the word? Does fifth place change the same way?

teacher.summary: Separates fraction nouns (three fifths) from ordinal adjectives (fifth place), which share morphological material.
teacher.explain: A fractional noun denotes a denominator and heads the nominal in a fraction NP, with the numerator in determiner function (one fifth). It's a count noun and inflects for number: one third, two thirds. Half and quarter are suppletive, not formed with -th. The same form can be an ordinal adjective in another use: fifth in fifth place is adjectival and takes no plural, while fifths in three fifths takes plural marking and a cardinal determiner. This dictionary, which is provisional, treats these as separate categories despite the shared form.
teacher.terms: Fraction word, with numerator and denominator, are the traditional terms. Ordinal number is the traditional name for what this dictionary calls an ordinal adjective.

contrasts.note: Fractional noun, plural, with a cardinal determiner.
Ordinal adjective, no plural marking.

watch_for: A learner might add plural marking to fifth in fifth place, as if it were the fraction noun.
A learner might expect half and quarter to be formed with -th like fifth.
teacher.activity: Give students a pie drawn in fifths. They shade one, two and three pieces and write the fraction in words each time, then write a sentence using fifth to give a position in a race and compare the two uses.

child.hook: What happens to the word third when you have two pieces?
child.explain: A fraction word names the size of the pieces. One third has one piece. With two pieces you say two thirds, adding an s. Half and quarter are special words.

examples.text: I coloured [two thirds] of the picture.
She ate [one quarter] of the pizza.

child.play: Say one third, then two thirds. Now try one fifth and two fifths. Which part of the word changes when there's more than one piece?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Fractional Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-fractional-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Fused-head Numerative

dimensions.form: Numerative DP without overt head noun
dimensions.meaning: Quantity reference with recoverable noun from context
dimensions.function: Fused determiner-head in NP structure
dimensions.distribution: Elliptical contexts; may license partitive of-complement

1.definition: Numerative used as a standalone DP/NP without an overt head noun

examples.form: She bought twenty books, but I bought [twenty-two].

examples.note: Factor substitution (fragment answering the factor constituent, not a fused head)

constraints.description: Functions as a fused determiner-head in NP structure; may license partitive of-complements.

projection.target: In Lee bought thirty books and I bought forty, the second numerative fills the object NP and can recover the kind from context. In Forty is even, the bare form can instead name the number. Stand-alone shape does not fix the analysis.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s fused-head comparison and Reynolds’s cardinal-noun diagnostics separate the corresponding readings.

curious.title: Number words that stand in for a whole phrase
curious.summary: A number word can stand alone when the thing counted is clear from the situation.
curious.body: In She bought twenty books, but I bought twenty-two, the second number does the work of a whole phrase. It means twenty-two books, and we recover books from the first half of the sentence. Not every bare number works this way. In Forty is even, the number names the number itself. And an answer like Two to the question How many thousand? fills in only the multiplier part of a number such as two thousand. This dictionary treats these as different readings of a similar-looking form.

examples.text: She bought twenty books, but I bought [twenty-two].

curious.try: Say a sentence with a number and a counted thing, then repeat it with the thing left out of the second half. What does the listener fill in?

teacher.summary: Shows number words standing alone for a whole noun phrase, and separates that use from bare numbers that name numbers.
teacher.explain: A numerative can fill a whole NP by itself, with the noun recovered from context. This dictionary calls this a fused determiner-head: one word has both the determiner function and the head function. A partitive of-complement may follow. Stand-alone shape doesn't settle the analysis: in Lee bought thirty books and I bought forty, forty fills the object NP and recovers books, but in Forty is even the bare form can name the number. The fragment Two, answering How many thousand?, substitutes for the factor in two thousand and isn't a fused head. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Fused determiner-head is the term used here. Traditional grammar might describe these as numerals used without a noun.

examples.text: She bought twenty books, but I bought [twenty-two].

contrasts.text: Lee bought thirty books and I bought [forty].
contrasts.note: Fused head, noun recovered from context.
The bare form can name the number instead.

watch_for: A learner might treat the fragment answer Two, given to a question about thousands, as a fused head, when it replaces only the factor.
A learner might read Forty in Forty is even as standing for forty things, when it can name the number.
teacher.activity: Write short pairs of sentences where the second leaves out the counted noun. Students underline the number word and say what noun the reader recovers.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Fused-head Numerative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-fused-head-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Magnitude Head Numerative

dimensions.form: Magnitude determinative (hundred, thousand, million, etc.)
dimensions.meaning: Denotes base magnitude value (powers of ten > 10)
dimensions.function: Head of magnitude phrase; licenses factor modifier
dimensions.distribution: Requires factor in most contexts; heads DP

1.definition: Denotes a base magnitude (hundred, thousand, million, etc.) that can scale a quantity

examples.note: Magnitude determinative head; factor two is its modifier
Magnitude head inside an additive coordination

projection.target: Hundred remains singular in exact two hundred books and supplies its scale. In hundreds of books, the same base has count plural morphology and an oblique dependent. These diagnostics separate the head’s lexical uses.
projection.evidence: Reynolds identifies a determinative magnitude head in the exact phrases and distinguishes plural magnitude nouns in the categorial analysis.

curious.title: Hundred, thousand and million as base amounts
curious.summary: Hundred, thousand and million are base amounts that other numbers can scale.
curious.body: Words like hundred, thousand and million stand for a base amount. In two hundred, the two scales that base: it says how many hundreds. This dictionary says such a word needs a number in front of it in most contexts. The same base can also be a plural noun. Hundred stays singular in two hundred books, but hundreds of books has a plural ending and an of phrase. The dictionary treats these as different uses of the same word. A base can also sit inside a longer number, as in twelve thousand and forty-one.

examples.text: two hundred books and [hundreds] of books

curious.try: Compare two hundred books with hundreds of books. Which one has a plural ending, and which one has an of?

teacher.summary: Shows how hundred, thousand and million work as the head of a number phrase, and how that differs from their plural noun uses.
teacher.explain: A magnitude head is a determinative such as hundred, thousand or million, denoting a base value that can scale a quantity. It's the head of the magnitude phrase and licenses a factor modifier (two hundred). This dictionary says it requires a factor in most contexts. Hundred stays singular in exact two hundred books and supplies its scale. In hundreds of books, the same base is a plural count noun with an of dependent, which is a separate lexical use. The head can also appear inside an additive coordination (twelve thousand and forty-one). This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Numeral is the traditional word for number words in general. This dictionary calls hundred, thousand and million magnitude determinatives when they head a number phrase.

contrasts.note: Exact quantity, singular magnitude head with a factor.
Plural count noun with an of dependent.

watch_for: A learner might add a plural ending to hundred in two hundred books, as in hundreds of books, when the two uses differ.
A learner might treat hundreds of books as the same construction as two hundred books.
teacher.activity: Students sort phrases such as two hundred books, hundreds of books and twelve thousand into exact quantities and plural noun uses, then say which has a factor in front.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Magnitude Head Numerative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-magnitude-head-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Ordinal Adjective
pattern: Cardinal base → ordinal form (-th or suppletive)

entry.name: Ordinal Adjective
entry.pattern: Cardinal base → ordinal form (-th or suppletive)

dimensions.form: Cardinal base + -th suffix or suppletive (first, second, third)
dimensions.meaning: Specifies rank or position in an ordered sequence
dimensions.function: Heads AdjPs; attributive modifier or predicative complement
dimensions.distribution: Pre-nominal modifier; licenses factors in complex ordinals

1.definition: Specifies rank or order position within a sequence

constraints.description: Ordinal adjectives typically function as modifiers in NPs and can co-occur with determiners.

projection.target: Third can premodify chapter alongside a separate determiner, as in the third chapter. In three thirds the homophonous ordinal base supplies a count noun with plural marking and a preceding numeral.
projection.evidence: CGEL and Reynolds distinguish the ordinal adjective from the fractional noun by its NP distribution.

curious.title: Words for position in a line
curious.summary: Words like first and twenty-second say where something comes in an ordered sequence.
curious.body: Words like first, second and twenty-second give rank or position. They're built from a number word by adding -th, or they're special forms, as with first, second and third. They work like describing words. In the third chapter, third sits before the noun alongside the word the. This dictionary separates that use from three thirds, where the same-looking word is a noun naming a fraction, with a plural ending and a number in front.
curious.try: Line up five objects and name their positions. Which position words have special forms?

teacher.summary: Helps explain ordinal words as adjectives, and how they differ from fraction nouns that look the same.
teacher.explain: Ordinal adjectives specify rank or position. They're formed from a cardinal base plus -th or are suppletive (first, second, third). They head AdjPs and function as attributive modifiers or predicative complements, and they can co-occur with determiners: the third chapter. Twenty-second is a further example, at rank 22. The same form can be a fractional noun: in three thirds, third is a count noun with plural marking and a preceding numeral. This dictionary, which marks the analysis as provisional, uses distribution in the NP to tell the two apart.
teacher.terms: Ordinal number or ordinal numeral is the traditional name for these words. This dictionary treats ordinals as adjectives, and fractions such as thirds as nouns.

contrasts.note: Ordinal adjective, modifying chapter beside the determiner the.
Fractional noun with plural marking and a numeral in front.

watch_for: A learner might treat third in three thirds as the same word class as third in the third chapter.
A learner might expect every ordinal to have a special form, when only first, second and third are listed as suppletive here.
teacher.activity: Students stand in a line and each says their position (first, second, third). Then they write one sentence using an ordinal before a noun, such as the third chapter, and one using a fraction such as three thirds, and say which is which.

child.hook: What words tell you who is first, second and third in a race?
child.explain: Some words tell you the place in a line. First, second and third are special words. Some others are made by adding th to the number. They can go before a noun, like the third chapter.
child.play: Line up toys and say each one's place, like the first one and the second one. Then make up a sentence that puts a place word before a noun.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain no longer offers twenty-second as an example of a factor (the entry licenses factors in complex ordinals but does not say twenty-second has one); it is now just an example of rank 22. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; irregular changed to suppletive as in the entry. Second round: fixed child.explain, Others changed to Some others (the entry's twenty-second is not formed by adding th); teacher.terms now gives the traditional names for these words rather than for a word class.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Ordinal Adjective." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-ordinal-adjective-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Rightmost-base Ordinal Formation in Numeratives
pattern: [numerative] + ordinal suffix on rightmost simple base

entry.name: Rightmost-base Ordinal Formation in Numeratives
entry.pattern: [numerative] + ordinal suffix on rightmost simple base

dimensions.form: Complex numerative with ordinal morphology on rightmost base only
dimensions.meaning: Ordinal meaning applies to entire numerative
dimensions.function: Morphological targeting rule for ordinal/fractional formation
dimensions.distribution: Defines constituent boundary before noun; key evidence against cascading NumP

1.definition: Ordinal morphology targets the rightmost simple base within a numerative

constraints.description: Ordinal/fractional morphology selects the rightmost simple base in the numerative constituent.
Irregular bases (first/second/third) are lexically specified.

projection.target: In two hundred forty-second, the only overt ordinal form is the last part of the numerative, while the ordinal interpretation applies to the whole rank. Ordinalizing an earlier component cannot freely substitute for that realization.
projection.evidence: Reynolds uses the placement of ordinal morphology among the constituency tests, independently of spelling conventions.

curious.title: Where the ordinal ending goes in a long number
curious.summary: In a long ordinal such as twenty-fourth, only the last part of the number takes the ordinal form.
curious.body: To turn a number into a position word, you change the last part only. Twenty-four becomes twenty-fourth, and two hundred becomes two hundredth. The special forms work the same way: in twenty-second, the last word two becomes second. The whole phrase gives one rank, but only the final piece shows it. In two hundred forty-second, the only marked word is the last one. This dictionary says that ending on an earlier part can't freely take its place.
curious.try: Say your house number as a position, such as the thirty-first house. Which part of the number changed?

teacher.summary: Shows where the ordinal ending goes in complex numbers, and why it only marks the final part.
teacher.explain: Ordinal and fractional morphology targets the rightmost simple base in a complex numerative: twenty-fourth (on four), two hundredth (on the magnitude base hundred), twenty-second (the suppletive ordinal for two). The irregular bases first, second and third are lexically specified. The ordinal meaning applies to the whole numerative, but the form shows it only on the last part. In two hundred forty-second, only the final element is overtly ordinal. This dictionary uses this placement as evidence about constituent structure, independently of spelling. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Ordinal number or ordinal numeral is the traditional name for these forms.
watch_for: A learner might try to put the ordinal ending on an earlier part of a long number, when the ending goes on the last part.
A learner might think the ordinal meaning belongs only to the final word, when it applies to the whole number.
teacher.activity: Give students cardinal numbers (twenty-four, two hundred, twenty-two) and have them write the ordinal for each, underlining the part that changed. Then they say a longer number of their own as a position.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Rightmost-base Ordinal Formation in Numeratives." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-ordinal-rightmost-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Single-digit Numerative

dimensions.form: Monomorphemic lexemes (one through nine, plus zero)
dimensions.meaning: Specifies cardinality from zero to nine
dimensions.function: Factor, addition, determiner; most versatile numerative subclass
dimensions.distribution: All numerative positions; combine freely in compounds

1.definition: Specifies a cardinal value from zero to nine

projection.target: The digit 0 participates as the lexeme zero and can determine a plural in zero defects. One differs in selecting a singular count nominal. The single-digit class therefore does not predict uniform agreement or determiner selection.
projection.evidence: CGEL gives the cardinal distribution and Reynolds includes zero in the basic lexical inventory. The comparison separates numerical representation from grammatical number.

curious.title: The words for zero to nine
curious.summary: The single-word numbers from zero to nine can do any job a number word does, though they don't all behave alike.
curious.body: The numbers from zero to nine are single words: one, two, three and so on up to nine, plus zero. They can stand in front of a noun, multiply a bigger number, or be added to one, as in forty-two. They don't all act the same. One goes with a singular noun, while zero can go with a plural, as in zero defects. This dictionary says that being a single-digit number doesn't tell you how a word will agree or what kind of noun follows it.
curious.try: Say one apple, then zero apples. Which has a plural ending on the noun?

teacher.summary: Covers the digit words zero to nine, and why they don't all select the same kind of noun.
teacher.explain: Single-digit numeratives are the monomorphemic lexemes zero to nine. They specify cardinality and can function as a factor, as an addend or as a determiner, and they combine freely in compounds. They don't predict uniform agreement or determiner selection. Zero participates as the lexeme zero and can determine a plural (zero defects). One selects a singular count nominal. This dictionary separates the numerical representation, the digit, from grammatical number. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Numeral, or cardinal numeral, is the traditional name. Digit refers to the written symbol 0 to 9, which this dictionary distinguishes from the lexeme.
watch_for: A learner might expect one to go with a plural noun in the way five does.
A learner might think zero must go with a singular noun, because it stands for none.
teacher.activity: Students write a noun phrase for each word from zero to nine (for example zero defects, one chapter, five dogs) and sort them by whether the noun is singular or plural.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Single-digit Numerative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-single-digit-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Regular Teen Numerative (-teen)

dimensions.form: Single-digit base + -teen suffix (thirteen through nineteen)
dimensions.meaning: Specifies cardinality from thirteen to nineteen
dimensions.function: Same distribution as single-digit numeratives
dimensions.distribution: Determiner, factor, addition; lexically atomic

1.definition: Specifies a cardinality from thirteen to nineteen via -teen morphology

projection.target: The -teen word form gives a value ten greater than the base related to it. The same base element can give a different value with -ty, as thirteen versus thirty shows. The two endings do not have the same lexical or prosodic distribution.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates the teen and decade formations. Reynolds counts both among the basic lexemes.

curious.title: Thirteen to nineteen
curious.summary: The numbers from thirteen to nineteen are built from a single-digit word plus -teen.
