curious.body: Thirteen through nineteen are formed by adding -teen to a single-digit word. The -teen word has a value ten greater than the base it comes from, so thirteen is ten more than three. The ending -ty works differently: the same base gives a different value, as thirteen and thirty show. The two endings also don't have the same distribution as words. Once built, a -teen word acts as one unit and can do the same jobs as a single-digit number.
curious.try: Say thirteen and thirty. What differs in the sound, and what differs in the amount?

teacher.summary: Explains the -teen numbers from thirteen to nineteen and how they differ from the -ty numbers.
teacher.explain: The regular teen numeratives are formed from a single-digit base plus -teen and specify cardinalities from thirteen to nineteen. They're lexically atomic and have the same distribution as single-digit numeratives: determiner, factor and addition. The -teen form is ten greater than its base, while -ty gives a different value from the same base, as thirteen versus thirty shows. CGEL separates the teen and decade formations, and the two endings differ in lexical and prosodic distribution. Eleven and twelve are treated in a separate entry. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Teens is the traditional name for these numbers. This dictionary calls them teen numeratives and treats each as a single word.

contrasts.note: -teen, ten greater than the base three.
-ty, a different value from the same base.

watch_for: A learner might confuse thirteen and thirty, which have different values.
A learner might treat thirteen as two separate words, when it works as one unit.
teacher.activity: Students pair -teen and -ty words (thirteen and thirty, for example) and say each in a short sentence about a quantity, noting how the endings differ in sound.

child.hook: What is the difference between thirteen and thirty?
child.explain: Thirteen ends in teen and is ten more than three. Thirty ends in ty and is a different amount. Both start from the same word.
child.play: Say two number words that end in teen and two that end in ty. Can your friend hear the difference? Make a sentence with each.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Regular Teen Numerative (-teen)." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-teen-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Irregular Teen Numerative (eleven/twelve)

dimensions.form: Suppletive forms not derived by -teen suffixation
dimensions.meaning: Specifies cardinality of eleven or twelve
dimensions.function: Same distribution as regular teens
dimensions.distribution: Determiner, factor, addition; lexically atomic

1.definition: Suppletive teen numeratives for 11 and 12

constraints.description: Not derived by -teen suffixation.

projection.target: Eleven and twelve occupy the first two positions after ten but do not use productive -teen suffixation. Their related ordinals eleventh and twelfth can be compared with thirteenth without analyzing eleven and twelve as -teen stems.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the distinct forms inside the numeral inventory. Current morphological structure is the criterion here.

curious.title: Eleven and twelve
curious.summary: Eleven and twelve sit right after ten, but they aren't built with -teen.
curious.body: Eleven and twelve come right after ten in the counting order, but they don't use the -teen ending that thirteen and the rest use. They're their own forms, not made by adding anything to a single-digit word. This dictionary treats them as separate words with the same jobs as the -teen numbers: in front of a noun, as a multiplier, or added to another number. Their position-words, eleventh and twelfth, can be compared with thirteenth without treating eleven and twelve as -teen words.
curious.try: Count from eleven up to nineteen. Which words don't end in teen?

teacher.summary: Explains eleven and twelve as irregular forms that aren't treated as -teen words.
teacher.explain: Eleven and twelve are suppletive teen numeratives for 11 and 12. They aren't derived by -teen suffixation, though they come in the first two positions after ten. They're lexically atomic and have the same distribution as the regular teens: determiner, factor and addition. Their ordinals eleventh and twelfth can be compared with thirteenth without analyzing eleven and twelve as -teen stems. This dictionary takes current morphological structure as its criterion. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls these forms irregular (in its name for the pattern) and suppletive, not derived by -teen suffixation.

contrasts.note: Suppletive form, not made with -teen.
Regular -teen form.

watch_for: A learner might expect eleven and twelve to be built like thirteen, with -teen on a single-digit base.
A learner might think eleven and twelve behave differently from the -teen numbers in a noun phrase, when they have the same distribution.
teacher.activity: Students write the numbers from eleven to nineteen, circle the two that don't end in -teen, and write a short sentence using each of them before a noun.

child.hook: Do eleven and twelve end in teen like thirteen does?
child.explain: Thirteen ends in teen. Eleven and twelve don't. They're special words that don't follow the teen pattern. You use them just like the other numbers.
child.play: Count from eleven up to nineteen out loud. Clap on the two words that don't end in teen.

checked.note: Fixed: the teacher activity and child play said to go from ten to nineteen and pick out the two numbers without -teen, but ten also lacks it; the ranges now start at eleven. Also fixed (unflagged): the same range in the curious try question. Second round: fixed curious.body, which described the factor use as multiplying a larger number (this dictionary sets no size condition); fixed teacher.terms, which called irregular the traditional word and defined suppletive as not derived by -teen, and now gives this dictionary's own wording. Also fixed (unflagged): teacher.summary no longer promises to explain why the forms are irregular.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Irregular Teen Numerative (eleven/twelve)." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-teen-irregular-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: ten Numerative

dimensions.form: Monomorphemic lexeme; base for teen and decade derivation
dimensions.meaning: Specifies cardinality of ten
dimensions.function: Determiner, factor; morphological base for -teen and -ty
dimensions.distribution: All basic numerative positions

1.definition: Specifies a cardinality of ten

projection.target: Ten chapters uses ten directly with a plural nominal. In two tens, the separate cardinal two quantifies two realizations of the value and tens inflects. An independent use of ten does not force either analysis across contexts.
projection.evidence: Reynolds lists ten among the basic determinative forms and uses token nouns to establish separate noun distribution.

curious.title: The word ten
curious.summary: Ten is a single word that other number words, such as -teen and -ty ones, are built from.
curious.body: Ten is a single word that specifies the amount ten. It can stand in front of a plural noun, as in ten chapters, and it's the base that the -teen and -ty numbers are formed from. Ten can also be counted. In two tens, the number two counts two portions of the value ten, and tens takes a plural ending. This dictionary says that ten used on its own doesn't force either analysis in every context.
curious.try: Compare ten chapters with two tens. Which one has an s on ten, and what is two doing in it?

teacher.summary: Explains ten as a basic numerative and how it differs from the noun use in two tens.
teacher.explain: Ten is a monomorphemic lexeme specifying a cardinality of ten. It occurs in all basic numerative positions, including determiner and factor, and is the morphological base for -teen and -ty. Ten chapters uses ten directly with a plural nominal. In two tens, the separate cardinal two quantifies two realizations of the value and tens inflects, as a noun would. This dictionary doesn't force either analysis for an independent use of ten across contexts. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Cardinal number is the traditional name. This dictionary also uses cardinal noun for the countable use in two tens.

contrasts.note: Ten used directly with a plural noun.
Tens inflects for number and is counted by two.

watch_for: A learner might read tens in two tens as a plural of the determiner in ten chapters, when it takes plural marking as a noun.
A learner might assume a bare ten has one fixed analysis, when this dictionary leaves that open across contexts.
teacher.activity: Students write one phrase with ten before a noun and one with two tens, and explain in their own words what two counts in the second.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "ten Numerative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerative-ten-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Numerical Label Construction

dimensions.form: Cardinal noun (basic or complex) following an embellishment noun; bare NP
dimensions.meaning: Rigid designation of a unique entity via numerical identifier
dimensions.function: Names/identifies specific entities (rooms, highways, addresses, etc.)
dimensions.distribution: Subject, object, complement positions; typically without determiner

1.definition: A cardinal proper noun heads a bare NP used as a proper name, identifying a unique entity through direct reference

examples.note: Numerical label identifying a specific room
Numerical label for a specific highway

constraints.description: Cardinal noun heads a bare NP; resists determiners and attributive modifiers.
Rigidly designates a unique entity; reference is direct, not mediated by descriptive content.
The non-numeral element (Room, Highway, etc.) functions as embellishment, not attributive modifier.

relatedConstructions.notes: This subtype restricts the identifier to numerical forms. The wider pattern also admits letters and mixed codes.
Reynolds treats 1066 in the year 1066 as an appositive (n. 10). A bare year such as 1066 can identify a calendar year on its own.

grounds.locator: §5, cardinal nouns used as labels (§5.2 [7a–b] and nn. 9–10); §2, terminology

grounds.note: CGEL lists Ward 17 among composite heads and calls Ward a descriptor inside the name. Its embellishments are semantically non-restrictive dependents outside the name, and they include nominal and adjectival attributive modifiers. So CGEL doesn't contrast embellishment with attributive modifier, as the third constraint (from Reynolds 2026, n. 9) does.

grounds.locator: Meeting Locations, Robert Purcell Community Center
grounds.note: Lists Room 101 as the code for the TV Lounge.

projection.target: In room six, six identifies a designated room in the labeling system. It does not say that six rooms are involved. Adding an external quantity in two Room Six signs can count the signs while leaving the label unchanged.
projection.evidence: Reynolds includes label uses among cardinal proper-noun uses and distinguishes the label from count determination.

known_boundary_items: In 20 Pheasant Street the number precedes the street name, unlike Room 101 and Flight 447.
Room 302A has the same naming function with a mixed code, as covered by the wider descriptor-plus-identifier entry.

curious.title: Names made of numbers
curious.summary: A word like Room or Highway followed by a number can work as the name of one particular thing.
curious.body: Some places and things are named with a number. Room 101 is one specific room, Highway 401 is one specific highway, and Flight 447 is one specific flight. In these names the number doesn't count anything. It says which room, which highway or which flight you mean. That's why the number behaves like part of a name rather than like a quantity. Compare Room 101 with 101 rooms: in the second, the number tells you how many rooms there are. In the first, it picks out a single room in a system of labels.
curious.try: Try swapping the number in a name you know, such as a room or a flight. Do you now mean a different thing, or a different amount of the same thing?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining why a number after a noun like Room can be a name rather than a quantity.
teacher.explain: In Room 101, the number is a cardinal noun that names the thing, and the whole phrase is a bare NP (it has no determiner of its own) used as a proper name. On this dictionary's analysis, the first word, Room, is an embellishment of the name rather than an attributive modifier, and it gives the kind of thing named. The number doesn't say how many: it points to one unique entity through a labelling system. Compare 101 rooms, where 101 is a quantity that counts rooms. In 20 Pheasant Street the number comes first, before the street name, unlike Room 101 and Flight 447.
teacher.terms: Cardinal noun: a number word used as a noun. Embellishment: this dictionary's label for the non-numeral word (Room, Highway). CGEL analyzes the comparable Ward in Ward 17 differently, as a descriptor inside the name.

contrasts.note: The number identifies one room.
The number counts rooms.

watch_for: A learner might read Room 101 as one hundred and one rooms.
A learner might think 20 Pheasant Street is a count of something rather than an address.
teacher.activity: Give pairs of cards, one showing a label (Highway 401, Flight 447) and one showing a quantity (401 highways, 447 flights). Students sort them into "names one thing" and "counts things", then say how they decided.

child.hook: If you're in Room 101, are you in a hundred and one rooms?
child.explain: Sometimes a number is a name. Room 101 is just one room, and the number tells you which one. In 101 rooms, the number tells you how many.
child.play: Find numbers on doors, buses or signs. For each one, decide if it names one thing or counts several.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms no longer glosses embellishment as CGEL's term for Room (CGEL treats the comparable Ward as a descriptor inside the name); teacher.explain marks the embellishment analysis as this dictionary's.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Numerical Label Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/numerical-label-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Object-Oriented Ascriptive Predicative

1.definition: Ascribes a property or status to the object referent.
1.details: In considered him a fool, the NP a fool describes him. The predicative does not add another participant or require a change of state. Passivizing can make the original object the subject while retaining its status as the referent described by the predicative.

examples.note: The predicative NP describes the person referred to by him.
Constructed passive with the adjectival predicative retained.

relatedConstructions.notes: The active VP contains an object and a predicative complement.
The resultative presents a property as a result of the event.
Two NPs can instead be two distinct objects. The predicative describes the object.

grounds.note: Documents object attribute frames.
Compares predicative complements, objects and resultatives.

projection.target: The predicative remains oriented to the original object under passivization. With consider, the sentence does not present the object as undergoing a change.
projection.evidence: CASA distinguishes NP and adjective realizations. CGEL treats them as predicative complements with the object as their predicand.

curious.title: Describing the person or thing after the verb
curious.summary: In some sentences the phrase after the object describes it, and isn't a second object.
curious.body: In She considered him a fool, the phrase a fool doesn't name another person. It describes him. The sentence ascribes a property or status to the person referred to by him. Nothing has to change for this to work: considering someone a fool doesn't present them as becoming one. The description stays attached to him even when the sentence is turned around, as in He was considered unreliable. This dictionary separates this pattern from sentences with two objects, such as handing someone a gift.
curious.try: Say She considered him a fool. Who does a fool describe?

teacher.summary: Separates an object plus a describing phrase from two objects, and from a result.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb, a direct object and a predicative complement (an NP or AdjP) that describes the object: in considered him a fool, a fool describes him. The predicative adds no participant and doesn't require a change of state. In the passive, the original object becomes the subject and the predicative still describes the same referent (He was considered unreliable). It contrasts with the double-object pattern, where two NPs are separate objects, and with the resultative, which presents the property as the result of the event. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: The predicative here is sometimes called an object complement. This dictionary's term is predicative complement, with the object as its predicand.

contrasts.note: A fool describes him, so there's one object plus a predicative.
Two separate objects, indirect then direct.
The property is the result of the event, which makes it a resultative.

watch_for: A learner might read the two NPs in considered him a fool as two objects, when a fool describes him.
A learner might expect considered unreliable to mean the person changed, when the pattern doesn't require a change of state.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with two phrases after the verb. They decide whether the second phrase describes the first phrase or is a second object, and explain how they know.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Object-Oriented Ascriptive Predicative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/object-ascriptive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Object Control in a to-Infinitival Complement
pattern: VP[V + NPᵢ + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

entry.name: Object Control in a to-Infinitival Complement
entry.pattern: VP[V + NPᵢ + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

1.definition: Interprets a selected object as the participant in the infinitival situation.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. Negation in the subordinate clause applies to waiting. Kai remains the persuadee.

relatedConstructions.notes: Persuaded Kai to stay requires a persuadee. Expected there to be trouble permits dummy there in the corresponding position.

projection.target: Kai is both the person persuaded and the understood subject of stay. Dummy there cannot serve as a persuadee.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Persuading someone to do something
curious.summary: In Jo persuaded Kai to stay, Kai is both the person persuaded and the one who stays.
curious.body: In Jo persuaded Kai to stay, one person does two jobs. Kai is the person who was persuaded, and Kai is also the one who stays, even though stay has no subject of its own. The same holds when the second part is negative: in They persuaded Kai not to wait, the not applies to waiting, and Kai is still the person persuaded. This dictionary calls the pattern object control, because the object of the first verb controls who does the second action.
curious.try: Say Jo persuaded Kai to stay. Who was persuaded? Who stays?

teacher.summary: Explains verbs like persuade, where the object is also the understood subject of the infinitive.
teacher.explain: In object control, the NP after the verb is a selected object that is also interpreted as the subject of the to-infinitival. Kai is the person persuaded and the one who stays. Because the object is a participant in the main verb's situation, persuaded Kai to stay requires a persuadee, so dummy there can't fill the slot. Negation in the infinitival applies to the subordinate situation (persuaded Kai not to wait). It differs from object raising, as in expected there to be trouble, where the corresponding position permits dummy there. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Object control is the term used here. Equi is another textbook name for this idea.

contrasts.text: They persuaded Kai not to wait.
contrasts.note: The negation applies to waiting. Kai remains the persuadee.

contrasts.text: They expected there to be trouble.
contrasts.note: Object raising. The corresponding position permits dummy there.

watch_for: A learner might read Kai in persuaded Kai to stay as only the subject of stay, when Kai is also the person persuaded.
A learner might read the negation in persuaded Kai not to wait as applying to the persuading, when it applies to waiting.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with persuade, a person and an infinitive. They then underline who was persuaded and who does the second action, and confirm these are the same person.

child.hook: In Jo persuaded Kai to stay, who is going to stay?
child.explain: Kai is the one who gets persuaded. Kai is also the one who stays. One person does both jobs in the sentence.
child.play: Make up a sentence with persuaded, a friend's name, to, and something to do. Then ask who gets persuaded and who does the thing.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Object Control in a to-Infinitival Complement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/object-control-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Object Raising with a to-Infinitival
pattern: VP[V + raised NPᵢ + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

entry.name: Object Raising with a to-Infinitival
entry.pattern: VP[V + raised NPᵢ + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

1.definition: Presents an assessment of a subordinate situation whose subject is realized in the higher complement sequence.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. A passive counterpart preserves the embedded predication.

projection.target: The raised slot admits dummy there, and an ordinary raised NP can correspond to the subject of a passive with verbs such as believe. It need not independently participate in the believing.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Expecting something about someone
curious.summary: In They expected there to be trouble, what is expected is a whole situation, not the word after expected.
curious.body: In They expected there to be trouble, the thing expected is that there would be trouble. The little word there isn't a person or a place, so it can't be someone the verb is about. It simply fills the position after the verb. This dictionary calls the pattern object raising. An ordinary noun phrase after the verb can correspond to the subject of a passive, as Jo does in Jo was expected to win. It need not take part in the expecting or believing itself. The pattern presents an assessment of a situation, here Jo winning.
curious.try: Say They expected there to be trouble. Is there a person or thing that does the expecting besides they?

teacher.summary: Explains verbs like expect, where the noun phrase after the verb belongs to the situation being assessed.
teacher.explain: In object raising, the NP after the verb is the subject of the to-infinitival situation but appears in the higher complement sequence. The pattern presents an assessment of that subordinate situation. The slot admits dummy there (expected there to be trouble), and an ordinary raised NP can correspond to the subject of a passive with verbs such as believe. It need not independently participate in the believing. A passive counterpart preserves the embedded predication (Jo was expected to win). It contrasts with object control, as in persuaded Kai to stay, where Kai is the person persuaded. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Raising to object is another name for the same pattern. This dictionary treats object control separately.

contrasts.text: They expected there to be trouble.
contrasts.note: Dummy there is possible after the verb.
Control. Kai is the person persuaded.

watch_for: A learner might think the NP after the verb must take part in the main verb's action, when with expect it need not.
A learner might treat there in expected there to be trouble as a place, when it is a dummy.
teacher.activity: Students compare sentences with expected and persuaded, and ask of each whether the noun phrase after the verb is a person the verb acts on or only the subject of what is expected.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer calls Jo in the passive 'a noun phrase in that position' (it is the passive subject corresponding to the NP after the verb); teacher control contrast no longer claims dummy there is excluded or that the object 'must' be a participant (the entry does not say so). Second round: dismissed the three flags on the object-control contrast (this dictionary's object-control entry links back to this one with the same contrast, persuaded Kai to stay against expected there to be trouble, and says Kai is the person persuaded); teacher.terms now says this dictionary treats object control separately. Also fixed: This dictionary is provisional changed to marks the analysis as provisional.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Object Raising with a to-Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/object-raising-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Object-Oriented Resultative Construction

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb with an NP direct object followed by an object-oriented predicative complement
dimensions.meaning: The direct-object referent comes to have the property or status expressed by the predicative complement as a result of the verbal event
dimensions.function: Adds a secondary result predication whose predicand is Od
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal in complex-transitive clauses; the PredComp may be lexically selected or constructionally licensed and may be obligatory or optional

1.definition: The direct-object referent is in the state expressed by PredComp at the end of the process denoted by the VP
1.details: PredComp is a syntactic complement oriented toward Od, and resultative is its semantic interpretation. Unlike a depictive, a resultative entails a change culminating in the PredComp state. CGEL recognizes obligatory and optional object-oriented resultatives; optional resultatives remain complements, whereas optional depictives are analyzed as adjuncts. In a related passive, the active Od becomes subject and the PredComp is correspondingly subject-oriented (CGEL Ch. 4 §§1.1, 5, 5.3, pp. 217, 251–62).

examples.note: Optional resultative PredComp clean is predicated of Od it
The fence comes to be blue as a result of the painting

2.definition: An agentive activity verb licenses a reflexive Od as predicand for an obligatory resultative PredComp
2.details: In He talked himself hoarse, talk does not require internal complementation on its own, but himself and hoarse are licensed together: dropping both yields He talked, while dropping only PredComp does not preserve the analysis because himself is then not Od. CGEL restricts this subtype to a reflexive predicand; an arbitrary affected NP is excluded (Ch. 4 §5.3, pp. 261–62).

examples.note: Constructionally licensed reflexive Od plus obligatory resultative PredComp

constraints.description: The NP is Od and the following AdjP or NP is PredComp, not a second object; PredComp is oriented toward Od in the active VP.
PredComp denotes a resultant state of its predicand, not a state merely holding during the verbal situation.
An optional resultative is still a complement; an optional depictive such as almost raw in ate the steak almost raw is an adjunct in CGEL's analysis.
Marked state-goal PPs such as to sleep and into a stupor are locative complements rather than PredComp and therefore fall outside this pattern.
With an agentive intransitive base such as talk, the resultative subtype requires a reflexive Od; the reflexive and PredComp are jointly licensed.

projection.target: An Od followed by an object-oriented resultative PredComp predicts an end-state entailment for the Od referent, reorientation of PredComp to the subject under passive, and complement behavior distinct from optional depictive adjuncts and marked locative state goals
projection.evidence: CGEL's predicand orientation, passive correspondence, resultative-depictive contrast, and obligatory/optional complementation tests converge on this profile (Ch. 4 §§1.1, 5, 5.3, pp. 217, 251–62).

diagnostics: joint omission of reflexive and PredComp

known_boundary_items: ate the steak almost raw: optional depictive adjunct, not a resultative PredComp
cried himself to sleep or drank himself into a stupor: to/into PPs express marked state goals and are locative complements
considered Ed a fool: object-oriented PredComp but depictive rather than resultative
caused motion uses an object-oriented locative Comp:PP, not PredComp

relatedConstructions.notes: Object-oriented resultatives are VP-level complement constructions
The result predicand is realized by an NP direct object; PredComp itself may also be an NP
Both express caused change, but caused motion uses a locative Comp:PP where the resultative uses PredComp
Head–Od–PredComp is complex-transitive, not the Head–Oi–Od double-object pattern
Marked state goals such as to sleep are locative complements rather than PredComp
Time-away contains Od plus a particle PP complement and does not predicate a result property of Od

grounds.note: PredComp is a core complement oriented toward a predicand; in transitive clauses the predicand is normally Od
Result interpretation, optionality, adjunct contrast, and reflexive licensing provide convergent diagnostics

curious.title: Doing something until the object ends up a certain way
curious.summary: In He painted the fence blue, the last word says what state the fence ends up in.
curious.body: In He painted the fence blue, the fence comes to be blue as a result of the painting. The word blue describes the fence, and it describes the outcome. He washed it clean works the same way: it ends up clean. There's a related pattern with a reflexive word. In He talked himself hoarse, the talking leaves him hoarse. This dictionary says it works only with a reflexive, not with any affected person. It's different from describing how something is while the action goes on, as in He ate the steak almost raw.
curious.try: After someone paints a fence blue, what colour is the fence? Does the word blue describe the fence before or after the painting?

teacher.summary: Explains a result state attached to the direct object, and how it differs from depictives and from state-goal PPs.
teacher.explain: The object-oriented resultative is a verb with a direct object (Od) followed by a predicative complement (an AdjP or NP) that is predicated of that object. The Od is in the state the predicative names at the end of the verbal process. Unlike a depictive, a resultative entails a change culminating in that state. An optional resultative still counts as a complement, while an optional depictive such as almost raw in ate the steak almost raw is an adjunct. Marked state goals such as to sleep are locative complements. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Resultative is the traditional name. The predicative is also sometimes called an object complement. Depictive is the name for a description that holds during the event.

contrasts.note: Resultative. The fence comes to be blue as a result of the painting.

contrasts.text: He ate the steak almost raw.
contrasts.note: Depictive. Almost raw describes the steak while he ate it, and it's an adjunct.
To sleep is a marked state goal, a locative complement, so it isn't a resultative predicative.

watch_for: A learner might read painted the fence blue as having two objects, when blue describes the fence.
A learner might treat cried herself to sleep as the same pattern as talked himself hoarse, when to sleep is a locative complement.
A learner might take almost raw in ate the steak almost raw as a result, when it describes the steak during the eating.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with a verb, an object and a descriptive word. They ask whether the object ends up in that state because of the action (resultative) or is simply that way while the action happens (depictive), and sort them.

child.hook: After someone paints a fence blue, what colour is it?
child.explain: In He painted the fence blue, the last word tells how the fence ended up. The painting made it blue. The word comes after the thing and says what it became.
child.play: Pick a job, like wiping or painting. Say the thing, then a word for how it ends up. For example, wiped the table dry. Trade turns with a friend.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Object-Oriented Resultative Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/object-resultative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Accusative Subject in a Gerund-Participial
pattern: gerund-participial[Subject:NP in accusative if a personal pronoun + V-ing VP]

entry.name: Accusative Subject in a Gerund-Participial
entry.pattern: gerund-participial[Subject:NP in accusative if a personal pronoun + V-ing VP]

1.definition: Expresses the subject of an -ing clause without genitive marking where the environment allows it.

examples.form: We objected to [them blocking the exit].

projection.target: The prepositional context can license them as the embedded subject, and blocking still takes a direct object. Alternatives with a genitive vary with syntactic environment and style.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Them blocking the exit
curious.summary: An -ing phrase can have its own subject, and a pronoun there can take its object form, as in them blocking the exit.
curious.body: In We objected to them blocking the exit, the -ing phrase them blocking the exit has its own subject, them. The pronoun has the form used for objects, not a genitive form such as their. The word them is the doer of the blocking, not the thing objected to. And blocking still has its own object, the exit. This dictionary says that where a genitive form is an alternative, the choice varies with the surrounding grammar and with style, and that this pattern is the one with no genitive marking.

examples.text: We objected to [them blocking the exit].
She was annoyed at [him leaving early].

curious.try: Say We objected to them blocking the exit. Who is doing the blocking?

teacher.summary: Explains an -ing clause whose subject is a pronoun in its object form, as in objected to them blocking the exit.
teacher.explain: A gerund-participial clause can have a subject NP that, if it's a personal pronoun, is accusative: them blocking the exit. This dictionary says the prepositional context (objected to) can license them as the embedded subject, while blocking still takes a direct object. The alternative with a genitive subject varies with the syntactic environment and with style. The pattern expresses the subject of an -ing clause without genitive marking where the environment allows it. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats the clause as gerund-participial.

examples.text: We objected to [them blocking the exit].
She was annoyed at [him leaving early].

watch_for: A learner might take them as the object of the preposition to, when it is the subject of the -ing clause.
A learner might read the exit as the object of the preposition to, when it is the direct object of blocking.
teacher.activity: Students underline the subject and the verb of the -ing clause in sentences like We objected to them blocking the exit, then identify which words are the clause's subject and its object.

checked.note: Fixed: replaced the watch_for item that treated omitting the object as a learner error with a confusion the entry supports (blocking still takes the exit as direct object). Dismissed: none. Second round: fixed teacher.terms by cutting the claim about how traditional grammar frames the choice between them blocking and their blocking (this dictionary makes no such claim).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Accusative Subject in a Gerund-Participial." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/oblique-ing-subject-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: X of one’s own
pattern: NP[... N + PP[of + NP[dependent genitive pronoun + own]]]

entry.name: X of one’s own
entry.pattern: NP[... N + PP[of + NP[dependent genitive pronoun + own]]]

1.definition: Presents an entity as set aside for someone’s ownership or independent use.
1.details: My own uses the dependent genitive form. CGEL contrasts a car of my own and a car of mine. Harjo’s motel-room example specifies independent use through rental. Comparing a room of her own with her own room and a room of hers in the same new rental context would help show which contribution belongs to the of pattern.

examples.form: I’ve got [a car of my own].

examples.note: Harjo imagines renting space to sleep and paint.

relatedConstructions.notes: Of mine is the corresponding pronoun pattern without own.
Both involve of and genitive forms. The own phrase uses the dependent form of the pronoun.

projection.target: The construction can describe independent use without legal ownership, and uses my own where the simple genitive would have mine.
projection.evidence: CGEL's form contrast and Harjo's rental example. The pre-head own comparison remains a proposed test.

curious.title: A car of my own
curious.summary: A phrase like a car of my own presents something as set aside for your ownership or use.
curious.body: A car of my own presents the car as set aside for someone's ownership or independent use. The pattern is a noun, then of, then a genitive pronoun such as my, then own. The same idea without own uses a different pronoun form: a car of mine. It needn't mean legal ownership. Someone imagining renting a room to sleep and paint in can still call it a room of my own. The word all can add emphasis, as in a room all of my own.

examples.text: I've got [a car of my own].

curious.try: Finish the sentence: I'd like a ___ of my own. Does your phrase mean you own it, or only that you can use it?

teacher.summary: Explains the pattern a room of my own and how it contrasts with a room of mine.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a noun followed by of plus a dependent genitive pronoun and own (a car of my own). It presents an entity as set aside for someone's ownership or independent use, and it can describe independent use without legal ownership. CGEL contrasts a car of my own with a car of mine: my own uses the dependent genitive form, where the simple pattern uses the independent form mine. All can emphasize the relation (a room all of my own). This dictionary proposes comparing a room of her own, her own room and a room of hers in a new rental context, but that remains a proposed test. It is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar calls my a possessive adjective or determiner and mine a possessive pronoun. This dictionary says dependent genitive and independent genitive.

examples.text: I've got [a car of my own].

contrasts.note: Dependent genitive plus own, after of.
Independent genitive, without own.
The comparison phrase this dictionary proposes; no claim made here about the difference.

watch_for: A learner might assume a car of my own requires legal ownership, when it can describe independent use.
A learner might blend the two patterns, when this dictionary pairs my own with of and mine with the pattern without own.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences such as I'd like a ___ of my own with a noun of their choice. They then rewrite each with of mine and discuss whether they still mean set aside for me.

child.hook: What does a room of your own mean?
child.explain: A room of my own is a room that's just for me. After of, we say my own. Without own, we say mine, as in a room of mine.

examples.text: I've got [a car of my own].
She wants [a room of her own].

child.play: Finish the sentence for yourself. I'd like a ___ of my own. Then ask a friend what they'd pick.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "X of one’s own." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/of-genitive-own-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Necessary Condition only if

1.definition: Restricts the circumstances in which a consequence holds or a permission applies.

examples.form: We’ll go [only if the ferry runs].

projection.target: The ferry running is required for going. Its running alone need not guarantee going, since further conditions can remain open.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Only if as a requirement
curious.summary: Only if says that something has to be the case for a consequence to hold or a permission to apply.
curious.body: In We'll go only if the ferry runs, the ferry running is required for going. Without it, we don't go. That doesn't mean the ferry running is enough on its own. Other conditions can remain open, so the ferry might run and we might still stay home. This dictionary describes only if as restricting the circumstances in which a consequence holds or a permission applies, and treats it as a more specific kind of if sentence.

examples.text: We'll go [only if the ferry runs].
You can borrow it [only if you ask first].

curious.try: Say We'll go only if the ferry runs. If the ferry runs, are we sure to go?

teacher.summary: Explains only if as marking a necessary condition, not a guarantee.
teacher.explain: A main clause plus only if plus a finite clause restricts the circumstances in which a consequence holds or a permission applies. In We'll go only if the ferry runs, the ferry's running is required for going. Its running alone need not guarantee going, since further conditions can remain open. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the if-conditional and relates it to even if. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Necessary condition is the logical term for what only if marks. Conditional clause is the traditional name for the if part.

examples.text: We'll go [only if the ferry runs].
You can borrow it [only if you ask first].

contrasts.text: We'll go only if the ferry runs.
contrasts.note: The ferry running is required for going.

contrasts.text: We'll go if the ferry runs.
contrasts.note: Plain if, for comparison. This dictionary treats only if as a specialization of the if-conditional.

watch_for: A learner might think that if the ferry runs, we're sure to go, when only if doesn't say that.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentence stems that start with a consequence and only if, such as I'll come only if ___, then say what else could still stop the outcome.

child.hook: We'll go only if the ferry runs. What if the ferry runs?
child.explain: Only if names something that has to be true. If the ferry doesn't run, we don't go. But other things might still matter, so running isn't a promise.

examples.text: We'll go [only if the ferry runs].
You can come [only if you ask first].

child.play: Finish the sentence I'll come only if ___. Then think of something else that could still stop you.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says the condition has to happen first or that the ferry runs before the trip (the dictionary makes the condition required, with no order of events); curious.summary reworded from 'before a consequence holds' to 'for a consequence to hold'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Necessary Condition only if." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/only-if-restriction-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Open Interrogative Clause

dimensions.form: Clause headed by a VP and marked by an interrogative phrase; a non-subject interrogative phrase is normally fronted and triggers inversion in a main clause, while an interrogative Subject retains basic position
dimensions.meaning: Characteristically presents an open proposition whose variable is assigned a value by an answer
dimensions.function: Characteristically asks an open question, while also supporting rhetorical, directive, and other indirect uses
dimensions.distribution: Tensed and infinitival main clauses and subordinate open-interrogative content clauses

1.definition: A headed clause type marked by an interrogative phrase and characteristically used to ask for a variable's value
1.details: The interrogative phrase is based on who, whom, whose, which, what, when, where, why, how, or a phrase containing one of these. If it is Subject, it occupies the same basic position as a declarative Subject and does not trigger inversion. A non-subject interrogative phrase is normally fronted and triggers subject–auxiliary inversion in a main clause, but subordinate clauses normally retain Subject–Predicator order. Reduced interrogative phrases are outside this headed-clause entry and belong with clause-analogue semantics (CGEL pp. 853–57, 872–76, 902–18).

examples.note: Interrogative phrase as Subject; basic order and no subject–auxiliary inversion
Fronted non-subject interrogative phrase triggering inversion
Subordinate open interrogative with basic Subject–Predicator order

examples.form: [Why are you making such a fuss?]
examples.note: Open interrogative whose actual force may be rhetorical rather than information-seeking

constraints.description: The construction is a Clause headed by VP and contains an interrogative phrase. Main-clause inversion follows normal fronting of a non-subject interrogative phrase, not interrogativity alone.
An interrogative Subject remains in basic Subject position; subordinate open interrogatives normally lack subject–auxiliary inversion.
A phrase-only reduction such as Which one? is not an instance of this headed construction; its clausal interpretation belongs under clause-analogue-001.
A request for information is characteristic but not necessary; open interrogatives can be rhetorical or convey indirect directives and evaluations.

projection.target: The grammatical role of the interrogative phrase predicts whether main-clause fronting and inversion occur, while its variable predicts answer congruence; subordinate status independently predicts retention of basic Subject–Predicator order
projection.evidence: Subject, non-subject main-clause, and subordinate interrogative phrases show the predicted three-way order contrast, while all contribute a variable to the characteristic question interpretation

grounds.note: The interrogative phrase's role projects order, inversion, answer congruence, and subordinate behavior
The role-sensitive profile recurs across main and subordinate open interrogatives

diagnostics: fronting plus inversion for a non-subject in a main clause
normally no inversion in a subordinate clause

relatedConstructions.notes: The interrogative property percolates from the word through its phrase to mark the open-interrogative Clause
Open and closed interrogatives are distinct primary clause types with different syntactic marking
Echo marking is independent of clause type and can preserve the stimulus order instead of showing open-interrogative order
Phrase-only open-question expressions are interpreted clausally without being headed Clauses

grounds.note: Open-interrogative marking, role-sensitive order, variable questions, and interrogative-phrase percolation

curious.title: Questions built around a question word
curious.summary: Questions starting with a word like who, what or why typically ask for a missing piece of information, and word order depends on what the question word does.
curious.body: A question such as Who broke the window? asks for a missing piece, and the answer supplies it. The question word comes from the set who, whom, whose, which, what, when, where, why and how. When the question word is the subject, as in Who broke the window?, the order stays as in a statement. When it's something else, as in Which report did Kim finish?, it is normally moved to the front, and in a main question like this one a helping verb comes before the subject. A question tucked inside a sentence, as in I know which report Kim finished, normally keeps the statement order. Not every such question is a real request: Why are you making such a fuss? can be a complaint.

examples.text: [Why are you making such a fuss?]

curious.try: Turn Kim finished the report into a question with which. Where does the helping verb go? Then put the question inside I know ... and see what changes.

teacher.summary: Covers wh-questions, and how the role of the question word affects word order in main clauses, with subordinate clauses normally keeping subject-predicator order.
teacher.explain: An open interrogative is a headed clause marked by an interrogative phrase, characteristically asking for the value of a variable. If the interrogative phrase is the Subject, it keeps basic position and there's no inversion (Who broke the window?). A non-subject interrogative phrase is normally fronted and triggers subject-auxiliary inversion in a main clause (Which report did Kim finish?). Subordinate open interrogatives normally keep Subject-Predicator order (I know which report Kim finished). A request for information is characteristic but not necessary: these clauses can also be rhetorical or convey indirect directives and evaluations. Reduced phrases such as Which one? aren't instances of this clause type.
teacher.terms: Wh-question is the traditional name; this dictionary's term is open interrogative. Subject-auxiliary inversion is the traditional name for the change in order.

examples.text: [Why are you making such a fuss?]

contrasts.note: Interrogative Subject. Basic order, no inversion.
Fronted non-subject, so inversion in the main clause.

contrasts.text: I know which report Kim finished.
contrasts.note: Subordinate clause, basic order retained.

watch_for: A learner might carry the main-clause inverted order into a subordinate question, when subordinate clauses normally retain Subject-Predicator order.
A learner might invert the subject and a helping verb in a question whose question word is the subject, when an interrogative subject keeps its basic position.
A learner might take every such question as a request for information, when it can be rhetorical.
teacher.activity: Students turn statements such as Kim finished the report into questions with who, which and why. They sort the results by whether the question word is the subject, then embed each one after I know and compare the order.

child.hook: Which words start a question, like who, what, where and why?
child.explain: Some questions start with a word like who, what, where or why. They usually ask for a missing piece, and the answer fills it in. Who broke the window? asks who did it.
child.play: Ask a friend a question with each of who, what, where, when and why. They answer with just the missing piece, like under the bed.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body now limits the helping-verb-before-subject order to main-clause questions with a fronted non-subject and says subordinate questions normally keep statement order; teacher summary says the role of the question word affects order in main clauses and that subordinate clauses normally keep subject-predicator order; teacher watch_for now concerns inversion with an interrogative subject rather than the presence of a helping verb. Second round: fixed teacher.terms, cutting the mapping of yes/no question onto closed interrogative (the entry does not equate them) and the label information question (the entry defines the clause type by form and includes rhetorical uses).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Open Interrogative Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/open-interrogative-clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Open let Imperative
pattern: imperative let + non-inclusive NP + bare infinitival

entry.name: Open let Imperative
entry.pattern: imperative let + non-inclusive NP + bare infinitival

1.definition: Presents a wish, stipulation, or instruction involving the referent of the post-let NP.

projection.target: The expected action is attributed to everyone, and the sentence need not request permission from a gatekeeper. Inclusive let’s has a separate person interpretation.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Let everyone draw a ticket
curious.summary: A sentence starting with let can state a wish or instruction about whoever the noun phrase after let refers to.
curious.body: Let everyone draw a ticket tells us what everyone is to do. The action is attributed to everyone, and the sentence doesn't need to be a request for permission from someone in charge. It can state a wish, a rule or an instruction involving whoever the noun phrase after let refers to. This dictionary separates it from let's, which has a different person interpretation, and from the let that means giving permission.
curious.try: Say Let everyone draw a ticket. Who is supposed to draw? Is anyone being asked for permission?

teacher.summary: Explains imperatives with let plus a noun phrase and a bare infinitive, such as Let everyone draw a ticket.
teacher.explain: The pattern is imperative let plus a non-inclusive NP plus a bare infinitival. It presents a wish, stipulation or instruction involving the referent of the NP after let. The expected action is attributed to that referent (everyone draws a ticket), and the sentence needn't request permission from a gatekeeper. Inclusive let's has a separate person interpretation. This dictionary relates the pattern to the permissive let and to let's as neighbouring constructions. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
watch_for: A learner might read the sentence as a request for permission from a gatekeeper, when it needn't be one.
A learner might read Let everyone draw a ticket as having the person interpretation of let's, when this dictionary says let's has a separate one.
teacher.activity: Students write three rules for a class game using let plus a group (everyone, each team) and a verb. They then say who is expected to act in each rule.

child.hook: Let everyone draw a ticket. Who is going to draw one?
child.explain: This sentence tells what everyone should do. It's an instruction or a wish about them. Let's is a different pattern.
child.play: Make up rules for a game that start with Let. Who does each rule say should act?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary now speaks of whoever the noun phrase after let refers to, not someone other than the speaker; teacher.watch_for no longer treats a speaker-inclusive reading as an error and says only that let's has a separate person interpretation.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Open let Imperative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/open-let-imperative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Ostensive NP

dimensions.form: Extra-clausal NP with marked prosody; NP-internal licensing is preserved but differs between vocative and directive-ostensive packaging
dimensions.meaning: Directs attention to a referent (addressee or environmental)
dimensions.function: Attention-securing utterance; not an argument of any predicator
dimensions.distribution: Stand-alone or supplement position; resists embedding, tags, and questioning

1.definition: An extra-clausal NP whose utterance directs attention to its referent, with packaging-specific NP-internal syntax preserved
1.details: The structural parent of vocative-001 (addressee-directed: securing the channel) and directive-ostensive-001 (environment-directed: securing joint attention). Ordinary determination applies in the directive-ostensive packaging, while vocative function independently licenses bare common-noun NPs such as Mum, driver, officer, and buddy (CGEL pp. 522–23). The packagings shade into each other: Taxi! is ambiguous between hailing the driver and alerting companions, and reminders (Your keys!) sit between alerting and addressing. The construction cross-cuts exclamation-001: tag vocatives instantiate this profile without exclamatory force.

examples.note: Boundary case, ambiguous between the two packagings

constraints.description: Determination is packaging-sensitive: directive-ostensives preserve ordinary determination (a snake, the bus), while vocative function licenses restricted bare common-noun NPs (Mum, driver, buddy).
Not selected by any predicator; resists embedding, tags, and question formation.

projection.target: Membership predicts packaging-specific NP syntax despite extra-clausal status, introduction of a discourse referent available to anaphora, an orientation-type rather than verbal response, and marked prosody
projection.evidence: Directive-ostensives preserve ordinary determination where block language sheds it, while vocatives license a restricted bare-NP inventory (CGEL pp. 522–23); both packagings retain referential and orientation behaviour unlike interjections

diagnostics: licensed bare common nouns in vocatives

stabilisers.evidence: Attention-securing must be fast; minimal structure with maximal prosodic salience
Plausibly continuous with pre-linguistic pointing and the one-word stage; testable in CHILDES

known_boundary_items: Taxi! (vocative/directive-ostensive ambiguity)
block language (form without prosody or determination)
clausal alerts (There's a fire!: function without the form)

grounds.note: Vocative function licenses restricted bare common-noun NPs

curious.title: A single noun phrase that calls for attention
curious.summary: A lone noun phrase, said with marked stress, can direct someone's attention to a person or thing.
curious.body: Sometimes a single noun phrase is a complete message. Calling Mom! gets the listener's attention. Pointing out A snake! gets everyone's attention for something in the surroundings. Both are said with marked stress and aren't part of a longer sentence. This dictionary separates two uses: calling to the person addressed, and drawing attention to something in the environment. They shade into each other. Taxi! could hail the driver or alert a friend. The phrase resists being questioned, tagged or tucked inside another sentence.
curious.try: Think of something you might shout in a crowd, like a name or a thing. Is it calling a person or pointing something out?

teacher.summary: Shows how a single noun phrase can serve as an attention-directing utterance, with two packagings that differ in determination.
teacher.explain: An ostensive NP is an extra-clausal NP that directs attention to its referent. It isn't an argument of any predicator, and it resists embedding, tags and question formation. It has two packagings: vocative (addressee-directed, securing the channel) and directive-ostensive (environment-directed, securing joint attention). Directive-ostensives keep ordinary determination (a snake, the bus), while vocative function licenses restricted bare common-noun NPs (Mum, driver, officer, buddy). Taxi! is ambiguous between the two, and reminders such as Your keys! sit between alerting and addressing. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: The addressee-directed use is the vocative. Directive-ostensive is this dictionary's term for the environment-directed use.

contrasts.note: Directive-ostensive, with ordinary determination.
Vocative, a bare common noun allowed in calling.
A clausal alert, which has the function but not this form.

watch_for: A learner might think a vocative such as Mum needs a determiner like a or the.
A learner might take Taxi! as having one fixed use, when it is ambiguous between the two.
A learner might treat a lone noun phrase as an interjection, when it keeps its referential behaviour.
teacher.activity: Students list short shouts from a playground or street scene. They decide for each whether it calls a person (vocative) or points something out (directive-ostensive), and mark the ambiguous ones.

child.hook: What do you shout when you see a snake?
child.explain: Sometimes just a name or a thing is the whole message. A snake! tells everyone to look. Mom! calls someone over. You don't need a verb.
child.play: Take turns shouting just a thing or a name. Can your friend tell whether you're calling someone or pointing something out?

checked.note: Audit: fixed curious.body, can't be changed to resists being (the entry says the construction resists embedding, tags and questioning, and allows supplement position); also This dictionary is provisional changed to marks the analysis as provisional.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Ostensive NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/ostensive-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: out of Causative with an -ing Clause
pattern: VP[Head:V + Od:NPᵢ + Comp:PP[out of + gerund-participial Clause with understood subjectᵢ]]

entry.name: out of Causative with an -ing Clause
entry.pattern: VP[Head:V + Od:NPᵢ + Comp:PP[out of + gerund-participial Clause with understood subjectᵢ]]

1.definition: Presents the object referent as caused to abandon an action or prevented from carrying it out.
1.details: Talk someone out of leaving can prevent a prospective departure. Other uses involve stopping an ongoing course of action or losing an opportunity through deception. The object supplies the understood subject of the gerund-participial. A report of trying, intending, or planning to bring this about does not assert that the prevention occurred.

examples.note: Constructed prospective action. Lee is understood as the person who would leave.

examples.form: I [cheated you all out of being in my life].
examples.note: Published corpus example. The opportunity is lost rather than supplied.

relatedConstructions.notes: Both link the matrix object to the understood subject of a gerund-participial and contrast in the result.
The literal counterpart can have a spatial source after out of.

grounds.note: Examines the form and semantic range of the gerund-participial construction.

grounds.locator: sense groups for the NP-taking form
grounds.note: Documents the separately analyzed NP complement.

projection.target: The affected object is understood as the participant in the action that is prevented, abandoned, or made unavailable. The paired into-frame can express the opposite outcome.
projection.evidence: Kim and Sim analyze 725 COCA examples. The noun-taking out of frame in Hunston’s inventory supplies a point of comparison.

curious.title: Talked out of doing something
curious.summary: In They talked Lee out of leaving, the person after the verb is steered away from an action.
curious.body: In They talked Lee out of leaving, Lee is the person who would have left, and the talking is aimed at stopping that. The person after the verb is understood as the doer of the action in the -ing phrase. This dictionary describes the meaning as causing someone to abandon an action or preventing them from carrying it out. Other uses involve stopping an ongoing course of action, or losing an opportunity through deception, as in I cheated you all out of being in my life. A report of trying to talk someone out of something doesn't say that it worked.

examples.text: I [cheated you all out of being in my life].
They tried to [talk Lee out of leaving].

curious.try: Say They talked Lee out of leaving. Did Lee leave? Now say They tried to talk Lee out of leaving. What do you know now?

teacher.summary: Explains verb + object + out of + -ing phrase, where the object is the understood doer of the -ing action.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb, a direct object, and a PP complement headed by out of whose complement is a gerund-participial clause. The object supplies the understood subject of that clause. The meaning is that the object referent is caused to abandon an action, or is prevented from carrying it out. Uses include a prospective action (talked Lee out of leaving), stopping an ongoing course of action, and losing an opportunity through deception (cheated you all out of being in my life). A report of trying, intending or planning to bring this about doesn't assert that the prevention occurred. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Gerund-participial is this dictionary's term for the -ing clause. Traditional grammar might call it a gerund phrase.

examples.text: I [cheated you all out of being in my life].

contrasts.text: They talked Lee out of leaving.
contrasts.note: Lee is the understood subject of leaving.

contrasts.text: They tried to talk Lee out of leaving.
contrasts.note: A report of trying doesn't assert the prevention occurred.

watch_for: A learner might conclude from tried to talk Lee out of leaving that Lee stayed, when the sentence doesn't assert it.
A learner might read out of as spatial, as in a literal movement out of a place, when here it introduces an action that's abandoned or prevented.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with talked someone out of plus an -ing phrase. They then rewrite each with tried to, and discuss what each version tells the reader about whether the action took place.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "out of Causative with an -ing Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/out-of-ing-causative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Paired-NP Introduction
pattern: Vocative:NP + pause + NP[name or definite description]

entry.name: Paired-NP Introduction
entry.pattern: Vocative:NP + pause + NP[name or definite description]

1.definition: Introduces the referent of the second NP to the addressee picked out by the first.
1.details: A pause separates the two NPs. Gaze or gesture often helps identify the participant being introduced. The introduced referent can be presented by name or by description without a preceding clause to complete. In the shelter example, Alex can learn that Teacup is the kitten’s name in the course of being introduced. The construction alone gives no evidence about when the name was established or whether the hearer stores a separate noun lexeme.

examples.note: Constructed. A volunteer addresses Alex and indicates the kitten called Teacup.
Published example of introducing Casey to Elise.
Constructed. A definite description identifies the person being introduced.

relatedConstructions.notes: The first NP has vocative function.
The introduced-referent slot can be filled by a strong name NP.
The two phrases conventionally perform an introduction without a VP at the construction’s level.

grounds.note: Analyzes a paired-NP introduction with a vocative and a name or definite description.

projection.target: In an introduction context, the first NP sets the addressee and the second identifies the introduced referent. The second slot admits descriptions as well as names, without requiring an overt introducing verb or a linguistic antecedent.
projection.evidence: Goldberg and Perek give the paired example and describe its use with a pause and typically a gesture. The kitten and definite-description cases illustrate the contrast.

curious.title: Introducing someone with two names
curious.summary: Saying someone's name, pausing, then naming or describing someone else can introduce that second person or thing to the first.
curious.body: A volunteer at an animal shelter says Alex, Teacup. Alex is the person being spoken to, and Teacup is the kitten being pointed out. A pause separates the two phrases, and pointing or looking helps show who's being introduced. There's no verb, and none is needed. The second phrase can be a name, as in Elise, Casey, or a description, as in Alex, the new vet. This dictionary describes the first phrase as addressing someone and the second as identifying who is being introduced.
curious.try: Introduce a friend to someone using only two phrases and a pause. Does the listener work out who is who?

teacher.summary: Shows how two noun phrases with a pause can serve as a complete introduction.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a vocative NP, a pause, then an NP that is a name or a definite description. The first NP picks out the addressee, and the second identifies the referent being introduced to that addressee. A pause separates the two, and gaze or gesture often helps identify the person or animal introduced. The introduced referent can be presented by name or by description, without a preceding clause to complete. This dictionary treats the pair as a clause analogue: the two phrases conventionally perform an introduction without a VP at the construction's level. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Vocative is the traditional name for the first NP. This dictionary calls the whole pattern a paired-NP introduction.
watch_for: A learner might read the two phrases as a list of two people being addressed, when the first is the addressee and the second the person introduced.
A learner might expect an introducing verb, when none is required.
teacher.activity: Students role-play introductions with a pause between a vocative and a name, then with a description in place of a name. Observers say who is addressed and who is being introduced.

child.hook: How can you introduce a friend with just two names?
child.explain: Say the name of the person you're talking to. Pause. Then say the name of the person you're introducing. Pointing or looking helps.
child.play: Pair up. Introduce a toy or a classmate to your partner using only two names and a pause.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary no longer says the two are introduced to each other; it gives the entry's direction (the second referent is introduced to the person addressed by the first). Also fixed (unflagged): provisional sentence in teacher.explain.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Paired-NP Introduction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/paired-np-introduction-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subjectless Participial Supplement
pattern: nonfinite supplement[V-ing or V-en + dependents] anchored to main clause

entry.name: Subjectless Participial Supplement
entry.pattern: nonfinite supplement[V-ing or V-en + dependents] anchored to main clause

1.definition: Adds a circumstance whose understood subject is normally recovered from the anchor.

examples.form: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
Lee shut the door, [startled by the noise].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. The past-participial supplement takes Lee as its understood subject.

projection.target: Jo is the ordinary understood hearer. A separate overt subject would instead support an absolute supplement, while some fixed discourse adjuncts use contextual subjects.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Extra -ing and -ed phrases beside a sentence
curious.summary: A phrase starting with an -ing or -ed verb can add a circumstance to a sentence, with its doer understood from the main clause.
curious.body: In Hearing footsteps, Jo switched off the light, the phrase hearing footsteps adds a circumstance but doesn't say who heard. We understand that it was Jo. In Lee shut the door, startled by the noise, the -ed phrase is understood to be about Lee. The doer is normally taken from the main part of the sentence. If the added phrase has its own subject, it's a different pattern, which this dictionary calls an absolute supplement. Some fixed phrases get their understood subject from the situation instead.

examples.text: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
Lee shut the door, [startled by the noise].

curious.try: Say Hearing footsteps, Jo switched off the light. Who heard the footsteps? Where does the sentence tell you?

teacher.summary: Explains -ing and -ed phrases added to a main clause, and how their understood subject is recovered.
teacher.explain: A subjectless participial supplement is a nonfinite phrase (V-ing or V-en plus dependents) anchored to a main clause. It adds a circumstance, and its understood subject is normally recovered from the anchor: Jo is the hearer in the first example, and Lee is the startled one in the second. A separate overt subject would support an absolute supplement instead. Some fixed discourse adjuncts use contextual subjects. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Participial phrase is the traditional name. This dictionary calls the pattern a supplement because it's added to the clause and not required by it.

examples.text: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
Lee shut the door, [startled by the noise].

contrasts.text: [Hearing footsteps], Jo switched off the light.
contrasts.note: The understood hearer is Jo, recovered from the main clause.

contrasts.text: [Jo having left], Lee switched off the light.
contrasts.note: A separate overt subject supports an absolute supplement instead.

watch_for: A learner might look for the understood subject inside the phrase, when it is recovered from the main clause.
A learner might expect the subject of startled by the noise to be the door, when this dictionary takes it to be Lee.
teacher.activity: Students underline the participial phrase in each of several sentences and circle who or what it is understood to be about. They then say how they know.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subjectless Participial Supplement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/participial-clause-supplement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Past Tense -ed

1.definition: Marks temporal/modal/social distance
1.details: Core meaning potentially involving displacement from a reference point (temporal, modal, or interpersonal) - though this unification remains debatable

2.details: Marks situation as occurring before reference time (but see cases like sports commentary where this breaks down)

3.details: Indicates displacement from actual/current reality

4.details: Creates interpersonal distance, often for politeness

projection.target: Regular -ed can mark a preterite or past participle. In Jo checked the key it marks finite preterite, while in Jo has checked the key it realizes the participle selected by have. Remote and backshifted preterites need not locate the event before speech time.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the syncretism and the independent distribution of the temporal and remote interpretations.

curious.title: The -ed ending on verbs
curious.summary: Adding -ed to a verb can place something in the past, but it can also mark something imagined or add politeness.
curious.body: The -ed ending (or -d or -t, with more than one pronunciation) places something in time, as in She walked home and They finished yesterday. But it does more. In If I owned a car, it marks something that isn't actual. In I wanted to ask you, it adds social distance, which can make a request or offer more polite. This dictionary also gives Did you want coffee? as a polite offer, with the past form did. This dictionary lists these as separate meanings and notes that whether one idea, displacement from a reference point, unites them remains debatable. Past time doesn't fit every use: Jones passed to Smith! in a sports commentary describes an immediate past.
curious.try: Compare They finished yesterday with Did you want coffee? Is the second one about the past, or about being polite?

teacher.summary: Explains the -ed ending as more than past time, covering hypothetical and politeness uses, and how its preterite use differs from its participle use.
teacher.explain: Regular -ed (with the allomorphs -d, -t, /d/, /t/ and /ɪd/) marks the preterite. This dictionary lists four meanings: displacement from a reference point (temporal, modal or interpersonal), temporal anteriority (They finished yesterday), non-actual or hypothetical marking (If she studied more; I wish I lived there), and social distancing (Did you want coffee?; I hoped we could talk). The first, unifying meaning remains debatable. Temporal anteriority has exceptions such as sports commentary (Jones passed to Smith!). Remote and backshifted preterites need not locate the event before speech time. Regular -ed also marks the past participle, as in Jo has checked the key. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Past tense is the traditional name; CGEL says preterite. The -ed form after have is the past participle.

contrasts.note: Finite preterite.
Participle selected by have.
Contrary-to-fact desire, not past time.

watch_for: A learner might assume every -ed form locates the event in the past, when this dictionary lists hypothetical and politeness uses.
A learner might read Did you want coffee? only as asking about a past wanting, when it can be a polite offer.
A learner might treat the -ed in has checked as a preterite, when it is the participle selected by have.
teacher.activity: Students sort -ed sentences into past time, imagined situations and polite requests or offers, using examples such as They finished yesterday, If she studied more and I wanted to ask you. They then explain what each use has in common with the others, if anything.

child.hook: What happens to a verb when you add ed?
child.explain: Adding ed can make a verb tell about the past, as in She walked home. It can also talk about something that isn't real, as in If I owned a car. It can also make something sound more polite, as in I wanted to ask you.
child.play: Say three sentences with ed words, one about yesterday, one about something you wish for, and one polite one, like I wanted to ask you. Which job does the ed do in each?

checked.note: Fixed: child explain and the teacher activity used Did you want coffee? as an -ed example, but it has the irregular preterite did and plain want; they now use I wanted to ask you (this dictionary's social-distance example with -ed), and the child play matches. The curious body now ties the -ed ending to I wanted to ask you and presents Did you want coffee? as a separate polite offer. Second round: removed the bracketed example Did you want coffee? from the curious and teacher example lists (its did is irregular and want is plain, so neither shows -ed) and gave the teacher list I hoped we could talk instead; teacher.watch_for[1] now says the question can be a polite offer, without ruling out a question about past wanting. Curious.body says the polite offer uses the past form did instead of saying it works 'in the same way'; teacher.summary now contrasts the preterite and participle uses of the ending.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Past Tense -ed." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/past-tense-ed-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Path Locative-Complement Construction

dimensions.form: Verb head with a path-denoting PP in locative-complement function
dimensions.meaning: Intermediate location or route traversed during motion, without itself necessarily specifying either terminal point
dimensions.function: Locative complement of the verb, bearing the semantic role path
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal with motion verbs and motion construals; compatible with separate source- and goal-role complements
