1.definition: A VP contains a locative PP complement that identifies the route or intermediate location traversed by the moving theme
1.details: Path is a semantic role, while locative complement is the CGEL syntactic function. Via uniquely marks path in its central spatial use, and along is strongly path-associated. PPs headed by across, through, up, and similar prepositions can instead express location, source, or goal; a path construal identifies an intermediate portion of a larger trajectory. Path complements are integrated into the motion VP and fall within do so scope (CGEL Ch. 8 §4.3, pp. 684–88).

examples.note: Along-PP identifying a route without a terminal point

examples.form: They [walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre].
examples.note: Path up the hill occurs between separate source and goal complements

constraints.description: The path PP is an integrated locative complement in a motion VP, not a clause-level location adjunct.
The PP identifies the route or an intermediate location; it need not identify the initial or final location.
A path complement normally leaves the motion unbounded and therefore permits a for-duration phrase; a syncretic path-goal reading can instead bound the event and license an in-duration phrase.
Source, path, and goal may be separately realized in one VP; their co-occurrence does not impose an invariant surface order.
This entry establishes V-hosted path complementation only; it makes no claim that a path PP is selected inside a larger PP without independent attachment evidence.

projection.target: Identifying an integrated PP as a path complement predicts an intermediate-location interpretation, compatibility with separate source and goal complements, and absence of event bounding unless the PP simultaneously receives a goal construal
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts path and goal readings by terminal-point entailments and in/for duration, identifies via and along as central path markers, and shows paths co-occurring between source and goal (Ch. 8 §4.3, pp. 684–88).

core.property: Path role borne by a locative PP complement

diagnostics: compatibility with an overt following goal

known_boundary_items: ran across the bridge: across the bridge can be goal when it supplies the final location, or path when a later goal is expressed
walked through the forest in eight hours: the in-duration phrase selects a goal construal in which the end of the forest is reached
A location adjunct describes where the situation occurs; a path complement describes the trajectory of the moving theme and is included in do so scope
No PP-internal path-complement attachment is asserted by this VP-level entry

relatedConstructions.notes: The path-role locative complement is licensed within VP structure
The path-role dependent is a PP in locative-complement function
Sister locative role; a goal supplies the final location and typically bounds a motion event
Sister locative role; source, path, and goal can co-occur in a single motion VP
The object-oriented locative complement in caused motion can bear the path role

grounds.note: Path dependents in motion VPs are locative complements, with path distinct from source, goal, and direction
Role, realization, co-occurrence, and aspectual diagnostics converge on the path profile

curious.title: Naming the route of a journey
curious.summary: Some verbs of moving are followed by a phrase that says which way the traveller went, without saying where the journey started or ended.
curious.body: In She came via the bridge, the phrase via the bridge tells us the route. It names a place along the way, not the starting point or the destination. In They strolled along the castle wall, the same thing happens: we learn the route and nothing about where the stroll ended. This dictionary calls that role the path. A route phrase can sit in the same sentence as a starting point and a destination, as in They walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre, where up the hill is the middle stretch. Via and along are strongly tied to routes, but a phrase starting with across, through or up can name a place, a starting point or a destination instead, depending on the sentence.

examples.text: They [walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre].

curious.try: Think of a trip you made. Which words in your sentence name the route, and which name where you started or finished?

teacher.summary: Helps students tell route phrases (path) from starting-point and destination phrases after verbs of motion.
teacher.explain: In a motion VP, a PP in locative-complement function can bear the semantic role path: the route or intermediate location the moving thing traverses. Path is a role; locative complement is the syntactic function. Via marks path in its central spatial use, and along is strongly path-associated. PPs with across, through or up can instead express location, source or goal. A path complement normally leaves the motion unbounded, so it permits a for-duration phrase; a reading that also bounds the event can license an in-duration phrase. Source, path and goal can all appear in one VP, with no fixed surface order. A path complement is part of the VP, unlike a location adjunct, and it falls within do so scope.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes group these with adverbials of place or direction. In this grammar, path is a semantic role and locative complement is the syntactic function.

examples.text: They [walked from the station up the hill to the new Civic Centre].

contrasts.text: They walked through the forest for hours.
contrasts.note: A for-duration phrase fits when the PP names a route and the motion has no endpoint.

contrasts.text: They walked through the forest in eight hours.
contrasts.note: An in-duration phrase selects a reading where the end of the forest is reached, so the PP also supplies a goal.

watch_for: A learner might read every PP after a motion verb as the destination, when up the hill in the station-to-Civic-Centre example names the middle of the journey.
A learner might assume across or through marks a route every time, though they can also express location, source or goal.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a short map with a start, a destination and two landmarks. Each pair writes one sentence naming the route only, then one adding the start and the destination. They underline the phrase that names the route.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Path Locative-Complement Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/path-complement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Perception with a Bare Infinitival

1.definition: Presents something directly perceived as an occurrence.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. Progressive-shaped comparison presents a phase of the perceptible event.

relatedConstructions.notes: Heard Kai close the latch presents the occurrence as a whole. Heard Kai closing the latch presents it in progress.

projection.target: The plain form follows the perceived participant. The construction can present the closing as a whole, while heard Kai closing the latch can target an ongoing phase.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Hearing or seeing something happen
curious.summary: A verb of perceiving, a person or thing, and a plain verb form together present what was perceived as an event.
curious.body: In We heard Kai close the latch, the closing is something we perceived directly, and the plain verb form close names it. Here the closing can be presented as a whole event. Compare We heard Kai closing the latch. The -ing form presents the closing as it was going on, a stretch of the event rather than the whole of it. Both sentences report hearing, and the choice between the plain form and the -ing form changes how the event is framed.
curious.try: Say We heard Kai close the latch and We heard Kai closing the latch. Which one sounds like you caught only part of it?

teacher.summary: Useful for showing how a plain verb form after see or hear frames an event as a whole, compared with an -ing form.
teacher.explain: In this pattern a perception verb is followed by an NP and a bare infinitival: heard Kai close the latch. The NP is the perceived participant and the plain form follows it. The construction can present the event as a whole, while the gerund-participial alternative (heard Kai closing the latch) can target an ongoing phase. This dictionary marks this contrast as provisional, with medium confidence, and cites CGEL on perception complements.
teacher.terms: A bare infinitival is the plain form of the verb with no to. Textbooks sometimes call the two patterns the bare infinitive and the -ing participle after verbs of perception.

contrasts.text: We heard Kai close the latch.
contrasts.note: The occurrence presented as a whole.

contrasts.text: We heard Kai closing the latch.
contrasts.note: The occurrence presented in progress.

watch_for: A learner might treat the two forms as interchangeable, when this dictionary says they present the event differently.
A learner might add to before the plain verb after heard Kai.
teacher.activity: Describe a short action (a door shutting, a ball being kicked). Students write one sentence with the plain verb form and one with the -ing form after saw or heard, then say which presents the whole event.

child.hook: What is the difference between hearing someone close a door and hearing someone closing it?
child.explain: Both sentences tell what you heard. We heard Kai close the latch can mean the whole closing. We heard Kai closing the latch can mean it was happening as we listened.

examples.text: We heard Kai close the latch.
We heard Kai closing the latch.

child.play: Take turns doing a short action, like shutting a book. The others say what they saw, once with the plain verb and once with the -ing word.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Perception with a Bare Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/perception-bare-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Perception with a Gerund-Participial

1.definition: Presents a perceived participant in the course of an activity or event.

projection.target: Seeing Kai crossing the square is compatible with leaving before Kai reached the other side. The -ing complement can describe the phase perceived.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Seeing something while it happens
curious.summary: A verb of perceiving, a person, and an -ing verb together present the person as in the middle of an activity.
curious.body: In I saw Kai crossing the square, Kai is caught in the course of crossing. The -ing form describes the stretch of the event that was seen. That's why the sentence is compatible with leaving before Kai reached the other side. Seeing Kai crossing the square doesn't require seeing the crossing finished.
curious.try: Could you say I saw Kai crossing the square if you left before Kai got to the other side?

teacher.summary: Shows that see plus an NP and an -ing form can present only the phase of an event that was perceived.
teacher.explain: In this pattern a perception verb takes an NP followed by a gerund-participial predicate: saw Kai crossing the square. The -ing complement can describe the phase perceived. Seeing Kai crossing the square is compatible with leaving before Kai reached the other side. This dictionary presents this as provisional, with medium confidence, and cites CGEL on perception complements.
teacher.terms: Gerund-participial is the form in -ing. Textbooks sometimes call it the present participle or -ing participle in this use.

contrasts.text: I saw Kai crossing the square.
contrasts.note: Kai is seen in the course of the activity.

contrasts.text: We heard Kai close the latch.
contrasts.note: The plain form can present the closing as a whole (see the bare-infinitival entry).

watch_for: A learner might assume that saw Kai crossing the square means the whole crossing was seen, when the -ing form can describe only the phase perceived.
teacher.activity: Show a short video clip and stop it midway. Students write what they saw, using saw plus a name and an -ing verb, and discuss whether the sentence needs the action to be finished.

child.hook: If you see someone crossing a street, did you see them get to the other side?
child.explain: The -ing word shows the person in the middle of doing something. You can say I saw Kai crossing the square even if you left before Kai got across.

examples.text: I saw Kai crossing the square.
We saw Mia painting a fence.

child.play: Look out of a window for one minute. Write what you saw people doing, using saw, a name and an -ing word.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Perception with a Gerund-Participial." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/perception-gerund-participial-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Perfect have + V-en

1.definition: Places a prior situation relative to a temporal anchor

examples.note: Prior event relative to a past reference time

1.details: The present perfect has a present anchor and often suggests current relevance. In many varieties it resists an explicitly finished past-time setting. The preterite perfect instead uses a past anchor.

2.definition: Marks experiential or repeatable prior occurrence

3.definition: Marks a continuing situation spanning up to the reference time (universal/continuative perfect)

examples.form: I have lived there for three years

examples.note: Ongoing state with inception in the past

relatedConstructions.notes: The perfect auxiliary and participial complement form a VP headed by have

projection.target: Perfect have selects a past participle. With a past anchor, had left precedes that past time. A present anchor is only one possibility, even when no time expression is overt.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates perfect anteriority from primary tense and from the contextual interpretation of current relevance.

curious.title: Have plus a past participle
curious.summary: Have followed by a verb's past-participle form relates a situation to a point in time, such as now. The situation can be earlier than that point, or continue up to it.
curious.body: In She has finished the report, the finishing came before now, and it matters now. In They had already left, the leaving came before some time in the past. The same build also covers I have visited Japan and We have met before, which report something that happened earlier, and I have lived there for three years, where the living continues up to now. This dictionary notes that the present version often suggests current relevance, and that in many varieties it resists an explicitly finished past-time setting.

examples.text: I [have lived there for three years].

curious.try: Compare I have lived there for three years with I lived there for three years. What does each tell you about whether I still live there?

teacher.summary: Core pattern for the perfect, with its present, past, experiential and continuing uses.
teacher.explain: Perfect have selects a past participle and relates a situation to a temporal anchor. With a present anchor (has finished) the situation is prior to now or, in the continuing use, runs up to now; with a past anchor (had left) it precedes that past time. A present anchor is only one possibility, even when no time expression is overt. This dictionary distinguishes three uses: a prior situation relative to the anchor (has finished the report, had already left), experiential or repeatable prior occurrence (have visited Japan), and a continuing situation spanning up to the reference time (have lived there for three years, has worked here since 2020). It also separates perfect anteriority from primary tense and from the contextual interpretation of current relevance. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call these the present perfect and the past perfect. This dictionary's preterite perfect is the version with a past anchor. The continuing use is also called the universal or continuative perfect.

examples.text: I [have lived there for three years].

contrasts.note: Present anchor; prior completion relevant now.
Past anchor; leaving precedes a past reference time.

watch_for: A learner might read has finished as a plain past event, missing the link to the present anchor.
A learner might read I have lived there for three years as ending in the past, when the residence continues up to now.
teacher.activity: Give students three cards (finished the report, visited Japan, lived there for three years). They write a have-sentence for each and a one-line note saying whether it is a completed event, an experience, or a situation continuing up to now.

child.hook: When someone says I have finished, what happened before now?
child.explain: Have or has plus a word like finished can tell us something already happened. She has finished the report. They had already left means the leaving came before some time in the past.
child.play: Say what you have done today, starting with I have. Then a partner says what they had already done before lunch, starting with I had.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary and teacher.explain no longer define the whole pattern as placing a situation before the anchor (the continuing use extends up to it); teacher.explain's first use is now 'a prior situation relative to the anchor', with current relevance left as the present perfect's suggestion; cut 'pluperfect'; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'. Second round: fixed child.explain, tells us changed to can tell us (the entry also has a use where the situation continues up to now); curious.title now says past participle, as the entry requires. Dismissed the low flag on teacher.explain (its examples are prior situations, and the continuing use follows in the same paragraph).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Perfect have + V-en." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/perfect-have-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Personal Determination with we or you

1.definition: Locates the named group in relation to the speaker or addressee.

projection.target: The nominal survives after the personal expression. In many varieties a non-subject parallel can use us volunteers, showing that case and reference matter independently.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: We or you before a group name
curious.summary: The words we, us or you can come right before a plural noun to say which group is meant, in relation to the speaker or the person spoken to.
curious.body: In We volunteers need a break, the word we ties the group to the speaker: the volunteers in question include the speaker. The plural noun volunteers still follows and says which group it is. This dictionary says the noun survives after the personal word. In many varieties, a version that isn't the subject can use us volunteers, which shows that the person-and-case choice and the reference are separate matters.
curious.try: Replace volunteers with another group name, such as teachers or neighbours. Does the sentence still work?

teacher.summary: Explains we or you followed by a plural noun, as in We volunteers need a break.
teacher.explain: In this pattern a personal expression (we, us or you) is followed by a plural nominal. The personal expression locates the named group in relation to the speaker or addressee. The nominal survives after it. In many varieties a non-subject parallel can use us volunteers, which shows that case and reference matter independently. This dictionary files this under noun phrases with a determiner and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars call we, us and you personal pronouns. Here the personal word functions as a determiner before the nominal.
watch_for: A learner might think the noun volunteers is optional decoration, when it names the group the personal word is tied to.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences about their own group (We students, We neighbours), then say who is included and who is addressed in a version with you.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Personal Determination with we or you." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/personal-determiner-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Phrase

dimensions.form: Headed constituent; the immediate head may be a word or phrase, and the ultimate head is a word of a lexical category
dimensions.meaning: The head's semantic contribution, elaborated by its dependents
dimensions.function: Whatever functions the head's category makes available (argument, modifier, predicate, ...)
dimensions.distribution: Determined principally by the head: an NP distributes as its nominal head allows, a PP as its preposition head allows, and a Clause as its VP head allows

1.definition: A constituent organized around a head, which licenses its dependents and principally determines its distribution
1.details: Phrases contrast with coordinations and other non-headed constituents (see coordination-001 and clause-analogue-001). Clause, VP, NP, Nom, AdjP, AdvP, PP, and DP are phrasal categories. A Clause is headed immediately by a VP and may also contain a Subject; the VP is ultimately headed by V. Constituents that CGEL calls verbless clauses are not Clauses in this Constructionary: they instantiate a separate clause-analogue construction. Other phrases likewise may have a phrasal immediate head, such as Nom in NP. A phrase may consist of its head alone (outside as a complete PP, Kim as a complete NP).

examples.note: Clause; Subject Kim plus Head VP left early, whose head is V
Subjectless imperative Clause; Head is the VP leave early

constraints.description: Exactly one immediate head; dependents are licensed by that head and its ultimate lexical head. In a Clause the Head is VP and Subject is optional. A constituent without a head is not a Phrase, and one without a VP head is not a Clause.

projection.target: Identifying a constituent's immediate and ultimate heads predicts its external distribution and internal function structure, including the optional Subject plus Head:VP organization of Clauses and the exclusion of clause-analogue constructions from the Clause category
projection.evidence: Distribution inheritance and head-dependent licensing hold across the phrasal categories; CGEL Ch. 1, pp. 22–25 explicitly includes Clause and analyses Predicate/VP as its head

grounds.note: Head category predicts external distribution and internal dependent functions
The head-dependent profile recurs across the phrasal categories

relatedConstructions.notes: The non-headed constituent type; the contrast is definitional
A non-headed constituent may have clausal semantics, but it is neither a Phrase nor a Clause

grounds.note: Clause included among headed constituents; Predicate/VP as clause head
Clause is defined as a Phrase headed by VP with an optional Subject; CGEL's 'verbless clauses' are assigned to a separate clause-analogue construction

curious.title: Groups of words built around a key word
curious.summary: A phrase is a group of words organized around one main word, which decides what else can come with it and where it can go.
curious.body: In the old house, the word house is the main word, called the head. The words around it elaborate it. In in the garden, the head is in, and in very old, it's old. The head decides which other words can join it and where the whole phrase can go in a sentence. A phrase can also be just its head: outside can be a complete phrase, and so can Kim. A short sentence such as Kim left early counts as a phrase too, built around the verb phrase left early.
curious.try: Pick any phrase from a sign or book. Which word in it could you not remove without losing the phrase's point?

teacher.summary: Defines headed constituents (phrases and clauses) and what counts as a head.
teacher.explain: A phrase is a constituent organized around a head, which licenses its dependents and principally determines its distribution. An NP distributes as its nominal head allows, a PP as its preposition head allows, and a clause as its VP head allows. A phrase may consist of its head alone (outside as a PP, Kim as an NP). Clause, VP, NP, Nom, AdjP, AdvP, PP and DP are phrasal categories here. A Clause is headed immediately by a VP and may also contain a Subject. This dictionary does not treat CGEL's verbless clauses as Clauses; they fall under a separate clause-analogue construction. Coordinations are also non-headed.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars sometimes speak of the main word of a phrase. Here the head is the word or phrase that licenses the dependents, and the ultimate head is a word of a lexical category. This dictionary calls constituents without a head non-headed rather than phrases.

contrasts.note: A Clause with a Subject (Kim) and a VP head (left early).
A subjectless imperative Clause, still headed by the VP leave early.

watch_for: A learner might treat the first word in a phrase as its head, though in the old house the head is house.
A learner might think a phrase must have two or more words, when a single word such as Kim or outside can be a complete phrase.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of phrases (in the garden, the old house, very old). They circle the head of each and say what category the head belongs to.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/phrase-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: make Causative with a Bare Infinitival
pattern: VP[make + NP + bare infinitival]; passive be made + to-infinitival

entry.name: make Causative with a Bare Infinitival
entry.pattern: VP[make + NP + bare infinitival]; passive be made + to-infinitival

1.definition: Presents one participant as causing the other to undertake or undergo a situation.

relatedConstructions.notes: Compare They made Kai wait and Kai was made to wait. The infinitival marker is required in the passive counterpart.
Made Kai wait and let Kai wait share an NP followed by a bare infinitival. Make presents a cause and let presents permission or non-prevention.

projection.target: In the active make selects the bare infinitival, while the corresponding passive Lee was made to laugh uses to. The interpretation retains Lee as the laugher.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Making someone do something
curious.summary: Make, a person or thing, and a plain verb together present one participant as causing another to do or go through something.
curious.body: In The joke made Lee laugh, the joke causes Lee to laugh, and Lee is still the one who laughs. The verb after Lee is in its plain form, with no to. The passive version does use to: Lee was made to laugh. The to is required there. Compare They made Kai wait and Kai was made to wait.
curious.try: Say The joke made Lee laugh. Now turn it around starting with Lee. Where does to appear?

teacher.summary: Explains make plus an NP and a plain verb, and the to that appears in the passive.
teacher.explain: In the active, make takes an NP followed by a bare infinitival: The joke made Lee laugh. The sentence presents one participant as causing the other to undertake or undergo a situation, and Lee remains the laugher. In the passive counterpart the infinitival marker is required: Lee was made to laugh. Make shares the NP plus bare infinitival shape with let (let Kai wait); make presents a cause and let presents permission or non-prevention. This dictionary marks the pattern as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call this the causative use of make, or make plus bare infinitive.

contrasts.note: Active, plain verb after the NP.
Passive, with to.
Same shape with let, which presents permission or non-prevention rather than a cause.

watch_for: A learner might add to after the NP in the active, when the active selects the plain form.
A learner might leave out to in the passive, though the infinitival marker is required there.
teacher.activity: Give students five active make-sentences. They rewrite each as a passive and mark where to appears, then add one sentence with let and say how its meaning differs.

child.hook: When something makes you laugh, who is the one laughing?
child.explain: Make can be followed by a name and then a plain verb. The joke made Lee laugh. Lee is the one who laughs. If you start with Lee, you add to: Lee was made to laugh.
child.play: Make up sentences with made, a name and a plain verb. Then turn each one around so it starts with the name, and add to.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "make Causative with a Bare Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/plain-make-causative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Plural Construction
pattern: Applies to common and proper nouns, pronouns, and determinatives

entry.name: Plural Construction
entry.pattern: Applies to common and proper nouns, pronouns, and determinatives

dimensions.form: Plural morphology (-s, -es, irregular, zero); agreement marking
dimensions.meaning: Non-singular reference; more than one or construed as aggregate
dimensions.function: Signals non-singular construal; triggers agreement
dimensions.distribution: Nouns, pronouns, determinatives; agreement targets in clause

1.notes: Bidirectional; plural form cues non-singular construal, non-singular construal licenses plural form

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional syntax-semantics interface for number
Paradigmatic contrast in the number system
Regular plural suffix is specialization of plural construction

projection.target: The form controls ordinary plural agreement in the scissors are blunt. The lexical description can nevertheless be about one instrument.
projection.evidence: CGEL’s discussion of plural-only nouns separates grammatical number from the number of objects described.

curious.title: Words that mean more than one
curious.summary: Plural forms mark more than one thing, or a group of things taken together, and they trigger matching forms elsewhere in a sentence.
curious.body: Plural forms appear in nouns, pronouns and some other small words, not just nouns: cats, they and these all point to more than one. Some plurals name a group, as in Kennedys, or types rather than a mass, as in wines. Others mark recurring instances, as in headaches. The plural form controls ordinary plural agreement, as in The scissors are blunt. Yet the description can be about one instrument. So the plural form tells us how the grammar treats the word, not strictly how many objects there are.
curious.try: Name something you use that is described with a plural word but is a single object. What verb goes with it?

teacher.summary: Overview of plural forms across nouns, pronouns and determinatives, and what they signal.
teacher.explain: Plural morphology (-s, -es, irregular, zero) applies to common and proper nouns, pronouns and determinatives. It signals non-singular construal and triggers agreement. This dictionary lists four uses: non-singular entities (cats, they, these), countable aggregates (Kennedys, many), countable taxonomic categories, that is, types rather than non-count (wines), and recurring instances (headaches). Form and number of referents can come apart: the scissors are blunt has plural agreement but can describe one instrument, because grammatical number is separate from the number of objects described. This dictionary marks this as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Words like scissors are sometimes called plural-only nouns. This dictionary contrasts plural with singular.

contrasts.note: Plural agreement, though the description can be about one instrument.

watch_for: A learner might assume a plural form must mean more than one object.
A learner might read wines as several bottles only, when it can mean types of wine.
teacher.activity: Students sort words (cats, they, these, Kennedys, wines, headaches) by which use of the plural they show, then add one example of their own for each use.

child.hook: Why do we say the scissors are, when you hold only one pair?
child.explain: Plural words like cats and they mean more than one. Some words, like scissors, look plural even when you mean one tool. We say The scissors are blunt.
child.play: Make a list of plural words. Which ones go with are? Find something you use that is one thing but has a plural word.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Plural Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/plural-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Plural -s

1.specialization: Realizes plural number on an eligible nominal stem

2.specialization: Realizes plural number when the noun is used to count types or varieties

3.specialization: Realizes plural number in a construction that describes recurring instances

4.specialization: Forms common nouns denoting groups from proper nouns used as names

projection.target: With transparent regular plural formation, the final sound of the stem predicts the suffix pronunciation. Compare the /s/ in cats, /z/ in dogs, and /ɪz/ in horses. A variety interpretation additionally depends on count use of the noun.
projection.evidence: CGEL describes the sibilant allomorphy and separately documents contextual count readings.

curious.title: Adding -s to make a plural
curious.summary: Adding -s or -es to a common noun makes it plural, and the same ending can also count types, repeated events or members of a family.
curious.body: The ending -s turns cat into cats, marking more than one. The ending is pronounced differently depending on the last sound of the word: an s sound in cats, a z sound in dogs, and an extra syllable, like iz, in horses. The same ending does other jobs. Wines counts types of wine. I get headaches describes headaches that come back. And the Kennedys names the members of a family or dynasty, built from a name. Which job the ending does depends on how the noun is being used.
curious.try: Say cats, dogs and horses aloud. Can you hear the three different endings?

teacher.summary: Covers regular plural -s/-es, its pronunciation, and its extensions to types, recurring instances and family names.
teacher.explain: Plural -s or -es attaches to a common-noun stem and realizes plural number. In regular formation the final sound of the stem predicts the pronunciation of the suffix: /s/ in cats, /z/ in dogs, /ɪz/ in horses. The same suffix realizes plural number in several uses: non-singular (cats), types or varieties of a substance (wines), recurring instances (I get headaches), and groups formed from proper names (the Kennedys, meaning Kennedy family or dynasty members). A variety reading depends on the noun being used as a count noun. This dictionary marks this as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: The sibilant ending is sometimes called an allomorph of the plural suffix.

contrasts.note: Three pronunciations of one suffix, set by the last sound of the stem.

watch_for: A learner might pronounce the ending the same way in cats, dogs and horses.
A learner might read wines only as more than one bottle, when it can count types of wine.
teacher.activity: Students sort a list of plural nouns by the ending sound (s, z, iz) and say what the last sound of the singular is each time.

child.hook: Does the s on cats sound the same as the s on dogs?
child.explain: Adding s to a word can mean more than one. Cats ends with an s sound. Dogs ends with a z sound. Horses ends with an extra bit, like iz.
child.play: Say a list of plural words aloud. Sort them by the ending you hear: s, z or iz.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Plural -s." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/plural-s-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Finite Auxiliary in a Polar Short Answer
pattern: answer particle + Subject pronoun + finite Aux, optionally negated

entry.name: Finite Auxiliary in a Polar Short Answer
entry.pattern: answer particle + Subject pronoun + finite Aux, optionally negated

1.definition: Resolves an antecedent polar question with an overt indication of the proposition’s polarity.

relatedConstructions.notes: Compare Yes, she did with Hell yeah. The first can retain a subject and finite auxiliary from the antecedent clause. The second adds emphasis to the response word.

projection.target: Did presents a positive answer and helps identify the elided predicate. Responses to negative questions can vary in the use of the answer particle across speakers and contexts.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Answering yes or no with a short reply
curious.summary: A short reply to a yes/no question can say yes or no, then a pronoun, then a helper verb, and leave the rest out.
curious.body: Asked Did Jo lock up?, you can answer Yes, she did. The answer uses the pronoun she for Jo, repeats the helper word did from the question, and drops the rest of the verb phrase. The helper verb in the reply tells you the answer is positive, and it helps you work out what is left out: lock up. Replies to negative questions can vary from speaker to speaker and context to context in how the answer word, yes or no, is used.
curious.try: Ask a friend a yes/no question about their day. Does their short answer repeat a helper word from your question?

teacher.summary: Shows how a reply to a yes/no question can be built from yes or no, a subject pronoun and a finite auxiliary.
teacher.explain: A polar short answer resolves an antecedent polar question with an overt indication of polarity. The pattern is an answer particle, a subject pronoun and a finite auxiliary, optionally negated. Did presents a positive answer and helps identify the elided predicate. Responses to negative questions can vary in the use of the answer particle across speakers and contexts. This dictionary marks this as provisional, with medium confidence, and relates it to auxiliary VP ellipsis.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call these short answers or elliptical answers. This dictionary's answer particle is the word yes or no.
watch_for: A learner might treat the reply to a negative question as having a single fixed form, when this dictionary notes variation in the answer particle.
teacher.activity: Pairs ask each other five yes/no questions with different auxiliaries (did, can, is, has, will) and reply with a full short answer, then say what part of the verb phrase was left out.

child.hook: When someone asks Did you lock up? what short answer can you give?
child.explain: You can answer a yes/no question with a short reply. Did Jo lock up? Yes, she did. The reply uses did from the question and leaves out the rest.

examples.text: Did Jo lock up? Yes, she did.
Can Sam swim? Yes, he can.

child.play: Ask each other yes/no questions. Give short answers like Yes, she did.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body now says the reply uses the pronoun she for Jo (not 'repeats a pronoun') and that the left-out predicate is lock up, as in the question; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'. Cut an unflagged teacher watch_for item implying a different auxiliary in the answer is wrong (not supported by the entry). Second round: fixed child.play, which made copying the question's helper word a rule (this dictionary says the reply can retain it); the game now models Yes, she did. Curious.try now asks whether the reply repeats a helper word instead of assuming it does.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Finite Auxiliary in a Polar Short Answer." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/polarity-short-answer-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Count NP for a Portion or Variety
pattern: NP[count determination + substance noun, with ordinary plural marking where appropriate]

entry.name: Count NP for a Portion or Variety
entry.pattern: NP[count determination + substance noun, with ordinary plural marking where appropriate]

1.definition: Counts servings or other contextually standardized portions of a substance.
1.details: In two coffees in a café, the relevant units are servings. Their size and the containers used are supplied by the situation. Two of the same blend can satisfy the request.

examples.note: Constructed café example. Two portions can both be the same variety.

2.details: In two coffees at a tasting the units can be varieties. One small sample of each variety would suffice. A later third serving of the first variety does not add to the number of varieties.

examples.form: The roaster sells [two coffees] from that region.

relatedConstructions.notes: A normally non-count substance description supplies what is portioned or classified.
The examples use ordinary count NP syntax.

grounds.note: Distinguishes portion and variety constructions and their sources of contextual interpretation.

projection.target: With the same counted noun and cardinal, portion and variety readings have different counting units. Identical servings count separately in the portion reading.
projection.evidence: FrameNet gives both readings with beer and treats them as two construals of a substance noun. The contrast adds an explicit constructional dependency to the existing non-count noun entry.

curious.title: Counting servings or kinds
curious.summary: A noun for a substance, like coffee, can be counted either as servings or as varieties.
curious.body: In Could we have two coffees? in a café, the units are servings. Their size and the containers used come from the situation, and two of the same blend satisfy the request. In The roaster sells two coffees from that region, the units are varieties. Here two coffees means two different kinds, and one small sample of each would do. A third serving of the first kind wouldn't add to the number of kinds.

examples.text: The roaster sells [two coffees] from that region.

curious.try: What could two teas mean if you said it to a waiter? What could it mean at a shop that sells different kinds of tea?

teacher.summary: Shows that a count noun phrase with a substance noun can count portions or varieties.
teacher.explain: A normally non-count substance noun can appear in an ordinary count NP, with plural marking where appropriate. The portion reading counts servings or contextually standardized portions: in two coffees in a café, size and container are supplied by the situation, and two servings of the same blend still count as two. The variety reading counts varieties: in two coffees at a tasting, one sample of each would suffice, and a later serving of the first variety does not add to the count. With the same noun and the same cardinal, the two readings have different counting units. This dictionary marks this as provisional, with high confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes describe both as count uses of a non-count noun.

examples.text: The roaster sells [two coffees] from that region.

contrasts.note: Portions; two servings of the same blend can count as two.

contrasts.text: The roaster sells two coffees from that region.
contrasts.note: Varieties; two distinct kinds.

watch_for: A learner might think two coffees can only mean two cups.
A learner might think a count noun phrase with a substance noun is ungrammatical, when this dictionary shows ordinary count NP syntax.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a menu and a shop list. They write one sentence counting servings and one counting varieties, and underline the context words that signal each reading.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Count NP for a Portion or Variety." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/portion-variety-count-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Comparative Quantification with more of

1.definition: Compares amounts drawn from a specified set or whole.

examples.form: We should keep [more of these samples].

projection.target: The of-phrase fixes the group counted over. More can quantify a plural count domain or an amount of a non-count substance, depending on the complement.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: More of a particular set
curious.summary: More of followed by a group or a substance compares amounts taken from that group or substance.
curious.body: In We should keep more of these samples, the phrase after of says which set we're drawing from: these samples. Keeping more of them means a bigger share of that set. The word more can count things in a plural group, as in more of these samples, or measure an amount of a substance, as in more of this soup. Which one it is depends on what follows of.

examples.text: We should keep [more of these samples].
Could I have [more of this soup]?

curious.try: Say more of these cookies and more of this milk. Which one counts items, and which one measures an amount?

teacher.summary: Covers more of plus a domain expression, which compares amounts drawn from a specified set or whole.
teacher.explain: In NP[more + PP[of + domain expression]], the of-phrase fixes the group counted over. More can quantify a plural count domain (more of these samples) or an amount of a non-count substance, depending on the complement. This dictionary describes the pattern as comparing amounts drawn from a specified set or whole, and relates it to the true partitive. It is marked provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats this as a specialization of the true partitive.

examples.text: We should keep [more of these samples].
Could I have [more of this soup]?

watch_for: A learner might treat more of these samples and more samples as the same, though the of-phrase fixes a specified set to draw from.
teacher.activity: Show a bowl of items and a jug of juice. Students write one sentence with more of plus a plural count noun phrase and one with more of plus a non-count substance.

child.hook: What is the difference between more cookies and more of these cookies?
child.explain: More of these cookies means more from a set you can point to. The words after of tell which set you mean.

examples.text: We should keep more of these samples.
Could I have more of this soup?

child.play: Point at a pile of things and say what you want more of, starting with more of these or more of this.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Comparative Quantification with more of." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/positive-degree-partitive-more-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Positive Paucal a few and a little
pattern: NP[Det:a few + plural count nominal, or Det:a little + non-count nominal]

entry.name: Positive Paucal a few and a little
entry.pattern: NP[Det:a few + plural count nominal, or Det:a little + non-count nominal]

1.definition: Presents a small quantity as a positive amount.

projection.target: A little asserts some available time. Bare little favours an inadequate-amount reading and patterns differently in environments sensitive to negative orientation.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A few and a little
curious.summary: A few and a little present a small quantity as a positive amount.
curious.body: In We still have a little time, the speaker presents the time as available. A little goes with a non-count word like time, and a few goes with a plural count word, as in a few minutes. This dictionary contrasts a little with plain little. Bare little favours a reading where the amount is inadequate, and it behaves differently in some settings that are sensitive to negative orientation.
curious.try: Compare We have a little time with We have little time. Which one presents the time as available?

teacher.summary: Contrasts a few and a little, which present a small amount as positive, with bare little.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a determiner a few with a plural count nominal, or a little with a non-count nominal, presenting a small quantity as a positive amount. A little asserts some available time. Bare little favours an inadequate-amount reading and patterns differently in environments sensitive to negative orientation. This dictionary files the pattern as a specialization of the noun phrase with a determiner and relates it to an absolute negator determinative. It is provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls this positive paucal, paucal meaning a small number, in contrast with bare little.

contrasts.text: We still have a little time.
contrasts.note: Presents the time as available.

watch_for: A learner might use a little with a plural count noun, when the pattern pairs a little with a non-count nominal.
A learner might read bare little as the same as a little, when bare little favours an inadequate-amount reading.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences about their week using a few with plural nouns and a little with non-count nouns, then swap and check that each pairing fits.

child.hook: If you have a few minutes, is there time to play?
child.explain: A few and a little name a small amount. We still have a little time. We still have a few minutes. A few goes with things you can count.

examples.text: We still have a little time.
We still have a few minutes.

child.play: Look in your pencil case. Say what you have a few of and what you have a little of.

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer says the expressions mean 'you have some' (availability comes from the sentence; the entry gives a quantity meaning); curious summary no longer says 'not as too little'; try question asks which presents the time as available, matching the entry. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Positive Paucal a few and a little." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/positive-paucal-a-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Genitive whose Relative
pattern: relative[NP[whose + Nom]ᵢ + clause with linked positionᵢ]

entry.name: Genitive whose Relative
entry.pattern: relative[NP[whose + Nom]ᵢ + clause with linked positionᵢ]

1.definition: Relativizes the genitive dependent inside a larger NP.

examples.form: I called the engineer [whose report had leaked].

projection.target: Whose tracks the antecedent engineer, but the whole NP whose report is the subject of had leaked. The antecedent can also be nonhuman.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Whose in a describing clause
curious.summary: Whose can join a describing clause to a person or thing, and the noun it belongs to stays attached to it.
curious.body: In I called the engineer whose report had leaked, whose points back to the engineer. The noun that comes with it, report, travels along: the whole phrase whose report is what the clause is about, and it's the one that had leaked. So whose links the clause to the engineer, but whose report, as a unit, is the part doing the leaking. The person or thing it points back to can also be nonhuman.

examples.text: I called the engineer [whose report had leaked].

curious.try: Finish this sentence with a clause starting with whose. I met the woman ...

teacher.summary: Explains relative clauses that begin with whose plus a noun, as in the engineer whose report had leaked.
teacher.explain: This relative clause relativizes the genitive dependent inside a larger NP. Whose tracks the antecedent (engineer), but the whole NP whose report is the subject of had leaked. The antecedent can also be nonhuman. The relative word is contained in the construction, which interfaces with the integrated relative modifier. This dictionary marks it as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Whose is sometimes called a possessive relative pronoun. This grammar says genitive: whose is the genitive form of the relative word.

examples.text: I called the engineer [whose report had leaked].

watch_for: A learner might think whose alone is the subject of had leaked, when the whole NP whose report is the subject.
A learner might assume whose must refer to a person, though the antecedent can be nonhuman.
teacher.activity: Students combine two sentences (I called the engineer. Her report had leaked.) into one with whose, then identify the subject of the relative clause.

child.hook: How can you join two sentences about the same person using whose?
child.explain: Whose can join two ideas about the same person. In I called the engineer whose report had leaked, whose points back to the engineer. The words whose report stay together.

examples.text: I called the engineer whose report had leaked.
We met a girl whose dog can swim.

child.play: Think of a person and something of theirs, like a girl and her dog. Finish this sentence: I know a girl whose ...

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says the engineer owns the report (the dictionary says only that whose points back to the engineer and whose report is the subject of had leaked) and no longer uses the term clause; child.play reworded to match; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Genitive whose Relative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/possessive-relative-whose-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Preposition Phrase
pattern: Head:P (+ Obj:NP / PredComp:NP/AdjP / Comp:PP/AdvP/clause; or no complement)

entry.name: Preposition Phrase
entry.pattern: Head:P (+ Obj:NP / PredComp:NP/AdjP / Comp:PP/AdvP/clause; or no complement)

dimensions.form: Phrase headed by a preposition; NP complements may be objects or predicatives, and PP, AdvP, or clause complements are also licensed
dimensions.meaning: Relates an entity or situation to another in space, time, comparison, reason, or abstract structure
dimensions.function: Complement, modifier, adjunct, or predicative complement in a containing construction
dimensions.distribution: Complement of verbs and nouns, modifier in NPs and clauses, and complement of prepositions

1.definition: Phrase headed by a preposition, with or without a complement
1.details: The head may take an NP object (in the garden), a predicative NP or AdjP (as a liability, as reasonable), an AdvP (until recently), a clause (because it rained), a PP (from under the bed), or no complement (outside). A single complementless preposition constitutes a complete PP (CGEL Ch. 2 §7, p. 58).

examples.note: P with PP complement; under the bed expresses the source location
Complete PP consisting of one complementless preposition

constraints.description: The phrase is headed by a preposition; locative members accept such modifiers as right and straight.

relatedConstructions.notes: The head is a preposition

projection.target: A preposition can head a phrase even without an NP after it, as in We waited outside. Some heads take a different category, as with because it rained, and a PP can itself be selected, as with from under the stairs.
projection.evidence: CGEL classifies PPs by their heads and documents complement types and functions rather than identifying them through the presence of an NP alone.

curious.title: Phrases built around words like in and until
curious.summary: A preposition phrase is a group of words whose main word is a preposition, such as in, as, until or because.
curious.body: In in the garden, the preposition in is the main word, and the garden follows it. The same kind of phrase can be built with other kinds of follower: as a liability, until recently, because it rained, and from under the bed. A preposition can also stand alone as a complete phrase. Outside is a whole phrase on its own, as in We waited outside. What makes each of these a preposition phrase is its main word, not the kind of word that comes after it.
curious.try: Pick a short preposition like in, until or because. What can you put after it to make a phrase?

teacher.summary: Defines the PP and the range of complements a preposition can take, including none.
teacher.explain: A PP is a phrase headed by a preposition, with or without a complement. The head may take an NP object (in the garden), a predicative NP or AdjP (as a liability, as reasonable), an AdvP (until recently), a clause (because it rained), a PP (from under the bed), or no complement (outside). A single complementless preposition constitutes a complete PP. PPs are classified by their heads, not by an NP being present. Locative members accept modifiers such as right and straight. A PP can function as a complement, modifier, adjunct or predicative complement in a larger construction.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars sometimes treat words like outside, until and because as adverbs or conjunctions when no NP follows. Here each is a preposition heading a PP.

contrasts.note: Preposition with an NP object.
A complete PP with no complement.

watch_for: A learner might think a preposition needs an NP after it, when outside can be a complete phrase.
A learner might analyze because it rained as a clause only, when this dictionary takes because as the head of a PP with a clause complement.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of PPs (in the garden, until recently, outside). They underline the preposition, then say what, if anything, follows it.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Preposition Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/pp-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Preference would rather
pattern: VP[would rather + plain infinitival or finite subordinate clause]

entry.name: Preference would rather
entry.pattern: VP[would rather + plain infinitival or finite subordinate clause]

1.definition: Expresses preference between actual or imagined alternatives.

projection.target: A finite clause can have its own subject and a modally remote preterite. In I would rather stay, the subject of stay is understood as the matrix subject.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying what you would prefer
curious.summary: Would rather expresses a preference between real or imagined alternatives, and can be followed by a plain verb or a whole clause.
curious.body: I would rather you stayed says what the speaker prefers: that you stay. After would rather there can be a clause with its own subject, here you, and the verb in that clause takes a past-looking form, stayed, which has a remote, imagined feel rather than a past one. With a plain verb, as in I would rather stay, the person doing the staying is understood to be the speaker.
curious.try: Say what you would rather do tonight, then say what you would rather a friend did. How does the verb change?

teacher.summary: Explains would rather with a plain infinitival or a finite clause.
teacher.explain: Would rather expresses preference between actual or imagined alternatives. It can be followed by a plain infinitival or a finite subordinate clause. A finite clause can have its own subject and a modally remote preterite, as in I would rather you stayed. In I would rather stay, the subject of stay is understood as the matrix subject. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the VP and relates it to the irrealis were. It is provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: This dictionary describes would rather as a pattern followed by a plain infinitival or a finite subordinate clause.

contrasts.note: The subject of stay is understood as the speaker.
A finite clause with its own subject and a remote preterite.

watch_for: A learner might read stayed in I would rather you stayed as past time, though this dictionary describes it as modally remote.
A learner might take the subject of stay in I would rather stay to be someone other than the speaker.
teacher.activity: Pairs write five would-rather sentences about weekend plans, two with a plain verb and three with a clause having its own subject, then underline each verb form.

child.hook: How do you say what you want to do instead of something else?
child.explain: Would rather tells what you prefer. I would rather stay. You can also say what you want someone else to do. I would rather you stayed.
child.play: Tell a partner what you would rather do on a rainy day. Then say what you would rather a friend did.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Preference would rather." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/preference-would-rather-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Predeterminer all before a Determined NP

1.definition: Applies universal quantification outside a following determiner phrase or constituent.

projection.target: All can precede those and the in the same NP. Each and every do not generally occupy that same position before an existing central determiner.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: All before this, that or the
curious.summary: All can stand before a determiner such as those or the, applying to the whole group named.
curious.body: In They catalogued all those shells, all comes before those and takes in every shell in the group that those picks out. The two words sit one after the other in the same phrase. All can also come before the, as in all the shells. This dictionary notes that each and every don't generally take that same place before a determiner that is already there.
curious.try: Try putting all before the, these and my. Which ones work?

teacher.summary: Explains all before another determiner, as in all those shells and all the shells.
teacher.explain: In the pattern NP[all + Det + Nom], all applies universal quantification outside a following determiner phrase or constituent. All can precede those and the in the same NP. Each and every do not generally occupy that same position before an existing central determiner. This dictionary files this as a specialization of the noun phrase with a determiner, and relates it to each-of partitives. It is provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call all in this position a predeterminer. In CGEL terms, determiner is a function and determinative a category.
watch_for: A learner might think all has to replace the determiner, when it can come before it.
A learner might expect each and every to take the same position before the or those.
teacher.activity: Students write six noun phrases with all plus a determiner (the, those, these, my) and a plural noun, then compare with a partner and discuss which ones they find natural.

child.hook: Can the word all go in front of the, like in all the kids?
child.explain: The word all can come before words like the and those. They catalogued all those shells. All means every one of them.
child.play: Say a sentence about your class starting with all the. Then change the to those or my.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Predeterminer all before a Determined NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/prenominal-all-the-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Bare Plural with Prenominal Modifier

1.definition: Category/kind modification with property attribution

examples.note: Prototypical property-denoting usage; Direct property modification (age attribute)
Requires contextual reference set; Complementary set relation

constraints.description: The modifier function must be realized by an AdjP; the lexical head is the plural noun
Head must be plural

relatedConstructions.notes: The old men shows the same modification inside an article-marked NP.

projection.target: In a clause such as Old men were waiting, the modified bare plural can be an ordinary subject without an article. In the same episodic use an old man needs the article. The difference in bare licensing follows the head’s count and number profile and survives expansion to very old.
projection.evidence: CGEL gives the range of attributive AdjPs and the ordinary order within the nominal.

curious.title: Plural nouns with an adjective in front
curious.summary: A plural noun with an adjective before it, such as old men, can stand as a subject without a word like the or a.
curious.body: In old men, the adjective old tells us a property of the men, here their age. In other men, the adjective needs a surrounding set of men to make sense, because other points to the rest of a set. A plural noun like this can be a sentence subject without a small word in front: Old men were waiting. A single man isn't the same: in the same kind of sentence, an old man needs the article a. Adding words such as very to the adjective, as in very old men, doesn't change that.
curious.try: Say Old men were waiting. Then try it with one man. What word do you need to add?

teacher.summary: Covers plural nouns modified by a prenominal adjective, which can serve as subjects with no article.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a plural noun as lexical head of a nominal, with an AdjP modifier before it: old men. It expresses category or kind modification with property attribution. Old men is direct property modification (an age attribute); other men requires a contextual reference set and expresses a complementary-set relation. The modifier must be an AdjP and the head must be plural. In an episodic clause such as Old men were waiting, the modified bare plural can be an ordinary subject without an article, while an old man needs the article. The licensing follows the head's count and number profile and survives expansion to very old. This dictionary marks this as provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call the modifying adjective an attributive adjective. This dictionary also calls old men a bare plural with a prenominal modifier.

contrasts.note: The same modification inside an NP marked with the.

watch_for: A learner might think a subject needs the or a, when a plural noun with a modifier can stand alone as a subject.
A learner might read other men as simply more men, when other needs a contextual reference set.
teacher.activity: Students list plural noun phrases with an adjective (old men, tall trees) and use each as a bare subject, then mark in each one whether the adjective attributes a property or points to a set.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Bare Plural with Prenominal Modifier." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/prenominal-modifier-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Preposed Verbal Predicate
pattern: Clause[preposed VP + Subject + stranded licensing auxiliary]

entry.name: Preposed Verbal Predicate
entry.pattern: Clause[preposed VP + Subject + stranded licensing auxiliary]

1.definition: Repeats or validates a salient predicate by putting the verbal material first.

examples.form: They said Jo would run, and [run she did].

grounds.locator: Ch. 16 §3, complement preposing; Ch. 3 §2.1.4, stranding and preposing

projection.target: The auxiliary remains in the nucleus and the preposed VP is plain after do. Preposing the lexical predicate does not require inverting the subject and auxiliary.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Putting the action first
curious.summary: The verb part of a clause can move to the front to repeat or confirm something already mentioned, with did left behind in its usual place.
curious.body: In They said Jo would run, and run she did, the speaker confirms the prediction by putting the verb first: run. Then comes the subject, she, and then did. The pattern repeats or validates a salient predicate. The front part is the plain form after did. The subject and did don't swap places; the verb part is simply moved in front.

examples.text: They said Jo would run, and [run she did].

curious.try: Someone says Sam will win. Can you finish this: And win ...?

teacher.summary: Covers sentences where the verb part comes first and the auxiliary is left behind, as in run she did.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause consisting of a preposed VP, the subject and a stranded licensing auxiliary, as in run she did. It repeats or validates a salient predicate by putting the verbal material first. The auxiliary remains in the nucleus, and the preposed VP is plain after do. Preposing the lexical predicate does not require inverting the subject and auxiliary. This dictionary relates it to complement preposing, auxiliary VP ellipsis and finite do-support. It is provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes describe this as VP fronting. This dictionary calls it a preposed verbal predicate.

examples.text: They said Jo would run, and [run she did].

watch_for: A learner might expect the subject and auxiliary to swap places, when this dictionary says preposing the lexical predicate does not require inversion.
A learner might use an inflected verb in the fronted part, when it is plain after do.
teacher.activity: Give students a prediction (They said Jo would run). They continue each with a confirming clause that fronts the verb, then compare the order with a plain version.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Preposed Verbal Predicate." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/preposed-predicate-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Preposition

dimensions.form: Mostly short, closed-class lexemes; no inflection
dimensions.meaning: Relates an entity or situation to another in space, time, or abstract structure
dimensions.function: Head of PP; PPs serve as complements, modifiers, and adjuncts
dimensions.distribution: NP objects and other complements are optional for much of the class; a few exceptional heads follow their complement

1.definition: Lexical category heading preposition phrases, with optional complements for much of the class
1.details: The CGEL category is much larger than the traditional one: it includes the traditional prepositions (in, on, of), objectless members traditionally called adverbs (home, abroad, ashore, upstairs; ago, with its obligatory pre-head measure modifier), the rare complement-head members (notwithstanding), and clause-taking members traditionally called subordinating conjunctions (because, although, while). See data/lexicon/gold/prepositions.yaml for the curated inventory.

examples.note: Transitive: the garden bears the object function within the PP
Intransitive, with an obligatory pre-head measure modifier (cf. ten years before Christ); the Constructionary rejects CGEL's complement analysis on p. 632

constraints.description: Heads a PP; accepts right/straight modification in locative uses (right outside, straight home).

projection.target: Category membership predicts PP distribution (goal and locative complement positions, from-embedding for locative members, modifier positions), right/straight modifiability for locatives, and non-inflection
projection.evidence: Distributional convergence across the traditional prepositions, the intransitive members, and the clause-taking members (CGEL Ch. 7)

grounds.note: The expanded category projects PP-head distribution across traditional, objectless, and clause-taking members
Shared distributional behavior supports the stable expanded preposition profile
Prepositions head PPs and include objectless and clause-taking members beyond the traditional class

curious.title: Words like in, outside and because
curious.summary: In this dictionary, a preposition is a word that heads a preposition phrase, and the group is wider than you may expect.
curious.body: Words like in, on and of are prepositions. So are some words that traditional grammar puts elsewhere: outside, home and ago, which need no noun after them, and because, which takes a whole clause. Prepositions relate one thing or event to another in space, time or other ways. They don't change form. In the garden, she waited outside and ten years ago all contain a preposition, and so does because it rained. In place uses, you can add right or straight: right outside, straight home.
curious.try: Find a sign or a book page and look for small words like in, on or because. Which ones are followed by a noun, and which by a clause or nothing?

teacher.summary: Defines the wider category of preposition, including words that traditional grammar calls adverbs or subordinating conjunctions.
teacher.explain: A preposition is a lexical category heading PPs, with optional complements for much of the class. The CGEL category is much larger than the traditional one. It includes traditional prepositions (in, on, of), objectless members traditionally called adverbs (home, abroad, ashore, upstairs; ago, with an obligatory pre-head measure modifier), the rare complement-head member notwithstanding, and clause-taking members traditionally called subordinating conjunctions (because, although, while). Prepositions are closed-class and don't inflect. In locative uses they accept right and straight. The Constructionary departs from CGEL on the analysis of ago.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar calls home, outside and upstairs adverbs, and because, although and while subordinating conjunctions. This grammar calls them prepositions.
watch_for: A learner might think a preposition must be followed by a noun phrase, when this dictionary gives intransitive members such as outside.
A learner might treat because as a different kind of word from in, when this dictionary places both in one category.
teacher.activity: Give students a list (in, outside, home, ago, because, although). They try each in a sentence, then say whether anything follows it, and what.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Preposition." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/preposition-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Preposition Fronting in a Relative
pattern: relative [PP[P + relative NP] + clause with linked gap]

entry.name: Preposition Fronting in a Relative
entry.pattern: relative [PP[P + relative NP] + clause with linked gap]

1.definition: Places a preposition and relative expression together at the front of the relative clause.

examples.form: The terminal [from which they departed] is closed.

relatedConstructions.notes: To whom Jo spoke fronts the preposition with its complement. Jo was spoken to leaves the preposition behind when its complement is realized as passive subject.

projection.target: A fronted P can take which or whom. The comparable relative with that requires stranding rather than forming an initial PP from that.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Carrying a preposition to the front
curious.summary: In a describing clause, the preposition can move to the front together with the word which or whom.
curious.body: In The terminal from which they departed is closed, the little word from travels to the front of the clause together with which. The two stay together as a unit. The word that after from can't be used this way: with that, the preposition has to stay behind, as in The terminal that they departed from is closed. A fronted preposition can take which or whom.

examples.text: The terminal [from which they departed] is closed.
The terminal that they departed from is closed.

curious.try: Turn I spoke to the woman into a clause that begins with to whom.

teacher.summary: Explains relative clauses where a fronted preposition travels with which or whom.
teacher.explain: In a relative clause with a fronted preposition, the preposition and the relative expression form a PP at the front of the clause, and the rest of the clause contains a linked gap. A fronted P can take which or whom. The comparable relative with that requires stranding rather than forming an initial PP from that. Compare To whom Jo spoke, which fronts the preposition with its complement, with Jo was spoken to, which leaves it behind. This dictionary relates the pattern to integrated relative modifiers, selected prepositional complements and the prepositional passive, and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call this preposition fronting or pied-piping. Stranding is the term for leaving the preposition behind.

examples.text: The terminal [from which they departed] is closed.

contrasts.text: The terminal from which they departed is closed.
contrasts.note: Preposition fronted with which.

contrasts.text: The terminal that they departed from is closed.
contrasts.note: With that, the preposition is stranded at the end.

watch_for: A learner might split the preposition from which, when the fronted PP stays together.
A learner might expect to front the preposition in a relative with that, when that requires stranding.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs of sentences (I spoke to the woman. She called) and ask them to join them two ways, with a fronted preposition and with a stranded one, and say which relative word each needs.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Preposition Fronting in a Relative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/preposition-pied-piping-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Prepositional Passive
pattern: Clause[NPᵢ + be + V-en + stranded P with gapᵢ]

entry.name: Prepositional Passive
entry.pattern: Clause[NPᵢ + be + V-en + stranded P with gapᵢ]

1.definition: Allows the complement of a preposition to correspond to the subject of a passive.

relatedConstructions.notes: Selected prepositions are a major source. Some independently licensed locatives can also be stranded.

projection.target: To remains part of the passive VP. Selection by the verb strongly supports the construction, and some independently licensed adjunct PPs can also occur under restricted conditions.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Passives that leave a small word behind
curious.summary: The thing that follows a preposition can become the subject of a passive sentence, leaving the preposition behind after the verb.
curious.body: In This proposal was referred to repeatedly, the subject, this proposal, would follow to in an ordinary active sentence. In the passive it becomes the subject, and to stays behind after the verb. Selected prepositions, the ones a verb takes, are a major source of this pattern. Jo was spoken to works the same way. This dictionary also notes that some other prepositional phrases can take part under restricted conditions.
curious.try: Turn Someone spoke to Jo into a sentence that starts with Jo. What word is left at the end?

teacher.summary: Covers passives whose subject corresponds to the complement of a preposition, with the preposition stranded.
teacher.explain: In a prepositional passive the complement of a preposition corresponds to the subject of the passive: This proposal was referred to repeatedly. The preposition is stranded after the verb and remains part of the passive VP. Selection by the verb strongly supports the construction, and some independently licensed adjunct PPs can also occur under restricted conditions. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the be-passive, and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call this the pseudo-passive or passive with a stranded preposition.

contrasts.text: They referred to this proposal repeatedly.
contrasts.note: Active; this proposal follows to.
