contrasts.text: This proposal was referred to repeatedly.
contrasts.note: Passive; this proposal is the subject and to is left behind.

watch_for: A learner might drop to from was referred to, when it remains part of the passive VP.
A learner might think any adverbial phrase can be turned into a passive subject, when this dictionary notes this works under restricted conditions.
teacher.activity: Students rewrite active sentences with a selected preposition (They referred to this proposal) as passives, then underline the preposition that is left behind.

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary no longer says the preposition ends the sentence (the entry's own example continues with repeatedly). Also fixed (unflagged): removed the 'To whom Jo spoke' comparison, which the entry does not support, and replaced it with an active/passive contrast built on the entry's example; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Prepositional Passive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/prepositional-passive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Selected Prepositional Complement
pattern: VP[Head:V + PP with lexically selected P]

entry.name: Selected Prepositional Complement
entry.pattern: VP[Head:V + PP with lexically selected P]

1.definition: Links a verbal argument through a preposition selected by the lexical sense.

relatedConstructions.notes: Compare relied on Jo with picked the book up. Jo is the object of selected on. The book is an object of the verb and can precede the particle up.

projection.target: The preposition in this sense can be stranded in Who did you rely on? It remains adjacent to its NP in the ordinary order and does not undergo particle shift.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Verbs that go with a particular small word
curious.summary: Some verbs link an argument through one particular preposition that belongs with that sense of the verb.
curious.body: In We relied on Jo, the preposition on isn't a free choice. The verb sense chooses it. Jo is the object of on, and the on-phrase is tied to the verb relied. Compare picked the book up. There, the book is the object of the verb, and it can go before the little word up. Relied on Jo doesn't work that way. In the ordinary order the preposition stays next to Jo, but it can be left at the end in a question like Who did you rely on?
curious.try: Which small word goes with rely in We relied on Jo? Say a new sentence with rely and that word.

teacher.summary: Shows verbs that select a specific preposition for a complement, such as rely on.
teacher.explain: In this pattern a verb head takes a PP with a lexically selected preposition: relied on Jo. The lexical sense links the argument through that preposition. Jo is the object of selected on. Compare picked the book up, where the book is an object of the verb and can precede the particle up. The selected preposition can be stranded in Who did you rely on?, remains adjacent to its NP in the ordinary order, and does not undergo particle shift. This dictionary relates the pattern to verb-particle-object constructions, and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call these prepositional verbs. This dictionary contrasts them with the verb-particle-object pattern of picked the book up.

contrasts.note: Jo is the object of the selected preposition on.
The book is an object of the verb and can precede the particle up.

watch_for: A learner might think the preposition after rely can be changed freely, when it is selected by the verb sense.
A learner might try to move on away from its NP the way up moves in picked the book up.
teacher.activity: Students make a card list of verbs with their selected prepositions (rely on). They write a statement and a question for each, with the preposition at the end of the question.

child.hook: Which little word goes with the verb rely?
child.explain: Some verbs go with a certain small word. We relied on Jo. The word on belongs with rely here. In this sentence it sits right next to Jo.
child.play: Make up sentences with rely on. Then turn them into questions, like Who did you rely on?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary says the verb links an argument through a selected preposition (Jo is the object of on, not of the verb); teacher.terms now ties the contrast to the verb-particle-object pattern in the entry; replaced 'The entry' with this dictionary. Second round: fixed curious.body and child.explain, which stated adjacency to Jo without the entry's restriction to the ordinary order (the preposition can be stranded in Who did you rely on?).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Selected Prepositional Complement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/prepositional-verb-frame-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Backshift in Reported Content

1.definition: Allows a preterite in the subordinate report to correspond to a present-tense original or to overlap the reporting reference time.

projection.target: The hunger can coincide with the speaking. Present-tense is also possible in appropriate contexts, especially where the reporter treats the content as still current.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Why a report uses the past form
curious.summary: When you report what someone said earlier, the verb in the report can take a past form even if the original speaker used the present.
curious.body: In Yesterday Jo said she was hungry, the report uses was, though Jo's own words could have been present tense, as in I'm hungry. The past form matches the past setting of the reporting. The hunger can still coincide with the speaking, so was doesn't have to mean Jo was hungry before she spoke. A present-tense form is also possible in suitable contexts, especially where the reporter treats the content as still current.
curious.try: Report something a friend said earlier today, once with a past verb and once with a present verb. When does each feel right?

teacher.summary: Explains how a past-tense form in a report can correspond to a present-tense original or overlap the reporting time.
teacher.explain: In a past reporting setting, a subordinate preterite can correspond to a present-tense original or overlap the reporting reference time. In Yesterday Jo said she was hungry, the hunger can coincide with the speaking. A present-tense form is also possible in appropriate contexts, especially where the reporter treats the content as still current. This dictionary relates the pattern to declarative content clauses and marks it provisional, with medium confidence.
teacher.terms: Textbooks sometimes call this backshift or the sequence of tenses.
watch_for: A learner might read was in she was hungry as meaning the hunger came before Jo spoke, when it can coincide with the speaking.
A learner might think the report must use a past form, when a present form is possible where the reporter treats the content as still current.
teacher.activity: Give students direct statements (I'm hungry, I like it). They report each as said yesterday, then discuss whether a present form could also work.

child.hook: If Jo says I'm hungry, how do you tell it tomorrow?
child.explain: When you tell what someone said before, the verb can take a past form. Yesterday Jo said she was hungry. She could have been hungry right when she said it.

examples.text: Yesterday Jo said she was hungry.
Yesterday Sam said he was tired.

child.play: One person says a sentence with I am. Another tells it later starting with said, using a past form.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Backshift in Reported Content." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/present-backshift-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Present Futurate

1.definition: Presents a future occurrence as scheduled or fixed by an arrangement.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. A calculable future event with the simple present.

projection.target: The plain present can locate a scheduled departure in the future. Compare the heat will crack the pane tomorrow, where the ordinary simple present would suggest a more settled prediction or scenario.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: The plain present talking about tomorrow
curious.summary: A verb in the plain present tense can describe something that hasn't happened yet, when it's scheduled or fixed by an arrangement.
curious.body: In The ferry leaves at dawn tomorrow, the verb leaves is in the present tense, yet the event is in the future. The word tomorrow anchors it there, and the sentence presents the departure as scheduled, something arranged in advance. The same goes for The Sun sets at five tomorrow, where the event isn't arranged by anyone but can be calculated. Compare The heat will crack the pane tomorrow, where will is used instead. This dictionary treats its account of the present-tense pattern as provisional.
curious.try: Think of something coming up this week that's on a schedule, such as a bus or a class. Can you describe it with a plain present-tense verb and a word like tomorrow?

teacher.summary: Useful when learners ask why a present-tense verb can refer to a scheduled future event.
teacher.explain: The plain present can locate an event in the future when a future time expression (tomorrow, at dawn tomorrow) anchors it. The reading is of an event scheduled or fixed by an arrangement, and a calculable event such as a sunset fits too. Compare will, as in The heat will crack the pane tomorrow. The dictionary's account is marked provisional, so present it as a description of these examples rather than a complete rule for when learners should choose the present over will.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the 'present for future' or 'simple present with future time reference'; this dictionary calls it the present futurate.

contrasts.text: The heat will crack the pane tomorrow.
contrasts.note: A will-version of a future event, for comparison.

watch_for: A learner might read leaves as describing the present moment instead of a scheduled future departure.
A learner might think the present-tense pattern can replace will in any prediction about the future.
teacher.activity: Students write three sentences about a school timetable or transit schedule using a plain present-tense verb and a future time word, then swap with a partner who says whether each event is scheduled.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Present Futurate." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/present-futurate-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Locative and Temporal Subject–Dependent Inversion
pattern: Clause[locative or temporal dependent + V(P) + postposed Subject:NP]

entry.name: Locative and Temporal Subject–Dependent Inversion
entry.pattern: Clause[locative or temporal dependent + V(P) + postposed Subject:NP]

1.definition: Presents a referent or event after giving the location or time that anchors it.
1.details: In Three days later came another eight offers, the temporal phrase is an adjunct and the offers are the subject. With be, the fronted phrase is often a locative complement. The preposed material normally links more closely to the preceding discourse than the subject. The verb need not be auxiliary be.

examples.form: [Three days later came another eight offers.]
examples.note: After mention of the first fourteen credit offers.
Constructed locative example with a lexical verb.

relatedConstructions.notes: The clause nucleus includes a subject after the verb.
Ordinary complement preposing does not send the subject after the verb.

grounds.note: Documents the noun phrase subject after the verb and the discourse conditions on inversion.
Provides the catalogue pointers. The diagnostics come from CGEL.

projection.target: The frame admits a lexical verb and a temporal adjunct. Relative discourse familiarity matters even for syntactically permissible sequences.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the temporal and locative subtypes of the wider subject–dependent inversion family and compares the information status of the two dependents.

curious.title: Putting a place or time first, and the subject last
curious.summary: A phrase giving a place or time can open a sentence, with the verb next and the subject coming after it.
curious.body: In Three days later came another eight offers, the sentence opens with a time phrase, then comes the verb, and only then the thing being introduced: another eight offers. In On the wall hung a portrait, a place phrase opens the sentence and the portrait arrives last. The pattern introduces a person, thing or event after first saying where or when it belongs. The opening phrase normally links back to what was said before. The verb doesn't have to be a form of be. This dictionary treats the account as provisional.

examples.text: [Three days later came another eight offers.]

curious.try: Read a sentence that begins with a place, such as On the wall. Can you build a sentence that ends with the thing that was there?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, sentences that front a locative or temporal phrase and put the subject after the verb.
teacher.explain: In this frame a locative or temporal dependent comes first, then a verb, then a postposed subject NP. In Three days later came another eight offers, the temporal phrase is an adjunct and another eight offers is the subject. With be, the fronted phrase is often a locative complement. The fronted material normally links more closely to the preceding discourse than the subject does. The verb need not be auxiliary be, and relative discourse familiarity matters even for syntactically possible sequences. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional. It differs from ordinary complement preposing, which doesn't send the subject after the verb.
teacher.terms: Often grouped under 'locative inversion' (place phrase) and 'temporal inversion'; this dictionary uses subject-dependent inversion.

examples.text: [Three days later came another eight offers.]

watch_for: A learner might take the fronted phrase to be the subject, since it comes first.
A learner might read the final NP as an object because it follows the verb.
teacher.activity: Give students the pairs "A portrait hung on the wall" and "On the wall hung a portrait". They mark the subject in each and discuss what the opening phrase connects back to in a short paragraph.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Locative and Temporal Subject–Dependent Inversion." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/presentational-dependent-inversion-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Presentational there with a Lexical Verb
pattern: Clause[dummy there + lexical V + postverbal NP]

entry.name: Presentational there with a Lexical Verb
entry.pattern: Clause[dummy there + lexical V + postverbal NP]

1.definition: Introduces an entity through an event of appearance, presence or emergence.

examples.form: [There appeared a crack in the plaster].

projection.target: Only certain lexical predicates license dummy there in this frame. The opening there need not locate the crack, and ordinary event-transitive verbs are excluded.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: There introducing something that appears
curious.summary: A sentence can begin with there, then a verb of appearing, then the thing that appears.
curious.body: In There appeared a crack in the plaster, the word there doesn't point to a place. It opens the sentence, the verb appeared follows, and then comes the thing being introduced, a crack. The pattern introduces something through an event of appearance, presence or emergence. Only certain verbs fit this frame, and the opening there need not say where the crack is. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.

examples.text: [There appeared a crack in the plaster].

curious.try: Can you think of other verbs about appearing or emerging that could follow there at the start of a sentence?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, there plus a lexical verb of appearance introducing a new entity.
teacher.explain: Here dummy there is followed by a lexical verb and a postverbal NP, as in There appeared a crack in the plaster. The pattern introduces an entity through an event of appearance, presence or emergence. Only certain lexical predicates license dummy there in this frame, and the opening there needn't locate the crack. This dictionary says ordinary event-transitive verbs are excluded. The analysis is provisional, and this dictionary gives only one illustration, so check examples with a reference before teaching others as equivalents.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called existential or presentational there; this dictionary calls this one presentational there with a lexical verb.

examples.text: [There appeared a crack in the plaster].

watch_for: A learner might read there as a place adverb meaning in that location.
A learner might assume any verb can follow dummy there.
teacher.activity: Show the sentence and ask students to say where the crack is. Discuss that the information about location comes from the phrase in the plaster, not from there.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Presentational there with a Lexical Verb." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/presentational-there-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Preterite with Present-Time Politeness
pattern: Clause[preterite of a request-related predicate + complement]

entry.name: Preterite with Present-Time Politeness
entry.pattern: Clause[preterite of a request-related predicate + complement]

1.definition: Softens a present request by presenting it as an already entertained thought or intention.

examples.form: [I wanted to ask] if a seat was available.

projection.target: The request can be made at the time of speaking. The morphology also has a literal past interpretation in a context that supplies a past intention.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Past tense for a polite request now
curious.summary: A past-tense verb can soften a request being made right now.
curious.body: In I wanted to ask if a seat was available, the person is asking now. The past tense wanted presents the request as a thought or intention they've already had, which softens it. The same form can also have a literal past meaning, if the situation supplies a past intention. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.

examples.text: [I wanted to ask] if a seat was available.

curious.try: How would you ask for something politely using a past-tense verb? Does it feel gentler than a present-tense version?

teacher.summary: Explains why a past-tense verb can make a present request more polite.
teacher.explain: The preterite of a request-related predicate plus a complement can soften a present request by presenting it as an already entertained thought or intention. In I wanted to ask if a seat was available, the request is made at the time of speaking. The same morphology can also be literally past, in a context that supplies a past intention. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional, so present it as a description of this example, and point out that tense can express more than time.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the 'past tense of politeness' or 'tentative past'; this dictionary uses preterite for the past tense form.

examples.text: [I wanted to ask] if a seat was available.

watch_for: A learner might take wanted as describing something that happened only in the past.
A learner might not realize the speaker is asking now.
teacher.activity: Students role-play asking for a seat or a favour, first with a plain request and then with a past-tense softened one, and say how each might sound to the listener.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Preterite with Present-Time Politeness." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/preterite-politeness-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Finite Auxiliary with not

1.definition: Expresses clausal negation with not associated with the finite auxiliary.

projection.target: Not follows the finite auxiliary in an ordinary declarative, and lexical verbs generally require do in this frame. Nonfinite negation places not differently.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Where not goes in a sentence
curious.summary: In an ordinary statement, not comes right after the first helping verb.
curious.body: In She has not received it, the word not follows has. The helping verb has is the finite one, and not attaches to it to make the whole clause negative. This dictionary also says that verbs like receive generally need do in this kind of sentence when there's no other helping verb, and that when the verb has no tense, not goes elsewhere. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Take a statement with a helping verb, such as She has finished. Where does not go to make it negative?

teacher.summary: Shows where not sits relative to the finite auxiliary in a negative statement.
teacher.explain: In an ordinary declarative, not follows the finite auxiliary: She has not received it. Lexical verbs generally require do in this frame, and nonfinite negation places not differently. This dictionary treats not as associated with the finite auxiliary, expressing clausal negation. It marks the analysis as provisional and the example is constructed, so use it as a starting pattern rather than a full account of negation.
teacher.terms: This dictionary's term for the verb that not follows is finite auxiliary.
watch_for: A learner might place not before the auxiliary instead of after it.
A learner might negate a lexical verb directly with not, without do.
teacher.activity: Give students affirmative sentences with has, is and will. They rewrite each as negative and underline the finite auxiliary and the not that follows it.

child.hook: Where does the word not go when you say you haven't done something?
child.explain: Look at She has not received it. The little word not comes right after has. A helper word like has comes first, and not follows it.
child.play: Pick a sentence with a helper word, such as She has finished. Make it say the opposite by adding not. Say where you put it.

checked.note: Audit: fixed teacher.terms, cutting primary auxiliary (such as have, be, do), since the entry covers any finite auxiliary and the activity uses will. Also replaced the entry with this dictionary in curious and teacher text, and the curious body now says receive needs do when there is no other helping verb.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Finite Auxiliary with not." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/primary-auxiliary-negation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Privative Adjective in -less

1.definition: Characterizes something by absence of a feature or entity named by the noun base.

projection.target: The default interpretation is a room with no windows. Context and lexicalization can supply an evaluative reading, as with careless, rather than literal absence alone.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Words ending in -less
curious.summary: Adding -less to a noun makes an adjective meaning that something lacks what the noun names.
curious.body: In The room was windowless, the adjective windowless is built from the noun window plus the ending -less. It describes a room with no windows. The ending says that what the noun names is missing. Context and the history of a particular word can sometimes shift the meaning toward a judgment of someone, as with careless, rather than only a literal absence. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Take a noun like door or sun and add -less. What would the new word describe?

teacher.summary: Shows how -less turns a noun into an adjective meaning without that thing.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an adjective formed from a noun base plus -less, and it characterizes something by the absence of a feature or entity named by the noun. The default interpretation of The room was windowless is a room with no windows. Context and lexicalization can supply an evaluative reading, as with careless, rather than literal absence alone. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and gives one constructed example, so treat other -less words as separate vocabulary items and check them.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a privative suffix; this dictionary calls the pattern a privative adjective in -less.

examples.text: The family was [homeless] for a month.

watch_for: A learner might read careless as literally lacking care rather than as an evaluation of a person.
A learner might assume every noun can take -less.
teacher.activity: Students list nouns and add -less, then write a sentence for each new word and a partner says whether the word means literally without the noun.

child.hook: What do you call a room with no windows?
child.explain: Some words end in -less. The ending tells you something is missing. A windowless room has no windows.
child.play: Put -less on the end of a noun, like sun or roof. Say what the new word would describe. Make up a sentence with it.

checked.note: Frequency pass: added the constructed teacher example The family was homeless for a month (homeless about 4,800th in SUBTLEX-UK, with the literal without reading the block gives as the default) beside the entry's windowless (about 57,700th); activity already has students choose their own nouns, so left as is.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Privative Adjective in -less." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/privative-less-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Pro-Nominal one and ones
pattern: Nom[one/ones as anaphoric head + optional nominal dependents]

entry.name: Pro-Nominal one and ones
entry.pattern: Nom[one/ones as anaphoric head + optional nominal dependents]

1.definition: Recovers a nominal description while allowing independent determination and number.

projection.target: Ones can take plural morphology and an adjective. It normally recovers count nominal content, while the separate numeral one can answer a question about cardinality.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: One and ones standing in for a noun
curious.summary: The words one and ones can stand in for a noun that was already mentioned, so we don't repeat it.
curious.body: In I preferred the larger ones, the word ones picks up a description from earlier, such as shoes or cups. It carries that description, and it can still take its own the, an adjective like larger, and a plural ending. This dictionary says it normally stands in for something countable. The number word one is a separate thing: it can answer a question about how many. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Say a sentence about some things, then refer back to them with ones and an adjective, as in the larger ones.

teacher.summary: Explains one and ones as substitute words that recover a noun and can take their own determiner, adjective and plural.
teacher.explain: Pro-nominal one(s) is an anaphoric head that recovers a nominal description while allowing independent determination and number. In I preferred the larger ones, ones can take plural morphology, a determiner (the) and an adjective (larger). It normally recovers count nominal content. The numeral one is separate and can answer a question about cardinality. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and gives one constructed example, so check further cases before generalizing.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the 'prop-word one' or 'substitute one' in traditional grammars; this dictionary calls it pro-nominal one.
watch_for: A learner might read ones as the numeral one with a plural ending.
A learner might think ones can recover any kind of noun, when this dictionary says it normally recovers count nominal content.
teacher.activity: Students get a sentence with a repeated noun, such as one about two kinds of cups, and replace the second noun with one or ones and an adjective. They compare their versions.

child.hook: How can you talk about some things again without saying the same word twice?
child.explain: The word ones can stand in for a word we've already used. If we're talking about shoes, we can say the larger ones. It means the larger shoes.
child.play: Name a group of things, like pencils. Then say which ones you like using ones, such as the sharp ones.

checked.note: Audit: fixed curious.body, which gave a causal link (because it carries that description) that the entry does not make, and the child hook and explain, which called the noun shoes a name. Also replaced the entry with this dictionary in curious and teacher text, Often with Sometimes in teacher.terms, and restated the count limit with the entry's normally.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Pro-Nominal one and ones." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/pro-nominal-one-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Progressive Futurate

1.definition: Presents a future event as already arranged, planned or settled in the relevant circumstances.

projection.target: An explicit future anchor selects an arrangement interpretation. With an ordinary predicted natural event, as in the time of sunset, the plain present is often preferred to the progressive futurate.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Being plus -ing for plans
curious.summary: A be plus -ing verb with a future time can describe something already planned.
curious.body: In We're meeting Jo on Tuesday, the verb form is the same one used for things happening right now, but the words on Tuesday point to the future. The sentence presents the meeting as already arranged, planned or settled. An explicit future time selects that reading. For an ordinary natural event like sunset, this dictionary says the plain present is often preferred. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of something you've already planned for next week. Can you say it with am, is or are plus an -ing verb and a day?

teacher.summary: Explains the be plus -ing form with a future time word for arranged events.
teacher.explain: A progressive clause with an explicit future anchor can present a future event as already arranged, planned or settled in the relevant circumstances: We're meeting Jo on Tuesday. The future anchor selects the arrangement interpretation. With an ordinary predicted natural event, such as the time of sunset, this dictionary says the plain present is often preferred. The analysis is provisional, with one constructed example.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called 'present progressive for future'; this dictionary calls it the progressive futurate.

contrasts.text: The Sun sets at five tomorrow.
contrasts.note: A natural event, where this dictionary says the plain present is often preferred.

watch_for: A learner might read We're meeting Jo as describing a meeting in progress.
A learner might use the progressive for a future event that has no arrangement behind it.
teacher.activity: Students write a plan for the week in be plus -ing sentences with a day each, then trade with a partner who says what has already been arranged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Progressive Futurate." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/progressive-futurate-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Progressive -ing

1.definition: Marks an ongoing or unfolding situation at a reference time (imperfective viewpoint; endpoints are not asserted)

examples.note: Ongoing event in past time frame
Ongoing process; does not entail completion

2.definition: Marks current-phase or contingent construal (often contrasted with a default habitual/simple-present reading)

examples.form: The server is running slow today

relatedConstructions.notes: The progressive auxiliary and gerund-participial complement form a VP headed by be

projection.target: Be plus a gerund-participle typically presents an activity in progress or a current phase. An -ing complement in Jo avoided staying does not itself have progressive aspect. A future adjunct can instead give the progressive an arrangement reading.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes progressive be from other gerund-participial structures and discusses futurate uses.

curious.title: Being plus -ing for things in progress
curious.summary: A form of be plus a verb ending in -ing presents something as ongoing or unfolding at a particular time.
curious.body: In She is reading, the action is in progress. In They were walking home, it was going on at some time in the past. In She was building a house, the house building is ongoing, and the sentence doesn't say it was ever finished. Compare She built a house, which does tell us it was completed. The same form can also frame something as current or temporary, as in He is living in Chicago or The server is running slow today. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Say She was building a house, then She built a house. In which one do you know the house got finished?

teacher.summary: Core explanation of the be plus -ing progressive, with its two readings and a contrast with the simple past.
teacher.explain: The progressive is be plus a gerund-participle. Its first reading marks an ongoing or unfolding situation at a reference time (imperfective viewpoint), where endpoints aren't asserted: She was building a house doesn't entail completion, while She built a house does. Its second reading marks a current-phase or contingent construal, often contrasted with a default habitual or simple-present reading (He is living in Chicago). The progressive auxiliary and its gerund-participial complement form a VP headed by be. This dictionary marks the account provisional. A future adjunct can give the progressive an arrangement reading.
teacher.terms: Often called the continuous or progressive aspect; the -ing form is a gerund-participle.

contrasts.note: Ongoing process; does not entail completion.
Perfective contrast with completion entailment.

watch_for: A learner might think any -ing form after a verb is a progressive, such as the -ing form in Jo avoided staying, which isn't progressive.
A learner might think She was building a house means the house was finished.
teacher.activity: Students match sentence pairs, such as She was building a house and She built a house, to the question "Is the house finished?" and explain their answer.

child.hook: Is the house finished if she was building it?
child.explain: Words like is, was and were plus an -ing word can show something going on. She was building a house means she was in the middle of it. She built a house means it got done.
child.play: Say what you are doing right now with is or am and an -ing word. Then say what you did yesterday without -ing. Does it sound finished or still going?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Progressive -ing." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/progressive-ing-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Proper Name
pattern: Any linguistic form that functions to uniquely identify

entry.name: Proper Name
entry.pattern: Any linguistic form that functions to uniquely identify

dimensions.form: Variable; typically proper noun, but can be any form (common NP, clause, etc.)
dimensions.meaning: Unique identification; rigid designation; individual-tracking across discourse
dimensions.function: Creates cognitive access points; anchors encyclopedic and episodic knowledge
dimensions.distribution: Wherever referential expressions appear; subject to pragmatic naming conventions

1.definition: Refers to a unique individual, entity, place, event, etc.
1.details: Names create cognitive access points, allowing discourse participants to track and accumulate information about the referent over time. They serve as anchors for both encyclopedic and episodic knowledge.

2.details: Names don't just label but can constitute social reality. They can confer status, rights, responsibilities, and social relationships.

3.details: Names often carry cultural, social, and categorical information through their form. Company names, book titles, personal names each tend to follow recognizable patterns that help hearers identify the type of entity being named.

examples.form: If on a winter's night a traveler

4.details: The choice of which form of a name to use (full name, first name, nickname, title + name, etc.) can indicate social distance, formality, power relationships, and discourse context.

5.details: Certain name elements (Inc., Ltd., Co., etc.) have legal force, indicating corporate structure, liability status, and regulatory compliance. The presence or absence of these elements can affect legal standing.

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional interface; proper-name intention licenses proper noun choice, proper nouns cue proper-name interpretation
Proper names can be realized as proper-noun-headed NPs

projection.target: A standing name such as Jo can identify its bearer in subject or object position. Two Jos can instead count people sharing the name. A capital letter or name-shaped form alone does not fix which interpretation is used.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts ordinary name uses with description and counting uses. The construction account separates standing designation from its syntactic realization.

curious.title: Names and what they do
curious.summary: A proper name picks out one particular person, place, organization or thing, and it can do more than label.
curious.body: A name like Brett Reynolds or The Boring Company points to one individual, so people can keep track of that individual and add what they learn. A name's form can hint at what kind of thing it names: company names, book titles and personal names each follow recognizable patterns. Names can also carry social meaning. Professor Smith signals a formal relationship, His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama establishes an institutional role, and Inc. in Apple Inc. has legal force. A capital letter alone doesn't settle things, since two Jos can count people who share a name. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of how you'd address a teacher, a friend and a stranger. How does the form of their name change?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining names as a meaning category, including titles, company designations and the difference between a name and a proper noun.
teacher.explain: A proper name is a semantic category: any form that functions to identify a unique individual or entity. It is typically a proper noun but can be another form, such as a common-noun phrase (The Boring Company) or a title. Names refer to unique entities, can create social or institutional facts (the Dalai Lama's institutional role), signal membership in name categories, index social relations (Professor Smith), and can mark legal status (Inc., Ltd.). Proper name is a semantic category and proper noun a syntactic one, with a two-way link between them. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional. A standing name such as Jo can identify its bearer, but two Jos can count people sharing the name.
teacher.terms: Proper noun: the syntactic category; proper name: the semantic category. Titles and honorifics (Professor, His Holiness) and corporate designations (Inc., Ltd.) are separate semantic refs in this dictionary.

examples.text: [If on a winter's night a traveler]

watch_for: A learner might think any capitalized word is a proper name.
A learner might treat proper name and proper noun as the same thing.
A learner might use a first name where a title and surname are expected.
teacher.activity: Students list names for the same person (full name, first name, nickname, title plus surname) and say what social relationship each suggests.

child.hook: What's the difference between a girl and Jo?
child.explain: A name points to one particular person or thing. Jo is one person. Sometimes two people share a name, and then we can say two Jos.

examples.text: There are [two Jos] in our class.

child.play: Think of a name that two people you know share. Say a sentence about each one using the same name.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Proper Name." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/proper-name-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Proper Name in a Descriptive NP
pattern: NP[Determiner + Nominal based on a proper name, optionally plural or modified]

entry.name: Proper Name in a Descriptive NP
entry.pattern: NP[Determiner + Nominal based on a proper name, optionally plural or modified]

1.definition: Counts or distinguishes bearers of the same name.
1.details: In two Kims, two individuals satisfy the description ‘has the name Kim’. A modifier can select one Kim from that group. This use can be created even if Kim has never previously been used as an ordinary count noun in that community.

examples.form: There are [two Kims] on the committee.

2.definition: Describes a person by resemblance to a salient bearer of the name.
2.details: In another Einstein, the person evaluated need not have the name Einstein. A name can contribute properties of the bearer, selected by the context. With no Einstein the interpretation concerns the absence of those properties.

examples.form: They were hoping to recruit [another Einstein].

3.definition: Selects a manifestation, product, or copy associated with the named entity.
3.details: The Paris of her youth identifies a period or version of Paris. A Rembrandt can refer to a painting. Some Beethoven can refer to music. A copy of a publication can be described by the title with a possessive determiner.

examples.note: Constructed example with count syntax and an artwork interpretation.

relatedConstructions.notes: The descriptive NP is built around a form otherwise used as a name.
A strong proper name independently supplies a definite referent without a determiner.
An introduction can establish which entity a form names. Secondary constructions can then use a standing name descriptively.

grounds.note: Documents name-bearer and resemblance uses and leaves the number of constructions open.
Distinguishes name bearers, resemblance, manifestations, products and copies.

projection.target: Numeral and plural marking can count bearers, and an indefinite NP can describe resemblance, including when the described person has a different name. Product uses independently admit count and non-count construals.
projection.evidence: FrameNet supplies name-bearer and resemblance uses of the same form family. CGEL documents those readings along with manifestations, products and copies. Their differing entailments motivate keeping the readings visible while leaving the number of constructions open.

curious.title: Names used like ordinary nouns
curious.summary: A name can be counted, compared with, or used to mean something connected to the named person or place.
curious.body: In There are two Kims on the committee, Kim is used to count people who share a name. In They were hoping to recruit another Einstein, the person wanted needn't be called Einstein; what's meant is someone with the relevant qualities of Einstein. A name can also pick out a version of something, a product or a copy: They bought a Rembrandt can mean they bought a painting, and some Beethoven can mean music. This dictionary keeps these readings visible without saying how many separate constructions they are, and marks the account as provisional.

examples.text: There are [two Kims] on the committee.
They were hoping to recruit [another Einstein].

curious.try: Can you think of a name that stands for a type of person, such as someone known for a quality? How would you say you wanted another one?

teacher.summary: Explains how names can behave like count nouns with number, determiners and modifiers.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a NP with a determiner and a nominal based on a proper name, optionally plural or modified. This dictionary distinguishes readings: counting or distinguishing bearers of the same name (two Kims, where a modifier can select one Kim), resemblance (another Einstein, where the person needn't have that name), and a manifestation, product or copy associated with the named entity (a Rembrandt, some Beethoven, the Paris of her youth). Numeral and plural marking can count bearers, and an indefinite NP can describe resemblance. Product uses admit count and non-count construals. This dictionary leaves open how many constructions there are. It's marked provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary describes these as proper names in descriptive NPs.

examples.text: There are [two Kims] on the committee.
They were hoping to recruit [another Einstein].

watch_for: A learner might expect another Einstein to mean a person called Einstein, when the person need not have that name.
A learner might think a Rembrandt refers to the painter.
A learner might think a name cannot take a determiner or a plural ending.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences using names in descriptive NPs into three groups (same name, resembles, product or copy) and justify their choices.

child.hook: What do you call it when two kids are both named Kim?
child.explain: A name can be counted. If two people are named Kim, we can say two Kims.

examples.text: There are [two Kims] on the committee.

child.play: Think of a name shared by two people you know. Count them aloud, then say a sentence about each one.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.watch_for no longer presents two Kims needing two bearers as a learner mistake (it requires two bearers of the name); removed the 'proper-to-common conversion' term (conversion implies a category change the entry does not claim); removed a Rembrandt from the child edition. Also fixed (unflagged): curious.body says a Rembrandt can mean a painting; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Proper Name in a Descriptive NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/proper-name-secondary-use-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Proposition Affirmation with Fronted so

1.definition: Confirms or acknowledges the proposition just put into play.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. Inversion instead adds Jo as another promiser.

relatedConstructions.notes: So I did confirms the proposition. So did Jo extends the predicate to another subject. Subject–auxiliary order distinguishes the two.

projection.target: The same subject normally resumes the prior assertion, with subject before auxiliary. Inverted so did I typically adds a parallel case instead.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: So I did
curious.summary: Starting a short reply with so, then the subject and a helping verb, confirms what someone just said.
curious.body: If someone says You did promise, a reply of So I did agrees with them: yes, that's true. The reply confirms the point just made. Changing the order changes the meaning. So did Jo doesn't confirm that you promised; it adds Jo as another person who promised. The same subject normally resumes the earlier statement when it comes before the helping verb. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Say You did promise, then reply So I did. Now reply So did Jo. How do the two replies differ?

teacher.summary: Shows how word order after so distinguishes confirming a statement from adding another person.
teacher.explain: Fronted so with a subject before the finite auxiliary (So I did) confirms or acknowledges the proposition just put into play. With subject-auxiliary inversion (So did Jo) the meaning changes: Jo is added as another subject who did the same thing. The same subject normally resumes the prior assertion, with subject before auxiliary, and inverted so did I typically adds a parallel case instead. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional. Make the order contrast the focus.
teacher.terms: The inverted order (so did Jo) is the pattern in 'so do I'; this dictionary treats the two orders as distinct constructions.

contrasts.note: Same subject; confirms the proposition.
Inversion adds Jo as another promiser.

watch_for: A learner might use So did I to confirm their own earlier action.
A learner might read So did Jo as agreeing that you promised.
teacher.activity: Pairs read a statement with did, such as You did promise, and take turns answering with So I did or So did another name. The partner says whether the reply confirms or adds someone.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Proposition Affirmation with Fronted so." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/proposition-affirmation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Pseudo-Cleft
pattern: Clause[Subject:NP[fused relative] + be + PredComp:XP[value]], or reversed alignment

entry.name: Pseudo-Cleft
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:NP[fused relative] + be + PredComp:XP[value]], or reversed alignment

1.definition: Specifies the value of a variable defined by a fused relative.
1.details: The fused relative in What I need is a long cool drink defines what is to be identified. The value can precede be in the reversed version. Clausal values are common, including a bare or to-infinitival when the relative has do. A copular clause that evaluates what they did as a disgrace is ascriptive and does not specify the action.

examples.form: [What I need is a long cool drink.]
examples.note: The drink supplies the value of what I need.

examples.form: [A long cool drink is what I need.]
[What you must do is apply for special leave.]
examples.note: Bare infinitival value. To is also possible here.

relatedConstructions.notes: The matrix clause is headed by a copular VP.
Both foreground a value. Their backgrounded relatives occupy different positions.
The variable is defined by a fused relative.

grounds.note: Lists multiple phrase and clause types in the post-be position.

projection.target: A do pseudo-cleft can take an infinitival value which the corresponding it-cleft generally excludes.
projection.evidence: CGEL compares the two clefts with matched clausal values and distinguishes specifying and ascriptive be. CASA catalogs the wh-cleft pattern.

curious.title: What I need is...
curious.summary: A sentence can start with a what clause, then a form of be, and finish with the thing being named.
curious.body: In What I need is a long cool drink, the first part sets up a gap: what is it that I need? The last part fills it in: a long cool drink. Putting the answer last gives it emphasis. The order can be flipped, as in A long cool drink is what I need. The answer can also be an action, as in What you must do is apply for special leave. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.

examples.text: [What I need is a long cool drink.]
[A long cool drink is what I need.]
[What you must do is apply for special leave.]

curious.try: Start with what I want is, and finish with the thing you want. Then flip it around.

teacher.summary: Covers sentences like What I need is a drink, where a what clause is paired with the value that completes it.
teacher.explain: A pseudo-cleft specifies the value of a variable defined by a fused relative. In What I need is a long cool drink, what I need defines what is to be identified, and the drink supplies the value. The value can precede be in the reversed version (A long cool drink is what I need). Clausal values are common, including a bare or to-infinitival when the relative has do (What you must do is apply for special leave; to is also possible). This dictionary says the do pseudo-cleft can take an infinitival value which the corresponding it-cleft generally excludes. It's marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a wh-cleft; the part beginning with what is a fused relative in this dictionary's terms.

examples.text: [What I need is a long cool drink.]
[A long cool drink is what I need.]
[What you must do is apply for special leave.]

contrasts.text: What they did was a disgrace.
contrasts.note: A copular clause that evaluates what they did, not one that specifies the action.

watch_for: A learner might treat What they did was a disgrace as a pseudo-cleft, when it evaluates the action instead of naming it.
A learner might leave out the be that links the two parts.
teacher.activity: Students turn plain sentences such as I need a long cool drink into pseudo-clefts and then into the reversed version, and say which part is the value.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Pseudo-Cleft." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/pseudo-cleft-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Quasi-count Plural Noun

1.definition: Denotes aggregates of discrete individuals with weakened individuation, yielding a mixed countability profile

constraints.description: Plural-only morphology with plural agreement; resists singular and a/an.
Individuation is weakened; tight count properties (low cardinals, distributives) are degraded.
Tight cardinality uses surface mainly in specialized registers.

relatedConstructions.notes: Many cattle has a lexically restricted plural count profile. Some rabbit uses a noun productively in non-count syntax to refer to material.

core.property: Plural-only morphology with loose count diagnostics

stabilisers.evidence: High-frequency quasi-count lexemes stabilize the profile.
Singulative reference is offloaded to functional alternatives (cow, officer).
Iterated transmission preserves the ordered dissociation pattern.

projection.target: Cattle admits many and plural agreement, while an individual count normally uses a classifier or counting expression such as three head of cattle. No claim about novel forms follows automatically from those facts.
projection.evidence: CGEL documents the restricted cardinal patterns and plural agreement of plural-only nouns.

perturbations: Loss of functional singulatives pushes toward full count or non-count profiles.

known_boundary_items: folks
people

coupling.mechanism: bidirectional inference between construal and count morphosyntax

curious.title: Plural words with no single form
curious.summary: Some nouns, such as cattle, are plural in form with no singular, and only partly behave like ordinary count nouns.
curious.body: Cattle works with many and takes plural verbs: many cattle. But it has no singular, and a cattle isn't something you say. These nouns refer to groups of separate individuals, yet they don't let us pick out one at a time in the usual way. To count individuals, English uses a counting expression such as three head of cattle, or a different word altogether, like cow. This dictionary marks the account as provisional, though it treats the pattern as stable.
curious.try: Try saying a cattle and then a cow. Which one lets you talk about a single animal? What would you say for several?

teacher.summary: Low priority for most classes: cattle is relatively infrequent (about 3,700th among word forms in the SUBTLEX-UK subtitle counts), so treat it if it comes up rather than teaching it. Explains plural-only nouns like cattle that take many but resist a, one and low numbers.
teacher.explain: Quasi-count plural nouns are plural-only, with plural agreement, and resist singular forms and a/an. They allow loose count diagnostics (many, few, high round numerals) but tight ones (a/an, low cardinals, distributives) are degraded. Individuals are counted with specialized frames such as three head of cattle, or by a different word (cow, officer). Tight cardinality uses surface mainly in specialized registers. This dictionary marks the account provisional and says no claim about novel forms follows automatically. Folks is a boundary item showing instability.
teacher.terms: Related to plural-only or collective nouns in traditional grammars; this dictionary calls these quasi-count nouns, with a mixed countability profile.

contrasts.note: Loose count property is fine.
Tight count property rejected.

watch_for: A learner might think three cattle is the standard way to count three animals, when this dictionary gives three head of cattle.
A learner might use a with cattle to refer to a single animal.
A learner might treat all plural-only nouns as having the same profile.
teacher.activity: If cattle comes up in a reading, students list plural-only nouns they know and test each with many, a and three, recording which tests fit.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.summary now opens by marking the entry low priority (cattle about 3,700th in SUBTLEX-UK); activity, which tests plural-only nouns students know, now starts from cattle coming up in a reading.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Quasi-count Plural Noun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/quasi-count-noun-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Quasi-Modal be to

1.definition: Presents a requirement, official arrangement, or projected event.

projection.target: The required or arranged reading occurs without a predicative NP or adjective. It can use preterite was/were for a past arrangement without asserting fulfilment.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Are to, for rules and arrangements
curious.summary: A form of be followed by to and a verb can express a requirement, an official arrangement or a planned event.
curious.body: In Staff are to report at eight, the words are to tell staff what's required or arranged. There's no ordinary adjective or noun after are; the to plus verb carries the meaning. The same pattern can use was or were for an arrangement made in the past, and that doesn't assert the arrangement was carried out. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of an instruction that might be posted at a workplace or school. Can you put it in the form people are to do something?

teacher.summary: Explains be plus to-infinitive for requirements, arrangements and projected events.
teacher.explain: A finite form of be followed by a to-infinitival can present a requirement, an official arrangement or a projected event: Staff are to report at eight. The required or arranged reading occurs without a predicative NP or adjective. It can use preterite was or were for a past arrangement without asserting fulfilment. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional and calls this a quasi-modal, a VP of finite be plus a to-infinitival.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a semi-modal or periphrastic modal; this dictionary calls it quasi-modal be to.
watch_for: A learner might read are to as plain be plus a preposition to.
A learner might think a past form such as was to means the event happened.
teacher.activity: Students rewrite a short list of rules as are to sentences, such as visitors are to sign in, and discuss who is giving the instruction.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Quasi-Modal be to." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/quasi-modal-be-to-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Question
pattern: Host:SyntacticExpression => Meaning:Question[set of logically possible answers]

entry.name: Question
entry.pattern: Host:SyntacticExpression => Meaning:Question[set of logically possible answers]

dimensions.form: No unique syntactic form: the semantic category applies to headed Clauses of more than one type, coordinations, and constructionally licensed non-clausal expressions
dimensions.meaning: A structured set of logically possible answers, closed or open according to the variables and alternatives presented
dimensions.function: Makes resolution of an informationally incomplete answer space relevant; inquiry is the prototype but not a condition of membership
dimensions.distribution: A semantic layer over syntactic hosts, including interrogative and declarative Clauses, multi-Clause coordinations, and reduced or non-headed question expressions

1.definition: A semantic category in which an expression defines a set of logically possible answers
1.details: Question is not a clause type and is not identified with the pragmatic act of making an inquiry. A question determines answerhood conditions: a closed question presents a delimited answer set, while an open question contains a variable whose possible values differentiate the answers. An answer supplies the relevant missing information; a conversational response need not do so. Questions can serve acknowledgement, wondering, examination, exposition, and indirect speech acts as well as information-seeking inquiry, and the same semantic category can be realized by syntactically different hosts (CGEL Ch. 10 §§4.1–4.3, pp. 865–72).

examples.note: Closed-interrogative Clause defining positive and negative answers
Open-interrogative Clause defining answers by values of the variable who
Declarative Clause carrying question meaning without becoming interrogative
Reduced syntactic host with question meaning; it is not thereby a Clause

constraints.description: Membership is determined by the answer set an expression defines, not by interrogative morphology, word order, punctuation, or any single clause type.
An answer must resolve the relevant alternative or assign a value to the relevant variable; other conversational responses can be appropriate without constituting answers.
Information-seeking inquiry is a prototypical use rather than the definition: acknowledgement, wondering, quiz, expository, rhetorical, and indirect-act uses remain possible.
When the host is a Clause, it independently satisfies (Subject +) Head:VP. A coordination or constructionally licensed fragment may host question meaning without being reclassified as a Clause.
Independent dimensions distinguish polar, alternative, and variable questions; information and direction questions; neutral and biased questions; and ordinary and echo questions.

projection.target: Recognizing Question meaning predicts a structured class of congruent answers, a principled distinction between answers and merely appropriate responses, informational incompleteness resolvable by an answer, and semantic contrasts of answer-space, bias, direction, and echo status that remain independent of the host's clause type
projection.evidence: Closed, open, declarative, coordinated, and reduced realizations differ formally but preserve answer-set organization; the same organization persists across inquiry, acknowledgement, wondering, examination, exposition, and indirect-act uses

grounds.note: Defines questions by answer sets, distinguishes answers from responses, and cross-classifies questions independently of clause type
The answer-set generalizations recur across closed, open, declarative, coordinated, and reduced hosts

known_boundary_items: Interrogative is a syntactic property of particular words, phrases, and Clauses; it is neither necessary nor by itself a definition of Question meaning.
Question punctuation is an orthographic cue and does not determine semantic membership by itself.
A reduced or non-headed question expression may have Question meaning without satisfying the VP-headed definition of Clause.

relatedConstructions.notes: Many questions have a Clause host, which remains independently defined as (Subject +) Head:VP
Closed interrogatives are the characteristic syntactic host of closed questions, but clause type and Question meaning are distinct
Open interrogatives characteristically host variable questions without defining the semantic category
Declarative Clauses can host Question meaning while retaining declarative clause type
A coordination of Clauses may jointly present one alternative question while remaining a non-headed coordination
Constructionally licensed non-headed expressions may carry Question meaning without becoming Clauses

grounds.note: Treats question at the semantic level as an answer-set category and distinguishes it from both clause type and pragmatic inquiry
Question is a semantic category applied to syntactic hosts; clausal hosts retain the strict (Subject +) Head:VP ontology

curious.title: What makes something a question
curious.summary: A question is defined by the set of possible answers it opens, not by its word order or question mark.
curious.body: Have you seen it? leaves two possible answers, yes or no. Who broke it? leaves open who did it. Which one? is a short phrase that does the same job, and You're leaving? shows that a statement can also act as a question. So what makes something a question is the set of answers it defines, not one particular grammar. This dictionary says a question isn't the same as an act of inquiry either: questions can also acknowledge, wonder, examine or explain. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Find a sentence that doesn't look like a question but would still get an answer if you said it to someone. What answer would it get?

teacher.summary: Frames question as a meaning category (a set of possible answers) that different sentence types can carry.
teacher.explain: Question is a semantic category: an expression defines a set of logically possible answers. It is not a clause type and is not the same as the act of inquiry. A closed question presents a delimited answer set (Have you seen it?), an open question contains a variable (Who broke it?), a declarative clause can carry question meaning (You're leaving?) and a reduced expression can too (Which one?, which isn't thereby a Clause). An answer supplies the missing information; a conversational response needn't. This dictionary says punctuation and word order don't fix membership, and it marks the account provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary separates the clause types (closed and open interrogative) from the semantic category Question.
watch_for: A learner might think a question must start with an auxiliary or a question word.
A learner might think a question mark makes something a question.
A learner might treat any reply as an answer, when an answer resolves the open alternatives.
teacher.activity: Give students four cards, each carrying a different question form. They list the possible answers each defines and sort replies into answers and merely appropriate responses.

child.hook: How do you know something is a question?
child.explain: A question comes with a set of possible answers. Have you seen it? can be answered with yes or no. Who broke it? can be answered by saying who.
child.play: Ask a friend a question that needs a yes or no. Then ask one that starts with who. Which kind was easier to answer?

checked.note: Fixed: child explain no longer defines a question as asking for an answer or says Who broke it? needs a name (this dictionary lists rhetorical and other uses, and an answer need only identify who); curious body says Who broke it? leaves open who did it; teacher terms drops the yes/no and wh-question equations, which this dictionary keeps apart from the clause types. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' wording.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Question." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/question-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Quotative Inversion
pattern: quoted utterance + V[speech] + non-pronominal or otherwise licensed Subject

entry.name: Quotative Inversion
entry.pattern: quoted utterance + V[speech] + non-pronominal or otherwise licensed Subject

1.definition: Places a reporting verb before its subject after or within direct speech.

projection.target: Full NP subjects readily follow the reporting verb. Plain personal pronouns usually precede it in contemporary neutral prose, though literary inverted variants occur.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Said the clerk
curious.summary: After a quotation, the verb of speaking can come before the speaker.
curious.body: In “I can explain,” said the clerk, the verb said comes first and the clerk, who is speaking, follows. It reports the words just quoted, and it can come after or within the quotation. This dictionary says full noun phrases such as the clerk readily follow the verb. Plain personal pronouns usually come first in neutral modern prose, though literary variants with the verb first occur. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Look at some dialogue in a book you're reading. Find a quotation followed by said and a name or a noun. Does the verb come first?

teacher.summary: Explains why a reporting verb can come before its subject after direct speech.
teacher.explain: In quotative inversion the reporting verb comes before its subject after or within direct speech: “I can explain,” said the clerk. Full NP subjects readily follow the verb. Plain personal pronouns usually precede it in contemporary neutral prose, though literary inverted variants occur. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional and notes the link with the subject-dependent inversion family.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called 'speech-verb inversion'; this dictionary calls it quotative inversion.

contrasts.note: The same report with the subject before the verb.

watch_for: A learner might think said the clerk is a question because the verb comes first.
A learner might use the inverted order with a plain pronoun in everyday writing.
teacher.activity: Students take dialogue from a story and rewrite each quotation tag with the verb first and then with the subject first, comparing how each reads.

child.hook: Why does the speaker come second in a story?
child.explain: In stories, a person's words can be followed by a speaking word and then the speaker. In “I can explain,” said the clerk, the word said comes before the clerk.
child.play: Open a story and find some speech. Does the speaker come before or after the speaking word? Rewrite one to flip the order.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Quotative Inversion." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/quotative-inversion-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Iterative re- on a Verb

1.definition: Forms a verb describing another performance of the relevant action.

projection.target: The normal reading presupposes an earlier check. A word that merely starts with the same letters, such as reject, need not support an again analysis.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Re- meaning do it again
curious.summary: Putting re- on the front of some verbs makes a new verb meaning to do the action again.
curious.body: In Please recheck the numbers, recheck means to check them another time. The normal reading takes it for granted that there was an earlier check. A word that only starts with the same letters, such as reject, doesn't necessarily mean again in the same way. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Put re- on a verb like read or write. What does the new word mean, and what has to have happened first?

teacher.summary: Shows how re- builds verbs meaning to perform an action again.
teacher.explain: The prefix re- plus a suitable verbal base forms a verb describing another performance of the relevant action: Please recheck the numbers. The normal reading presupposes an earlier check. A word that merely starts with the same letters, such as reject, need not support an again analysis, so students shouldn't segment every re- word. This dictionary marks the account provisional and is built on one constructed example.
teacher.terms: Re- is traditionally a prefix; this dictionary calls the pattern iterative re- on a verb.

examples.text: After the flood, they had to [rebuild] the bridge.

watch_for: A learner might split reject into re- plus ject and look for an again meaning.
A learner might use recheck when there was no earlier check.
teacher.activity: Students list re- verbs they know and sort them into again meanings and words where re- only appears at the start, then check each against a dictionary.

child.hook: What does the re- at the start of recheck do?
child.explain: Re- can mean again. To recheck is to check again. Something has to be checked first.
child.play: Add re- to verbs like read, write or play. Say what each new word means. Then use it in a sentence.

checked.note: Frequency pass: added the constructed teacher example After the flood, they had to rebuild the bridge (rebuild about 6,000th in SUBTLEX-UK, about 3,500th counting its other forms) beside the entry's recheck (about 63,100th); activity already has students list re- verbs they know, so left as is.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Iterative re- on a Verb." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/re-iterative-prefix-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Reaction Object

1.definition: Expresses a reaction through the action named by the verb.
1.details: In smiled her thanks, the smile is the means of expressing thanks. The NP can denote an attitude, communicative response, or emotion. The verb need not ordinarily take an object of this type. The sources distinguish the pattern from a cognate object naming the event itself and report restrictions on passive versions.

examples.note: Published example. The NP denotes the attitude expressed by the nod.
COCA example of a bare response NP.

relatedConstructions.notes: The verb and reaction expression form a VP.
A cognate NP characterizes the action itself.
Smiled her sweetest grades the smile rather than identifying a reaction expressed by it.

grounds.note: Documents lexical diversity and possible sources of the reaction object.
Reports reaction examples and passive diagnostics.

projection.target: An action verb can combine with an NP describing what the action expresses, even when its ordinary intransitive use has no such NP.
projection.evidence: Bouso documents varied reaction nouns. Bouso, Hundt and Van Driessche compare reaction, cognate and superlative patterns and their distinct transitivity profiles.

curious.title: Nodding satisfaction
curious.summary: An action verb can take a noun naming the reaction it expresses.
curious.body: In She nodded satisfaction, the nod is how the satisfaction is shown. In He grunted assent, the grunt expresses agreement. The noun can name an attitude, a communicative response or an emotion. The verb needn't ordinarily take an object of this kind. In smiled her thanks, the smile is the means of expressing thanks. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of a gesture or sound, such as a shrug or a sigh. What reaction could you say it expressed?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, action verbs followed by a noun naming the reaction they express.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a VP with an expression or action verb and an NP naming the reaction expressed: She nodded satisfaction. The NP can denote an attitude, communicative response or emotion, and the verb need not ordinarily take an object of this type. In smiled her thanks, the smile is the means of expressing thanks. This dictionary distinguishes this from a cognate object, which names the event itself, and reports restrictions on passive versions. It is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: A cognate object names the event itself; this dictionary keeps the reaction object separate from it.
watch_for: A learner might think the noun names the action itself rather than the reaction expressed.
A learner might assume the verb can't take an object because it doesn't ordinarily take one.
teacher.activity: Write She smiled her thanks on the board. Students rephrase it as She smiled to express her thanks, then do the same for She nodded satisfaction, and say what each gesture expressed.

checked.note: Frequency pass: added the constructed teacher example She smiled her thanks (from the entry's details; smile and thanks are both within the top 2,500 word forms of SUBTLEX-UK); teacher.activity no longer has students combine nod, grunt and sigh with reaction nouns (grunt about 21,500th, assent about 29,800th) and now rephrases smiled her thanks and the entry's nodded satisfaction; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Reaction Object." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/reaction-object-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Recipient Passive with a Retained Object
pattern: Clause[Subject:recipient NP + passive be + V-en + retained theme NP]

entry.name: Recipient Passive with a Retained Object
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:recipient NP + passive be + V-en + retained theme NP]

1.definition: Makes the recipient the passive subject while keeping the theme in object position.

examples.form: [A replacement key was sent to Lee].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. Theme subject with an oblique recipient.

relatedConstructions.notes: The recipient corresponds to the indirect object of the active frame.

projection.target: The replacement key remains an ordinary NP complement of sent. In A replacement key was sent to Lee, the theme instead controls agreement and the recipient is an oblique.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Being sent something
curious.summary: A passive sentence can make the person who receives something the subject while the thing received stays after the verb.
curious.body: In Lee was sent a replacement key, Lee is the recipient and the subject of the sentence. The replacement key still sits after the verb, as an ordinary part of it. Compare A replacement key was sent to Lee, where the key is the subject and Lee comes in a phrase with to. The two sentences describe the same sending but arrange the people and things differently. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.

examples.text: [A replacement key was sent to Lee].

curious.try: Turn Someone sent Lee a key into a sentence beginning with Lee, and then into one beginning with the key. How do the endings differ?

teacher.summary: Connects the passive of double-object verbs to the two ways of choosing the subject.
teacher.explain: The recipient becomes the passive subject while the theme stays in object position: Lee was sent a replacement key. The recipient corresponds to the indirect object of the active frame. The replacement key remains an ordinary NP complement of sent. In A replacement key was sent to Lee, the theme controls agreement and the recipient is an oblique. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional, and its examples are constructed.
teacher.terms: The remaining NP is sometimes called a retained object; this dictionary uses that term. See also the double-object (ditransitive) pattern.

contrasts.text: Lee was sent a replacement key.
contrasts.note: Recipient as subject; the theme is a retained object.

contrasts.text: A replacement key was sent to Lee.
contrasts.note: Theme as subject; recipient in a to-phrase.

watch_for: A learner might think the replacement key must be the subject because it is the thing sent.
A learner might look for a missing object after sent in the first sentence.
