teacher.activity: Students start from Someone sent Lee a replacement key and write both passives, underlining the subject in each and saying what the other participant becomes.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body no longer says Lee received the key (the entry names Lee the recipient of the sending) and now says 'sending' rather than 'giving'; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Recipient Passive with a Retained Object." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/recipient-passive-retained-object-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Reciprocal Predicative NP with a with-Phrase
pattern: PredComp:NP[N[pl] + PP[with + NP]], with the other participant supplied by the predicand

entry.name: Reciprocal Predicative NP with a with-Phrase
entry.pattern: PredComp:NP[N[pl] + PP[with + NP]], with the other participant supplied by the predicand

1.definition: Ascribes a reciprocal relation whose participants are expressed separately.
1.details: With friends, the predicand supplies one side of the relationship and the with-phrase supplies the other. CGEL observes that the predicative noun can be plural even with a singular subject. Lee-Goldman and Petruck report that good friends with the president can describe the quality of the relationship, whereas powerful friends with the president fares poorly on the reading where powerful describes the people. Extension of that modifier contrast to other relation nouns remains open.

examples.note: The subject is singular and the predicative noun is plural.

examples.form: They are [good friends with the president].
examples.note: Published judgment. Good can describe the friendship.

relatedConstructions.notes: The plural noun heads a predicative NP in CGEL's analysis.

grounds.note: Analyzes the reciprocal relation and compares modifiers of friends with and friends of.

projection.target: For friends with, the split predication permits a singular subject and licenses modifiers that assess the relationship.
projection.evidence: CGEL gives the singular-subject case. FrameNet's published modifier comparison holds the plural subject fixed.

curious.title: Friends with someone
curious.summary: A plural noun like friends plus with can describe a two-way relationship, even when the sentence is about one person.
curious.body: In I'm no longer friends with him, the subject I is one person, yet the noun is plural. That's because a friendship involves two sides: I supply one and with him supplies the other. A modifier such as good can then describe the relationship itself: They are good friends with the president. This dictionary notes that on the reading where an adjective like powerful describes the people, this form fares poorly. Whether other relationship nouns work this way is left open. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.

examples.text: They are [good friends with the president].

curious.try: Think of other relationship words, like partners or neighbours. Do they fit with someone in the same way?

teacher.summary: Explains a plural predicative noun with a with-phrase for reciprocal relationships, including with a singular subject.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a predicative NP with a plural noun and a with-phrase, where the predicand supplies one side of the relationship and the with-phrase the other. The predicative noun can be plural even with a singular subject (I'm no longer friends with him). A modifier can assess the relationship: good in good friends with the president can describe the friendship, whereas powerful friends with the president fares poorly on the reading where powerful describes the people. Extension to other relation nouns remains open. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: The plural noun heads a predicative NP in this dictionary's analysis.

examples.text: They are [good friends with the president].

watch_for: A learner might make friend singular after a singular subject.
A learner might read good as describing the people rather than the relationship.
teacher.activity: Students write pairs such as Mia is friends with Tom, underline the two sides of the relationship, and say which part supplies each side.

child.hook: Why do we say friends when it's just one of you?
child.explain: A friendship has two sides. One side is the person the sentence is about. The other side comes after with.
child.play: Say who you're friends with using friends with and a name. Then try it with someone else.

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer says a friendship has two people or that only one side is said (each side can be more than one person, as in They are good friends with the president); cut the term 'reciprocal complement' (not in the entry); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Reciprocal Predicative NP with a with-Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/reciprocal-noun-with-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Recurrent Progressive with always

1.definition: Presents a habit as a recurring series of occurrences, often with a speaker evaluation.

projection.target: The frame can describe repeated gate-leaving even if the gate is closed now. Irritation suits this example but an evaluatively positive action can support praise in the same frame.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: You're always doing that
curious.summary: Be plus always plus an -ing verb describes a habit as a series of repeated occurrences, often with the speaker's opinion in it.
curious.body: In You're always leaving the gate open, the speaker is talking about a repeating pattern, a series of times the gate was left open. The gate doesn't have to be open right now. The speaker's feelings often come through, and irritation suits this example. But the same frame can carry praise when the action is a good one. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Say something you notice someone doing again and again, using are or is plus always and an -ing verb. Does it sound like a complaint or praise?

teacher.summary: Explains be plus always plus -ing for habits seen as recurring events, often with an evaluation.
teacher.explain: The frame is be plus always plus a V-ing form. It presents a habit as a recurring series of occurrences, often with a speaker evaluation: You're always leaving the gate open. The frame can describe repeated gate-leaving even if the gate is closed now. Irritation suits this example, but an evaluatively positive action can support praise in the same frame. This pattern is a specialization of the progressive. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional and the example is constructed.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called the 'emphatic' or 'habitual' use of the progressive; this dictionary calls it the recurrent progressive with always.

contrasts.note: A positive action in the same frame, which can express praise.

watch_for: A learner might read the sentence as describing something happening right now.
A learner might assume the frame can only express a complaint.
teacher.activity: Students make pairs of sentences with be plus always plus -ing, one that could be said with irritation and one with praise, and read them aloud with matching tone.

child.hook: When do people say you're always doing something?
child.explain: You're always leaving the gate open means it keeps happening, again and again. It might be something annoying. It might be something good.
child.play: Think of something a friend or family member does again and again. Say it with are or is plus always and an -ing word.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Recurrent Progressive with always." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/recurrent-progressive-always-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Reflexive Beneficiary in a Double-Object VP
pattern: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + reflexive indirect objectᵢ + direct object NP]

entry.name: Reflexive Beneficiary in a Double-Object VP
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + reflexive indirect objectᵢ + direct object NP]

1.definition: Presents the subject’s action as securing goods or a resource for the subject.

relatedConstructions.notes: Its two postverbal NPs are indirect and direct object.
Here the reflexive is indirect rather than direct object.

projection.target: Jo is understood as the intended beneficiary and room is the acquired resource. In found herself in a quieter room, herself is instead the direct object and the PP locates Jo.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Finding yourself a room
curious.summary: A sentence can show someone securing something for themselves by using a reflexive word, like herself, right after the verb.
curious.body: In Jo found herself a quieter room, Jo is both the finder and the person who benefits. The word herself comes right after found, and the room follows. The sentence presents Jo's action as securing a resource for Jo. Compare Jo found herself in a quieter room, where herself is the direct object and the phrase in a quieter room says where Jo was. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Take a sentence such as Jo found a quieter room. Can you add herself to show that the room was for Jo?

teacher.summary: Explains a reflexive indirect object that shows the subject benefiting from the action.
teacher.explain: In this frame a reflexive indirect object follows the verb, with a direct object after it: Jo found herself a quieter room. Jo is understood as the intended beneficiary and room is the acquired resource. The two postverbal NPs are the indirect and the direct object. In Jo found herself in a quieter room, by contrast, herself is the direct object and the PP locates Jo. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: The Birmingham English Constructicon, which this dictionary cites, has a related record titled Getting V oneself N. This dictionary describes the pattern as a reflexive beneficiary in a double-object VP.

contrasts.text: Jo found herself in a quieter room.
contrasts.note: Here herself is the direct object and the PP says where Jo is.

watch_for: A learner might treat herself as the direct object in both sentences.
A learner might read a quieter room as describing Jo.
teacher.activity: Students compare Jo found herself a quieter room and Jo found herself in a quieter room, and mark the role of herself in each (indirect object or direct object).

checked.note: Fixed: in Jo found herself in a quieter room, herself is now described as the direct object (with a phrase locating Jo) rather than 'the thing found'; matching change in the teacher activity; replaced the unsupported 'sometimes called' term with the entry's cited constructicon record. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Reflexive Beneficiary in a Double-Object VP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/reflexive-benefactive-ditransitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: State Goal with a Construction-Licensed Reflexive
pattern: VP[V + reflexive direct object + PP denoting a resulting state]

entry.name: State Goal with a Construction-Licensed Reflexive
entry.pattern: VP[V + reflexive direct object + PP denoting a resulting state]

1.definition: Extends a goal expression to a state caused by an activity whose verbal head need not otherwise license the reflexive object.

relatedConstructions.notes: A state is construed as a goal.
CGEL distinguishes these PPs from adjective and noun phrase predicatives.

grounds.locator: Chs. 7–8, caused motion and resultative constructions

projection.target: To sleep describes the state reached, not the destination of an actual motion. Omitting the PP removes the interpretation that licenses the reflexive object after cry.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Crying yourself to sleep
curious.summary: A verb can take a reflexive word and a phrase naming the state that results, even if the verb wouldn't normally take that word.
curious.body: In The child cried herself to sleep, the crying caused a result: the child ended up asleep. The word herself follows cried, and to sleep names the state reached. The pattern itself, not the verb cry, makes room for that word. The phrase to sleep describes a state reached, not a place travelled to. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of an activity that could tire someone into a state. Can you say it with the person, herself or himself, and a to phrase?

teacher.summary: Explains the reflexive-plus-PP frame where an activity leads to a resulting state.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a VP with a verb, a reflexive direct object and a PP denoting a resulting state: The child cried herself to sleep. It extends a goal expression to a state caused by an activity, and the verb need not otherwise license the reflexive object. To sleep describes the state reached, not the destination of an actual motion. Omitting the PP removes the interpretation that licenses the reflexive object after cry. This dictionary notes that CGEL distinguishes these PPs from adjective and noun phrase predicatives. It's marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Often grouped with resultative constructions; this dictionary treats it as a specialization of caused motion, with a state construed as a goal.
watch_for: A learner might read to sleep as movement to a place.
A learner might assume cry is an ordinary verb that takes an object.
teacher.activity: Students list activities (cry, sing, run) and complete each as a sentence with a reflexive and a state to phrase, then discuss which describe a state reached.

child.hook: What happened if someone cried herself to sleep?
child.explain: She cried, and then she fell asleep. The crying caused the sleep. The words to sleep tell you the state she ended up in.
child.play: Pick an activity and a result, like singing and sleep. Put them in a sentence with herself or himself. Say what state the person ends up in.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "State Goal with a Construction-Licensed Reflexive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/reflexive-state-goal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Supplementary which with a Clausal Anchor
pattern: Clause or larger discourse unit + supplement with relative which

entry.name: Supplementary which with a Clausal Anchor
entry.pattern: Clause or larger discourse unit + supplement with relative which

1.definition: Refers back to a situation or proposition conveyed by an anchor.

examples.form: The train had already left, [which was unfortunate].

projection.target: Which can refer to the departure situation as a whole. Number from an incidental NP inside the anchor does not determine the reference of which.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Which pointing back at a whole situation
curious.summary: A which can follow a statement and refer back to the whole situation it describes, not to a single thing in it.
curious.body: In The train had already left, which was unfortunate, the word which doesn't point at the train. It points at the whole situation: the fact that the train had already left. That's what was unfortunate. The pattern is a comment tacked onto the end of a statement. It's a special case of a larger family of add-on remarks that begin with which. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, so treat the details as a working proposal.

examples.text: The train had already left, [which was unfortunate].
The shop was closed, [which surprised us].

curious.try: Add a which remark to the end of a sentence you just said. What exactly is the which referring to?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why which can refer to a whole preceding statement, not just a noun.
teacher.explain: A supplementary relative clause beginning with which can take as its anchor a clause (or a longer stretch of discourse), not only a noun phrase. In The train had already left, which was unfortunate, which refers to the departure situation as a whole. Number on a noun phrase inside the anchor, such as the singular noun train, doesn't determine what which refers to. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the ordinary supplementary relative, and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a sentential relative. In this dictionary: supplementary relative with a clausal anchor.

examples.text: The train had already left, [which was unfortunate].
The shop was closed, [which surprised us].

watch_for: A learner might take which to refer only to the nearest noun, such as the train, when it refers to the whole situation.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a short statement on a card. Each student adds a which comment, then partners say aloud what which stands for. Collect a few and discuss which ones refer to the whole situation.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Supplementary which with a Clausal Anchor." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/relative-clausal-which-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Relative Use of Indeterminates

dimensions.form: Restricted subset of the indeterminate series; what and how join only in fused relatives
dimensions.meaning: The open variable is bound by the head nominal (integrated) or supplies it (fused)
dimensions.function: Relativization; links the variable to a discourse referent
dimensions.distribution: Integrated and supplementary relatives; fused relatives for what, how, and the -ever series

1.definition: The indeterminate's variable is identified with the relativized element
1.details: Membership differs from the interrogative packaging: what and how are excluded from integrated relatives (*the thing what he said in standard English); why is limited (the reason why). Relative that is a subordinator in CGEL, not a member of this series. Fused relatives (what she saw; whatever you choose) supply their own head; on the deitality inventory, ignorance-reading fused relatives pattern deitally while free-choice readings are mixed.

constraints.description: Integrated-relative membership excludes what and how; fused relatives have their own syntax and may deserve a separate entry as coverage grows.

relatedConstructions.notes: Ignorance-reading fused relatives are deital; free-choice readings mixed (Reynolds, deitality inventory)

projection.target: Whose in the writer whose essay won links the possessor to writer. The whole phrase whose essay occupies subject position of won. A relative may front a larger phrase, unlike treating the relativizing form alone as the entire dependent.
projection.evidence: CGEL analyzes percolation in relative phrases and compares fused, integrated, and interrogative distributions.

curious.title: Question words that link a description to a noun
curious.summary: Words like who, which and where can tie a description to the noun it describes.
curious.body: In the woman who called, the word who links the description called to the woman. The same family of words, which also asks questions, does this job: who, whom, whose, which, where, when and why. Not all of them fit every slot. Why, for instance, is limited: the reason why she left works. Related words, such as whatever, work in a different way. In I'll take whatever you're offering, the whole phrase whatever you're offering names the thing taken, with no separate noun before it. The details of this analysis are marked provisional in this dictionary.
curious.try: Finish the phrase the person who ... in three different ways. Then try the place where ... and the time when ...

teacher.summary: Helps explain how question words work as relative words, and which ones are excluded from ordinary relatives.
teacher.explain: A restricted subset of the question-word series (who, whom, whose, which, where, when, why) works as relative words, with the open variable bound by the head noun (integrated relatives). Fused relatives, which supply their own head, use what, how and the -ever series (what she saw, whatever you choose). Membership differs from the question use: what and how are excluded from integrated relatives, and why is limited (as in the reason why). Following CGEL, relative that isn't treated as part of this series. A relative can also front a larger phrase, as in the writer whose essay won. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: In these relative uses, who, whom, whose and which are sometimes called relative pronouns, and where, when and why relative adverbs. In this dictionary they are the relative use of the indeterminate series. Fused relatives are sometimes called nominal or free relatives.

contrasts.note: Excluded in standard English, according to this dictionary.

watch_for: A learner might carry the question uses of what and how over into integrated relatives.
A learner might treat that in the woman that called as the same kind of word as who.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body no longer says the relative word builds a noun phrase by itself or stands in for the thing offered (in the fused relative the whole expression supplies the head); teacher.explain no longer says why is limited to the reason why, only that it is limited, with that as the example. Second round: fixed teacher.explain, which assigned fused relatives to the seven listed words; it now ties those words to integrated relatives and what, how and the -ever series to fused relatives, as this dictionary does. Teacher.terms now applies the traditional labels to the relative uses only. Also fixed (unflagged): curious.body said whatever was one of the listed words, and said only some of them fit every slot; it now calls whatever a related word and says not all of them fit every slot.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Relative Use of Indeterminates." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/relative-word-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Repeated Bare Noun with a Preposition
pattern: Nᵢ + P + Nᵢ, with bare noun forms and a choice of preposition tied to the reading

entry.name: Repeated Bare Noun with a Preposition
entry.pattern: Nᵢ + P + Nᵢ, with bare noun forms and a choice of preposition tied to the reading

1.definition: Presents successive instances over an interval.
1.details: After presents a succession of distinct instances of one kind. CGEL also gives upon in mile upon mile. Nominal uses such as flight after flight of stairs coexist with adjunct uses. The construction's interpretation and the question of what heads each subtype can be evaluated separately.

examples.note: An NP use discussed by CGEL in the chapter on prepositions.

2.definition: Presents a process in successive units with by.
2.details: The repeated noun supplies the units by which an event proceeds. Which prepositions can express a particular reading is a property of the subtype. This entry records the productive succession patterns.

examples.note: The process advances by successive mouthfuls.

examples.form: We checked the total [invoice by invoice].
examples.note: Constructed test of the stepwise reading with a different noun.

relatedConstructions.notes: From N to N can relate two different nouns that restrict the endpoints.

grounds.note: Documents distinct readings by preposition and distinct nominal and adjunct distributions.

projection.target: The preposition and the matched noun slots together distinguish iteration over instances from a description of how an event proceeds.
projection.evidence: CGEL's matched forms and distributional contrasts. Jackendoff documents productive subtypes and lexical exceptions.

curious.title: The same noun twice with a word between
curious.summary: Repeating a noun around a small word, as in day after day, shows a series of separate instances or a job done in stages.
curious.body: Say a noun, put after in the middle, say the noun again, and you get a long stretch made of one thing following another: day after day, flight after flight of stairs. The little word matters. With by the sense changes to a task done in steps, as in mouthful by mouthful. The pattern lets a phrase work in more than one role. Flight after flight of stairs acts like a noun phrase, while others work as add-ons to a sentence. Which little word fits depends on which of the two meanings you want. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: We checked the total [invoice by invoice].

curious.try: Pick a noun, say it twice with after between, and put it in a sentence. Then try by in the middle. Does the picture change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain N after N (a succession of instances) and N by N (a process in stages).
teacher.explain: The pattern repeats a bare noun around a preposition. With after, it presents a succession of distinct instances of one kind (day after day); CGEL also gives upon in mile upon mile. With by, the repeated noun supplies the units by which an event proceeds (mouthful by mouthful). Which preposition can express a given reading is a property of the subtype, so teach the pairings as patterns. Some uses are noun phrases (flight after flight of stairs) and others are adjuncts. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: We checked the total [invoice by invoice].

contrasts.note: A succession of instances.

contrasts.text: We checked the total invoice by invoice.
contrasts.note: The process advances in stages, one invoice at a time.

watch_for: A learner might use after where the by reading (a process in stages) is wanted.
A learner might repeat the noun in the plural, when the pattern as described here uses a bare noun form.
teacher.activity: Write nouns (page, step, drop, hour) on cards. Pairs make one N after N phrase and one N by N phrase with each noun in a sentence, then explain how the two sentences differ.

child.hook: What do we call it when one day follows another again and again?
child.explain: Say a word twice with after in the middle. Day after day means day, then another day, and another. With by it means doing something one piece at a time.

examples.text: She ate her dinner [mouthful by mouthful].

child.play: Pick a noun, like step or page. Make up a sentence with it twice around after. Then try it around by and see how the meaning changes.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Repeated Bare Noun with a Preposition." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/repeated-noun-preposition-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Double-Object Obligation with owe

1.definition: Presents a person as entitled to something that remains outstanding.

relatedConstructions.notes: An apology can be owed to someone without ever being delivered.

projection.target: Lee is the person to whom the apology is owed. The construction can be true when the apology has not been offered and describes an obligation rather than an intended gift.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Owing someone something
curious.summary: With owe, the person you owe comes first and the thing owed comes second, and the thing may not yet have been given.
curious.body: In I owe Lee an apology, Lee is the person who is entitled to the apology, and the apology is still outstanding. The verb owe is followed by two noun phrases in a row: first the person, then the thing. This is a version of the two-object pattern found with verbs like send and give. But owing isn't giving. The sentence can be true even if the apology hasn't been offered, because it describes an obligation, not a gift on its way. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of something you owe a friend. Say it with the friend's name first, then the thing owed.

teacher.summary: Helps explain owe with two objects and how an obligation differs from a transfer.
teacher.explain: Owe takes an indirect object (the creditor, or entitled participant) followed by a direct object (the outstanding thing): I owe Lee an apology. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the ditransitive VP. The meaning is an obligation, not an intended gift: Lee is the person to whom the apology is owed, and the sentence can be true when the apology has not been offered. Contrast this with verbs of giving, where the pattern suggests a transfer.
teacher.terms: Indirect object and direct object are the usual terms. In this dictionary, the pattern is a double-object construction.

contrasts.note: Obligation; the apology is outstanding.
A transfer, which the sentence presents as completed.

watch_for: A learner might read owe Lee an apology as saying the apology has already been delivered.
teacher.activity: Students write three things they owe someone (a call, a thank-you, a book) using the double-object pattern. Partners say whether each thing has been handed over yet and how they can tell.

child.hook: If you owe a friend a game, has the friend got it yet?
child.explain: Owe is followed by the person and then the thing. I owe Lee an apology means Lee should get an apology. It doesn't mean Lee has it yet.
child.play: Say what you owe someone, with the name first. Then ask a friend, "Has it happened yet?"

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Double-Object Obligation with owe." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/response-obligation-ditransitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Integrated Appositive Name
pattern: Nom[descriptive noun + proper-name expression identifying the referent]

entry.name: Integrated Appositive Name
entry.pattern: Nom[descriptive noun + proper-name expression identifying the referent]

1.definition: Identifies the bearer of a nominal description by appending a name without a supplementary break.

projection.target: Both parts concern the same river. A name replacement changes the referent identified. An ordinary modifier like river water gives no comparable identification.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A name added right after a description
curious.summary: A name can follow a descriptive noun with no pause, so the two together pick out one particular thing.
curious.body: In The river Wye flooded, river describes the thing and Wye names it. There's no comma or break between them, so the two sit together as one unit. Both parts are about the same river. Swapping the name changes which river you mean. That's what makes this different from an ordinary describing word: river water, for example, doesn't name the particular river in the same way. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of a description plus a name, such as a kind of place followed by its name. Does the name still pick out one particular place?

teacher.summary: Helps explain a name attached to a descriptive noun without a supplementary break.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a Nom made of a descriptive noun plus a proper-name expression that identifies the referent: the river Wye. Because there's no supplementary break, the name is integrated into the phrase. Both parts concern the same river, and replacing the name changes the referent identified. An ordinary modifier, such as river in river water, gives no comparable identification. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the Nom, and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar sometimes calls this restrictive apposition. In this dictionary: integrated appositive name.

contrasts.note: The name identifies which river.
River is an ordinary modifier of water and names no particular river.

watch_for: A learner might treat Wye in the river Wye as an ordinary describing word, like river in river water.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Integrated Appositive Name." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/restrictive-appositive-name-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Scalar Endpoint Adjective in a Resultative
pattern: resultative VP with an adjectival result construed as a reachable state

entry.name: Scalar Endpoint Adjective in a Resultative
entry.pattern: resultative VP with an adjectival result construed as a reachable state

1.definition: Presents the result as an attained point or region on a scale.

grounds.locator: discussion of result predicates and endpoint construal

projection.target: On the completed-event reading, the rail reaches contextual smoothness. Replacing smooth with a property that does not readily supply an attainable endpoint can lower acceptability even when the verb and object are unchanged.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Doing something until it reaches a state
curious.summary: A describing word after the object can show the point on a scale that the action brought something to.
curious.body: In They polished the railing smooth, the word smooth tells you where the polishing ended up. The railing ended up smooth, and the sentence reports that it got there. The describing word works like a point on a scale, such as how smooth something is. According to this dictionary, swapping smooth for a quality that doesn't readily supply an endpoint can make the sentence less acceptable, even when the verb and object stay the same. The analysis is marked provisional.
curious.try: Think of something you can do to an object until it's clean, flat, dry or smooth. Say it as one sentence with the describing word last.

teacher.summary: Helps explain resultatives whose adjective names an attainable endpoint on a scale.
teacher.explain: In a resultative VP like polished the railing smooth, the adjective gives the result as an attained point or region on a scale. On the completed-event reading, the rail reaches contextual smoothness. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the object resultative, and notes that replacing smooth with a property that doesn't readily supply an attainable endpoint can lower acceptability, even with the same verb and object. Present the adjective as the state the action brings about.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar sometimes speaks of a resultative predicate or result phrase. In this dictionary: scalar endpoint adjective in a resultative.

contrasts.note: No result is stated; compare with polished the railing smooth.

watch_for: A learner might read smooth in polished the railing smooth as describing how the polishing was done, when it names the state reached.
teacher.activity: Give students verb and object pairs (wipe the table, paint the fence, press the shirt). They add an adjective that names the state reached, then compare which adjectives name a clear endpoint.

child.hook: What do you call a table after you wipe it until it's clean?
child.explain: Some sentences end with a word that tells how things turned out. They polished the railing smooth. After the polishing, the railing was smooth.
child.play: Pick something to do, like wipe, wash or paint. Say what you did and add a word for how it ended up.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the railing started out rough or dull (the entry does not specify an initial state).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Scalar Endpoint Adjective in a Resultative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/resultative-scalar-state-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Right Argument-Cluster Coordination

1.definition: Coordinates corresponding postverbal bundles that need not form ordinary independent phrases.

examples.form: I took [Jo to the station and Lee home].

projection.target: Each person pairs with a separate goal under one overt verb. Lee home is the object and goal sequence, and is not an ordinary nominal constituent.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Joining pairs of things after one verb
curious.summary: One verb can serve two pairs of things joined by and, even though each pair isn't an ordinary phrase.
curious.body: In I took Jo to the station and Lee home, the verb took appears once but works for two jobs. Jo goes with the station, and Lee goes with home. Each person pairs with a separate destination. What's joined by and isn't an ordinary phrase: Jo to the station and Lee home are bundles of two things that follow the verb. Lee home, for example, is a person plus a destination. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: I took [Jo to the station and Lee home].
She gave [Ann a book and Bo a pen].

curious.try: Say a sentence with two people each going to a different place or getting a different thing, with only one verb.

teacher.summary: Helps explain coordination of postverbal bundles under a single verb.
teacher.explain: In this coordination, corresponding sequences of postverbal arguments are coordinated, and the sequences need not be ordinary independent phrases. In I took Jo to the station and Lee home, each person pairs with a separate goal under one overt verb. Lee home is the object and goal sequence, and it isn't an ordinary nominal constituent. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of coordination and marks the analysis as provisional. Present it as the same verb serving two parallel bundles.

examples.text: I took [Jo to the station and Lee home].
She gave [Ann a book and Bo a pen].

watch_for: A learner might read Lee home as an ordinary phrase, when it is a person plus a goal.
A learner might look for a second verb in the coordinated part, though one overt verb serves both bundles.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Right Argument-Cluster Coordination." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/right-argument-cluster-coordination-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Right Dislocation with a Pronoun

1.definition: Clarifies or reiterates a referent expressed by a pronoun in the preceding clause nucleus.
1.details: The following NP can disambiguate a pronoun or restate a referent that is already clear. CGEL contrasts a topic that is already evoked or accessible through the prior context with an attorney introduced for the first time, for which right dislocation is infelicitous. The observation concerns this pronoun-linked NP subtype.

examples.note: The final NP specifies the intended referent of him.
From a passage in which the book is already identified.

relatedConstructions.notes: The clause nucleus supplies Head:VP.
The left pattern can introduce a new referent.
Extraposition has a different status for the pronoun and the final expression.

grounds.note: Gives a clause-first sequence with the co-referential final NP.

projection.target: Right dislocation favours an accessible referent. It can clarify a choice between already available referents, including when the pronoun is embedded.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts clarification, reiteration and discourse-new contexts. CASA notes the role of an active topic.

curious.title: Saying who you mean at the end
curious.summary: A speaker can use a pronoun and then add a noun phrase after the clause to say exactly who or what it was.
curious.body: In I really like him, your dad, the word him already refers to someone. Then your dad is added at the end to make clear who. It can also simply restate a person or thing that's already clear, as in It's fascinating, this book. The added phrase works best for something already in the conversation. A new person who hasn't been mentioned doesn't fit well in this slot: this dictionary notes that an attorney introduced for the first time is a poor fit here.
curious.try: Say something about a person or thing using only him, her or it, then add the name or noun at the end.

teacher.summary: Helps explain a tag-like noun phrase after a clause that repeats a pronoun's referent.
teacher.explain: In right dislocation, a clause with an overt personal pronoun is followed by an NP referring to the same thing: I really like him, your dad. The final NP can disambiguate the pronoun or restate a referent that is already clear. CGEL contrasts a topic that has been evoked or is accessible from the context with an attorney introduced for the first time, for which right dislocation is infelicitous. The observation concerns this pronoun-linked subtype. The pronoun can be embedded in the clause, and the pattern favours an accessible referent.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an antitopic or a tag NP. This dictionary also contrasts it with left dislocation, which can introduce a new referent.

contrasts.note: The pronoun alone; the listener must work out who him is.

contrasts.text: I really like him, your dad.
contrasts.note: The final NP specifies the intended referent.

watch_for: A learner might use the final NP to introduce someone new to the conversation, when the pattern fits an accessible referent.
A learner might drop the pronoun and keep only the final noun phrase.
teacher.activity: Give students two people in a picture. They say a sentence using him or her, and a partner adds a final noun phrase that says exactly who is meant.

child.hook: When you say "him", how does a friend know who you mean?
child.explain: You can say it first, then say the name at the end. I really like him, your dad. The end part tells who "him" is.
child.play: Say a sentence with him, her or it. Then add the person or thing at the end, after a little pause.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Right Dislocation with a Pronoun." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/right-dislocation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Identity Comparison with same … as

1.definition: Compares items for identity of referent or identity of relevant type.

examples.form: We chose [the same model as Lee].

projection.target: The same model can identify a shared model without asserting that we bought one and the same physical object. As supplies the standard of comparison.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Being the same as something else
curious.summary: The same followed by as compares two things and says they match.
curious.body: In We chose the same model as Lee, the phrase after as is the standard we compare with. The two choices are the same model, but we needn't have bought one and the same physical object. It means the kind matches. So the same can point to a shared kind of thing or to a single shared thing. The word as introduces what we compare against. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: We chose [the same model as Lee].
She ordered [the same soup as Ravi].

curious.try: Say what you have in common with a friend using the same ... as.

teacher.summary: Helps explain the same + noun + as for identity of referent or of type.
teacher.explain: The same plus a noun, followed by an as-phrase, compares items for identity of referent or identity of relevant type. In We chose the same model as Lee, the same model can identify a shared model without asserting that we bought one and the same physical object. As supplies the standard of comparison. This dictionary relates the pattern to the equative as ... as construction, and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Related in this dictionary to the equative as ... as comparison.

examples.text: We chose [the same model as Lee].
She ordered [the same soup as Ravi].

watch_for: A learner might read the same model as meaning one single physical object, when it can mean the same type.
A learner might leave out as before the standard of comparison.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences about what they share with a partner (the same colour, the same bus) using the same ... as. Then they decide whether each shows one shared object or a shared type.

child.hook: How can two people have the same lunch?
child.explain: The same ... as tells you two things match. We chose the same model as Lee. We each chose that kind, so they match.

examples.text: We chose [the same model as Lee].
She ordered [the same soup as Ravi].

child.play: Look at a friend's bag, shoes or lunch. Say what's the same using the same ... as.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Identity Comparison with same … as." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/same-as-comparison-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: you call that X Challenge

1.definition: Challenges the appropriateness of a category label in a dismissive or corrective context
1.details: Challenges category membership rather than scalar degree (though the two are related via prototype structure). Implies "that doesn't deserve the label X" or "let me show you what X really is." A speaker can reject the label without offering a replacement exemplar. A literal inquiry about what to call an object is also possible.

examples.form: [You call that a sandwich]? It's just bread with lettuce.
examples.note: Challenges category membership; implying it fails to meet criteria

examples.form: [You call that clean]? There's dust everywhere.
examples.note: With predicative adjective; challenges threshold for category
Dismissive; implies speaker has higher standards

examples.form: [You call that an apology]? You didn't even say sorry.
examples.note: Challenges whether token meets criteria for type

constraints.description: Declarative clause with 2nd person subject and "call" as main verb; typically layered with the declarative-question construction
Complement is a category label (N or predicative expression)
Challenges appropriateness of categorization

relatedConstructions.notes: The challenge frame retains declarative clause type
Question prosody conventionally layers onto the declarative challenge frame
Shares addressee-directed challenge function; targets category membership rather than scalar degree

grounds.locator: Ch. 10 §§4.7.2, 6.4, declarative questions and challenges to question presuppositions, for comparison

projection.target: Keeping the wording You call that a repair? fixed, dismissive intonation and a visibly broken object invite a challenge to repair. In a cooperative question about terminology, the wording can instead check what label the addressee uses.
projection.evidence: The source describes the surrounding question architecture. The proposed challenge reading is illustrated by a constructed contextual contrast and its conventionality remains open.

curious.title: Doubting that something deserves its name
curious.summary: You call that a sandwich? can say the thing doesn't deserve the label, rather than ask what to call it.
curious.body: When someone says You call that a sandwich? with a dismissive tone, they're saying the thing doesn't deserve the name. It's just bread with lettuce. The same words can also be a plain question, if someone really wants to know what label you use. A dismissive tone and a visibly poor example point to the challenge. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and treats the challenge reading as a proposal whose status as a settled convention remains open.

examples.text: [You call that a sandwich]? It's just bread with lettuce.
[You call that clean]? There's dust everywhere.
[You call that an apology]? You didn't even say sorry.

curious.try: Think of something that barely deserves its name. Challenge it with You call that ...? and say what's missing.

teacher.summary: Helps explain a dismissive question that challenges whether a label fits.
teacher.explain: The frame You call that (a) N/PRED? has a declarative clause with a second person subject and call as the main verb, and its complement is a category label (a noun or a predicative expression). It challenges whether the label is appropriate: that doesn't deserve the label X. It challenges category membership, not scalar degree, though the two are related. The speaker can reject the label without offering a replacement. A literal inquiry about what to call an object is also possible, so tone and context decide. Question prosody is typically layered onto the declarative frame. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: In this dictionary it overlaps in function with declarative scalar recalibration, which targets degree rather than category membership.

examples.text: [You call that a sandwich]? It's just bread with lettuce.
[You call that clean]? There's dust everywhere.
[You call that an apology]? You didn't even say sorry.

watch_for: A learner might answer You call that a sandwich? as a vocabulary question, when it can be a challenge.
A learner might miss the dismissive tone that signals a challenge rather than a cooperative question about words.
teacher.activity: Show pictures of poor examples (a plain piece of bread as a sandwich). Students say You call that a ...? in a dismissive voice, then in a curious voice, and the class says which reading each one gave.

child.hook: What do you say when someone calls something by a grand name it doesn't deserve?
child.explain: You call that a sandwich? can say the thing is not good enough to have that name, instead of asking about the word. The tone of voice helps.

examples.text: [You call that a sandwich]? It's just bread with lettuce.

child.play: Pick something that's not a good example of its name. Say You call that ...? in a surprised voice and add one reason.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary and child.explain now say the sentence can be a challenge rather than that it always is (the entry also allows a literal question about what label to use); curious.body no longer rules out the question reading; teacher.explain says question prosody is typically layered, as in the entry; removed a scalar-recalibration example not given in this entry; reworded one watch_for.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "you call that X Challenge." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/scalar-challenge-call-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Differential by in Scalar Change

1.definition: Quantifies the amount of change on an ordered scale.

examples.form: The water level fell [by twelve centimetres].
The water level fell [to twelve centimetres].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. To introduces the attained value, not the difference.

projection.target: By measures the difference between starting and ending values. To with an endpoint instead names the final value, which can co-occur with a differential.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: How much something changed
curious.summary: After a verb of rising or falling, by plus an amount says how big the change was, while to says where it ended up.
curious.body: The water level fell by twelve centimetres tells you the size of the drop: the difference between the starting and ending levels. The water level fell to twelve centimetres tells you something else: the level it reached. Same verb, different question answered. The word by measures the gap between where something started and where it finished. The word to names the final value. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: The water level fell [by twelve centimetres].
The water level fell [to twelve centimetres].

curious.try: Say how much a price, a temperature or a score changed, once with by and once with to. Which tells you the change, and which tells you the new value?

teacher.summary: Helps explain by plus a measure phrase for the amount of change, versus to for the endpoint.
teacher.explain: With a verb of scalar change (fall, rise and the like), a PP headed by by plus a measure NP quantifies the amount of change on an ordered scale. By measures the difference between starting and ending values. To with an endpoint instead names the final value, and it can co-occur with a differential. This dictionary treats the by-phrase as a specialization of the PP and relates it to differential measure phrases in comparatives. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: The by-phrase here is sometimes called a differential or amount phrase.

examples.text: The water level fell [by twelve centimetres].
The water level fell [to twelve centimetres].

contrasts.text: The water level fell by twelve centimetres.
contrasts.note: The size of the drop.

contrasts.text: The water level fell to twelve centimetres.
contrasts.note: The value reached.

watch_for: A learner might read fell to twelve centimetres as a drop of twelve centimetres.
A learner might choose by or to without checking whether the number is a difference or an endpoint.
teacher.activity: Show a simple graph with start and end values. Students write one by sentence and one to sentence about it, then swap and check which number each sentence reports.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Differential by in Scalar Change." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/scalar-change-by-measure-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Declarative Scalar Recalibration

1.definition: Can introduce a comparison that shifts the operative standard on a scale
1.details: The surface form attributes a belief to the addressee, but the constructional meaning is scalar recalibration: the speaker has Z that exceeds X on the Y dimension. Direction is flexible - the speaker may exceed from superiority (dismissive) or from being worse off (self-deprecating, ironic). Typically followed by the speaker's evidence for exceeding.

examples.form: [You think you're upset]. I wrote a paper predicting that this wouldn't happen.
examples.note: Self-deprecating; speaker exceeds on upset-scale due to embarrassing wrong prediction (Joshua Gans)

examples.form: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
examples.note: With declarative-question construction layered; speaker exceeds on tiredness scale

examples.form: [You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.
examples.note: With demonstrative subject; introduces something more expensive

examples.form: [You think you know stress]. Try raising triplets.

constraints.description: Matrix clause with 2nd person subject and "think" as main verb
Embedded predicate must be gradable (scalar)
Requires follow-up providing speaker's evidence for exceeding on the scale

relatedConstructions.notes: The scalar-recalibration frame retains declarative clause type
Question prosody commonly layers onto the declarative scalar frame
Shares addressee-directed scalar-challenge function; differs in matrix verb and targets category membership rather than degree

grounds.locator: Ch. 13 §3, metalinguistic comparison; Ch. 16 §3.2, proposition assessment, for comparison

projection.target: You think that is loud can introduce an instance that shifts the operative degree standard. In a literal conversation about the hearer’s beliefs, the same sentence need not introduce a higher degree. The comparison depends on the following discourse.
projection.evidence: The source provides related scale and proposition-assessment analyses. The paired contexts illustrate the proposal and do not determine whether the reading has conventionalized.

curious.title: Topping someone's claim with your own
curious.summary: You think you're tired? can set up a comparison in which the speaker's own case goes further on the same scale.
curious.body: You think you're tired? I've been up for 36 hours. The first part looks like a remark about what you believe, but it can shift the scale. The speaker can be saying they're beyond tired, in a way that makes the listener's tiredness look smaller. Whether the sentence really works this way depends on what follows. A follow-up that gives the speaker's evidence, such as the 36 hours, supplies the comparison. In a literal conversation about what someone believes, the same sentence need not do this. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
[You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.
[You think you know stress]. Try raising triplets.

curious.try: Think of a time someone said they were really tired, cold or busy. How would you top that with You think ...?

teacher.summary: Helps explain a belief-sounding frame that can top the listener's point on a scale.
teacher.explain: The frame You think you're/NP is [GRADABLE-PRED] has a matrix clause with a second person subject and think as the main verb, and the embedded predicate must be gradable. Its meaning can be scalar recalibration: the speaker has something that exceeds the addressee's example on the relevant dimension. The direction is flexible, since the speaker may exceed from superiority (dismissive) or from being worse off (self-deprecating, ironic). The pattern needs a follow-up giving the speaker's evidence. The comparison depends on the following discourse. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: In this dictionary it overlaps in function with a related scalar-challenge construction that has a different matrix verb and targets category membership rather than degree.

examples.text: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
[You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.
[You think you know stress]. Try raising triplets.

watch_for: A learner might hear You think you're tired? only as a remark about the listener's belief, when a follow-up can show the speaker is topping it.
A learner might use the frame without a follow-up that supplies the speaker's own, bigger case.
teacher.activity: Students write a complaint about a mild condition (tired, cold, busy), pass it on, and the partner replies with You think ...? and an exaggerated case that tops it.

child.hook: What do you say when you've got it even worse than your friend?
child.explain: You think you're tired? can sound like a question about what you think. Sometimes it means "I'm even more tired." What the speaker says next shows which.

examples.text: [You think you're tired]? I've been up for 36 hours.
[You think that's expensive]. Wait till you see the repair bill.

child.play: Take turns. One person says "I'm tired" or "I'm cold". The other answers You think ...? and tops it with a reason.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer dismisses the literal belief reading and now says what follows shows which reading is meant; curious.summary, curious.body, teacher.summary and teacher.explain say the comparison can be introduced rather than always is, as the entry says it depends on the following discourse. Also fixed (unflagged): teacher.watch_for no longer treats the literal reading as a mistake; teacher.terms no longer quotes a constructed You call that X? form.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Declarative Scalar Recalibration." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/scalar-recalibration-declarative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Secondary Verbal Negation

1.definition: Negates a non-finite or subjunctive clause without do-support

examples.form: It is vital that he [not] be told.
a plan [not] approved by the board
It looks bad for them [not] to smile.

constraints.description: Not premodifies the secondary VP; do-support is unavailable.
In to-infinitivals, not may appear before or after to (e.g., "for them to not smile").

relatedConstructions.notes: Secondary not premodifies the VP that heads the non-finite or subjunctive Clause
Secondary verbal negation applies within headed non-finite and subjunctive Clauses

projection.target: The negative to-infinitival in a plan not to leave and the mandative that Lee not leave both keep the following verb in the plain form without do. The corresponding finite declarative Lee did not leave uses do.
projection.evidence: CGEL treats these as secondary verbal negation and distinguishes them by form from primary negation.

curious.title: Negating a verb without do
curious.summary: In certain verb forms, not negates the verb without the helper do.
curious.body: Plain sentences like Lee did not leave need the helper do. But some verb forms get their negation another way. In It is vital that he not be told, not stands directly in front of be. In Not locking the doors is unwise, it stands before locking. In a plan not to leave, it comes before to. This works with forms that aren't tensed sentences: a plain-form verb after that, an -ing form, a form like approved in a plan not approved by the board, and a to form. In each, no do is used. With to, not can come before or after it, as in for them not to smile and for them to not smile. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: It is vital that he [not] be told.
a plan [not] approved by the board
It looks bad for them [not] to smile.

curious.try: Compare Lee did not leave with a plan not to leave. What helper verb appears in the first and not in the second?

teacher.summary: Helps explain not before non-finite and subjunctive verb phrases, where do-support is unavailable.
teacher.explain: In secondary verbal negation, not premodifies a VP in a non-finite or subjunctive clause, and do-support is unavailable. The four cases are the subjunctive (that he not be told), the gerund-participial (not locking the doors), the past-participial (a plan not approved by the board) and the infinitival (for them not to smile). In to-infinitivals, not may appear before or after to (for them to not smile). The negative to-infinitival in a plan not to leave and the mandative that Lee not leave both keep the following verb in the plain form without do. By contrast, the finite declarative Lee did not leave uses do. CGEL treats these as secondary verbal negation, distinguished by form from primary negation.
teacher.terms: Subjunctive, gerund-participial, past-participial and infinitival are the clause types named in this dictionary. CGEL distinguishes secondary verbal negation by form from primary negation; the finite declarative Lee did not leave, which uses do, is the comparison case.

examples.text: It is vital that he [not] be told.
a plan [not] approved by the board
It looks bad for them [not] to smile.

contrasts.note: Finite declarative; negation uses do.
Negative to-infinitival; no do.
Not may also follow to.

watch_for: A learner might add do to the verb after not in a to-infinitive or subjunctive clause.
A learner might look for not only after to, when it may come before or after.

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary and body no longer say not comes directly before the verb in every case (this dictionary allows not before or after to); the clause forms are described more carefully; teacher terms no longer defines primary negation as finite with do-support and instead names the comparison case this dictionary uses. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' wording; curious title.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Secondary Verbal Negation." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/secondary-verbal-negation-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Simple Intransitive VP
pattern: VP[Head:V, without a core complement slot in the use at issue]

entry.name: Simple Intransitive VP
entry.pattern: VP[Head:V, without a core complement slot in the use at issue]

1.definition: Presents a one-place predication without a core object or predicative complement.

projection.target: An adjunct may be added without changing the verb's core frame. An NP after the verb can instead require a separately licensed construction, as with a cognate event object.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Verbs that stand alone
curious.summary: Some verbs need nothing after them to make a complete statement about someone or something.
curious.body: In The guests laughed, the verb laughed is enough. It says one thing about one thing, the guests, and needs no object or other required partner. Extras can still be added, such as when or where it happened, without changing what the verb itself needs. This dictionary calls this the simple intransitive pattern. A noun phrase after such a verb isn't automatically part of it. Something like a cognate event object, where the object repeats the verb's meaning, is treated as a separate pattern. The analysis is marked provisional.
curious.try: Think of verbs that make a complete sentence with just a subject, like laughed. Then add where or when without changing what the verb needs.

teacher.summary: Helps explain verbs used with no object or predicative complement.
teacher.explain: In a simple intransitive VP, the head verb has no core complement slot in the use at issue: it presents a one-place predication without a core object or predicative complement. In The guests laughed, only the subject is required. An adjunct may be added without changing the verb's core frame. An NP after the verb can instead require a separately licensed construction, as with a cognate event object. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the VP and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Intransitive verb is the traditional term. This dictionary stresses the use in a given sentence, not the verb as a whole.

contrasts.note: Subject plus verb only.
An adjunct is added and the verb's core frame stays the same.

watch_for: A learner might treat an adjunct such as at noon as a required object.
A learner might take laughed as a verb that can't be followed by anything, when this dictionary describes only the use at issue.
teacher.activity: Give students verb cards (laugh, sleep, arrive). They write a bare sentence with each, then add an adjunct, and underline the part the verb actually needs.

child.hook: Which words can finish a sentence all by themselves?
child.explain: Some verbs need nothing after them. The guests laughed is a whole sentence. You can add more, like when or where, but you don't have to.
child.play: Make up short sentences with just a doer and a verb. Then add where or when and see that the verb didn't change.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Simple Intransitive VP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/simple-intransitive-vp-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Temporal since with a Reference Anchor
pattern: PP[since + date/NP/finite clause] with a later reference time

entry.name: Temporal since with a Reference Anchor
entry.pattern: PP[since + date/NP/finite clause] with a later reference time

1.definition: Supplies the earlier boundary of the interval under discussion.

examples.form: They’ve lived abroad [since the factory closed].

projection.target: The closure anchors the beginning of the relevant span. Substitution of because preserves a causal interpretation in some cases but removes this temporal-bounding contribution.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Where a stretch of time begins
curious.summary: Since marks the starting point of the period being talked about.
curious.body: In They've lived abroad since the factory closed, the closing of the factory is the starting point. The period in question runs from then up to the later time we're talking about, which here is now. The part after since can be a date, a noun phrase or a whole clause. Swapping since for because changes things. Because can keep a cause-and-effect reading in some cases, but it drops the contribution of marking when the period began. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: They've lived abroad [since the factory closed].

curious.try: Finish the sentence I've known my best friend since ... in two ways, with an event and with a date.

teacher.summary: Helps explain since as the earlier boundary of an interval, and how it differs from because.
teacher.explain: A PP headed by since supplies the earlier boundary of the interval under discussion, relative to a later reference time. Its complement can be a date, an NP or a finite clause. In They've lived abroad since the factory closed, the closure anchors the beginning of the relevant span. Substituting because preserves a causal interpretation in some cases but removes this temporal-bounding contribution. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the PP and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Since here is a preposition in CGEL's sense, including when its complement is a clause.

examples.text: They've lived abroad [since the factory closed].

contrasts.text: They've lived abroad since the factory closed.
contrasts.note: The closing marks the start of the span.

contrasts.text: They've lived abroad because the factory closed.
contrasts.note: Because gives a reason and doesn't mark the start of the span.

watch_for: A learner might read since the factory closed as giving a reason, as because would.
A learner might leave out the later reference time that the period runs up to.
teacher.activity: Students put an event on a timeline and write one since sentence marking the start of the period. A partner draws the span from the since point to the reference time.

child.hook: When did something start? How do you say it?
child.explain: Since tells when a long stretch of time began. They've lived abroad since the factory closed. The closing was the start.

examples.text: They've lived abroad [since the factory closed].

child.play: Say how long you've done something using since and the day it began, like since my birthday.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Temporal since with a Reference Anchor." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/since-time-anchor-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Singular Construction
pattern: Applies to common and proper nouns, pronouns, and determinatives

entry.name: Singular Construction
entry.pattern: Applies to common and proper nouns, pronouns, and determinatives

dimensions.form: Singular morphology (often zero); singular agreement marking
dimensions.meaning: Single entity reference; unity/wholeness for non-count nouns
dimensions.function: Signals singular construal; triggers singular agreement
dimensions.distribution: Nouns, pronouns, determinatives; agreement targets in clause

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional syntax-semantics interface for number

projection.target: The singular grammatical pattern travels across count and non-count uses. The water is cold has singular agreement although no distinct unit of water need have been selected.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates number agreement and countability, including singular morphology for non-count nouns.

curious.title: What singular means
curious.summary: Singular is a form that nouns, pronouns and similar words can have, and it makes other words in the sentence agree with it.
curious.body: Singular is a form that nouns, pronouns and similar words can have. With a count noun like cat it points to one thing, and so do it and this. The singular form is often just the plain word with nothing added, as in cat. The pattern also reaches words for substances, like rice. There it signals wholeness, not a count of one: the rice is treated as one undivided mass. The water is cold has a singular verb, even though no distinct unit of water has to be picked out. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Compare The cats are asleep with The rice is ready. Which verb form goes with the plural, and which goes with the singular?

teacher.summary: Helps explain singular form and agreement across count and non-count nouns, pronouns and determinatives.
teacher.explain: The singular construction applies to common and proper nouns, pronouns and determinatives. Its form is singular morphology (often zero) plus singular agreement marking, and it signals singular construal. For count uses it specifies exactly one countable entity; this dictionary's examples are the noun cat, the pronoun it and the determinative this. For non-count nouns it marks unity or wholeness, as with rice, an undivided substance. The pattern travels across count and non-count uses: The water is cold has singular agreement although no distinct unit of water need have been selected. CGEL separates number agreement from countability. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Non-count nouns are traditionally called mass or uncountable nouns. This dictionary follows CGEL in saying non-count.

contrasts.note: A count noun, one entity, singular agreement.
A non-count noun, singular agreement, no count of one.

watch_for: A learner might think singular agreement with a non-count noun like rice means a single item.
A learner might match the verb to the meaning of a word (a lot of water) instead of its form.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of nouns (cat, rice, water, idea). They write a sentence with each and mark the verb. Then discuss which nouns count a single item and which mark wholeness.

child.hook: What word do we use for just one thing, like it or this?
child.explain: A singular word can stand for one thing, like it or this. Words like rice and water are singular too, even though you don't count them one by one.
child.play: Look at things around you. Say the cat is or the rice is, and see which words go with is.

checked.note: Fixed: title, summary and curious.body no longer define singular as single-thing reference (non-count singulars are a separate use); teacher.explain no longer groups it and this under count nouns; child.explain no longer says 'Singular means one'; child.hook reworded to match.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Singular Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/singular-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Singular Anaphoric they
pattern: anaphoric NP[they/them/their] with a singular referent or antecedent

entry.name: Singular Anaphoric they
entry.pattern: anaphoric NP[they/them/their] with a singular referent or antecedent

1.definition: Uses the they paradigm for a single antecedent, including a bound variable or a known person.

projection.target: The antecedent can be singular while they takes ordinary they-agreement, such as were. The construction is compatible with bound readings and with specific references in suitable contexts.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: They for one person
curious.summary: They, them and their can point back to a single person, and the verb still agrees as it does with they.
curious.body: In Every applicant said they were ready, the word they refers back to every applicant, taken one at a time. The verb is were, the same form used when they means several people. The pattern is also compatible with they for a specific person in a suitable context. The word that they refers back to is singular, while the pronoun still takes its usual they forms. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Say a sentence beginning Everyone said ... and finish it with they. Which verb form follows?

teacher.summary: Helps explain they, them and their with a singular antecedent.
teacher.explain: The they paradigm (they, them, their) can have a singular antecedent, including a bound-variable reading (as with every applicant) or a known person. In Every applicant said they were ready, the antecedent is singular, yet they takes ordinary they-agreement, such as were. The pattern is compatible with bound readings and with specific references in suitable contexts. This dictionary treats it as a specialization of the personal pronoun NP and relates it to verb number agreement. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called singular they. In this dictionary: singular anaphoric they.
watch_for: A learner might expect the verb to agree with the singular antecedent (every applicant), when they takes ordinary they-agreement, such as were.
A learner might assume they can only refer to more than one person.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences starting Each student said ... and Every player thought ... using they, then circle the verb and discuss its form.

child.hook: Can they ever mean just one person?
child.explain: Sometimes they points back to one person at a time. Every applicant said they were ready. The verb is were, just like when they means a group.
child.play: Start a sentence with Every kid said or Each player said. Finish it using they and a verb.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher explanation no longer calls every applicant the 'bound variable' (it is the antecedent; they gets the bound-variable reading); reworded an unflagged watch_for item that implied was is wrong, which the entry does not state.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Singular Anaphoric they." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/singular-anaphoric-they-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Degree so with a Result Content Clause

entry.name: Degree so with a Result Content Clause

1.definition: Identifies a high degree through a resulting or evidentially linked situation.

examples.form: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn’t turn].

relatedConstructions.notes: So cold that the locks froze has degree marking on an adjective. Such a cold morning that the locks froze uses a nominal expression. Both specify degree or kind through a stated result.

projection.target: The result clause identifies the relevant scale threshold and ordinarily presents a realized situation. Compare too narrow to turn, which describes an obstacle without reporting an attempt.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: So much that something happens
curious.summary: So plus a describing word, followed by a clause about a resulting or linked situation, shows how high a degree is.
curious.body: The street was so narrow that the van couldn't turn. The word so marks a high degree of narrowness, and the part after that tells what resulted. That result shows how narrow the street was. The result clause sets the level that counts. It ordinarily presents something that really happened. Compare too narrow to turn, which describes an obstacle without reporting that anyone tried. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn't turn].
The soup was [so hot that she couldn't eat it].

curious.try: Finish this: The room was so cold that ... What result shows how cold it was?

teacher.summary: Helps explain so plus an adjective plus a that-clause that gives a result.
teacher.explain: The pattern is so plus a gradable expression plus a content clause, in which that is optional. It identifies a high degree through a resulting or evidentially linked situation. The result clause identifies the relevant scale threshold and ordinarily presents a realized situation. Compare too narrow to turn, which describes an obstacle without reporting an attempt. This dictionary also notes the overlap with such a cold morning that the locks froze, where the degree is specified through a nominal expression instead of an adjective. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: The that-clause is a declarative content clause; the that may be omitted.

examples.text: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn't turn].
The soup was [so hot that she couldn't eat it].
