contrasts.text: The street was so narrow that the van couldn't turn.
contrasts.note: The result is presented as having happened.

contrasts.text: The street was too narrow to turn in.
contrasts.note: An obstacle is described, and no attempt is reported.

contrasts.text: It was such a cold morning that the locks froze.
contrasts.note: The nominal counterpart with such.

watch_for: A learner might read the that-clause as a separate sentence, when it states the situation linked to the degree.
A learner might use too narrow to turn when a reported result is wanted.
teacher.activity: Give students adjectives (cold, noisy, heavy). They write a so ... that sentence with a realized result, then rewrite it with too ... to and say how the meaning shifts.

child.hook: How would you show that something was REALLY hot?
child.explain: You can say how much by saying what happened. The street was so narrow that the van couldn't turn. The result shows how narrow it was.

examples.text: The street was [so narrow that the van couldn't turn].
The soup was [so hot that she couldn't eat it].

child.play: Finish the sentence The box was so heavy that ... in three different ways.

checked.note: Fixed: the optional element is the word that, not the whole clause; curious summary no longer implies the clause must be introduced by that or that the degree causes the situation (the entry allows a resulting or evidentially linked situation); watch_for no longer treats a clause without a causal result as a learner error. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Degree so with a Result Content Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/so-degree-result-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Inverted Additive so and neither

1.definition: Affirms a parallel predication under matching polarity.

examples.form: Lee has finished, and [so has Jo].
Lee hasn’t finished, and [neither has Jo].

grounds.locator: Ch. 3 §2.1.2, inversion after additive so/neither; Ch. 8 §19, connective adjuncts

projection.target: A positive antecedent licenses additive so, a negative one neither or nor. The new subject follows the auxiliary and the prior predicate is recoverable.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying me too with so and neither
curious.summary: So has Jo and neither has Jo add another person to what's just been said, with the helper verb coming before the new subject.
curious.body: After Lee has finished, you can add and so has Jo. This says Jo has finished too. For a negative statement, you use neither: Lee hasn't finished, and neither has Jo. In both, the helper verb (has) comes before the person (Jo), and the rest of the earlier statement is understood without being repeated. A positive statement before it calls for so, a negative one for neither or nor. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: Lee has finished, and [so has Jo].
Lee hasn't finished, and [neither has Jo].

curious.try: Say something you've done, then add and so ... with a friend's name. Then try a negative one with neither.

teacher.summary: Helps explain so, neither and nor with subject-auxiliary inversion for additive agreement.
teacher.explain: In this additive pattern, so, neither or nor is followed by a finite auxiliary and then the subject. It affirms a parallel predication under matching polarity: a positive antecedent licenses so, and a negative one licenses neither or nor. The new subject follows the auxiliary, and the prior predicate is recoverable. This dictionary relates it to auxiliary VP ellipsis. CGEL discusses it under inversion after additive so and neither. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Subject-auxiliary inversion is the order of auxiliary before subject.

examples.text: Lee has finished, and [so has Jo].
Lee hasn't finished, and [neither has Jo].

contrasts.text: Lee has finished, and so has Jo.
contrasts.note: Positive antecedent, so.

contrasts.text: Lee hasn't finished, and neither has Jo.
contrasts.note: Negative antecedent, neither.

watch_for: A learner might use so after a negative statement, when matching polarity calls for neither or nor.
A learner might put the subject before the auxiliary after so or neither.
teacher.activity: Students write a statement about themselves on a slip. Partners respond with and so ... or and neither ..., matching the polarity, and read the pair aloud.

child.hook: How do you say "me too" in a longer way?
child.explain: You can add another person with so or neither. Lee has finished, and so has Jo. Say neither when the first part is negative.

examples.text: Lee has finished, and [so has Jo].
Lee hasn't finished, and [neither has Jo].

child.play: Say a sentence about one person, like Lee has finished. A friend adds a new person, starting with and so has. For Lee hasn't finished, the friend starts with and neither has.

checked.note: Fixed: child.play no longer has the friend reuse the first speaker's name; the friend now adds a new person after so or neither plus the helper word, as in the examples.

name: Intensifying so with a Nominal
pattern: Clause[Subject:NP + be + PredComp:[stressed so + nominal expression]]

entry.name: Intensifying so with a Nominal
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:NP + be + PredComp:[stressed so + nominal expression]]

1.definition: Attributes a conspicuous degree of a quality associated with the nominal expression.
1.details: In you’re so glass half full today, the final expression makes a description such as optimism available to be graded. A familiar name can work similarly when speakers associate the bearer with a style or quality. A name in this use can contribute associated qualities while retaining its independent use to identify its bearer in other contexts. The construction does not settle the lexical category of every filler.

examples.note: KABC spoken example, transcribed in the Research Constructicon. Stress is on so.
KABC spoken example. The situation is characterized by a feature associated with college.
Published example using a personal name as the basis for characterization.

relatedConstructions.notes: The construction invites a degree interpretation from a contextually retrieved property.
A name can supply the source of an associated property.
Both can invite evaluation with a stressed expression and nominal material.

grounds.note: Distinguishes referring to an individual from grading a property associated with that individual.

projection.target: Stressed so in the predicative frame makes a degree interpretation available even with an expression that elsewhere names an individual or describes a situation.
projection.evidence: Senger records two spoken examples. Bylinina studies the individual-denoting nominal and the inferred scale of comparison.

curious.title: So plus a noun to mean a quality
curious.summary: With stress on so, a noun or name can work like a describing word that you can have a lot of.
curious.body: In It's so college, the word college isn't naming a place. It stands for a quality we associate with college, and so tells us there's a lot of it. In You're so glass half full today, the expression makes an optimistic attitude available to be graded. A familiar name can work this way too, as in This is so Obama!, when speakers link the person with a style or quality. The name still names its bearer in other settings. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of a name or a place that stands for a style. Say That's so ... with stress on so. What quality do you mean?

teacher.summary: Helps explain stressed so before a noun or name to grade an associated quality.
teacher.explain: In the frame Subject + be + stressed so + nominal expression, so invites a degree interpretation from a contextually retrieved property. The final expression makes a description, such as optimism, available to be graded. A familiar name can work similarly when speakers associate its bearer with a style or quality, while keeping its ordinary use to identify the bearer elsewhere. The pattern doesn't settle the lexical category of every filler. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and relates it to degree, to proper names and to stressed some exclamatives.
teacher.terms: Intensifier so is traditional. Here it is stressed, and it grades a property associated with the nominal.
watch_for: A learner might read so college as saying that something is a college, when it characterizes the situation by a feature associated with college.
A learner might read so Obama as referring to the person, when it grades an associated quality.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Intensifying so with a Nominal." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/so-nominal-predication-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: some X or other
pattern: NP[some + singular count Nom + or other]

entry.name: some X or other
entry.pattern: NP[some + singular count Nom + or other]

1.definition: Introduces an individual while leaving a more specific identification open.
1.details: The whole pattern licenses bare other. An immediate identifying continuation with namely is degraded in Abenina-Adar’s comparison with an ordinary indefinite. CGEL suggests a modifier analysis for the tail. A coordinate analysis is also compatible with the pairing. The use by speakers who know the identity but choose to omit it needs a separate test.

examples.form: [Some student or other] was waiting outside the door.
examples.note: Introduces a student with their identity left open.
Published comparison with a book and an immediate identifying continuation.

relatedConstructions.notes: A form of indefinite NP with a specific discourse effect.
Related or another forms make coordination a live analysis of the tail.

projection.target: The form permits bare other and makes immediate identification by the same speaker awkward.
projection.evidence: CGEL records the form and its vague-identity reading. Abenina-Adar tests immediate identification.

curious.title: Some something or other
curious.summary: Some student or other introduces someone while leaving open who exactly it was.
curious.body: In Some student or other was waiting outside the door, there was a student, and the sentence doesn't say which. The words or other signal that the identity is left open. The pattern is an ordinary kind of indefinite phrase with a particular effect. One published comparison found that following it straight away with an identifying remark is degraded, compared with a plain some book. Whether it fits a speaker who knows the identity but leaves it out is something this dictionary says still needs testing. The analysis is marked provisional.

examples.text: [Some student or other] was waiting outside the door.

curious.try: Say Some ... or other about a thing you can't pin down, such as a person, a book or a song.

teacher.summary: Helps explain some + singular count noun + or other for an unidentified individual.
teacher.explain: The pattern is some plus a singular count Nom plus or other. It introduces an individual while leaving a more specific identification open, and the whole pattern licenses bare other. This dictionary treats it as an indefinite NP with a specific discourse effect. An immediate identifying continuation with namely is degraded in one published comparison with an ordinary indefinite. For the tail, CGEL suggests a modifier analysis, and a coordinate analysis is also compatible with the pairing. The use by speakers who know the identity but choose to omit it needs a separate test. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Compare the indefinite NP some student. In this dictionary the tail or other is analyzed either as a modifier or as coordination.

examples.text: [Some student or other] was waiting outside the door.

watch_for: A learner might follow some student or other directly with an identification such as namely, though this dictionary notes that it is degraded in one comparison.
A learner might use a plural noun after some in this pattern, when it is described here with a singular count noun.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences about unnamed people and things (some teacher or other, some song or other). Partners guess what the sentence leaves open and discuss whether it sounds natural to name it straight away.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "some X or other." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/some-n-or-other-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Source Locative-Complement Construction

dimensions.form: Verb head with a source-denoting PP in locative-complement function, headed centrally by from, away, off, or out
dimensions.meaning: Origin or initial location of motion, derivation, or change
dimensions.function: Locative complement of the verb, bearing the semantic role source
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal with motion and change verbs; compatible with a following goal-role locative complement

1.definition: A VP contains a locative complement bearing the source role, marking the initial location of motion or change
1.details: Source is a semantic role, while locative complement is the CGEL syntactic function. Source complements are generally headed by from, away, off, or out. From takes an NP or locative-PP complement; the inner PP in from under the bed expresses the source location and is not another source complement. Away occurs alone or with a from-PP complement; off occurs alone or with an NP object; out occurs alone or with an of- or from-PP complement (CGEL pp. 257–59, 687).

examples.note: The whole from-PP is the source-role locative complement; the inner PP expresses the source location
Source- and goal-role locative complements co-occurring

constraints.description: The whole source-denoting PP is integrated as a locative complement of the verb, not added as a locative adjunct.
The complement denotes the initial location or state and can co-occur with a separate goal-role locative complement.

projection.target: In their central motion uses, integrated locative PPs headed by from, away, off, or out predict an initial-location construal, head-specific complementation, and compatibility with a separate goal-role complement
projection.evidence: CGEL gives the four-head realization inventory and its distinct complement patterns on p. 687; spatial, state, and possession examples distinguish initial-location source from final-location goal on pp. 258–60

grounds.note: Head choice projects initial-location interpretation, complementation, and source-goal compatibility
The source-role profile recurs across motion, state, and possession domains

core.property: Source role borne by a locative PP complement
diagnostics: integration in a motion or change frame

known_boundary_items: Away from can express retrospective direction, and off has restricted goal uses; the containing event distinguishes these from the central source uses
path or route complements such as through the tunnel and via Chicago instantiate the distinct path-complement construction
derivational sources such as made from grapes: extension beyond literal motion

relatedConstructions.notes: The source-role locative complement is licensed within VP structure
The source-role locative complement is a PP headed centrally by from, away, off, or out

grounds.note: Source is a semantic role borne by a PP in locative-complement function

curious.title: Saying where something started
curious.summary: A small phrase with from, away, off or out can tell where a movement or change began.
curious.body: In She came from Toronto, the phrase from Toronto says where the coming started. Phrases beginning with away, off or out do a similar job: Kim jumped off the pier, He came out of the room, She walked away. This dictionary treats these phrases as built into the verb phrase, not added on as extras. A starting point can also go together with a separate end point, as in They flew from Toronto to Ottawa. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Describe a trip with where it started and where it ended, such as I walked from ... to ...

teacher.summary: Helps explain phrases with from, away, off or out that name the starting point of motion or change.
teacher.explain: Source is a semantic role: the initial location of motion, derivation or change. In CGEL terms, it's borne by a locative complement of the verb, a PP headed by from, away, off or out, integrated into the VP and not added as an adjunct. From takes an NP or locative PP (from under the bed). Away occurs alone or with a from-PP. Off occurs alone or with an NP object. Out occurs alone or with an of-PP or from-PP. A separate goal-role locative complement can follow (from Toronto to Ottawa). This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: In this dictionary, such a phrase is called a source-role locative complement.

contrasts.text: They flew from Toronto to Ottawa.
contrasts.note: Source and goal complements together.

watch_for: A learner might treat the inner PP in from under the bed as a second source complement, when the whole from-PP is the complement.
A learner might pair away or off with the wrong complement, since each head has its own complement pattern.
teacher.activity: Students trace a route on a map and write sentences using from, away, off and out for starting points. They then add a goal phrase to at least one.

child.hook: How do you say where a trip started?
child.explain: Words like from, off and out can tell where something started. She came from Toronto. Kim jumped off the pier. They flew from Toronto to Ottawa.
child.play: Act out a short trip. Say where you started with from, off or out, and where you ended with to.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the verb needs these phrases (the entry says they are integrated complements, not adjuncts, without claiming they are obligatory); teacher summary no longer implies the verb is incomplete without the phrase; removed the traditional-grammar label 'adverbial phrases of place or direction', which the entry does not make and which is broader than the construction.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Source Locative-Complement Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/source-complement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Specificational Copular Clause

1.definition: Identifies a value for a description made salient by the other copular expression.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. The reversed copular order identifies the same obstacle.

projection.target: The permit supplies a value rather than a general property. The reverse order can preserve the identification while changing the informational packaging.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Sentences that fill in an answer
curious.summary: Some sentences with is set up a description and then name what fits it.
curious.body: The main obstacle is the permit. The phrase the main obstacle sets up a description, and the permit fills it in. It names which thing fits. This is different from a sentence that just says what something is like. You can reverse the order: The permit is the main obstacle. It still identifies the same obstacle, though the information is packaged differently. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Complete The biggest problem is ... and then reverse it. What does each order put first?

teacher.summary: Helps explain be-clauses that identify a value for a description.
teacher.explain: A specificational copular clause pairs a variable NP with a value expression and be: it identifies a value for a description made salient by the other copular expression. In The main obstacle is the permit, the permit supplies a value rather than a general property. The reverse order, The permit is the main obstacle, can preserve the identification while changing the informational packaging. This dictionary treats the pattern as a specialization of the clause and relates it to pseudo-clefts and to subject-ascriptive clauses. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Compare ascriptive clauses, which ascribe a property. In this dictionary the related pattern is subject-ascriptive.

contrasts.text: The main obstacle is the permit.
contrasts.note: The variable comes first and the value second.

contrasts.text: The permit is the main obstacle.
contrasts.note: The reversed order identifies the same obstacle.

watch_for: A learner might read the permit as describing a property of the obstacle, when it supplies a value.
A learner might treat the reversed order as changing which obstacle is identified.
teacher.activity: Students write a description-then-value sentence (The winner is ...), reverse it, and say what each order puts first.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Specificational Copular Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/specificational-copular-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Speech-Act Adverbial
pattern: supplementary adverbial oriented to the utterance act

entry.name: Speech-Act Adverbial
entry.pattern: supplementary adverbial oriented to the utterance act

1.definition: Characterizes the speaker’s manner or purpose in making the utterance.

projection.target: Frankly characterizes the speaker’s statement, not the repair's manner of failing. A paraphrase can mention speaking frankly without changing the content asserted.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Words about how you're speaking
curious.summary: An adverb like frankly can describe how or why the speaker is making the statement, not what the statement is about.
curious.body: In Frankly, the repair won't last, the word frankly isn't about the repair. It describes the speaker's way of speaking: the speaker is being frank in saying this. You can check by paraphrase. Something like I'm speaking frankly captures it, and the content asserted stays the same: the repair won't last. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Add a word like honestly or briefly to the start of a statement. Is it about the thing you're describing, or about how you're saying it?

teacher.summary: Helps explain an adverbial that characterizes the speaker's manner or purpose in making the utterance.
teacher.explain: A speech-act adverbial is a supplementary adverbial oriented to the utterance act: it characterizes the speaker's manner or purpose in making the utterance. In Frankly, the repair won't last, frankly characterizes the speaker's statement, not the repair's manner of failing. A paraphrase can mention speaking frankly without changing the content asserted. This dictionary relates it to evaluative sentence adverbs and to participial clause supplements. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: In this dictionary: speech-act adverbial.
watch_for: A learner might read frankly as describing how the repair fails, when it describes the speaker's statement.
A learner might think the adverb changes the content asserted, when a paraphrase like I'm speaking frankly leaves it unchanged.
teacher.activity: Write statements with a speech-act adverb on cards. Students paraphrase each as I'm saying this ..., and check that the asserted content doesn't change.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Speech-Act Adverbial." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/speech-act-adverbial-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Aspectual still and Negative yet
pattern: clause with still or polarity-sensitive yet and a temporal reference point

entry.name: Aspectual still and Negative yet
entry.pattern: clause with still or polarity-sensitive yet and a temporal reference point

1.definition: Locates persistence or non-occurrence against an expected course of events.

projection.target: Not yet says that stopping has failed to occur up to the reference point and can suggest it remains expected. Still can instead present the existing state as persisting.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Still and not yet
curious.summary: Not yet and still place something against an expected course of events: one reports what hasn't happened, the other what carries on.
curious.body: In The alarm hasn't stopped yet, hasn't and yet together set the stopping against a point in time, here the present, and say it hasn't happened by then. Together they can also suggest that the stopping is still expected to come. Still works from the other side. It can present a state that already exists as carrying on. So not yet reports something that hasn't happened, and the word still reports something that continues. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and illustrates it with a single constructed example, so take it as a first sketch.
curious.try: Think of something you're waiting for. Say that it hasn't happened yet. Does your sentence suggest you expect it to happen?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining how not yet can suggest an expected change and how still can present a continuing state.
teacher.explain: This dictionary covers clauses with still or a negative yet and a temporal reference point, such as now. Not yet says the event has failed to occur up to that point, and it can suggest the event remains expected. Still can instead present an existing state as persisting. Both words are heard against an expected course of events. This dictionary treats the pattern as provisional and illustrates it with one constructed example, so treat these as starting observations for a lesson, not a full account of either word.
watch_for: A learner might read not yet as a plain negative and miss that the event can still be expected.
A learner might treat still as only a time word and miss that it presents an existing state as continuing.
teacher.activity: Give pairs a situation, such as a kettle on the stove. Each partner writes one sentence with not yet and one with still describing it at different moments. They swap and say what each sentence suggests about what the speaker expects next.

child.hook: What do you mean when you say the kettle hasn't boiled yet?
child.explain: Not yet says something hasn't happened up to the time we're talking about. It can hint that it is still expected. Still says something is carrying on.
child.play: Look at a clock. Say one thing that hasn't happened yet today and one thing that is still going on. Take turns with a friend.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body and teacher.explain now call the only example a constructed illustration; curious.summary no longer restricts both words to negative sentences or to now; child.explain says not yet can hint the event is still expected, with no claim about how soon, and refers to the time being talked about; replaced 'This entry' with this dictionary. Second round: fixed curious.body, which gave the non-occurrence meaning to yet alone (the entry gives it to not yet), and the child hook likewise; teacher.summary now says not yet can suggest an expected change and still can present a continuing state, as the entry does.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Aspectual still and Negative yet." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/still-yet-aspectual-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Exclamation with Stressed some

1.definition: Presents an instance as remarkable for its kind, with positive or negative evaluation.
1.details: CGEL compares emotive one. Anderson’s wine comparison distinguishes this pattern from ordinary exclamation. The wine we drank can express surprise purely at quantity. That was some wine we drank resists that reading. Anderson develops an account from focus, some, and properties of exclamatives. The scope of the parallel with one remains open.

examples.form: [SOME hotel that was!] An utter disgrace!
examples.note: Negative evaluation, with stress as marked by CGEL.
Anderson's mass-noun comparison constrains the available kind of surprise. Capitals mark stress here.

relatedConstructions.notes: The pattern realizes exclamation as an utterance-level function.
An independent use of some associates the NP with a different discourse contribution.

projection.target: The stressed predication favours noteworthy character or quality over surprise solely at quantity.
projection.evidence: CGEL's positive and negative examples and Anderson's contrast between stressed some and a plain nominal exclamation.

curious.title: Exclaiming that something was quite a specimen
curious.summary: Said with heavy stress, some in an exclamation presents something as remarkable for its kind.
curious.body: When some is said with strong stress in an exclamation, it marks what you're describing as remarkable of its kind. SOME hotel that was! can carry a negative judgment, as the next sentence shows (An utter disgrace!), and the same pattern can express a positive one. This dictionary compares it with the ordinary wine we drank, which can express surprise purely at how much there was. That was SOME wine we drank! doesn't easily mean that. It points to the character or quality of the wine instead. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [SOME hotel that was!] An utter disgrace!

curious.try: Say That was some meal! first with ordinary stress, then with heavy stress on some. Does the second version sound more like a judgment on the meal itself?

teacher.summary: Optional enrichment on exclamations with stressed some, which judge the quality of a thing rather than its quantity.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an exclamation whose predicative complement is an NP with stressed SOME plus a nominal. It presents an instance as remarkable for its kind, with positive or negative evaluation. CGEL compares emotive one. A contrast from the cited work separates this from an ordinary exclamation: The wine we drank can express surprise purely at quantity, whereas That was some wine we drank resists that reading. This dictionary leaves open how far the parallel with one extends and marks the analysis provisional, so present it as a tentative description. In the examples, capitals show where the stress falls.
teacher.terms: CGEL compares this use of some with emotive one. No other standard traditional name is given in this dictionary.

examples.text: [SOME hotel that was!] An utter disgrace!

watch_for: A learner might hear SOME in That was SOME wine as a quantity word meaning a lot of wine.
A learner might read the pattern as only praise, when the evaluation can be negative, as in SOME hotel that was.
teacher.activity: Students write a short exclamation about a film, a meal or a trip using stressed some. Classmates say whether the speaker is praising or complaining and point to the words that tell them.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Exclamation with Stressed some." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/stressed-some-exclamative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Strong Proper Name Construction
pattern: NP[Head:Nom[sg]; no Det] with naming semantics, in referential use

entry.name: Strong Proper Name Construction
entry.pattern: NP[Head:Nom[sg]; no Det] with naming semantics, in referential use

dimensions.form: Singular NP with no determiner. Its head may be a proper noun (Kim, Ukraine) or a common noun in naming use (Mom, Grandma).
dimensions.meaning: Naming semantics: the NP identifies its referent as the bearer of a conventional name, and is inherently definite.
dimensions.function: Referential use in argument functions: subject, object in a VP, object in a PP.
dimensions.distribution: Not names with the article (weak proper names: the Thames, the Philippines), not bare vocatives (Waiter!, Sally!), whose bareness comes from the vocative function.

1.definition: Identifies its referent as the bearer of a conventional name, with no determiner
1.details: CGEL distinguishes strong proper names, with no determiner (Kim, New York), from weak ones, where the article marks definiteness redundantly (the Thames). The construction is the strong kind, stated as a form-meaning pairing: a determinerless singular NP with naming semantics in referential use. Proper name is a semantic classification; strong and weak describe the form of the NP; the head belongs to the NP, not to the name.

examples.note: Proper-noun head, object in a PP
Common-noun head in naming use; the same noun takes a determiner in its relational use (my mom called)

examples.form: You wanna roll the ball to [Mommy]?
examples.note: Attested, object in a PP; mother to child (CHILDES Brent/Siskind, s1/010224.cha, line 1826)

examples.form: Did you tell [Grampa] you went out to see him?
examples.note: Attested, object in a VP; father to child (CHILDES Demetras2, Jimmy/father/020702.cha, line 281)

2.definition: Takes non-restrictive embellishments without a determiner
2.details: A small set of emotive adjectives can embellish a strong name in a bare NP, without selecting among bearers. An ordinary singular count noun takes the same adjective only with a determiner (the poor dog needs a rest).

examples.note: Emotive embellishment of a proper-noun-headed name
Constructed; the same pattern with a common-noun head in naming use

constraints.description: No determiner, and the NP is singular. Names plural in form (Naples, the surname Fields) are fine; syntactically plural names (the Alps) are always weak.
Requires a conventional naming relation between the form and its referent; identifiability alone is not enough (the doctor can identify one person without being a name).
Proper nouns are specialized for heading the NPs used as names, but a common noun in naming use can head the construction; on CGEL's analysis kin terms used as names remain common nouns.
Referential use only. Bare vocatives are not instances: the vocative function allows bare common nouns too (Waiter!).

relatedConstructions.notes: Specializes the bare-NP individual-reference use (meaning 4) to NPs with naming semantics
Realizes the proper-name function in a determinerless singular NP; proper name stays the semantic classification

Overlap is the strong proper-noun-headed NPs (London); weak names (the United Nations) are proper-noun NPs outside the construction, and common-noun heads in naming use (Mom) are inside it but not proper-noun NPs
Proper nouns are specialized for heading NPs used as names but are not required by the construction
Strong proper names are inherently definite, so the construction needs no determiner to mark definiteness
Bare vocatives share the bare form but not the construction; their bareness is licensed by the vocative function

grounds.note: Proper names in primary use have NP status; strong (no determiner) vs weak (redundant the); plural proper names are always weak; proper nouns specialized for heading proper names
Kin terms used as proper names belong syntactically to the category of common nouns
Emotive adjectives as embellishments in bare NPs (poor Henry)
A construction is a learned pairing of form with semantic or discourse function

grounds.locator: Brent/Siskind s1/010224.cha line 1826; Demetras2 Jimmy/father/020702.cha line 281
grounds.note: Bare kin-term arguments in caregiver speech (object in a PP, object in a VP)
Only the strong kind is treated as a construction; names are semantic and have no heads, the NPs used as names do (a deliberate departure from CGEL's usage); bare vocatives are excluded

projection.target: Knowing that a singular form is someone's conventional name predicts its bare use as an argument (Mom called, Ask Mom), its definite reading, and its bare emotive embellishment (poor Mom), where the same noun in relational use requires a determiner (my mom)
projection.evidence: CGEL's descriptions of strong names, kin-term names and emotive embellishment (pp. 517-520), and attested bare kin-term arguments in CHILDES caregiver speech

diagnostics: no article or genitive determiner in argument functions

known_boundary_items: Gambia / the Gambia (optional article)
titles such as If on a winter's night a traveler (not NPs; CGEL excludes titles from the strong/weak account)

curious.title: Names that stand alone
curious.summary: Names like Kim and New York need no the, a or my in front of them, and some family words can work the same way.
curious.body: A name like Kim or New York stands on its own in a sentence: Kim called. She lives in New York. A family word can do the same job when it works as a name. Mom called uses Mom as her name, while my mom called uses the same word to say what she is to me, and then it needs a determiner such as my in front. A few feeling words, such as poor, can also sit in front of a name with nothing else: Poor Henry needs a rest. Names that take the, such as the Thames, belong to a different kind. Calling out someone's name, as in Sally!, is also a separate matter. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Say Mom called and then my mom called. In which one is Mom what you call her?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why names appear without a determiner, including a family word like Mom when it is used as a name.
teacher.explain: The construction is a singular NP with no determiner, naming semantics, and referential use in an argument function (subject, object in a VP, object in a PP). Its head may be a proper noun (Kim, Ukraine) or a common noun in naming use (Mom, Grandma). Naming semantics means a conventional name, not mere identifiability: the doctor can identify someone without being a name. Names with the article (the Thames) are weak proper names and outside the construction. So are bare vocatives, whose bareness comes from the vocative function (Waiter!). A small set of emotive adjectives can embellish a strong name without a determiner. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and departs from CGEL's usage: it treats proper name as a semantic classification and the NP as the unit with a head.
teacher.terms: CGEL: strong proper names (no determiner) and weak ones (with the, as in the Thames). Proper name is a semantic category; proper nouns are the word class specialized for heading such NPs. Kin terms used as names remain common nouns on CGEL's analysis.

examples.text: You wanna roll the ball to [Mommy]?

contrasts.note: Naming use; no determiner.
Relational use; the same noun takes a determiner.

contrasts.text: The poor dog needs a rest.
contrasts.note: An ordinary singular count noun takes the same adjective with a determiner.
A weak proper name, with the article; outside this construction.

watch_for: A learner might assume Mom must take a determiner like any other singular count noun.
A learner might treat a bare vocative such as Waiter! as an instance, when its bareness comes from the vocative function.
A learner might treat the Thames as the same kind of name as Kim.
teacher.activity: Students list names from their lives (people, places, family words). They test each in a subject slot and in a relational version with my, then sort into names that stand alone and nouns that need a determiner.

child.hook: Why do we say Mom called but my mom called?
child.explain: Names like Kim and New York stand on their own. Mom can be a name too, when it's what you call her. When you say my mom, you're saying who she is to you.
child.play: Say Kim called. Then put Grandma in place of Kim. Then try my grandma called. Which ones can stand alone?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body now says the relational use needs a determiner such as my, not only my; teacher.summary no longer suggests Mom changes noun category (it is a common noun in naming use); child.play gives the sentence frame and drops the city option. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; teacher.terms drops 'usual'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Strong Proper Name Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/strong-proper-name-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subject-Oriented Ascriptive Predicative

1.definition: Attributes a property, class or condition to the subject referent.

projection.target: The complement describes Jo, and the corresponding stative property can often be predicated with be. An ordinary object cannot replace the adjective in the same role.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Verbs that describe the subject
curious.summary: Some verbs link the subject to a word or phrase that tells you what the subject is like.
curious.body: In Jo seems unusually calm, the part after seems doesn't name something Jo acts on. It describes Jo. The verb simply links the person to a quality, a class or a condition. One sign of this is that the same description can be given with be: Jo is unusually calm. Another is that an ordinary object can't take the place of the describing word in that role. This dictionary marks the pattern as provisional and bases it on a single illustration.
curious.try: Take a sentence like Jo seems calm and replace seems with is. Does the description of Jo stay the same?

teacher.summary: Helps students see that the word after a linking verb describes the subject rather than acting as an object.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause with a subject, a linking verb, and a predicative complement that attributes a property, class or condition to the subject referent. In Jo seems unusually calm, the complement describes Jo, and the corresponding stative property can often be predicated with be. An ordinary object cannot replace the adjective in the same role, which is one way to tell this complement from an object. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional and offers one constructed illustration, so use it as a starting point for classroom examples.
teacher.terms: Predicative complement is the CGEL term; textbooks sometimes call it a subject complement. This dictionary sets it beside an object-oriented counterpart.
watch_for: A learner might treat the word after seems as an object, when it describes the subject.
A learner might read seems as describing an action by Jo, when it links Jo to a description.
teacher.activity: Give students sentences with seems, looks and is plus a description. They underline the person or thing being described and swap seems for is, checking that the description still applies to the same subject.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subject-Oriented Ascriptive Predicative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subject-ascriptive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subject Control in a to-Infinitival Complement
pattern: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

entry.name: Subject Control in a to-Infinitival Complement
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

1.definition: Interprets the matrix subject as undertaking, intending, or experiencing the subordinate situation.

relatedConstructions.notes: Jo promised to return assigns Jo a role in the promising. There seems to be a leak allows dummy there because the subject is selected through the infinitival.

projection.target: Jo is the promiser and the understood returner. A dummy there cannot replace Jo as the promiser.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Who does the infinitive's action?
curious.summary: In some sentences, the person named at the start is also the one who does the action in the to-phrase.
curious.body: In Jo promised to return, Jo is the one who promises and also the one who returns. The to-phrase has no subject of its own, so we understand it as Jo. What matters is that Jo has a role in the promising: Jo takes on the undertaking, intention or experience described. A stand-in subject like the there of There seems to be a leak can't take over that role in the promising. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and bases it on one constructed illustration.

examples.text: There seems to be a leak.

curious.try: In Jo promised to return, who returns? Who promises? Is it the same person?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining who performs the action in a to-infinitive after verbs like promise.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause whose subject is understood as the subject of the to-infinitival complement. The matrix subject undertakes, intends or experiences the subordinate situation: in Jo promised to return, Jo is both promiser and returner, so Jo is assigned a role in the promising. A dummy there cannot replace Jo as the promiser. That separates subject control from subject raising: in There seems to be a leak, dummy there is allowed because the subject is selected through the infinitival. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration.
teacher.terms: This dictionary’s term is subject control; the related pattern is subject raising. Textbooks sometimes describe the infinitival's missing subject as an understood subject.

contrasts.note: Jo has a role in the promising; control.

contrasts.text: There seems to be a leak.
contrasts.note: Dummy there is possible because the subject is selected through the infinitival; raising.

watch_for: A learner might think the to-phrase has no subject at all, when it is understood as the subject of the main verb.
A learner might treat promise and seem as the same pattern because both are followed by to.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with verbs like promise, try and hope followed by a to-phrase. For each they say who does the second action and mark the link from the subject to the infinitive.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subject Control in a to-Infinitival Complement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subject-control-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subject-determiner (Genitive NP)

1.definition: Genitive NP realizes determiner function with a subject-like semantic relation to the head nominal

examples.note: Genitive NP corresponds to the subject/agent of the nominalization

examples.form: the committee's approval of the plan
examples.note: Genitive NP corresponds to the notional subject of the event noun

constraints.description: Genitive NP occupies the determiner position in NP structure.
Genitive NP stands in a subject-like relation to the head noun (e.g., agent/experiencer of a nominalized predicate), not mere possession.

projection.target: In the committee’s approval of the plan, the committee can map to the subject of approved the plan. In the committee’s photograph, an ownership or other relation remains possible. Genitive position alone does not license an agent interpretation.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts argument-realizing genitives with the wider range of ordinary genitive relations.

curious.title: A genitive that acts like a subject
curious.summary: Sometimes the word with 's before a noun tells you who did the action the noun names, not who owns something.
curious.body: In the committee's approval of the plan, the committee is the one who approved. The noun approval names an action, and the committee plays the part a subject would play in the matching sentence, the committee approved the plan. Compare the committee's photograph. There the link can be ownership or some other relation. So the 's form alone doesn't tell you the committee is the doer; it depends on the noun. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Turn the committee's approval of the plan into a sentence with a verb. Who is the subject? Now do the same with the committee's photograph. What changes?

teacher.summary: Explains genitives that match a verb's subject, as in the committee's approval, against ordinary genitives that show ownership.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a genitive NP in determiner function whose relation to the head noun resembles that of a subject. In Brett's use of the microphone and the committee's approval of the plan, the genitive corresponds to the notional subject of the event noun's verb, an agent or experiencer. This is not mere possession. In the committee's photograph, an ownership or other relation remains possible, so genitive position alone does not license an agent interpretation. The distinction is argument-realizing versus the wider range of ordinary genitive relations. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a subjective genitive. CGEL: genitive NP in determiner function. Avoid possessive as a label, since ownership is only one possible relation.

contrasts.text: the committee's approval of the plan
contrasts.note: The committee maps to the subject of approved the plan.
Ownership or another relation remains possible.

watch_for: A learner might read every genitive as showing ownership.
A learner might take the genitive in the committee's approval as the thing approved instead of the one who approved.
teacher.activity: Give students noun phrases with a genitive and a noun such as approval, arrival or photograph. They try to turn each into a sentence with a verb and decide whether the genitive becomes the subject.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subject-determiner (Genitive NP)." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subject-determiner-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subject Extraposition
pattern: Clause[Subject:dummy it + VP[... + extraposed content clause or infinitival]]

entry.name: Subject Extraposition
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject:dummy it + VP[... + extraposed content clause or infinitival]]

1.definition: Puts the situation under discussion after the predicate, leaving dummy it in subject position.
1.details: A that-clause, an interrogative clause, or an infinitival may occur in the later position. The basic initial-clause version is often less natural when the information is presented as new. A referential NP does not ordinarily alternate in this way. In a right dislocation like It’s fascinating, this book, it refers to the book.

examples.form: [It worries me that he hasn’t phoned.]
examples.note: Compare the basic That he hasn’t phoned worries me.

examples.form: [It is unclear why she told him.]

relatedConstructions.notes: The matrix clause has its own subject and predicate.
The pronoun is referential in the dislocated NP construction.
In It surprised me that Jo left, dummy it is subject. In I find it surprising that Jo left, it is object and the content clause follows the predicative.

grounds.note: Lists finite and infinitival patterns with dummy it.

projection.target: A clause can appear after the predicate with dummy it. The same predicate need not allow an ordinary NP in that position. Extraposition is especially useful with newly introduced information.
projection.evidence: CGEL gives matched clauses, an excluded ordinary NP, and an attested text opening. CASA lists finite and infinitival forms separately.

curious.title: Saving the clause for the end
curious.summary: A sentence can start with it and put a clause after the verb to say what the situation is.
curious.body: Instead of saying That he hasn't phoned worries me, we can say It worries me that he hasn't phoned. The clause that tells what the worry is about moves to the end, and the small word it fills the subject spot as a stand-in with nothing of its own to refer to. The later part can be a that-clause, a question clause or a to-phrase. This dictionary points out that the version with the clause up front is often less natural when the information is new. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [It worries me that he hasn't phoned.]
[It is unclear why she told him.]

curious.try: Take It would be pointless to resist and try putting the to-phrase at the start. Which version fits better when you tell someone a piece of news?

teacher.summary: Teaches the it ... that/to pattern and how to tell dummy it from a pronoun that refers.
teacher.explain: The matrix subject is dummy it, and the situation under discussion comes after the predicate as an extraposed content clause or infinitival. A that-clause, an interrogative clause or a to-infinitival may occur in the later position. The basic initial-clause version is often less natural when the information is presented as new. A referential NP doesn't ordinarily alternate in this way. Dummy it has no referent. This differs from right dislocation, where the pronoun does refer to the dislocated noun phrase. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, with high confidence.
teacher.terms: CGEL: extraposition with dummy it. Textbooks sometimes call this anticipatory or expletive it.

examples.text: [It worries me that he hasn't phoned.]
[It is unclear why she told him.]

contrasts.text: That he hasn't phoned worries me.
contrasts.note: The basic version, with the clause in subject position.

contrasts.text: It surprised me that Jo left.
contrasts.note: Dummy it is the subject of the matrix clause.

contrasts.text: I find it surprising that Jo left.
contrasts.note: Here it is an object and the clause follows the predicative; a separate pattern.

watch_for: A learner might look for a noun that it stands for, when dummy it refers to nothing.
A learner might mix up It surprised me that Jo left with I find it surprising that Jo left, where it is an object.
teacher.activity: Students are given sentences with a clause at the start and rewrite them with it and the clause at the end. They then decide which version sounds better when the news is new.

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary no longer calls the later clause the real subject (this dictionary keeps dummy it as the subject); teacher summary no longer calls the pattern common (no frequency claim in this dictionary). Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' wording.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subject Extraposition." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subject-extraposition-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subject-Linked Genitive Superlative

1.definition: Presents the performance at an extreme on a scale associated with the subject.
1.details: In worked our hardest, our refers to the people doing the work and hardest characterizes their effort. The postverbal expression has no overt noun and supplies a degree or standard. A linked at-pattern is available with some verbs. Its range differs, as in be at one’s best. The label objoid in the cited work notes the position and the unusual object profile. The present entry leaves the grammatical function of the bare phrase open.

examples.form: Kate and I have [worked our hardest] to raise them that way.
examples.note: COCA example in CASA. Our is linked to the subject.
Published comparison with the separate at-pattern, using the same verb.
Published illustration of the bare variant.

relatedConstructions.notes: The superlative supplies a degree standard.
The examples have no overt noun after the superlative. The head analysis remains open.

grounds.note: Documents conventional collocations and productivity from COCA.
Distinguishes the bare and at-patterns and provides corpus examples.
Reports asymmetric priming and discusses what this can support about their relation.

projection.target: The genitive normally tracks the subject while the bare superlative supplies a high degree for the performance. A related phrase with at can broaden the interpretation to a condition.
projection.evidence: Bouso’s corpus analysis and CASA’s contrasted records. The published priming study reports an asymmetry between the two forms.

curious.title: Worked our hardest
curious.summary: A verb followed by a genitive and a superlative, as in worked our hardest, says the effort reached its highest point.
curious.body: In worked our hardest, the word our points back to the people doing the work, and hardest describes their effort. There's no noun after hardest. The phrase supplies a degree, a standard of how hard. A version with at is also possible with some verbs: They worked at their hardest. The two don't have exactly the same range. Be at one's best is another at-pattern. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and leaves open what grammatical role the bare phrase has.

examples.text: Kate and I have [worked our hardest] to raise them that way.

curious.try: Say They worked their hardest and They worked at their hardest. Do they feel the same to you?

teacher.summary: Optional enrichment on worked their hardest and the related at-pattern.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a clause with a subject and a verb followed by a phrase whose genitive is linked to the subject and whose superlative sets a high degree: our refers to those doing the work, and hardest characterizes their effort. The postverbal expression has no overt noun. A linked at-pattern is available with some verbs, with a different range (be at one's best). The cited work uses the label objoid for the position and unusual object profile. This dictionary leaves the grammatical function of the bare phrase open, and the head analysis is open, so avoid presenting one analysis as settled.
teacher.terms: Objoid is the label in the cited work. This dictionary leaves the function of the bare phrase open.

examples.text: Kate and I have [worked our hardest] to raise them that way.

contrasts.note: The at-pattern, with the same verb.
The bare variant.

watch_for: A learner might look for a noun after hardest, when the phrase has no overt noun.
A learner might read our or their as owning something, when it tracks the subject.
teacher.activity: Students complete They worked ___ hardest and We tried ___ hardest with the matching genitive for each subject. They check that the genitive refers to the people doing the work.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subject-Linked Genitive Superlative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subject-genitive-superlative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subject Raising with a Catenative Verb
pattern: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

entry.name: Subject Raising with a Catenative Verb
entry.pattern: Clause[Subject NPᵢ + V + to-infinitival with understood subjectᵢ]

1.definition: Combines a verbal assessment or aspectual predicate with a subject selected through its complement.

examples.form: [Jo seems to have checked the lock].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. The corresponding passive, The lock seems to have been checked by Jo, preserves the subordinate event being assessed.

projection.target: Dummy there is acceptable, and active and passive descriptions of the subordinate event preserve what seems to hold. This distinguishes raising from subject control.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Sentences where the subject belongs to the next verb
curious.summary: With verbs like seem, the subject of the sentence really belongs to the to-phrase that follows.
curious.body: In There seems to be a leak, the word there can't be doing anything of its own. It is the subject because the to-phrase, to be a leak, selects it. The verb seems gives an assessment of what follows. That's why Jo seems to have checked the lock and The lock seems to have been checked by Jo describe the same thing that seems to hold. The subordinate event is what's being assessed. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and bases it on constructed illustrations.

examples.text: [Jo seems to have checked the lock].
The lock seems to have been checked by Jo.

curious.try: Say Jo seems to have checked the lock. Then say The lock seems to have been checked by Jo. Does what seems to be the case change?

teacher.summary: Useful for contrasting seem-type verbs with promise-type verbs and for showing why dummy there works with them.
teacher.explain: The pattern combines a verbal assessment or aspectual predicate with a subject selected through its complement. Two tests show it. Dummy there is acceptable (There seems to be a leak), and active and passive descriptions of the subordinate event preserve what seems to hold (Jo seems to have checked the lock; The lock seems to have been checked by Jo). Subject control, as in Jo promised to return, differs on both counts. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional and bases it on constructed illustrations.
teacher.terms: Subject raising is this dictionary's name for it. Sometimes called subject-to-subject raising. The contrast is with subject control.

examples.text: [Jo seems to have checked the lock].

contrasts.text: Jo seems to have checked the lock.
contrasts.note: Active; the subordinate event is what seems to hold.

contrasts.text: The lock seems to have been checked by Jo.
contrasts.note: The passive preserves what seems to hold.
Control; Jo has a role in the promising.

watch_for: A learner might think the subject of seems is doing the seeming.
A learner might treat seems to and promised to as the same pattern, when only one allows dummy there.
teacher.activity: Students try the dummy there and the passive tests on sets of verbs followed by to-phrases. They sort the verbs into those that pass both tests and those that do not.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body no longer says seems adds a stage in time (the entry's examples use seems to assess a situation); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subject Raising with a Catenative Verb." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subject-raising-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Subject-Oriented Resultative
pattern: VP[Head:V + PredComp:XP predicated of the subject]

entry.name: Subject-Oriented Resultative
entry.pattern: VP[Head:V + PredComp:XP predicated of the subject]

1.definition: Uses a postverbal complement to specify the state the subject reaches.

projection.target: Solid describes the outcome of freezing, whereas a depictive predicate ordinarily holds during the event. No separate object licenses solid in this use.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Saying how the subject ends up
curious.summary: A word after the verb can tell you what state the subject reaches, as in froze solid.
curious.body: In The basin froze solid, the word solid says what state the basin ended up in. It describes the outcome of the freezing, and no other object is needed to make it work. That makes it different from a word that describes how someone was while an action happened. This dictionary notes that this second kind ordinarily holds during the event, while the result word marks where the event ends up. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one illustration.
curious.try: Take the basin froze and add a word that says what it became. What happens to the meaning?

teacher.summary: Helps students distinguish a result state that the subject reaches from a description that holds during the action.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb followed by a predicative complement that specifies the state the subject reaches. In The basin froze solid, solid describes the outcome of freezing. A depictive predicate, by contrast, ordinarily holds during the event, as in Jo arrived hungry. No separate object licenses solid here. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional, rests on one constructed example, and names a related object-oriented resultative as a separate entry.
teacher.terms: Resultative is the usual textbook term. Depictive is the usual term for the description that holds during the event.

contrasts.note: Solid is the outcome of the freezing; resultative.
Hungry describes Jo during the arriving; depictive.

watch_for: A learner might read solid as a description that holds during the freezing, when it names the outcome.
A learner might look for an object after froze, when the complement is predicated of the subject.
teacher.activity: Give students verbs such as freeze, melt and dry. They add a word that says the end state, then check that it describes the subject at the end of the event, not during it.

child.hook: What word tells you how the water ended up after it froze?
child.explain: Some words after a verb tell how something ended up. The pond froze solid. Solid is how the pond ended up after it froze.
child.play: Pick a verb such as froze or melted. Add a word that says how the thing ended up. Read your sentence to a friend and see if they can say how it ended.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Subject-Oriented Resultative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subject-resultative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Mandative Subjunctive

1.definition: Presents the content of a requirement, recommendation, or request.

examples.form: They requested [that the gate remain closed].
They requested [that the gate not be opened].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. The subjunctive uses plain be after not, without support from do.

projection.target: Remain does not carry third-person singular marking. With negative not the plain form can occur without finite do, as in that it not remain closed.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Clauses that state a requirement
curious.summary: After words like requested, a that-clause can use the plain form of the verb to say what is required or recommended.
curious.body: In They requested that the gate remain closed, the clause after that gives the content of a request. The verb remain is in its plain form: it doesn't take an -s even though the gate is singular. The plain form also shows up with not. In that the gate not be opened, not comes before plain be, and no do is needed. The grammar books call this the subjunctive. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and gives only constructed examples.

examples.text: They requested [that the gate remain closed].
They requested [that the gate not be opened].

curious.try: Say They requested that the gate remain closed. What would the verb be in an ordinary statement, The gate remains closed? How does remain differ?

teacher.summary: Explains why a that-clause after request-type words takes the plain verb form and does not mark person or tense.
teacher.explain: The mandative subjunctive is a content clause with (that), a subject and a plain-form verb, presenting the content of a requirement, recommendation or request. Remain does not carry third-person singular marking. With negative not, the plain form can occur without finite do, as in that it not remain closed. In They requested that the gate not be opened, plain be follows not without support from do. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and a separate entry covers the related mandative should construction.
teacher.terms: Mandative subjunctive is a textbook name. In CGEL terms the verb is a plain form in a declarative content clause.

examples.text: They requested [that the gate remain closed].
They requested [that the gate not be opened].

contrasts.text: They requested that the gate remain closed.
contrasts.note: Plain form; no third-person singular marking.

contrasts.text: They requested that the gate not be opened.
contrasts.note: Plain be after not, without support from do.

watch_for: A learner might expect -s on remain because the gate is third-person singular.
A learner might expect do to support not in the clause, when plain be follows not directly.
teacher.activity: Students complete sentences beginning with demand, insist, recommend and request followed by a that-clause. They circle the verb form and say whether it carries person or tense marking.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Mandative Subjunctive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/subjunctive-mandative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Exemplifying such as
pattern: Nom or NP + such as + example XP or coordination

entry.name: Exemplifying such as
entry.pattern: Nom or NP + such as + example XP or coordination

1.definition: Introduces one or more illustrative members of the class just described.

examples.form: Bring safety gear [such as gloves and goggles].

projection.target: The examples do not exhaust the class. Other suitable safety gear can meet the instruction without being on the example list.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Giving examples with such as
curious.summary: Such as introduces some examples of the kind of thing you've just named.
curious.body: In Bring safety gear such as gloves and goggles, such as introduces examples of safety gear. The phrase is an offer of illustration, not a full list. That means other safety gear can still meet the instruction. Someone who brings a helmet hasn't ignored the request just because a helmet wasn't in the list. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration.

examples.text: Bring safety gear [such as gloves and goggles].
We need fruit [such as apples and pears].

curious.try: Write a sentence naming a kind of thing, then add such as and two examples. Could something not on your list still count?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining how such as introduces examples without listing everything.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a noun or NP followed by such as and one or more illustrative members of the class just described, given as a phrase or coordination. The examples do not exhaust the class: other suitable safety gear can meet the instruction without being on the example list. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration. It lists same-as comparison and integrated relative modifiers as related patterns in separate entries.
teacher.terms: Exemplification is the term the cited grammar uses for this role.

examples.text: Bring safety gear [such as gloves and goggles].
We need fruit [such as apples and pears].

watch_for: A learner might read the examples after such as as a complete list.
A learner might think a helmet wouldn't count in the safety gear example because it isn't listed.
teacher.activity: Students write instructions that name a class and give examples with such as, for example "Pack warm clothes such as ...". A partner suggests another item that fits the class but isn't on the list.

child.hook: When you say such as, do you name everything?
child.explain: Such as lets you name a few examples. It doesn't have to name everything. Other things of the same kind can fit too.

examples.text: Bring snacks [such as apples and crackers].
Bring safety gear [such as gloves and goggles].

child.play: Name a group, like pets or fruit. Say it with such as and two examples. Then a friend adds one more thing that fits.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Exemplifying such as." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/such-as-exemplification-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Degree such with Nominal and Result Clause

entry.name: Degree such with Nominal and Result Clause

1.definition: Characterizes the extent or kind of something through an associated result.

examples.form: It was [such a cold morning that the locks froze].

projection.target: In the singular count pattern such precedes a. A plural nominal such as such cold mornings uses no a, while the result dependency remains available.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Such a cold morning that the locks froze
curious.summary: Such plus a noun phrase can describe how extreme something was by giving what resulted from it.
curious.body: In It was such a cold morning that the locks froze, the second part tells how cold the morning was: cold enough to freeze the locks. The result clause that follows measures the extent or kind of morning it was. With a single countable noun, such comes before a. With a plural, as in such cold mornings, there is no a, and the result clause is still possible. The word that can be left out in the pattern. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: It was [such a cold morning that the locks froze].
It was [such a loud noise that the dog jumped].

curious.try: Finish this sentence in your own words. It was such a hot day that ...

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining such a/an plus a result clause, and the plural version without a.
teacher.explain: The pattern is such followed by a nominal expression and a content clause (that is optional) which gives a result. It characterizes the extent or kind of something through that associated result. In the singular count pattern, such precedes a. A plural nominal such as such cold mornings uses no a, while the result dependency remains available. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and has one constructed illustration. A related so-nominal pattern has its own entry.
teacher.terms: Result clause and such ... that are textbook labels for the pattern. The cited grammar treats such as a word in its own right.

examples.text: It was [such a cold morning that the locks froze].

contrasts.note: Singular count noun; such comes before a.
Plural; no a, and the result clause is still possible.

watch_for: A learner might put a before such in the singular pattern.
A learner might add a to a plural nominal after such.
A learner might read the that-clause as a relative clause instead of a result.
teacher.activity: Students complete such a ... that and such ... that sentences with their own results, then compare singular and plural versions of the same idea.

child.hook: How cold was the morning if the locks froze?
child.explain: You can use such to say how big or strong something was. Then you say what happened because of it. The locks froze because the morning was so cold.

examples.text: It was [such a cold morning that the locks froze].
It was [such a loud noise that the dog jumped].

child.play: Start with It was such a big ... and finish it with that and something that happened. See whose ending is the funniest.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Degree such with Nominal and Result Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/such-nominal-result-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Conditional provided that

1.definition: States a proviso under which a proposal or promise holds.

examples.form: You can use the room [provided that you lock up].

projection.target: In a permission context the phrase gives a condition on permission. It does not report the locking as already true.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Giving permission on one condition
curious.summary: Provided that adds a condition under which a promise or permission holds.
curious.body: In You can use the room provided that you lock up, the last part sets a condition. Locking up is the condition on permission to use the room. The phrase doesn't say that locking up has already happened. It sets a condition on the permission. The word that can be left out: provided you lock up works the same way in the pattern. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: You can use the room [provided that you lock up].
You can play outside [provided that you wear a coat].

curious.try: Give someone permission to do something, then add provided that and a condition. Does the condition sound like it has already happened?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining provided that as a way to attach a condition to a permission or promise.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a conditional PP formed from provided (that) and a finite clause. It states a proviso under which a proposal or promise holds. In a permission context the phrase gives a condition on permission: it does not report the locking as already true. This dictionary treats the whole phrase as a PP with a finite clause, one of the clause-taking prepositions. This analysis is provisional, and a separate entry covers the related unless pattern.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a subordinating conjunction in traditional grammar. CGEL: a preposition taking a finite clause.

examples.text: You can use the room [provided that you lock up].

watch_for: A learner might read provided that you lock up as saying you have already locked up.
A learner might think provided is only a verb, when here it introduces a condition.
teacher.activity: Students write permissions with provided that, for example about homework or the school library. A partner restates each as what you may do and what the condition is.

child.hook: In You can play outside provided that you wear a coat, what is the condition?
child.explain: Provided that gives a rule for something you're allowed to do. You can do it if the rule is met.

examples.text: You can use the room [provided that you lock up].
You can play outside [provided that you wear a coat].

child.play: Make up a rule using provided that. Say what you may do, then the condition. Your friend says which part is the condition.

checked.note: Fixed: child hook now asks for the condition in a given sentence instead of asking what a rule 'needs'; child game no longer says the condition 'has to happen first' (the entry treats it as a condition on permission); 'the entry' replaced by 'this analysis'. Second round: fixed child.explain by cutting 'but only', which made the proviso a necessary condition (this dictionary says it states a condition under which permission holds); curious.body now calls locking up the condition on permission rather than something permission depends on or requires.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Conditional provided that." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/sufficiency-provided-that-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Scalar Superlative with a Comparison Set
pattern: superlative AdjP/AdvP, optionally with of/in domain expression

entry.name: Scalar Superlative with a Comparison Set
entry.pattern: superlative AdjP/AdvP, optionally with of/in domain expression

1.definition: Places the chosen instance at an extreme relative to a contextually delimited set.

examples.form: Jo chose the [narrowest of the three aisles].

projection.target: Of the three restricts the comparison set. The aisle need not count as narrow by an independent contextual standard.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: The most extreme of a group
curious.summary: A word like narrowest picks one item as the extreme within a set the speaker has in mind.
curious.body: In Jo chose the narrowest of the three aisles, narrowest picks out one aisle at the extreme end of a comparison. The comparison set is the three aisles, and of the three marks it. The set limits what the word is compared with. So the chosen aisle needn't be narrow by any other standard. It's the narrowest only among those three. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration.

examples.text: Jo chose the [narrowest of the three aisles].
Sam picked the [smallest of the four puppies].
