curious.try: Choose three objects near you. Say which is the tallest or the lightest of the three. Would your answer change with a different set?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining superlatives and the set they are measured against.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a superlative adjective or adverb phrase, optionally with an of or in expression naming the domain. It places the chosen instance at an extreme relative to a contextually delimited set. Of the three restricts the comparison set, so the aisle need not count as narrow by an independent contextual standard. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and has one constructed illustration. A related entry covers the subject-linked genitive superlative, as in worked their hardest.
teacher.terms: Superlative grade of an adjective or adverb. Gradation is a separate entry.

examples.text: Jo chose the [narrowest of the three aisles].
Mia is the [tallest in her class].

watch_for: A learner might think the narrowest aisle must be narrow by an outside standard, when it is only the narrowest among the three.
A learner might leave out the comparison set or ignore of the three and in her class.
teacher.activity: Show students a set of three or four items. They write superlative sentences with of and in phrases naming the set, then change the set and see how the sentence changes.

child.hook: Which pet is the smallest of your three?
child.explain: Words like smallest and narrowest pick one thing from a group. The group is the set you're comparing. Change the group and the answer can change.

examples.text: Jo chose the [narrowest of the three aisles].
Sam picked the [smallest of the four puppies].

child.play: Line up three toys. Say which is the biggest of the three. Swap one toy and say it again.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Scalar Superlative with a Comparison Set." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/superlative-grade-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Supplementary Appositive NP
pattern: anchor NP + supplementary NP with a co-referential interpretation

entry.name: Supplementary Appositive NP
entry.pattern: anchor NP + supplementary NP with a co-referential interpretation

1.definition: Adds a second description or identification of a discourse referent.

projection.target: The second NP can be set off prosodically and contributes its own identification or characterization. Removing it leaves the anchor available for the same matrix role.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A second description added to a name
curious.summary: A second noun phrase beside the first adds another way of identifying the same person or thing.
curious.body: In Lee, our treasurer, signed the form, our treasurer refers to the same person as Lee. It adds a second description to a person already named. The added phrase can be set off in speech by its own rhythm, and it contributes its own identification or characterization. If you take it out, Lee signed the form still works with the same role in the sentence. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration.
curious.try: Take a sentence naming someone, add a phrase between commas that tells who they are, then remove it. Does the rest still work?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining added noun phrases set off by commas, such as Lee, our treasurer.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an anchor NP followed by a supplementary NP with a co-referential interpretation. It adds a second description or identification of a discourse referent. The second NP can be set off prosodically and contributes its own identification or characterization. Removing it leaves the anchor available for the same matrix role. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and has one constructed illustration. Related separate entries cover a restrictive appositive name and the supplementary relative clause.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar sometimes calls this non-restrictive apposition. CGEL: supplementary apposition.

contrasts.text: Lee, our treasurer, signed the form.
contrasts.note: Supplementary NP adds a second identification.
With the added NP removed, the anchor still fills the same role.

watch_for: A learner might treat Lee and our treasurer as two different people.
A learner might think the added phrase is needed to complete the sentence.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences naming a person or place and adding a second description in a comma-set phrase. They test whether removing the phrase leaves a complete sentence and say what the phrase adds.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Supplementary Appositive NP." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/supplementary-appositive-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Supplementary Relative

1.definition: Adds a separate predication about a referent or a larger anchor.

examples.form: Jo visited Bath, [which she had never seen before].

projection.target: The clause can add information about an already identified referent. Substituting bare that-relative syntax generally fails in the same supplementary reading.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: A which clause that adds extra information
curious.summary: A which clause after a name can add a separate piece of information about it.
curious.body: In Jo visited Bath, which she had never seen before, the which clause adds a second statement. It tells us something more about Bath, a place already identified. It doesn't help us work out which place is meant. A which clause can also add information about a larger anchor than a single noun. This dictionary notes that swapping in a bare that-relative generally fails to give the same added-information reading. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration.

examples.text: Jo visited Bath, [which she had never seen before].

curious.try: Add a which clause after the name of a place you know, and say what extra information it gives.

teacher.summary: Helps explain which clauses that add information about an already identified referent, set off by commas.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an anchor followed by a supplementary wh-relative clause. It adds a separate predication about a referent or a larger anchor: in Jo visited Bath, which she had never seen before, the clause adds information about Bath, an already identified referent. Substituting bare that-relative syntax generally fails in the same supplementary reading. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and has one constructed illustration. It lists the relative word as a part of this pattern.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammar sometimes calls this a non-restrictive relative clause. CGEL: supplementary relative clause.

examples.text: Jo visited Bath, [which she had never seen before].

watch_for: A learner might read the which clause as helping to pick out which place is meant, when it adds information about a place already identified.
A learner might swap in that for which and expect the same added-information reading.
teacher.activity: Students write a sentence naming a place, then add a which clause with extra information about it. A partner explains what the clause adds and whether it helps identify the place.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Supplementary Relative." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/supplementary-relative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deverbal Synthetic Noun Compound
pattern: N[participant nominal base + derived deverbal noun]

entry.name: Deverbal Synthetic Noun Compound
entry.pattern: N[participant nominal base + derived deverbal noun]

1.definition: Builds a compound whose first element supplies a participant associated with the verbal base.

projection.target: In the agentive reading the eventual cleaner cleans windows. Ordinary nondeverbal compounds can connect their two nouns through a much wider range of contextually inferred relations.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Nouns like window-cleaner
curious.summary: In its agentive reading, a compound like window-cleaner names a person by the thing they work on and what they do.
curious.body: In They hired a window-cleaner, the first part, window, names what is acted on, and cleaner names the one who does the action. A window-cleaner is someone who cleans windows. Other compounds are looser. A compound made of two ordinary nouns can connect them through a much wider range of relations, which the listener works out from context. In the pattern here, the first part matches a participant in the action of the verb. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and gives one constructed illustration.
curious.try: Think of someone whose job is named by a thing plus a person who does something to it. Can you say it with a verb, like cleans windows?

teacher.summary: Explains compounds like window-cleaner, where the first noun is a participant of the verb in the second word.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a compound noun whose first element supplies a participant associated with the verbal base of the second element, a deverbal noun. In the agentive reading, a window-cleaner is someone who cleans windows. Ordinary nondeverbal compounds can connect their two nouns through a much wider range of contextually inferred relations. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and gives one constructed illustration. A related entry covers deverbal nouns in -er.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called synthetic compounds.

contrasts.note: The first noun is what the verb acts on; the second names the doer.
An ordinary compound; the link between the nouns is inferred from context.

watch_for: A learner might read window-cleaner as a cleaner that belongs to windows, rather than someone who cleans windows.
A learner might expect every two-noun compound to link its parts the way window-cleaner does.
teacher.activity: Students list compounds like window-cleaner, where a participant noun is followed by a noun derived from a verb. They say what each person does with a verb, as in cleans windows, then compare them with compounds like coffee cup, whose link is looser.

child.hook: What does a window-cleaner do?
child.explain: Some words put what you work on first, then the person who does the job. A window-cleaner cleans windows. A dog-walker walks dogs.
child.play: Make a job word like this from a thing and a doer. What does the person do? Say it with a verb.

checked.note: Fixed: the teacher activity no longer treats an -er ending as enough for an object paraphrase (the entry requires a derived deverbal noun with a participant first element); curious summary marks the agentive reading. Dismissed: none. Second round: fixed teacher.terms, which attributed synthetic compounds to traditional grammar (the entry uses the term in its name without that attribution); curious.body now says this dictionary gives one constructed illustration rather than that the analysis rests on it.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deverbal Synthetic Noun Compound." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/synthetic-noun-compound-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Tag Question
pattern: Anchor:Clause[declarative | exclamative] + Tag:Clause[Head:VP[Head:V[auxiliary]]; Subject:NP[personal pronoun]; surface Auxiliary–Subject (+ not)] => Meaning:Question

entry.name: Tag Question
entry.pattern: Anchor:Clause[declarative | exclamative] + Tag:Clause[Head:VP[Head:V[auxiliary]]; Subject:NP[personal pronoun]; surface Auxiliary–Subject (+ not)] => Meaning:Question

dimensions.form: A declarative or exclamative Anchor Clause followed by a supplementary short closed-interrogative Tag Clause; the tag has a personal-pronoun Subject and an auxiliary-headed VP, with surface subject–auxiliary inversion
dimensions.meaning: A normally biased polar question anchored to the proposition of the first Clause; polarity relation and prosody distinguish reversed- and constant-polarity interpretations
dimensions.function: Seeks verification, acknowledgement, agreement, or uptake of the anchor, with exclamative anchors normally supporting acknowledgement or rhetorical force rather than doubt
dimensions.distribution: Independent utterances in which a declarative or exclamative Clause licenses a following supplementary Tag Clause

1.specialization: A reversed-polarity tag presents a biased polar answer set whose salient positive member confirms the anchor proposition. A rising tag asks for verification or expresses doubt; a falling tag seeks acknowledgement and may be rhetorical. Exclamative anchors normally take this falling pattern because the truth of their proposition is presented as not at issue.

examples.note: Positive declarative Anchor Clause plus negative Tag Clause; reversed polarity
Tag auxiliary agrees with plural tag Subject they, not directly with singular anchor Subject everybody

examples.form: [What a mess I've made of things], [haven't I]?
examples.note: Exclamative Anchor Clause with the normally falling, acknowledgement-oriented reversed tag

2.specialization: A constant-polarity tag has the same polarity as its typically positive declarative anchor. With its characteristic slight rise, it commonly attributes the anchor content to the addressee and conveys acknowledgement, surprise, disapproval, reproach, or sarcasm rather than speaker doubt.

examples.note: Positive declarative anchor and positive tag; constant polarity

examples.form: [So you have forgotten your homework again], [have you]?
examples.note: Constant-polarity tag with reproachful or disapproving force

constraints.description: The construction combines an Anchor Clause with a supplementary Tag Clause; it does not turn their combination into a single Clause. Each Clause independently has the strict structure (Subject +) Head:VP.

The Anchor is a declarative or exclamative Clause. The Tag is a short closed-interrogative Clause with a personal-pronoun Subject and a VP headed by an auxiliary; subject–auxiliary inversion determines surface order.
If the relevant anchor Predicator is auxiliary-headed, the tag normally selects the same auxiliary lexeme; otherwise it selects do. The tag auxiliary normally has the anchor's tense.

The personal-pronoun tag Subject repeats a pronominal anchor Subject or is anaphorically selected for a non-pronominal one. Person–number agreement is controlled by the tag Subject, as Everybody has read it, haven't they? demonstrates.
A negative tag permits synthetic auxiliary negation in ordinary style or analytic final not in more formal style.

The tag has polarity opposite to the anchor in the frequent reversed-polarity variant and the same polarity in the constant-polarity variant; semantically negative anchors such as Few of them liked it select a positive reversed tag.

Prosody is constructionally significant: a reversed rising tag normally requests verification, a reversed falling tag seeks acknowledgement, and a constant tag characteristically has a slight rise with attributional or emotive effects.

projection.target: Recognizing Tag Question membership predicts an anaphoric personal-pronoun Subject, same-auxiliary selection or do-support, preservation of relevant tense, agreement with the tag Subject, a systematic reversed-or-constant polarity relation, and prosody-sensitive verification, acknowledgement, or emotive force
projection.evidence: The predictions jointly distinguish direct tags from arbitrary interrogative supplements: anchor Subject and Predicator determine pronoun, auxiliary, tense, and agreement, while polarity relation and contour predict the characteristic interpretations

grounds.note: Provides the direct tag-formation procedure and the polarity-by-prosody interpretation contrasts
The pronoun, auxiliary, tense, agreement, polarity, and prosody cluster recurs across declarative and exclamative anchors

known_boundary_items: CGEL also attests tags with closed-interrogative and imperative anchors; those lie outside this declarative-or-exclamative-anchor constructional node.
Lovely day, isn't it? has a non-clausal anchor under the strict VP-headed Clause ontology and therefore is not an instance of this Clause-anchored node.
Interrogative parentheticals such as don't you think? are larger interrogative supplements, not auxiliary-plus-pronoun tags.

relatedConstructions.notes: Tag Question inherits answer-set semantics and specializes it as an anchor-dependent, normally biased polar question
Both Anchor and Tag satisfy (Subject +) Head:VP; their supplemented combination is not itself a Clause
A declarative Clause is the default Anchor realization
An exclamative Clause can anchor a normally falling reversed-polarity tag
The short Tag is a closed-interrogative Clause with surface subject–auxiliary inversion
The tag auxiliary agrees with the personal-pronoun tag Subject, including singular-anchor/plural-they cases
The Tag Clause retains an auxiliary-headed VP despite surface inversion
A declarative question applies Question meaning to one declarative Clause; a Tag Question adds a distinct Tag Clause to its Anchor
Non-clausal anchors in forms such as Lovely day, isn't it? require a separate host analysis

grounds.note: Describes anchor-plus-tag questions, direct tag formation, polarity classes, agreement, and prosodically conditioned interpretations

Tag Question is a semantic specialization realized by a declarative or exclamative Anchor Clause plus a Tag Clause with a pronominal Subject and auxiliary-headed VP; every Clause remains strictly VP-headed

curious.title: Questions tacked onto the end of a statement
curious.summary: A short question such as isn't he? can follow a statement to ask the listener to confirm it or react to it.
curious.body: In He is ill, isn't he?, a short question follows the statement. It's built from an auxiliary verb and a pronoun that refers back to the person in the statement: isn't he. In the frequent version the question has the opposite polarity from the statement, positive then negative. A rising voice asks for confirmation, and a falling one invites agreement or acknowledgement. A tag can also repeat the statement's polarity: He is ill, is he? This version can express surprise, disapproval or sarcasm, not doubt. The pronoun decides the verb's form, as in Everybody has read it, haven't they? This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.

examples.text: [What a mess I've made of things], [haven't I]?
[So you have forgotten your homework again], [have you]?

curious.try: Say He is ill, isn't he? once with your voice rising at the end and once with it falling. Which version asks and which one invites agreement?

teacher.summary: Core material for tag questions: how the tag is formed and how polarity and intonation change its force.
teacher.explain: A tag question pairs an anchor clause (a declarative or exclamative) with a short closed-interrogative tag clause. The tag has a personal-pronoun subject and an auxiliary-headed VP, with subject-auxiliary inversion. If the anchor's predicator is headed by an auxiliary, the tag normally selects the same auxiliary; otherwise it uses do. The tag normally keeps the anchor's tense, and the verb agrees with the tag's pronoun. In the frequent reversed-polarity variant, a rising tag asks for verification and a falling tag seeks acknowledgement. A constant-polarity tag characteristically has a slight rise and can convey surprise, disapproval, reproach or sarcasm. Prosody is part of the construction. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional, though confidence in the pattern is marked high.
teacher.terms: Question tag is a textbook name. CGEL: tag clause attached to an anchor clause. The polarity relation is reversed or constant.

examples.text: [What a mess I've made of things], [haven't I]?
[So you have forgotten your homework again], [have you]?

contrasts.note: Reversed polarity; positive anchor, negative tag.
Constant polarity; slight rise, attributing the content to the addressee.

contrasts.text: Few of them liked it, did they?
contrasts.note: A semantically negative anchor takes a positive reversed tag.

watch_for: A learner might choose the tag verb to agree with a singular anchor subject such as everybody, when the tag's pronoun, they, controls agreement.
A learner might repeat the full verb from the anchor instead of using do when the anchor has no auxiliary.
A learner might ignore the intonation and miss whether the speaker wants confirmation or only agreement.
teacher.activity: Pairs say the same anchor, such as It's cold today, with different tags and intonation. The listener decides whether each version asks for confirmation, invites agreement or sounds surprised. Then they swap roles with new anchors.

child.hook: How do you ask a friend to agree with something you just said?
child.explain: A tag question is a tiny question stuck on the end of a sentence. It uses a short helper word like is, has or does, and a pronoun like he or she. Your voice rising or falling changes what you mean.
child.play: Say a sentence about a friend, then add a tiny question to check it. Say it twice, with your voice going up and then down. Does it sound different?

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says the tag repeats the helper word (the dictionary has the tag use do when the anchor's predicator has no auxiliary, as in She likes tea, doesn't she?); teacher.explain now ties auxiliary repetition to the anchor's predicator and says the constant-polarity rise is characteristic and its effects possible; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary' and 'the usual textbook name' with 'a textbook name'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Tag Question." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/tag-question-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Temporal Genitive Determiner

1.definition: Locates the nominal referent or event at a contextually identified time.

relatedConstructions.notes: In [the day after the election]’s agenda, the genitive gives a time and the marker attaches at the edge of the phrase, after election rather than day.

grounds.locator: Ch. 5 §§16.3, 16.5, relations expressed by genitive determination

projection.target: Tomorrow dates the event without denoting a participant in the inspecting. The inspector’s inspection can instead relate an argument to the nominal predicate.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Tomorrow's inspection
curious.summary: A time word with 's before a noun says when the thing happens.
curious.body: In They cancelled tomorrow's inspection, tomorrow's tells you when the inspection is due. It dates the event. It doesn't name anyone who takes part in the inspecting. Compare the inspector's inspection, where the inspector is a participant in the event. So the 's form can do different jobs, depending on the word before it. A time phrase can also take the 's at its end, as in the day after the election's agenda, where the 's attaches after election rather than day. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of a time word that can take 's before a noun, like last week's news. What does the time word say about the noun?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining genitives that give a time, as in tomorrow's inspection, as opposed to genitives that name a participant.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an NP whose determiner is a time-denoting genitive NP, followed by a nominal. It locates the nominal referent or event at a contextually identified time. Tomorrow dates the event without denoting a participant in the inspecting, whereas the inspector's inspection relates an argument to the nominal predicate. The genitive can also be a longer phrase with the marker at its edge, as in the day after the election's agenda, where the marker attaches after election rather than day. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and has one constructed illustration.
teacher.terms: CGEL: genitive NP in determiner function. Avoid possessive as a label here, since the genitive gives a time, not ownership.

contrasts.note: The genitive dates the event; no participant.
The genitive relates a participant to the nominal predicate.

watch_for: A learner might read tomorrow's as naming who or what is inspected or who inspects.
A learner might put the 's after day instead of at the end of the phrase the day after the election.
teacher.activity: Students list time words that take 's before a noun, such as today's, last week's and next year's. They write sentences with each and underline the time word, then say what it tells us about the noun.

child.hook: Why do we say tomorrow's trip?
child.explain: You can put 's on a time word to say when something is. Tomorrow's trip is the trip that's tomorrow. The word tomorrow tells you when.
child.play: Pick a time word like today or yesterday. Add 's and a noun, like yesterday's game. Make up three of your own.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Temporal Genitive Determiner." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/temporal-genitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Reduced than Comparative Clause
pattern: comparative governor + than + finite clause with constructionally unexpressed element

entry.name: Reduced than Comparative Clause
entry.pattern: comparative governor + than + finite clause with constructionally unexpressed element

1.definition: Supplies a comparison standard through a subordinate clause with predictable reduction.

examples.form: It took longer [than we had expected it to take].

projection.target: The duration slot corresponding to longer is understood without an overt degree expression. The gap can occur inside a nonfinite complement of the standard clause.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Comparisons that leave a word out
curious.summary: In a than-clause, part of the clause can be missing but still understood.
curious.body: In It took longer than we had expected it to take, the clause after than gives the standard for the comparison. It is missing something. We understand how long we expected it to take, though that duration isn't spelled out. That missing element corresponds to the word longer. The gap can even sit inside a to-phrase within the than-clause, as in expected it to take. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and rests on one constructed illustration.

examples.text: It took longer [than we had expected it to take].

curious.try: Finish this sentence in your own words. The trip took longer than ...

teacher.summary: Optional enrichment on than-clauses with an understood missing element.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a comparative governor, than and a finite clause with a constructionally unexpressed element. The clause supplies a comparison standard and its reduction is predictable. In It took longer than we had expected it to take, the duration slot corresponding to longer is understood without an overt degree expression. The gap can occur inside a nonfinite complement of the standard clause, here the to-phrase. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and has one constructed illustration, so use it as a starting point rather than a full account of comparative clauses.
teacher.terms: Comparative clause is the standard textbook term. This dictionary’s own label for the missing element is a constructionally unexpressed element.

examples.text: It took longer [than we had expected it to take].

watch_for: A learner might look for an overt expression of how long after take and think something is missing by mistake.
A learner might not link the gap in the than-clause back to the comparative word longer.
teacher.activity: Students write a sentence with a comparative word and than plus a clause, such as longer than we had expected. They then say what the missing amount is and which word in the first part it matches.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Reduced than Comparative Clause." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/than-reduced-clause-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Special Fused-Head NP with the and an Adjective

entry.name: Special Fused-Head NP with the and an Adjective

1.definition: Refers to a class of people or to an abstract domain characterized by the adjective.
1.details: With the very wealthy, the default special interpretation is plural and human. With the utterly impossible, the abstract interpretation has singular agreement. The adjective retains its ability to take adverbial modifiers. Anaphoric examples like the long in the short route and the long recover their nominal description from context and have independent agreement.

examples.note: Constructed human-class reading with plural agreement.
Constructed abstract reading with singular agreement.

relatedConstructions.notes: The special interpretation is available without a recoverable antecedent noun.
The overt constituent retains adjectival modification.

grounds.note: Contrasts human, abstract and anaphoric uses.
Distinguishes special readings and noun conversion.

projection.target: The same article-plus-adjective frame can show plural agreement in the human reading and singular agreement in the abstract reading. Adverbial modification of the adjective survives in both.
projection.evidence: FrameNet separates human, abstract and anaphoric patterns. CGEL supplies the count-noun conversion comparison and contrasts the special reading with contextually recovered readings.

curious.title: The wealthy, the impossible
curious.summary: The plus an adjective can stand for a class of people or an abstract domain, with no noun after it.
curious.body: In The very wealthy are exempt, the adjective with the in front refers to a class of people. There's no noun after it, yet the phrase works as the subject, and the verb is plural. The same frame can be abstract. In The seemingly impossible is now routine, the phrase means a domain of things, and the verb is singular. In both, the adjective keeps its ability to take adverbs such as very and seemingly. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, though it's confident in the main pattern.
curious.try: Say The very wealthy are exempt and The seemingly impossible is now routine. How does the verb differ, and what does each phrase refer to?

teacher.summary: Explains the plus adjective as a noun phrase for a class of people or an abstract domain, with agreement that follows the reading.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an NP with the as determiner and a fused modifier-head adjective phrase, with no overt noun. The default special interpretation is plural and human: the very wealthy. The abstract interpretation takes singular agreement: the utterly impossible. The adjective keeps its ability to take adverbial modifiers. Anaphoric examples such as the long in the short route and the long recover their nominal description from context and have independent agreement. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional and marks high confidence.
teacher.terms: CGEL: fused head, where the head is fused with its modifier. Traditional grammar sometimes describes the adjective as used as a noun. This dictionary distinguishes the special reading from noun conversion.

contrasts.note: Human class reading; plural agreement.

contrasts.text: The seemingly impossible is now routine.
contrasts.note: Abstract reading; singular agreement.

contrasts.text: the short route and the long
contrasts.note: Anaphoric use; the noun route is recovered from context.

watch_for: A learner might use singular agreement with a human class reading, such as the very wealthy.
A learner might think the adjective has become a noun and can no longer take an adverb.
A learner might read the long in the short route and the long as a class of people instead of a recovered noun.
teacher.activity: Students list phrases with the and an adjective, such as the rich and the impossible. They mark each as a class of people, an abstract domain or a recovered noun, and choose the matching verb form.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.activity model phrase the very wealthy (wealthy about 4,500th in SUBTLEX-UK) replaced by the rich; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Special Fused-Head NP with the and an Adjective." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/the-adjective-np-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Time-away Construction

dimensions.form: Verb head with an activity construal followed by a construction-licensed time-period direct object and the one-word PP away
dimensions.meaning: The subject uses up a bounded interval by engaging continuously or repeatedly in the verbal activity
dimensions.function: Construes a time interval as wholly occupied by an activity, often with a defeasible heedless, pleasurable, or time-wasting implication
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal; canonical Head–Od–away order, with Head–away–Od available especially for a heavy time NP

1.definition: An agentively engaged subject uses up the time interval denoted by the direct object in carrying out the verbal activity
1.details: The time NP is a genuine Od licensed by the construction, not a temporal adjunct: it passivizes, enters the tough construction, and cannot be stranded by VP ellipsis. Away is fixed and is syntactically a particle; in CGEL category terms it is an intransitive preposition heading a one-word PP complement, since particle is not a lexical category. The VP receives an activity construal: a lexical activity is normally atelic, while a repeatable bounded event such as sneeze is coerced to iteration. The heedless, pleasurable, or time-wasting implication is defeasible (Jackendoff 1997: 534–43; CGEL pp. 280–84).

examples.note: Repeatable bounded event coerced to repeated sneezing

examples.form: The evening had been nearly slept away.
examples.note: Passive evidence that the time NP is Od rather than adjunct

constraints.description: The time NP occupies Od position and excludes a lexical direct object: Fred drank the night away, not *Fred drank scotch the night away; obligatorily transitive verb uses are excluded.
Canonical order is Head–Od–away. Away may precede a sufficiently heavy NP, but modified away must follow the NP.
The NP must denote a time period; resource and activity-denoting NPs are excluded, though journey-context distance NPs can metonymically measure elapsed time.
The external subject is construed as agentively engaged and the VP denotes an activity rather than a state; the lexical verb may instead denote a repeatable bounded event.
The base activity is atelic, or a repeatable bounded event receives an iterative reading; nonrepeatable achievements are excluded.
The construction construes the interval as bounded or used up; the heedless-pleasure or should-have-done-something-else implication is conventional but defeasible.

projection.target: Recognizing Head–Od[time]–away predicts that the time NP behaves as a direct object despite lacking verb-level licensing, that away is a one-word intransitive-preposition PP in particle syntax, and that the VP denotes a bounded interval occupied by an agentive activity or iterated event
projection.evidence: Passivization, tough-construction, VP-ellipsis, particle placement, and lexical-object exclusion converge on direct-object status; independent activity, agentivity, and time-use diagnostics establish the semantic profile (Jackendoff 1997: 535–41)

grounds.note: Independent object, particle-placement, aspectual, and semantic diagnostics
The recurrent diagnostic cluster supports the stable constructional profile

diagnostics: cannot be stranded by VP ellipsis

known_boundary_items: Ordinary aspectual Head + away (work away) is atelic and has no time object; it is not the time-away construction.
The construction is distinct from the resultative and way constructions.
Distance-as-time readings are contextual extensions; activity-nominal objects are excluded.

relatedConstructions.notes: Time-away fixes away as the particle and restricts the direct object to a time-period NP
The construction-licensed time direct object is realized by an NP
Away heads the one-word PP in particle function

grounds.note: Time-object licensing, activity construal, ordering, and constructional semantics
Away is an intransitive preposition heading a one-word PP in particle use

curious.title: Sleeping the afternoon away
curious.summary: A verb, a stretch of time and the word away together say that someone spent the whole stretch on an activity.
curious.body: In Bill slept the afternoon away, the afternoon is a stretch of time that Bill fills up with sleeping. The pattern says the interval was used up by the activity, and it can suggest that the time was spent heedlessly or pleasurably, or wasted. That hint can be cancelled. The time phrase behaves like an object of the verb. It can become the subject of a passive, as in the evening had been nearly slept away. The pattern also works with a verb for a repeatable event, as in Saul sneezed the afternoon away, which means sneezing again and again. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of an activity you could do for a long time, like reading or chatting. Can you say it with a stretch of time and away?

teacher.summary: Teaches how a verb, a time period and away together describe an activity that uses up an interval.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a verb with an activity construal, a time-period NP and the word away: the subject uses up the interval by engaging in the activity. The time NP is a genuine direct object licensed by the construction, not an adjunct: it passivizes and cannot be stranded by VP ellipsis. The verb gets an activity construal, so a lexical activity is atelic and a repeatable bounded event such as sneeze is read as iterated. A lexical object is excluded, as in Fred drank the night away. The heedless, pleasurable or time-wasting implication is defeasible. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional, though its confidence is marked high.
teacher.terms: Away is traditionally called a particle or adverb. In CGEL terms it is an intransitive preposition heading a one-word PP. Od is the direct object.

contrasts.note: The time NP is the object.

contrasts.text: Fred drank scotch the night away.
contrasts.note: A lexical direct object is excluded.

contrasts.text: The evening had been nearly slept away.
contrasts.note: Passive evidence that the time NP is an object, not an adjunct.

watch_for: A learner might read the time phrase as an adjunct, when it is an object that can become the subject of a passive.
A learner might treat away as meaning leaving, when here it marks the interval as used up.
A learner might think the sentence must mean the time was wasted, when that implication can be cancelled.
teacher.activity: Give students verbs such as sleep, chat, read and sneeze. They write sentences with a time phrase and away, then decide whether the activity could fill the whole interval.

child.hook: Can you read the whole afternoon away?
child.explain: You can say you spent a whole stretch of time doing one thing. You name the time and add away. Bill slept the afternoon away means he slept for all of it.
child.play: Think of something you could do for a long time. Say it with a time like the whole morning, then away. Who can make the funniest one?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Time-away Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/time-away-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Measure before ago

1.definition: Locates an event or point by measuring backwards from the relevant deictic time.

relatedConstructions.notes: Four days ago locates an event relative to the deictic time. Since Monday gives the start of an interval.

projection.target: The time can usually be paraphrased as four days before now. Ago normally takes its measure before it, in contrast to temporal before with a following reference complement.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Four days ago
curious.summary: A length of time followed by ago tells you how far back something happened.
curious.body: In The review arrived four days ago, the phrase four days ago measures backwards from the time of speaking. You can paraphrase it as four days before now. The measure comes before ago, as in four days ago. This is different from before, which is followed by the point it refers back to, as in before Monday. A related pattern, since Monday, gives the start of a stretch of time instead. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Pick something that happened this week. Say how long ago it was using a number and ago.

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining how ago works with a measure phrase to count backwards from now.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a PP made of a measure NP and ago. It locates an event or point by measuring backwards from the relevant deictic time, so four days ago paraphrases four days before now. Ago normally takes its measure before it. By contrast, temporal before takes a reference complement after it. Since Monday gives the start of an interval, whereas four days ago locates an event relative to the deictic time. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats the whole of four days ago as a PP.

contrasts.note: Measures backwards from the deictic time.
Gives the start of an interval.
Temporal before takes a reference complement after it.

watch_for: A learner might read ago as a word that comes first and takes a point of reference, like before.
A learner might think since Monday and four days ago do the same thing.
teacher.activity: Students put events on a timeline from today. For each, they write one sentence with a number and ago, and another with since or before and a named day.

child.hook: How long ago did you last eat?
child.explain: Ago counts backwards from now. Four days ago means four days before now. The time measure goes before ago.
child.play: Say something that happened today, yesterday and last week using ago. Count backwards from now with a friend.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher terms no longer mentions the adverb classification (the entry gives only the prepositional analysis); child explanation now says the whole time measure, not the number, goes before ago, and uses the entry's 'before now'. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Measure before ago." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/time-measure-ago-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Title with a Personal Name

1.definition: Uses a personal name and a convention for identifying the bearer’s office, qualification, or style.
1.details: The title helps determine the form of the associated name. In the conventional British uses illustrated here, Sir precedes a given name, with a surname optionally following. Dr ordinarily precedes the surname or a full name in the standard formal style. Some professional conventions and familiar styles use a title with a given name.

examples.note: Constructed example showing the given-name form.
Constructed example showing the surname form.

relatedConstructions.notes: These forms can be determinerless personal names.
A titled personal name may be used in direct address.

grounds.note: Distinguishes class-specific title positions and name shapes.
Contrasts surname and given-name vocative examples with different titles.

projection.target: Substituting a surname alone for the given name in the standard British Sir pattern loses the conventional name form. A professional title such as Dr can use the surname alone.
projection.evidence: CASA distinguishes academic title plus surname from title plus given name. CGEL gives examples of both as possible personal names in vocative function.

curious.title: Titles that go with names
curious.summary: A title such as Sir or Dr can sit in front of a person's name, and the title helps decide which form of the name follows.
curious.body: In Sir James opened the ceremony, the title Sir goes with a given name. In Dr Patel wrote the report, the title Dr goes with a surname. The title tells us something about the person, such as an office or a qualification, and it also shapes the name that comes after it. The dictionary describes this as a convention, and marks its account as provisional. In the conventional British uses covered here, Sir precedes a given name, and a surname may follow it. Dr ordinarily precedes the surname or a full name in the standard formal style. Some professional conventions and familiar styles use a title with a given name.
curious.try: Think of a title you know, such as Dr or Sir. Which kind of name do you put after it, a first name or a surname?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining which part of a person's name follows a title such as Sir or Dr.
teacher.explain: A title is a pre-head element in a noun phrase whose head is a personal name, and the title is tied to a conventional name form. In the conventional British uses this dictionary illustrates, Sir precedes a given name, with a surname optionally following. Dr ordinarily precedes the surname or a full name in the standard formal style, though some professional conventions and familiar styles pair a title with a given name. This dictionary says that replacing the given name with a surname alone in the standard Sir pattern loses the conventional name form, while a professional title such as Dr can use the surname alone. This dictionary marks the analysis provisional, so present these as conventions, not rules for every variety.
teacher.terms: Title is the traditional name for Sir and Dr in this use. This dictionary treats the whole sequence as a noun phrase with a personal name.

contrasts.note: Title with a given name.
Title with a surname.

watch_for: A learner might assume the same part of the name follows every title.
A learner might use a surname alone after Sir, though this dictionary says this loses the conventional name form.
teacher.activity: Give students a list of titles and a list of people's names. In pairs they match each title with the name forms the conventions allow, then compare with the teacher's list.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Title with a Personal Name." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/title-personal-name-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Excess Degree too with an Infinitival

1.definition: Presents a degree as exceeding a threshold set by an action or outcome.

examples.form: The gap was [too narrow for the crate to fit through].

projection.target: The crate could count as large enough for other purposes. The relevant threshold is whether it can fit through that gap, not a universal degree of narrowness.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Too much for an action
curious.summary: Too plus a describing word and an action can say that something goes past the limit that action sets.
curious.body: In The gap was too narrow for the crate to fit through, the word too doesn't just say the gap is very narrow. It says the gap is narrow past a certain point, and that point is set by what has to happen: the crate fitting through. So the sentence says nothing general about how narrow the gap is. The same crate could count as large enough for other purposes. What matters is only whether it can fit through that gap. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: The gap was [too narrow for the crate to fit through].
The box was [too heavy to lift].

curious.try: Finish this sentence in your own words, then say what action sets the limit: The soup was too hot to ...

teacher.summary: Helps explain too used with an action to say that a degree passes a threshold.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an adjective or adverb phrase with too, a gradable head and a to-infinitival. It presents a degree as exceeding a threshold set by an action or outcome. In this dictionary’s example, the threshold is whether the crate can fit through the gap, not a universal degree of narrowness: the same crate could count as large enough for other purposes. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional. Teach the pattern as a way of linking a degree word to a purpose or outcome, and compare it with plain degree modification.
teacher.terms: Too is a degree modifier here. Textbooks sometimes call the whole pattern the too ... to construction.

examples.text: The gap was [too narrow for the crate to fit through].
The box was [too heavy to lift].

contrasts.text: The gap was too narrow for the crate to fit through.
contrasts.note: Narrow relative to the crate's passage.
Describes a degree with no threshold set by an action.

watch_for: A learner might read too narrow as simply very narrow, with no limit set by the action.
A learner might take the sentence to claim the crate is small in every respect, though this dictionary notes the crate could count as large enough for other purposes.
teacher.activity: Show pictures of objects and tasks (a tall shelf, a short child). Students write one sentence per picture with too, an adjective and a to-infinitive, and name the action that sets the limit.

child.hook: Why can't a big dog fit through a small cat flap?
child.explain: Sometimes too means more than the limit for a job. The cat flap is too small for the dog to fit through. The job is fitting through.

examples.text: The box was [too heavy to lift].
The soup was [too hot to eat].

child.play: Finish sentences that start "This is too big to ..." and "That is too far to ...". Say which job sets the limit each time.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Excess Degree too with an Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/too-degree-infinitival-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Monotransitive Transfer with to
pattern: VP[Head:V + Theme NP + PP[to + recipient NP]]

entry.name: Monotransitive Transfer with to
entry.pattern: VP[Head:V + Theme NP + PP[to + recipient NP]]

1.definition: Packages a transferred item as direct object and its intended recipient as a to-phrase.

relatedConstructions.notes: Send licenses both frames. Other verbs, including explain in mainstream standard English, select only the to frame in this sense.

projection.target: The Theme can be the ordinary passive subject, and certain verbs such as explain allow a recipient to-phrase while resisting double objects in mainstream standard usage.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Passing something to someone with to
curious.summary: A verb can name the thing passed along, followed by a to-phrase naming who it is meant for.
curious.body: In Kim sent the keys to Lee, the keys are what is passed along and Lee is the person they are meant for. The thing comes right after the verb, and the receiver comes in a phrase beginning with to. Some verbs, such as send, also allow a version with the receiver first and no to: Kim sent Lee the keys. Other verbs allow only the to version. According to this dictionary, explain is one of these in mainstream standard English. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: She [explained the rules to the class].

curious.try: Say Kim sent the keys to Lee, then say Kim sent Lee the keys. Now try the same two moves with explained the rules to the class.

teacher.summary: Helps explain verbs of transfer that take a direct object plus a to-phrase for the recipient.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a monotransitive VP: the head verb, a Theme noun phrase as direct object, and a prepositional phrase with to whose noun phrase is the recipient. It is a specialization of the monotransitive VP. Send licenses this frame and the double-object frame, so the two alternate. Other verbs, including explain in mainstream standard English, select only the to frame in this sense. The Theme can be the ordinary passive subject. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional, so present verb-by-verb licensing as something to check, not predict.
teacher.terms: Dative alternation is sometimes used as a textbook name for the choice between the to-phrase form and the double-object form.

examples.text: She [explained the rules to the class].

contrasts.text: Kim sent the keys to Lee.
contrasts.note: Direct object plus a to-phrase.
Double-object frame, also licensed by send.

watch_for: A learner might assume every verb that takes a to-phrase can also take two objects, though this dictionary says explain selects only the to frame.
A learner might treat the to-phrase as an object, when the Theme is the direct object.
teacher.activity: Give students verb cards (send, explain, give). They write one sentence per verb with a to-phrase, then test whether a double-object version also works, and sort the verbs.

child.hook: What do you say when you hand the keys to someone?
child.explain: Some sentences name what is passed first. Then they say who it is for, starting with to. Kim sent the keys to Lee.
child.play: Pass a small object around a circle. Each player says what they did, like "I passed the ball to Sam."

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary, curious.body and child.explain now say the to-phrase names the intended recipient (who the thing is meant for), not that the person gets it; replaced 'the entry' with this dictionary; hedged the dative alternation term.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Monotransitive Transfer with to." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/transitive-to-recipient-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: True Partitive with of
pattern: NP[quantificational head or fused head + PP[of + definite/domain-establishing NP]]

entry.name: True Partitive with of
entry.pattern: NP[quantificational head or fused head + PP[of + definite/domain-establishing NP]]

1.definition: Selects a subset from an established domain.

examples.form: They bought [three of the cartons of milk].
examples.note: Constructed comparison. Of the cartons supplies an established group of containers. Of milk identifies the contents of each.

relatedConstructions.notes: Three of the cartons selects members of a set. Three litres of the milk specifies quantity. A definite NP after of is compatible with either analysis.

projection.target: The of-phrase supplies the domain counted over. The boxes can be more numerous than three. In three boxes of apples, of apples instead identifies the content or measure domain.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Picking some out of a group
curious.summary: A phrase like three of the boxes picks out a smaller number from a group we already have in mind.
curious.body: In They opened three of the boxes, the words after of name a group already established: the boxes. The words before of say the number chosen from it. The boxes can be more numerous than three. Compare three boxes of apples. There, of apples says what is inside the boxes, not which boxes were chosen. A longer sentence can show both: They bought three of the cartons of milk. Of the cartons names the set that three comes from, and of milk says what each carton holds. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: They bought [three of the cartons of milk].

curious.try: Say three of the apples and three boxes of apples. In which one are you choosing from a set already in view?

teacher.summary: Helps explain how of-phrases pick a subset from an established group, as opposed to naming contents or a measure.
teacher.explain: In a true partitive, a quantificational head or fused head combines with an of-phrase whose noun phrase is definite or otherwise establishes a domain. The of-phrase supplies the domain counted over, so the boxes can be more numerous than three. In three boxes of apples, of apples instead identifies the content or measure domain. In three of the cartons of milk, of the cartons gives the domain and of milk identifies the contents of each. This dictionary notes that a definite noun phrase after of is compatible with either analysis: three of the cartons selects members of a set, while three litres of the milk specifies quantity. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Partitive is the traditional name. The contrast case is the measure pseudopartitive, covered in a related entry.

examples.text: They bought [three of the cartons of milk].

contrasts.text: Three of the cartons selects members of a set.
contrasts.note: Partitive reading.

contrasts.text: Three litres of the milk specifies quantity.
contrasts.note: Measure reading, though the definite noun phrase after of looks the same.

watch_for: A learner might read the of-phrase in three boxes of apples as the group chosen from, when it names the contents.
A learner might assume a definite noun phrase after of must signal a partitive, though this dictionary says it is compatible with either analysis.
teacher.activity: Lay out ten counters. Students say "I took three of the counters" and compare it with "three counters of plastic", then discuss which phrase names the group chosen from.

child.hook: If you take three cookies from a plate, what is left behind?
child.explain: We say three of the cookies when we pick some from a group we can already see. The group comes after of.
child.play: Put toys on a table. Take some and say "I took two of the toys." Then swap and let a friend say what you left.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "True Partitive with of." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/true-partitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Open Exhaustive Conditional
pattern: adjunct[interrogative XP or wh-ever + finite clause]

entry.name: Open Exhaustive Conditional
entry.pattern: adjunct[interrogative XP or wh-ever + finite clause]

1.definition: Makes the main claim hold across values for an open variable.

examples.form: [Whatever Jo suggests], we need a vote.

projection.target: The adjunct does not fill a nominal argument role. The main claim is to hold across suggestions, unlike an object fused relative denoting the suggestion itself.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Whatever happens, the same thing holds
curious.summary: A phrase beginning with a question word, or one with ever added, says the main claim holds across all the possible answers.
curious.body: In Whatever Jo suggests, we need a vote, the first part doesn't name one suggestion. It covers whatever suggestion Jo might make, and the main claim holds across all of them. We need a vote whichever suggestion it is. This differs from a phrase that stands for the suggestion itself, as in We accepted whatever Jo suggested. There, whatever Jo suggested names the thing accepted. In the pattern here, the opening phrase doesn't fill a role like that. It sets the range of cases over which the main claim is true. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: [Whatever Jo suggests], we need a vote.

curious.try: Complete this: Whoever wins, ... Does what you wrote hold for every possible winner?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, whatever- and wh-clauses that make a claim hold across all values.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an adjunct built from an interrogative phrase or a wh-ever word plus a finite clause. It makes the main claim hold across values for an open variable. In Whatever Jo suggests, we need a vote, the adjunct does not fill a nominal argument role: the main claim holds across suggestions. This contrasts with an object fused relative, where the wh-phrase denotes the suggestion itself. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional and links related entries on exhaustive alternative conditionals and fused relative noun phrases.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an unconditional clause or a free-choice conditional. This dictionary’s name is open exhaustive conditional.

examples.text: [Whatever Jo suggests], we need a vote.

contrasts.text: Whatever Jo suggests, we need a vote.
contrasts.note: Adjunct; the claim holds across suggestions.

watch_for: A learner might read whatever Jo suggests as the thing needed, when it frames the claim.
A learner might confuse the adjunct with a fused relative that names a thing.
teacher.activity: Students write three sentences beginning Whatever, Whoever or Wherever plus a clause, then a main claim that holds in every case. Pairs read them aloud and check whether the claim really holds for all cases.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Open Exhaustive Conditional." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/unconditional-wh-adjunct-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Exceptive Conditional unless

1.definition: Presents the condition as an exception to the main claim.

examples.form: The door will stay locked [unless Lee comes back].

projection.target: Outside cases in which Lee comes back, the door remains locked. The sentence need not determine what happens if Lee does return.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Unless as an exception
curious.summary: A phrase starting with unless presents a condition as an exception to the main claim.
curious.body: In The door will stay locked unless Lee comes back, the part with unless presents a condition as the exception. Outside the cases in which Lee comes back, the door remains locked. The sentence doesn't need to say what happens if Lee does return. It only tells us what to expect in the ordinary case, and flags the exception. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: The door will stay locked [unless Lee comes back].

curious.try: Say what you expect to happen on Saturday, then add an unless part naming an exception.

teacher.summary: Helps explain unless as marking the exception to the main claim.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a prepositional phrase headed by unless plus a finite clause. It presents the condition as an exception to the main claim. In The door will stay locked unless Lee comes back, the door remains locked outside cases in which Lee comes back, and the sentence need not determine what happens if Lee does return. This dictionary marks its analysis as provisional and relates it to the if-conditional. Teach it as an exception marker with its own meaning, and compare it with if.
teacher.terms: Unless is a preposition here.

examples.text: The door will stay locked [unless Lee comes back].

contrasts.text: The door will stay locked unless Lee comes back.
contrasts.note: Names the exception; the return case is left open.

watch_for: A learner might think the sentence says what happens when Lee does return, though this dictionary says it need not.
A learner might treat unless as a plain synonym of if not.
teacher.activity: Students write a rule for the classroom with unless, then swap and identify the exception in each other's rule.

child.hook: What could change your plan?
child.explain: The word unless names an exception. We'll eat outside unless it rains. Rain is the exception.

examples.text: The door will stay locked [unless Lee comes back].

child.play: Say a plan, then add unless and an exception. Take turns, and make the exceptions silly but possible.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary and curious.try no longer say the unless phrase names the one case in which the claim fails or that it changes the outcome (the entry leaves open what happens if the condition is met); 'one exception' changed to 'an exception' in the title, child.hook and child.explain. Also fixed (unflagged): removed the 'negative conditional' term; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Exceptive Conditional unless." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/unless-exceptive-conditional-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Resultative with a Nonselected Object
pattern: VP[V + NP[not the ordinary object of V] + result predicate]

entry.name: Resultative with a Nonselected Object
entry.pattern: VP[V + NP[not the ordinary object of V] + result predicate]

1.definition: Licenses an affected participant through a result predicate, including when the base verb normally takes no such object.

examples.note: Constructed comparison. An addressee reading is possible without attributing a change of state to the baby.

relatedConstructions.notes: This family includes unselected non-reflexive objects. CGEL’s narrower agentive intransitive pattern is recorded in the linked entry.

projection.target: The baby need not be an addressee of shouting. The result requires an affected participant, and dropping awake removes that reading. This goes beyond the reflexive-only subtype in the CGEL comparison.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Verbs that get an object they wouldn't normally take
curious.summary: A result word can let a verb take an object that the verb alone wouldn't take, so the object is changed by the action.
curious.body: In The neighbours shouted the baby awake, the verb shouted is used with an object, the baby. The baby need not be the one being shouted at. What matters is the result: the baby ends up awake. Compare The neighbours shouted at the baby. Here the baby can be the one addressed, and nothing says the baby changes. Drop awake from the first sentence and the affected-baby reading goes with it. The result word is what gives the baby its role. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Compare shouted the baby awake with shouted at the baby. In which one is the baby changed by the shouting?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, resultatives where the object is not the verb's ordinary object.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a VP with a verb, a noun phrase that is not the ordinary object of that verb, and a result predicate. It licenses an affected participant through the result predicate, including when the base verb normally takes no such object. In shouted the baby awake, the baby need not be an addressee, and the result requires an affected participant. Dropping awake removes that reading. This dictionary says this family goes beyond the reflexive-only subtype in the CGEL comparison, and records CGEL's narrower agentive intransitive pattern in a linked entry. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Resultative is the traditional name. The noun phrase is sometimes called a nonselected or unselected object.

contrasts.text: The neighbours shouted the baby awake.
contrasts.note: The baby is an affected participant; awake gives the result.

contrasts.text: The neighbours shouted at the baby.
contrasts.note: An addressee reading is possible, with no change of state attributed to the baby.

watch_for: A learner might read shouted the baby awake as meaning the baby was spoken to, when the result word supplies the affected-participant reading.
A learner might think awake can be dropped without changing the meaning.
teacher.activity: Give students intransitive verbs such as laugh, sing and shout. In groups they try to add an object and a result phrase, then discuss what each object has become.

checked.note: Frequency pass: teacher.activity verb whisper (about 5,200th in SUBTLEX-UK, counting its other forms) replaced by shout, the entry's own verb; entry examples unchanged.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Resultative with a Nonselected Object." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/unselected-object-resultative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Temporal until with an Endpoint

1.definition: Supplies the boundary up to which a situation holds or an occurrence is delayed.

projection.target: The opening ends the wait on the ordinary reading. Under negation as in didn’t leave until noon, the earlier interval is associated with absence of the event.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Until, the endpoint
curious.summary: Until names the point up to which something goes on, or before which something doesn't happen.
curious.body: In We waited until the shutters opened, the opening of the shutters ordinarily ends the wait. Until supplies the boundary: the waiting held up to that point. Until can also work with a negative. In She didn't leave until noon, the time before noon is the period when leaving didn't happen. Until can be followed by a date, a noun phrase, or a whole clause. This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Say what you did until a certain time today. Then say something you didn't do until that time.

teacher.summary: Helps explain until as marking the endpoint of a situation or the delay of an event.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a prepositional phrase headed by until, followed by a date, a noun phrase or a finite clause. It supplies the boundary up to which a situation holds, or up to which an occurrence is delayed. In We waited until the shutters opened, the opening ends the wait on the ordinary reading. Under negation, as in didn't leave until noon, the earlier interval is associated with absence of the event. This dictionary treats until phrases as prepositional phrases and relates the pattern to since. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Until is a preposition here.

contrasts.text: We waited until the shutters opened.
contrasts.note: The wait holds up to the boundary.
Under negation, the earlier interval is a time without leaving.

watch_for: A learner might read didn't leave until noon as saying she left before noon, when the time before noon is the period without leaving.
A learner might read until as marking the start of something, when it supplies the boundary up to which a situation holds or an occurrence is delayed.
teacher.activity: Students make a timeline of a school day. They write sentences with until for what holds up to each time, and sentences with didn't ... until for delayed events.

child.hook: What do you do until the bell rings?
child.explain: The word until tells us up to when something goes on. We waited until the shutters opened. Then the waiting was over.
child.play: Say what you do until a time or event, like "I play until dinner." Then let a friend say what happens next.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body now says the opening ordinarily ends the wait, as this dictionary qualifies it; teacher watch_for items restated in terms of this dictionary's boundary and absence-of-event wording; child explain no longer says until only tells where something stops. Also fixed (unflagged): cut the claim that until is sometimes grouped with conjunctions and the description of the phrases as adjuncts, neither of which this dictionary states; 'the entry' wording.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Temporal until with an Endpoint." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/until-time-boundary-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Verb Number Agreement
pattern: Subject NP[singular/plural] + finite verb agreeing in number

entry.name: Verb Number Agreement
entry.pattern: Subject NP[singular/plural] + finite verb agreeing in number

1.definition: Finite verb inflects to match the grammatical number of the subject NP

constraints.description: Agreement is realized on finite verbs/auxiliaries that bear number morphology (e.g., present -s, is/are).
Collective and notional agreement can override strict grammatical number in some varieties.

relatedConstructions.notes: Agreement links an overt Subject to the finite verbal head within Clause structure
Number is realized on the finite verb or auxiliary in the VP head of the Clause

projection.target: In the key to the cabinets is missing, agreement tracks the subject head rather than the nearest plural noun. The number-transparent pattern a number of keys are missing needs a separate account.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes ordinary agreement and independently conditioned overrides.

curious.title: The verb matches the subject
curious.summary: In a clause, a verb that has number forms changes to match whether the subject is singular or plural.
curious.body: In This dog runs, the subject is one dog and the verb takes the form runs. In These dogs run, the subject is more than one dog and the verb is run. The verb matches the subject in number. In The key to the cabinets is missing, the verb goes with key, the subject's main word, not with the nearer plural word cabinets. Sometimes a speaker's sense of the group can override strict number in some varieties. This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Say The key to the cabinets is missing. Which word does the verb match, key or cabinets?

teacher.summary: Core to teaching subject-verb agreement, and to explaining why a nearby plural does not decide the verb.
teacher.explain: A finite verb inflects to match the grammatical number of the subject noun phrase. Agreement is realized on finite verbs and auxiliaries that bear number morphology, such as the present -s and is/are. In the key to the cabinets is missing, agreement tracks the subject head rather than the nearest plural noun. This dictionary says collective and notional agreement can override strict grammatical number in some varieties, and that the number-transparent pattern a number of keys are missing needs a separate account. The analysis is marked provisional.
teacher.terms: Known in teaching as subject-verb agreement. This dictionary places number on the finite verb or auxiliary in the head of the verb phrase.

examples.text: The key to the cabinets is missing.

contrasts.note: Singular subject, singular verb.
Plural subject, plural verb.

watch_for: A learner might make the verb agree with cabinets in the key to the cabinets is missing, when the subject head is key.
A learner might treat a number of keys are missing like an ordinary agreement case, though this dictionary says it needs a separate account.
teacher.activity: Give students sentence frames with a singular head and a plural noun inside a phrase after it. They underline the subject head and choose the verb form that matches it.

child.hook: Why do we say the dog runs but the dogs run?
child.explain: Some words, like runs, change to match the subject. In This dog runs, the subject is this dog. When this dog changes to these dogs, runs changes to run.
child.play: Change cat to cats in "The cat sleeps." What happens to sleeps? Try it with five more sentences.

checked.note: Fixed: curious.summary now limits agreement to verbs with number forms and grammatical number; child.explain no longer says the verb matches 'who is doing it' (agreement follows the grammatical subject); curious.body tied the subject-head point to the key example; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'. Second round: fixed child.explain, which tied agreement to whether the subject is one or more than one and implied that every verb changes (this dictionary bases agreement on grammatical number and limits it to finite forms that mark number); it now works through This dog runs and These dogs run, and the game starts from The cat sleeps. Teacher.terms no longer calls subject-verb agreement the usual name.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Verb Number Agreement." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/verb-number-agreement-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Prepositional Verb-Particle-Object Construction
pattern: Head:V + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]] + Od:NP ↔ Head:V + Od:NP + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]]

entry.name: Prepositional Verb-Particle-Object Construction
entry.pattern: Head:V + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]] + Od:NP ↔ Head:V + Od:NP + Comp:PP[particle, Head:P[intransitive]]

dimensions.form: VP headed by a verb with an NP direct object and a separate one-word PP complement in particle use, ordered either Head–particle–Od or Head–Od–particle
dimensions.meaning: Ranges from transparent spatial or directional combinations to aspectual and idiomatic verb-particle combinations
dimensions.function: Allows a one-word PP complement to occur exceptionally between the verb head and its NP direct object
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal in transitive clauses; post-object order is required with an unstressed personal-pronoun Od, while lexical and information-weight factors affect the two orders elsewhere

1.definition: A one-word PP complement in particle use combines with a verb and a distinct NP direct object
1.details: Particle is a syntactic use, not a lexical category. In the central case, the particle is a one-word PP headed by an intransitive preposition. In She took off the label, off is a complement of take and the label is a separate Od; this differs from She jumped off the wall, where off is a transitive preposition and off the wall is a single PP complement. The particle construction is diagnosed by order alternation, obligatory pre-particle placement of an unstressed pronoun, and the failure of particle + Od to behave as a constituent (CGEL Ch. 4 §6.2, pp. 280–83).

examples.note: Head–particle–Od order with down as a one-word PP complement
Post-object particle; compare the impossible unstressed-pronoun order *took off it

constraints.description: The particle is a Comp:PP of the verb and the NP is a separate Od of the verb; particle + NP is not a PP constituent.
In the central prepositional subtype recorded here, the particle is a one-word PP headed by an intransitive P; the term particle identifies its syntactic use rather than a lexical category.
An ordinary non-pronominal Od generally permits Head–particle–Od and Head–Od–particle orders, but an unstressed personal-pronoun Od must immediately follow the verb: take it off, not *take off it.
Particle + Od cannot normally be fronted, foregrounded in an it-cleft, or repeated as a coordinated phrase; these failures distinguish the sequence from a transitive PP.
Heavy-NP postposing and lexical fossilisation can obscure the ordinary alternation, so no single placement test is necessary in every token.

projection.target: The ability of a one-word PP complement to intervene between Head:V and a non-pronominal Od predicts a corresponding post-object placement, obligatory pre-particle placement of an unstressed pronoun, and non-constituency of particle + Od
projection.evidence: CGEL's order, pronoun-substitution, fronting, coordination, and adverb-insertion contrasts jointly distinguish the particle construction from V + transitive-PP structure (Ch. 4 §6.2, pp. 280–83).

core.property: One-word PP complement in particle use

diagnostics: unstressed personal pronoun immediately follows V

core.property: Particle plus Od is not a constituent

activation_states.effect: End placement of the Od may be licensed independently of the particle construction
One of the two particle positions may be strongly preferred or excluded
