known_boundary_items: jump off the wall: off heads a transitive PP containing its own Obj, rather than a particle PP followed by Od
read through the prospectus versus read the prospectus through: CGEL treats this as alternation between a transitive PP and NP plus non-particle intransitive PP
Adjectival and verbal particles occur in a small set of idioms, but the present entry records the central PP subtype

relatedConstructions.notes: The particle and direct object are dependents in a VP headed by V
The separate direct object is realized by an NP
The particle is a one-word PP complement
Literal directional particles can realize the locative complement in caused-motion VPs, while idiomatic particles need not express motion

grounds.note: Particle is a syntactic use; central particles are one-word PPs headed by intransitive prepositions
Convergent order, pronoun, constituency, coordination, and insertion diagnostics

curious.title: Little words before or after an object
curious.summary: A short word like down or off can come before or after the object of a verb, as in brought down the bed and brought the bed down.
curious.body: In She brought down the bed, the small word down goes with the verb brought, and the bed is what she brought. The same thing can be said the other way: She brought the bed down. In the dictionary's account, down isn't the start of a phrase down the bed. It stands on its own beside the verb, and the bed is a separate object. The dictionary marks this account as provisional, and says no single test works in every case.
curious.try: Say took the label off, then try replacing the label with it. Where does it go?

teacher.summary: Helps explain verb-particle combinations with an object, including word-order flexibility and the pronoun restriction.
teacher.explain: In this construction a verb takes a separate noun phrase as direct object and a one-word prepositional phrase complement in particle use. The particle is a syntactic use, not a word category. In She took off the label, off is a complement of take and the label is a separate direct object. This differs from She jumped off the wall, where off heads a prepositional phrase containing its own object. An ordinary object generally allows both orders, but an unstressed personal-pronoun object must immediately follow the verb: take it off. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional, and notes that heavy objects and fixed idioms can obscure the alternation.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a verb-particle combination or a phrasal verb; the second label also covers cases without an object. In this grammar the particle is a one-word prepositional phrase complement of the verb.

contrasts.note: Verb, particle, object.
Verb, object, particle.
An unstressed pronoun object cannot follow the particle; this dictionary gives take it off.

watch_for: A learner might read down the bed in brought down the bed as a single phrase, when this dictionary treats down and the bed as separate.
A learner might treat take off it like take off the label, though an unstressed pronoun must come before the particle.
teacher.activity: Give students phrasal verbs on cards (take off, bring down, put on). They build sentences with a noun object in both orders, then replace the object with it and say where the particle must go.

child.hook: Can you say "took the label off" and "took off the label"?
child.explain: Some small words like off and down can go before or after the object. She took the label off. She took off the label. With it, the little word goes after it.
child.play: Take a sticker off a page and say what you did two ways. Then say what you did with it, like "I took it off."

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer says the particle goes on either side of 'what the verb moves' (many combinations involve no movement); now says before or after the object; curious title reworded likewise; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'; phrasal verb hedged as a broader label. Second round: fixed child.explain, comes last changed to goes after it (the entry requires the particle to follow an unstressed pronoun object, not to end the sentence); cut the curious claim that separateness is why both orders are possible; teacher.explain now says an ordinary object generally allows both orders, as the entry does.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Prepositional Verb-Particle-Object Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/verb-particle-object-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Vocative Construction

1.definition: Addresses the hearer directly, identifying them as the intended recipient
1.details: Forms its own intonation phrase, typically with fall-rise or level contour; summons use may have high sustained "calling" contour. Not syntactically integrated as a clause argument. NP is either bare or determined by 1st/2nd person forms only (genitive my/our/your, or determinative you).

examples.note: Summons with calling contour (high sustained pitch)

constraints.description: NP is bare or determined only by 1st/2nd person forms (my, our, your, you); 3rd-person and non-deictic determiners excluded
Requires addressee to be present (real or imagined)
Forms separate intonation phrase with fall-rise, level, or calling contour
Can occur clause-initially, clause-medially, or clause-finally

1.notes: Vocatives strongly favour bare NPs, especially for proper names and kinship terms

relatedConstructions.notes: Addressee-directed packaging of the ostensive NP (securing the channel)
Only the summons/call use is exclamatory; tag and address vocatives are not
Vocative function licenses bare NP for kinship terms that would otherwise require determination
Proper names freely occur as vocatives

projection.target: An overt imperative subject and a vocative can co-occur, as in Lee, you take the first shift. Moving Lee to the end can preserve the address reading while you continues to supply the subject. The name in the vocative is therefore not the only potential subject expression.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts vocatives and subjects in imperative clauses. The constructed position and co-occurrence test illustrates the proposed distribution without relying on corpus frequencies or kin-term acquisition claims.

diagnostics: kinship terms bare in vocative but determined elsewhere

stabilisers.evidence: Need to secure attention and identify addressee
High frequency of vocative proper names and kinship terms in child-directed speech
Early-acquired; vocative kinship terms among first multi-word uses

coupling.mechanism: Vocative use licenses bare form; bare form signals vocative construal

curious.title: Calling someone by name
curious.summary: A name or title said directly to the person you're speaking to, set apart from the rest of the sentence.
curious.body: In Mom, can you help me?, the word Mom isn't part of what is being asked. It addresses the hearer directly and picks them out as the person meant. This is a vocative. It sits in its own stretch of speech, with its own tone, such as a fall-rise, a level tone, or a high held calling tone when summoning someone. It can come at the start, the middle or the end: I think, Brett, you're wrong. The noun phrase is either bare, as in Mom or Ladies and gentlemen, or begins with my, our, your or you, as in My friend, let me explain. A drawn-out, high Moooom! is the calling version. This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of how you get a friend's attention across a room. Do you say their name on its own, in a calling tone?

teacher.summary: Helps explain direct address, its separate intonation and the determiners it allows.
teacher.explain: A vocative addresses the hearer directly. It forms its own intonation phrase, with a fall-rise or level contour, or a high sustained calling contour for a summons. It is not selected by the verb and is not syntactically integrated as a clause argument. The noun phrase is either bare or determined only by first- and second-person forms (the genitives my, our, your, or the determinative you). It can occur clause-initially, clause-medially or clause-finally, and it needs an addressee, real or imagined. In an imperative, an overt subject and a vocative can co-occur, as in Lee, you take the first shift. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: Genitive is used here for my, our and your, rather than possessive.

contrasts.text: Lee, you take the first shift.
contrasts.note: Vocative Lee, with you as the subject.

watch_for: A learner might treat the vocative as the subject of the clause, when in an imperative the vocative and an overt subject can co-occur.
A learner might read the vocative as part of the clause, when it forms its own intonation phrase.
teacher.activity: Students read a short dialogue aloud, first with vocatives placed at the start, then in the middle and at the end. They notice how the vocative is set apart from the rest of the sentence.

child.hook: When you call someone's name, what happens to your voice?
child.explain: When we speak straight to someone, we can say their name. Mom, can you help me? The name stands apart from the rest of the sentence.
child.play: Say the same sentence three times, with a friend's name at the start, middle and end. Does the name sound set apart each time?

checked.note: Fixed: curious list of forms no longer excludes bare noun phrases such as Ladies and gentlemen; replaced the 'pause on either side' and 'shouted' wording with the entry's contours (fall-rise, level, high sustained calling); removed the 'rising tone' option; child and teacher activities no longer rest on pauses; removed the unsupported 'noun of address' term and the punctuation-based watch_for. Dismissed: none. Second round: fixed teacher.terms by cutting 'Vocative is the traditional name' (this dictionary uses the label but makes no claim about its history).

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Vocative Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/vocative-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Verb Phrase

dimensions.form: Phrase headed by a verb, with complements and modifiers licensed in the VP; no Subject occurs within the VP
dimensions.meaning: A situation profile contributed by the head verb and elaborated by its internal dependents
dimensions.function: Head (Predicate) of a Clause, or dependent in constructions that license a VP
dimensions.distribution: Occurs as the Head of a Clause and in selected embedded or modifying environments

1.definition: A phrase headed by a verb, containing any complements and modifiers but excluding the Subject
1.details: The verb is the Head of the VP and the ultimate Head of any Clause headed by that VP. Its lexical sense and constructional frame jointly determine which complements are required or permitted. The Subject, when present, is a dependent of Clause rather than VP; a VP can therefore serve as the Head of a Clause with an overt Subject or as the whole overt content of a subjectless Clause.

examples.note: Head V left with modifier early; Kim is Subject of Clause, not part of the VP
Head V sent with indirect and direct object complements
Head V slept with a construction-licensed object and PP complement

constraints.description: The Head is a verb; its inflectional form and lexical sense constrain the VP's internal syntax.
Complements and VP-level modifiers are dependents within the VP.
A Subject is never a dependent within VP structure; it belongs to the Clause headed by the VP.

projection.target: Once a constituent is identified as a VP, the head verb and its constructional frame predict the inventory and order of internal complements, while the constituent type is eligible to serve as the Head of both subject-bearing and subjectless Clauses
projection.evidence: CGEL states that the verb is Head of VP and that properties of the verb determine which other elements are required or permitted; the Clause/VP contrast independently locates Subject outside the VP

grounds.note: The verbal head and its sense license complement inventory, while VP category predicts Clause-head distribution
Verb as Head of VP and ultimate Head of Clause; verb properties govern permitted and required dependents

diagnostics: Subject combines with VP at Clause level
manner, temporal, aspectual, and other integrated modifiers

relatedConstructions.notes: VP specializes the headed Phrase pattern with V as Head

grounds.note: VP is a phrasal category headed by V and serves as the Predicate/Head of Clause

curious.title: The verb and what goes with it
curious.summary: A verb phrase is a verb together with the words that complete or modify it, not including the subject.
curious.body: In Kim left early, the verb is left and early adds to it. Together, left early is the verb phrase. Kim, who did the leaving, stands outside it. A verb phrase can be bigger. In I sent Sue a copy, the verb sent comes with two objects, Sue and a copy. In They slept the afternoon away, the verb comes with an object and another word that finishes it. The verb's meaning and the pattern it appears in together decide which other words are required or allowed, and the subject is never inside the verb phrase. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Take Kim left early and cover up the subject, Kim. What's left, left early, is the verb phrase.

teacher.summary: Core grammar category: the verb phrase, with its head verb and dependents, excluding the Subject.
teacher.explain: A verb phrase (VP) is a phrase headed by a verb, containing any complements and modifiers but excluding the Subject. The verb is the head of the VP and the ultimate head of any clause headed by that VP. Its lexical sense and constructional frame jointly determine which complements are required or permitted. The Subject is a dependent of the clause, not of the VP. A VP can therefore head a clause with an overt Subject, or be the whole overt content of a subjectless clause. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: Verb phrase is the standard term. In this grammar the VP excludes the Subject, and Predicate names the VP's function in the clause.

contrasts.note: Kim is the Subject of the clause, not part of the VP.

watch_for: A learner might include the Subject in the verb phrase, when the Subject belongs to the clause.
A learner might assume a verb takes any complements, though its sense and frame decide which are required or permitted.
teacher.activity: Students take simple sentences with a clear subject and bracket the verb phrase, leaving out the subject. They then compare brackets in pairs.

name: way-Motion Construction

dimensions.form: VP headed by make or a manner-denoting verb, followed by the direct-object NP x's way and a change-of-location PP complement, centrally bearing a path, goal, or direction role
dimensions.meaning: The participant identified by x progresses along a route, in a direction, or toward a goal by the activity or means expressed by the verb
dimensions.function: The fixed way-object frame licenses a change-of-location complement and allows the verb to specify the manner or means of progress
dimensions.distribution: VP-internal; found in the make one's way idiom and a productive extension with manner or means verbs

1.definition: A participant progresses along the path, in the direction, or toward the goal expressed by the locative complement
1.details: CGEL analyzes x's way as an Od, not as a preposition or as part of the following PP. Make one's way is an idiom meaning approximately 'progress' that licenses change-of-location complements although make alone does not do so. This idiom provides the basis for a productive construction in which another verb supplies the manner or means of progress (CGEL Ch. 8 §4.3, p. 685; Ch. 4 §8.1.3, p. 305).

examples.form: We [made our way to the station].
examples.note: Make one's way idiom with a goal-role locative complement

examples.form: Jill had to [elbow her way to the exit].
examples.note: Productive manner/means verb; the frame supplies progress toward the goal

examples.form: They [pushed their way to the front].
examples.note: Way Od precedes a goal-role locative complement

constraints.description: The fixed-form NP x's way is Od of the verb; the following PP is a separate change-of-location Comp:PP, centrally bearing a path, goal, or direction role.
The way NP contains a genitive determiner form and way as nominal head; the genitive identifies the participant whose progress is described.
Make licenses the frame idiomatically; productive alternatives contribute the manner or means by which progress is achieved.
The VP denotes directed progress along a route, in a direction, or toward a goal rather than ordinary creation or possession of a way referent.
In CGEL's account, the movement consists of a series of stops and starts rather than uninterrupted continuous motion.

projection.target: The fixed x's way Od followed by a change-of-location complement predicts a progress interpretation, constructional licensing of path, goal, or direction with non-motion manner verbs, and interpretation of the verb as the manner or means of progress rather than as selecting an ordinary way object
projection.evidence: CGEL relates the make one's way idiom to productive manner/means replacements such as elbow and push, while retaining Od and locative-complement functions (Ch. 8 §4.3, p. 685; Ch. 4 §8.1.3, p. 305).

core.property: Manner or means supplied by Head:V

known_boundary_items: made a way through the wall: ordinary creation of a path-denoting object lacks the fixed genitive way-object profile
caused motion: its Od denotes the moving theme, whereas the way construction's Od is the fixed x's way NP
An ordinary goal-complement VP lacks the construction-specific way object

relatedConstructions.notes: Way-motion is a VP-level argument-structure specialization
The fixed x's way constituent is an NP functioning as Od
Non-pronominal x's way NPs realize the determiner through the genitive-s construction
The route, direction, or endpoint is expressed by a locative PP complement
The final locative complement can express the route traversed
The final locative complement can express the endpoint of progress
Both combine manner or means with motion, but they assign different functions and roles to Od

grounds.note: x's way is Od and the following change-of-location dependent is a locative complement
Fixed way object, productive manner-verb replacement, and locative licensing form a recurrent profile

curious.title: Making your way somewhere
curious.summary: Phrases like "elbowed her way to the exit" say how someone moved forward and where they were heading.
curious.body: We made our way to the station. Jill had to elbow her way to the exit. They pushed their way to the front. In each, the person makes progress toward a place. In the last two, the verb (elbow, push) says how they managed it. The pattern needs a word like our, her or their, plus way, followed by a phrase saying where. It isn't about a way that someone builds or owns. It describes getting forward along a route, in a direction or toward a goal. On the account this dictionary follows, the movement goes in a series of stops and starts, not in one smooth motion.

examples.text: We [made our way to the station].
Jill had to [elbow her way to the exit].
They [pushed their way to the front].

curious.try: Replace elbowed with another action, such as squeezed or fought, in She elbowed her way to the exit. Does the sentence still say she was making progress toward the exit?

teacher.summary: Explains how verbs like push can describe progress toward a place when followed by x's way and a locative phrase.
teacher.explain: In We made our way to the station, make one's way is an idiom meaning roughly "progress". It licenses a change-of-location complement even though make alone doesn't. A productive extension replaces make with a verb of manner or means (elbow, push), which then says how the progress is achieved. In CGEL's analysis, x's way is the direct object, not part of the preposition phrase. The genitive determiner (her, their, Kim's) identifies the person making progress, and way is the head. The following PP is a separate locative complement giving the path, goal or direction. In CGEL's account, the movement is a series of stops and starts.
teacher.terms: Direct object (Od): x's way. Complement (Comp): the PP of path, goal or direction. Genitive: the form identifying whose way, such as her or Kim's.

examples.text: We [made our way to the station].
Jill had to [elbow her way to the exit].
They [pushed their way to the front].

contrasts.text: They pushed their way to the front.
contrasts.note: The way phrase is the object, and the PP says where.

contrasts.text: They made a way through the wall.
contrasts.note: Ordinary creation of a path, without the fixed genitive way-object.

watch_for: A learner might read their way as an ordinary object naming a route someone owns.
A learner might take the PP as part of the way phrase rather than as a separate complement.
A learner might read pushed their way to the front as pushing the way itself, rather than pushing in order to move forward.
teacher.activity: Give students a destination (the exit, the front, the station) and cards with verbs (push, fight, make). They build sentences with a person's own way and a phrase of place, then discuss how each verb changes the picture of getting there.

child.hook: When you squeeze through a crowd, how would you say it with the word "way"?
child.explain: Some sentences use someone's own way to show them making progress toward a place. He pushed his way to the front. Here pushed tells how he moved, and the last part tells where he was going.

examples.text: We [made our way to the station].
He [elbowed his way to the door].
They [pushed their way to the front].

child.play: Pick a place, like the door or the front. Then say how you'd get there with your way, using words like pushed, squeezed or made.

checked.note: Fixed: curious body no longer says the verb always tells how the person managed it (in made our way, make is the idiom and the manner or means verbs are the productive extension); stops-and-starts claim attributed to the account this dictionary follows rather than stated as a plain feature; child explanation describes progress toward a place rather than 'how they got somewhere'. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'. Frequency pass: teacher.summary now names push only, and the activity verb elbow (about 5,600th in SUBTLEX-UK, counting its other forms) is replaced by fight, as in the curious try; the entry example with elbow is unchanged.

name: Article in a Weak Proper Name

entry.name: Article in a Weak Proper Name

1.definition: Realizes a conventional proper name that uses an article in ordinary argument position.

relatedConstructions.notes: A different dedicated syntactic host for the primary name use.

projection.target: The article forms part of the ordinary naming pattern, while a label or compound can omit it in a suitable form. Arbitrary replacement with a does not preserve the primary name use.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Names that come with the
curious.summary: Some names include the word the as part of the name, as in the Thames.
curious.body: In They crossed the Thames, the word the isn't an extra. It belongs to the way this name is used in an ordinary sentence. The name and the article go together. That differs from names that need nothing in front of them. The dictionary describes the article here as part of the ordinary naming pattern. A label or compound can leave it out in a suitable form, but arbitrarily swapping in a does not keep the main name use. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of another name you can't say without the. What happens if you drop it?

teacher.summary: Helps explain proper names that conventionally take an article.
teacher.explain: A weak proper name is a noun phrase in which a lexically conventional article combines with a name expression, as in the Thames. It realizes a conventional proper name in ordinary argument position. The article forms part of the ordinary naming pattern, while a label or compound can omit it in a suitable form. Arbitrary replacement with a does not preserve the primary name use. This dictionary contrasts this with strong proper names, which have no such article, and marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: The and a are determinatives, often called articles. This dictionary’s weak proper name contrasts with strong proper name.

contrasts.note: Name with its conventional article, in argument position.

watch_for: A learner might leave out the before a name that conventionally has it.
A learner might replace the with a, though this dictionary says arbitrary replacement does not keep the name use.
teacher.activity: Students list names of places or things they know, and sort them into names with the and names without it. They check each list against a reference.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Article in a Weak Proper Name." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/weak-proper-name-article-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Topic Proposal with what about
pattern: what about + NP or gerund-participial expression

entry.name: Topic Proposal with what about
entry.pattern: what about + NP or gerund-participial expression

1.definition: Introduces something for consideration, often as a related topic or proposed activity.

projection.target: An activity can be proposed without asking for the identity of an object. With a referent such as the spare key, the intended issue is supplied by the conversation.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: What about this idea?
curious.summary: What about, followed by a thing or an action, puts something forward for the other person to think about.
curious.body: What about asking Lee first? isn't really a request for information. It proposes an action, asking Lee, for the listener to consider. The words after what about can name an action, as here, or a thing. With something like the spare key, the conversation supplies what the issue is. The speaker doesn't need to ask what the object is. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Suggest something to a friend using What about. Does the friend answer with information or with a decision?

teacher.summary: Helps explain what about as a way to propose an activity or raise a related topic.
teacher.explain: The pattern is what about followed by a noun phrase or a gerund-participial expression. It introduces something for consideration, often as a related topic or proposed activity. An activity can be proposed without asking for the identity of an object. With a referent such as the spare key, the intended issue is supplied by the conversation. This dictionary classes it as pragmatic and relates it to questions. It marks its analysis provisional, so present a proposed activity and a related topic as two uses, and note that context supplies what is at issue.
teacher.terms: Gerund-participial is this dictionary's term for an -ing expression such as asking Lee first. Textbooks may call the -ing form a gerund.

contrasts.note: Proposes an action; no object is asked for.
The conversation supplies the issue.

watch_for: A learner might answer What about asking Lee first? by naming an object, when it proposes an action.
A learner might look for a missing noun phrase after about, when the proposal is complete.
teacher.activity: Pairs plan a weekend. One suggests with What about and an -ing phrase, the other accepts, rejects or changes the plan.

child.hook: How do you suggest a game to a friend?
child.explain: Sometimes What about is a way to suggest an idea. What about asking Lee first? It isn't a question about a thing.
child.play: Take turns suggesting an activity with What about. The next player says yes or suggests another.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain no longer ranks the proposal use above the related-topic use; teacher.terms now says gerund-participial applies to an -ing expression such as asking Lee first; removed the unsupported list of possible issues for the spare key; replaced 'the entry' with this dictionary.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Topic Proposal with what about." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/what-about-topic-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: Deliberative what if

1.definition: Raises a hypothetical circumstance and invites consideration of its consequences.

examples.form: [What if the last bus has already gone?]

projection.target: A response can discuss a plan for that circumstance. The string can stand alone without a stated matrix consequence, unlike a fully expressed ordinary conditional.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: What if something happened?
curious.summary: What if plus a clause raises a possible situation and invites talk about what would follow.
curious.body: What if the last bus has already gone? doesn't ask for a fact. It raises a possibility and invites the listener to think about it. A reply can discuss a plan for that situation, such as walking or calling a taxi. The string can stand alone without a stated result, unlike a fully expressed if sentence such as If the last bus has gone, we'll walk. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: [What if the last bus has already gone?]

curious.try: Ask a friend What if with something that could happen on the way home. What do they say you should do?

teacher.summary: Helps explain what if as a way to raise a hypothetical and invite discussion of consequences.
teacher.explain: The pattern is what if followed by a finite clause. It raises a hypothetical circumstance and invites consideration of its consequences. A response can discuss a plan for that circumstance. The string can stand alone without a stated matrix consequence, unlike a fully expressed ordinary conditional. This dictionary relates it to if-conditionals and to questions, classes it as pragmatic, and marks its analysis provisional. Teach it as a way of raising a scenario that can stand without a stated consequence.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a what-if question. This dictionary treats it as a deliberative use.

examples.text: [What if the last bus has already gone?]

contrasts.text: What if the last bus has already gone?
contrasts.note: Stands alone; no consequence stated.

contrasts.text: If the last bus has gone, we'll walk.
contrasts.note: Ordinary conditional with both parts.

watch_for: A learner might wait for a main clause after what if, when the string can stand alone.
A learner might answer with yes or no as to a plain question, when it invites discussion of the scenario.
teacher.activity: Students pose What if questions about a story's plot. Partners respond with a plan or consequence.

child.hook: What would you do if you missed the last bus?
child.explain: What if raises something that might happen. What if the last bus has already gone? Then we talk about what we could do.

examples.text: [What if the last bus has already gone?]

child.play: Take turns asking a What if question. The other player says what they would do.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.explain no longer says the pattern is not a conditional with something left out (the entry says only that it can stand alone without a stated consequence); child.explain no longer calls it a pretend problem. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

name: Phrasal Exclamation with what
pattern: independent NP[exclamative what + optional a/an + Nom]

entry.name: Phrasal Exclamation with what
entry.pattern: independent NP[exclamative what + optional a/an + Nom]

1.definition: Expresses an affective evaluation through an apt nominal description.

projection.target: The singular count example includes a, whereas What lovely weather! does not. The independent pattern needs no finite predication to convey the evaluation.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: What a mess!
curious.summary: What plus a noun description can express a feeling about something, with no verb at all.
curious.body: What a mess! expresses a reaction. There's no verb and no complete statement, yet the feeling about the mess comes through clearly. The words that follow what describe the thing aptly and give the speaker's evaluation. In What a mess!, the word a comes between what and the singular noun. Not every case has it: What lovely weather! doesn't. The pattern needs no verb to carry its meaning. This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: React to something in the room using What a ... or What ... Does your reaction need a verb?

teacher.summary: Helps explain verbless what-exclamations as a way to evaluate something.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an independent noun phrase with exclamative what, an optional a or an, and a nominal. It expresses an affective evaluation through an apt nominal description. The singular count example includes a, as in What a mess!, whereas What lovely weather! does not. The independent pattern needs no finite predication to convey the evaluation. This dictionary relates it to exclamative words and clauses and marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats what here as an exclamative form in a noun phrase.

contrasts.note: Singular count noun, with a.
No a.

watch_for: A learner might look for a verb in What a mess!, when none is needed.
A learner might add a before lovely weather, though this dictionary's example has none.
teacher.activity: Students look at pictures and write one What a ... or What ... exclamation for each, then sort them by whether they include a.

child.hook: What do you say when you see a huge mess?
child.explain: What a mess! shows how we feel. It has no action word. The words after What describe the thing.
child.play: Show a friend a picture. They shout a reaction starting with What a ... for it. Then try one without a, like What lovely weather!

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary no longer calls the pattern a noun phrase after what or a strong feeling; the body no longer singles out a (this dictionary allows a or an) and ties a to the What a mess! example; teacher explain says nominal, not nominal head. Also fixed (unflagged): 'the entry' wording; child play wording. Second round: fixed teacher.terms, cutting Exclamation is the traditional name (the entry makes no claim about traditional names).

name: what with Circumstantial Adjunct
pattern: adjunct[what with + NP, non-finite or verbless predication, or coordination]

entry.name: what with Circumstantial Adjunct
entry.pattern: adjunct[what with + NP, non-finite or verbless predication, or coordination]

1.definition: Presents one or more circumstances as explaining the main situation.
1.details: What with the trains being late describes a reason for the delay. A plain with phrase can also depict an accompanying circumstance with no explanatory force, as in She waited with her arms folded. Adding what invites a reason reading. A simple NP such as the weather can fill the same slot.

examples.form: [What with the trains being late and the roads blocked], we stayed put.
[What with the weather], we never left the house.
examples.note: Constructed example with a simple NP.

relatedConstructions.notes: Both can express circumstances with their own predication.
The form includes fixed with and can contain an NP.

grounds.note: Tests addition of what in the depictive use.
Records the reason adjunct and the coordinated complement.

projection.target: Adding what to the relevant with frame imposes an explanatory interpretation. Its complement can also be a simple circumstance-denoting NP.
projection.evidence: FrameNet tests explanatory versus depictive interpretations. CGEL records what with as an idiom introducing a reason adjunct.

curious.title: What with, giving reasons
curious.summary: What with and one or more circumstances offers them as the reason for what happened.
curious.body: What with the trains being late and the roads blocked, we stayed put. The part before the comma lists the circumstances, and they explain why we stayed. A simple noun phrase can fill the same slot: What with the weather, we never left the house. A plain with phrase can show an accompanying circumstance with no explanation, as in She waited with her arms folded. Adding what invites a reason reading. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: [What with the trains being late and the roads blocked], we stayed put.
[What with the weather], we never left the house.
She waited with her arms folded.

curious.try: Explain why you were late using What with and two reasons. Does it sound like an excuse?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, what with as a way to present circumstances as the reason for a situation.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an adjunct beginning with what with, followed by a noun phrase, a non-finite or verbless predication, or a coordination. It presents one or more circumstances as explaining the main situation. A plain with phrase can depict an accompanying circumstance with no explanatory force, as in She waited with her arms folded. Adding what invites a reason reading. A simple noun phrase such as the weather can fill the same slot. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats what with as an idiom introducing a reason adjunct, and relates it to absolute supplements, which can also express circumstances with their own predication.

examples.text: [What with the trains being late and the roads blocked], we stayed put.
[What with the weather], we never left the house.

contrasts.text: What with the weather, we never left the house.
contrasts.note: Reason reading.

contrasts.text: She waited with her arms folded.
contrasts.note: Accompanying circumstance, no explanation.

watch_for: A learner might read what with as a question about what, when it introduces a reason.
A learner might take a plain with phrase to explain the main situation, when it can depict an accompanying circumstance.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with with in two uses, one a depiction and one with what added as a reason, and say which is which.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher.terms no longer calls the clause-like part after with 'absolute' (the entry only relates the construction to absolute supplements); 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

name: Deliberative why not with a Bare Infinitival

entry.name: Deliberative why not with a Bare Infinitival

1.definition: Invites consideration of an action by asking for a reason against it.

projection.target: The usual response can accept the suggestion instead of reporting a cause. The plain form can follow not without finite auxiliary do.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Why not do it?
curious.summary: Why not plus an action suggests doing it, by asking whether there is any reason against.
curious.body: Why not call again tomorrow? looks like a question about a reason, but it works as a suggestion. It invites the listener to consider calling again, by asking what stands in the way. A reply can simply accept the idea, such as "Good idea", instead of giving a cause. The verb after not is in its plain form, call, with no extra helper like do. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Suggest something to a friend with Why not. Do they answer with a reason or with a yes?

teacher.summary: Helps explain why not as a way of suggesting an action.
teacher.explain: The pattern is why not followed by a plain verbal predicate. It invites consideration of an action by asking for a reason against it. The usual response can accept the suggestion instead of reporting a cause. The plain form can follow not without finite auxiliary do. This dictionary classes it as pragmatic, relates it to what-if and to directive entries, and marks its analysis provisional. Teach it as a suggestion that has the form of a question.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called a suggestion or proposal. The plain form is the bare infinitive of traditional grammar.

contrasts.note: A suggestion made by asking for a reason against the action; a reply can simply accept it.

watch_for: A learner might read it only as a request for a cause, when a reply can simply accept the suggestion.
A learner might look for do before not, when the plain form follows not directly.
teacher.activity: Pairs take turns making Why not suggestions about a weekend plan. The partner accepts, declines or counters, and the pair notes which replies give reasons and which don't.

child.hook: How do you suggest an idea without saying "You should"?
child.explain: Why not can be a way to suggest something. Why not call again tomorrow? It asks for a reason not to, and a friend can just say Good idea.
child.play: Take turns making a Why not suggestion. The next player says yes or gives a different idea.

checked.note: Fixed: teacher contrast and watch_for no longer say no reason is asked for or that giving one is a learner error (the entry defines the proposal as asking for a reason against the action, while a reply may accept without a cause); child explanation now says it asks for a reason not to; 'the entry' replaced by 'this dictionary'.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Deliberative why not with a Bare Infinitival." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/why-not-proposal-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: X with a capital Y Construction

dimensions.form: PP headed by with, followed by capital + letter name.
dimensions.meaning: Signals uppercase orthography and a proper/institutional sense for the label.
dimensions.function: Disambiguates official or proper-name use from ordinary descriptive use.
dimensions.distribution: Postposed adjunct or parenthetical after a label.

1.specialization: Specifies uppercase orthography for the relevant label, favoring an institutional/proper sense.

relatedConstructions.notes: Lexical variant using uppercase.
Uppercase specification aligns with proper-noun readings.
Uppercase specification often cues proper-name interpretation.

projection.target: Democrat with a capital D specifies the writing of the label and can imply party affiliation. In chaos with a capital C, there need be neither an organization nor a name. The capital instruction can support emphatic construal.
projection.evidence: The dictionary directly documents both the literal terminology and the emphatic idiom. The constructed comparison holds the frame constant.

curious.title: With a capital letter
curious.summary: Adding with a capital D (or another letter) to a word says how it is written, and can point to an official or named meaning.
curious.body: Democrat with a capital D tells us how the word is written, and it can point to the party-affiliated sense. Church with a capital C does the same for the institutional sense. So the phrase is a spelling instruction that can also point to the meaning. This dictionary notes that in chaos with a capital C, there need be neither an organization nor a name. The capital instruction can support an emphatic reading. This dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Say one word and add with a capital and its first letter. Does the word's meaning change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain with a capital letter as a way to specify spelling and signal a proper or institutional sense.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a prepositional phrase headed by with, followed by a, capital and a letter name. It is a postposed adjunct or parenthetical after a label. It specifies uppercase orthography for the label, favouring an institutional or proper sense. It disambiguates official or proper-name use from ordinary descriptive use. In democrat with a capital D, the sense can be party-affiliated. In chaos with a capital C, there need be neither an organization nor a name, and the capital instruction can support an emphatic reading. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional. A sibling entry covers with an uppercase letter.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats this as a spelling specification, with an uppercase variant.

contrasts.note: Party-affiliated sense.
Institutional sense.

watch_for: A learner might think the phrase must name an organization, when this dictionary says chaos with a capital C needs neither an organization nor a name.
A learner might take it as only a spelling instruction, when it can also point to a proper sense.
teacher.activity: Write pairs of words on the board, such as democrat and church. Students say them with with a capital and a letter, then discuss what meaning each choice points to.

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation now matches the entry (capital C marks the institutional sense of church, not a particular church); teacher explain describes the phrase itself as the postposed adjunct or parenthetical; emphatic reading hedged as the entry has it. Dismissed: none. Second round: removed the child edition, whose institutional and party-affiliated senses need adult background to follow (an adult-register pattern); teacher.explain now says democrat with a capital D can imply party affiliation, as this dictionary has it; cut the claim that capital letter is the everyday term.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "X with a capital Y Construction." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/with-a-capital-letter-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).

name: X with a lowercase Y Construction

dimensions.form: PP headed by with, followed by lowercase + letter name.
dimensions.meaning: Signals lowercase orthography and an ordinary/common sense for the label.
dimensions.function: Disambiguates descriptive use from institutional/proper use.
dimensions.distribution: Postposed adjunct or parenthetical after a label.

1.specialization: Specifies lowercase orthography for the relevant label using lowercase.

relatedConstructions.notes: Lexical variant using small.
Lowercase specification aligns with common-noun readings.

projection.target: With a lowercase r and with a small r can direct a reader to the same written form in a literal clarification. The named letter generally matches the relevant initial or contrasted position in the label.
projection.evidence: The case contrast is documented for small and capital. The lowercase substitution illustrates the independently meaningful case terminology in the same slot.

curious.title: With a lowercase letter
curious.summary: Adding with a lowercase r (or another letter) says how a word is written, and can point to an ordinary meaning.
curious.body: Republican with a lowercase r points to the ordinary descriptive sense of the word, not an institutional one. Romantic with a lowercase r works the same way. The phrase is a spelling instruction. It can say which written form is meant, as small does in with a small r. The letter named generally matches the initial of the label. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Say a word and add with a lowercase and its first letter. What written form are you pointing to?

teacher.summary: Helps explain with a lowercase letter as a spelling clarification pointing to an ordinary sense.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a prepositional phrase headed by with, followed by a, lowercase and a letter name. It is postposed after a label or used parenthetically. It specifies lowercase orthography and signals an ordinary or common sense, disambiguating descriptive use from institutional or proper use. With a lowercase r and with a small r can direct a reader to the same written form in a literal clarification. The named letter generally matches the relevant initial or contrasted position in the label. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional. A sibling entry covers with a small letter.
teacher.terms: Lowercase letter is the everyday term. This dictionary lists with a small letter as a variant.

contrasts.note: Non-institutional sense.

watch_for: A learner might name a letter that doesn't match the initial being discussed, though this dictionary says the letter generally matches it.
A learner might treat with a lowercase r and with a small r as different instructions, when they can point to the same written form.
teacher.activity: Students pair words such as republican and romantic with the phrase with a lowercase and the initial. They then restate each using with a small and the initial, and confirm the written form is the same.

curious.summary: Adding with an uppercase I (or another letter) says a word is written with a capital, which can point to an official or named meaning.
curious.body: Internet with an uppercase I points to the institutional or official sense. Reformation with an uppercase R points to the proper, historical-event sense. name: Year Name Construction

dimensions.form: Cardinal noun (typically four-digit); bare NP or in PP complement
dimensions.meaning: Rigid designation of a specific calendar year
dimensions.function: Temporal reference via proper naming rather than counting
dimensions.distribution: In PPs (in 1066), as appositive (the year 1066), subject position

1.definition: Cardinal noun names a specific year through direct reference

examples.form: The year [1066] saw the Norman Conquest.
examples.note: Year as appositive to embellishment noun

constraints.description: Heads a bare NP; resists determiners and attributive modifiers.
Typically uses basic numeratives and 'oh' (ten sixty-six, not one thousand sixty-six).
Rigidly designates a unique temporal point.

projection.target: In They met in 2002, the numerative identifies a calendar year without specifying an amount of elapsed time. In They waited two years, the cardinal instead quantifies a duration. Spelling with digits can obscure the distinction.
projection.evidence: CGEL distinguishes temporal location from duration and Reynolds analyzes the label use of cardinal nouns.

curious.title: Years as names
curious.summary: A number like 1994 can name a particular year, working like a name rather than a count.
curious.body: In born in 1994, the number doesn't count anything. It names one particular year. We can also say the year 1066 saw the Norman Conquest, or 2025 will be different, with the number standing on its own as the subject. Compare They met in 2002 with They waited two years. The first uses a number to identify a year, with no length of time. The second counts a stretch of time. Writing with digits can hide the difference. A year name resists words like the or an adjective in front of it. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: The year [1066] saw the Norman Conquest.

curious.try: Say They met in 2002 and They waited two years. Which one tells you how long, and which one tells you when?

teacher.summary: Helps explain years as name-like numbers, and how they differ from counting.
teacher.explain: A year name is a cardinal noun that names a specific year through direct reference. It heads a bare noun phrase and resists determiners and attributive modifiers. It occurs as the complement of a preposition (in 1994), as an appositive (the year 1066) and as a subject (2025 will be different). This dictionary describes the spoken form as typically using the basic numeratives (and oh), as in ten sixty-six rather than one thousand sixty-six. In They met in 2002 the number identifies a calendar year without specifying elapsed time. In They waited two years the cardinal quantifies a duration. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: Calendrical label is the term in the source cited by this dictionary. This dictionary treats the year name as a proper-name-like use of a cardinal noun.

examples.text: The year [1066] saw the Norman Conquest.

contrasts.note: Names a year, with no amount of time.
Counts a duration.

watch_for: A learner might read in 2002 as a length of time, when it names a calendar year.
A learner might read the digits of a year as a quantity, since digits can obscure the distinction.
teacher.activity: Students sort sentences with numbers into year names and durations. They then read the year names aloud in the form this dictionary describes, such as ten sixty-six.

child.hook: Does the number in "born in 1994" count something?
child.explain: A year's number is its name. Born in 1994 tells us which year. Two years is different. It counts how long.
child.play: Say a year, like the year you were born. Then say how many years something took. Which one is a name and which one counts?

checked.note: Fixed: curious.body now says year names resist (rather than never take) determiners and adjectives, as in the entry; teacher.explain now gives the spoken-form pattern as typical (ten sixty-six) with oh mentioned separately; replaced 'the entry' with 'this dictionary'.

name: Zero Plural of Selected Count Nouns
pattern: N[plural] realized with the same stem form as N[singular]

entry.name: Zero Plural of Selected Count Nouns
entry.pattern: N[plural] realized with the same stem form as N[singular]

1.definition: Realizes count plural without a distinct suffix on a restricted set of nouns.

projection.target: The numeral and verb agree with a plural even though sheep lacks a plural suffix. A singular determiner can combine with the same stem form in a sheep.
projection.evidence: See the cited discussion and the constructed illustration.

curious.title: Plurals with no ending
curious.summary: A few nouns, such as sheep, look the same in the singular and the plural.
curious.body: In Three sheep were left outside, there's more than one sheep, and the word sheep has no plural ending like -s. We can tell it's plural because of three and because the verb is were. The same form of the word works for one: a sheep. The dictionary describes this as a restricted set of nouns, not a pattern for all words. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
curious.try: Say Three sheep were left outside and A sheep was left outside. What changes besides the number word and the verb?

teacher.summary: Helps explain nouns whose plural has the same form as the singular.
teacher.explain: A zero plural realizes count plural without a distinct suffix on a restricted set of nouns. In Three sheep were left outside, the numeral and verb agree with a plural even though sheep lacks a plural suffix. A singular determiner can combine with the same stem form, as in a sheep. This dictionary relates it to the regular plural -s and to grammatical number, and marks its analysis provisional. Teach it by showing that number is carried by the determiner, numeral and verb, not only by the noun.
teacher.terms: Sometimes called an unchanged plural. This dictionary treats these as count nouns whose plural has no suffix.

contrasts.note: Plural, no suffix.
Singular, same stem form.

watch_for: A learner might add -s to sheep, when it is one of the restricted set with no plural suffix.
A learner might think a noun without a suffix is singular, when the numeral and verb show it is plural.
teacher.activity: Students read sentences containing sheep, noticing which word shows the number. Then they find other cues, such as the verb form, in each sentence.

child.hook: Why is there no -s on sheep when there are three of them?
child.explain: Sheep stays the same for one or for three. A sheep. Three sheep. We know it's plural from three and were.
child.play: Say a sentence with one sheep, then with three. Which words change and which stay the same?

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Zero Plural of Selected Count Nouns." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/zero-plural-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
